article_title: Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC
citation: Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-policy-in-washington-dc
title: District discipline policy changes require monitoring of school-level implementation, because schools may not comply with bans on suspensions for low-level offenses
description: This principle holds that a district code-of-conduct reform is not self-implementing: schools vary in how they put a new policy into practice, and some do not comply. The Philadelphia experience summarized in this publication showed "significant variation in how schools implemented this new policy" and that "many Philadelphia schools did not comply" with the suspension prohibition, so districts changing discipline policy should monitor school-level implementation.
requirements: Districts adopting discipline policy changes need a way to observe how individual schools implement the change, as the Philadelphia study did.
constraints: The publication reports non-compliance for a ban on out-of-school suspension for low-level offenses in Philadelphia; it does not establish compliance levels for other policy types or districts.
target_learners: K-12 students in districts revising student codes of conduct
target_learning_goals: Reducing exclusionary discipline for non-violent, low-level offenses
examples: The School District of Philadelphia prohibited suspensions and expulsions for failure to follow classroom rules and use of profane language in 2012-2013, and the study summarized here found significant variation in implementation and non-compliance by many schools.
key_sources: Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-policy-in-washington-dc

article_title: The Impact of Healthy Harlem on the Prevalence of Child Overweight and Obesity and Contributing Factors: Interim Evaluation Report
citation: Mabli, J., Bleeker, M., & Fox, M. K. (2017). The Impact of Healthy Harlem on the Prevalence of Child Overweight and Obesity and Contributing Factors: Interim Evaluation Report. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Universal prevention plus targeted intensive goal-setting tier for students needing additional support
description: The program combines a universal tier delivered to all participants with an intensive targeted tier for students identified as needing more support. All students are exposed to Prevention, "which includes physical activity, healthy snacks, nutrition education lessons, and parent workshops," while students who are overweight or obese "also participate in Get Fit, an intensive, 12-week program in which students identify and work on specific goals." This layered structure lets a broad educational base coexist with individualized goal work for a higher-need subgroup.
requirements: A universal delivery setting reaching all students (here, after-school programs)
A criterion for identifying students for the intensive tier (here, overweight or obesity status)
constraints: The intensive tier is limited to middle and high school students who are overweight or obese and runs for a fixed 12-week period
target_learners: All students in an after-school program, plus a targeted subgroup of middle and high school students who are overweight or obese
target_learning_goals: Nutrition knowledge and attitudes
Goal-setting for improving eating and physical-activity habits
examples: HCZ after-school students all received Prevention; those overweight or obese additionally received Get Fit, and the evaluation found BMI reductions for students receiving both components

article_title: Multi-Armed RCTs: A Design-Based Framework
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2017). Multi-Armed RCTs: A Design-Based Framework. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Researchers conducting multi-armed RCTs should adapt estimation, multiplicity testing, and CACE methods from two-group practice
description: The report's guidance is that analysts running studies with several intervention arms should not simply reuse two-group methods: estimators "need to be modified for the multi-armed design," hypothesis tests across pairwise contrasts require multiple comparison adjustments, and CACE estimation demands attention to its complex identifying assumptions. The principle directs evaluation design and analysis choices in multi-armed education studies.
requirements: Analysts must define the pairwise contrasts of interest before selecting estimators and adjustment procedures
constraints: Guidance is framed for design-based analysis in social policy research, including education evaluations
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluation methodologists
target_learning_goals: Applying sound statistical practice when evaluating several interventions in one randomized study
examples: The report walks through pairwise-contrast estimation, multiplicity adjustment, and multi-armed CACE identification as the three analytic tasks needing adaptation

Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/multi-armed-rcts-a-design-based-framework

article_title: Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation
citation: Tim Kautz, Peter Z. Schochet, Charles Tilley. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Align analytic assumptions across methods when comparing impact estimation approaches
description: When evaluating whether choice of impact estimation method matters, the article indicates analysts should align the underlying analytic assumptions across the methods being compared. It notes the design- and model-based methods are most similar "when the underlying analytic assumptions (such as the weights used to aggregate clusters and blocks) are aligned". This makes method comparisons interpretable rather than confounded by differing weighting choices.
requirements: Access to the same RCT data across methods, with the ability to specify matching aggregation weights for clusters and blocks
constraints: Similarity of findings depends on the assumptions being aligned; the article does not claim equivalence when they differ
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators analyzing RCT impact data
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation and comparison of intervention impacts in education evaluations
examples: The study re-analyzed nine past education RCTs, estimating impacts with design-based, HLM, and robust standard error methods and comparing the resulting estimates and significance levels.
key_sources: Tim Kautz, Peter Z. Schochet, Charles Tilley. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?
citation: Neil Seftor. (2016). What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Education decision-makers should examine what a null-effect study means before making program decisions
description: This principle holds that practitioners considering a program change, such as "switching curricula or implementing a new schoolwide intervention aimed at behavior," should not take a null finding at face value. The brief advises readers on "what to look for in a study that finds no effect and how you can think about what to do next," treating interpretation of null results as a necessary step before acting.
requirements: Access to the study of the program under consideration, so its null finding can be examined rather than accepted at face value
constraints: The brief addresses school or district decision-makers weighing program choices; its guidance is framed for that audience
target_learners: school and district decision-makers evaluating education programs
target_learning_goals: informed interpretation of evaluation evidence when choosing or continuing education programs
examples: The brief opens with the scenario of a school or district staff member picking up a study of a program and reading that there is no effect, then asks what caused the result and what it means

article_title: Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://behavioralsciencepolicy.org
title: Make greater use of professional accountability in education
description: The review recommends that policymakers "make greater use of professional accountability, which has historically been underutilized in education." Professional accountability is one of the four forms in the review's taxonomy, and the authors argue its underuse represents an opportunity as states redesign accountability systems under ESSA. The recommendation rests on the review's synthesis of laboratory and field evidence on how each accountability form motivates educators.
requirements: Policymakers with discretion over accountability system design, as afforded by the Every Student Succeeds Act
target_learners: K-12 public school students
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of educational practice
examples: The review positions professional accountability as historically underutilized relative to outcome-based high-stakes testing since NCLB.
key_sources: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reimagining-accountability-in-k12-education

article_title: Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://behavioralsciencepolicy.org
title: Combine multiple, complementary forms of accountability to support continuous improvement
description: The review concludes that policymakers should "use multiple, complementary forms of accountability, creating a complete system that encourages and supports the continuous improvement of educational practice." Rather than relying on a single form such as outcome-based high-stakes testing, the recommendation is to combine forms so their distinct motivational mechanisms complement one another. This follows from the review's analysis of favorable and unfavorable effects of each form.
requirements: State-level discretion over accountability design, as provided by the Every Student Succeeds Act
target_learners: K-12 public school students
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of educational practice
examples: The review's third concluding recommendation is a complete system combining complementary accountability forms.

article_title: Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report

title: Allow sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation in partnership-based family engagement initiatives
description: Among the formative findings on the viability of leveraging public-private partnerships, the report identifies "the importance of (1) allowing sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation." This principle directs funders, communities, and organizations to budget adequate transition time between planning and implementation phases of family engagement initiatives.

examples: The report lists allowing sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation as the first of six formative findings from FEIP grantees' implementation experiences.

citation: Dana Petersen, Megan Shoji, Adam Dunn, Natasha Nicolai. (2016). Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Emphasize the supports professionals need, especially teachers and schools, to foster family engagement
description: The report's formative findings include "emphasizing supports professionals need, especially teachers and schools, to foster family engagement." This principle holds that partnership-based family engagement initiatives should direct attention and resources to the professional side—teachers and schools—so that practitioners are equipped to foster family engagement.

citation: John Deke. (2016). Design and Analysis Considerations for Cluster Randomized Controlled Trials That Have a Small Number of Clusters. Evaluation Review, vol. 40, issue 5. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/design-and-analysis-considerations-for-cluster-randomized-controlled-trials-that-have-a-small-number-of-clusters
title: Design small cluster randomized trials deliberately: use blocked randomization, Type I error-safe analysis, and corrected power calculations
description: The article offers best practices for designing and analyzing cluster randomized controlled trials with ten or fewer clusters, contexts where it says meaningful effects may still be detectable. Its stated objective is "to offer recommendations for best practices in design and analysis for small CRCTs," grounded in simulations of alternative approaches. The practices cover analytic choice, blocking, power estimation, and cluster-count planning.

constraints: Small effects remain very difficult to detect with just four clusters
Covariate adjustment for blocking depends on whether precision gains offset degrees of freedom loss

examples: The author used simulations to examine which analytic approaches control Type I errors, which designs yield the most power, the design effect of spurious correlations, and scenarios under which impacts of different sizes can be detected with high probability

citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Kristin Hallgren. (2015). The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making. Issue Brief, Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Develop a teacher of record definition that reflects all professionals and educational settings
description: The brief recommends that states adopting teacher of record definitions craft a definition that covers every professional contributing to instruction and every educational arrangement, citing co-teaching as an example. A definition limited to traditional single-teacher classrooms would misattribute students in shared-instruction settings. article_title: Adding Design Elements to Improve Time Series Designs: No Child Left Behind as an Example of Causal Pattern-Matching
citation: Manyee Wong, Thomas D. Cook, Peter M. Steiner. (2015). Adding Design Elements to Improve Time Series Designs: No Child Left Behind as an Example of Causal Pattern-Matching. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Strengthen short interrupted time series evaluations by adding multiple design elements rather than relying on the basic single-group ITS structure
description: Because the basic single-group ITS depends on extrapolating the pretest functional form as a counterfactual, an assumption the authors call problematic, evaluators should add multiple design elements to the basic ITS structure. Each element limits alternative interpretations, and together the elements provide a strong causal warrant when predictions are complex and results cohere with them.
requirements: Design elements must be chosen so that the predictions they engender are complex enough that no alternative explanation fits the same pattern.
constraints: No added design element is perfect by itself; the warrant is collective and conditional.
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators of state and national programs
target_learning_goals: Strengthening causal inference in interrupted time series program evaluations
examples: The article demonstrates the approach using No Child Left Behind as an example of evaluating a national program with a short ITS.

citation: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data
title: Develop a coherent plan for effectively using data before or alongside building data systems
description: The brief's central recommendation is that education agencies should develop a coherent plan for using data effectively, treating data use as something that requires deliberate planning rather than assuming data alone drives improvement. The brief states it "focuses on developing a coherent plan for effectively using data", positioning planning as one of three companion topics alongside developing a data system and supporting its effective use.
requirements: A coherent plan must be developed deliberately by the education system seeking effective data use
target_learners: state education officials
district-level staff
system developers
target_learning_goals: using data to inform decisions that improve classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement
examples: The brief is one of a series; the other two briefs address considerations for developing or enhancing a data system and supporting the effective use of a data system.
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data

article_title: Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief)
citation: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data
title: Decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data
description: The brief endorses data-informed decision making across every level of the education system. It observes that "Most agree that decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data", framing good data as an input to decisions at classroom, district, and state levels alike, while acknowledging that achieving this in practice is difficult.
requirements: Good data must be available to decision makers at classroom, central office, and state education agency levels
constraints: In practice, data often fails to move decision makers or overwhelms them with extraneous information
target_learners: classroom educators
central office staff
state education agency staff
target_learning_goals: making data-informed decisions to improve instruction and student achievement
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data

article_title: Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief)
citation: Mathematica Policy Research. (2013). Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design education data systems so they drive instructional and improvement decisions rather than drown educators in extraneous information
description: The brief argues that data systems should be developed and enhanced with decision use in mind, from the classroom to the central office and state education agency. It warns that "it is all too easy for data to leave educators and policymakers unmoved—or, worse yet, to drown them in extraneous information, rather than drive decisions that will improve classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement." The brief therefore treats decision relevance as a core design consideration for data systems.
requirements: Data must be usable by decision makers and educators at any level of the education system
target_learners: state education officials
district-level staff
system developers
target_learning_goals: improving classroom instruction
improving school performance
improving student achievement
examples: The brief is one of a series offering recommendations and strategies for promoting effective data use by decision makers and educators.
key_sources: Mathematica Policy Research. (2013). Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-and-enhancing-data-systems

article_title: Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models
citation: Eric Isenberg, Bing-ru Teh, Elias Walsh. (2013). Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models. Working Paper 23, Chicago, IL: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Researchers using elementary administrative data for value-added models should attend to teacher/student link accuracy before estimation
description: Because unconfirmed administrative data can link "about one in six teachers in these grades and subjects" to a subject they do not teach, researchers using value-added models with elementary school data should verify teacher/student links, for example through a roster confirmation process, before estimation. The paper motivates this by comparing confirmed and unconfirmed links in DC Public Schools data.
requirements: Access to a roster confirmation process or equivalent means for teachers to verify the subjects and students they taught
constraints: Mislinking arises specifically from departmentalization of instruction in math and reading/English language arts in grades 4 and 5
target_learners: elementary school students
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of teacher effects in value-added models
examples: The working paper compares roster-confirmed teacher/student links to unconfirmed administrative links in DC Public Schools
key_sources: Eric Isenberg, Bing-ru Teh, Elias Walsh. (2013). Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models. Working Paper 23, Chicago, IL: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/elementary-school-data-issues-implications-for-research-using-valueadded-models

article_title: First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact
citation: Joanne Pfleiderer. (2013). First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Effective dissemination requires getting the right message to the right people at the right time in the right form
description: The guide's core principle is that dissemination must be matched to audience and medium: "Today, effective dissemination depends on getting the right message to the right people at the right time in the right form." To break through the clutter of competing communications, researchers are advised to assemble the elements the guide enumerates rather than relying on a single channel.
requirements: Researchers need the right elements: a compelling story, engaging visuals, and a set of electronic tools, including email, video, and social media
target_learners: decision makers
stakeholders
practitioners
target_learning_goals: effective communication of research findings to intended audiences
examples: The guide contrasts past practice—posting a report on the web or sending out a press release—with the current need to combine story, visuals, and electronic tools in one communication.
key_sources: Joanne Pfleiderer. (2013). First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/first-impressions-creating-newsflashes-with-impact

article_title: What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models?
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2013). What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 38, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates for high-stakes educator decisions
description: This principle holds that before using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions about educators, decision-makers should account for the likely error rates of the measurement system. The article's results show nontrivial misclassification rates, and it concludes that "policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions regarding educators." The principle operationalizes the article's error-rate findings as a design consideration for educator evaluation systems.
requirements: A value-added measurement system whose likely error rates can be estimated from the amount of data available, such as one versus three years of test score gain data.
constraints: The stated error rates apply to measuring teacher and school performance in the upper elementary grades using student test score gain data.
target_learners: Upper elementary grade students whose teachers and schools are evaluated
target_learning_goals: Accurate classification of teacher and school performance for accountability decisions
examples: The article derives error rates of about 25 percent with three years of data and 35 percent with one year of data for comparing a teacher to the average, and 10 percent and 20 percent for overall false positives and false negatives.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2013). What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 38, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/what-are-error-rates-for-classifying-teacher-and-school-performance-using-value-added-models

article_title: Do Low-Income Students have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers?
citation: Steven Glazerman and Jeffrey Max. (2011). Do Low-Income Students Have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers? NCEE Evaluation Brief, NCEE 2011-4016. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20114016/pdf/20114016_app.pdf
title: Policymakers concerned with equitable access to teacher quality should attend to the distribution of teacher effectiveness measured by classroom performance, not credentials
description: The brief argues that because credentials inequitably distributed across schools are only weakly associated with classroom performance, equity policy should target performance-based measures. It states that those who want to assure disadvantaged students have access to teachers at least as good "need to attend to the distribution of teacher effectiveness, measured in terms of classroom performance, rather than to the distribution of teacher credentials." As policy shifts toward performance measures, information on the distribution of high-performing teachers can help assure the best teachers are deployed where most needed.
requirements: District data systems that measure teacher effectiveness through value-added analysis of student achievement growth
constraints: Findings pertain to ten purposefully selected large districts and are not necessarily applicable to other districts
Few districts systematically collect or use data on teacher effectiveness
target_learners: Economically disadvantaged K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to high-performing teachers
examples: The brief analyzed prevalence of top-20-percent value-added teachers across school poverty quintiles in ten districts to inform such equity policy
key_sources: Steven Glazerman and Jeffrey Max. (2011). Do Low-Income Students Have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers? NCEE Evaluation Brief, NCEE 2011-4016. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20114016/pdf/20114016_app.pdf

article_title: Passing Muster: Evaluating Teacher Evaluation Systems
citation: Glazerman, S., Goldhaber, D., Loeb, S., Raudenbush, S., Staiger, D. O., Whitehurst, G. J., & Croft, M. (2011). Passing Muster: Evaluating Teacher Evaluation Systems. Washington, DC: Brown Center on Education Policy at Brookings. https://www.brookings.edu
title: Fund districts for recognizing exceptional teachers against a uniform standard without imposing a uniform evaluation system
description: A design principle for education policy: funding decisions that reward districts for identifying exceptional teachers can be standardized at the level of the funding rule while leaving the design of the underlying teacher evaluation system to each district.
requirements: Districts must operate local teacher evaluation systems whose results can be compared against the uniform funding standard
constraints: The available text states the proposal as a design aim; no implementation or test is described
target_learners: School districts and state education agencies designing teacher evaluation and incentive-funding policies
target_learning_goals: Comparing teacher evaluation systems across districts
Dispensing funds to recognize exceptional teachers under a uniform standard
examples: The report proposes ways to achieve a uniform standard for dispensing funds to districts without imposing a uniform evaluation system on those districts.

article_title: Precision Gains from Publically Available School Proficiency Measures Compared to Study-Collected Test Scores in Education Cluster-Randomized Trials
citation: John Deke, Lisa Dragoset, Ravaris Moore. (2010). Precision Gains from Publically Available School Proficiency Measures Compared to Study-Collected Test Scores in Education Cluster-Randomized Trials. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Collect student-level baseline test scores for covariate adjustment in cluster-randomized trials when precision matters, treating school-level proficiency data as a lower-cost but weaker substitute
description: The report frames a design trade-off: student-level pretest scores "can be costly to collect," while school-level proficiency data are "available at low cost." Because the cheaper school-level measure yields smaller precision gains, studies that need statistical precision should budget for collecting student-level baseline scores rather than relying on the free aggregate data.
requirements: Access to student-level baseline test scores collected by the study, which the report notes can be costly to collect.
constraints: School-level proficiency data are publicly available at low cost but, on average, do not increase statistical precision as well as student-level baseline test scores.
target_learners: K-12 school populations studied in education cluster-randomized trials
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of intervention impacts on student achievement outcomes
examples: The report based its comparison on data from five large-scale randomized control trials conducted for the U.S. Department of Education's Institute of Education Sciences.
key_sources: John Deke, Lisa Dragoset, Ravaris Moore. (2010). Precision Gains from Publically Available School Proficiency Measures Compared to Study-Collected Test Scores in Education Cluster-Randomized Trials. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2010). Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Policymakers should carefully consider likely system error rates before using value-added estimates for high-stakes educator decisions
description: The report recommends that performance measurement systems based on value-added estimates account for their statistical error before being used for high-stakes decisions about educators. Because simulations show error rates of roughly 25 to 35 percent for teacher comparisons under typical data conditions, the authors conclude that "policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions regarding educators."
requirements: Performance measurement systems should be designed and evaluated using hypothesis-testing error rate calculations, as the report does with its OLS and Empirical Bayes error rate formulas.
constraints: Findings apply to value-added models applied to student test score gain data in the upper elementary grades; error rates depend on the number of years of data available.
target_learners: Upper elementary grade students whose teachers and schools are evaluated
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of teacher and school performance for accountability decisions
examples: The report develops error rate formulas based on OLS and Empirical Bayes estimators and applies them in simulations of realistic performance measurement system schemes.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2010). Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results from a Randomized Controlled Study
citation: Glazerman, S., Isenberg, E., Dolfin, S., Bleeker, M., Johnson, A., Grider, M., & Jacobus, M. (2010). Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results from a Randomized Controlled Study. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Sustain comprehensive induction supports for new teachers across two years to affect student achievement
description: Because the randomized evaluation found achievement impacts only for teachers receiving two years of comprehensive induction and none for one year, induction supports for new teachers should be sustained across two years rather than compressed into a single year. The report states that "two years of comprehensive induction can boost student achievement" while for one year "there was no impact."
requirements: Comprehensive induction components (trained full-time mentors, intensive curriculum, observation opportunities, assessment tools) sustained over two years
constraints: One year of induction showed no impact; no other outcomes were affected
target_learners: New (novice) K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Raise student achievement through improved early-career teaching
examples: The evaluation compared teachers receiving one versus two years of comprehensive induction with business-as-usual induction programs
key_sources: Glazerman, S., Isenberg, E., Dolfin, S., Bleeker, M., Johnson, A., Grider, M., & Jacobus, M. (2010). article_title: An Approach for Addressing the Multiple Testing Problem in Social Policy Impact Evaluations
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). An Approach for Addressing the Multiple Testing Problem in Social Policy Impact Evaluations. Education Review, vol. 33, no. 6.
title: Address the multiple testing problem in impact evaluations using a framework that balances Type I and Type II errors
description: When an evaluation tests many outcomes and subgroups, the article recommends addressing the resulting multiple testing problem with a framework that "balances Types I and II errors". This directs evaluators to choose testing procedures that jointly manage the risk of spurious impact findings and the risk of missing true effects, rather than focusing on only one error type.
requirements: An evaluation design involving hypothesis tests across multiple outcomes and/or subgroups
target_learners: Education and social policy researchers conducting impact evaluations
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of impact findings across multiple tested outcomes and subgroups
examples: The article discusses this balancing framework as its proposed approach for social policy impact evaluations.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). An Approach for Addressing the Multiple Testing Problem in Social Policy Impact Evaluations. Education Review, vol. 33, no. 6. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-approach-for-addressing-the-multiple-testing-problem-in-social-policy-impact-evaluations

article_title: Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues
citation: May, Henry, Irma Perez-Johnson, Joshua Haimson, Samina Sattar, and Phil Gleason (2009). Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues (NCEE 2009-013). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Collect and use baseline state test data as covariates to increase statistical power and reduce study costs
description: The paper recommends that studies using student achievement outcomes generally aim to collect and use baseline data, because analyses using more than one wave of data typically have much greater statistical power than posttest-only analyses. Using prior state test results as baseline covariates can substantially reduce overall study costs, since the power improvement allows the sample size to be greatly reduced while maintaining the target power level. Baseline data also help establish treatment-control equivalence and assess potential nonresponse bias.
requirements: Researchers must link pretest and posttest scores for individual students under student-level random assignment, or link individual and/or aggregate data under school- or district-level random assignment
constraints: Substantial effort may be required to link longitudinal data; costs of linking must be evaluated separately for each state because database quality varies
target_learners: Education researchers designing randomized experiments
target_learning_goals: Increased statistical power for detecting intervention impacts on student achievement
examples: The paper cites Bloom, Richburg-Hayes, and Black (2005) showing that even aggregate school-level baseline covariates can dramatically increase the power of a school-level RCT
key_sources: May, Henry, Irma Perez-Johnson, Joshua Haimson, Samina Sattar, and Phil Gleason (2009). Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues (NCEE 2009-013). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/using-state-tests-in-education-experiments-a-discussion-of-the-issues

article_title: Technical Methods Report: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley Chiang. (2009). Technical Methods Report: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use correct variance formulas when estimating the CACE parameter in education RCTs
description: The report's methodological contribution is to work out the correct variance formulas for the CACE estimator under clustered designs and to compare them with "those that are typically used in practice". Analysts estimating CACE in education RCTs should apply the correct variance formulas when assessing significance of the estimator, measured in nominal and standard deviation units.
requirements: Access to compliance information and outcome data from a clustered education RCT
constraints: The report's empirical comparison finds the variance correction terms matter little, so the practical gain from the correction may be small
target_learners: education researchers conducting RCT analyses
target_learning_goals: correct significance testing of complier average causal effect estimates
examples: The authors compared significance findings for the CACE estimator using the correct variance formulas with those typically used in practice across ten large-scale RCTs
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley Chiang. (2009). Technical Methods Report: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. article_title: Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Plan evaluation sample sizes around the larger requirements of clustered RD designs before choosing between RD and experimental designs
description: Because clustered RD designs typically demand substantially larger samples than clustered experiments for equivalent statistical precision, evaluators should assess power implications before committing to an RD design. The report finds that "three to four times larger samples are typically required under RD than experimental clustered designs to produce impacts with the same level of statistical precision." This principle directs researchers to weigh that power cost against RD's applicability when the assignment point, pretests, and research questions make RD feasible.
requirements: Sufficient sample size at the cutoff to offset the power disadvantage relative to a clustered experimental design
constraints: Viability depends on the point of treatment assignment, the availability of pretests, and key research questions, and may be limited for new impact evaluations of educational interventions
target_learners: Students in education evaluations using clustered RD designs
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of intervention effects on student test scores
examples: The report's empirical work focuses on commonly used designs in education research testing intervention effects on student test scores under clustered RD designs
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/technical-methods-report-statistical-power-for-regression-discontinuity-designs-in-education-evaluations

article_title: Statistical Power for Random Assignment Evaluations of Education Programs (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Statistical Power for Random Assignment Evaluations of Education Programs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 33, no. 1. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Set precision standards for education trials before determining required school samples
description: The article recommends that evaluators discuss "appropriate precision standards" and then determine, for each random-assignment design, "the required number of schools to achieve those standards" using empirical parameter values. This makes precision targets, rather than convenience, drive sample planning in education experiments. The principle applies the article's unified framework to practical evaluation design.
requirements: Empirical values of intraclass correlations, regression R2 values, and other parameters for the outcome and population of interest
constraints: Illustrated for standardized test scores of elementary school students
target_learners: elementary school students
target_learning_goals: designing education experiments with adequate statistical power
examples: The article discusses appropriate precision standards and, for each design, the required number of schools to achieve those standards.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Statistical Power for Random Assignment Evaluations of Education Programs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 33, no. 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/journal-article-statistical-power-for-random-assignment-evaluations-of-education-programs

article_title: Human-AI Collaboration for Qualitative Analysis in Participatory Design: Refining the Writing Analytics Tool
citation: Potter, A.; Serhan, Z.; Patne, N. A.; Öncel, P.; Ahmed, I.; Arner, T.; Islam, R.; Roscoe, R. D.; Allen, L. A.; Crossley, S. A.; McNamara, D. S. (2026). Human-AI Collaboration for Qualitative Analysis in Participatory Design: Refining the Writing Analytics Tool. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1. https://osf.io/8j9y6/?view_only=3a21ed900475418a8c258ea595cbe53b
title: Why–When–How feedback framework for presenting writing metrics
description: WAT-C presents each advanced metric's written feedback in a Why–When–How structure: "The Why section explains the rationale for the feedback", the When section "describes situations or genres where the writing behavior is most appropriate", and the How section "provides concrete revision strategies students can apply to improve their work". The pattern operationalizes feedback principles holding that effective feedback details both the task and improvement strategies, aiming to make advanced analytics interpretable, actionable, and instructionally relevant for student revision.
requirements: Underlying metrics with defined levels and revision guidance so each Why, When, and How component can be populated
constraints: Instructors in the focus groups critiqued the clarity, tone, and contextual relevance of the feedback comments, prompting revisions
target_learners: College writing students reviewing automated feedback on essays
target_learning_goals: Interpreting metric feedback, understanding communicative context, and performing meaningful revisions
examples: For Word Variety, students read why lexical diversity enhances engagement, when to prioritize consistency over variation, and how to revise by replacing repeated words with synonyms.
key_sources: Potter, A.; Serhan, Z.; Patne, N. A.; Öncel, P.; Ahmed, I.; Arner, T.; Islam, R.; Roscoe, R. D.; Allen, L. A.; Crossley, S. A.; McNamara, D. S. (2026). Human-AI Collaboration for Qualitative Analysis in Participatory Design: Refining the Writing Analytics Tool. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1. https://osf.io/8j9y6/?view_only=3a21ed900475418a8c258ea595cbe53b

article_title: Integrating Topic Modeling and LLM Prompt Engineering into a Human-driven Approach to Analyze Interview Transcripts
citation: Teresa M. Ober, Karyssa A. Courey, Michael Flor. (2026). Integrating Topic Modeling and LLM Prompt Engineering into a Human-driven Approach to Analyze Interview Transcripts. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1.
title: Maintain human oversight throughout AI-assisted qualitative analysis to ensure contextual alignment and mitigate hallucination risk
description: The article's implications section holds that computational tools should augment rather than replace human interpretive work in qualitative analysis. As the authors state, "Human oversight remained essential throughout, ensuring contex- tual alignment and mitigating risks of hallucination or conceptual drift." The human-in-the-loop design positions researchers as validators of LLM outputs, reviewing labels for accuracy, relevance, and alignment with underlying sentence examples and bestwords.
requirements: Researcher judgment to validate and refine LLM outputs at each stage
Clear construct definitions embedded in prompts
constraints: The human-in-the-loop design mitigates but does not eliminate risks of hallucination and misalignment, and the interpretive process introduces subjectivity
target_learners: educational researchers
qualitative research teams adopting AI tools
target_learning_goals: rigorous and interpretable AI-assisted qualitative coding
examples: The research team reviewed all LLM-generated labels for accuracy and alignment, and no clear instances of hallucination were observed
key_sources: Teresa M. Ober, Karyssa A. Courey, Michael Flor. (2026). Integrating Topic Modeling and LLM Prompt Engineering into a Human-driven Approach to Analyze Interview Transcripts. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/1008

article_title: Modelability as a Strategy for Improving the Generalizability and Scalability of Predictive Models
citation: Alice Xu, Icy (Yunyi) Zhang, Adam B. Blake and James W. Stigler. (2026). Modelability as a Strategy for Improving the Generalizability and Scalability of Predictive Models. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9099
title: Triangulate trace data with other sources to strengthen validity of inferences about learning
description: Because trace logs capture what learners do but not the underlying cognitive or metacognitive processes, the article advises that "To strengthen the validity of inferences drawn from trace data, it is important to triangulate with other data sources that offer more direct insight into learners' thinking". Modelable systems should combine trace data with embedded assessments and self-report measures so aligned sources collectively enhance inferential validity.
requirements: Additional data sources offering direct insight into learners' thinking, such as embedded assessments and self-report surveys, must be collected alongside trace data.
constraints: Logging behavior alone is not sufficient, as it captures only what learners do, not the processes underlying those actions.
target_learners: learners interacting with digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of engagement, cognition, and metacognition for learning analytics
examples: CourseKata triangulates enGauge trace data with over 1,500 embedded formative assessments and multi-point self-report surveys on motivation and interest.
key_sources: Alice Xu, Icy (Yunyi) Zhang, Adam B. Blake and James W. Stigler. (2026). Modelability as a Strategy for Improving the Generalizability and Scalability of Predictive Models. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9099

article_title: 12 Heuristics for Learning Analytics in Simulation-Based Professional Learning
citation: Susan Harrington and Charlott Sellberg. (2026). 12 Heuristics for Learning Analytics in Simulation-Based Professional Learning. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 130-142. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9141
title: Twelve LXD heuristics for evaluating learning analytics in simulation-based professional learning
description: The article's core artifact is a set of twelve heuristics organized across four dimensions: technical-pedagogical (e.g., "Enable appropriate assessment of individual and group performance", "Support temporal and spatial awareness of unfolding scenarios"), socio-technical (fostering professional vision, integrating with existing tools), socio-pedagogical (role-playing, socialization into professional values, professional language), and ethical (appropriate data use, privacy, accessibility). The heuristics are intended "to be used as a type of mnemonic in prompting the evaluator to think carefully and critically about features of the LA system".
requirements: Application during early prototyping to align design decisions with intended learning goals
Evaluation should focus on how the system supports learning outcomes, not only technical usability
constraints: The heuristics do not address potential technical issues related to system functionality or usability; established heuristics such as Nielsen's should be used for those
Developed with a relatively small group of experts and only two iterations
Applied only to early-stage prototypes, not a fully functional implementation
target_learners: UX and LX designers evaluating learning analytics systems
professional learners in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: evaluation of learning analytics dashboards supporting professional skill development in simulators

article_title: Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective
citation: Ohsaki, A., Tan, Y., Eagan, B., Shaffer, D. W., & Swiecki, Z. (2026). Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 190–207. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.8959
title: Attend to disciplinary differences when facilitating interdisciplinary knowledge creation teams
description: This principle holds that educators facilitating knowledge creation in interdisciplinary teams should recognize that different disciplines bring distinct epistemic agency patterns to collaborative work. The article states educators may "grasp the characteristics of different disciplines, determine the timing of interventions, and design scaffolding" accordingly. It emerged from finding that engineers, product designers, and service designers showed significantly different KC patterns during prototyping.
requirements: Educators need awareness of disciplinary frameworks shaping team members' collaborative problem-solving approaches
constraints: Based on analysis of three teams from three specific disciplines in a Japanese educational context
target_learners: interdisciplinary design teams
higher education students
target_learning_goals: knowledge creation
collaborative problem-solving
examples: The study compared engineering, product design, and service design teams during wallet prototyping, finding distinct epistemic agency patterns for each discipline

citation: Ohsaki, A., Tan, Y., Eagan, B., Shaffer, D. W., & Swiecki, Z. (2026). Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 190–207. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.8959
title: Provide timely educator support for concept creation during knowledge creation activities
description: This principle recommends that educators offer timely support to help teams move from information gathering toward concept creation and idea improvement. The article's Notes for Practice states results suggest "supporting concept creation" as a design recommendation for KC learning environments. It is grounded in findings that teams differed in when and whether they reached generative collaborative actions across session phases.

higher education students

idea improvement

title: Use short task durations to encourage sharing of incomplete ideas in knowledge creation activities
description: This principle recommends setting short time frames for collaborative activities to encourage learners to share incomplete and imperfect ideas rather than waiting for polished contributions. The article states "setting short time frames for activities to encourage sharing of incomplete ideas" as a design recommendation. The 30-minute session duration was chosen because it "could be embedded into typical 45- to 90-minute lessons in Japanese schools."

K-12 and higher education students

sharing incomplete ideas
design-mode thinking

article_title: Function Art: Understanding the Artistic Transformation of Mathematical Functions through Learning Analytics
citation: Bautista, G. Jr., Cacuyong, R., Lavicza, Z., Sabitzer, B., & Emara, M. (2026). Function Art: Understanding the Artistic Transformation of Mathematical Functions through Learning Analytics. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9037
title: Three types of function art: pure, organic, and hybrid
description: The article categorizes function art into three types based on how mathematical functions are used in artistic expression. Pure function art consists solely of function graphs (e.g., linear, quadratic, sine). Organic function art primarily uses functions but incorporates mathematical objects such as conics when needed. Hybrid function art blends functions with geometric primitives, image overlays, and annotations. Classification rules distinguish organic from hybrid based on whether functions were used whenever possible.
requirements: Classification requires examining whether curves could have been achieved with functions but the student chose not to use them
constraints: Circles and vertical line segments cannot be straightforwardly represented as functions in GeoGebra, so artworks using only these alongside functions are classified as organic
target_learners: Grades 8-12 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Understanding function families and their graphical representations
Distinguishing between function-based and non-function-based mathematical objects
examples: Artworks using only functions and circles were classified as organic; artworks including arcs that fail the vertical line test were classified as organic; artworks with general line segments, polygons, or imported images were classified as hybrid
key_sources: Bautista, G. Jr., Cacuyong, R., Lavicza, Z., Sabitzer, B., & Emara, M. (2026). Function Art: Understanding the Artistic Transformation of Mathematical Functions through Learning Analytics. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9037

article_title: Early Detection of Students at Risk - Predicting Student Dropouts Using Administrative Student Data from German Universities
citation: Johannes Berens, Kerstin Schneider, Simon Görtz, Simon Oster, Julian Burghoff. (2019). Early Detection of Students at Risk - Predicting Student Dropouts Using Administrative Student Data from German Universities and Machine Learning Methods. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 11, No 3. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM
title: Set the at-risk identification threshold using the average dropout rate of previous cohorts, balancing reach against misidentification
description: An EDS assigns each student a dropout probability and needs a threshold above which students are flagged as at risk. The article frames this as a trade-off: "lowering the threshold will reach more potential dropouts at the cost of a higher misidentification rate; alternatively, raising the threshold will increase the accuracy of the EDS while decreasing the identification rate of at-risk students." It recommends that, when applied to current students, the threshold be based on the average dropout rate of previous cohorts, and notes a low threshold may harm student-body acceptance of the system.
requirements: Estimated dropout probabilities for each student, and knowledge of the average dropout rate of previous cohorts
constraints: Deviations in dropout rates between cohorts establish a margin of error when distinguishing probable from actual dropouts
target_learners: Students flagged as at risk by an early detection system
target_learning_goals: Targeting dropout-prevention interventions to students in danger of dropping out
examples: For validation, the authors set a 'true' threshold so identified dropouts match known dropouts in the test cohort, and an 'average' threshold based on the 2010-2012 cohort dropout rates

article_title: Using Demographic Data as Predictor Variables: a Questionable Choice
citation: Baker, R. S., Esbenshade, L., Vitale, J., & Karumbaiah, S. (2023). Using Demographic Data as Predictor Variables: a Questionable Choice. Journal of Educational Data Mining, 15(2). https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/
title: Use demographic variables to validate fairness across groups rather than as predictors within at-risk models
description: The article's central recommendation is that demographic data serve model validation rather than prediction. The authors conclude that "there are greater benefits to fairness if demographic variables are used to validate fai rness rather than as predictors within models". In practice this means analyzing a model's goodness of fit broken down by demographic group to ensure comparable model quality across groups, while keeping actionable, malleable variables as predictors. This preserves the ability to detect group-level disparities without embedding immutable characteristics in individual predictions.
requirements: Models should be checked for fairness and equal accuracy across demographic groups as part of validation
constraints: The authors scope this argument to at-risk prediction models in education; they discuss alternate uses such as cost-sensitive classification separately
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students subject to at-risk or dropout prediction models
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate prediction of student outcomes such as dropout or graduation risk
examples: The article notes commercial systems such as BrightBytes and Infinite Campus adopt the validation approach, analyzing model fit broken down by demographic group

article_title: Effects of Scenario-Based Assessment on Students' Writing Processes
citation: Hongwen Guo, Mo Zhang, Paul Deane, Randy E. Bennett. (2020). Effects of Scenario-Based Assessment on Students’ Writing Processes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 12, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/
title: Place lead-in tasks before the essay in a single-scenario design to reduce working-memory load during writing
description: The article’s theoretically motivated scenario-based design presents a topical scenario with source materials, then lead-in tasks (reading, summarizing, critiquing, analyzing arguments) before the essay. The authors conclude that “the original single-scenario & essay-last form with the theoretically motivated assessment design may have reduced students’ working memory load while they planned and reviewed their essays,” yielding more efficient and fluent text production and freeing attention for monitoring and revising text. The design simulates a condensed writing project in the order a skilled practitioner might follow.
requirements: A single coherent scenario shared by lead-in tasks and the essay; lead-in tasks that engage students with the sources and activate needed skills
constraints: The benefit was observed for the single-scenario design; a mixed-scenario essay-last design lowered scores, possibly via added working-memory load and reduced motivation; the authors note results may not generalize to broader populations or different conditions
target_learners: Middle-school (eighth-grade) students writing argumentative essays from sources
target_learning_goals: Argumentative writing from sources
Efficient and fluent text production
Self-monitoring and revision of text
examples: Students randomly assigned within classrooms to four test forms; the essay-last single-scenario group produced essays of similar quality in less time with fewer words than essay-first students
key_sources: Hongwen Guo, Mo Zhang, Paul Deane, Randy E. Bennett. (2020). Effects of Scenario-Based Assessment on Students’ Writing Processes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 12, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/443

article_title: Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels
citation: Gomathy Ramaswami, Teo Susnjak and Anuradha Mathrani. (2023). Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels. Journal of Learning Analytics, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2023.7935
title: Three reference frames for student-facing dashboards: social, achievement, and progress comparisons
description: The article adopts Jivet et al.'s (2017) categorization of student-facing LAD reference frames: social (comparison with peers), achievement (distance toward goals), and progress (comparison with an earlier self). Social comparison is described as "the most widely used reference frame for LADs." The pattern holds that combining internal and external frames lets students build academic self-concept, set re-adjusted goals, and monitor progress over time.
requirements: A dashboard must present data in ways students can interpret against at least one reference frame (peer, goal, or prior self)
constraints: For some students, external peer comparison could be detrimental and needs careful presentation (Roberts et al., 2017, as cited)
target_learners: tertiary students
online and blended learners
target_learning_goals: self-awareness of learning progress
motivation
self-regulated learning
examples: SensEnablr's first column compares a student's weekly engagement score against the class average; the third column reflects the internal achievement frame (distance toward goals)
key_sources: Gomathy Ramaswami, Teo Susnjak and Anuradha Mathrani. (2023). Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels. Journal of Learning Analytics, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2023.7935

article_title: Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels
citation: Gomathy Ramaswami, Teo Susnjak and Anuradha Mathrani. (2023). Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels. Journal of Learning Analytics, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2023.7935
title: Integrate explainability into predictive LADs to build trust and support uptake
description: The article argues that predictive LADs should expose how models work and why specific predictions were made, since students engage more when they understand outputs. It notes that "detailing the reasons why students receive a particular recommendation has been shown to increase their trust in the system and the likelihood of them following the advice." SensEnablr implements this via SHAP feature-importance visualizations and Anchors rule-based explanations presented in simplified form on the dashboard.
requirements: Explanatory technologies (e.g., SHAP, Anchors) must be integrated alongside predictive models; explanations should be simplified for student comprehension
constraints: When a model produces unexpected or erroneous output, trust is further eroded and could result in rejection by the end user
target_learners: tertiary students using predictive dashboards
target_learning_goals: informed study-related decision-making
trust in analytics tools
examples: SensEnablr displays a simplified SHAP feature-importance plot showing top features and their relative strengths, plus Anchors-based IF-ELSE rule explanations for individual predictions

article_title: A Participatory Approach to Designing a Student-Facing Dashboard for Online and Distance Education
citation: Herodotou, C., Shrestha, S., Comfort, C., Andrews, H., Mulholland, P., Bayer, V., Maguire, C., Lee, J. & Fernandez, M. (2025). A Participatory Approach to Designing a Student-Facing Dashboard for Online and Distance Education. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(2). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8481
title: Select dashboard features through a combination of student-reported usefulness, frequency of agreement, and data feasibility
description: This principle holds that participatory dashboard design should decide which features to include by weighing three factors together rather than frequency alone: what students explain as useful, how many students agree, and whether the data can actually be retrieved. The authors used it because their small, self-selected sample made frequency-based decisions invalid. It operationalizes student voice in learning analytics design.
requirements: Student explanations of usefulness collected alongside frequency counts
Access to institutional data sources to judge feasibility
constraints: With a small, self-selected sample, frequency alone cannot validly determine feature inclusion
target_learners: online and distance learning undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: study progress awareness
study planning
self-regulation
examples: The team included assignment scores, credits passed, tutorials attended, forecasts, and contact features, and excluded extensions, credits failed, and comparison data, citing usefulness, agreement, and feasibility in Table 5.

title: Student-facing dashboards should prescribe actionable solutions, not only describe performance
description: The article argues that dashboards for online students should go beyond displaying descriptive performance data and offer prescriptive information — recommended materials to study and easy ways to contact tutors or support teams — so students can act to overcome performance challenges. Prescriptive data is described as of special significance to online students because it moves beyond describing their data to offering actions they should undertake.

study planning
seeking help

article_title: Towards Data-Informed Teaching Practice: A Model for Integrating Analytics with Teacher Inquiry
citation: Saar, M., Rodríguez-Triana, M. J., & Prieto, L. P. (2022). Towards Data-Informed Teaching Practice: A Model for Integrating Analytics with Teacher Inquiry. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 88–103. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7505
title: Design TLA models to start with purpose rather than problems, keep the inquiry question central, and complement student data with teaching data
description: The article derives design principles for analytics-informed teacher inquiry models from its three DBR iterations. A TLA model "should not focus on problems but should inform teaching practice in general", should "draw attention to an inquiry question", should indicate "how student data could be complemented by teaching data", and should help teachers "divide their teaching analysis into different but logically linked steps". These principles respond to teachers' difficulties with interpretation steps and their tendency to pose questions only about students.
requirements: Models should provide explanations, examples, and prompts for data variety to assist teachers at each step
constraints: The authors note more assistance should be provided to teachers in formulating inquiry questions, as teachers do not always start analysis with them
target_learners: Novice and experienced primary and secondary school teachers
target_learning_goals: Conducting analytics-informed inquiry into teaching practice
examples: The AMTI starts with "purpose" rather than "problem identification" and was reshaped into a circular diagram to emphasize iterative inquiry

article_title: Examining the English Language Arts Course Placement System at the College of the Marshall Islands
citation: Shannon, L., Gruber, J., Rentz, B., Vila, C., Erichsen, K., & Nastasi, J. (2026). Examining the English language arts course placement system at the College of the Marshall Islands (REL 2026–006). U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, Regional Educational Laboratory Pacific. https://ies.ed.gov/use-work/resource-library/reports
title: Weight placement measures by their demonstrated predictive value: rely on high school GPA more heavily and drop components that do not predict outcomes
description: This principle holds that course placement systems should weight placement measures in proportion to their demonstrated ability to predict student outcomes, and drop measures that predict nothing. The study found the multiple-choice test and GPA "similarly able to predict passing these credit- bearing courses," while the writing component predicted none, yet the test carried 75 percent of the placement weight. The authors recommend either using GPA alone or dropping the writing component and increasing GPA's weight to streamline placement and cut costs.
requirements: Predictive validity evidence for each placement measure, such as logistic regression against course passing outcomes, as conducted in this study.
constraints: Using GPA alone would come at the cost of slightly reduced placement precision, as the report states.
target_learners: First-year community college students
target_learning_goals: Appropriate placement into credit-bearing versus developmental English language arts coursework
examples: The report recommends CMI consider using only high school GPA to place students or weighting GPA more heavily and removing the writing component to ensure appropriate and logistically efficient course placement.

article_title: CCSR: A New Model for the Role of Research in Supporting Urban School Reform
citation: Melissa Roderick, John Q. Easton, and Penny Bender Sebring. (2009). A New Model for the Role of Research in Supporting Urban School Reform. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago Urban Education Institute. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Five organizational commitments for research that builds district capacity
description: CCSR's three themes for capacity-building research are institutionalized in five commitments that organize how the organization conducts and communicates research: 'developing an extensive data archive on CPs, (2) extensive stakeholder engagement and strong ongoing relationships with the district, (3) conducting scientifically rigorous research while making findings broadly accessible, (4) building knowledge of core problems across time and across studies, and (5) an extensive outreach of providing information to the public.' The pattern treats the how of research—interaction, organization, dissemination—as capacity-building mechanisms in their own right.

Governance structures (steering committee) that institutionalize stakeholder consultation
High internal standards of quality and review

examples: Biennial CCSR surveys of principals, teachers, and students in grades six through twelve, with individual school reports benchmarking each school against similar schools

article_title: Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour
citation: de Vreugd, L., van Leeuwen, A., Jansen, R., & van der Schaaf, M. (2024). Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(3), 249–262. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8529
title: Do not rely solely on stakeholder input for LAD content; provide literature-based constructs for stakeholders to weigh
description: This principle holds that needs assessment for a learning analytics dashboard should combine stakeholder preferences with constructs drawn from literature. The article recommends that "developers do not solely rely on stakeholder input" because users may be unaware of LAD possibilities; presenting potentially relevant constructs from literature lets stakeholders weigh their added value against their own ideas, resulting in better-informed preferences. In this study, focus groups rated a predetermined literature-based list and could add new topics.
requirements: Stakeholders such as students and tutors must be given a predetermined list of potentially relevant constructs from literature alongside the option to suggest new topics
constraints: Relying solely on prospective user preferences is advised against, as users may not be aware of LAD possibilities or mechanisms of data collection
target_learners: University students
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of study behaviour
examples: Focus group participants rated predetermined constructs (e.g., self-efficacy, intrinsic goal orientation) on Likert scales and could add new topics; two newly suggested topics per group made the final ranking lists.

article_title: Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour
citation: de Vreugd, L., van Leeuwen, A., Jansen, R., & van der Schaaf, M. (2024). Learning Analytics Dashboard Design and Evaluation to Support Student Self-Regulation of Study Behaviour. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(3), 249–262. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8529
title: Plan an explicit usability exploration and adjustment phase before evaluating a LAD's perceived usefulness
description: The article recommends that LAD developers "plan an explicit phase of usability exploration and design adjustments before evaluating a LAD's usefulness." Think-aloud protocols provided in-depth insight into usability problems and, most importantly, the reasons for them, allowing design adjustments (e.g., an introduction video, reorganized exercises) before the usefulness evaluation. Needs assessment, usability testing, and perceived usefulness evaluation are described as all essential elements of a LAD's final evaluation of effectiveness.
requirements: Think-aloud interviews or comparable qualitative exploration to identify why usability problems occur, followed by design adjustments before usefulness assessment
target_learners: University students
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of study behaviour
examples: Think-aloud interviews (n=8) revealed participants struggled with navigating an empty LAD and interpreting acceptable scores; adjustments such as an introduction video and Prepare–Act–Reflect categorization preceded the SUS reassessment.

citation: Hiroyuki Yamada. (2024). New Normal in Early Elementary Mathematics Learning: Part III - Learning from Variation in Grade 3. E4 Center, Northwestern University. https://e4.northwestern.edu
title: Prioritize foundational Algebra/Algebraic Thinking and Number and Operations skills when students struggle across mathematics domains
