article_title: New Normal in Early Elementary Mathematics Learning: Part I -- Initial Findings on Growth and Domains in Grade 1 through Grade 2
citation: Hiroyuki Yamada. (2024). New Normal in Early Elementary Mathematics Learning: Part I - Initial Findings on Growth and Domains in Grade 1 through Grade 2. E4 Center, Northwestern University. https://e4.northwestern.edu
title: Prioritize foundational skills in Algebra and Algebraic Thinking and Number and Operations when students struggle across all mathematics domains
description: The article recommends that because AL and NO best predict later performance across domains, instruction for struggling students should prioritize these foundational domains. It states "it would be critical to prioritize working on skills in these foundational domains if students struggled with all domains of mathematics", suggesting focal skills such as addition, subtraction, and place value, and leveraging assessment results from online learning systems to fine-tune interventions.
requirements: Assessment results identifying students struggling across all domains
Recommended skill development activities from online learning systems
constraints: Recommendation derives from observational cross-lagged panel associations, not an intervention test
target_learners: Grade 1–2 students struggling across all mathematics domains
target_learning_goals: Foundational arithmetic and algebraic thinking skills
examples: The article suggests focal skills could include addition and subtraction and place value, with educators leveraging online learning system assessment results and recommended activities
key_sources: Hiroyuki Yamada. (2024). New Normal in Early Elementary Mathematics Learning: Part I - Initial Findings on Growth and Domains in Grade 1 through Grade 2. E4 Center, Northwestern University. https://e4.northwestern.edu/2024/06/25/new-normal-in-early-elementary-mathematics-learning-part-i-initial-findings-on-growth-and-domains-in-grade-1-through-grade-2/

article_title: Classroom Composition Affects Teacher Performance Ratings
citation: Delgado, W., & Sartain, L. (2026). Classroom composition affects teacher performance ratings. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 48(2).
title: Interpret teacher performance ratings as partly reflecting classroom composition, since teachers working with more challenging students may be systematically undervalued
description: The article's central principle is that "Teacher performance ratings do not purely reflect teaching quality—they are also shaped by the students in the classroom." Evaluation systems should therefore account for classroom context when interpreting ratings, because teachers assigned more challenging students may be undervalued, with equity consequences for groups such as Black teachers.
requirements: Awareness of the classroom composition measures (prior achievement, attendance, behavior, demographics, class size) that influence ratings.
constraints: Effects were driven by academic and behavioral factors rather than demographics for observation ratings; the bias interpretation rests on the absence of corresponding effects in student growth measures.
target_learners: K-12 teachers in urban public school districts
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate measurement of teaching quality for tenure, promotion, and dismissal decisions
examples: In Chicago Public Schools data, teachers received higher ratings when assigned students with higher prior achievement, more regular attendance, and fewer behavioral challenges.
key_sources: Delgado, W., & Sartain, L. (2026). Classroom composition affects teacher performance ratings. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 48(2). https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/classroom-composition-affects-teacher-performance-ratings

article_title: Infographic: Adopting and Adapting
citation: Adopting & Adapting: Skyline ELA curriculum launch infographic. (2021). University of Chicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Five organizational capacity levers leaders used to support Skyline ELA implementation
description: The infographic identifies five domains of strategic investment through which school leaders strengthened organizational capacity for curriculum implementation: "Championed professional learning", "Protected teacher time", "Expanded staff support", "Engaged external support", and "Strengthened collaboration structures". Leaders who targeted these key organizational levers supported teachers' engagement with the Skyline ELA curriculum. The pattern organizes implementation support as leadership investment across these five domains rather than as a single intervention.
requirements: Leaders must have discretion to allocate resources across professional learning, teacher time, staffing, external support, and collaboration structures.
constraints: Documented in the context of the K-2 Skyline ELA curriculum launch in Chicago Public Schools.
target_learners: Elementary school teachers in grades K-2
target_learning_goals: Implementation of a new literacy (ELA) curriculum with instructional change
examples: Leaders in the studied schools made strategic investments across the five domains during the 2021 Skyline launch.
key_sources: Adopting & Adapting: Skyline ELA curriculum launch infographic. (2021). University of Chicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Change That Matters
citation: Sharon Greenberg & Anthony S. Bryk. (2024). Change that matters: Progress made by Chicago Public Schools shows that successful change takes time, focus, and patience. Kappan, V105 N6. https://kappanonline.org
title: Sustainable system change targets a small number of high-leverage processes and improves them continuously over time (Pareto Principle)
description: Drawing on the Pareto Principle from improvement science, the article argues that sustainable and effective change involves identifying the primary drivers of weak outcomes, "targeting a small number of high-leverage processes for change, and then devoting attention to their continuous improvement over time." Chicago leaders saw the system producing unsatisfactory outcomes, used reliable research evidence to select targets, built execution capacity, and kept the public informed to build trust and patience.
requirements: Reliable research evidence to identify high-leverage processes and inform continuous improvement; capacity-building to move from promising practices to quality enactment at scale; sustained attention over years
constraints: Quick, broad-based implementation generally promises more and faster results than is realistically possible; achieving quality equitably at scale becomes the casualty
target_learners: District and school system leaders
target_learning_goals: Designing and sustaining system-level improvement of instructional outcomes
examples: CPS targeted the principalship and Algebra 1 instruction as high-leverage processes; Arne Duncan emphasized keeping only a handful of priorities pursued in a world-class way
key_sources: Sharon Greenberg & Anthony S. Bryk. (2024). Change that matters: Progress made by Chicago Public Schools shows that successful change takes time, focus, and patience. Kappan, V105 N6. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/change-that-matters

article_title: Q&A: Grades & Test Scores
citation: Key Questions: How important are course grades as predictors of students' future success? (2025). UChicago Consortium / FutureEd. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Use course grades as the primary indicator for assessing academic readiness, with standardized tests as supplementary information
description: The article recommends that when choosing a single measure for assessing academic readiness, course grades should come first because they are the most comprehensive indicator of preparation, while tests like the SAT and ACT "provide some additional information." Grades are likened to a full scouting report and tests to a sprint-time measure: useful but partial. The principle applies to admissions, advising, and readiness decisions discussed in the interview.
requirements: Grades must be interpreted knowing that grading practices differ across teachers and schools, though GPAs average out those differences.
constraints: Some studies using restricted samples or weighted or self-reported GPAs reach different conclusions, so data quality and study design matter.
target_learners: secondary and postsecondary students being assessed for academic readiness
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of students' general academic preparation and readiness for further academic work
examples: The interview advises that if focusing on one measure for assessing academic readiness, grades provide the most comprehensive information, with SAT/ACT scores adding some additional information.
key_sources: Key Questions: How important are course grades as predictors of students' future success? (2025). UChicago Consortium / FutureEd. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: The Impact of Rhode Island's Charter School Performance Review System
citation: Margaret E. Raymond, PhD; Marzena Sasnal, PhD. (2025). The Impact of Rhode Island's Charter School Performance Review System on the Education Landscape. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu
title: Rhode Island's new performance framework sets rigorous, multidimensional quality standards across academic achievement, governance, financial stability, and mission alignment
description: The article describes an enumerated set of quality standards that the new performance framework imposes on existing charter schools. Schools must "demonstrate strong academic gains, measured through standardized assessments" and match or exceed sending district performance; governing boards are accountable for oversight and culture; schools must show long-term financial viability; and they are evaluated on mission fulfillment and service to diverse populations including English learners and students with disabilities. The framework applies these standards from the initial application through renewal, with annual dashboards supporting continuous improvement.
requirements: Applicants must meet very rigorous criteria to be authorized to open a new charter in Rhode Island
Schools receive ongoing performance indicators and annual dashboards so expectations are understood
constraints: Some charter school leaders argued that using the SAT to evaluate career and technical education schools is not an adequate measure of success
target_learners: Rhode Island charter school students, including English learners and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement and growth
Organizational and governance health
Financial stability
Mission alignment and community engagement
examples: RIDE developed the updated framework after a year of research with charter school practitioners, collecting feedback from parents, community members, advocacy groups, and school leaders
key_sources: Margaret E. Raymond, PhD; Marzena Sasnal, PhD. (2025). The Impact of Rhode Island's Charter School Performance Review System on the Education Landscape. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu/reports/item/rhode-island-2025/

article_title: City Studies: Project Meta-Analysis
citation: Margaret E. Raymond, Won Fy Lee. (2022). City Studies Project Meta-Analysis by CREDO of Stanford University: Cohort 1 Cities. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu/city-studies/
title: Locally driven solutions and implementation flexibility may be necessary conditions for successful student learning
description: Drawing on the heterogeneous city-level growth patterns in the meta-analysis, the report's discussion proposes that effective learning practices are highly localized rather than a single uniform solution. It states that "schools' ability to ﬁnd locally driven solutions to the locally identiﬁed problems and to allow ﬂexibility in implementing a proposed set of remedies could be necessary conditions for successful student learning." The principle frames school-level autonomy and local problem identification as design conditions for improving learning growth in urban school systems.
requirements: Schools must have the ability to identify problems locally and devise locally driven solutions
Flexibility in implementing a proposed set of remedies
constraints: The report presents this as an interpretation of observed heterogeneous trends, not a tested manipulation; it is stated as a possibility ("could be necessary conditions")
target_learners: K-12 public school students in urban districts, mainly low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: Academic performance growth in reading and mathematics
examples: The report's discussion links the positive charter contributions across heterogeneous city trends to locally driven solutions and implementation flexibility
key_sources: Margaret E. Raymond, Won Fy Lee. (2022). City Studies Project Meta-Analysis by CREDO of Stanford University: Cohort 1 Cities. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Stanford University. https://credo.stanford.edu/city-studies/

article_title: 2023 Pace of Learning Report
citation: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/
title: Dosage-based add-on interventions yield only a student's prevailing pace of learning, so students needing the most help gain the least
description: The brief argues that interventions adding instructional time at the margin — longer days, extra school days, tutoring — cannot retire learning losses because "during the additional period of instruction, a student’s prevailing POL is the best we can expect to realize." It advises treating the pre-COVID POL as an upper bound on gains from added time, since "the students who need the extra help the most are likely to gain the least from the broad application of added learning time."
requirements: Any added-time intervention must be evaluated against the student's historical pace of learning rather than assumed full yield
constraints: The brief lists further drawbacks: interventions are time-limited and funding-constrained, supply challenges exist in needy communities, long-term persistence of short-term impacts is unknown, and voluntary programs may disproportionately serve those who least need them
target_learners: K-12 students with COVID learning losses, especially those with below-average pace of learning
target_learning_goals: Recovering pandemic learning losses toward grade-level benchmarks
examples: A 6th-grade student with a POL of 50 percent and 90 days of loss would reach only 9th-grade level after twelve years, and full tutoring benefit over two years would advance him only a half year
key_sources: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/

article_title: 2023 Pace of Learning Report
citation: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/
title: Deploy high-impact teachers to more students via incentives, since better teachers derive more learning
description: The brief recommends shifting students' pace of learning upward by ensuring higher-quality instruction, arguing "better teachers derive more learning from their students than their peers." One deployment approach offers more effective teachers additional pay or sabbatical/training credit for taking on additional students, so each student drawn from the lower portion of the POL distribution receives "a high quality teacher and higher performing peers, both of which stimulate student performance."
requirements: Use qualitative and quantitative information, including multi-cohort test-based impact estimates strengthened by principal and peer assessments, to identify teachers with outsized impacts
constraints: The brief flags open questions: whether expanded classes taught by top teachers produce the expected gains for added students is listed among the things yet to learn
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those in the lower portion of the POL distribution
target_learning_goals: Increasing students' rate of learning through higher-quality instruction
examples: The brief suggests offering more effective teachers additional pay for taking on additional students, or credit toward later sabbatical or special training
key_sources: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/

article_title: Training and Retaining Effective School Leaders
citation: Rivkin, S.G., Sartain, L., & Schiman, J.C. (2023). Training and retaining effective school leaders: Results from efforts to improve principal effectiveness in Chicago Public Schools. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Invest in principal training and support, but design policies to avoid shifting effort away from noncognitive skill development
description: The brief's forward-looking recommendation is that because principals have lasting impacts on students, "investments in principal training and support are likely well spent." At the same time, it cautions that accountability policies focused primarily on test scores may shift effort away from noncognitive skills, which principals can influence and which recent research shows is much more valuable for young adults' long-term success. Districts should therefore pair principal-effectiveness investments with policy designs that do not crowd out noncognitive skill development.
requirements: District capacity to fund and sustain principal training and support programs over multiple years
constraints: Accountability policies focused primarily on student test scores may shift efforts away from developing students' noncognitive skills
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public school districts
target_learning_goals: Cognitive and noncognitive skill development shaped by school leadership
examples: CPS partnered with local universities on the Chicago Leadership Collaborative residency program and introduced merit bonuses of up to $20,000 for principals of schools with the highest achievement growth
key_sources: Rivkin, S.G., Sartain, L., & Schiman, J.C. (2023). Training and retaining effective school leaders: Results from efforts to improve principal effectiveness in Chicago Public Schools. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/training-retaining-effective-school-leaders

article_title: Investing in Adolescents
citation: Shanette C. Porter, C. Kirabo Jackson, Sebastián Kiguel and John Q. Easton. (2023). Investing in Adolescents: High School Climate and Organizational Context Shape Student Development and Educational Attainment. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Effective high schools feature supportive environments, ambitious instruction, and collaborative teachers
description: The study identifies a pattern of school organizational characteristics shared by high schools that supported students' development on all dimensions of growth. Such schools featured "Supportive environments in which students feel safe, supported, and find teachers trustworthy and responsive to their needs", ambitious instruction with challenging, engaging, well-structured classes that build on prior knowledge, and collaborative teachers active in school improvement, committed to their school, and engaged in professional development.
requirements: Schools must combine a rigorous instructional environment with strong and supportive school-based relationships, which the release says adolescents may be particularly responsive to.
target_learners: high school students (grades 8-9 transition)
target_learning_goals: socioemotional development
academic achievement
educational attainment
examples: The study characterized high schools supporting growth on all dimensions using 5Essentials Survey measures of school climate completed by high school students and teachers.
key_sources: Shanette C. Porter, C. Kirabo Jackson, Sebastián Kiguel and John Q. Easton. (2023). Investing in Adolescents: High School Climate and Organizational Context Shape Student Development and Educational Attainment. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/investing-in-adolescents

article_title: Reaching for Improvement
citation: Shyjka, A. (2022). Reaching for improvement: Teacher evaluation and its role in instructional improvement. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.cps.edu/about/departments/talent/
title: Integrate elements of the teacher evaluation system into the school's Instructional Improvement Support System for coaching purposes
description: The article recommends that if REACH-related coaching is to be feasible for schools, it would likely be both most efficient and effective to integrate relevant elements of the REACH evaluation system into the IISS of a school. As the article states, "If REACH-related coaching is to be feasible for schools, it would likely be both most efficient and effective to integrate relevant elements of the REACH evaluation system into the IISS of a school." This means using the Framework for Teaching as a shared vision language and connecting evaluation feedback to ongoing collaborative improvement work.
requirements: Schools must have existing collaborative structures and instructional leadership capacity to absorb integration demands
Coaching systems or willingness to build them must be present
constraints: Coaching toward improvement may place additional demands on schools' already strained capacities if coaching systems are not already present
target_learners: K-12 teachers in public schools undergoing teacher evaluation
target_learning_goals: Instructional improvement driven by evaluation feedback and coaching
examples: Docherty High School integrated the FFT as a shared vision of instructional quality, connected improvement initiatives to FFT practice change goals, and offered optional weekly REACH domain-focused professional development
key_sources: Shyjka, A. (2022). Reaching for improvement: Teacher evaluation and its role in instructional improvement. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.cps.edu/about/departments/talent/

article_title: Supporting Change in Instructional Practices to Meet the Common Core Mathematics and Next Generation Science Standards
citation: District supports for teachers' standards-aligned instructional practices in the Chicago Public Schools. (2015). AERA Open. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Education leaders should prioritize professional learning, especially colleague collaboration around instruction, when supporting standards-aligned math and science teaching
description: The article's findings imply that leaders deciding how to support standards-aligned math and science instruction get the strongest association from professional learning opportunities, particularly collaboration with colleagues around instruction, which "had consistently positive relationships with instructional practices in math and science." The authors state: "We discuss implications for education leaders as they make decisions about how to best support teachers in standards-aligned math and science instruction."
requirements: Districts must be able to organize professional learning opportunities and structured collaboration with colleagues around instruction.
constraints: The evidence is a mixed-methods exploratory study of the Chicago Public Schools; relationships are correlational, and curriculum and instructional resources showed more modest and mixed relationships.
target_learners: K-12 math and science teachers in public school districts
target_learning_goals: Enacting standards-aligned instructional practices in mathematics and science
examples: The study compared district implementation supports in the Chicago Public Schools and found collaboration around instruction positively related to practices even among teachers perceiving many barriers.
key_sources: District supports for teachers' standards-aligned instructional practices in the Chicago Public Schools. (2015). AERA Open. https://journals.sagepub.com

article_title: Meeting Families' Needs
citation: Ehrlich, S.B., Allensworth, E.M., & Tansey, J. (2021). Meeting families' needs: Attendance rates in full-day vs. half-day pre-k. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Expand access to full-day pre-k, prioritizing students and families facing the greatest logistical and economic barriers to attendance
description: The article recommends that policymakers increase full-day pre-k availability because it better fits families' daily lives and raises attendance, particularly for groups with historically lower attendance. It states that "Increasing opportunities for full- day programs is especially beneficial for these families" with fewer economic resources, and that districts should consider which students benefit most when deciding program location and enrollment processes.
requirements: Full-day pre-k is more expensive for districts to offer than half-day pre-k, so expansion requires additional investment in teachers and classes.
constraints: The article states full-day programs address some, but not all, logistical barriers; families with limited economic resources still face challenges such as childcare, transportation, and healthcare access.
target_learners: pre-kindergarten three- and four-year-old students
families with fewer economic resources
Black students and other groups with historically lower attendance
target_learning_goals: regular pre-k attendance
kindergarten readiness
equitable access to early learning
examples: CPS opened new full-day classrooms in under-enrolled, high-priority neighborhoods and where elementary schools had space; enrollment in full-day pre-k grew from roughly 1,700 students in 2012-13 to more than 6,000 in 2015-16.
The NLCI funded four elementary schools' transition from half-day to full-day pre-k, where the most consistently significant effects of the initiative were found.
key_sources: Ehrlich, S.B., Allensworth, E.M., & Tansey, J. (2021). Meeting families' needs: Attendance rates in full-day vs. half-day pre-k. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/meeting-families-needs

article_title: The Preventable Failure
citation: Roderick, M., & Kelley-Kemple, T., with Johnson, D. W., & Ryan, S. (2021). The Preventable Failure: Improvements in High School Graduation Rates when High Schools Focus on the Ninth-Grade Year. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-preventable-failure
title: Use an early-warning indicator of ninth-grade course performance as the primary lever for dropout prevention rather than a packaged program
description: The report argues that effective dropout prevention should operationalize an early indicator of ninth-grade course performance and give school staff data tools to act on it, rather than purchase a packaged solution. CPS "placed the onus of the work in the hands of the principals," providing data tools that let educators identify at-risk students, monitor performance, and target recovery, while decentralized schools constructed their own approaches. The intervention supports staff to get ninth-graders to attend, complete homework, and get extra help when needed.
requirements: Requires giving principals access to real-time data linking attendance and course outcomes, plus clear evidence on the indicator's link to graduation
constraints: The article cautions the indicator is a very minimum standard of course performance, and that researchers could not isolate which component (data access, information, or principal commitment) contributed most
target_learners: Ninth-grade students in traditional urban high schools, particularly those at risk of course failure
target_learning_goals: Staying on-track to graduate through credit completion and passing core courses
examples: CPS included the Freshman OnTrack rate in its high school accountability system starting in 2007, and the Graduation Pathways office provided watch lists, monthly success reports, and credit recovery reports to schools
key_sources: Roderick, M., & Kelley-Kemple, T., with Johnson, D. W., & Ryan, S. (2021). The Preventable Failure: Improvements in High School Graduation Rates when High Schools Focus on the Ninth-Grade Year. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-preventable-failure

article_title: Improvements in Math Instruction and Student Achievement Through Professional Learning Around the Common Core State Standards in Chicago
citation: Key Questions: How did students' reports of instructional practices, their test scores, grades, and pass rates in math change with implementation of the CCSS-M, based on their schools' level of participation in standards-related PL?. (2018). AERA Open. https://aeraopen.org
title: Evaluate standards implementation by implementation strategy, student subgroups, and outcomes beyond test scores
description: The article argues that existing literature on the Common Core State Standards in Math showed little benefit but had not examined variation by implementation strategies, student subgroups, or outcomes other than test scores. It therefore designs its evaluation around "different levels of participation in professional learning around the standards," subgroup achievement levels, and grades, pass rates, and practice reports. This broadens what counts as evidence of a standards policy's effects.
requirements: Outcome data beyond test scores, such as student reports of instructional practices, grades, and pass rates, must be available
constraints: Findings are from one district (Chicago) and the middle grades, so generalization to other settings is not established in the available text
target_learners: middle grades students
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement under standards-based reform
examples: The study compared pre- and post-standards years across Chicago middle-grade schools with different levels of professional-learning participation using a difference-in-differences approach with school fixed effects.
key_sources: Key Questions: How did students' reports of instructional practices, their test scores, grades, and pass rates in math change with implementation of the CCSS-M, based on their schools' level of participation in standards-related PL?. (2018). AERA Open. https://aeraopen.org

article_title: Closer to Home
citation: Ehrlich, S.B., Connors, M.C., Stein, A.G., Francis, J., Easton, J.Q., Kabourek, S.E., & Farrar, I.C. (2020). Closer to home: More equitable pre-k access and enrollment in Chicago. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research, NORC at the University of Chicago, and Start Early. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Use the geographic distribution of school-based pre-k classrooms—particularly full-day classrooms—as a policy lever for equitable access and enrollment
description: The article concludes that where districts place pre-k classrooms, especially full-day ones, shapes which student groups can access and enroll in pre-k, and that deliberately reallocating classrooms toward under-enrolled, high-need neighborhoods can reduce enrollment inequities. As the authors state, "the geographic distribution of school-based pre-k (particularly full-day) may be an important policy lever for addressing inequities in student access and enrollment in Chicago." Chicago reallocated classrooms and converted half-day to full-day classrooms in neighborhoods with high poverty and low pre-k enrollment.
requirements: Districts must be able to reallocate or convert classrooms across neighborhoods and fund full-day options, as Chicago did through strategies including a federal Preschool Development Grant-Expansion.
constraints: The study is descriptive and does not directly test policy effectiveness or identify access as a causal mechanism for enrollment changes; findings are interpreted as observed patterns and initial evidence of potential levers.
target_learners: four-year-old pre-k students, particularly students of color, English Learners, and students from low-income families
target_learning_goals: equitable access to and enrollment in high-quality early childhood education
examples: CPS reallocated pre-k classrooms to neighborhoods with a history of under-enrollment, expanded full-day options in high-need neighborhoods, and centralized the application process with prioritization for high-priority students.
key_sources: Ehrlich, S.B., Connors, M.C., Stein, A.G., Francis, J., Easton, J.Q., Kabourek, S.E., & Farrar, I.C. (2020). Closer to home: More equitable pre-k access and enrollment in Chicago. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research, NORC at the University of Chicago, and Start Early. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/closer-to-home

article_title: The Forgotten Year
citation: Seeskin, A., Mahaffie, S., & Usher, A. (2020). The forgotten year: Applying lessons from Freshman success to Sophomore year. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-forgotten-year-applying-lessons-freshman-success-sophomore-year
title: Sophomore educators should use a layered indicator system combining on-track status, course failures, attendance, and a 3.0 GPA threshold to target supports
description: The report recommends that sophomore educators combine multiple predictive indicators rather than relying on on-track status alone. "By using an indicator system that combines all of these key predictive indicators—a GPA threshold of 3.0, in addition to the three warning indicators for high school graduation—sophomore educators could differentiate their students" and target supports effectively. The GPA threshold matters because GPA is the strongest indicator of college access, while failures and attendance best flag non-graduation risk.
requirements: Access to timely, actionable data on grades, attendance, and course failures for each student
constraints: Indicators alone cannot change a system; they must be paired with monitoring structures and supports such as freshman success teams extended to sophomore year
target_learners: High school sophomores, including students off-track or showing early warning signs
target_learning_goals: High school graduation
College enrollment and readiness
examples: CPS freshman teams already use eighth-grade attendance and grades at entry, then monitor Freshman OnTrack status and GPA throughout the year; the report proposes extending this structure to sophomore year.
key_sources: Seeskin, A., Mahaffie, S., & Usher, A. (2020). The forgotten year: Applying lessons from Freshman success to Sophomore year. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/the-forgotten-year

article_title: Teacher Evaluation in Chicago Public Schools
citation: Sartain, L., Zou, A., Gutiérrez, V., Shyjka, A., Hinton, E., Brown, E.R., & Easton, J.Q. (2020). Teacher Evaluation in CPS: Perceptions of REACH Implementation, Five Years In. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Make evaluator feedback specific, actionable, task-focused, relevant, balanced, and collaborative for it to improve practice
description: Teachers consistently reported that the value of observation feedback depends on its qualities. As the researchers summarize, "Teachers said that for feedback to be meaningful and useful, it must be specific, actionable, task-focused, relevant, balanced, and collaborative." Evaluators and school leaders should therefore design feedback conversations around these six characteristics rather than delivering generic ratings.
requirements: Evaluators must deliver feedback that is specific, actionable, task-focused, relevant, balanced, and collaborative
constraints: The article reports teachers' stated preferences about feedback qualities; it does not experimentally test which qualities cause practice change
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers in evaluated schools
target_learning_goals: improving classroom instructional practice through evaluation feedback
examples: Teachers reported the REACH observation process accurately represented their teaching practice, provided opportunities to reflect, and resulted in practice changes
key_sources: Sartain, L., Zou, A., Gutiérrez, V., Shyjka, A., Hinton, E., Brown, E.R., & Easton, J.Q. (2020). Teacher Evaluation in CPS: Perceptions of REACH Implementation, Five Years In. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: English Learners in Chicago Public Schools
citation: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Allensworth, E.M., & Freire, S. (2019). English Learners in CPS: A new perspective. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Report academic performance for all students who began as English Learners, not only active ELs, to give an unbiased picture of EL progress
description: The report argues that accountability and public reporting should follow a consistent group of students who began school as ELs, including former ELs, rather than the changing active-EL subgroup. It states "The best way to understand the average performance of the EL students... is to look at all students who began their schooling as ELs together." This regrouping showed performance of never-EL and ever-EL students was very similar. The report also suggests early identification of students with low first-grade ACCESS scores for additional support.
requirements: Longitudinal data linking students across years so the same cohort can be followed regardless of current EL status
constraints: Results apply to students continuously enrolled from kindergarten; the report states its results would not apply to recent immigrants entering in later grades, whom it hopes to study later
target_learners: English Learners in elementary and middle grades
district and school decisionmakers reporting EL outcomes
target_learning_goals: English proficiency
academic achievement across attendance, test scores, grades, and high school readiness
examples: The report regrouped 2018 eighth-grade ELA PARCC data to show former ELs passed at 31.5 percent versus 25.9 percent for students never classified as ELs
The report compared three kindergarten cohorts continuously enrolled through expected eighth-grade year

article_title: Do Classroom Environments Matter for Noncognitive Aspects of Student Performance and Students' Course Grades?
citation: Camille A. Farrington, Shanette Porter, Joshua Klugman. (2019). Do Classroom Environments Matter for Noncognitive Aspects of Student Performance and Students' Course Grades? University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Teachers have more influence over student motivation than they may often assume
description: Because within-student analyses showed a sizable relationship between classroom environment and students' self-reported motivation in a specific class (β=0.234), the article concludes that teacher practice shapes motivation rather than motivation being a fixed student trait. The article states: "This suggests that teachers have much more influence over student motivation than they may often assume." Classrooms with more teacher support, organization, goal clarity, relevance, meaningful work, and positive community were associated with higher student motivation in that class.
requirements: Teachers shape classroom environments through behaviors and instructional practices that students perceive, such as support, goal clarity, and relevance
constraints: The evidence is correlational within-student; the article calls for rigorous experimental or quasi-experimental designs to build causal knowledge
target_learners: Middle and high school students
target_learning_goals: Supporting student motivation to work hard in class
examples: Students reported greater motivation to do well in classrooms their classmates rated more highly on teacher support, organization, goal clarity, relevance, and community than in their own lower-rated classrooms

article_title: Ten Criteria for Describing and Selecting SEL Frameworks
citation: Blyth, D.A.; Borowski, T.; Farrington, C.A.; Kyllonen, P.; Weissberg, R.P. (2019). Ten Criteria for Describing and Selecting SEL Frameworks. Establishing Practical Social-Emotional Competence Assessments Work Group, Frameworks Briefs introductory series 3 of 3. https://measuringsel.casel.org
title: Prioritize SEL framework criteria by context and practice needs before selecting a framework
description: Because the ten criteria are not equally important in all situations, the brief recommends that practitioners first build a profile of what they need, then seek frameworks that score high on their highest-priority criteria. For example, a group wanting staff alignment should weight professional-development supports, while one seeking youth-facing materials should weight resources for children and youth. The brief states: "we hope they are helpful to practitioners who are trying to describe and decide what they need in a framework."
requirements: Practitioners build a profile that prioritizes what they need based on the criteria before seeking a framework
constraints: Not all criteria are equally important in all situations; the degree of balance needed depends in part on the intended purpose and use of a framework
target_learners: preschool to high school students
target_learning_goals: social and emotional competencies
examples: The brief suggests paying particular attention to Implementation Support Criteria 2 when seeking staff alignment, and Criteria 3 when seeking resources for use with children and youth.

article_title: Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K-12 Students
citation: Camille A. Farrington, Joseph Maurer, Meredith R. Aska McBride, Jenny Nagaoka, J. S. Puller, Steve Shewfelt, Elizabeth M. Weiss, and Lindsay Wright. (2018). Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K–12 Students: Developing a Theory of Action. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/arts-education-and-social-emotional-learning-outcomes-among-k–12-students
title: Three domains of social-emotional competencies developed through art practices
description: The report organizes the social-emotional outcomes of arts learning into three domains. As printed, these are "three main domains of social-emotional competencies that are developed and exercised through the social-emotional components of art practices: self-management and discipline (intrapersonal); social and relationship skills (interpersonal); and self-expression and identity." Each art practice may afford work on several components across these domains depending on how the instructor frames it and the learners' ages.
requirements: Art practices must be described specifically, since it is the practices rather than the art discipline label that carry the social-emotional components
constraints: The connected social-emotional components depend in part on the age of the learners
target_learners: K–12 students in visual arts, music, dance, theatre, and media arts programs
target_learning_goals: Self-management and self-discipline, interpersonal and relationship skills, self-expression and identity
examples: Peer critique of self-portraits is given components of listening skills, clear communication with peers, and managing emotions; learning a new brushstroke is given building self-control, focusing attention, and building self-confidence and positive identity

article_title: Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K-12 Students
citation: Camille A. Farrington, Joseph Maurer, Meredith R. Aska McBride, Jenny Nagaoka, J. S. Puller, Steve Shewfelt, Elizabeth M. Weiss, and Lindsay Wright. (2018). Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K–12 Students: Developing a Theory of Action. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/arts-education-and-social-emotional-learning-outcomes-among-k–12-students
title: Be intentional about the social-emotional contexts arts lessons create, because effects occur regardless of instructor intent and can be negative
description: The report's central practical implication is that arts education produces social-emotional effects whether or not instructors plan for them. As the executive summary states, "arts education has social-emotional effects regardless of instructor intent—and these effects can be either positive or negative." Students may feel deeply exposed or ashamed, or conclude they lack artistic talent, and avoid arts thereafter. Educators should therefore consciously design lessons so students take advantage of social-emotional components and are guided toward improved competencies.
requirements: Deliberate planning and awareness by a skilled instructor to shape lessons into spaces for social-emotional development
constraints: The report cautions instructors should not shy away from uncomfortable or challenging content, since challenge in a safe space is one of the catalytic opportunities in arts education
target_learners: K–12 students in arts education settings
target_learning_goals: Positive social-emotional competency development and avoidance of negative social-emotional effects
examples: The report notes that even where evidence showed significant effects, there was much variation in outcomes among participants and across settings, motivating the call for intentional design

article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Early Education Essentials: Testing Measurement Validity of an Organizational Conditions and Practices Tool for Early Childhood Education Settings. (2018). https://www.tandfonline.com
title: Use organizational-conditions survey data to give ECE leaders actionable information about supports for practitioner effectiveness
description: The article positions organizational-conditions measurement as a leadership tool: the survey "has the potential to provide leaders and practitioners with actionable data about organizational supports that enable ECE practitioners to be more effective in their daily work with children and families." Programs should thus measure organizational conditions alongside classroom-level quality metrics to guide improvement.
requirements: Reliable, site-sensitive survey administration with teacher and parent perceptions
constraints: The overview states potential; the associations with quality metrics held for some, but not all, measured conditions
target_learners: ECE program leaders and practitioners
target_learning_goals: identifying organizational supports that improve daily work with children and families
examples: Site-level essential scores were related to teacher–child interaction scores and student attendance in 81 ECE sites

article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research.
title: Strong instructional leadership: purpose-driven vision, relational trust, and protected collaboration
description: When Effective Instructional Leaders is strong, leaders hold a vision "rooted in developmental science and developmentally appropriate practice," view teachers as professional educators, build relational trust with staff, maneuver around incompatible mandates by reframing them toward shared purpose, and cultivate family partnerships. Weak programs instead show compliance-driven visions, micromanagement, and transactional leadership, as contrasted in the report's Table 1.
requirements: Leaders need knowledge of child development and early childhood instructional practices to ground the vision
constraints: Leaders in strong sites still face frequent central/grantee office mandates, some incompatible with their vision, which they must reframe
target_learners: preschool children and the teachers, staff, and families surrounding them
target_learning_goals: consistent, developmentally appropriate early learning and staff capacity for improvement
examples: One leader protected the first two days of the school year for collaboration and split another day across the year for professional learning groups
A leader scheduled around staff family commitments, asking whether a 5:30pm finish was too late for a staff member's husband's birthday
key_sources: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research.
title: Strong collaborative teachers: protected, structured, data-driven peer collaboration
description: When Collaborative Teachers is strong, leaders ensure teachers have "routine protected time, weekly and monthly" to meet, with collaboration that is structured by goals, data, and protocols focused on real problems of practice. Teachers observe each other's classrooms, bring up problems of practice, and share innovations; weak programs show individual accountability, minimal feedback, and no routine peer observation (Table 2).
requirements: Leaders must allocate and protect collaboration time and facilitate it with clear purpose and structured processes
constraints: Teachers reported struggles using collaboration time productively and that the work demands being highly multitask oriented
target_learners: preschool teaching teams, including special education and dual-language learner contexts
target_learning_goals: meeting diverse learning needs of young children and continuous improvement of teaching practice
examples: A teaching team met weekly to discuss individual children and set goals across social-emotional, cognitive, language, and literacy areas
Peer learning groups broke out during staff meetings several times a quarter to visit each other's classrooms
key_sources: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). article_title: Early Education Essentials
citation: Pacchiano, D.M., Wagner, M.R., & Lewandowski, H., with Ehrlich, S.B. & Stein, A.G. (2018). Early Education Essentials: Illustrations of Strong Organizational Practices in Programs Poised for Improvement. Chicago, IL: The Ounce of Prevention Fund and the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research.
title: Strong involved families: welcoming routines, multi-channel communication, and partnership in learning
description: When Involved Families is strong, staff treat partnerships with families as critical to teaching effectiveness: families are welcomed "in every part of the building throughout the day," staff "use multiple, ongoing strategies to build relationships and communicate with families," and teachers partner with families to extend learning at home. Weak programs limit family engagement to funder requirements, homework folders without context, and inconsistent formal communication.
requirements: Staff must treat engaging and partnering with families as a critical part of the job, equally as important as work directly with children
target_learners: preschool children and their families, including grandparents and extended family
target_learning_goals: family understanding of children's development and extension of learning opportunities at home
examples: Leaders and staff greeted families and children by name at drop-off and pick-up, and families walked all the way to classrooms
Classroom webpages posted photos of units and home-connection suggestions alongside newsletters

article_title: Changes in Math Instruction and Student Outcomes since the Implementation of Common Core State Standards in Chicago
citation: Julia A. Gwynne and Sarah Cashdollar. (2018). Changes in Math Instruction and Student Outcomes since the Implementation of Common Core State Standards in Chicago. UChicago Consortium working paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Three-tier train-the-trainer professional development cascade through school networks
description: A district-scale professional development delivery pattern in which each school network sends experienced teachers to full-day district-sponsored sessions three to four times per year; these teacher facilitators "replicated these sessions at network Teacher Leader Institutes," and teacher leaders then share the content with colleagues in their own schools. The district considered this three-tier distributed approach the best way to reach its sizeable workforce. The pattern trades reach for control: the district had less assurance that every teacher received the professional development, and participation levels varied widely across schools.
requirements: Organized school networks with identified experienced teacher facilitators and time for Teacher Leader Institutes
Coordination of session content across years
constraints: The district had less control over making sure each and every teacher received professional development on the new standards
target_learners: All district math teachers, network leaders, and administrators
target_learning_goals: Building capacity to teach to new, more challenging standards
examples: CPS delivered CCSS-M professional learning through network facilitators attending district sessions, network Teacher Leader Institutes, and school-level sharing

article_title: A Community Effort to Support the Transition from Pre-K to Kindergarten
citation: Spain, A.K., Ehrlich, S.B., Cowhy, J.R., Dasgupta, D.K., & Lockaby, T. (2018). A community effort to support the transition from pre-K to kindergarten. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Provide an external facilitator for multi-school transition programs to sustain collaboration and communicate a consistent vision
description: The report recommends that programs bringing together staff from multiple schools use an external facilitator and coordinator. Planning professional learning community meetings, field trips, and family learning activities took substantial time, and "Having BPI as an external facilitator and coordinator provided leadership around these responsibilities" that teacher ownership would have been hard to sustain. An external facilitator is also positioned to reflect on designing future meetings to better meet the needs of all teachers and families.
requirements: An external facilitator with capacity to plan meetings, field trips, and family learning activities and to communicate a consistent vision of the work
constraints: Especially relevant in the context of teacher and administrator turnover from one year to the next
target_learners: pre-K and kindergarten teachers and families across multiple schools and centers
target_learning_goals: sustained cross-school collaboration supporting children's transition to kindergarten
examples: BPI, a public interest law and policy center, staffed PKTP and provided leadership around planning and coordination across the six Altgeld-Riverdale sites.

article_title: A Community Effort to Support the Transition from Pre-K to Kindergarten
citation: Spain, A.K., Ehrlich, S.B., Cowhy, J.R., Dasgupta, D.K., & Lockaby, T. (2018). A community effort to support the transition from pre-K to kindergarten. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Co-design transition programs around key components rather than a structured curriculum, while communicating a consistent vision
description: The report finds that focusing on key components rather than a structured curriculum, and co-developing the program with rather than for teachers, allowed flexibility for practitioners. Teachers reported that "not having a transitions curriculum created important fl exibility to respond to teacher and student needs in local community context and across diverse educational settings," and as co-designers they felt the common classroom practices aligned with student needs. The report cautions that this flexible approach must also include communication of a consistent vision to support future engagement and participation.
requirements: Communication of a consistent vision for the program to support engagement and participation
constraints: Variation in perceptions of alignment with curricula, goals, and visions of schools and centers created implementation barriers for some teachers
target_learners: pre-K and kindergarten teachers implementing transition practices in diverse educational settings
target_learning_goals: classroom and community transition practices aligned to local student needs
examples: PKTP teachers co-designed the common classroom practices, developed content for family learning activities, and established priorities for their professional learning community.

article_title: The Information Content of Employee Awards
citation: Signaling effects of merit awards: Evidence from school principals in Chicago. (2023). Economics of Education Review. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/economics-of-education-review
title: Design merit award programs to reduce the loss of more effective school leaders
description: Because merit awards can signal effectiveness to outside employers and increase exit among winners, award programs should be modified to retain the leaders they identify. The article states the findings "highlight the importance of program modifications that reduce the loss of more effective school leaders." Program design should therefore anticipate labor-market signaling consequences alongside incentive benefits.
requirements: An award program with an explicit effectiveness threshold whose winners can be observed by outside employers
constraints: The recommendation rests on evidence from one merit award program for Chicago principals
target_learners: school principals
district policymakers
target_learning_goals: retaining effective school leaders while maintaining incentive effects
examples: The Chicago principal merit award program, whose incentives increased achievement while award winners exited at over twice the rate of near-threshold non-winners

article_title: Why Do Students Get Good Grades, or Bad Ones? The Influence of the Teacher, Class, School, and Student
citation: Elaine M. Allensworth and Stuart Luppescu. (2016). Why do students get good grades, or bad ones? The influence of the teacher, class, school, and student. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research working paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Interpret course grades in light of observable context—attendance, course conditions and class composition—rather than treating them as incomparable across teachers and schools
description: The article argues that because most grade variation is explained by observable factors, practitioners can use contextual information when interpreting grades. It finds "there are observable factors that systematically explain most of the differences in the grades that students receive in different types of schools, and with different teachers." Grades remain useful for early warning and readiness indicators, but a low grade may reflect course conditions, schedule demands, or attendance patterns rather than idiosyncratic grading.
requirements: Knowledge of the course conditions (subject, level, peer achievement, period, term, class size) and the student's attendance in the course
constraints: Attendance and test scores are incomplete measures of effort and skills, so the study likely underestimates how much grades reflect real differences in effort and skills
target_learners: High school students
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of course grades and GPAs as indicators of academic readiness in educational decision-making
examples: The study used the universe of core-course grades from 118 Chicago public high schools to quantify how much teacher, school and course-condition variation remains after accounting for attendance and test scores
key_sources: Elaine M. Allensworth and Stuart Luppescu. (2016). Why do students get good grades, or bad ones? The influence of the teacher, class, school, and student. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research working paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Organizing Early Education for Improvement
citation: Ehrlich, S.B., Pacchiano, D.M., Stein, A.G., Wagner, M.R., Luppescu, S., Park, S., Frank, E., Lewandowski, H., & Young, C. (2018). Organizing early education for improvement: Testing a new survey tool. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and the Ounce of Prevention Fund. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Measure organizational conditions in ECE settings because existing quality tools do not capture them
description: The report argues that ECE improvement efforts focused only on classrooms miss a key lever: the organizational climate and conditions surrounding teachers. It states that "The ECE field is missing a statistically valid tool that measures these organizational conditions in ECE settings and provides actionable information from which to design improvement strategies." Reliable tools exist for classroom structural quality, interactions, and administrative practices, but not for the interdependent organizational conditions that support or impede educators' daily practice.
requirements: Survey measures must be statistically valid and provide actionable information that program staff can use to design improvement strategies
constraints: Survey data are not expected to map perfectly onto other quality measures; they should provide consistent information while also identifying practices other tools do not capture
target_learners: ECE program leaders, practitioners, and stakeholders in school- and community-based preschool programs
target_learning_goals: strengthening organizational conditions that enable effective teaching and improvements in children's learning
examples: The Ounce and UChicago Consortium partnered to develop and test the Early Ed Essentials surveys to fill this measurement gap
key_sources: Ehrlich, S.B., Pacchiano, D.M., Stein, A.G., Wagner, M.R., Luppescu, S., Park, S., Frank, E., Lewandowski, H., & Young, C. (2018). Organizing early education for improvement: Testing a new survey tool. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and the Ounce of Prevention Fund. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/organizing-early-education-improvement-testing-new-survey-tool

article_title: Organizing Early Education for Improvement
citation: Ehrlich, S.B., Pacchiano, D.M., Stein, A.G., Wagner, M.R., Luppescu, S., Park, S., Frank, E., Lewandowski, H., & Young, C. (2018). Organizing early education for improvement: Testing a new survey tool. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and the Ounce of Prevention Fund. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Use explicit Rasch-based criteria (reliability, item fit, difficulty spread, DIF) when developing survey measures
description: The report used the Rasch IRT model rather than raw-score methods because IRT "creates measures that are on linear scales," provides a person standard error, and handles missing data without bias. Measure refinement followed explicit criteria: person reliability of at least 0.70 (preferably above 0.80), item fit with infit mean square below 1.30, adequate spread of item difficulty, and removal of items with significant and large DIF contrasts. Rasch also "allows for comparisons over time" by equating measures across respondent samples.
requirements: Items must fit the restricted one-parameter Rasch model; some items may need to be discarded or modified to fit
Measures should reach person reliability of at least 0.70, with reliabilities greater than 0.80 preferred
constraints: A disadvantage of Rasch analysis is that some items may need to be discarded or modified to fit the model
target_learners: survey developers and researchers measuring organizational or educational constructs
ECE program staff who receive survey reports
target_learning_goals: producing reliable, unidimensional survey measures that validly capture respondents' perceptions and can be tracked over time
examples: Items with significant (p < 0.05) and large (p > 0.50) DIF contrasts were considered for removal, though some large-DIF items were retained when they fit within each group

article_title: How Do Principals Influence Student Achievement?
citation: Elaine Allensworth. (2019). Elementary School Case Studies. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/how-do-principals-influence-student-achievement
title: Distributed leadership with monitoring routines in elementary schools
description: A school-level organizational pattern in which principals delegate leadership functions to staff (coaches, counselors, teachers) while maintaining regular instructional monitoring routines such as progress-report reviews, assignment feedback, and team data meetings. Both case schools distribute work among staff: at Foxglove the principal's philosophy is "putting the right people in the right place", and at Ivy the principal empowers staff to set goals. The cases suggest distribution works best paired with coordination and shared monitoring structures.
requirements: Staff members with capacity to own delegated functions, as at Ivy where the principal cites a strong staff
constraints: Foxglove's distributed model operated with few mechanisms to coordinate work within and across groups, and teachers reported limited scheduled collaboration time
target_learners: Elementary school students
target_learning_goals: School-wide academic achievement, growth targets, and student support
examples: Foxglove delegates discipline, finances, lesson-plan checking, attendance supports, and hiring; Ivy's grade-level teams create academic goals that the whole school reviews.

article_title: Making Sense out of Incentives
citation: NO AUTHOR LINE. (2018). Incentive-Based Approaches to Improving Attendance. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk (JESPAR). https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/cjep20
title: Align incentive design with the nature of specific attendance barriers
description: The article recommends that incentive design begin with diagnosis: policymakers and practitioners need guidance on "how to design incentives in ways that align with the nature of specific attendance barriers and problems." Because attendance barriers differ, a single incentive design will not fit every school's situation.
requirements: Practitioners must first identify the specific attendance barriers and problems their students face before choosing or designing incentives
constraints: The article notes varied levels of success when incentives are employed without such alignment
target_learners: chronically absent students in pre-K to grade 12
target_learning_goals: improving attendance
examples: The framework prompts schools to decide whether incentives are an appropriate intervention for their particular attendance problem before implementing one

article_title: Illuminating the Mechanisms of Character Development
citation: Key Questions: How might learning environments "build character" in children and youth?. (2017). Journal of Character Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Theorize character-education mechanisms by leveraging theory and empirical work from other disciplines
description: Because program evaluations and extant character-development studies make identifying promising practices difficult, the article recommends a more thorough use of theoretical and empirical work from other disciplines. It suggests "a more thorough leveraging of both theoretical work and empirical studies in other disciplines (e.g., neuroscience, cognitive science, social psychology, developmental psychology, sociology, philosophy) to theorize about potential mechanisms whereby school practices develop character."
