Feinberg (Eds.), Integrating Timing Considerations to Improve Testing Practices, Routledge. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-cessation-of-measurement-identifying-test-taker-disengagement-using-response-time-book/

article_title: Assessment education: Bridging research, theory, and practice to promote equity and student learning
citation: Tarasawa, B., Gotwals, A., & Jackson, C. (2020). Assessment education: Bridging research, theory, and practice to promote equity and student learning. Rowman & Littlefield. https://rowman.com
title: Use assessment in a way that balances addressing opportunity gaps, especially under COVID-era schooling challenges
description: The book promotes using assessment not only for accountability but deliberately balanced to address opportunity gaps. Its description calls this balancing "a critical element now more than ever as schools face the challenge of education in the era of COVID." The principle frames assessment as an equity tool for educators pursuing data-informed instruction rather than purely punitive measurement.
requirements: Educators such as teachers, administrators, and other educational leaders striving toward data-informed instruction must have access to practical uses of assessment in education
constraints: The book presents this as especially critical in the era of COVID, when schools face heightened challenges
target_learners: K-12 students in schools addressing opportunity gaps
target_learning_goals: Equitable learning outcomes supported by data-informed instruction
examples: The book compiles resources and strategies for teachers, administrators, and educational leaders who strive toward data-informed instruction that balances assessment use to address opportunity gaps.
key_sources: Tarasawa, B., Gotwals, A., & Jackson, C. (2020). Assessment education: Bridging research, theory, and practice to promote equity and student learning. Rowman & Littlefield. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/assessment-education-bridging-research-theory-and-practice-to-promote-equity-and-student-learning/

article_title: NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools
citation: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Exclude insufficiently engaged examinees when building assessment norms to protect validity
description: This norming principle holds that test events from examinees who did not engage with the assessment should be removed before estimating norms, because disengaged responses distort the score distributions that norms are built from. The report states: "To improve the validity of norming results, examinees who were not sufﬁciently engaged during the test were not included in the analyses." The 2020 MAP Growth norming study applied this screening as part of its data eligibility criteria.
requirements: A operational way to flag insufficiently engaged test events in the assessment data
target_learners: K-12 students taking interim assessments
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of achievement and growth scores
examples: The 2020 MAP Growth norming study excluded insufficiently engaged examinees from its analyses
key_sources: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/nwea-2020-map-growth-achievement-status-and-growth-norms-for-students-and-schools/

article_title: NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools
citation: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Use school instructional calendars to reflect each student's instructional exposure when norming
description: This principle holds that norms should be calibrated to the amount of instruction a student actually received before testing, using school-specific calendars rather than a uniform assumption. The report states: "we continued to reﬁne the use of sch ool calendars to better reﬂect the level of instructional exposure available to the student when she/h e/they test." Instructional days are computed by accounting for non-instructional days within each school's calendar, and growth is modeled against instructional exposure.
requirements: Accurate instructional calendar information for each school, including non-instructional days
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: fair comparison of achievement and growth across students with differing instructional time
examples: The report includes a chapter on instructional exposure with instructional calendars, non-instructional days, and calculation of instructional days, illustrated by an instructional calendar example figure
key_sources: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/nwea-2020-map-growth-achievement-status-and-growth-norms-for-students-and-schools/

article_title: Do response styles affect estimates of growth on social-emotional constructs? Evidence from four years of longitudinal survey scores
citation: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Do response styles affect estimates of growth on social-emotional constructs? Evidence from four years of longitudinal survey scores. Multivariate Behavioral Research. https://www.tandfonline.com
title: When estimating growth from Likert survey scores, compare scoring models that do and do not account for response styles
description: Because response styles can affect growth parameter estimates, the article's approach is to score longitudinal surveys using IRT models that do and do not account for response styles, then compare the growth-model results. The authors "conducted empirical and simulation analyses in which we scored surveys using item response theory (IRT) models that do and do not account for response styles." This dual-scoring comparison serves as a sensitivity check for growth inferences.
requirements: Longitudinal survey data on the construct of interest
Access to IRT scoring models both with and without response-style parameters
constraints: Effects vary by psychological construct, response style, and IRT model used, so results of the comparison are not uniform
target_learners: K-12 students assessed on social-emotional constructs
target_learning_goals: Valid estimation of growth on survey-measured constructs
examples: The study scored four years of survey data under both model types and compared slope estimates in growth models
key_sources: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Do response styles affect estimates of growth on social-emotional constructs? Evidence from four years of longitudinal survey scores. Multivariate Behavioral Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/do-response-styles-affect-estimates-of-growth-on-social-emotional-constructs-evidence-from-four-years-of-longitudinal-survey-scores-journal/

article_title: The impact of a technology-enhanced math performance task on student cognitive engagement in mathematics
citation: Meg Guerreiro. (2017). The impact of a technology-enhanced math performance task on student cognitive engagement in mathematics. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Technological affordances in assessments should be purposefully implemented; simply putting tests on computers may not be enough
description: The article's design recommendation is that technology in assessment should be implemented deliberately for its affordances rather than applied as a default conversion of tests to computer delivery. It states that "just putting tests on computers may not be enough and technological affordance should be purposefully implemented." This follows from the null platform effect on cognitive engagement combined with student appreciation of specific interactive features.
requirements: A purpose for each technological affordance, such as the interactivity and animations students cited as helping them visualize and work through problems
constraints: The between-subjects ANOVA found no relationship between platform modality and cognitive engagement, so platform choice alone did not change measured engagement
target_learners: students in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: cognitive engagement during mathematics assessment
examples: The study compared technology-enhanced (animation and interactivity), technology-enabled (computer-based without animation and interactivity), and paper-and-pencil platforms on the same mathematics performance task
key_sources: Meg Guerreiro. (2017). The impact of a technology-enhanced math performance task on student cognitive engagement in mathematics. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-impact-of-a-technology-enhanced-math-performance-task-on-student-cognitive-engagement-in-mathematics/

article_title: Instructors’ technology experience and iPad delivered intervention implementation: A mixed methods replication study
citation: Lina Shanley, Mari Strand Cary, Ben Clarke, Meg Guerreiro, Michael Thier. (2017). Instructors’ technology experience and iPad delivered intervention implementation: A mixed methods replication study. Educational Technology Research and Development 65, 815–830.
title: Plan for instructor facilitation and professional development when implementing technology-based interventions in authentic school settings
description: The article positions instructor facilitation as central to whether technology-based interventions are implemented successfully in real classrooms: "Instructor facilitation is an essential element in the successful implementation of technology-based interventions in authentic school settings." Because instructors' varying technology experience and reported barriers corresponded with variable student use, the authors draw implications for technology-based intervention implementation and professional development.
requirements: Instructors with sufficient technology experience and support, since instructor-reported experience and barriers corresponded with student use patterns
constraints: Instructors with moderate iPad experience and/or no reported barriers to technology integration demonstrated the least desirable student use patterns, so experience and barrier profiles alone do not guarantee desirable implementation
target_learners: kindergarten teachers and other instructors implementing technology-based interventions
target_learning_goals: successful implementation of technology-based interventions as measured by student use
examples: The two KinderTEK development studies related instructor-reported iPad experience and technology-integration barriers to student use of the iPad-delivered intervention
key_sources: Lina Shanley, Mari Strand Cary, Ben Clarke, Meg Guerreiro, Michael Thier. (2017). Instructors’ technology experience and iPad delivered intervention implementation: A mixed methods replication study. article_title: Are all biases bad? Collaborative grounded theory in developmental evaluation of education policy
citation: Anderson, R., Guerreiro, M., & Smith, J. (2016). Are all biases bad? Collaborative grounded theory in developmental evaluation of education policy. Journal of Multidisciplinary Evaluation 12(27), 44-57.
title: Varied perspectives should be a critical component in the methodological and analytical choices of education research when the goal is deeper understanding of program or policy impact
description: This principle holds that education research should deliberately build varied perspectives into its methodological and analytical choices. The authors argue that "varied perspectives should be a critical component in the methodological and analytical choices of education research", especially "when the sought after outcome is deeper understanding of the impact, both positive and negative, of an education program or policy". It directs evaluators to treat interpretive diversity as a design feature rather than a threat to be controlled.
requirements: At least two researchers with distinct perspectives participating in analysis and theory generation
constraints: Argued for in the context of education policy and program evaluation seeking deeper understanding of impacts
target_learners: education researchers
policy evaluators
target_learning_goals: deeper understanding of the positive and negative impacts of education programs and policies
examples: In the study, two researchers with distinct perspectives cogenerated themes and theory from interviews of education leaders in Kentucky and California.
key_sources: Anderson, R., Guerreiro, M., & Smith, J. (2016). Are all biases bad? Collaborative grounded theory in developmental evaluation of education policy. Journal of Multidisciplinary Evaluation 12(27), 44-57. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/are-all-biases-bad-collaborative-grounded-theory-in-developmental-evaluation-of-education-policy/

article_title: The learning curve: Revisiting the assumption of linear growth across the school year
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). The learning curve: Revisiting the assumption of linear growth across the school year. NWEA Research working paper. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19345747.2020.1839990
title: Do not assume linear within-year growth when estimating learning from achievement data
description: Analyses that estimate how much students learn during the school year — for school-year-length policy, summer-loss studies, or gap research — should test rather than assume that within-year growth is linear. The article's own finding is that "assuming linear within-year growth is often not justified, particularly in reading," so linear-growth assumptions can distort such estimates, especially in reading.
requirements: Achievement data at multiple within-year time points (e.g., fall, winter, spring) to check growth shape before fitting linear models
constraints: The evidence reported covers math and reading in grades K-8 in 2016-17; the abstract notes the problem is particularly pronounced in reading
target_learners: Kindergarten through 8th grade students
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement and modeling of within-year academic growth
examples: The authors examined fall, winter, and spring scores for over seven million K-8 students and found the linear assumption often unjustified
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). The learning curve: Revisiting the assumption of linear growth across the school year. NWEA Research working paper. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19345747.2020.1839990

article_title: How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School (Expanded Edition)
citation: John D. Bransford, Ann L. Brown, and Rodney R. Cocking, editors, National Research Council. (2000). How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School: Expanded Edition. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/9853
title: Bridge the science of learning to actual classroom practice as a distinct follow-up step
description: The volume treats linking research on learning to practice as a distinct effort requiring its own committee and report. The Preface states that after the original science-of-learning volume, "a second NRC committee, the Committee on Learning Research and Educational Practice, was formed to carry that volume an essential step further by exploring the critical issue of how better to link the findings of research on the science of learning to actual practice in the classroom." The principle is that synthesis of learning science and translation into practice are separate, both necessary steps.
requirements: A body of learning-science findings already synthesized
target_learners: teachers
teacher educators
curriculum designers
target_learning_goals: applying learning research to instructional design and classroom practice
examples: The Committee on Learning Research and Educational Practice produced How People Learn: Bridging Research and Practice, published in June 1999, whose material was drawn on for this expanded edition.
key_sources: John D. Bransford, Ann L. Brown, and Rodney R. Cocking, editors, National Research Council. (2000). How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School: Expanded Edition. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press. https://doi.org/10.17226/9853

article_title: Transforming education through COVID-19 recovery and learning acceleration: research findings, policy recommendations, and lessons from the ground
citation: Michael Conner, PhD, Beth Tarasawa, Deb Delisle, Janet Murguía, Chris Minnich, Marc Morial. (2021). Transforming education through COVID-19 recovery and learning acceleration: research findings, policy recommendations, and lessons from the ground. NWEA Research webinar. https://www.nwea.org
title: Treat the post-pandemic moment as an opportunity to reimagine education and build more equitable systems
description: The webinar positions pandemic recovery not merely as restoration but as a chance for systemic redesign toward equity. The page states that "we can use this critical moment in education to reimagine education and build more equitable systems that provide all children with an excellent education," tying recovery spending to longer-term equity goals.
requirements: Coordination among policymakers, education leaders, and advocacy organizations during the recovery period
constraints: Tied to the specific post-COVID recovery context and the availability of federal recovery funding
target_learners: All children
Historically underserved students
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to an excellent education
System-level transformation
examples: The webinar pairs NWEA trend research with policy recommendations from equity-focused organizations

article_title: Incorporating person covariates and response times as collateral information to improve person and item parameter estimations
citation: Wang, S., & Jiao, H. (2011). Incorporating Person Covariates and Response Times as Collateral Information to Improve Person and Item Parameter Estimations. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the National Council on Measurement in Education, New Orleans, LA.
title: Use routinely collected response times and student background data as collateral information rather than discarding them as test byproducts
description: The article argues that in computer-based testing, response times, background information and academic history are "all simultaneously collected (or available) during the test administration along student responses," yet common practice ignores them. Because using RT "does not change the construct measured by a test, but increases the accuracy of estimations," testing programs should incorporate such collateral information into IRT parameter estimation for scoring, equating and scaling. The authors frame this as making tests fair by accounting for differences in personality or cognitive style among test takers, analogous to DIF analysis for gender and ethnicity.
requirements: Computerized test administration that records item-level response times and collects examinee auxiliary information
constraints: Few studies have examined the consequence of not using CI in real applications; the GLIMMIX estimation approach may fail to converge with large item counts or much missing data
target_learners: K-12 examinees in large-scale computerized assessment programs
target_learning_goals: Improved precision of person and item parameter estimates supporting scoring, equating, scaling and test quality monitoring
examples: The study compared nested joint models with and without raw score, gender and ethnicity covariates on two MPG Skills Checklist tests, finding CI models generally fit better.
key_sources: Wang, S., & Jiao, H. (2011). Incorporating Person Covariates and Response Times as Collateral Information to Improve Person and Item Parameter Estimations. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the National Council on Measurement in Education, New Orleans, LA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/incorporating-person-covariates-and-response-times-as-collateral-information-to-improve-person-and-item-parameter-estimations/

article_title: A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time. NWEA Research presentation, National Council on Measurement in Education 2020 virtual conference. https://www.nwea.org
title: Exclude rapid guesses from scoring because they represent a test taker's choice to opt out of the measurement process
description: The principle holds that because rapid guesses do not reflect what a test taker knows and can do, they do not contribute to measurement and should be excluded from scoring. The authors base this on the belief that "rapid guessing on an item represents a test taker's choice to 'opt out' of the measurement process." The presentation supports the principle through data analyses and previous research findings.
requirements: Response-time data from computer-based test administration must be available to identify rapid-guessing behavior.
constraints: Applies to computer-based tests where disengaged item responses can be identified as rapid-guessing behavior.
target_learners: Test takers on computer-based achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of knowledge, skills, and abilities
examples: The authors contend rapid guesses should be excluded from scoring and provide evidence through data analyses and previous research findings.
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time. NWEA Research presentation, National Council on Measurement in Education 2020 virtual conference. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-cessation-of-measurement-identifying-test-taker-disengagement-using-response-time/

article_title: The impact of test-taking disengagement on item content representation
citation: Steven Wise. (2020). The impact of test-taking disengagement on item content representation. Applied Measurement in Education, 33(2), 83-94. https://doi.org/10.1080/08957347.2020.1732386
title: Address test-taking disengagement to preserve the content representation of test scores
description: Because disengaged responses can distort the content representation of a test event, the article discusses implications for test-score validity "along with suggestions for addressing the problem." The principle is that test developers and users should act on test-taking disengagement so that the engaged responses underlying scores maintain the content representation intended by the test blueprint.
requirements: Awareness of which items or content categories elicit disengaged responses, such as rapid guessing
constraints: The available text states only that suggestions are discussed; it does not print the specific remedies.
target_learners: students taking achievement tests
target_learning_goals: valid test-score interpretation across the intended content domain
examples: The article reports two studies of rapid-guessing behavior and discusses implications for test-score validity along with suggestions for addressing the problem.
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2020). The impact of test-taking disengagement on item content representation. Applied Measurement in Education, 33(2), 83-94. https://doi.org/10.1080/08957347.2020.1732386

article_title: Estimating student growth on psychological and social-emotional constructs: A comparison of multiple scoring approaches
citation: Kuhfeld, Megan, and James Soland. (2020). Estimating Student Growth on Psychological and Social-emotional Constructs: A Comparison of Multiple Scoring Approaches. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-193. https://www.edworkingpapers.com/ai20-193
title: When survey responses from all timepoints are available, use MIRT calibration that accounts for latent variable covariances over time before fitting growth models
description: The article recommends that researchers scoring longitudinal survey measures of psychological and social-emotional constructs calibrate items with a multidimensional IRT model spanning all timepoints rather than sum scores or unidimensional calibration. The authors conclude that "a MIRT approach is likely preferable when survey responses from all timepoints are available at the time of calibration," because such models better recover true developmental trajectories and variance components. The recommendation rests on the simulation and empirical comparisons showing non-MIRT approaches understate slopes and variances.
requirements: Item responses from all timepoints available at the time of calibration
Consistent item set administered across timepoints
constraints: The article states MIRT models are "not a panacea for all measurement issues"; results were not examined under failures of longitudinal measurement invariance or shifting item composition across timepoints
target_learners: elementary and middle school students
target_learning_goals: accurate recovery of growth trajectories and variance components on psychological and social-emotional constructs
examples: The two simulation studies and the growth mindset empirical study each compared sum score, unidimensional IRT, and MIRT scoring approaches feeding latent growth curve models
key_sources: Kuhfeld, Megan, and James Soland. (2020). Estimating Student Growth on Psychological and Social-emotional Constructs: A Comparison of Multiple Scoring Approaches. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-193. https://www.edworkingpapers.com/ai20-193

article_title: School effectiveness, summer loss, and federal accountability: Applying the compound polynomialmodel in a program evaluation context
citation: Soland, J. & Thum, Y.M. (2019). School effectiveness, summer loss, and federal accountability: Applying the compound polynomial model in a program evaluation context. The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper.
title: Accountability systems should account for the seasonality of achievement data, since ignoring summer loss changes which schools are identified as effective
description: The article argues that because school effectiveness estimates differ depending on whether fall-to-spring or spring-to-spring growth is used, accountability models should not ignore summer learning loss. The authors state that "a broader policy conversation is likely needed about the extent to which schools should be responsible for how learning changes during the summer months," and show that no correlation they produced reached the .90 threshold at which rank orderings would agree.
requirements: Requires assessment data collected at multiple points within the year (e.g., fall and spring) and a growth model that can parameterize within-year growth, since states testing only once per year cannot model within-year growth
constraints: The authors note the CP findings are sensitive to parameterization choices such as the centering grade, so the model cannot definitively identify effective and ineffective schools
target_learners: elementary and middle school students
target_learning_goals: accurate and fair estimation of school contributions to student growth for accountability determinations
examples: The authors compared school-level fall-to-spring and spring-to-spring growth estimates from CP models fit to five years of MAP Growth data and found all correlations below the .90 threshold
key_sources: Soland, J. & Thum, Y.M. (2019). School effectiveness, summer loss, and federal accountability: Applying the compound polynomial model in a program evaluation context. The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/school-effectiveness-summer-loss-and-federal-accountability-applying-the-compound-polynomialmodel-in-a-program-evaluation-context/

article_title: The relationship between test-taking disengagement and performance on MAP Growth retests
citation: Wise, S. (2019). The Relationship Between Test-Taking Disengagement and Performance on MAP Growth Retests. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org
title: Retest disengaged students, but first focus on increasing their motivation so engagement improves
description: The article recommends that educators retest students who showed rapid guessing, because disengaged students who re-engage on retest are likely to show sizable gains and produce more valid scores. It stresses that "Simply retesting will accomplish little if engagement does not improve", so increasing the student's motivation before retesting is central to the recommendation.
requirements: The student's motivation must be addressed before retesting so that engagement actually improves
constraints: Educators should be cautious if they do not retest students showing high levels of rapid guessing, since those scores threaten the validity of test score interpretations
target_learners: K-12 students taking MAP Growth assessments who show rapid guessing
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of what students know and can do
examples: Analysis of over 100,000 tests retested within one day showed disengaged students who rapid-guessed less on retest tended to see gains sometimes exceeding 10 RIT points.
key_sources: Wise, S. (2019). The Relationship Between Test-Taking Disengagement and Performance on MAP Growth Retests. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-relationship-between-test-taking-disengagement-and-performance-on-map-growth-retests/

article_title: Identifying students who are off-track academically in ninth grade – the role of social-emotional learning trajectories
citation: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld. (2019). Identifying students who are off-track academically in ninth grade – the role of social-emotional learning trajectories. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Incorporate social-emotional development trajectories into identification of students not on track for high school success
description: The article's stated implication is that early-warning identification of academically off-track students should draw on how students develop socially-emotionally, not only on academic indicators. As the summary puts it, “understanding how a student develops social-emotionally can improve identification of students not on track to succeed in high school.” The principle applies in middle school, where SEL level and growth can be measured before the 9th-grade transition.

constraints: The page prints no evidence on how such identification should be implemented operationally
target_learners: middle school students
ninth-grade students
target_learning_goals: academic readiness for high school
social-emotional learning
examples: The study related students' 6th-grade SEL level and 6th-to-8th-grade SEL growth to their successful transition to secondary school

article_title: The impact of proctor notification when students disengage
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2019). The impact of proctor notification when students disengage. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Monitor and respond to disengagement during testing because engagement shapes the effort students give
description: Test administrations should include active monitoring of student engagement with a mechanism for responding when students disengage, because disengagement undermines the effort students give on testing day. The brief's framing question, "How do you help make sure students give their best effort on testing day?", ties best effort directly to managing engagement during the test.
requirements: Proctors or staff tasked with engagement monitoring during test sessions
target_learners: K-12 students taking standardized tests
target_learning_goals: Accurate achievement measurement through best-effort test performance
examples: NWEA research on student test engagement studied proctor notification as the response mechanism
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2019). The impact of proctor notification when students disengage. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-impact-of-proctor-notification-when-students-disengage/

article_title: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models
citation: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models. (2019). NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Account school accountability models for summer learning loss
description: School accountability models should incorporate seasonal learning patterns rather than assuming uniform growth across the calendar year. The brief's rationale is that "ignoring summer loss can impact which schools are identified as low performers", meaning models that omit summer loss risk misclassifying schools. The principle directs accountability designers to use growth estimates that separate school-year learning from summer learning before labeling schools.
requirements: Assessment data collected across seasons, including fall and spring (or summer-adjacent) administrations, so summer loss can be estimated separately from school-year growth
constraints: The supplied text does not print the specific modeling procedure the brief recommends
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate school accountability classifications
examples: The brief examines how estimates of school effectiveness change when seasonality is taken into account
key_sources: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models. (2019). NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/reconciling-long-term-education-policy-goals-with-short-term-school-accountability-models/

article_title: The utility of adaptive testing in addressing the problem of unmotivated examinees
citation: Steven Wise. (2014). The utility of adaptive testing in addressing the problem of unmotivated examinees. Journal of Computerized Adaptive Testing, 2(1), 1–17. https://jcat.psychstat.org
title: Use computerized adaptive tests in low-stakes programs to mitigate unmotivated examinees
description: The article recommends, through its integrative review, that low-stakes testing programs address examinee motivation by using computerized adaptive tests, which it finds "can have important advantages over conventional tests" both in identifying low-effort instances and in "effectively addressing the validity threat posed by unmotivated examinees." The principle treats test format as a lever for managing examinee motivation alongside conventional test-quality work.
requirements: A computerized adaptive testing delivery platform
constraints: The advantage is stated for low-stakes testing programs where unmotivated examinees threaten score validity
target_learners: Examinees in low-stakes testing programs
target_learning_goals: Valid achievement scores despite variable examinee effort
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2014). The utility of adaptive testing in addressing the problem of unmotivated examinees. Journal of Computerized Adaptive Testing, 2(1), 1–17. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-utility-of-adaptive-testing-in-addressing-the-problem-of-unmotivated-examinees/

article_title: Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data
citation: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/
title: Measurement professionals have a responsibility to identify invalid scores to individuals making achievement inferences from them
description: This principle holds that measurement professionals should actively flag invalid scores — those "materially distorted by non-effortful test taking" — to the individuals who make inferences about student achievement on the basis of those scores. The article recommends this as a professional responsibility so that score users are not misled by scores biased by low test-taking motivation.
requirements: Measurement professionals must be able to apply effort-related individual score validation to identify which scores are invalid before reporting them
constraints: Applies to scores distorted by non-effortful test taking; the article does not claim it covers all sources of invalidity
target_learners: K-12 students whose achievement test scores are interpreted by educators
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of student achievement from test scores
examples: The article recommends that measurement professionals identify invalid scores to individuals who make inferences about student achievement on the basis of those scores
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/

article_title: Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data
citation: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/
title: Trust in an achievement score requires that the test event not be unduly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors
description: This principle states a validity precondition for achievement testing: users can trust that a score "accurately reflects what that student knows and can do" only if the test event is not unduly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors that could distort it. The article uses this premise to justify screening individual scores for distortion from low test-taking motivation before drawing inferences about achievement.
requirements: Score users must be able to assume the test event was not unduly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors before trusting the score for achievement inferences
constraints: Test-taking motivation is presented as one such construct-irrelevant factor, not the only possible one
target_learners: K-12 students taking achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Valid inference about what a student knows and can do from test scores
examples: The article's abstract presents this trust assumption as the foundation for its argument that non-effortful test taking must be detected
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2015). Effort analysis: Individual score validation of achievement test data. Applied Measurement in Education, 28(3), 237–252. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/effort-analysis-individual-score-validation-of-achievement-test-data/

article_title: Students improve even amid evaluation controversy
citation: NWEA Research. (2016). Students improve even amid evaluation controversy. Phi Delta Kappan 98 (2), 58-65. https://www.nwea.org
title: Strengthen evaluation procedures, systematic evidence collection, and data use rather than relying on a punitive approach
description: The article recommends improving the teacher evaluation process by emphasizing "the importance of strong evaluation procedures, the systematic collection of evidence of teacher performance, and the use of data to inform the process." It argues this approach has promise for improving educator effectiveness far more than a narrower punitive approach, and is most likely to gain the support of administrators and teachers.
requirements: Strong evaluation procedures, systematic collection of evidence of teacher performance, and use of data to inform the evaluation process
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Improving educator effectiveness and student achievement over time
examples: New York's APPR system combined a student-growth component (40%) with classroom observations (60%) as an instance of structured, evidence-based evaluation
key_sources: NWEA Research. (2016). Students improve even amid evaluation controversy. Phi Delta Kappan 98 (2), 58-65. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/students-improve-even-amid-evaluation-controversy/

article_title: Propensity score stratification using multilevel models to examine charter school achievement effects
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Yun Xiang. (2015). Propensity score stratification using multilevel models to examine charter school achievement effects. Journal of School Choice, 9(2), 179–196. https://www.tandfonline.com
title: Use propensity score stratification with multilevel models when estimating school achievement effects from observational data
description: When estimating the achievement effects of school transfer or school choice from non-experimental data, the article recommends combining propensity score stratification with multilevel models. The authors report that this combination "reduces selection bias which arises from confounding variables and improves the accuracy of charter school effect estimations". The multilevel component addresses the clustered structure of students within schools in cross-state samples.
requirements: Key covariates must be available to balance treatment and control groups via propensity scores
constraints: Applicable in quasi-experimental contexts; the article does not claim equivalence to randomized designs
target_learners: K-12 students in charter and traditional public schools
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of school effects on standardized achievement and growth
examples: The authors applied the approach to a cross-state sample of students to estimate charter school achievement and growth effects relative to traditional public schools.
key_sources: Beth Tarasawa, Yun Xiang. (2015). Propensity score stratification using multilevel models to examine charter school achievement effects. Journal of School Choice, 9(2), 179–196. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/propensity-score-stratification-using-multilevel-models-to-examine-charter-school-achievement-effects/

article_title: An investigation of examinee test-taking effort on a large-scale assessment
citation: Steven Wise, J. Carl Setzer, Jill R. van den Heuvel, Guangming Ling. (2013). An investigation of examinee test-taking effort on a large-scale assessment. Applied Measurement in Education, 26(1), 34–49.
title: Monitor examinee effort in low-stakes assessments using item response times because low effort can distort results
description: Assessment results collected under low-stakes conditions are vulnerable to low examinee effort: "Assessment results collected under low-stakes testing situations are subject to effects of low examinee effort." Because even a small amount of rapid guessing can impact institutional rankings, test users should check for rapid-guessing behavior via response times before interpreting low-stakes scores.
requirements: Computer-based testing that records item response times, enabling classification of responses as rapid guessing or solution behavior.
constraints: The principle addresses low-stakes testing situations; the article does not claim high-stakes results show the same effort problem.
target_learners: K-12 and institutional examinees taking large-scale low-stakes assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of assessment results for accountability and institutional comparison
examples: The study quantified rapid guessing in a commercially available low-stakes instrument and found it averaged 1% of item responses yet could still affect institutional rankings.
key_sources: Steven Wise, J. Carl Setzer, Jill R. van den Heuvel, Guangming Ling. (2013). An investigation of examinee test-taking effort on a large-scale assessment. Applied Measurement in Education, 26(1), 34–49. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/an-investigation-of-examinee-test-taking-effort-on-a-large-scale-assessment/

article_title: Increasing parental involvement of English language learner families: What the research says
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Jacqueline Waggoner. (2015). Increasing parental involvement of English language learner families: What the research says. Journal of Children and Poverty, 21(2), 129–134. https://epsl.asu.edu/epru/documents/EPSL-0801-250-EPRU.pdf
title: Increase ELL parental involvement through both traditional and nontraditional family engagement implemented in culturally and linguistically appropriate practices
description: The brief recommends that schools seeking to increase ELL parental involvement implement "both traditional and nontraditional approaches to family engagement" within practices that are culturally and linguistically appropriate. It argues this dual approach is needed because schools often struggle to meet ELL students' instructional and linguistic needs and because parent communication barriers differ from those of mainstream families. The brief presents this as its central recommendation, supported by its research overview and illustrated by a district case study.
requirements: Practices must be culturally and linguistically appropriate to the families served
constraints: Schools often struggle to meet the unique instructional and linguistic needs of ELL students
target_learners: English language learner students and their families
target_learning_goals: Increased parental involvement in children's education
examples: The brief concludes with a case study of one public school district's successful outreach efforts implementing such engagement.
key_sources: Beth Tarasawa, Jacqueline Waggoner. (2015). Increasing parental involvement of English language learner families: What the research says. Journal of Children and Poverty, 21(2), 129–134. https://epsl.asu.edu/epru/documents/EPSL-0801-250-EPRU.pdf

article_title: Is Moneyball the next big thing in education?
citation: James Soland. (2015). Is Moneyball the next big thing in education? Phi Delta Kappan 96(4), 64–67. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Adapt predictive analytics to schooling rather than copying industry practice
description: The article recommends that educators apply predictive analytics in ways that respect how schooling differs from industry, because "Predictive analytics in education can offer a benefit as long as educators heed the differences" between the two settings. It works by treating analytics as a supplement to, not a replacement for, teacher knowledge of students. The article uses this principle to frame its warnings about misidentification and teacher perceptions.
requirements: Educators must recognize and act on the differences between industrial and educational use of the tools
constraints: Ignoring these differences may misidentify at-risk students and negatively influence teacher views, per the article's warning
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those at risk of dropping out
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of student risk and support needs
examples: The article contrasts teachers' knowledge of students with an investor's knowledge of a stock or a scout's knowledge of a pitcher
key_sources: James Soland. (2015). Is Moneyball the next big thing in education? Phi Delta Kappan 96(4), 64–67. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/is-moneyball-the-next-big-thing-in-education/

article_title: The phantom collapse of student achievement in New York
citation: John Cronin, Nate Jensen. (2014). The phantom collapse of student achievement in New York. Phi Delta Kappan 96(2), 60-66. https://www.nwea.org
title: States should closely coordinate new assessment data with existing data when switching measuring instruments
description: This principle holds that when a state adopts a different measuring instrument, the new results must be interpreted against, and coordinated with, the existing data stream so that changes in scores are not mistaken for changes in achievement. The article draws this as an explicit lesson from New York's Common Core release: "states need to closely coordinate new data with existing data when they switch to different measuring instruments." It is used to explain why the new exam results were misread as a collapse in achievement.
requirements: Existing achievement data from the prior instrument must be available for comparison when new exam results are released
constraints: The article states this need specifically for states switching to different measuring instruments, such as the move to Common Core exams
target_learners: K-12 students in states adopting new assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement trends across assessment transitions
examples: New York released the first results of exams under the Common Core State Standards, and the results were misread as dramatic declines in achievement
key_sources: John Cronin, Nate Jensen. (2014). The phantom collapse of student achievement in New York. Phi Delta Kappan 96(2), 60-66. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-phantom-collapse-of-student-achievement-in-new-york/

article_title: Is teacher value added a matter of scale? The practical consequences of treating an ordinal scale as interval for estimation of teacher effects
citation: Soland, J. (2017). Is teacher value added a matter of scale? The practical consequences of treating an ordinal scale as interval for estimation of teacher effects. Applied Measurement in Education, 30(1), 52–70. https://www.nwea.org
title: Treat ordinal test scales cautiously when using them for teacher value-added decisions
description: The article argues that assuming a test scale is equal-interval "can be problematic, especially when the assessment is being used to achieve a policy aim like evaluating growth over time," and that treating an ordinal scale as interval "might lead to erroneous conclusions about teacher quality." Because mild scale transformations can multiply classification odds by a factor of 5, users of value-added estimates should check scale sensitivity before acting on high/low classifications.
requirements: Users should verify how value-added classifications change under mild nonlinear transformations of the score scale before using them for personnel decisions
constraints: The concern applies when assessments serve policy aims such as evaluating growth over time or teacher quality
target_learners: K-12 students assessed on standardized achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate teacher evaluation and accountability decisions
examples: The article re-estimated teacher value added under transformed scales and found classification odds changed by up to a factor of 5 while rankings stayed largely stable
key_sources: Soland, J. (2017). Is teacher value added a matter of scale? The practical consequences of treating an ordinal scale as interval for estimation of teacher effects. Applied Measurement in Education, 30(1), 52–70. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/is-teacher-value-added-a-matter-of-scale-the-practical-consequences-of-treating-an-ordinal-scale-as-interval-for-estimation-of-teacher-effects/

article_title: The potential of adaptive assessment
citation: Freeman, E. (2014). The potential of adaptive assessment. Education Leadership, 71(6).
title: Use adaptive assessment results to differentiate instruction to current academic needs
description: The principle is that assessment should feed instruction directly: because computerized adaptive testing yields immediate, informative results, teachers can use them to tailor teaching. The article states that "The immediate, informative test results enable teachers to differentiate instruction to meet individual students’ current academic needs." It presents this as the instructional payoff of adopting CAT in place of uniform, factory-style testing.
requirements: An adaptive assessment that produces immediate, informative results available to teachers
constraints: The article's supporting text reports no study testing this instructional use
target_learners: K-12 students with varied current achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Instruction matched to individual students' current academic needs
examples: The article describes schools using computerized adaptive testing whose teachers receive immediate results for differentiating instruction
key_sources: Freeman, E. (2014). The potential of adaptive assessment. Education Leadership, 71(6). https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-potential-of-adaptive-assessment/

article_title: Rapid‐guessing behavior: Its identification, interpretation, and implications
citation: Steven Wise. (2017). Rapid‐guessing behavior: Its identification, interpretation, and implications. Educational Measurement Issues and Practice 36 (4) 52-61. https://doi.org/10.1111/emip.12189
title: Exclude rapid guesses from scoring because they do not contribute to measurement
description: The article recommends that rapid guesses not be counted in scores: "because rapid guesses do not contribute to measurement, it makes little sense to include them in scoring." The rationale follows from the conceptualization of rapid guessing as a momentary opt-out and from the finding that inclusion tends to negatively distort scores and diminish validity. Implementing the principle requires identifying rapid guesses from very short response times before scoring.
requirements: A method for identifying rapid guesses from item-level response time data before scoring occurs
constraints: The article notes there are misconceptions regarding the dynamics of rapid guessing that must be handled for proper interpretation; the supplied text does not print those details
target_learners: Test takers taking computer-based multiple-choice assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate, validity-preserving test scores
examples: The article argues that rapid guesses identified via very short response times should be removed from the scored record
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2017). Rapid‐guessing behavior: Its identification, interpretation, and implications. Educational Measurement Issues and Practice 36 (4) 52-61. https://doi.org/10.1111/emip.12189

article_title: Moving from data to making a difference
citation: Andrew Hegedus. (2013). Moving from data to making a difference. TASA INSIGHT Magazine 28(2), 17-21. https://www.nwea.org
title: Treat data use as a complete process that ends with evaluating progress, not as a one-time report
description: Because educational problems lack clear definitions, many potential causes, and simple solutions, the article recommends approaching data use as a structured process rather than an isolated event. The process it outlines is one "that begins with collecting data and ends with evaluating progress," meaning schools should plan for evaluation of progress as an explicit final stage whenever they begin collecting data for improvement.
requirements: Data collection must be initiated with the intention of following through to a progress-evaluation stage
constraints: The article's supporting detail for this recommendation is not visible in the available abstract text
target_learners: educators and school leaders
target_learning_goals: using assessment data to make a difference in educational outcomes
examples: The article outlines key characteristics of a process that begins with collecting data and ends with evaluating progress
key_sources: Andrew Hegedus. (2013). Moving from data to making a difference. TASA INSIGHT Magazine 28(2), 17-21. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/moving-from-data-to-making-a-difference/

article_title: Moving from data to making a difference
citation: Andrew Hegedus. (2013). Moving from data to making a difference. TASA INSIGHT Magazine 28(2), 17-21. https://www.nwea.org
title: Data-to-evaluation improvement cycle pattern for complex educational problems
description: This pattern captures the article's overall shape for improvement work in education: a cycle whose endpoints are data collection and progress evaluation. The abstract frames it as a response to problems that "lack clear definitions, have many potential causes, lack simple solutions, and defy straightforward measurement," suggesting the cycle's key characteristics are meant to bring structure to otherwise ill-defined problems. The pattern operates at the school- or system-improvement level rather than the individual lesson level.
requirements: A functioning data collection step and a progress evaluation step at the cycle's endpoints
constraints: Only the endpoints of the cycle are visible in the available text; the intermediate key characteristics are not shown
target_learners: schools and school systems
target_learning_goals: systematic improvement of teaching and learning through data
examples: The article outlines key characteristics of a process spanning data collection to progress evaluation
key_sources: Andrew Hegedus. (2013). Moving from data to making a difference. TASA INSIGHT Magazine 28(2), 17-21. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/moving-from-data-to-making-a-difference/

article_title: An information-based approach to identifying rapid-guessing thresholds
citation: Wise, S. (2019). An information-based approach to identifying rapid-guessing thresholds. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(4), 325-336.
title: Rapid-guessing threshold methods should be reliable and aligned with test taker behavior
description: The article argues that effective methods for identifying rapid guesses require threshold methods with two properties: they must be reliable, and they must be "aligned with test taker behavior." It presents common threshold methods based on response accuracy or visual inspection of response-time distributions as sharing limitations, and offers the information-based approach as meeting these requirements without those limitations.
requirements: Threshold methods must be reliable
Threshold methods must be aligned with test taker behavior
constraints: Common threshold methods based on response accuracy or visual inspection of response-time distributions are described as having limitations
target_learners: test takers of low-stakes achievement tests
target_learning_goals: valid achievement score interpretation
examples: The article introduces information-based threshold methods as an alternative that avoids the limitations of accuracy-based and visual-inspection methods.
key_sources: Wise, S. (2019). An information-based approach to identifying rapid-guessing thresholds. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(4), 325-336. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/an-information-based-approach-to-identifying-rapid-guessing-thresholds/

article_title: The (non)impact of differential test taker engagement on aggregated scores
citation: Steven Wise, James Soland, Yuanchao Bo. (2019). The (non)impact of differential test taker engagement on aggregated scores. International Journal of Testing 20 (1), 55-77. https://www.tandfonline.com/
title: Do not assume low-stakes aggregated school scores are invalid solely because of differential test-taker engagement; check whether disengagement effects cancel or dilute
description: The article argues that differential engagement on low-stakes tests does not necessarily invalidate aggregated school-level scores. In its PISA-Based Test for Schools data, school means were "highly stable due to two factors": dilution by engaged students and cancellation of positive and negative individual distortions. The principle directs measurement users to examine these mechanisms before discounting aggregated scores.
requirements: Evidence about the proportion of students exhibiting no non-effortful behavior and the direction of individual score distortions in the assessment of interest
constraints: The finding is specific to the computer-based version of the PISA-Based Test for Schools; the abstract notes disengagement is most prevalent with low-stakes tests
target_learners: K-12 students taking low-stakes school-level assessments
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of aggregated school-level achievement scores
examples: The study examined distortive effects of differential engagement on aggregated school-level scores using data from the computer-based version of the PISA-Based Test for Schools
key_sources: Steven Wise, James Soland, Yuanchao Bo. (2019). The (non)impact of differential test taker engagement on aggregated scores. International Journal of Testing 20 (1), 55-77. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-nonimpact-of-differential-test-taker-engagement-on-aggregated-scores/

article_title: The effects of effort monitoring with proctor notification on test-taking engagement, test performance, and validity
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2018). The effects of effort monitoring with proctor notification on test-taking engagement, test performance, and validity. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(2), 183-192.
title: Monitor test-taking effort in real time and alert proctors to disengagement to protect score validity on low-stakes tests
description: On low-stakes computer-based tests, disengaged test taking poses a serious threat to score validity. This principle recommends detecting rapid guessing as it occurs and notifying proctors so they can re-engage the test taker, because the study found that "after a proctor notification was triggered, test-taking engagement tended to increase, test performance improved, and test scores exhibited higher convergent validation evidence."
requirements: A computer-based testing platform capable of detecting rapid-guessing behavior in real time and proctors positioned to respond to notifications.
constraints: The evidence comes from one empirical study of a low-stakes testing context; the available text prints no effect sizes.
target_learners: Students taking low-stakes computer-based achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Valid and reliable measurement of achievement
examples: The study administered computer-based achievement tests with the effort monitoring feature enabled and triggered proctor notifications upon rapid-guessing detection.
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2018). The effects of effort monitoring with proctor notification on test-taking engagement, test performance, and validity. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(2), 183-192. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-effects-of-effort-monitoring-with-proctor-notification-on-test-taking-engagement-test-performance-and-validity/

article_title: Finding root causes effectively: A powerful way to improve schools
citation: Andrew Hegedus. (2010). Finding root causes effectively: A powerful way to improve schools. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Improve SIP quality through better determination of root causes so staff efforts are focused on improving results
description: The paper recommends improving School Improvement Plan quality by determining root causes more effectively, because plans that address symptoms are unlikely to improve achievement. As printed, improving SIP quality through better root-cause determination means "staff and administrative efforts will be more focused and directed in ways that have a higher likelihood of improving results." The recommendations also support developing a collaborative, inquiry-based culture.
requirements: School teams must determine root causes rather than surface symptoms when building improvement plans
constraints: NCLB-mandated consequences increase pressure to address root causes but do not themselves help schools determine or remove them
target_learners: school staff and administrators
target_learning_goals: focused school improvement efforts with a higher likelihood of improving student results
examples: The paper provides proposals for the entire SIP process and for school district central office support based on lessons learned developing the recommended process, protocols and tools
key_sources: Andrew Hegedus. (2010). Finding root causes effectively: A powerful way to improve schools. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/finding-root-causes-effectively-a-powerful-way-to-improve-schools/

article_title: Controlling construct-irrelevant factors through computer-based testing: Disengagement, anxiety, & cheating
citation: Steven Wise. (2018). Controlling construct-irrelevant factors through computer-based testing: Disengagement, anxiety, & cheating. Education Inquiry 10(1), 21-33. https://www.tandfonline.com/
title: Weigh benefits against costs, disadvantages, and challenges when deciding whether to move from paper-and-pencil to computer-based tests
description: The article frames the decision to move from paper-and-pencil to computer-based tests as a weighing problem: "A decision of whether to move from paper-and-pencil to computer-based tests is based largely on a careful weighing of the potential benefits of a change against its costs, disadvantages, and challenges." Within that weighing, the article argues that control of construct-irrelevant factors should count among the benefits, since "the potential for expanded control may prove to be one of the most important benefits of computer-based tests."
requirements: Decision-makers must identify and weigh the potential benefits of a change against its costs, disadvantages, and challenges, as the article states.
target_learners: K-12 and other students taking computer-based or paper-and-pencil assessments
target_learning_goals: Valid assessment of achievement through reduced construct-irrelevant variance
examples: The article presents the paper-to-computer transition decision as a trade-off analysis and then examines one benefit side of that analysis: control of disengagement, anxiety, and cheating.
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2018). Controlling construct-irrelevant factors through computer-based testing: Disengagement, anxiety, & cheating. Education Inquiry 10(1), 21-33. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/controlling-construct-irrelevant-factors-through-computer-based-testing-disengagement-anxiety-cheating/

article_title: Predicting time to reclassification for English learners: A joint modeling approach
citation: Tyler Matta, James Soland. (2018). Predicting time to reclassification for English learners: A joint modeling approach. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics. https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998618791259
title: Model English proficiency development jointly with reclassification timing when predicting EL outcomes
description: Because the joint model outperformed the conventional approach, the article supports designing EL policy analytics that estimate proficiency growth and reclassification timing together rather than separately. The SREM treats "student-specific random effects as latent covariates in the time to reclassification model," yielding more accurate predictions of the grade of reclassification.
requirements: Access to longitudinal English proficiency measures linked to reclassification records
constraints: Evidence comes from one large Arizona school district
target_learners: English learners (ELs)
target_learning_goals: Accurate prediction of reclassification to fluent English proficient status
examples: The authors fit the SREM to Arizona district data and compared its prediction accuracy (93%) with a conventional discrete-time hazard model (85%).
key_sources: Tyler Matta, James Soland. (2018). Predicting time to reclassification for English learners: A joint modeling approach. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics. https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998618791259

article_title: Are achievement gap estimates biased by differential student test effort? Putting an important policy metric to the test.
citation: James Soland. (2018). Are achievement gap estimates biased by differential student test effort? Putting an important policy metric to the test. Teachers College Record, 120(12), 1-26. https://www.tcrecord.org
title: Interpret test scores as achievement only to the extent that students are willing and able to demonstrate what they have learned
description: Because low test effort biases observed test scores downward and effort differs by subgroup, score-based comparisons such as achievement gaps reflect achievement only conditionally on student engagement. The article states that "test scores reflect achievement only to the extent that students are willing and able to demonstrate what they have learned," reminding users of policy metrics to consider effort when interpreting subgroup score differences.
requirements: Test interpretation should account for, or at least consider, measures of student test effort such as rapid guessing.
constraints: The bias introduced into achievement gap estimates by differential test effort is hard to quantify.
target_learners: K-12 students in subgroup comparisons used for policy and accountability
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of achievement gap estimates and subgroup score differences
examples: The study conditioned achievement gap estimates on measures of rapid guessing to test the sensitivity of gap conclusions to differential effort.
key_sources: James Soland. (2018). Are achievement gap estimates biased by differential student test effort? Putting an important policy metric to the test. Teachers College Record, 120(12), 1-26. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/are-achievement-gap-estimates-biased-by-differential-student-test-effort-putting-an-important-policy-metric-to-the-test/

article_title: The changing landscape of assessment and accommodation policies
citation: Elizabeth Barker. (2019). The changing landscape of assessment and accommodation policies. Accessibility, Compliance, & Equity, 72-77. https://www.nwea.org
title: Include accommodations in educational assessments in pursuit of accessibility for all
description: The article's opening design recommendation is that "Educational assessments must include accommodations in the pursuit of accessibility for all." It treats accommodations as a necessary component of accessible assessment design, while cautioning that their role is unsettled and evolving. The article uses this principle to motivate its review of the accommodations landscape across past, present, and future policy developments.
requirements: Assessment developers must treat accommodations as part of assessment design rather than an afterthought, per the article's statement that assessments "must include accommodations."
constraints: The article notes accommodations, once adopted, "feel transitional" and rarely seem like an organic and fully equal part of an assessment.
target_learners: All students taking educational assessments, including students requiring accommodations
target_learning_goals: Accessible and equitable measurement of student achievement
examples: The article frames its review of the accommodations landscape as motivated by this accessibility requirement.
key_sources: Elizabeth Barker. (2019). The changing landscape of assessment and accommodation policies. Accessibility, Compliance, & Equity, 72-77. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-changing-landscape-of-assessment-and-accommodation-policies/

article_title: Evaluating the relationships between poverty and school performance
citation: Andrew Hegedus. (2018). Evaluating the Relationships Between Poverty and School Performance. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Evaluate schools, especially high-poverty schools, using growth measures alongside achievement data because achievement alone clouds how much learning is occurring
description: The article recommends that school evaluation should not rest on achievement data alone, because "the heavy weighting of achievement data in the evaluation of U.S. schools clouds how much learning may actually be occurring." Growth measures should accompany achievement data since the study shows they offer a clearer, more accurate picture of learning, particularly for high-poverty communities. The principle applies to school-level evaluation and accountability contexts.
requirements: Both achievement data and growth measures must be available for the schools being evaluated, as the article treats achievement data as playing a critical role in tracking student progress.
constraints: The article's scope is evaluation of U.S. schools, with particular relevance to high-poverty communities.
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. schools, particularly in high-poverty communities
target_learning_goals: Accurate evaluation of how much learning is occurring in schools
examples: The report investigates how achievement-weighted evaluation clouds learning in high-poverty communities and presents its findings through an interactive data visualization gallery.

article_title: Lessons From Implementing Courseware in Gateway Statistics Courses
citation: Barbara Means, Julie Neisler, Daniel Parker, Vanessa Peters Hinton, and Emily Pressler. (2026). Lessons From Implementing Courseware in Gateway Statistics Courses. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: High-engagement high-achievement courseware classes share transparent guidance, mindset attention, active learning, and emphasis on understanding
description: Across five spotlight classes that achieved both above-average affective engagement and higher-than-expected achievement, instructors used different instructional models yet shared common themes: "transparent guidance about what to do and why it mattered, repeated attention to students' mindsets and statistics anxiety, active learning structures that supported participation, and deliberate efforts to emphasize understanding rather than procedures alone." All treated the courseware as a resource to teach with, not a substitute for instruction.
requirements: Instructor willingness to blend courseware use with active in-class facilitation rather than delegating teaching to the technology
constraints: Identified from a small set of five outlier classes; themes are descriptive, not experimentally validated
target_learners: College students in introductory statistics courses using digital courseware
target_learning_goals: Statistics conceptual understanding, affective engagement, and course success
examples: Spotlight approaches included combining direct instruction with group work, collaborative active learning emphasizing understanding, group problem solving, interactive online instruction, and alternating whole-class framing with peer learning
