article_title: Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas
citation: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163
title: Include researchers from diverse backgrounds and communities most targeted by intersectional structural inequality to guide equity-relevant research
description: The article's first recommendation is that equity-relevant research teams must include researchers from diverse backgrounds and diverse research methods. It argues that "these lived experiences give insights about issues of equity that those without the experiences cannot easily see or always keep at the forefront of their thinking," and that without intentional inclusion it is too easy to only include dominant perspectives. Diversity is needed both in the people on the team and in the development process.
requirements: Intentional inclusion of diverse perspectives, since without it dominant ones dominate
Research enabling active, equitable, and real participation of historically excluded groups
target_learners: historically and systemically excluded students
education research teams
target_learning_goals: envisioning pathways that make learning accessible for all groups of students
examples: The SEERNet personas were created to provoke thinking about what different researchers bring to their work and make apparent new features or capabilities that might be needed
key_sources: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163

article_title: Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas
citation: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163
title: Engage teachers, students, and families as partners in research throughout the development process, using participatory design research
description: The article's second recommendation is to include research participants, not only researchers, through participatory design research (PDR) and community-engaged research. Engagement should happen "throughout the development process and not just at the end," enabling platform developers to acknowledge students' cultural diversity and accommodate multiple modes of learning. The article notes this inclusion leads to buy-in and increases the relevance of the work, but requires time, resources, and compensation for community members.
requirements: Time and resources to support community participation, with acknowledgment and compensation for their work
Careful attention to the traditional roles of power in research, as PDR works to create new roles and relations
constraints: Working to include community members takes time and resources to support
target_learners: teachers
students
families
historically excluded communities
target_learning_goals: improving equity in research
helping platforms interpret learners' preconceptions and experiences
examples: The article cites Hammond's point that cultural responsiveness informs practice so better teaching choices can be made for all students
key_sources: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163

article_title: Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas
citation: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163
title: Minimize bias in learning platforms by diversifying the developers, training data, and feedback sources behind algorithms
description: The article's third recommendation addresses algorithmic bias: any algorithm has the potential to be biased because it reflects the biases of the humans who develop and validate it. It recommends ensuring that algorithms and training data represent diverse learners by including developers with diverse backgrounds who use their lived experiences to shape algorithms in terms of race, ethnicity, gender, and nationality, plus feedback from parents, students, and teachers in communities where the algorithm will be used.
requirements: Developers with diverse backgrounds and perspectives shaping the algorithms
Feedback from parents, students, and teachers who represent communities where the algorithm will be used
constraints: Machine learning systems working with student data can learn biases from technical design errors and from existing patterns of inequality and discrimination in training data
Readily available data leads to overrepresentation of specific subsets of the population
target_learners: diverse learners
students in communities where platform algorithms are deployed
target_learning_goals: preventing algorithmic bias from influencing student learner performance and behavior
examples: The article cites studies on educational AI reflecting on origins of AI bias and potential harms in education
key_sources: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163

article_title: Computational Thinking Boosters: Algorithmic Thinking in K-2
citation: Computational Thinking Boosters: Algorithms in K-2. (2021). Webinar presentation, NSF grant #1923314. https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1923314
title: Recognize and name the algorithmic thinking already present in K-2 daily routines
description: The webinar asks teachers to consider "Where Am I Likely Already Integrating These Skills?" and notes that many K-2 skills are algorithmic in nature: following a daily schedule, collaboratively creating classroom procedures through testing and analyzing outcomes, and conversations about how sequence order affects outcomes. Teachers should surface these existing practices as computational thinking rather than adding wholly new content.
requirements: Teacher awareness of decomposition, pattern recognition, comparing and contrasting in existing routines
target_learners: K-2 students
target_learning_goals: Recognizing algorithmic thinking in daily life
Decomposition and pattern recognition
examples: Students and teachers collaborate to create classroom procedures through testing and analyzing outcomes
key_sources: Computational Thinking Boosters: Algorithms in K-2. (2021). Webinar presentation, NSF grant #1923314. https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1923314

article_title: Executive Summary: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity
citation: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity. (2024). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/2024/02/20/how-ai-for-education-can-address-digital-equity/
title: Make evaluating AI the most critical element of AI literacy rather than passive use
description: The brief states that "Evaluating AI is the most critical element of AI literacy," warning that people too often use AI passively without considering privacy, safety, or societal implications. To be truly AI literate, users must take an active approach with awareness of the data the algorithm is using and how it is being applied and shared.
requirements: Active user approach with awareness of the data the algorithm is using and how it is being applied and shared
constraints: Positioned within the AI literacy framework for educational settings
target_learners: learners
educators
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI systems
awareness of privacy, safety, and societal implications of AI use
examples: The framework emphasizes that understanding and evaluating AI are critical to making informed decisions about if and how to use AI in learning environments
key_sources: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity. (2024). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/2024/02/20/how-ai-for-education-can-address-digital-equity/

article_title: Executive Summary: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity
citation: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity. (2024). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/2024/02/20/how-ai-for-education-can-address-digital-equity/
title: Identify and mitigate bias in AI to keep educational AI compatible with digital equity commitments
description: The brief argues that because AI automates educational processes based on associations found in data, and "the associations in existing data often contain bias," automations built on biased associations could increase unfair and unlawful discrimination. Identifying and mitigating bias is therefore essential to using AI in ways compatible with commitments to Digital Equity, as discussed in the US Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights.
requirements: Identification and mitigation of bias in the data associations underlying AI automations
constraints: Grounded in the US Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
target_learners: all students
educational leaders
target_learning_goals: fair and equitable use of AI in education
examples: The brief links bias mitigation to the United States Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights as a digital equity commitment
key_sources: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity. (2024). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/2024/02/20/how-ai-for-education-can-address-digital-equity/

article_title: Practitioners at the Center: Catalyzing Research on Problems of Practice in Realistic Settings
citation: Pautz Stephenson, S., Banks, R., & Pakhira D. (2022, December). Practitioners at the center: Catalyzing research on problems of practice in realistic settings. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/164
title: Center practitioners in research via six guiding principles spanning inclusion, power-shifting, lived experience, problems of practice, feedback loops, and dissemination
description: Based on interviews with three SEERNet digital learning platform teams, the report identifies six principles to guide strategies for centering practitioners: include practitioners with diverse backgrounds; "Empower practitioners and intentionally shift power dynamics so that they have a voice, especially in research questions"; value practitioners' lived experiences as content and context experts; surface problems of practice and connect them to research goals; structure feedback loops that transform knowledge, actions, or goals of all involved; and disseminate findings so platforms are widely used, used well, and have positive impact.
requirements: Practitioners should help define research questions and objectives for the end result to be useful in practice
constraints: The models work well for iterative, agile, comparative improvement research; practitioner involvement could look different in effectiveness or scale-up studies or fundamental scientific research; equity in how partnership districts are selected must be addressed so partnerships broaden rather than perpetuate inequities
target_learners: K-12 educators, instructional and technology coaches, school administrators, and district-level staff
target_learning_goals: Research that impacts educational decision making and addresses consequential problems of practice
examples: SEERNet's Office Hours initiative was the network's first endeavor to apply these guiding principles, strategically advertising to K-12 Title I school districts
key_sources: Pautz Stephenson, S., Banks, R., & Pakhira D. (2022, December). Practitioners at the center: Catalyzing research on problems of practice in realistic settings. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/164

article_title: The Growing Diversity in Today’s Classroom
citation: Making Learning Personal for All: The Growing Diversity in Today's Classroom. (2016). https://global.digitalpromise.org
title: Personalize learning by connecting it to each individual's development, background, interests, and experiences
description: The paper defines personalized learning as "learning that is connected to each individual's development, background, interests, and experiences," an approach it says broadly and equitably supports educators' efforts to empower learners as individuals. It argues personalization means engaging, motivating, and inspiring learners with the right resources at the right time, in the right medium, and at the right pace, and warns that current overly simplistic personalization models risk leaving diverse learners behind.
requirements: Structured supports: curriculum, pedagogy, tools, and resources specifically designed to support personalization strategies
Knowledge about the individual learner, since personalization can only be based on what is known about the learner
constraints: The paper states current models that drive personalization remain overly simplistic and are rarely based on research
target_learners: Diverse K-12 learners, including students in poverty, English language learners, students with disabilities, and gifted students
target_learning_goals: Equitable support of diverse learners' academic success and engagement
examples: The paper cites adaptive working memory training and individualized phonological awareness and reading instruction as personalization approaches grounded in research
key_sources: Making Learning Personal for All: The Growing Diversity in Today's Classroom. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/7acc6442-9c20-42ff-b4b2-21645832493e

article_title: Market Signals for Research-Based Innovations
citation: Sierra Noakes. (2019). Market Signals for Research-Based Innovations. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/
title: Incorporate learning sciences research findings into edtech design and development to serve the full spectrum of learners
description: The report argues that because advances in learning sciences show how people learn and that people learn differently, developers who incorporate learning sciences research findings can create powerful learning experiences for the full spectrum of learners. It states research-driven edtech can meet this potential by "attending to the most difficult content to teach and learn; creating opportunities for differentiation; and providing guidance to support seamless implementation."
requirements: Developers must actually use learning sciences research findings in product design and development
constraints: Without established standards or clear signals, the report says it is challenging to demand that developers attend to authentic learner needs through research incorporation
target_learners: edtech product developers
the full spectrum of learners, including marginalized learner populations
target_learning_goals: equitable, high-quality learning opportunities and experiences for every learner
examples: Digital Promise's 2017 work with two districts piloting edtech for English Learners found few products are designed for marginalized learner populations
key_sources: Sierra Noakes. (2019). Market Signals for Research-Based Innovations. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/7c36b6fa-e221-437f-92d5-f4d3a89c0a1f

article_title: Emerging Technology Adoption Framework: For PK-12 Education
citation: Ruiz, P., Richard, E., Chillmon, C., Shah, Z., Kurth, A., Fekete, A., Glazer, K., Pattenhouse, M., Fusco, J., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Lin, L., Arriola, S., Lockett, D., Crawford-Meyer, V., Karim, S., Hampton, S., & Beckford, B. (2022). Emerging technology adoption framework: For PK-12 education. [Educator CIRCLS white paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/161
title: Include the whole education community in technology evaluation and adoption decisions
description: The framework's core principle is that educational leaders, technology specialists, teachers, students, and families should all participate in evaluating and adopting emerging technologies. It was "created with education community members to help ensure that educational leaders, technology specialists, teachers, students, and families are all part of the evaluation and adoption process." Questions are addressed to each stakeholder group, and some questions can be asked of multiple members of the community.
requirements: Questions listed under the procurement decision makers and district leaders section can usually also be asked of educators
target_learners: PK-12 students
target_learning_goals: equitable, community-informed technology procurement and implementation
examples: The framework gathers feedback from researchers, policy experts, the edtech community, educators, and families

article_title: Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate
citation: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205
title: Integrated Learning Pathways defined by four principles: competency-based, complementary, cumulative, and consistent
description: Learning pathways are system-wide learning progressions that "function according to four principles: They are competency-based, complementary to disciplinary learning, consistent across classrooms, and cumulative from year to year." Competency-based means Portrait Skill Sets are broken into actionable Practices learners demonstrate; complementary means pathways supplement rather than replace existing structures; cumulative means developmentally appropriate progressions articulated as "I can" statements across grade bands; and consistent means practice opportunities are designed into every classroom so attributes are "realistically attainable by each of their students." The design process is intended to be adapted to each district's Portrait.
requirements: Teachers, leaders, and experts work together to identify and map integration opportunities; a designated team of district, school, and teacher leaders guides development
constraints: Each competency-based Practice should not be integrated universally or indiscriminately across grade bands and disciplines; consistency does not mean pathways are blind to context
target_learners: K-12 students across all classrooms and grade bands
target_learning_goals: Portrait Skill Sets and Practices developed dispositionally across disciplines and grades
key_sources: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205

article_title: Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate
citation: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205
title: Align new district initiatives to an existing Portrait and Learning Pathway rather than adding new programs
description: The article recommends that, with an Integrated Learning Pathway in place, "each new learning priority—whether it be computational thinking, social-emotional learning, artificial intelligence, or another—can be aligned to the Skill Sets and Practices already present in the district's Portrait." This lets educators see how initiatives relate to one another and to existing teaching, identifies where relevant Practices already exist, and removes the burden from individual teachers of figuring out each new initiative, supporting equity through consistency. The authors suggest this weaving into shared priorities may alleviate "Initiative Fatigue."
requirements: An existing district Portrait and a developed Integrated Learning Pathway
constraints: The article notes this addresses curricular integration only; whole-child pedagogical approaches and competency-based rubrics are left to forthcoming work
target_learners: K-12 students in districts adopting multiple initiatives
target_learning_goals: Coherent alignment of district initiatives to graduate skill outcomes
examples: Indian Prairie SD used its Portrait to align computational thinking and is next aligning AI literacy skills to the same framework, mapping AI evaluation categories to Portrait Skill Sets
key_sources: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205

article_title: Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate
citation: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205
title: Shift from passive to active use of technology, using the Portrait to guide active integration
description: Drawing on the National Education Technology Plan's Digital Use Divide, the article recommends designing technology use so students engage in "active use" — "critical thinking, exploration, and creative expression" — rather than only skill-and-drill exercises and assessments, a passive pattern the article notes is more common for marginalized learners. It illustrates this with data practices: students may passively complete an online statistics module, or actively manipulate a data set to build a visualization presenting an argument to an audience, practicing the Portrait Skill Set of Communicating in All Media and Modalities while still computing the same descriptive values.
requirements: A Portrait framework identifying Skill Sets such as Communicating in All Media and Modalities to anchor what active use means
constraints: The article frames this as a promising framework rather than a tested intervention
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those experiencing marginalization
target_learning_goals: Active, creative technology use including data practices
examples: The article contrasts an online statistical-analysis module with learners manipulating a data set to argue for a relevant issue to an audience

article_title: Centering Wellbeing: Advancing Social Emotional Learning for All
citation: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177
title: Align professional learning initiatives with district leadership priorities and commitments to move ideas into action
description: The report identifies strategic alignment between a working group's focus and district leadership commitments as the first of three readiness factors accelerating implementation. Leaders who joined with clear aims—expanding SEL resources for deaf students, deepening existing wellness work, or advancing a superintendent's vision—moved from idea to action, which the report notes requires "commitment, effort, and—almost always—dedicated time and financial resources."
requirements: Dedicated time and financial resources, since moving from idea to action requires commitment, effort, and almost always dedicated time and financial resources
target_learners: district and school leaders
educators
target_learning_goals: strengthening SEL and wellbeing supports system-wide
examples: Dr. Tanner joined the working group specifically to expand adaptable SEL resources for deaf students; Dr. Moore built on existing district work to win wellness-center funding; Suffern's wellbeing focus was part of the superintendent's vision.
key_sources: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177

article_title: Centering Wellbeing: Advancing Social Emotional Learning for All
citation: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177
title: Engage both decision makers and implementors in professional learning experiences to ease translation into district practice
description: The report's second readiness factor holds that districts translate working-group lessons into action more easily when leaders with authority for both decision-making and implementation participate together. In Suffern, the director noted the superintendent "heard [the ideas] directly," removing the need to plead the case; in El Segundo, clarity in roles let the superintendent secure board funding while the associate superintendent led program work.
requirements: Participation by leaders with authority for both decision-making and implementation
target_learners: district leaders
superintendents
program implementors
target_learning_goals: adopting and enacting SEL and wellbeing strategies district-wide
examples: Suffern's superintendent and counseling director attended together; El Segundo's superintendent and associate superintendent divided roles for funding and program design.
key_sources: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177

article_title: Centering Wellbeing: Advancing Social Emotional Learning for All
citation: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177
title: Balance central curation of SEL resources with educator flexibility to respond to student needs
description: The report's third readiness factor describes districts providing school leaders and teachers easy access to curated materials while allowing flexibility to be responsive to student priorities. Fayette County is building resource folders organized by DESSA assessment categories; Suffern's director argued resources should be handed to teachers rather than relying on them to read through materials; El Segundo made wellbeing part of onboarding with self-paced professional development access.
requirements: Central district supports that offer easy access to curated materials
Flexibility for educators to be responsive to student priorities and needs
target_learners: teachers
school leaders
target_learning_goals: advancing SEL and wellbeing instruction tailored to student needs
examples: Fayette County folders organized by DESSA SEL categories; El Segundo onboarding includes wellbeing and teachers can access professional development resources at their own pace.
key_sources: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Use inclusive language and design in LER onboarding
description: This principle holds that LER onboarding should welcome users regardless of age, technological familiarity, or pathway shape. The report states that "LERs should reduce assumptions about linear career pathways so as not to invalidate the lived experiences of learners and workers," and recommends offering opportunities to elevate skills developed through community, cultural, and caregiving contexts. It also suggests querying learners' goals up front so prompts can be tailored to individual journeys.
requirements: Onboarding prompts must allow users to showcase a wide variety of skills and experiences, including contexts outside formal institutions
constraints: Onboarding prompts limited to transcripts and employment history may inadvertently exclude important aspects of skills and background
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded adult learners and workers, including multilingual learners and those experiencing poverty
target_learning_goals: successful onboarding and adoption of learning and employment record technology
examples: Workshop participants asked to change "work" experience to just "experience" and requested adding military credentials and cultural identity as skills
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Make the LER value proposition clear to learners and employers
description: This principle directs LER vendors to articulate, in plain language, why a learner should create an interoperable learner record and how employers and education institutions derive value from the data. The report found that "Many participants expressed confusion between LERs and LinkedIn, Indeed, and services like TopResume because the purpose of the LER was not immediately clear." It recommends embedding LER education in onboarding, using video, static visuals, plain-language text, and inline tips throughout the process.
requirements: Product descriptions must clearly differentiate LERs from social networking and resume-building tools
The value proposition for employers and education institutions must be articulated so learners understand how their data may be used
constraints: Value revealed only after completion is limited: outcomes like matched positions "were not apparent at the beginning of the journey"
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded adult learners and workers onboarding to LER technology
target_learning_goals: understanding the purpose and value of LERs and the tradeoffs of contributing personal data
examples: Participants suggested adding a "why" section in build prompts to explain things to people
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Communicate and create resources to ensure data integration accuracy
description: This principle requires that information auto-populated from third parties be correct and thorough, that users can edit it, and that vendors communicate where data comes from. The report states that "data integrations that populate incorrect or incomplete information without a mechanism for learners to correct the errors breeds frustration," and proposes a way to report inaccuracies and request edits without jeopardizing verification integrity, plus troubleshooting information and FAQs for broken or delayed integrations.
requirements: A mechanism for learners to report inaccuracies and request edits
Transparent communication about where the tool pulls information from
constraints: The value of a single, reliable, cumulative learning record depends on the accuracy of third-party data pulls
target_learners: adult learners and workers onboarding to LERs with integrated postsecondary transcripts
target_learning_goals: trusting and accurately representing skills and credentials in a learning and employment record
examples: A participant whose newly earned associate's degree was missing and bachelor's degree shown as completed could not edit the record
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Offer technology and content support during LER onboarding
description: This principle calls for live support options, examples and encouragement during profile creation, and explicit explanation of why different data types are required and when alternatives exist. The report observes that "Not all learners onboarding to LERs will have extensive digital or career navigation skills," and that some participants got stuck at login or were leery about which data were required versus optional, especially those with past extractive or exploitive experiences with technology.
requirements: Live support options for login and onboarding assistance
Explicit statements of how each step ensures safety and security and why sharing personal information is advantageous
constraints: Participants varied widely in digital literacy; chatbots may not suffice for those who do not know which questions to ask
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded adult learners and workers with limited digital literacy
target_learning_goals: completing LER account creation and onboarding independently
examples: Participants reported difficulty verifying email and phone and forgetting user IDs; one said a person to talk to would have helped where a chatbot would not
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Conduct ongoing user testing for continuous improvement of LERs
description: This principle directs vendors to iteratively solicit feedback from employers and end users, including people unaffiliated with institutions or on nonlinear journeys, to share timely updates on platform changes, and to provide an accessible in-platform space for suggestions. The report states that "Collecting user feedback is necessary for attaining buy-in and developing trust across demographics, especially for HSE communities," and that iterative testing signals the technology is of value and values its users, fostering intuitive onboarding and retention.
requirements: Iterative feedback collection from both employers and end users
An accessible space on the platform for users to share suggestions at any time
constraints: Targeted feedback on accessibility of language, design, and technology support is needed because HSE learners are disproportionately impacted by limited access to digital resources and skills training
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded learners and workers, including those with nonlinear journeys
target_learning_goals: sustained adoption and use of LER technology
examples: Participants reported limited skill and industry options, which vendors could use to build a more robust and accurate data library
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Nico & Nor Family Flyer
citation: Early Science with Nico and Nor. (2022). WGBH Educational Foundation. https://www.wgbh.org
title: Collaborative co-design process across five partner roles for early science curriculum development
description: The program was developed through a collaborative process in which five partner groups each contributed: children and families co-designed activities "helping identify everyday experiences and meaningful contexts in which science, math, and engineering could be promoted authentically"; researchers documented learning goals and facilitated research activities; curricula developers and media designers leveraged families' and educators' insights to create resources and digital tools; and teachers shared classroom needs to inform activity design. The process is summarized as "Building collaborative relationships, Centering children & families (asset-based approach), Co-designing, pilot testing and refining, Evaluating implementation & outcomes, Disseminating lessons and resources broadly."
requirements: Sustained collaboration among families, teachers, researchers, curricula developers and media designers
Iterative cycles of co-design, pilot testing and refinement
target_learners: preschool children and their families
preschool teachers and staff
target_learning_goals: early science, math and engineering learning grounded in everyday family experiences
examples: Families tested the activities and projects in their homes, and their insights informed iterations of the curricular resources and digital tools.

article_title: Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts
citation: Christina Luke and Viki M. Young. (2020). Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Build awareness and educator buy-in before embedding micro-credentials in professional learning systems
description: Introducing micro-credentials into an existing professional learning system can be jarring if educators are not involved. District administrators learned they needed to build awareness of what micro-credentials are, how they are assessed, and their rigor, and to encourage buy-in through clear communication about purpose and value plus tangible supports such as planning time, stipends, and recertification credit.
requirements: Clear communication about the purpose and value of pursuing micro-credentials and tangible support for educators
target_learners: K-12 classroom teachers and district administrators
target_learning_goals: Effective adoption of competency-based professional learning
examples: Districts offered incentives including planning and collaboration time, stipends for preparing or earning micro-credentials, leadership opportunities, and hours toward recertification.
key_sources: Christina Luke and Viki M. Young. (2020). Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/8960df64-de36-4121-8af2-651b343b0884

article_title: Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts
citation: Christina Luke and Viki M. Young. (2020). Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Tie micro-credentials to district outcomes and redesign professional learning systems around them
description: The report recommends aligning micro-credentials to district goals so teacher time and resources target meaningful student learning outcomes and professional learning is coherent rather than fragmented. Because micro-credentials are competency- and research-based, leaders said they "allow us to track the efectiveness of our PD" and document teachers actually implementing practices, not just sitting through a training.
requirements: Micro-credentials selected or developed to align with district outcomes and goals as determined by data
constraints: Districts may need to renegotiate local collective bargaining agreements and develop school leader buy-in to commit PD time
target_learners: District administrators and K-12 classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Coherent, goal-aligned professional learning and documented implementation of new practices
examples: One district leader described planning to use micro-credentials for PD in computational thinking and equity, aligned with focus areas the district had already implemented.

article_title: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE Family Literacy Program, Central Maine
citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE. (2012). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Use a virtual world to provide real community and human connection as an antidote to rural isolation in adult education
description: The article argues that a virtual world can supply the community and human support that adult learners need and that traditional distance education lacks. Because "every avatar has a real person behind it," learners interact with teachers and peers in real time, and the article claims the multiple digital channels for human support can provide more learner-educator connections than face-to-face programs. SPICE used this to address the loneliness its adult learners reported in a 2008 state audit.
requirements: Teachers trained to interact with every avatar so each learner experiences human connection
Understanding what your learners need before adopting the approach
constraints: Hughes notes family literacy programs in less rural areas might not have the same success with a virtual world if their learners have a physical place to meet
target_learners: rural adult learners experiencing isolation
target_learning_goals: community building, persistence, and confidence in adult and family literacy education
examples: SPICE educators went to learners' homes across RSU 3's 440 square miles before building the virtual Center, and learners report no longer feeling isolated
key_sources: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE. (2012). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE Family Literacy Program, Central Maine
citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE. (2012). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Blend online learning with human support rather than offering purely online or purely face-to-face learning for adults
description: The article cites a 2009 Department of Education analysis finding that "adult learners achieve the best learning outcomes in a blended environment of online and face-to-face learning (versus only online or only face-to-face)." The anytime, anywhere capability of online learning fits adults' many life commitments, while teacher support is critical for adults to believe they can succeed. SPICE's virtual Center operationalizes this blend by pairing flexible online access with real-time human support.
requirements: Support from teachers so adult learners believe they can be successful
constraints: The rural, decentralized nature of RSU 3 made traditional blended learning very difficult, if not impossible, which is why SPICE blended online rather than physically
target_learners: adult learners with many life commitments
target_learning_goals: adult basic education and family literacy outcomes
examples: The virtual Center lets learners who miss a session because a child gets sick or they are called into work do the work later, still with human support from avatars
key_sources: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE. (2012). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Delivering virtual K-8 computing professional development in rural KY
citation: Iwatani, E., Tackett, T., Ruiz, P., & Burke, Q. (2021). Delivering Virtual K-8 Computing Professional Development in Rural KY. Digital Promise / Bit Source. https://bit.ly/36szXLy
title: CT Booster session structure: timed segments for vocabulary, examples, micro-credentials, and Q&A
description: Each CT Booster session follows a repeating timed structure: a short introduction and vocabulary segment, a set of worked examples anchored by guiding questions, a pointer to a related micro-credential, and a closing question-and-answer period. The deck prints the structure as "5-10 minutes: Introduction & Vocabulary" followed by "15-20 minutes: 3-4 Examples" and "2-5 minutes: Question & Answer Session". Guiding questions frame the examples, for example how teachers collect, analyze, and store data to understand relationships in intermediate and middle grades.
requirements: Sessions need prepared example sets (3-4 examples) matched to a guiding question and a related micro-credential to point teachers toward
constraints: Structure is designed for short virtual booster sessions, not full-length courses
target_learners: K-8 teachers in rural Kentucky
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking: data analysis and algorithms
examples: The K-2 Data & Analysis session on November 10, 2020 and the 3-8 Algorithms session on January 19, 2021 both used this timed structure
key_sources: Iwatani, E., Tackett, T., Ruiz, P., & Burke, Q. (2021). Delivering Virtual K-8 Computing Professional Development in Rural KY. Digital Promise / Bit Source. https://bit.ly/36szXLy

article_title: Learning by Design: How Design Tech High School Uses Research
citation: Digital Promise. (2017). Learning by Design: How Design Tech High School Uses Research. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Integrate the learning sciences into a school's existing culture and practices so it becomes an ongoing practice
description: The report recommends that schools fold learning sciences principles, like retrieval practice and interleaving, into the decision-making processes, professional development, and program design structures they already use; this allowed d.tech to maintain it as an ongoing practice rather than a one-time initiative. Schools are advised to analyze their own mission and structures to find the easiest integration points.
requirements: An analysis of the institution's mission and structures to determine the easiest ways to integrate the science of learning
constraints: The account is drawn from a single charter school's experience
target_learners: School administrators and instructional leaders
target_learning_goals: Sustained school-wide adoption of evidence-based learning strategies
examples: d.tech folded learning sciences principles into its existing design thinking processes and made follow-on professional development throughout the year so it was not one-and-done.
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2017). Learning by Design: How Design Tech High School Uses Research. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/93bddee8-5856-4faf-8758-71aae4ce8716

article_title: Sustainability in Inclusive Innovation: District-Community Solutions, Mindsets, and Practices
citation: Viki M. Young, Ph.D. and Alexandra Merritt Johnson, Ph.D. (2024). Sustainability in Inclusive Innovation: District-Community Solutions, Mindsets, and Practices. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Plan for sustainability during the pilot's final phase, covering buy-in, stewardship, budgeting, and data collection
description: The article frames sustainability as a phase following implementation in which teams, with facilitators, plan explicitly for continuation. Teams "engaged in a sustainability planning process with Digital Promise facilitators" whose key topics included buy-in, community-level conditions for scale, ownership and ongoing stewardship, budgeting for ongoing costs, and data collection to evaluate the solution. Planning also sets expectations that the school or community will persist with the solution amid turnover and reform fads.
requirements: Anticipate declining or repurposed resources and address incentives, logistical barriers, and additional resource needs identified during initial implementation
constraints: Because pilots ended between December 2022 and March 2023, sustainability blurred with ongoing implementation through June 2023, and no additional data collection occurred in the 2023-24 school year
target_learners: District-community teams including students, families, teachers, and leaders
target_learning_goals: Sustaining community-developed education solutions and inclusive R&D processes
examples: Teams used meeting notes and sustainability planning templates in the last pilot phase to identify local action steps for sustaining their work
key_sources: Viki M. Young, Ph.D. and Alexandra Merritt Johnson, Ph.D. (2024). Sustainability in Inclusive Innovation: District-Community Solutions, Mindsets, and Practices. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/94695da1-ad96-49e5-b461-b759d617ae25

article_title: Partnering to promote equity and digital learning
citation: Wiley, K., Neisler, J., & Means, B. (2023, February). Partnering to promote equity and digital learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/167
title: Equitized syllabus with five equity characteristics
description: The report describes equitizing the course syllabus as a concrete equity mechanism taught in an ATD workshop and adopted by partner colleges. The equitized syllabus incorporates five characteristics: "Welcoming—Indicating that every student belongs in the class"; Representing Diversity through non-white and non-Western content, authors, or perspectives; Demystifying by communicating clearly about course expectations; Destigmatizing Support Services by describing them as useful for everybody; and Creating Partnership by portraying instructor and student as partnering for learning. BMCC standardized these syllabi across sections via a shared template.
requirements: Instructor participation in the Equitizing Your Syllabus workshop or equivalent guidance, and a shared template to standardize across sections
target_learners: Undergraduate students in high-enrollment gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging, clarity of course expectations, awareness of support services
examples: BMCC redesigned course syllabi based on principles from the Equitizing Your Syllabus workshop and created an equitized syllabus template shared with all faculty via Microsoft Teams
key_sources: Wiley, K., Neisler, J., & Means, B. (2023, February). Partnering to promote equity and digital learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/167

article_title: Continuous Improvement and Postsecondary Student Success
citation: Barbara Means and Julie Neisler. (2004). Continuous Improvement for Student Success. Digital Promise Global. https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2004/12/06/the-bell-curve
title: Plan comparison groups and data sources in advance, because rigorous courseware impact studies require comparable treatment and comparison groups and cannot be left to busy developers or faculty alone.
description: The article distills lessons from the NGCC evaluation about conducting impact studies: measuring impact requires an objective outcome measure, a comparison group, evidence of comparability, adequate numbers in both groups, and holding other influences constant. It warns that "Comparison groups and data sources need to be planned in advance if you want to get an apples-to-apples comparison of different versions of a course." It also cautions that busy technology developers, marketers, or faculty cannot be expected to design and execute rigorous impact studies without considerable help.
requirements: An objective and consistent outcome measure, a comparison group, evidence the groups are comparable, adequate numbers in both groups, and other potential influences held constant.
constraints: Strong traditions of faculty independence around learning goals, instructional approach, assessment and grading practices impede efforts to learn what works best.
target_learners: Higher education students in courseware-supported courses
target_learning_goals: Improving course outcomes and measuring the impact of digital courseware redesigns
examples: In the NGCC evaluation, 77 impact data sets were submitted but only 28 had adequate numbers of reasonably comparable students in the two conditions.
key_sources: Barbara Means and Julie Neisler. (2004). Continuous Improvement for Student Success. Digital Promise Global. https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2004/12/06/the-bell-curve

article_title: Preparing Teachers For Deeper Learning
citation: Karen Cator, Carri Schneider, Tom Vander Ark. (2014). Preparing Teachers for Deeper Learning: Competency-Based Teacher Preparation and Development. Digital Promise / Getting Smart. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Next-generation teacher preparation and PD should offer teacher control over time, place, path and/or pace, balanced goals, job-embedded integration, and competency-based progression
description: The paper's central design recommendation is that high-quality teacher preparation and ongoing professional learning should mirror the personalized learning advocated for students. Its stated principles are "some element of teacher control over time, place, path and/or pace;" balance between teacher-defined, administrative, and school/district goals; "job-embedded and meaningful integration into classroom practice;" and competency-based progression. The paper argues these same principles applied to students' blended learning can and should be applied to teacher learning.
requirements: Blended structures that combine online learning with onsite experiences
Adult learning conditions of adaptability, productivity and value given teachers' time and money constraints
constraints: The paper frames these as design principles for a envisioned system rather than tested interventions
target_learners: Pre-service teachers
Practicing K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Teaching competencies for personalized, blended Deeper Learning environments
Continuous development of teacher competency throughout their careers
examples: Western Governors University offers self-paced, competency-based teacher preparation in which student teachers can test out of subjects; Summit Public Schools gives teachers two-week self-directed PD chunks four times a year
key_sources: Karen Cator, Carri Schneider, Tom Vander Ark. (2014). Preparing Teachers for Deeper Learning: Competency-Based Teacher Preparation and Development. Digital Promise / Getting Smart. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/a1928fce-2d47-429b-8e81-fbeb9ce079c3

article_title: Improving Ed-Tech Purchasing
citation: Improving Ed-Tech Purchasing: Identifying the key obstacles and potential solutions for the discovery and acquisition of K-12 personalized learning tools. (2015). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/marketplace
title: Improve ed-tech procurement through formal needs assessment, better discovery infrastructure, structured pilots, and trusted evidence mechanisms
description: The brief recommends that schools and districts "conduct formal instructional needs assessments to more clearly define challenges" and publicize needs so providers can match them; that discovery be eased through RFIs and an online "Ed-tech Product Information Exchange"; that pilots be structured to generate efficacy evidence and a data-driven go or no-go decision; and that faster, cheaper evidence alternatives such as formal pilots, case studies, and small comparison-group designs bridge the evidence gap.
requirements: Districts need structured processes for assessing instructional needs and evaluating evidence
Trusted third parties or brokers are needed to verify effectiveness claims both sides accept
constraints: Most districts will not have resources to pay external consultants for vendor-relationship management, and digital platforms and brokers are not yet widespread in the ed-tech market
Evidence alternatives must not reduce instructional time or burden teachers
target_learners: K-12 students and teachers in U.S. public school districts
target_learning_goals: Access to personalized learning technology tools that meet identified instructional needs
examples: The brief recommends designing RFPs to focus on specific instructional needs rather than product features, creating collaborative purchasing guidelines including piggyback contracts, and researching pay-for-success approaches for the ed-tech market.
key_sources: Improving Ed-Tech Purchasing: Identifying the key obstacles and potential solutions for the discovery and acquisition of K-12 personalized learning tools. (2015). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/marketplace

article_title: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya Public Charter School, Washington, D.C.
citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya. (2016). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Integrate English language learning with digital literacy instruction in one curriculum for immigrant adult learners
description: Briya combines English learning and digital skills in a single curriculum: "All of their devices, software, and online programs use English, so their learners are integrating their English language learning (ELL) with their digital literacy work." Teachers also use traditional ELL strategies in digital literacy classes, such as having students read aloud website names, URLs, and email addresses to practice pronunciation. The case study's key takeaways state these "can be effectively combined in one curriculum, increasing practice with English while also learning digital skills."
requirements: Devices, software, and online programs that operate in English so learners practice the target language while building digital skills
target_learners: immigrant adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency
digital literacy skills
examples: Teachers have students read aloud website names, URLs, and email addresses so they hear and practice English pronunciations
key_sources: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya. (2016). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org

article_title: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya Public Charter School, Washington, D.C.
citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: Briya. (2016). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Provide free or low-cost technical support and device access so families can maintain the technology they need
description: Even when families own devices, they often lack affordable technical support. Briya therefore provides "full technical support to ensure their parents and children always have the devices they need," connects learners to a local program offering low-cost laptops, lets learners use the program's IT department for device issues, and opens its devices for use before and after school. The case study names opening the program's IT division to families "a creative way to solve this need."
requirements: An IT department or technical support capacity that can be opened to learners
Devices available on site before and after school
constraints: Applies when families have their own devices but lack access to affordable technical support
target_learners: adult learners and families without affordable technical support
target_learning_goals: sustained access to digital learning tools
examples: Briya connects learners to a local program that provides low-cost laptops for families who do not have their own devices

article_title: Driving Edtech Coherence and Intentionality: Denver Public Schools’ Innovative Procurement Process
citation: Noakes, S., Shell, A., & Karim, S. (2025). Driving Edtech Coherence and Intentionality: Denver Public Schools' Innovative Procurement Process. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/267
title: Cross-department collaborative edtech review team with content-area review teams
description: The pattern organizes edtech approval as a standing collaboration across district departments: four core teams (EdTech, DoTS, Purchasing, and Legal) plus 14 content teams review each tool before approval. The report states "the development work was driven by a cross-functional team that included staff members from DPS' DoTS, legal, purchasing, and curriculum departments." Content teams are trained as reviewers to judge whether a tool benefits instruction in their content area, and the collaborative team meets bi-weekly to iterate on the process and pipeline.
requirements: Requires representatives from multiple district departments with time and capacity to review tools, and training for content-team reviewers.
constraints: The report notes the process was designed to take about five weeks but could extend to months due to vendor back-and-forths and limited staff capacity, and that school staff are not yet part of the review team.
target_learners: K-12 students in district schools
target_learning_goals: Ensuring approved edtech tools are secure, accessible, standards-aligned, and instructionally effective
examples: DPS staff were divided into four core teams and 14 content teams, including Humanities, Math, SEL, ESS, and Library Services, each providing content expertise in reviews.
key_sources: Noakes, S., Shell, A., & Karim, S. (2025). Driving Edtech Coherence and Intentionality: Denver Public Schools' Innovative Procurement Process. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/267

article_title: Understanding and Supporting District Systems Change Around Computer Science Education
citation: Quinn Burke, Jeremy Roschelle, Pati Ruiz, & Josh Weisgrau. (2021). Understanding and Supporting District Systems Change Around Computer Science Education. AERA Annual Conference, Division L Structured Poster Session. https://bit.ly/36szXLy

Willingness of educators and district leaders to act on what students share

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Anchor adult learning design in learners' past experience and life relevance
description: The report's first principle holds that "At the heart of all of theories about how adults learn is the notion of experience." Learning succeeds when adults connect new information to past experience or see its relevance to their lives, so products should let learners do something with new knowledge in practical, authentic tasks.
requirements: Authentic activities must include "a variety of perspectives and examples so students will find something they can relate to and connect with."
constraints: Designers cannot assume a common background: "there is no one typical adult learner experience to rely on."
target_learners: adult learners with varied educational and employment backgrounds
adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: connecting new information to prior experience
vocabulary and skills for real tasks such as job applications
examples: USA Learns teaches job-application vocabulary "in the context of a sample job application," ending with students filling out an application for a real job; other named strategies include role-playing, simulations, case studies, and games.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Take a problem-solving orientation with authentic practice, immediate application, and feedback
description: Because adult learning is rooted in experience, the report recommends structuring problems on what learners encounter in work and life, then helping them practice strategies to solve them: "the more learners can practice in authentic situations and apply what they learn immediately, the more likely they are to develop new skills."
requirements: Build assessments and feedback loops into the problem-solving environment; the report states this "helps students monitor their learning."
constraints: Learners must be free to make mistakes while solving problems; the report ties making mistakes, reflecting, and trying another approach to building persistence.
target_learners: adult learners preparing for work in fields such as healthcare
low-skilled adult learners
target_learning_goals: problem-solving strategies for work and life situations
skill development through authentic practice
examples: A Pine Technical College game trains medical-career students through realistic avatar scenarios — dealing with death and sickness, talking to patients, engaging family members — with feedback on each choice and retries until the desired behavior occurs.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Build regular reflection opportunities into adult learning experiences
description: Drawing on experiential learning theory, the report holds that "time and space for reflection helps learners absorb and make sense of the experience." It recommends quick discussions with peers or coaches, journaling, mind mapping, and discussion groups, tying reflection to learners' everyday lives so new information is processed in smaller chunks and sticks.
requirements: Provide time and space for reflection throughout the learning experience, "including self-reflection, group reflection, and peer reflection."
target_learners: adult ESL and basic education students
target_learning_goals: making sense of learning experiences
consolidating new information
examples: Instituto del Progreso Latino's Cyber ESL program blends in-class and online learning with "a one-on-one coaching session for students via Skype," which staff report makes a big difference in learner confidence.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Give adult learners control over pace and support self-directed goal setting, planning, and monitoring
description: Self-directed learning theory posits that adults "can and should be active participants in their own learning." The report recommends pace control — replaying video, more practice, choosing order, anytime access — plus goal setting, planning, and progress monitoring, since students who do these "are more likely to persist in learning and ultimately achieve positive outcomes."
requirements: Offer self-assessments such as pre-tests "so students understand what they know and what they need to learn," plus tools for planning and goal setting.
constraints: Low-skilled learners "often struggle with these tasks because they lack confidence in their learning" and need help and guidance to develop goal-setting, planning, and persisting skills.
target_learners: low-skilled adult learners
adult literacy and language learners using mobile programs
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills
persistence and program completion
examples: Cell-Ed lets students choose when to call in for short lessons and when to text-practice, and "has found that students are completing lessons at a faster pace than they would in a traditional classroom"; myPlace Online guides learners through creating their own learning plans, with directors reporting increased retention and completion.

title: Support transformative learning through trust, triggering events, reflection, and action
description: The report recommends that educators "create an environment in which students open their minds to new possibilities about their lives and futures." The sequence is to build trust, facilitate a triggering event that surfaces alternative viewpoints, have learners reflect on those viewpoints, and take some kind of action that crystallizes the transformation.

openness to new perspectives and career possibilities

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Six design principles from adult learning theory for adult-learning technology
description: The report's summary distills its five theory sections into six considerations: base curriculum on "real world, authentic situations that learners are familiar with, and/or will encounter in the job market"; help learners do something with new information; create regular self, group, and peer reflection; design pace control; facilitate self-direction via self-assessments and planning tools; and incorporate alternative points of view.

adult education program students

adult basic education and ESL outcomes

article_title: Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide
citation: Culturally Responsive Assessment Collaborative. (2025, November). Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/276/
title: Four activity categories scaffold CRA learning from reflection to redesign
description: The guide organizes course activities into four categories that progress from self-examination to system redesign: positionality and reflection; understanding the on-the-ground ecosystem of assessment; critically examining and modifying existing assessment tools or systems; and designing a new reality. This sequence lets students first articulate how their own identities and social positions shape assessment work, then map real assessment ecosystems, critique and adapt existing instruments, and finally design culturally responsive assessments. The categories are presented as a flexible structure instructors adapt to their cohort.

develop reflexivity and critical examination of assessment tools
examples: Activity Category 1 is Positionality and Reflection; Activity Category 4 is Designing a New Reality

article_title: Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide
citation: Culturally Responsive Assessment Collaborative. (2025, November). Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/276/
title: Design assessment as a coherent system aligned with learning goals and equity outcomes
description: When assessment is defined as a system rather than a single test, the guide's coherence principle requires that all components—from individual items to high-stakes policy measures—align with contemporary models of learning and the equity outcomes of the broader curriculum and program context. In CRA, this means externally developed instruments must be intentionally designed to support the culturally responsive teaching and learning occurring in the local environment. No single test can be the sole driver of equity and improvement; the system's role is to complement broader instructional, community, and aspirational goals.
requirements: All components of the assessment system must align with contemporary models of learning and the desired learning goals and equity outcomes of the overarching curriculum
constraints: Externally developed assessment instruments require intentional design to fit the local culturally responsive context
target_learners: assessment developers and graduate measurement students
target_learning_goals: design coherent assessment systems that support culturally responsive teaching and equity
examples: The guide cites Evans et al. (forthcoming), Glaser et al. (2001), and Marion et al. (2024) on coherence in assessment systems

description: The Inclusive Innovation process moves iteratively across five stages: Connect & Commit, Inquire & Investigate, Design & Develop, Implement & Iterate, and Sustain & Scale. Each stage has its own goals, practices, tools for data collection and analysis, protocols, and guidance on roles. The graphic shows community as the central strand on which development and research work is anchored, with researcher, developer, and community paths intertwining and merging for equity and mutuality checks between stages.

title: Four cross-cutting practices keep equity at the center of the R&D process at all times
description: The framework holds that engagement, capacity building, reflection, and recognition must run through every stage of the innovation process. Engagement builds trusting, mutually beneficial relationships with each stakeholder group; capacity building treats community members as true co-experts whose lived experience is honored; reflection uses recurring facilitated mutuality checks; and recognition sustains energy and broadens participation. The paper states these four cross-cutting practices keep equity at the center of the process at all times.
requirements: Recurring facilitated mutuality checks so that the assets, expertise, and needs of marginalized communities do not get exploited or re-marginalized
Resources, training, and mentorships to develop community members' capacity to lead and engage in education R&D
target_learners: Community members, practitioners, researchers, and developers collaborating on education R&D
target_learning_goals: Sustaining equitable partnerships and continuous improvement across all stages of innovation
examples: Reflection is operationalized as regular check-ins supporting shared meaning-making, alignment to project goals, and continuous improvement

title: Two-by-two equity-innovation matrix for analyzing whether a solution is adapted or radical and who has access
description: The report offers a two-by-two matrix as a tool for analyzing innovation and equity in a given project or proposed solution. The x-axis indicates whether the project is closer to being adapted from something existing or closer to radical, i.e., significantly different and ready to scale; the y-axis analyzes who has access and whether access promotes equity or reinforces opportunity gaps. Inclusive Innovation seeks to move solution designs towards quadrants C and D, which are intentionally designed for the most marginalized.

target_learners: Education R&D teams designing solutions for marginalized populations
target_learning_goals: Designing solutions that are both novel and equitable in access and participation

article_title: Automated Essay Scoring in Middle School Writing: Understanding Key Predictors of Students’ Growth and Comparing Artificial Intelligence- and Teacher-Generated Scores and Feedback
citation: Greene Nolan, H. L., & Vang, M. C. (2023). Automated essay scoring in middle school writing: Understanding key predictors of students' growth and comparing artificial intelligence- and teacher-generated scores and feedback. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/187
title: Use human and automated essay scoring in complementary ways that draw on the strengths of each
description: The report recommends pairing AES/AWE tools with teacher scoring rather than substituting one for the other. It argues that "human and automated essay scoring should ideally be used in complementary ways that draw on the strengths of each"—the AI's time savings, class-level data, and immediate feedback on one hand, and the teacher's holistic judgment and attention to students' humanity on the other. It further urges designers to factor teachers' knowledge, priorities, and understanding of students into AES design, and cautions current users about potential differences and biases in AI scoring.

constraints: Current AES tools read and provide feedback line by line and cannot grasp essays holistically, detect voice, or judge whether ideas connect

examples: Topeka teachers who saw the score comparisons pivoted to teaching students how such systems work and how to judge whether AES feedback makes sense before addressing it
