article_title: Partnerships that Work: Tapping Research to Address Learner Variability in Young Readers
citation: Tare, M., Nobles, S., & Xiao, W. (2018). Partnerships that work: Tapping research to address learner variability in young readers. Washington, DC: Digital Promise Global. https://www.digitalpromise.org/
title: Design features to the edges of learner variability to support all students
description: The report's key takeaway is that designing features to the edges of learner variability actually supports all students. Teachers felt all students can benefit from optional supports such as audio, not just readers who struggle, because teachers are attuned to the varying needs of all their students and welcome the ability to easily provide optional supports. Use of these tools also serves classroom cohesion, allowing all students to discuss together after completing an individual activity online.
requirements: Supports should be optional and easy for teachers to provide so they can be matched to varying needs
target_learners: All learners in inclusive K-3 classrooms, including struggling readers and advanced readers
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and participation in shared classroom discussion
examples: Teachers provided the audio option to all students, reporting benefits for below-grade-level readers hearing fluent reading and above-grade-level readers encountering new words
key_sources: Tare, M., Nobles, S., & Xiao, W. (2018). Partnerships that work: Tapping research to address learner variability in young readers. Washington, DC: Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/e59c6e47-4209-4187-a0ef-b8da08283ec6

article_title: Designing Gateway Statistics and Chemistry Courses for Today’s Students: Case Studies of Postsecondary Course Innovations
citation: Peters, V., Pakhira, D., White, L., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Means, B. (2022). Designing gateway statistics and chemistry courses for today's students: Case studies of postsecondary course innovations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/162
title: Gateway course innovations combine peer-based active learning with a shift from computation toward concepts, reasoning, and application to students' lives
description: Across the case studies, the dominant design pattern pairs peer-based active learning (small groupwork, projects, peer tutoring) with a curricular shift away from computation. The report states that "All five of the five statistics course innovations and two of the three chemistry course innovations involved a shift away from computational approaches toward teaching focused on concepts and reasoning and the application of the discipline to students' lives and future goals." Supporting practices include flipped classrooms, low-stakes formative assessment in place of high-stakes exams, and interactive visualizations or simulations. The report notes these features are congruent with recent National Academies consensus recommendations.
requirements: Instructors willing to restructure class time around individual and peer-based active learning activities
constraints: Structural (department- or institution-level) innovations were less common, and the report notes barriers to departmental or institutional adoption remain
target_learners: first-year undergraduate students in gateway statistics or general chemistry courses, including Black, Latinx, and Indigenous students and students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: statistical reasoning and application of concepts to real research problems
conceptual understanding and critical thinking in chemistry
examples: Skyline's Data Path course uses a flipped classroom where students watch lecture videos before class and class time supports semester-long projects with SAS coding

The University of Arizona redesigned course engages students through three to seven instructional tasks per lecture asking them to analyze data, model chemical systems, and generate evidence-based arguments
key_sources: Peters, V., Pakhira, D., White, L., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Means, B. (2022). Designing gateway statistics and chemistry courses for today's students: Case studies of postsecondary course innovations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/162

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Learning theories should drive the design and evaluation of emerging learning technologies
description: The report argues that theories about how people learn should drive the design of emerging technologies, their implementation, and the metrics used to evaluate efficacy. It cites traditions including Dewey's experiential learning, Piaget's constructivism, Vygotsky's social constructivism, Bandura's social cognitive theory, and Papert's constructionism, which 'mutually reinforce that learning is actively constructed based on experiences and in connection with other humans.' Technology adopting these lenses should promote learner agency, open-ended problems, and human connection.
requirements: Developers consult a multidisciplinary team including learning scientists with technological, pedagogical, and content-area expertise
target_learners: all learners using emerging technology tools
target_learning_goals: subject-area learning grounded in research-based instructional models
examples: The report points to concrete-to-representational-to-abstract sequencing in math and science-of-reading frameworks in literacy as research-based models developers can apply
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Measure edtech efficacy with learning outcomes data, not satisfaction or engagement alone
description: The report recommends that efficacy of learning tools be measured by learning outcomes data, prioritizing research-validated assessments for their demonstrated validity and reliability, supplemented by formative or platform performance data. It warns that 'using satisfaction and usability data in isolation can give misleading perspectives on learner benefit,' and that behavioral measures like logins and time on platform are only proxies. Other data sources should be used in conjunction with validated assessments for a comprehensive understanding.
requirements: Measures must be directly tied to theory and evidence about learning
constraints: Research-validated assessments can be difficult to access or slow to return results
target_learners: learners using emerging technology tools in classrooms and at home
target_learning_goals: demonstrated understanding, application, or transfer of skills or knowledge
examples: The report describes ESSA Tiers of Evidence as a guide for developers choosing study designs matching their research questions and resources
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Co-design emerging technology tools with educators and learners as context experts
description: The report recommends that development teams partner with educators and learners throughout development, since developers cannot fully understand all contextual nuances of use. Co-design is defined as 'a process to collaboratively and iteratively design a solution that meets the authentic needs of the intended users in their contexts.' The process moves from clarifying roles through discovery of pain points, ideation, prototyping, and iterative refinement before broader deployment.
requirements: Partners should represent the diversity of lived experiences across intended user demographics; power dynamics should be shifted to elevate each voice, with fair compensation and formal acknowledgment
constraints: The report notes educators often have to retrofit what developers produce when they are left out of conversations
target_learners: educators and learners as intended users across classroom contexts
target_learning_goals: tools that authentically reflect user needs, goals, and intended use cases
examples: GIANT Remix co-designed with students, educators, and families through online bootcamps, in-person workshops, community stations, and school programs; Research-Practice-Industry Partnerships are offered as one approach
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Avoid overly automated personalization; preserve meaningful learner choice
description: The report supports personalization that tailors content, pacing, and assessment, but states that 'personalization alone is not sufficient to design for agency.' Personalization promotes agency when learners make meaningful choices about how, where, and what learning produces. The authors explicitly 'do not recommend personalized learning experiences that are overly automated, because providing learners limited opportunities to make informed decisions can detract from agency.'
requirements: Customizations must give learners freedom to engage in learning experiences that feel valuable and meaningful to them
target_learners: learners across ages and abilities, including those served by adaptive tools
target_learning_goals: learner agency, ownership of learning, engagement
examples: Mentu's AI suggests evidence-based strategies but educators remain final decision-makers, with explanations of why each strategy was selected
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: Student Empathy Interviews: An Instrument For Considering More Inclusive K-12 Computing Pathways
citation: Pati Ruiz, Kelly Mills, Quinn Burke, and Merijke Coenraad. (2021). Student Empathy Interviews: An Instrument For Considering More Inclusive K-12 Computing Pathways. Digital Promise White Paper. https://bit.ly/36szXLy
title: Listening to student voices is an essential feature of inclusivity efforts in computing education
description: This principle holds that districts designing inclusive computing pathways should treat listening to student voices as an essential, prioritized feature of their inclusivity efforts, rather than relying solely on adult perceptions. The paper's third finding states that "listening to student voices within the district is an essential feature of inclusivity efforts--and a priority." It works by having educators conduct empathy interviews with students about their CS/CT experiences and using what students identify to inform pathway design, especially where adult assumptions diverge from student-identified barriers.
requirements: Educators conduct empathy interviews with students about their CS/CT experiences
Districts treat student listening as a priority within inclusivity efforts
constraints: The paper offers no comparative test of listening versus not listening; the principle rests on the authors' findings from one district's work
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly minoritized students in computing programs
target_learning_goals: Broadening participation in K-12 computational thinking and computer science pathways
examples: In Iowa City, teacher committee members across high school, middle school, and elementary levels interviewed and surveyed students about their CS/CT experiences, and the district treated the findings as input to its inclusive pathway design
key_sources: Pati Ruiz, Kelly Mills, Quinn Burke, and Merijke Coenraad. (2021). Student Empathy Interviews: An Instrument For Considering More Inclusive K-12 Computing Pathways. Digital Promise White Paper. https://bit.ly/36szXLy

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Ground breakthrough solution development in existing theory or evidence
description: Breakthrough R&D teams should leverage existing basic and applied research — the note cites the science of reading, self-determination theory, and formative assessment — to guide development. The note states that "the core components of a breakthrough should be supported by existing evidence or should be considered hypotheses to be tested," so that untested design choices are treated explicitly as testable hypotheses rather than assumptions.
requirements: Teams must identify which core components rest on existing evidence and which remain hypotheses requiring testing
target_learners: education R&D development teams
target_learning_goals: designing breakthrough solutions grounded in learning science
examples: The note names science of reading, self-determination theory, and formative assessment as example research bases
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Use tightly bound iterative development cycles with rapid evaluation loops before scaling
description: Iterative development in breakthrough R&D starts from big bold ideas and uses iterative cycles to narrow focus. Teams "should establish continuous, tightly bound iterative development cycles using rapid evaluation loops to inform product development before taking the product to scale," and the solution's theory of change should be continually updated to incorporate new data and evidence.
requirements: A theory of change that is continually updated as new data and evidence arrive
target_learners: education R&D product development teams
target_learning_goals: developing and refining breakthrough solutions before scale-up
examples: The note describes starting from big bold ideas followed by iterative cycles to narrow the idea into focus
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Match methodological approach to research questions and broaden what counts as rigor
description: Teams must select the methodological approach that fits their research questions, and the field should extend rigor standards beyond causal impact studies. The note argues that "information about the usefulness of a product is as valuable as a study of the product's impact on learning outcomes," and that the field "needs to establish what rigor means for a wider range of methodological approaches beyond causal impact studies," especially as AI-based research methods emerge.
requirements: Both usefulness information and impact evidence are necessary to judge whether something will work and be used across implementation contexts
constraints: Especially important as new methodological approaches and tools, such as the use of AI in research methods, are introduced
target_learners: education R&D researchers and evaluators
target_learning_goals: rigorous evaluation of breakthrough solutions
examples: The note cites an emerging Digital Promise evidence framework for educational technologies as reference 2
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Tie measurement plans to the theory of change and prioritize theory-driven instrumentation from the start
description: Measurement plans must be closely tied to the breakthrough's theory of change. Teams "should prioritize deep, theory-driven instrumentation that captures key behavioral and cognitive constructs of interest rather than privileging measures that happen to already be available," and an evaluation plan with data-collection instrumentation should be in place from the start of a project.
requirements: An evaluation plan with instrumentation for collecting data in place from the start
target_learners: education R&D evaluation teams
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of behavioral and cognitive learning constructs
examples: The note contrasts theory-driven instrumentation with defaulting to measures that happen to already be available
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Collect implementation integrity and cross-context data, including how impact holds when implementation quality varies
description: Teams should gather data on implementation integrity and variability across contexts, addressing both whether a solution is implemented as intended and how it performs across a wide range of contexts. They should also "document the factors that support high quality implementation as well as the robustness of a breakthrough solution's impact on learning when implementation quality varies," for example under resource and staffing constraints.
requirements: Data collection on implementation integrity and contextual variability throughout development and evaluation
constraints: Implementation quality may vary due to resource and staffing constraints
target_learners: education R&D teams and implementation partners
target_learning_goals: robust solution performance across diverse implementation contexts
examples: The note gives resource and staffing constraints as an example source of implementation quality variation
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Build transdisciplinary teams that reflect served communities and balance power dynamics
description: Fresh perspectives, ideas from other sectors, and innovative partnerships — grounded in strong understanding of the education sector and problems of practice — are key to developing novel solutions to persistent challenges. Teams "should include representatives from research, industry, and education practice/policy" and "should reflect the communities they serve." Teams must also set up conditions for productive interdisciplinary participation and ensure that power dynamics do not favor one perspective over another.
requirements: Conditions for productive interdisciplinary participation; power dynamics balanced across perspectives
target_learners: transdisciplinary education R&D teams
target_learning_goals: developing completely novel ideas for persistent education challenges
examples: The note lists research, industry, and education practice/policy as the three team constituencies
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Disseminate actionable findings early, plan scale pathways, and govern data with FAIR principles and privacy-enhancing technologies
description: Teams should translate R&D findings into practical, actionable insights for stakeholders and industry developers, and consider scale pathways such as commercialization or licensing early so development aligns with dissemination needs. Data work requires "the technical, operational, and legal infrastructure required to protect student and educator privacy," going beyond traditional compliance to address challenges from emerging technologies like generative AI, with policies on data provenance, algorithmic transparency, and continuous monitoring. Data management should be grounded in the FAIR principles to lower access barriers, prevent redundant efforts, and support transparency and replicability.
requirements: Clear policies on data provenance, algorithmic transparency, and continuous monitoring; FAIR-grounded data management
constraints: Traditional compliance expectations are insufficient for ethical, safety, and privacy challenges introduced by emerging technologies like generative AI
target_learners: education R&D teams, learning providers, industry developers
target_learning_goals: responsible scaling and open sharing of breakthrough solutions
examples: The note names commercialization and licensing to established providers as example pathways to scale
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol
citation: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Pause, Collect, Reflect routine for portfolio touchpoints
description: The protocol structures portfolio work as recurring touchpoints: educators pause at intentional moments in the year, collect artifacts of learning into student portfolios, and provide scaffolded opportunities to reflect on those artifacts and the learning journey. The guide states the aim is that "educators can empower students to curate meaningful portfolio artifacts that showcase growth, celebrate personal wins, encourage self-evaluation, and set actionable goals for the future." It is designed for use in professional learning communities, faculty meetings, or leadership retreats.
requirements: Identify 2-3 intentional pause points over the year or unit of study
Communicate the purpose of collection and reflection to students and families
target_learners: K-12 students implementing Portrait of a Graduate portfolios
target_learning_goals: Self-evaluation and goal setting
Recognition of growth on Portrait of a Graduate competencies
examples: The guide prompts educators to brainstorm in blank spaces how their school or district might implement each step.
key_sources: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/12e194a7-3bd6-404c-8ccb-37aa237483d6

article_title: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol
citation: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Embed portfolio pauses into existing classroom structures
description: Portfolio routines work best when integrated into the classroom's existing rhythms rather than added on. The guide instructs educators to integrate the pause "directly into your existing classroom structures so it feels like a natural part of the learning cycle rather than an afterthought." It also recommends clearly communicating the purpose of the collection and reflection processes to students and families early.
requirements: Early communication of the portfolio purpose to students and families
Existing classroom structures into which the routine can be integrated
target_learners: K-12 students and their families
target_learning_goals: Sustained portfolio curation and reflection as part of classroom culture
examples: The guide suggests using the protocol in professional learning communities, faculty meetings, or leadership retreats to plan implementation.
key_sources: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/12e194a7-3bd6-404c-8ccb-37aa237483d6

article_title: Powerful Learning: Fostering Agency, Purpose, and Curiosity Through Connection
citation: Anton, G., Mills, K., Jacob, S., Chou, N., McNeil, K., & Wegemer, C. (2026, July). Powerful learning: Fostering agency, purpose, and curiosity through connection: Cultivating future-ready knowledge, skills, and dispositions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/307
title: Emerging technologies must be evidence-based, learner-centered, and skill-building to enable Powerful Learning
description: The report argues emerging technologies act as either a barrier to or an enabler of Powerful Learning, and to maximize potential they "must be thoughtfully designed and implemented, to be evidence-based, learner-centered, and skill-building." Evidence-based tools leverage foundational research with predefined metrics for whom and under what conditions they impact learning; learner-centered tools promote agency via personalization, immediate feedback, and removing barriers; co-design with educators and students increases usability.
requirements: Both product teams and educators articulate clear, predefined metrics to discern exactly for whom and under what conditions the technology impacts learning
constraints: Technologies are currently being adopted often without a sufficient evidence base for when, if, and how to best leverage them for learning
target_learners: K-12 learners using emerging technologies
target_learning_goals: Agency, purpose, curiosity, and connection supported by technology
examples: The report notes adaptive learning platforms can sequence rigorous content, evaluate understanding in real time, and maintain productive struggle, and that accessibility features can translate visual information and provide real-time language translation
key_sources: Anton, G., Mills, K., Jacob, S., Chou, N., McNeil, K., & Wegemer, C. (2026, July). Powerful learning: Fostering agency, purpose, and curiosity through connection: Cultivating future-ready knowledge, skills, and dispositions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/307

article_title: Classroom-Based Experimentation in a Digital Learning Platform
citation: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306
title: Embed experiments seamlessly into the natural flow of platform instruction
description: The report's first emerging insight is that classroom-embedded experiments "can and should be seamless and non-disruptive, requiring minimal, if any, burden on the part of the instructor." Embedded manipulations operate naturalistically within the existing flow of instruction, preserving the integrity of students' learning experiences without requiring teachers to modify practice or manage groups. Group random assignment keeps students in the same class or school in the same condition, avoiding perceived unfairness and visible differences, and supports ecological validity and generalizability.
requirements: UpGrade's flexible randomization schemes, including group random assignment, to preserve consistency of learning experiences across groups.
constraints: Particularly important in school settings where maintaining coherence within classroom structures has practical and pedagogical importance.
target_learners: K-12 students and their classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Rigorous experimental evidence generated without disrupting everyday instruction
examples: Metacognitive prompts and self-efficacy surveys were embedded fully in the MATHia instructional flow, with interventions randomized by classroom.
key_sources: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306

article_title: Classroom-Based Experimentation in a Digital Learning Platform
citation: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306
title: Build measurement into learning by using intrinsic platform data as outcome measures
description: The report's second insight is to measure outcomes during the learning activity itself rather than only through external assessments. In MATHia, transactions such as "problem attempts, hint requests, steps towards skill mastery" create rich behavioral data tracing the learning process in real time. Built-in measures like skill mastery, hint-seeking behavior, and error rates can serve as meaningful outcome measures, and platforms must be intentionally designed with fine-grained, structured data logging for research access.
requirements: The digital learning platform must be well-instrumented to collect, store, and export data, logging fine-grained student transactions with contextual information in structured formats.
constraints: Built-in measures reflect competencies the system is explicitly designed to track, which vary with the platform's goals.
target_learners: K-12 students using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Observing how learning progresses during interventions, not just whether students learned
examples: MATHia's skill mastery adaptation, hint-seeking behavior, and error rates are cited as inherent measures usable as outcomes.
key_sources: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306

article_title: Designing Student Success Systems Intentionally: How Warwick Public Schools and Panorama Bridge the Gap with Co-Designed Technical Solutions
citation: Cocuzza, B., Noakes, S., Aso, C., Goldschmidt, L., and Bennett, K. (2026). Designing student success systems intentionally: How Warwick Public Schools and Panorama bridge the gap with co-designed technical solutions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/303
title: Design AI-enabled tools around immediate teacher needs and preserve human oversight in AI workflows
description: The article recommends that AI in student success systems support routine tasks within larger workflows rather than open-ended deliverables, and that solutions be designed around immediate teacher needs rather than district priorities alone. It advises that "AI-embedded workflows should lessen administrative burden and produce consistent results," and that classroom, school, and district perspectives all be considered so solutions are needs-driven. Warwick's own shift after low uptake was from top-down to bottom-up AI development aligned with actual teacher pain points.
requirements: Involve teachers in co-design conversations from the outset
Ensure classroom, school, and district perspectives are considered in designing new functionalities
constraints: AI is suited to routine tasks where users know they need the task and have a clear perspective on the output; open-ended tasks requiring heavy scrutiny of prompting and product are not
target_learners: K-12 district leaders
Solution providers building AI-enabled education tools
target_learning_goals: Successful adoption of AI-enabled student success tools
Human-centered AI implementation in schools
examples: Warwick leadership used usage data to shift development of the next custom tools toward user pain points rather than district priorities
key_sources: Cocuzza, B., Noakes, S., Aso, C., Goldschmidt, L., and Bennett, K. (2026). Designing student success systems intentionally: How Warwick Public Schools and Panorama bridge the gap with co-designed technical solutions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/303

article_title: EdTech Quality Indicators Guide: Leveraging the Five EdTech Quality Indicators to save time and money, reduce risk, and improve student outcomes
citation: Digital Promise. (2026). EdTech Quality Indicators Guide: Leveraging the Five EdTech Quality Indicators to save time and money, reduce risk, and improve student outcomes. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Six-step edtech procurement process from needs analysis to sustain-and-scale
description: The guide structures district edtech procurement as six steps: Analyze & Inventory, Discover & Decide, Design & Plan, Mobilize & Implement, Evaluate & Reflect, and Sustain & Scale. Each step frames key questions and points to practical resources and templates. The guide says the steps "represent a comprehensive process that districts and schools can engage with to discover, pilot, and procure edtech tools to meet a given need," grounding the articulated need in data before exploring solutions and returning to Discover & Decide if a pilot shows a tool is not the right fit.
requirements: Cross-departmental teams analyze student and operational data first; a cross-functional team defines vision and purpose before piloting
constraints: Steps assume district capacity to run pilots and maintain meeting cadences with providers
target_learners: District and school education leaders involved in edtech procurement
target_learning_goals: Formalizing intentional, data- and evidence-driven procurement processes
examples: Step 5 directs teams to leverage interim and summative pilot data to decide whether a tool is the right fit or whether to return to Discover & Decide
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2026). EdTech Quality Indicators Guide: Leveraging the Five EdTech Quality Indicators to save time and money, reduce risk, and improve student outcomes. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f1e0fd08-9047-42e7-9a2d-190ccb4d10dd

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — The UX Design Loop
citation: Gartrell, J. and Johnson, E. (2026). ATS Field Note: The UX Design Loop. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/299
title: Plan UX research backwards from the product decisions you need to make
description: The article recommends planning research "backwards": "start with the product decisions you'll need to make and work back to what you need to learn in order to make those decisions." This keeps studies focused on decision-relevant learning rather than producing "interesting but inconclusive findings." It is operationalized in Phase 1 of the Design Loop, where teams align on decisions, learning needs, and how to learn them.
requirements: Teams must first identify the key product decisions at stake before selecting research methods
target_learners: education R&D and product teams

article_title: Rubrics for Examining Historical Thinking Skills in High School World History Activities and Student Work: Construct Validity Evidence from the Literature
citation: Hardy, A., Iwatani, E. (2021). Rubrics for examining historical thinking skills in high school world history activities and student work: Construct validity evidence from the literature. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/113
title: Treat literacy skills as embedded in historical thinking demonstration rather than as separate assessment categories
description: When assessing historical thinking, the report recommends not scoring reading and writing as distinct categories, because literacy is central to demonstrating historical thinking and other national frameworks treat literacy skills as embedded in its demonstration. The authors state: "we do not include reading or writing as distinct categories in ourrubrics." This follows their observation that literacy strategies with primary sources are often used as a proxy for historical thinking in standardized testing, and that overlap between skills and literacy complicates independent claims.
requirements: Rubric dimensions that already capture the literacy-dependent demonstration of historical thinking
constraints: Applies to rubrics of historical thinking skills, not to literacy assessment itself
target_learners: U.S. high school world history students
target_learning_goals: Historical thinking skills demonstrated through reading and writing with primary sources
examples: The rubrics score sourcing and historical argumentation directly rather than including separate reading or writing dimensions

article_title: Data Plus Theory Equals Codebook: Leveraging LLMs for Human-AI Codebook Development
citation: Zambrano, A.F., Wei, Z., Zhang, J., Baker, R.S., Ocumpaugh, J., Barany, A., Liu, X., Ginger, J., Paquette, L., Zhou, Y., & Borchers, C. (2026). Data Plus Theory Equals Codebook: Leveraging LLMs for Human-AI Codebook Development. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1. https://osf.io/g3z4x
title: Three-step theory-informed human-AI codebook development process
description: A reusable workflow in which researchers first prompt GPT-4o with references to foundational theory papers to generate a baseline codebook, then re-prompt with both the theory and the dataset so the model refines constructs against authentic examples, and finally have two human coders merge, rename, and exclude constructs. In Study 1 the authors "prompted GPT-4o to generate a baseline codebook drawing solely from its knowledge base about the two foundational SRL papers, explicitly including full references in the prompt", then supplied the full transcript dataset, then refined. The pattern operationalizes iterative, theory-guided codebook development at scale.
requirements: Access to GPT-4o via API with temperature set to 0 and each prompt run three times to verify consistency across iterations
Foundational theory papers well established enough that the model's training data covers them, verified by preliminary checks
Two human coders to review specificity and applicability of generated constructs
constraints: Constructs relevant to theory but absent from the data cannot be coded
Distinguishing fine-grained construct pairs may be impractical where full human inspection of large datasets is infeasible
target_learners: qualitative researchers in the learning sciences and educational data mining
target_learning_goals: theory-aligned qualitative coding of learner behavior, such as self-regulated learning and interest development
examples: Applied to 955 think-aloud utterances from fifteen students across three intelligent tutoring systems (stoichiometry and formal logic), yielding a final eleven-construct SRL codebook

article_title: Seeing Is Solving: MLLMs, Reasoning, and Refusal in Visual Math
citation: Croteau, E., & Heffernan, N. (2026). Seeing Is Solving: MLLMs, Reasoning, and Refusal in Visual Math. https://osf.io/ct7bg/
title: Gate automated scoring and learner-model updates on visual-evidence availability and reliability, treating no-image refusals as missing-context signals
description: For image-dependent math in tutoring systems, the article recommends a reliability-first stance: "gate automated feedback and scoring not on single-run accuracy, but onwithin-model stability and cross-model corroboration". When an item is Required, a system must distinguish learner error from missing-figure conditions before assigning credit or updating mastery; no-image refusals "can be treated as missing-context indicators and used to suppress automated scoring orlearner-model updates until the required visual information is provided". High-agreement items are stronger candidates for automated feedback; low-agreement items should trigger guardrails such as human-authored hints, visual-evidence-binding scaffolds, or deferral.
requirements: The system must log refusal behavior and run stability, and item-level agreement information must be available to set deployment gates
constraints: Applies to image-Required items in intelligent tutoring contexts; the article notes lucky-correct answers without images remain possible and possible training-data exposure is not fully ruled out
target_learners: middle-school mathematics students (Grades 6–8) using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: valid automated scoring and learner-model updating on image-dependent math problems
examples: The article recommends that high-agreement items (solved by ≥5 models at majority-correct) are stronger candidates for automated feedback, while low-agreement items should trigger guardrails by design
key_sources: Croteau, E., & Heffernan, N. (2026). Seeing Is Solving: MLLMs, Reasoning, and Refusal in Visual Math. https://osf.io/ct7bg/

article_title: Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention
citation: Wei Dai, Jionghao Lin, Flora Ji-Yoon Jin, Yi-Shan Tsai, Namrata Srivastava, Pierre Le Bodic, Dragan Gašević, and Guanliang Chen. (2025). Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 102–125. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8735
title: Regularly update at-risk prediction models with data from new cohorts to maintain reliable performance
description: Because predictive models for identifying at-risk students lose accuracy when transferred to new cohorts, this principle recommends periodic retraining. As the article's Notes for Practice state, "these models should be regularly updated using data from new cohorts" to maintain reliable performance across diverse student populations. The study's own post-hoc evaluation illustrates the risk it addresses: source-semester-trained models scored lower AUC on the target semester than models trained and tested within the target semester.
requirements: Availability of trace and academic data from each new cohort to refresh the training set.
A pipeline (Ed and Moodle data extraction, feature engineering, model evaluation) that can be rerun each semester.
constraints: Comprehensive historical data for model retraining are often limited in real-world educational contexts, which is why generalizable models matter.
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large higher-education courses
Institutions deploying early-warning systems
target_learning_goals: Early and accurate identification of students at risk of failing
examples: The study applied source-semester random-forest models to the target semester without retraining and observed lower cross-semester AUC (0.72 and 0.78) than for models trained and tested within the same semester (0.98 and 0.96).
key_sources: Wei Dai, Jionghao Lin, Flora Ji-Yoon Jin, Yi-Shan Tsai, Namrata Srivastava, Pierre Le Bodic, Dragan Gašević, and Guanliang Chen. (2025). article_title: Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention
citation: Wei Dai, Jionghao Lin, Flora Ji-Yoon Jin, Yi-Shan Tsai, Namrata Srivastava, Pierre Le Bodic, Dragan Gašević, and Guanliang Chen. (2025). Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 102–125. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8735
title: Give students flexible options regarding whether and when to receive analytics-informed feedback support
description: This principle addresses intervention frequency and student control. Because preferences for intervention frequency vary, the article recommends that "students should be given flexible options regarding whether and when to receive this support." It follows from the survey finding that 60% of respondents wanted the intervention more often than the twice-per-semester schedule used, while others did not; the study's emails accordingly told students they could ask the teaching team not to receive the feedback again.
requirements: A delivery mechanism (e.g., email integrated with the LMS) that can support variable frequency and opt-out.
A way for students to communicate their preferences to the teaching team.
constraints: The study itself implemented only a fixed twice-per-semester frequency, so flexible scheduling was recommended, not tested.
target_learners: Undergraduate students identified as at risk of failing a course
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement with feedback interventions across the semester
examples: The intervention emails included the sentence: If you do not wish to receive this feedback again, please let the teaching team know directly.

article_title: Using Student Achievement Data to Support Instructional Decision Making
citation: Hamilton, L., Halverson, R., Jackson, S., Mandinach, E., Supovitz, J., & Wayman, J. (2009). Using student achievement data to support instructional decision making (NCEE 2009-4067). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides/
title: Make data part of an ongoing cycle of instructional improvement
description: Teachers should adopt a systematic, cyclical process for using data: collect and prepare varied data, interpret it and form hypotheses about how to improve learning, then modify instruction to test those hypotheses. The guide advises that "not all instructional changes bear fruit immediately", so teachers should allow adaptation time before discarding an intervention. Teachers can begin the cycle at any point, including with a hypothesis or an instructional modification they want to evaluate.
requirements: Collect data from multiple sources including annual state assessments, interim assessments, and classroom performance data
Develop testable hypotheses that identify a promising intervention, a measurable effect, and comparison data
constraints: Overreliance on a single data source such as a high-stakes accountability test can lead to teaching to the test and false gains not reflected on other assessments
target_learners: K-12 classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Adapting lessons, goals, and grouping in response to students' needs evidenced in achievement data
examples: The guide's testable-hypotheses box: teaching struggling 3rd graders the trade first method for subtraction and examining changes in their subtraction scores on the interim assessment, with pre-teaching scores as comparison data
key_sources: Hamilton, L., Halverson, R., Jackson, S., Mandinach, E., Supovitz, J., & Wayman, J. (2009). Using student achievement data to support instructional decision making (NCEE 2009-4067). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides/
title: Use multiple data sources and triangulation because no single assessment suffices
description: The guide recommends gathering annual, interim, and classroom-level data and interpreting them together. "Triangulation" is defined as "the process of using multiple data sources to address a particular question or problem and using evidence from each source to illuminate or temper evidence from the other sources". When multiple sources show similar strengths and weaknesses, teachers can be more confident in their decisions; when tests disagree, teachers should examine items to identify the discrepancy.
requirements: Prepare data in aggregate forms that address teachers' own questions and highlight patterns
Supplement annual state results with beginning-of-year information since students' skills may have changed
constraints: Classroom-level assignments, conditions, and scores are not generally comparable across classrooms
target_learners: K-12 teachers and school data teams
target_learning_goals: Identifying class-wide and individual strengths and weaknesses to allocate instructional time and adapt assignments
examples: A teacher tracking four waves of interim math data by performance quartile on a line graph, ensuring each quartile group contained numerous students so results were not driven by outliers

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Partners
citation: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Three-part consistent tutoring session structure: tutor read-aloud, targeted skill introduction, student read-aloud practice with feedback
description: Each tutoring session follows a consistent structure with three phases. First, "The tutor reads to the student, stopping to ask comprehension questions." Second, "The tutor then uses specific materials to introduce specific reading skills." Third, "the student reads aloud to the tutor and practices the new skill," with the tutor providing "feedback and coaching following prompts built into the curriculum." This gives volunteer tutors a scripted, repeatable lesson routine.
requirements: Curriculum with built-in prompts and specific materials for introducing specific reading skills
target_learners: Grade 2-4 students reading below grade level
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and specific reading skills
examples: Tutor reads aloud with comprehension questions, introduces a skill with specific materials, then hears the student practice the new skill aloud with feedback
key_sources: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Partners
citation: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: House school-based tutoring programs in a dedicated in-school reading center managed by a full-time coordinator
description: Reading Partners requires partner schools to provide infrastructure for consistent delivery: "Reading Partners requires partner schools to have a dedicated space for a reading center, usually a classroom," and "Reading Partners then provides a full-time site coordinator to manage the program and recruits community volunteers as tutors." A fixed space plus dedicated coordination supports reliable volunteer recruitment, training, and session delivery within the school day.
requirements: A dedicated space for a reading center, usually a classroom, with an internet connection
A full-time site coordinator to manage the program
target_learners: Elementary students in grades 2-4 reading below grade level
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and foundational reading skills
examples: A classroom converted to a reading center with an internet connection, staffed by a full-time site coordinator
key_sources: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Success for All
citation: Success for All program evidence summary. (2015). https://www.successforall.org
title: Regroup students across grade lines by current reading level using frequent curriculum-based assessment
description: Within Success for All, "children are frequently assessed on curriculum-based measures, and these are used to regroup children into reading groups according to current reading level, across grade lines." This keeps reading instruction matched to each child's current level rather than to grade placement, and pairs with one-to-one or small-group tutoring for struggling students, especially first graders.
requirements: Frequent curriculum-based assessment of reading level
Flexibility to form reading groups across grade lines
Tutoring capacity (paraprofessionals) for struggling students
target_learners: K-5 students in high-poverty elementary schools, especially struggling early readers
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills matched to current reading level
examples: Beginning with phonetically-controlled mini-books in grades K-1, with cooperative learning used extensively at all grade levels
key_sources: Success for All program evidence summary. (2015). https://www.successforall.org

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Recovery
citation: Reading Recovery. (2020). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/reading-recovery
title: Pair intervention teachers with a district-employed teacher leader providing initial training and ongoing professional development
description: Reading Recovery requires teachers to "affiliate with a Reading Recovery teacher leader who is employed by a school district and provides initial training and ongoing professional development to teachers." One teacher leader may work with about 42 teachers, from one or multiple districts. Teachers complete a yearlong graduate-level course for university credit; teacher leaders complete up to five graduate courses at a registered university training site.
requirements: Teachers must successfully complete a yearlong graduate level course taught by a teacher leader for which university credit is received
Teacher leaders must successfully complete up to five graduate level courses offered over two semesters at a registered university training site
constraints: Reading Recovery should not be a teacher's assignment for the entire school day
target_learners: kindergarten or primary-grade teachers, Title I teachers, intervention specialists, ELL or special education teachers, literacy coaches and administrators
target_learning_goals: delivery of one-to-one beginning reading intervention
examples: One teacher leader may work with about 42 teachers, who may all be from one school district or from multiple school districts.
key_sources: Reading Recovery. (2020). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/reading-recovery

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Recovery
citation: Reading Recovery. (2020). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/reading-recovery
title: Plan intervention staffing around expected need of 20-30% of the first-grade population and part-day teacher assignments
description: The review advises that "a useful estimate to plan staffing is to expect between 20-30% of the first grade population to need Reading Recovery." Teachers deliver four individual 30-minute lessons daily in addition to other school roles, and "Reading Recovery should not be a teacher's assignment for the entire school day." Staffing depends on level of need and may change year to year and vary school to school.
requirements: Teachers able to teach four individual 30-minute lessons each day in addition to their other roles
constraints: Staffing depends on level of need in a school and may change slightly from year to year and vary from school to school
target_learners: first-grade students needing reading intervention
target_learning_goals: beginning reading
examples: Teachers work with four students individually for two and one half hours each school day, about 8-10 students over the school year, and in some other instructional role for the rest of the day.

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Corps
citation: Reading Corps program description and evaluation summary. (2024). https://www.readingcorps.org
title: Multi-level coaching model supporting tutor fidelity
description: Reading Corps tutors are supported by "a multi-level coaching model that includes site-based and external coaches". The school-appointed Internal Coach provides on-demand support and "monthly coaching and feedback that focuses on ensuring high fidelity to the program", while an assigned Coaching Specialist provides additional regular coaching to both tutor and school staff and "supports all data-driven decision-making practices".

A Coaching Specialist provided by Ampact in addition to headquarters staff.

target_learning_goals: Fidelity of implementation of evidence-based literacy instruction
examples: Coaching supports data-driven decisions such as eligibility, graph interpretation, and exit decisions.

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: ASSISTments
citation: ASSISTments evidence summary. (2020). https://www.assistments.org
title: Dual-content homework design: textbook-linked problem sets plus mastery-oriented skill practice
description: ASSISTments organizes its homework content along two complementary types: "the first is linked to existing textbook homework problems and provides teachers the flexibility to assign suitable problem sets and the second is intended for mastery-oriented skill practice." This pattern lets homework both follow the enacted curriculum and provide repeated practice toward mastery, with the platform returning assessment information to teachers.
requirements: existing textbook homework problems to link content to
a problem bank supporting mastery-oriented practice
constraints: as evaluated, the pattern applied to grade 7 math homework in middle school settings
target_learners: middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: math homework completion with assistance and mastery of math skills
examples: Teachers assigned suitable problem sets linked to their textbook while also drawing on mastery-oriented skill practice content

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Saga Math
citation: Saga Math (Evidence Summary). (2020). Evidence for ESSA program evidence summary. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Embedded high-dosage tutoring pattern: small ratios, in-schedule sessions, and classroom-aligned sequencing
description: The Saga approach instantiates a high-dosage tutoring design in which tutoring is "embedded in students' regular school schedules", occurs at least three times weekly for 90 minutes, uses small tutor-to-student ratios (1:2 to 1:4 traditional; up to 1:8 blended with ALEKS), and trails classroom instruction by 2-3 days to reinforce learning and address gaps. Program strategies are adjusted using assessment data, observations, survey feedback, and progress-monitoring tools.
requirements: Minimum three sessions per week totaling 90 minutes, scheduled within the school day
Small tutor-to-student ratios per session (3-8 students depending on model)
Weekly alignment meetings between tutor supervisors and primary math teachers
constraints: Must remain supplemental so it does not displace Tier 1 instruction or other responsibilities
target_learners: High school students at risk of dropping out in high-poverty schools
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement, course grades, and course passing
examples: The blended model has 9th grade students spend every other day with a tutor for an hour at a 2-students-to-1-tutor ratio, with off days on computer-assisted learning

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Math Corps
citation: Math Corps Program Description. (2024). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/program/math-corps
title: Use instructionally-relevant assessment data to select, monitor, and exit students from tutoring
description: Math Corps bases entry, continuation, and exit decisions on assessment data rather than teacher judgment alone: "School staff use instructionally-relevant data to determine students who are eligible for the program" and students remain in tutoring "until math assessment data indicate they meet eligibility for exiting the program." Data-driven decision practices extend to graph interpretation and exit decisions supported by a Coaching Specialist.
requirements: Ongoing math assessment data collection
A Coaching Specialist who supports all data-driven decision-making practices (e.g., eligibility; graph interpretation; exit decisions)
target_learners: Students in grades 4-8 receiving supplemental math tutoring
target_learning_goals: Math skill growth sufficient to exit intervention
examples: Students receive tutoring two or three times per week until assessment data indicate exit eligibility, after which they are monitored until the end of the school year

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Number Rockets
citation: Number Rockets. (2020). Number Rockets: first-grade math tutoring program description. Tutoring provided through AIR. https://www.air.org
title: Build struggling students' conceptual understanding by sequencing tutoring from concrete tasks toward abstract tasks and procedures
description: The Number Rockets curriculum orders instruction along a concreteness fading sequence: it is "intended to build students' conceptual understanding by starting with concrete tasks and moving toward abstract tasks and procedures, including math facts." This principle recommends that small-group tutoring for struggling math students begin with manipulable, concrete activity before transitioning to abstract procedures.
requirements: A scripted curriculum that supplies the concrete-to-abstract task sequence
Tutors trained to deliver the sequence as designed
constraints: Evaluated as a Tier 2 supplement for first graders below the 38th percentile in math
target_learners: first-grade students struggling in math
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of number and operations, math facts
examples: Number Rockets sessions move from concrete tasks to abstract tasks and procedures, including math facts, across 63 days of 40-minute sessions

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Identify the specifics of the problem behavior and the conditions that prompt and reinforce it before intervening
description: Before selecting an intervention, teachers should concretely describe the problem behavior and its effect on learning, observe and record its frequency and context, and identify its antecedents and consequences. The guide recommends that "teachers carefully observe the conditions in which the problem behavior of an individual student is likely to occur and not occur", then use that information to tailor intervention strategies to the individual student within the classroom context. This analytic step is rated moderate evidence and underlies functional behavioral assessment practice.
requirements: Concretely describe the behavior problem and its effect on learning
Observe and record the frequency and context of the problem behavior over a few days to a week until clear patterns emerge
Identify what prompts and reinforces the problem behavior
constraints: The panel does not suggest that general education teachers conduct formal functional behavioral assessments and analyses on their own
Much of the supporting evidence comes from students with school-identified emotional and behavioral disabilities
target_learners: Elementary general education students (K-5) with persistent problem behaviors
target_learning_goals: Reducing inappropriate classroom behavior that impedes learning
examples: Concrete descriptions the guide offers include a student who blurts out answers without raising his hand during whole-class instruction and a student who frequently leaves her seat without permission during small-group instruction.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012).
