citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, November). Year Up. https://whatworks.ed.gov.
title: Combine occupational training with an employer internship and layered supports to improve early career earnings for disadvantaged young adults
description: The reviewed evidence indicates that a program model pairing full-time technical training with a subsequent employer internship, wrapped in advising, mentoring, stipends, and post-program placement services, can substantially raise short-term earnings for low-income young adults. The WWC judged this combination likely to increase short-term earnings, with an improvement index of +28 percentile points across two randomized trials. The model embeds work-based learning directly into occupational instruction and connects participants to employers in their target occupational fields.
requirements: Six months of full-time occupational and technical training aligned to employer needs
A six-month internship placement in the student's selected occupational field
Ongoing supports including advising, mentoring, and financial assistance throughout the program
constraints: The earnings advantage was demonstrated on short-term outcomes; medium-term earnings and employment showed no discernible effects, so the model's sustained impact beyond one year is not established by this evidence
Implementation depends on employer payments for interns, foundation grants, and charitable donations, which financed nearly all operating costs
target_learners: Low-income young adults ages 18 to 24 with a high school diploma or equivalent
target_learning_goals: Occupational and technical skills for entry-level positions in information technology and financial services
Professionalism and workplace behavior skills
Career planning, job search, and placement
examples: Year Up enrolled students in learning communities of about 40, delivered full-time training four and a half days a week for six months, then placed students in six-month internships with local companies in their selected occupational fields
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, November). Year Up. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/722.

article_title: Integrated Basic Education and Skills Training (I-BEST)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, September). Integrated Basic Education Skills and Training (I-BEST). https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Six team teaching models for integrating basic skills and occupational instruction
description: I-BEST's signature feature is team teaching, in which a basic skills instructor and an occupational instructor are both present for at least half of instructional time. The report enumerates six forms: "Traditional team teaching", "Collaborative teaching", "Complementary-supportive teaching", "Parallel instruction", "Differentiated split class", and "Monitoring teacher". In the Accelerating Opportunity evaluation all six types were used, with complementary-supportive most popular; in ACE the complementary-supportive model was typical; in the Washington I-BEST study collaborative teaching and two variants of traditional team teaching were implemented.
requirements: Both the basic skills instructor and the occupational training instructor are required to be present in class for at least half of the total instructional time in an I-BEST course
Instructors collaborate to identify joint learning outcomes for students in their class
constraints: The ACE model prescribes a 50 percent minimum of team teaching while Accelerating Opportunity calls for a minimum of 25 percent
target_learners: Adult basic skills students in postsecondary occupational training programs
target_learning_goals: Basic skills in the context of a chosen occupational field
examples: In the Accelerating Opportunity evaluation, all six types of team teaching models were used, with the complementary-supportive model being most popular
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, September). Integrated Basic Education Skills and Training (I-BEST). https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/706

article_title: Exploring Coaching for Powerful Technology Use in Education
citation: Tina Ehsanipour & Florencia Gomez Zaccarelli. (2017). Exploring Coaching for Powerful Technology Use in Education. Center to Support Excellence in Teaching - Stanford University. https://ce.stanford.edu
title: Keep technology in a supportive rather than starring role, and have technology experts coach the coaches so content stays central
description: Because "technology integration is not the ultimate goal; rather the goal is to engage students in authentic problem-solving," technology should support learning goals rather than drive them. The paper recommends a coach-the-coaches model in which content-specific instructional coaches receive technology training, or alternatively a collaboration between a technology-expert coach and teachers who are content experts, so content stays in the starring role.
requirements: Coaches need expertise in the teacher's specific content area in addition to technology expertise
constraints: This may pose a challenge in schools where there is at most one technology coach to begin with
target_learners: K-12 teachers integrating technology
target_learning_goals: Meaningful technology integration in service of content-area learning goals
examples: The paper describes Dinse de Salas and colleagues' (2016) alternative: a coach expert in technology collaborating with coached teachers who are the experts in their domains' content
key_sources: Tina Ehsanipour & Florencia Gomez Zaccarelli. (2017). Exploring Coaching for Powerful Technology Use in Education. Center to Support Excellence in Teaching - Stanford University. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/2f8e7466-5d96-49c4-b8cc-5b70690e0db9

article_title: Bottom Line
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021). Bottom Line. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Intensive one-on-one advising across the college application, transition, and first years of college
description: The Bottom Line model pairs each student with an individualized advisor across sequential phases: application advising, financial aid support, college selection guidance, summer transition assistance, and continued campus support. Advisors interacted with students during high school, on average, 13 times during a 15-month period, entailing 10-15 hours of contact time, with support continuing at target colleges for up to six years.
requirements: Full-time advisors with college degrees who complete a first year learning the organization's curriculum and mastering advisor competencies; offices in served communities and at each target college.
constraints: Costs are nearly fully funded by private and corporate donors and foundations; students and families incur no costs.
target_learners: High school juniors and seniors from low-income backgrounds transitioning to college
target_learning_goals: Applying to and selecting high-quality, affordable colleges; persisting in college
examples: In the study, most meetings involved working on college applications or financial aid, and students attending target colleges were matched to a new advisor at their college.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021). Bottom Line. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/714

article_title: User Guide and FAQ: MAP Growth National Dashboard
citation: MAP Growth National Dashboard user guide and FAQ. (2026). https://www.nwea.org/map-growth-national-dashboard
title: Interpret dashboard data with more than one metric, looking at patterns over time and considering both achievement and growth
description: The guide's cautions section recommends that users avoid drawing conclusions from a single metric or term: "Avoid drawing conclusions from a single metric or term. Instead, look at patterns over time and consider both achievement and growth." Pairing growth with achievement is presented as yielding a more complete and nuanced picture of student progress, since achievement captures single-point performance while growth tracks progress between test events.
requirements: Access to both achievement and growth metrics, which on the dashboard means data from at least two testing terms
constraints: Growth metrics are unavailable in the fall dashboard update because they require two test scores
target_learners: District leaders
State and federal policymakers
target_learning_goals: Responsible interpretation of assessment data
Pandemic recovery analysis
examples: The Trends Over Time tab supports comparing changes in RIT scores since 2019 baselines, including differences by student group
The guide recommends using national reference lines to put local or state results in context rather than state-to-state comparisons
key_sources: MAP Growth National Dashboard user guide and FAQ. (2026). https://www.nwea.org/map-growth-national-dashboard

article_title: User Guide and FAQ: MAP Growth National Dashboard
citation: MAP Growth National Dashboard user guide and FAQ. (2026). https://www.nwea.org/map-growth-national-dashboard
title: Frame achievement and growth differences between student groups as opportunity gaps rather than shortcomings of students
description: In its cautions on group data, the guide states that examining outcomes by race and ethnicity is essential for exposing long-standing inequities, but that these differences reflect systemic barriers and uneven access to resources. It instructs that "these data should be framed as opportunity gaps, not shortcomings of students themselves, with the intent to highlight where additional support and investment are needed." The principle guides responsible communication of subgroup comparisons by district leaders and policymakers.
requirements: Care in interpreting differences in achievement and growth between student groups, per the guide's cautions section
constraints: The guide does not state that the dashboard's group comparisons establish causes; it attributes group differences to systemic barriers and uneven access to resources
target_learners: Student groups in K–8 public schools, including groups defined by race and ethnicity, poverty level, and school locale
target_learning_goals: Equity-focused interpretation of achievement and growth data
Identifying where additional support and investment are needed
examples: The Group Insights tab breaks down national achievement and growth data by student groups to help identify disparities in opportunity and outcomes
key_sources: MAP Growth National Dashboard user guide and FAQ. (2026). https://www.nwea.org/map-growth-national-dashboard

article_title: Fostering Powerful Use of Technology Through Instructional Coaching
citation: Bakhshaei, M., Hardy, A., Francisco, A., Noakes, S., & Fusco, J. (2018). Fostering Powerful Use of Technology Through Instructional Coaching: Results from the Pilot Year of the Dynamic Learning Project. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Six core attributes of an effective instructional coaching program
description: From pilot-year data across 50 schools, the authors identified six core attributes of an effective coaching program: "partnerships, personalization, voluntary nature, situated in school/classroom, non-evaluative, and sustained." Coaching works as a partnership in which the teacher drives decisions; it is personalized to each teacher's context; participation is voluntary rather than compliance-based; the coach is situated on site; the relationship is non-evaluative so teachers feel safe experimenting; and support is sustained across cycles.
requirements: Coaches must be protected from evaluative roles and other assignments; teachers must be able to choose to participate; coaching must provide sustained one-on-one time (on average at least 19 hours of coaching support over the school year).
constraints: The attributes were identified in one pilot year across underserved middle schools; the report notes the appropriate balance of coaching depth versus breadth may change depending on school characteristics and teacher aptitude.
target_learners: K-12 classroom teachers
instructional coaches and program designers
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional growth in technology integration
improved instructional practice through coaching
examples: 77 percent of participating DLP teachers received at least 30 minutes of one-on-one coaching per week, with 43 percent receiving more than an hour each week.
key_sources: Bakhshaei, M., Hardy, A., Francisco, A., Noakes, S., & Fusco, J. (2018). Fostering Powerful Use of Technology Through Instructional Coaching: Results from the Pilot Year of the Dynamic Learning Project. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/540c3325-fd5f-408e-a347-2409f57848dd

article_title: Summer Bridge Programs
citation: Summer Bridge Programs. (2016). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Supporting Postsecondary Success. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Summer bridge programs combine orientation, advising, college-success skills training, and accelerated coursework in the 2–4 week bridge period
description: Summer bridge programs occur in the summer period between high school and college and, although content varies across institutions and populations, share a characteristic multi-component design. The report states they "typically last 2–4 weeks and involve (a) an in-depth orientation to college life and resources, (b) academic advising, (c) training in skills necessary for college success (e.g., time management and study skills), and/or (d) accelerated academic coursework." Nonacademic components are designed to provide cultural and social capital and promote adjustment to college culture.
requirements: Programs must be delivered in the summer bridge period between high school and college
constraints: Content varies across institutions and by the population served; components are combined with 'and/or', so not all programs include all four
target_learners: Incoming college freshmen, historically targeting ethnic/racial minority, low-income, first-generation, or other at-risk populations
target_learning_goals: College readiness, adjustment to college culture, time management and study skills, academic preparation for college-level work
examples: The Challenge Program implemented this design with non-credit-bearing college-like courses, peer educators and coaches, and family integration activities
key_sources: Summer Bridge Programs. (2016). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Supporting Postsecondary Success. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/661

article_title: Cultivating a Culture of Coaching to Support Powerful Use of Technology: Results from the Challenge-based Coaching Model Pilot in Puerto Rico
citation: Carol Lopez and Odelia Younge. (2021). Cultivating a Culture of Coaching to Support Powerful Use of Technology: Results from the Challenge-based Coaching Model Pilot in Puerto Rico. Digital Promise report. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Support successful coaching implementation by assigning coaches fewer classes, securing school leader commitment, and building teacher enthusiasm
description: The report identifies conditions that supported successful coaching implementation in the Puerto Rico pilot: "Fewer classes assigned to the coach", "Commitment from school leaders to the coaching work", and "Enthusiasm from teachers about the coaching work". These conditions emerged from the pilot's evaluation of coaches, teachers, and leaders and informed leaders' proposals for new academic structures giving participating educators fewer classes for professional development time.
requirements: School structures must allow participating coaches fewer assigned classes to make time for coaching work
target_learners: Instructional coaches (MRUC technology resource teachers)
School leaders
target_learning_goals: Successful implementation of instructional coaching for technology integration
examples: School leaders wanted to propose new academic structures to the Department of Education where pre-selected educators in special projects would have fewer classes assigned to provide more time for professional development
key_sources: Carol Lopez and Odelia Younge. (2021). Cultivating a Culture of Coaching to Support Powerful Use of Technology: Results from the Challenge-based Coaching Model Pilot in Puerto Rico. Digital Promise report. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/71c26d6b-e789-4ca3-b643-dcc98422a36d

article_title: Improving Access to Interactive, Mother-Tongue Digital Science Content for Early Grade Learners in Rural Haiti
citation: Suzanne Cole, Blue Butterfly; April Williamson, Digital Promise. (2024). Improving Access to Interactive, Mother-Tongue Digital Science Content for Early Grade Learners in Rural Haiti. https://digitalpromise.org/haiti
title: Three-component pilot model combining infrastructure and technology, Creole digital content, and professional development with coaching
description: The pilot model organizes implementation into three components. Infrastructure & Technology includes "Solar power & internet connectivity for rural schools," "Tablets for coaches, teachers & students," and classroom speakers. Digital Content comprises "Standards-aligned, culturally relevant, interactive teaching & learning applications in Haitian Creole." Professional Development includes "Teacher training on pedagogy, content knowledge & technology" and "Ongoing classroom observations & coaching." A Monitoring, Evaluation & Learning strand measures impact using qualitative and quantitative methods.
requirements: Local partner capacity for infrastructure management; funding for solar and connectivity expansion
constraints: 57 of 70 schools used offline resources only; infrastructure expansion is pending funding
target_learners: Early grade primary students and teachers in rural Haitian schools
target_learning_goals: Blended learning implementation
improved learning outcomes in Creole science content
examples: 70 schools participated: 13 received solar power, 13 received internet connectivity, and 57 used offline resources only, across Gonayiv, Mibalè, Lagonav, and Pòsali
key_sources: Suzanne Cole, Blue Butterfly; April Williamson, Digital Promise. (2024). Improving Access to Interactive, Mother-Tongue Digital Science Content for Early Grade Learners in Rural Haiti. https://digitalpromise.org/haiti

article_title: Funding Coaching is Not Enough: The Role of the District Administrator in Coaching
citation: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Adopt a research-backed coaching model aligned with district goals that specifies roles and targeted outcomes
description: The report recommends that district leaders adopt an explicit coaching model that states the vision and targeted outcomes of coaching plus the roles and responsibilities of coaches, school leaders, and teachers. Without such a model, "coaches may not know where to focus their efforts, and teachers may misunderstand the coaches' role." The authors report the framework supports coach clarity, positive teacher-coach relationships, and strategic program planning.
requirements: The model must explicitly include the vision and targeted outcomes of coaching and the roles and responsibilities of coaches, school leaders, and teachers
Stakeholders such as curriculum and technology teams, building administrators, coaches, and teachers should be included in decision-making
target_learners: K-12 teachers
instructional coaches
school and district administrators
target_learning_goals: improved teacher practice
strategic implementation of coaching programs
examples: A coach in the study explained that adopting an explicit model "has allowed everyone on the team to be on the same page. We now have a common language and set of expectations."
key_sources: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/89f20796-22b4-44c1-889c-cc2fd46a19a2

article_title: Funding Coaching is Not Enough: The Role of the District Administrator in Coaching
citation: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Protect coaches', principals', and teachers' time for coaching from unrelated duties and oversized caseloads
description: The report recommends that districts safeguard the time coaches and teachers spend together so they can consistently plan, implement new strategies, and reflect, and that coaches and principals get adequate time for consistent collaboration. Districts should verify before assigning unrelated tasks that coaches "will still have adequate time to meet with teachers and visit classrooms," since other duties and large caseloads diminish coaching impact.
requirements: Teachers must be assured that time spent with their coach is protected
Principals and coaches need a recurring standing meeting for consistent collaboration
target_learners: K-12 teachers
instructional coaches
school principals
target_learning_goals: sustained teacher-coach collaboration
implementation of new instructional strategies
examples: The report advises districts to encourage principals and coaches to set a recurring standing meeting and to check coaching-time availability before assigning non-coaching tasks.
key_sources: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/89f20796-22b4-44c1-889c-cc2fd46a19a2

article_title: Funding Coaching is Not Enough: The Role of the District Administrator in Coaching
citation: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Foster a non-evaluative culture of coaching in which coaching is framed as continuous improvement, not evaluation
description: The report recommends that districts build a coaching culture in which teachers understand that reflection, practice, and feedback opportunities exist "without any evaluative purpose." Suggested actions include consistently communicating that coaching is for continuous improvement rather than evaluation, recognizing participating teachers, and celebrating bright spots and sharing teacher testimonials.
requirements: Districts must consistently communicate that the purpose of coaching is continuous improvement, not evaluation
Leaders must be willing to model vulnerability and take personal responsibility for shortcomings
target_learners: K-12 teachers
instructional coaches
district administrators
target_learning_goals: teacher participation in coaching
continuous improvement of teaching practice
examples: One district hosted monthly breakfasts on each campus where all teachers who had been coached during the year shared ideas and strategies, which the report says removed misconceptions that coaching was punitive or only for novice teachers.
key_sources: Hardy, A., & Bakhshaei, M. (2021). Funding coaching is not enough: The role of the district administrator in instructional coaching. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/89f20796-22b4-44c1-889c-cc2fd46a19a2

article_title: Deepening Science Engagement With Challenge Based Learning: Research Report
citation: Iwatani, E., Means, B., Romero, M. R., & Vang, M. C. (2020). Deepening Science Engagement with Challenge Based Learning: Research Report. San Mateo, CA: Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Professional learning for student-centered science instruction should be experiential, sustained, and relationship-based rather than sporadic half-day sessions
description: The report argues that transforming teachers' values and behaviors toward student-centered instruction requires professional learning that builds on existing expertise, is experiential and affective, professionally relevant, organized around value-laden goals, provides sustained critical reflection, and is founded on authentic relationships. Sporadic half-day sessions are deemed insufficient to overcome over-reliance on teacher-directed transmission.
requirements: Significant experiential component
Leadership support
Modeling of the target instructional approach
Ongoing learning community
Multiple iterations with feedback and reflection
constraints: Not all professional development can or should be as extended and participant-centered as this project's model
target_learners: middle school science teachers
target_learning_goals: student-centered NGSS-aligned instruction
challenge based learning implementation
examples: The project used two multi-day design workshops with participatory observation, reflection opportunities, and district-level instructional and emotional support
key_sources: Iwatani, E., Means, B., Romero, M. R., & Vang, M. C. (2020). Deepening Science Engagement with Challenge Based Learning: Research Report. San Mateo, CA: Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f928a607-e645-49d6-abbf-3d9b42cf7383

article_title: GADRRS: Guidance and Agreement for Data Harmony, Responsibility, Retention, and Sharing
citation: Lastinger Center for Learning, University of Florida. (2024). Guidance and Agreement for Data harmony, Responsibility, Retention, and Sharing (GADRRS). https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/
title: Tailor shared student data narrowly to what is essential for the authorized purpose
description: The agreement requires that disclosure of education records be for an education purpose and that access be narrowly tailored so that personally identifiable information is disclosed only as essential to carry out the evaluation, study, project, service, or program. It operationalizes this through checkbox exhibits listing Industry-Standard Data, Additional Data, and Excluded Data, so parties enumerate exactly which fields transfer. This gives education agencies a concrete mechanism for minimum-necessary data sharing when outsourcing services or research.
requirements: Parties must specify shared data in Exhibit D and may list excluded data; use of the data is limited to providing the Services under the agreement.
constraints: The article frames this within FERPA exceptions (Studies Exception and School Official exception); disclosure outside these exceptions is not addressed.
target_learners: K-12 students whose education records are shared
target_learning_goals: Protecting student privacy while enabling instructional improvement and authorized educational research
examples: Exhibit D Part 1 lists industry-standard fields such as names, IDs, demographics, and achievement measures, while Part 3 records data that will not be transferred.
key_sources: Lastinger Center for Learning, University of Florida. (2024). Guidance and Agreement for Data harmony, Responsibility, Retention, and Sharing (GADRRS). https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/

article_title: Human-Centred Development of Indicators for Self-Service Learning Analytics: A Transparency through Exploration Approach
citation: Joarder, S., & Chatti, M. A. (2026). Human-Centred Development of Indicators for Self-Service Learning Analytics: A Transparency through Exploration Approach. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 163-189. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.8921
title: Five design goals for user-controlled indicator implementation (interactive UI, datasets, filters, analysis, visualization)
description: The article derives five design goals (DG1–DG5) from the LA literature and the Goal-Question-Indicator approach: an interactive and exploratory UI, dataset exploration, data filters, analysis method selection, and visualization definition. Together they structure indicator creation as an iterative, step-by-step process where users "explore the datasets, apply filters, and choose the analysis and visualization methods."
requirements: The process should be iterative and exploratory, allowing users to go back and change previous decisions
constraints: Derived for basic statistical indicators, not ML-based ones
target_learners: students
teachers
target_learning_goals: implementing LA indicators that meet their needs and goals
examples: The final implementation uses a shopping cart checkout–like progression with accordion components, with subsequent steps disabled until previous ones are completed

article_title: Long-Term Impacts of KIPP Middle Schools on College Enrollment and Early College Persistence
citation: Thomas Coen, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Philip Gleason. (2019). Long-Term Impacts of KIPP Middle Schools on College Enrollment and Early College Persistence. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Use admissions lotteries at oversubscribed schools to estimate long-term school impacts with randomized treatment and control groups.
description: When a school is oversubscribed and allocates seats by lottery, the lottery creates a randomized controlled trial: students offered admission form the treatment group and non-offered applicants the control group. The article states this design ensures the groups are "similar on average" on observable characteristics such as prior test scores and unobservable characteristics such as motivation and parental support, supporting credible long-term impact estimates.
requirements: A school must be oversubscribed and use an admissions lottery so that offers are effectively randomly assigned among applicants
constraints: Applies to applicants of oversubscribed schools; estimates concern students who applied through the lottery, not all students
target_learners: K-12 students applying to oversubscribed charter middle schools
target_learning_goals: estimating school effects on long-run outcomes such as college enrollment
examples: The KIPP study used 5th or 6th grade admissions lotteries in 2008 or 2009 at 13 oversubscribed KIPP middle schools to form treatment and control groups
key_sources: Thomas Coen, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Philip Gleason. (2019). Long-Term Impacts of KIPP Middle Schools on College Enrollment and Early College Persistence. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/long-term-impacts-of-kipp-middle-schools-on-college-enrollment-and-early-college-persistence

article_title: An Impact that Lasts: KIPP Middle Schools Boost College Enrollment
citation: Thomas Coen, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Philip Gleason. (2019). An Impact that Lasts: KIPP Middle Schools Boost College Enrollment. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-impact-that-lasts-kipp-middle-schools-boost-college-enrollment
title: Use oversubscribed-school admissions lotteries to build randomized controlled trials for estimating long-term effects of attending a school of choice
description: When a school of choice has more applicants than seats, its admissions lottery can serve as the randomizer for a causal evaluation. The KIPP study 'uses a randomized controlled trial design to ensure' that students offered admission and students not offered admission 'are similar on average', on observable characteristics such as prior test scores and unobservable ones such as motivation and parental support, permitting unbiased long-term impact estimates.
requirements: The school must be oversubscribed, so that admission offers are determined by a lottery
Enough applicants must be tracked long enough for the outcome of interest to accrue
target_learners: Students applying to oversubscribed schools of choice, here 5th- and 6th-grade middle school applicants
target_learning_goals: Causal estimation of a school's effect on long-term outcomes such as four-year college enrollment
examples: The study followed 1,177 lottery applicants to 13 oversubscribed KIPP middle schools and compared students who received admission offers with those who did not
key_sources: Thomas Coen, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Philip Gleason. (2019). An Impact that Lasts: KIPP Middle Schools Boost College Enrollment. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-impact-that-lasts-kipp-middle-schools-boost-college-enrollment

article_title: Transforming Teachers' Practice: The Impact of EL Education's English Language Arts Curriculum and Professional Learning on Teacher Practices
citation: Jane Choi, Scott Richman, Sarah Dolfin. (2017). Transforming Teachers' Practice: The Impact of EL Education's English Language Arts Curriculum and Professional Learning on Teacher Practices. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Combine quality curriculum and professional learning so that teachers' instructional practices are directly aligned with the content they are teaching
description: The publication proposes combining a quality curriculum with professional learning as a pathway for developing teachers' practices under rigorous standards. It states that "A promising pathway is to combine quality curriculum and professional learning so that teachers' instructional practices are directly aligned with the content they are teaching." The study of EL Education's ELA curriculum and professional learning is presented as an instance of this approach.
requirements: Quality curriculum materials and professional learning must be combined so that instructional practices align with the content being taught
constraints: The publication characterizes this as a promising pathway whose effectiveness still requires further evidence
target_learners: K-12 teachers implementing rigorous state standards such as the Common Core State Standards
target_learning_goals: Aligning teachers' instructional practices with the content they teach to foster student skills needed for college and careers
examples: The study examines EL Education's English Language Arts curriculum and professional learning as a combined approach to transforming teacher practice

Transforming Teachers' Practice: The Impact of EL Education's English Language Arts Curriculum and Professional Learning on Teacher Practices. article_title: Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges
citation: Nan L. Maxwell and Ann E. Person, editors. (2016). Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Comprehensive community college reform packages three common elements: measurable student success, cohesive programmatic components, and a culture of evidence
description: The volume's reforms, spanning state, federal government, and foundation-sponsored initiatives, all emphasize three common elements. As the editors state, the reforms emphasize "a focus on measurable student success, an intentional and cohesive packaging of programmatic components to be implemented at scale, and a culture of evidence." This pattern describes how comprehensive reform is structured across institutional initiatives.
requirements: Reform must be implemented as an intentional and cohesive package of programmatic components rather than isolated pieces
constraints: The pattern is drawn from community college reform initiatives examined in the volume
target_learners: community college students
target_learning_goals: measurable student success outcomes
examples: The volume presents chapters examining several contemporary comprehensive reform efforts, including state and federal government and foundation-sponsored initiatives
key_sources: Nan L. Maxwell and Ann E. Person, editors. (2016). Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/comprehensive-reform-for-21st-century-success-new-directions-for-community-colleges

article_title: Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges
citation: Nan L. Maxwell and Ann E. Person, editors. (2016). Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Successful comprehensive reform requires executive leadership complemented by strong faculty involvement, guided by an explicit and shared vision for student success
description: Across the volume's chapters, the editors report that "a few components emerge as critical for the success of comprehensive reform efforts, in particular, executive leadership complemented by strong faculty involvement, guided by an explicit and shared vision for success." This principle directs reform designers to pair top-level leadership with faculty engagement around a common vision.
requirements: An explicit and shared vision for student success must guide the reform
target_learners: community college students
target_learning_goals: improved student success outcomes
examples: The editors synthesized this component from the original analyses presented across the volume's chapters
key_sources: Nan L. Maxwell and Ann E. Person, editors. (2016). Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/comprehensive-reform-for-21st-century-success-new-directions-for-community-colleges

article_title: Competency-Based Education in College Settings
citation: Ann Person. (2016). Competency-Based Education in College Settings. Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: CBE curriculum development was more collaborative and consistent than in traditional programs, relying on instructional designers and standardization tools
description: The evaluation found that CBE curriculum development differed from traditional program development: it "was more collaborative and consistent than in traditional programs and relied on instructional designers and tools to support standardization." This design pattern pairs faculty collaboration with dedicated instructional design staff and shared tools so that competencies, assessments, and course materials are consistent across a program. The brief reports this as a distinguishing implementation feature of the consortium's CBE programs.
requirements: Instructional designers and standardization tools to support consistent curriculum
Collaboration among curriculum developers
target_learners: college students in competency-based programs
target_learning_goals: job-aligned competencies delivered through standardized curricula
examples: The consortium relied on instructional designers and tools to support standardization of CBE curricula, per the evaluation's key findings
key_sources: Ann Person. (2016). Competency-Based Education in College Settings. Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/competency-based-education-in-focus

article_title: Implementation and Outcomes of Competency-Based Education in Three Community Colleges: Findings from the Comprehensive Evaluation of a TAACCCT Grant (Executive Summary)
citation: Person, A. E., Thomas, J., & Goble, L. (2016). Implementation and Outcomes of Competency-Based Education in Three Community Colleges: Findings from the Comprehensive Evaluation of a TAACCCT Grant (Executive Summary). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Offer competency-based education models as one of multiple options, since they appear best suited for mature, academically well-prepared students
description: Based on the evaluation, the authors recommend that "CBE models should be one of multiple options for college students, especially since they appear best suited for those who are mature and academically well prepared." Competency-based models let students move through material independently, advancing upon demonstrating content mastery, so they demand self-direction. The recommendation frames CBE as a complement to, not a replacement for, other course formats in community colleges.
requirements: Students need the maturity and academic preparation to move through material independently, advancing when they demonstrate content mastery.
constraints: The evaluation found CBE appears best suited for students who are mature and academically well prepared.
target_learners: community college students in online information technology programs
target_learning_goals: content mastery in career-relevant information technology programs of study
examples: The evaluation of online competency-based information technology programs at three community colleges informed this recommendation.
key_sources: Person, A. E., Thomas, J., & Goble, L. (2016). Implementation and Outcomes of Competency-Based Education in Three Community Colleges: Findings from the Comprehensive Evaluation of a TAACCCT Grant (Executive Summary). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/implementation-and-outcomes-of-competencybased-education-in-three-community-colleges-findings

article_title: Implementation of Competency-Based Education in Community Colleges: Findings from the Evaluation of a TAACCCT Grant
citation: Ann E. Person, Lisbeth Goble, Julie Bruch, Jessie Mazeika. (2015). Implementation of Competency-Based Education in Community Colleges: Findings from the Evaluation of a TAACCCT Grant. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Provide enhanced learner supports such as academic coaching, pacing charts, and just-in-time interventions to help students succeed in independent, often remote CBE courses
description: Because CBE courses and programs require students to work through their academic programs "independently and often remotely," the report recommends enhanced learner supports. It names academic coaching, pacing charts, and just-in-time interventions as supports that "can help students succeed." This principle arises from the consortium's implementation experience rather than from an experimental test.
requirements: Programs deliver content that students work through independently and often remotely, so supports must reach students outside a shared classroom schedule.
constraints: The report presents this as an implementation lesson from CBE programs, not as a tested intervention effect.
target_learners: Community college students in online competency-based education programs, including dislocated and low-skilled workers
target_learning_goals: Completion of CBE courses and programs through self-paced, remote study
examples: The consortium colleges implementing the WGU model under the TAACCCT grant developed student supports as part of curriculum delivery, examined under the evaluation's student supports strand.

article_title: Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings
citation: Luke Heinkel, Kristin Hallgren, Brian Gill, Megan Shoji. (2015). Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Process or analyze postsecondary data beyond raw form before using them to inform K-12 policy and practice
description: This principle holds that K-12 officials should not rely on raw postsecondary data extracts alone when trying to inform policy and practice. The brief's key findings state directly that "additional processing or analysis of postsecondary data is required to use these data in more sophisticated ways." The brief presents this processing step as the bridge between descriptive reporting and the three sophisticated analytic uses it describes.
requirements: Access to postsecondary outcomes data on former students, such as through the National Student Clearinghouse StudentTracker for High Schools
Analytic capacity to process or analyze the raw data beyond descriptive reporting
target_learners: K-12 state, district, and school officials
target_learning_goals: Using postsecondary outcomes data to inform K-12 policy and practice
examples: The brief's key findings list additional processing or analysis as the requirement for moving from descriptive use to sophisticated use of postsecondary data
key_sources: Luke Heinkel, Kristin Hallgren, Brian Gill, Megan Shoji. (2015). Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/making-effective-use-of-postsecondary-data-in-k-12-education-settings

article_title: Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings
citation: Luke Heinkel, Kristin Hallgren, Brian Gill, Megan Shoji. (2015). Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Disseminate postsecondary data to engage K-12 stakeholders
description: This principle addresses the communication side of postsecondary data use in K-12 settings. The brief's key findings state that "dissemination of postsecondary data is important for engaging stakeholders," and the brief's stated structure includes a section that discusses the importance of dissemination alongside its treatment of raw-data uses and sophisticated analyses. Dissemination is thus presented as a distinct, necessary component of effective data use, not merely an afterthought to analysis.
requirements: Postsecondary outcomes data that have been processed or analyzed for K-12 use
Channels for sharing findings with state, district, and school stakeholders
target_learners: K-12 state, district, and school officials
target_learning_goals: Engaging stakeholders through dissemination of postsecondary outcomes data
examples: The brief devotes one of its three stated parts to discussing the importance of dissemination of postsecondary data
key_sources: Luke Heinkel, Kristin Hallgren, Brian Gill, Megan Shoji. (2015). Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/making-effective-use-of-postsecondary-data-in-k-12-education-settings

article_title: Best Practices in Competency-Based Education: Lessons from Three Colleges (In Focus Brief)
citation: Ann Person. (2015). Best Practices in Competency-Based Education: Lessons from Three Colleges (In Focus Brief). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Let time vary while holding competencies fixed, inverting the traditional fixed-time model
description: The brief's organizing design principle is that students master required competencies while "the time a student takes to demonstrate each competency may vary." It explicitly contrasts this with traditional models "in which different students may experience different learning outcomes, but they all spend a fixed amount of time in each course."
requirements: Clearly defined and measurable competencies that students must demonstrate
constraints: The brief presents this as a defining feature and contrast, not as a tested effect
target_learners: Community college students in flexibly paced programs
target_learning_goals: Demonstration of defined competencies at individually varying pace
examples: The consortium colleges implemented flexibly paced CBE programs in information technology under a TAACCCT grant
key_sources: Ann Person. (2015). Best Practices in Competency-Based Education: Lessons from Three Colleges (In Focus Brief). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/best-practices-in-competencybased-education-lessons-from-three-colleges

article_title: Impact Evaluation of the RWJF Summer Medical and Dental Education Program (SMDEP)
citation: Clemencia Cosentino, Cecilia Speroni, Margaret Sullivan, Raúl Torres. (2015). Impact Evaluation of the RWJF Summer Medical and Dental Education Program (SMDEP). Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Multi-site pipeline program with mixed component offerings across sites
description: SMDEP is implemented as a single program model across "12 sites across the nation," with variation in offerings: "Three sites offer only the program's medical component, whereas the others offer both the medical and dental components." This multi-site structure with site-level component variation is the implementation pattern the evaluation documents across sites.
requirements: National multi-site delivery with consistent core program features across sites
constraints: Component offerings vary by site, with three sites medical-only
target_learners: Rising college sophomores and juniors interested in medical or dental careers
target_learning_goals: Science enrichment and professional school preparation

article_title: Determinants of Students' Success: The Role of Advanced Placement and Dual Enrollment Programs
citation: Cecilia Speroni. (2011). Determinants of Students' Success: The Role of Advanced Placement and Dual Enrollment Programs. National Center for Postsecondary Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Offer dual enrollment on college campuses rather than exclusively on the high school campus to support college access
description: The study's findings support locating dual enrollment courses on college campuses: only students who took "dual enrollment classes on college campuses" showed higher college-going and bachelor's degree attainment, while students who took "these classes exclusively on the high school campus showed no statistically significant gains." The article's summary presents the campus setting as the operative difference between the participating groups.
requirements: Dual enrollment courses must be taken on a college campus for the positive impacts to be expected, per the study's contrast between campus settings.
constraints: The evidence is observational, comparing participants with similar non-participants rather than randomly assigned students; no significant gains were found for the high-school-campus setting.
target_learners: high school seniors
target_learning_goals: college enrollment
bachelor's degree attainment
examples: The study tracked all of Florida's 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 high school seniors and compared dual enrollment participants by course location.

article_title: Teacher Career Paths, Teacher Quality, and Persistence in the Classroom: Are Public Schools Keeping Their Best?
citation: Dan Goldhaber, Betheny Gross, Daniel Player. (2011). Teacher Career Paths, Teacher Quality, and Persistence in the Classroom: Are Public Schools Keeping Their Best? Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, vol. 30, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Early-career teacher retention pattern: quality-graded sorting across the effectiveness distribution
description: The article describes a retention pattern in which the teachers who stay are, on average, the more effective ones: "more effective teachers remain in the profession and stay in their initial schools." At the same time, the pattern is not uniform, since "there appears to be heterogeneity in mobility behavior across the performance distribution," and mobility is also shaped by the student demographics and achievement levels of teachers' schools. The pattern therefore combines a positive average quality-retention gradient with context-dependent exceptions.
requirements: Teacher quality must be measured (here via value-added) to place teachers on the performance distribution
constraints: Pattern is documented for early-career public school teachers and is heterogeneous across the performance distribution
target_learners: early-career public school teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and managing teacher retention and quality
examples: The study tracks whether public schools keep their more effective early-career teachers, in the profession and in their initial schools
key_sources: Dan Goldhaber, Betheny Gross, Daniel Player. (2011). Teacher Career Paths, Teacher Quality, and Persistence in the Classroom: Are Public Schools Keeping Their Best? Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, vol. 30, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/teacher-career-paths-teacher-quality-and-persistence-in-the-classroom-are-public-schools-keeping-their-best

article_title: The Unknown World of Charter High Schools
citation: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2010). The Unknown World of Charter High Schools. Education Next, vol. 10, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Evaluate charter high schools on attainment outcomes such as diploma completion and college attendance, not test scores alone
description: The article argues that attainment outcomes should anchor evaluations of charter high schools because of their downstream stakes: "Given the impact of educational attainment on a variety of economic and social outcomes, a positive result could have significant implications for the value of school-choice programs that include charter high schools." The study therefore measures standard diploma receipt and college attendance rather than relying solely on achievement tests.
requirements: Longitudinal data linking high school attendance records to later diploma receipt and college enrollment
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in the authors' framing of attainment's economic and social importance, not in a tested comparison of evaluation methods
target_learners: high school students in schools of choice
target_learning_goals: high school completion
college attendance
examples: The study measured the likelihood of earning a standard diploma and of attending college as its primary outcomes for charter high school attendees in Chicago and Florida
key_sources: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2010). The Unknown World of Charter High Schools. Education Next, vol. 10, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-unknown-world-of-charter-high-schools

article_title: Achievement and Attainment in Chicago Charter Schools
citation: Kevin Booker, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer, Tim R. Sass. (2008). Achievement and Attainment in Chicago Charter Schools. Santa Monica, CA: RAND. https://www.rand.org
title: Evaluate charter schools on long-term attainment outcomes, not test scores alone
description: The report recommends that school evaluations extend beyond achievement test scores to long-term attainment measures such as high-school graduation and college entry, because its own large positive attainment results "demonstrate that evaluations limited to test scores may fail to capture important benefits of charter schools." It presents itself as the first report to examine charter effects on long-term attainment, including high-school graduation and college entry.
requirements: Evaluation designs must track long-term attainment outcomes such as high-school graduation and college entry, in addition to test scores
constraints: The recommendation rests on findings for Chicago's multi-grade charter high schools; no effect sizes are printed in the supplied text
target_learners: K-12 students in charter schools
target_learning_goals: Accurate evaluation of school effects on student attainment
examples: The report examined high-school graduation and college entry as attainment outcomes for Chicago charter schools, in addition to ACT scores
key_sources: Kevin Booker, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer, Tim R. Sass. (2008). Achievement and Attainment in Chicago Charter Schools. Santa Monica, CA: RAND. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/achievement-and-attainment-in-chicago-charter-schools

article_title: Upward Bound Math-Science Program: Description and Interim Impact Estimates
citation: Robert B. Olsen, Neil Seftor, Tim Silva, David Myers, David DesRoches, Julie Young. (2007). Upward Bound Math-Science Program: Description and Interim Impact Estimates. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Hands-on math-science exposure pattern: labs, computer facilities, field sites, and scientist contact
description: The UBMS design pattern combines practical STEM settings with expert contact: grantees "provide participants with hands-on experience in laboratories, computer facilities, and at field sites, as well as opportunities to learn from mathematicians and scientists at host institutions." The report presents this as the program's core design for building skills and experiences that prepare disadvantaged students for college success in math and science fields.
requirements: Host institutions (colleges and universities) with laboratories, computer facilities, and field sites
Access to mathematicians and scientists at host institutions
constraints: Implemented within the federal Upward Bound grant structure for disadvantaged high school students
target_learners: Disadvantaged high school students
target_learning_goals: Math and science preparation for college
Career exposure to mathematicians and scientists
examples: By 2004, 127 UBMS projects operated at colleges and universities serving nearly 7,000 students

article_title: A Study of the Effect of Talent Search on Secondary and Postsecondary Outcomes in Florida, Indiana, and Texas
citation: Jill M. Constantine, Neil S. Seftor, Emily Sama Martin, Tim Silva, David Myers. (2006). A Study of the Effect of Talent Search on Secondary and Postsecondary Outcomes in Florida, Indiana, and Texas. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Assist low-income students to overcome information barriers to college access
description: The report concludes that providing low-income students with practical college-access information supports their college aspirations. It states that "assisting low-income students to overcome information barriers may be effective in helping them achieve their aspirations to attend college," identifying guidance on financial aid and admission applications and campus orientation as key services.

constraints: The report frames this as a suggestion based on quasi-experimental findings from three states, not a tested causal decomposition of program components

First-generation college-going students

Financial aid application skills
College application skills

article_title: Towards More Transparency in Learning Analytics: Sharing Information with University Students Increases Their Awareness of Data Collection Practices
citation: Stoo Sepp. (2025). Towards More Transparency in Learning Analytics: Sharing Information with University Students Increases their Awareness of Data Collection Practices. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 34–46. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8713
title: Disclose to students both what data is collected and who has access to it, including third-party vendors
description: The article recommends that educational institutions provide transparency about learning analytics data collection as a practical ethical step, stating "Educational organizations should thus work to provide more transparency around the details of what data is collected about students as well as who has access to it." Disclosure statements should cover not only what is collected but which parties have access, including listing the names and locations of third-party vendors, so that students can give informed consent and institutions build more trusting relationships.
requirements: Disclosure statements must be detailed rather than generic, since only non-generic disclosures increased understanding
Disclosure should name which parties have access to the data, including third-party vendors and private companies
constraints: Disclosure alone did not change acceptance of data collection or opinions on who should have access, so transparency by itself does not shift attitudes
target_learners: university students in online and technology-supported courses
target_learning_goals: awareness of learning analytics data collection practices
informed consent regarding educational data use
examples: Participants saw one of three disclosure formats from a fictional University of Australia: a generic vague statement, a detailed text statement, or an icon-based nutrition label mimicking mobile app store disclosures

article_title: Balancing Act: Early, Fair, and Accurate Identification of At-Risk Students
citation: Alison Cheng, Bo Pei and Cheng Liu. (2025). Balancing Act: Early, Fair, and Accurate Identification of At-Risk Students. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 47–65. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8761
title: Incorporate fairness evaluation mechanisms into early at-risk student identification processes
description: The article recommends that at-risk identification practices, which traditionally emphasize early intervention and accuracy, should systematically evaluate fairness across demographic groups alongside predictive performance. It reports that "the findings also support the practice of incorporating fairness evaluation mechanisms into the process of identifying at-risk students", improving educator awareness of disparate impacts on underrepresented groups. This involves monitoring prediction rates and error types such as true positive and false negative rates across subgroups rather than pursuing overall accuracy alone.
requirements: Fairness metrics (e.g., demographic parity, equal opportunity differences) computed alongside performance metrics at each identification stage
Examination of prediction rates across demographic subgroups
constraints: Fairness metric choice depends on educational context, stakeholder goals, and normative beliefs; different metrics can yield divergent conclusions
target_learners: High school students, particularly those from historically underrepresented groups
target_learning_goals: Equitable and timely identification of students needing academic support
examples: The study evaluated four fairness metrics across three course stages and three protected features, and applied ThresholdOptimizer post-processing to reduce bias while maintaining balanced accuracy
key_sources: Alison Cheng, Bo Pei and Cheng Liu. (2025). Balancing Act: Early, Fair, and Accurate Identification of At-Risk Students. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 47–65. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8761

article_title: Privacy in LA Research: Understanding the Field to Improve the Practice
citation: Olga Viberg, Chantal Mutimukwe, Åke Grönlund. (2022). Privacy in LA Research: Understanding the Field to Improve the Practice. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 169–182. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7751
title: Define privacy explicitly in LA research and practice to enable responsible use of student data
description: The article's central design recommendation is that privacy must be explicitly defined before privacy-protecting models and tools can be built, because "poorly implemented frameworks for privacy protection may negatively impact LA outcomes and undermine trust in the discipline." Defining privacy in principle is not enough: specific situations must be operationalized through specifications of information content, flows, and access. The Smith et al. framework provides common ground for such situation-specific discussions.
requirements: A clear definition of privacy in the targeted study setting before designing privacy mechanisms
constraints: Privacy is not a simple checklist but concerns data handling in depth and detail; what privacy means differs across stakeholders and contexts
target_learners: learning analytics researchers
educational institutions
LA system developers
target_learning_goals: responsible, trust-preserving use of student data for analysis and decision-making
examples: The review shows 74% of LA articles omit definitions; the authors argue this gap slows effective data-driven decision-making in education
key_sources: Olga Viberg, Chantal Mutimukwe, Åke Grönlund. (2022). Privacy in LA Research: Understanding the Field to Improve the Practice. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 169–182. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7751

article_title: Causal Inference and Bias in Learning Analytics: A Primer on Pitfalls Using Directed Acyclic Graphs
citation: Weidlich, J., Gašević, D., Drachsler, H. (2022). Causal Inference and Bias in Learning Analytics: A Primer on Pitfalls Using Directed Acyclic Graphs. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 183–199. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7577
title: Use DAGs at the design stage of a study to decide which variables to control for and which to leave uncontrolled
description: The article recommends constructing a DAG before data collection so that decisions about when to control, what to control for, and when to avoid control can be derived by inspecting the graph. It notes that "statistical controlling for a variable requires that it has been measured in some way, highlighting the need for working with DAGs in the design stage of a research study." This principled approach replaces indiscriminate inclusion of correlated covariates, which the article calls garbage-can regression.
requirements: Variables considered for statistical control must be measured, so control decisions must be made before data collection
constraints: Statistical control's bias-reducing utility is proportional to the validity and reliability of the confounder's measurement
target_learners: learning analytics researchers
educational data mining researchers
target_learning_goals: designing studies that support valid causal inference about learning interventions
examples: In the dashboard example, tracing back-door paths showed controlling for SRL would block both open paths while controlling for study behaviour alone would not
key_sources: Weidlich, J., Gašević, D., Drachsler, H. (2022). Causal Inference and Bias in Learning Analytics: A Primer on Pitfalls Using Directed Acyclic Graphs. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 183–199. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7577

article_title: The Science Student Electronic Exit Ticket (SEET) System: Visualizations to Help Teachers Notice and Reflect on Classroom Inequalities
citation: Ali Raza, Tamara Sumner and William R. Penuel. (2024). The Science Student Electronic Exit Ticket (SEET) System: Visualizations to Help Teachers Notice and Reflect on Classroom Inequalities. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(1), 87-100. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8199
title: Design equity visualizations that embody simplicity and familiarity while providing access to disaggregated data
description: Because teachers underused the equity visualizations in favor of easier whole class displays, the article argues that designers need "further investigation into new visualization types that embody simplicity and familiarity while still providing access to finer-grained data on student participation by race/ethnicity and gender." The principle holds that ease-of-use, familiarity, and simplicity are prerequisites for adoption of learning analytics visualizations in practice, and that equity visualizations must reconcile this with their necessarily more complex data types. Trust is flagged as an important attribute for visualizations displaying sensitive data.
requirements: Visualization types familiar to teachers, such as bar and line charts, or supports that build visualization literacy
constraints: Equity visualizations necessarily embody more complex data types, suggesting new visualization literacies may be needed
target_learners: K-12 science teachers
target_learning_goals: sustained teacher use of equity analytics to reflect on instructional practice
examples: The disaggregated bar chart was ranked the most preferred of the equity visualizations, consistent with teachers' familiarity with bar charts

article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students
citation: Usher, A., Mahaffie, S., & Nagaoka, J. (2023). The educational attainment of Chicago Public Schools students: 2022. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/tool/cps/
title: Interpret disaggregated attainment data within the context of structural oppression and use it to question what can be done to change inequitable outcomes
description: The report disaggregates attainment data by race/ethnicity and gender, disability status, and English Learner status "to understand which students face more barriers to educational attainment and where different strategies and supports are needed." It urges readers to examine these rates within the context of systemic racism and to move beyond asking why disparities exist toward questioning what can be done, both within and outside education, to change them.
requirements: Readers should examine disaggregated rates while moving through stages of questioning needed to affect change, informed by research on systemic racism in Chicago's schools
constraints: The report lacks information on students pursuing non-college pathways such as workforce or military, and its race/ethnicity and gender categories are limited by the data CPS collects; rates for groups of fewer than 100 students are suppressed
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools students
target_learning_goals: Fostering equitable educational outcomes and disrupting policies contributing to inequitable outcomes
examples: The report recommends readers interrogate how disparities in attainment are due to issues of equity within the district and higher education institutions
key_sources: Usher, A., Mahaffie, S., & Nagaoka, J. (2023). The educational attainment of Chicago Public Schools students: 2022. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/tool/cps/

article_title: Standards-Driven Instructional Improvement
citation: New research: Chicago showed instructional improvements under standards reform, while many other places did not. (2022). UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Invest in teachers' learning, collaboration, and experimentation as the central lever for standards-driven instructional change
description: This principle holds that large-scale instructional change under new learning standards is achieved primarily by investing in teachers' own learning rather than by supplying curricula or ready-made materials. The release quotes report author Elaine M. Allensworth: "These findings point to the importance of investing in teachers’ learning, collaboration, and experimentation." It further states that large-scale instructional change is possible "when key supports are in place, but they have to be the right supports." In the study, professional learning — collaboration, coaching, and workshops — was the most important support strategy, and resources worked only when instruction-ready and tied to professional learning.
requirements: Professional learning supports must be in place, including teacher collaboration, coaching, and workshops
Instructional resources, if used, must be instruction-ready and tied to professional learning around instructional practices
constraints: The release notes that ready-made resources and particular curricula — levers policymakers often turn to — did not connect to changes in instruction and outcomes in this study
target_learners: K-12 students in mathematics and science classrooms in a large urban district
target_learning_goals: Standards-aligned instructional practices in mathematics and science
Improved student achievement in math and science
examples: Chicago Public Schools promoted change in math and science instruction aligned with CCSS-M and NGSS between 2014-15 and 2017-18 using districtwide surveys, interviews, and achievement data

The article states: "We apply math and reading college readiness benchmarks to rich longitudinal data for more than 360,000 students across the nation." It serves equity diagnosis by identifying who falls off track and when.

Student-level and school-level demographic data to model trajectory predictors

article_title: Identifying Students Who Are Off-Track Academically in 9th Grade: The Role of Social-Emotional Learning Trajectories
citation: Soland, J. & Kuhfeld, M. (2019). Identifying students who are off-track academically in 9th Grade: the role of social-emotional learning trajectories. (NWEA Collaborative for Student Growth Research Brief). https://www.nwea.org
title: SEL status-and-growth framework: middle school SEL constructs as developmental trajectories predicting 9th-grade off-track status
description: This framework treats social-emotional learning constructs (academic growth mindset, self-efficacy, self-management) as developmental processes with their own growth trajectories, asking "whether a student's mean SEL score in 6th grade (status) or growth between 6th through 8th grade is more predictive of being off track academically in 9th grade." The article operationalizes it with latent growth curve models, in which "the random intercept reflects the average 6th grade score and the latent growth factor represents the linear change between 6th and 8th grade." Status and growth factors are then used as predictors of 9th-grade off-track indicators.
requirements: Multiple waves of longitudinal SEL measures scored on a common metric (IRT scoring with tested longitudinal measurement invariance)
At least three data waves, which constrained the article to a linear growth trajectory
constraints: Findings come from a single urban, high-poverty district with many English learners and may not generalize to other settings
Only four years of survey data were available, so three years were used and nonlinear functional forms could not be tested
Measures are student self-report surveys, which may suffer from self-report and social desirability biases
target_learners: Middle school students (grades 6-8) in urban, high-poverty districts
target_learning_goals: Social-emotional competencies (growth mindset, self-efficacy, self-management) as indicators for identifying students off track to graduate
examples: The district administered spring SEL surveys each year; DIF analyses found no problematic differential functioning across grade comparisons before IRT calibration and scoring

It treats evidence as seldom unitary, with 'aspects that are more central and well-supported and aspects that are more thinly developed or in need of further investigation', and frames evidence use as a multi-step process spanning acceptability, adoption, implementation planning, and continuous improvement.

district decision makers

title: Trails Up a Mountain: stakeholder-specific evidence paths toward a shared peak
description: Trails Up a Mountain is a workshop visualization depicting 'different paths along a journey (or climb) to related destinations', recognizing that technology developers, school procurement leaders, and researchers each use evidence in different ways at different times. Unlike a strict tier ladder, it preserves the idea of a desirable peak of evidence that all perspectives are climbing towards, while allowing evidence journeys to intersect at key moments or conversations.
requirements: Requires recognizing that evidence needed for decision-making varies by audience and that each group's criteria must be considered by the others
constraints: The article notes researchers and practitioners often operate under different evidentiary standards, illustrated by disagreement over simulated-student evidence

technology developers
researchers
target_learning_goals: Aligning evidence generation and use across stakeholder roles
examples: School leaders might start by finding out what is working at schools like mine, while developers might start from proof of concept of a learning-process improvement

article_title: Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies
citation: Roschelle, J., Ruiz, P., Means, B., Griffiths, R., Lee, K. (2026 April). Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/289
title: The Stacks: parallel dimensions of process, usage, and outcomes evidence
description: The Stacks is a workshop visualization that 'allows for a small set of different, parallel dimensions of evidence rather than sequential levels'. The dimensions include process evidence revealing how students proceed through learning activities, usage evidence describing who uses the activities and how much, and outcomes evidence covering academic and durable skills. Unlike tier levels, evidence across stacks develops in parallel, and additional stacks such as safety and privacy can be added.
requirements: Requires methods complementary enough that different stakeholders can each find the evidence they require
constraints: An intervention does not necessarily progress through these dimensions as levels

edtech developers

title: EdTech Ladders and Chutes: evidence as feedback-and-improvement loops with setbacks
description: EdTech Ladders and Chutes is a workshop visualization in which evidence 'is not unidirectionally towards more or better but rather has the characteristic of feedback-and-improvement loops, which can include setbacks and require resilience'. A ladder is technology that enables acceleration; a chute is when evidence shows an innovation did not work as expected, requiring return to an earlier stage for redesign. It frames developers as needing to be part of an education ecosystem open to learning from both successes and failures.

article_title: AI in Education: A Set of Four Essential Resource Briefs for Educators

title: AI literacy framework: knowledge, skills, and dispositions for critically understanding, evaluating, and responsibly using AI
description: The briefs define AI literacy as "the knowledge, skills, and dispositions needed to critically understand, evaluate, and responsibly use AI systems in learning environments." The framework enumerates components for educators: identifying when AI is used, understanding how AI systems generate outputs, writing effective prompts, evaluating responses critically, recognizing bias and errors, and making informed instructional and ethical decisions. article_title: What States Say about Evaluating AI in Education
citation: Ruiz, P., Prado, Y., Roschelle, J., & Fusco, J. (2025). What States Say About Evaluating AI in Education: Reviewing Guidance From 32 States and Puerto Rico. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/280
title: Three-stage developmental framework for state AI-in-education evaluation efforts
description: The report organizes state AI evaluation guidance into three a priori refined developmental stages: Nascent and Exploratory (definitional, conceptual, exploratory activities like user feedback and vocabulary building), Emergent and Piloting (small-scale piloting of policies, practices, materials, and tools with user feedback and pre-procurement evidence checks), and Systematic and Evidentiary (larger-scale assessment of student outcome measures with continuous improvement cycles).
