Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. http://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/educational-attainment-chicago-public-schools-students-2015-focus-four-year-college

article_title: College Readiness Indicator Systems Resource Series
citation: Annenberg Institute for School Reform, Brown University; John W. Gardner Center for Youth and their Communities, Stanford University; & University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research. (2014). Beyond college eligibility: A new framework for promoting college readiness. College Readiness Indicator Systems Resource Series. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: CRIS Framework: a conceptual foundation linking college readiness indicators, supports, and a cycle of inquiry
description: The CRIS Framework provides a conceptual foundation for building college readiness indicator systems. It features indicators targeting academic preparedness, academic tenacity, and college knowledge across individual, setting, and system levels, with a Cycle of Inquiry connecting indicators to supports. The document states that "The Cycle of Inquiry constitutes the mechanism that connects indicators for each dimension and at each level with the appropriate supports." The framework sits within community, policy, and higher education contexts.

description: The CCSR noncognitive framework organizes research on concepts tied to academic success into five general categories: "academic behaviors, academic perseverance, social skills, learning strategies, and academic mindsets." It was designed to synthesize a vast research literature, clarify meanings, and reconcile disparities between researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds. In the framework, mindsets and learning strategies feed academic behaviors and perseverance, which together produce academic performance, all nested within school, socio-cultural, community, and policy contexts.

description: The report typologizes CPS seniors' overall schedules into five named coursetaking patterns: "Making Up Courses," "Vocationally Focused," "Elective Heavy," "Core Concentrators," and "Advanced Placement." The report states that "Their schedules fall into five distinct coursetaking patterns" and that these patterns are not simply a result of achievement differences, since similarly qualified seniors often take different schedules. The typology is used throughout to show that most seniors' schedules focus on completing graduation requirements rather than preparing for college.

It states: "For students who hope to attend college, senior year must be reinterpreted as more than the end of high school and should instead function as a bridge into college." Teachers and school leaders should collectively decide what skills and academic behaviors students need for postsecondary success and how these develop across grades nine through twelve. Coursework requirements alone do not address the low challenge of senior year courses.

description: The study organizes principal leadership effects through Bryk et al.'s framework of essential supports, in which "[the] framework of organizational supports for student learning starts with leadership as the driver for change" and leaders work across four domains: professional capacity of staff, learning climate, parent and community involvement, and ambitious instruction. description: A new school-level measure developed by the authors to capture whether teachers express shared goals, behaviors, and obligations regarding college attendance. The measure was constructed using Rasch rating scale analysis and represents the average of teacher reports in the high school. Approximately 4,000 teachers in 87 high schools responded.

title: College-going climate framework: two mechanisms by which high schools shape college enrollment
description: The article proposes that urban high schools shape college enrollment among low-income students through two mechanisms: (1) ensuring that seniors who aspire to a four-year degree take the steps to apply to and enroll in a four-year college, and (2) influencing whether students enroll in colleges with selectivity levels at or above the kinds of colleges they are qualified to attend (college match). This framework distinguishes between enrollment steps (planning, applying, acceptance, enrollment) and the quality of college choice (match/undermatch). It draws on Schneider's (2007) conceptualization that effective practice is embedded in school climate and shared norms rather than isolated counseling activities.

target_learning_goals: College aspiration follow-through

article_title: Potholes on the Road to College
citation: Roderick, M., Coca, V., & Nagaoka, J. (2011). Potholes on the Road to College: High School Effects in Shaping Urban Students' Participation in College Application, Four-year College Enrollment, and College Match. Sociology of Education, 84(3), 178-211. https://doi.org/10.1177/0038040711411280
title: Urban high schools should develop organizational norms and structures that guide students through the college application process to convert aspirations into four-year enrollment
description: The article argues that student qualifications and college aspirations alone are insufficient to produce four-year college enrollment; high schools must actively create norms, expectations, and concrete supports that guide students through planning, applying, gaining acceptance, and enrolling. This includes ensuring teachers hold high expectations, provide assistance outside class time, and embed college preparation across the curriculum rather than delegating it solely to counselors.
requirements: School-wide teacher buy-in and shared goals that all students can go to college
Concrete guidance on applications and financial aid
Organizational structures embedded in the academic program rather than isolated in the guidance department
constraints: The evidence is associational (HGLM with observational data), not causal; proxy measures of climate may partially reflect student composition rather than school practice
target_learners: Low-income urban high school seniors
First-generation college aspirants
target_learning_goals: Timely college application
FAFSA completion
Four-year college enrollment
College match
examples: The article's HGLM models found teacher assessment of college-going climate significantly associated with each enrollment step even after controlling for student qualifications and demographics
key_sources: Roderick, M., Coca, V., & Nagaoka, J. (2011). Potholes on the Road to College: High School Effects in Shaping Urban Students' Participation in College Application, Four-year College Enrollment, and College Match. Sociology of Education, 84(3), 178-211. https://doi.org/10.1177/0038040711411280

article_title: Passing Through Science
citation: Montgomery, N., & Allensworth, E. M., with Correa, M. (2010). Passing Through Science: The Effects of Raising Graduation Requirements in Science on Course-Taking and Academic Achievement in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/passing-through-science
title: Raising course requirements alone is insufficient to improve learning; policy must also address student engagement and the quality of classroom instruction
description: The report's central policy conclusion is that mandating course exposure changes transcripts but not learning: "Course content matters only when students are engaged in learning that content and are earning strong grades." In Chicago, most post-policy graduates earned Cs or lower in the new required science courses, suggesting minimal engagement and learning. The authors therefore argue that "policy solutions need to go beyond adding course requirements to address student engagement and the quality of classroom instruction in advanced science courses."
requirements: Schools must develop classroom instruction capable of advancing science learning in the required advanced courses, not merely schedule them.
constraints: The report grounds this in one policy, in one district, at one moment in time, in a setting where many students dropped out before benefiting from the requirements.
target_learners: All high school students subject to college-preparatory graduation requirements, including those with weak prior science preparation
target_learning_goals: Science content knowledge and college-preparatory science course completion
examples: CPS required three college-preparatory science courses beginning with 1997 ninth-graders; course completion more than doubled among graduates while most earned Cs or lower and college outcomes did not improve.
key_sources: Montgomery, N., & Allensworth, E. M., with Correa, M. (2010). Passing Through Science: The Effects of Raising Graduation Requirements in Science on Course-Taking and Academic Achievement in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/passing-through-science-effects-raising-graduation-requirements-science-course-taking

article_title: College Preparatory Curriculum for All
citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373709343471
title: Conceptual model of how curricular policy influences student outcomes through changes in the school's instructional program
description: The article proposes a conceptual model in which policy effects on academic outcomes must flow through changes in the school's instructional program: courses, content, and pedagogy. As the authors state, "any policy effects on students' academic outcomes must flow through changes in the instructional program of the school: the courses, content, and pedagogy that students receive." Enrollment combined with student response shapes ninth-grade learning, which in turn shapes later outcomes such as graduation and college enrollment. The model guided the study's three research questions distinguishing enrollment effects from total policy effects.
requirements: Schools' instructional programs must adjust to the policy as expected, and students must respond with better freshman-year performance, for beneficial effects to occur
constraints: Some schools may have difficulty enacting substantial changes in their instructional programs in ways that benefit students, and students who would otherwise take remedial classes may not respond as expected
target_learners: First-time ninth graders in urban public high schools
target_learning_goals: Ninth-grade academic performance in algebra and English, later high school achievement, graduation, and college enrollment
examples: The study traced the Chicago policy's effects through course enrollment changes, ninth-grade performance, and long-term outcomes including graduation and college enrollment
key_sources: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373709343471

article_title: College Preparatory Curriculum for All
citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373709343471
title: Universalizing college preparatory course work is unlikely to succeed without professional development, school-community support, and extra support for low-ability students
description: Drawing on the detracking literature, the article argues that a policy of universalizing college preparatory courses needs accompanying organizational supports. As the authors write, "a policy of universalizing college preparatory courses may have little chance of success if it does not address such issues as professional development around instruction, widespread support for the policy among the school community (teachers and parents), and extra support for low-ability students." Schools that detracked successfully shared staff belief in diversity, inclusive pedagogy from professional development, and supports such as extra support courses.
requirements: Professional development around instruction, widespread support among teachers and parents, and extra support courses for struggling students
constraints: Successful detracking schools' characteristics "seem to be exceptional"; resistance from parents, technical difficulties of teaching heterogeneous classrooms, and teachers' low expectations are common difficulties
target_learners: Ninth graders in comprehensive high schools, including low-ability students previously served by remedial tracks
target_learning_goals: Success in college preparatory course work in algebra and English
examples: Chicago's 1997 mandate ended remedial courses without the accompanying instructional supports the detracking literature identifies, and outcomes showed increased failure rates and no test-score gains
key_sources: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373709343471

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller. (2009). From High School to the Future: Making Hard Work Pay Off — The Road to College for Students in CPS's Academically Advanced Programs. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago, Urban Education Institute. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Five-part account of distinctive college-navigation challenges facing academically advanced first-generation students
description: The report draws on qualitative and quantitative analysis to identify five areas where academically advanced CPS students—most first-generation college students—face challenges in the college application process: not understanding the range of accessible colleges, lacking structured support for complicated applications to competitive colleges, competing demands from challenging coursework, and weak financial aid knowledge and participation. The report states "lack of knowledge of financial aid possibilities and lack of effective participation in financial aid prevent them from getting the aid they deserve." It argues high schools "must also fill the gaps in students'—and their parents'—understanding of college search, application, and selection."
requirements: High schools must provide specialized supports for college search and application beyond setting college-going expectations
constraints: The report states it is not intended to be a rigorous evaluation of the efficacy of selective enrollment schools, IB programs, or AP initiatives
target_learners: high-achieving high school students in selective enrollment, IB, and AP programs, most of whom are first-generation college students
target_learning_goals: navigating college search, application, selection, and financial aid
examples: The report compares the colleges students are qualified to attend with those to which they apply and enroll using CPS postsecondary tracking data, alongside qualitative analysis of the application process
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller. (2009). From High School to the Future: Making Hard Work Pay Off — The Road to College for Students in CPS's Academically Advanced Programs. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago, Urban Education Institute. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-future-making-hard-work-pay

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller. (2009). From High School to the Future: Making Hard Work Pay Off — The Road to College for Students in CPS's Academically Advanced Programs. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago, Urban Education Institute. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Benchmark advanced students' college outcomes by fully informed choice, not merely four-year attendance
description: The report recommends that for academically advanced students, schools and districts should measure success not by whether students attend any four-year college but by whether students and families make a fully informed choice among the wide range of accessible options. As it puts it, "our benchmark should be whether students and their families have made a fully informed college choice based on full knowledge of the wide range of college options available." This reframes college-going culture goals for high-achieving, largely first-generation populations.
requirements: High schools must fill gaps in student and parent understanding of college search, application, and selection, not only set college expectations
constraints: The report addresses a small group of programs and schools in CPS, though it argues lessons generalize as more schools build rigorous programs
target_learners: academically advanced high school students and their families
target_learning_goals: making informed college choices matched to qualifications
examples: The report urges practitioners building college-going cultures to meet the specific needs of academically advanced students rather than stopping at four-year enrollment
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller. (2009). From High School to the Future: Making Hard Work Pay Off — The Road to College for Students in CPS's Academically Advanced Programs. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago, Urban Education Institute. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-future-making-hard-work-pay

article_title: College Readiness for All
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, and Vanessa Coca. (2009). College Readiness for All: The Challenge for Urban High Schools. The Future of Children. https://www.futureofchildren.org
title: Four-pillar framework of college readiness skills
description: Drawing particularly on David Conley's work, the article defines college readiness through "four main areas of skill development that are critical in shaping college readiness: content knowledge and basic skills, core academic skills, non-cognitive skills and norms of performance, and 'college knowledge.'" Content knowledge is subject-specific; core academic skills such as writing and analytic thinking transfer across disciplines and are the areas where high school-college skill demands differ most; non-cognitive skills cover self-monitoring behaviors like study skills and time management; and college knowledge is the social-capital-based capacity to navigate admissions and financial aid. The article argues high schools must stress all four.
requirements: High schools must attend to all four skill areas rather than only the two commonly recognized ones
Schools must be explicit about which skills shape college access and how to measure them
constraints: The framework is developed for improving college access and readiness for low-income and minority students in urban high schools
target_learners: High school students, particularly low-income and minority students in urban high schools
target_learning_goals: College readiness across content knowledge, core academic skills, non-cognitive skills, and college knowledge
examples: The article distinguishes core academic skills from content knowledge using the American Diploma Project's English standards, which include writing, research, oral communication, and analytic thinking
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, and Vanessa Coca. (2009). College Readiness for All: The Challenge for Urban High Schools. The Future of Children. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/college-readiness-all-challenge-urban-high-schools

article_title: College Readiness for All
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, and Vanessa Coca. (2009). College Readiness for All: The Challenge for Urban High Schools. The Future of Children. https://www.futureofchildren.org
title: Districts and states should build data systems that link high school performance to graduates' college outcomes and set validated readiness standards
description: The article argues high schools cannot be held accountable for college readiness without knowing what happens to their graduates: "districts and states will require new feedback systems that both provide schools information on the college outcomes of their graduates and link their performance during high school with their college outcomes." Readiness standards must be validated at performance levels giving students a high probability of accessing four-year colleges, show where students stand, measure progress, and give clear improvement guidance.
requirements: New data systems linking high school indicators to actual college performance and outcomes
Readiness standards validated against outcomes such as credit-bearing course placement and degree attainment
Standards must allow districts to assess current standing, measure progress, and guide improvement
constraints: At present, no state uses its existing high school assessment system to benchmark college readiness, and only a few states have linked high school indicators to college performance
target_learners: High school students in urban districts, particularly low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: College readiness measurement, college access, and four-year college completion
examples: The authors developed readiness benchmarks from Chicago data, identifying an unweighted 3.0 GPA cutoff using National Student Clearinghouse outcomes
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, and Vanessa Coca. (2009). College Readiness for All: The Challenge for Urban High Schools. The Future of Children. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/college-readiness-all-challenge-urban-high-schools

article_title: Barriers to College Attainment
citation: Jenny Nagaoka, Melissa Roderick, and Vanessa Coca. (2008). Barriers to College Attainment: Lessons from Chicago. The Consortium on Chicago School Research at The University of Chicago / Center for American Progress. https://www.americanprogress.org
title: Three-category framework of college readiness skills: content knowledge and basic skills, core academic skills, and noncognitive skills and norms of performance
description: Drawing on David Conley's work on college readiness, the report identifies "three categories of skills that have been demonstrated as critical in determining college access, and more importantly, college performance." The first is basic skills in mathematics and reading plus content knowledge in core academic subjects. The second is core academic skills—"thinking, problem-solving, writing, and research skills" usable across subject areas. The third is noncognitive skills that let students manage new academic and social demands. The framework grounds the report's use of ACT scores and unweighted core-course GPAs as qualification measures.
requirements: Students must have basic skills and content knowledge, core academic skills, and noncognitive skills to move from high school to college-level work
target_learners: urban high school students, particularly low-income, minority, and first-generation college students
target_learning_goals: college readiness and preparation for college-level coursework
examples: The report operationalizes the framework using ACT scores and unweighted GPAs in core courses (English, mathematics, science, social science, and world language) rather than course completion requirements
key_sources: Jenny Nagaoka, Melissa Roderick, and Vanessa Coca. (2008). Barriers to College Attainment: Lessons from Chicago. The Consortium on Chicago School Research at The University of Chicago / Center for American Progress. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/barriers-college-attainment-lessons-chicago

article_title: College Preparatory Curriculum for All
citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Instructional-program mediation model of curriculum policy effects
description: A conceptual model (Figure 1) holding that a curriculum mandate affects student outcomes only through the school's instructional program: 'the courses, content, and pedagogy that students receive'. Enrollment depends on program structure and student background; courses and student response shape ninth-grade learning, which should translate into later achievement and postsecondary outcomes. Beneficial effects require schools to adjust instruction, students to respond, and early performance gains to persist.
requirements: Schools' instructional programs must adjust to the policy as expected
Students must respond to changing instruction with better freshman-year performance
Improved freshman performance must lead to better later outcomes
constraints: Some schools may have difficulty enacting substantial instructional changes, and students who would otherwise take remedial classes may not respond as expected
target_learners: All high school students, including low-ability and special education students
target_learning_goals: Ninth-grade math and English achievement, high school graduation, and college enrollment
examples: The study tested the model by tracing effects on 15 outcomes measured at the end of ninth grade and the end of high school
key_sources: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/college-preparatory-curriculum-all-consequences-ninth-grade-coursetaking-algebra-and

article_title: College Preparatory Curriculum for All
citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Universalizing college-preparatory coursework requires instructional support, school-community buy-in, and extra help for struggling students, not mandate alone
description: Drawing on detracking research, the article argues that simply mandating a common rigorous curriculum 'may have little chance of success' without professional development around instruction, widespread support among teachers and parents, and extra support courses for low-ability students. Schools that successfully detracked shared staff belief in diversity, inclusive pedagogy, and supports for struggling students. The Chicago evaluation's mixed outcomes illustrate the limits of a mandate without these accompanying conditions.
requirements: Professional development around instruction
Widespread support for the policy among teachers and parents
Extra support for low-ability students
constraints: Schools face resistance from parents, technical difficulties of teaching heterogeneous classrooms, and low teacher expectations
target_learners: High school students of all ability levels, particularly low-ability students in formerly remedial tracks
target_learning_goals: Rigorous coursework completion and achievement in heterogeneous college-preparatory classes
examples: Chicago implemented the 1997 mandate district-wide without the accompanying professional development and support conditions the detracking literature identifies
key_sources: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2008). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Consequences of Ninth-Grade Course Taking in Algebra and English on Academic Outcomes in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/college-preparatory-curriculum-all-consequences-ninth-grade-coursetaking-algebra-and

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: John Q. Easton, Stephen Ponisciak, Stuart Luppescu. (2008). From High School to the Future: The Pathway to 20. Research Report, Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: The Pathway to 20: prior achievement, school academic culture, and grades as the three determinants of ACT performance
description: This report frames college readiness as a trajectory measured by the EPAS sequence (EXPLORE, PLAN, ACT), in which ACT scores are influenced by "multiple factors—prior achievement as measured by test scores, the academic culture of high school, and the quality of student work in high school as measured by grades." Prior scores strongly predict outcomes but do not determine them; school culture (student-teacher trust, academic press, importance of high school, postsecondary expectations) and grades explain divergent outcomes among similar starters. The framework is used to position EXPLORE 17 as an interim benchmark and to argue elementary standards are misaligned with college readiness.
requirements: Matched longitudinal test-score data across the EPAS tests to track students' progress toward the ACT goal
constraints: The report addresses only selected aspects of academic culture (student-teacher trust, school-wide academic press for the future, importance of high school for the future, and expectations for postsecondary education) and only in relation to certain outcomes
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools high school students in grades 8-11
target_learning_goals: College readiness as measured by ACT composite performance
examples: CPS set a district-wide goal of an ACT composite of 20 and added the percentage scoring 20 or higher to high school score cards
key_sources: John Q. Easton, Stephen Ponisciak, Stuart Luppescu. (2008). From High School to the Future: The Pathway to 20. Research Report, Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-future-pathway-20

article_title: Small Schools on a Larger Scale
citation: Kahne, J. E., Sporte, S., de la Torre, M., with Easton, J. Q. (2006). Small High Schools on a Larger Scale: The First Three Years of the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/small-high-schools-larger-scale
title: CHSRI small schools theory of action
description: The report maps the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative's theory of action: district resources and policies create small voluntary schools with limited bureaucratic regulation, which foster a teacher context of "trust, collective responsibility, and teacher influence"; this context supports instructional-improvement activities leading to higher-quality instruction, while smaller personal environments plus shared curricular themes are expected to raise expectations and academic and personal support for students, ultimately improving outcomes. The report quantitatively tests Boxes 6 through 10 of this framework.
requirements: Appropriate district resources and policies to create the small schools
Balancing small school autonomy and flexibility with accountability and support from CHSRI staff and the district
constraints: The report examined only the theory elements assessable quantitatively (Boxes 6-10); qualitative work covered Boxes 1-5 but is not detailed in this report
target_learners: Low-income students of color in large urban public high schools, particularly Chicago ninth- and eleventh-graders
target_learning_goals: Improved attendance, on-track status, dropout prevention, and achievement test performance through supportive school contexts and instructional improvement
examples: The initiative converted three large underperforming high schools into twelve autonomous small schools between 2002 and 2004, sharing buildings but not administrative staff or discretionary funds
key_sources: Kahne, J. E., Sporte, S., de la Torre, M., with Easton, J. Q. (2006). Small High Schools on a Larger Scale: The First Three Years of the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/small-schools-larger-scale-first-three-years-chicago-high-school-redesign-initiative

article_title: Small Schools on a Larger Scale
citation: Kahne, J. E., Sporte, S., de la Torre, M., with Easton, J. Q. (2006). Small High Schools on a Larger Scale: The First Three Years of the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/small-high-schools-larger-scale
title: Small school reforms should pair supportive personal contexts with deliberate focus on instructional improvement to raise achievement
description: The report's central design implication is that creating small, personal, supportive school environments benefits teacher community and some engagement outcomes, but those conditions "do not appear to be spurring increased instructional reform activity, differing instructional practices, or improved student achievement test scores." District and initiative leaders therefore coordinated efforts to help small schools "focus more directly and productively on instructional improvement," since the authors suspect success there is essential to improving academic outcomes.
requirements: Small school structures alone are insufficient; a direct, sustained focus on instructional improvement is needed
Strong instructional leadership appears necessary for collaboration to alter instructional practices, per the Chicago qualitative work cited
constraints: Findings come from only the first three years of the reform, with only five schools operating the full three years, so broad efficacy claims were premature
target_learners: Students in newly created or converted urban small high schools serving low-performing, high-mobility populations
target_learning_goals: Translating improved school climate into improved instruction and academic achievement
examples: In response to the null achievement findings, district leaders coordinated with CHSRI staff to help schools focus on instructional improvement
key_sources: Kahne, J. E., Sporte, S., de la Torre, M., with Easton, J. Q. (2006). Small High Schools on a Larger Scale: The First Three Years of the Chicago High School Redesign Initiative. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/small-schools-larger-scale-first-three-years-chicago-high-school-redesign-initiative

article_title: School Improvement with External Partners
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf
title: Five Essential Supports for Student Learning as analytical framework for assessing external partners
description: The Five Essential Supports is a research-based framework for school improvement that identifies five interconnected conditions: school leadership, professional community, parent and community involvement, student-centered learning climate, and quality instruction. The report uses this framework as its primary analytical lens to assess external partners' accomplishments, stating it was 'derived from a synthesis of research across the country on school improvement.' Each support is elaborated with specific indicators in Figure 1 of the report.
requirements: All five supports must be considered together, as they represent an integrated account of what schools need to improve student learning
constraints: The framework represents a consensus of experienced educators within the Chicago Public Schools and is most applicable to urban school contexts
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: School-wide improvement in student achievement and learning conditions
examples: Used to organize the report's assessment of nine external partners' accomplishments and difficulties across 18 schools
key_sources: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf

article_title: School Improvement with External Partners
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf
title: Chicago Annenberg External Partner model for school improvement
description: The external partner model links intermediary organizations (university- or community-based) to networks of schools to provide outside expertise for improvement efforts. Partners sponsor activities including network meetings, instructional materials, school-based literacy coordinators, demonstration teachers, leadership teams, and parent assistants. The model emerged from Chicago's decentralization movement and the 1995 Annenberg Challenge, which provided $49.2 million to fund 45 networks of schools with external partners focused on goals such as improving literacy instruction and developing school leadership.
requirements: Requires networks of three or more schools with a committed external partner relationship
Partners must be voluntarily selected by schools
constraints: Partner involvement occupies only a minor part of schools' attention, limiting influence
Initial budget requirements limited external partners to only 10 percent of any total grant made to a network
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: Whole-school change in instruction, leadership, professional community, parent involvement, and learning climate
examples: Nine Chicago Annenberg partners studied from 1996-1999, including five university-based, two community-based, one community advocacy, and one cultural institution partner
key_sources: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf

article_title: School Improvement with External Partners
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf
title: Urban school improvement should prioritize building human resources over adopting specific practices
description: This principle holds that effective school improvement places major emphasis on developing the capacities of people within schools and sustaining long-term support from partner organizations, rather than primarily on importing specific programs or strategies. The report's findings across nine partners suggest that without committed, sustained human relationships, externally promoted practices do not take root. As the authors state, improvement requires 'building on human resources both within schools and in assisting partner organizations over the long term.'
requirements: Long-term commitment from supporting organizations and funders
Sustained relationships between partners and school staff
constraints: Adopting specific practices alone is insufficient without parallel investment in human capacity
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: Sustainable school-wide improvement in teaching quality and student learning
examples: The report's recommendation emerges from cross-case findings that partner success depended on sustained relationships with willing teachers rather than on program fidelity alone
key_sources: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf

article_title: The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools
citation: Zohal Shah, Marilys Galindo, Chioma Aso-Hernandez, Christina Luke Luna, Keun-woo Lee, Josh Weisgrau, Teresa Solorzano, Britney Jacobs. (2024). The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Competency-Based Education with its seven elements of instructional practice
description: Competency-based education (CBE) is an education model that recognizes and accredits learners for demonstration of their skills and competencies instead of seat-time. The report adopts the Aurora Institute definition providing "seven critical elements of instructional practice," spanning learner decision-making, meaningful assessment, differentiated support, mastery-based progression, varied pathways and pacing, embedded equity strategies, and transparent common expectations. The report uses this framework to ground its argument that CBE is more adaptable to nonlinear learner pathways than seat-time credentialing.
requirements: Students must demonstrate mastery prior to advancing
Formative assessments integrated to inform daily instruction
Teachers communicate learning expectations with consistent assessment methods
constraints: Systematic implementation in K-12 is relatively new; policies limiting graduation-requirement flexibility can be barriers
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly historically and systematically excluded youth
target_learning_goals: Demonstration of competencies and skills across disciplines
examples: The Chugach School District in Alaska implemented CBE for over 20 years, replacing letter grades with emerging, developing, proficient, and advanced terminology and building a customized information management system.

description: The Portrait of a Graduate model has school leaders, educators, families, and communities collaboratively define the attributes students should embody by the end of secondary schooling. In the report's analysis of portraits nationwide, "most tend to highlight six primary skill sets": Analyze to Understand; Care For and Contribute to Society; Collaborate Across Difference; Communicate in All Media and Modalities; Create to Solve and Share; and Practice Self-Awareness and Regulation. Most portraits contain six to eight attributes, and seventeen states have adopted statewide portraits.

title: Learning and Employment Record (LER) technologies and digital wallets
description: LER technologies digitally store, share, and collect records of a person's learning and employment, documenting learning wherever it occurs — education, workplace, credentialing, or military training. Their infrastructure is based on interoperability, giving learners transparent, secure records and the ability to curate profiles and control what is shared with employers and institutions. Examples include North Dakota's digital wallets for high school students, which allow sharing "digitally verifiable transcripts, diplomas, and other credentials with any employer or institution," and Canada's MyCreds credential wallet.
requirements: Interoperability standards and governance approaches
Long-term access to learning records at no additional cost after learners leave issuing institutions
constraints: Risk of compromising user data privacy without adequate protection; verifiable technical skills may take priority over durable skills in matching
target_learners: K-12 students, postsecondary learners, and workers
target_learning_goals: Documenting, verifying, and transmitting skills and qualifications across education and employment contexts
examples: North Dakota was the first state to launch digital wallets for high school students; MyCreds launched in Canada for secure credential storage and transfer.

title: Implementation science framework for assessing district readiness
description: The report grounds its conceptual framework in implementation science, a model for understanding how educational interventions are adopted and scaled that focuses on "fidelity, feasibility, and sustainability" rather than real-time effectiveness. Following McKay (2017), the authors examine contextual factors affecting a district's readiness to implement competency-based micro-credentials and LER technologies while centering HSE learners, identifying indicators such as community or institutional partnerships, data privacy and infrastructure, and student advising and career support. This yields a Readiness Framework (Appendix B) for district leaders.
requirements: Fostering and sustaining partnerships with districts, universities, community organizations, and workforce organizations
Intervention must match the needs of the target population and be possible to implement in the given context
constraints: Without technical assistance or research-practice partnership support, conditions for implementation in schools are often not ideal

target_learning_goals: Recognition of competencies through micro-credentials and LER technologies
examples: The team used the framework's criteria to select two districts for pilot planning and refined it through listening tours and cross-sector design sessions.

article_title: Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development
citation: Patti Constantakis and Sierra Noakes. (2019). Tapping Data for Frontline Talent Development. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: From a disconnected learning ecosystem to a worker-centered ecosystem
description: The report frames a transition model from a 'Disconnected Learning Ecosystem' — silos, insufficient analysis, data not in workers' hands — to a 'Worker-Centered Ecosystem' where workers access their own data, providers deliver personalized services, employers improve talent pipelines, and funders make informed investment decisions. The mechanism is data sharing and interoperability: 'Access to the right data will equip frontline workers with the agency and knowledge to make informed decisions about their future and will equip stakeholders with information needed to deliver high-quality services.'
requirements: Data must flow between stakeholders and back to frontline workers, which current processes and systems 'do not support'
constraints: Progress depends on resolving legal, incentive, and technical challenges the report identifies
target_learners: frontline workers in retail, healthcare, food service, and hospitality
target_learning_goals: career advancement and informed decisions about professional development
examples: The report contrasts a 'Here' state of disconnected silos with a 'There' state where workers can access their data to inform their decisions.

article_title: A Series of Briefs: Implementing AI Literacy Across Learning Environments
citation: Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., Karim, S., Dallas, D., Zachariah, I., Peters Hinton, V., Chillmon, C., & Gonzales, L. (2025). Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/268
title: AI literacy as a set of foundational skills and competencies spanning understanding, evaluation, and effective human-centered use
description: The briefs define AI literacy as "a set of foundational skills and competencies that enable individuals to understand how AI works, responsibly evaluate AI systems, and use AI effectively as a human-centered tool across various contexts, including learning, work, and civic applications, while adapting to its ongoing evolution." This definition synthesizes several prior frameworks (CSTA & AI4K12, OECD, EDSAFE AI Alliance, Mills et al., Long & Magerko) and organizes the brief series' recommendations for learners and leaders across settings.
requirements: Adoption requires adapting to AI's ongoing evolution, so the definition is framed as dynamic rather than fixed
constraints: The authors note the brief may not capture every recent advancement and should be treated as foundational guidance while readers stay informed
target_learners: K-12 students
postsecondary students
workforce learners
informal learning audiences
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI works
responsibly evaluating AI systems
using AI effectively as a human-centered tool
examples: The definition anchors four audience-specific briefs: PK-12, postsecondary, workforce, and informal learning environments
key_sources: Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., Karim, S., Dallas, D., Zachariah, I., Peters Hinton, V., Chillmon, C., & Gonzales, L. (2025). Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/268

title: Institutions should adopt proactive, thoughtful adaptation strategies rather than reacting to AI with urgency or fear
description: The briefs recommend that "Rather than reacting to AI developments with urgency or fear, institutions and communities need proactive, thoughtful adaptation strategies." Effective integration, they argue, requires deliberate planning with an emphasis on human connection, learning, and equity so that all learners and workers can thrive in an AI-integrated future. This principle guides the tone and pacing of the implementation guidance across the brief series.

constraints: AI technology is ever-evolving, so adaptation strategies must remain dynamic
target_learners: all learners and workers preparing for an AI-integrated future
target_learning_goals: safe and effective engagement with AI
equitable participation in AI-integrated environments
examples: The briefs advise policymakers to consider the interconnected implications of AI-related policies across settings for comprehensive, coordinated responses

article_title: Catching up or falling behind: Measuring middle school achievement trajectories for college readiness
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, and Greg King. (2020). Catching up or Falling Behind: Measuring Middle School Achievement Trajectories for College Readiness. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-233, Annenberg Institute at Brown University.
title: Trajectory-based early indicator framework monitoring on-track status for college readiness across middle school
description: The article presents a framework that applies college readiness benchmarks to longitudinal middle-grades assessment data, assigning each student a series of up to six on-track status indicators and grouping students into six trajectory patterns. As the authors state, this study demonstrates an early academic indicator approach that continuously monitors students' on-track status from the beginning of 6th grade to the end of 8th grade. The framework identifies when achievement growth acceleration and deceleration happen using vertically scaled scores.
requirements: At least one test score in each grade between 6th and 8th grade (fall of 6th, fall or spring of 7th, spring of 8th) to construct a full trajectory
constraints: The analyses are descriptive, and the estimates should not be taken as causal links
The GRD sample may not be nationally representative
target_learners: Middle school students (6th through 8th grade)
target_learning_goals: Academic college readiness in math and reading

article_title: Catching up or falling behind: Measuring middle school achievement trajectories for college readiness
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, and Greg King. (2020). Catching up or Falling Behind: Measuring Middle School Achievement Trajectories for College Readiness. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-233, Annenberg Institute at Brown University.
title: Monitor individual student performance regularly and consistently against college readiness benchmarks to enable timely intervention
description: The article recommends that schools continuously track students' on-track status relative to benchmarks throughout middle school rather than relying on annual state tests. As the authors argue, individual student performance should be measured regularly and consistently relative to a set of benchmarks to ensure timely provision of instructional intervention. Analyzing achievement relative to on-track benchmarks requires very little computation and the interpretation of results is straight-forward, making the approach easy for schools and districts to implement.
requirements: Regular, consistent measurement of individual student performance relative to a benchmark set (e.g., MAP Growth ACT benchmarks)
Benchmarks that link middle school scores to later college readiness criteria
constraints: The benchmarks capture one aspect of college readiness and are not deterministic of eventual college enrollment and success
The authors do not advocate using benchmarks to group and label students for academic tracking; multiple indicators such as course grades and attendance are recommended

target_learning_goals: Academic college readiness in math and reading
examples: Schools monitor as students move on-track, fall off track, or sustain their status, and respond by targeting programs and services accordingly; support services should be offered to boys and Black and Hispanic students on the margin of college readiness

description: The article describes Early College as a dual-enrollment model whose design rests on a "four-pronged approach": whole-school enrollment, added academic and social supports, early exposure to college-level rigor, and credit accumulation. article_title: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models
citation: Soland, J., Thum, Y.M., & King, G. (2019). Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models: Evidence and implications from a longitudinal study. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org
title: Compound Polynomial (CP) growth model for jointly estimating within-year and between-year growth
description: The CP model is a multilevel growth model whose design matrix combines a within-year (fall-to-spring) matrix with a between-year (spring-to-spring) polynomial matrix, so that both kinds of growth are estimated in one model. The authors use it "to simultaneously estimate fall-to-spring (within-year) and spring-to-spring (between-year) growth over five years using a single model," producing conditional Z-scores via contrast matrices that allow school effectiveness comparisons across timespans on a consistent sample. The preferred specification treats all coefficients as random except the within-year quadratic, which is fixed at the school level.
requirements: Requires vertically scaled test scores on a common scale (here the RIT scale) administered fall and spring so within- and between-year growth are comparable
A consistent sample of students across timespans, handled here via conditional multivariate distribution Z-scores
constraints: Excludes schools serving fewer than 10 students at a test administration as potentially anomalous
The cohort is not intact: students need at least one valid test score to remain in the sample
target_learners: Elementary school students in grades 2–6
target_learning_goals: Estimating school contributions to student academic growth in math and reading
examples: Applied to a Southern-state cohort taking MAP Growth in fall and spring of grades 2–6, estimating school effects for 570 schools

title: Policymakers should examine whether short-term growth accountability aligns with long-term goals like college and career readiness
description: Because school effectiveness estimates are highly sensitive to the timespan over which growth is measured, the article recommends that policymakers openly discuss how schools should be held accountable for long-term objectives. It argues policymakers "may need to ask themselves whether accountability policies based on short-term growth are creating incentives that jibe with their broader goal of college and career readiness," noting the current emphasis may be producing unintended consequences relative to long-term goals.

Awareness of the .90 correlation threshold below which accountability determinations are likely to change

Findings come from one state using a low-stakes assessment, so generalization is limited

examples: The article compared school effectiveness estimates from a single year, three years, and five years of data for 570 schools using the CP model

article_title: Combining academic, noncognitive, and college knowledge measures to identify students not on track for college: A data-driven approach
citation: James Soland. (2017). Combining Academic, Noncognitive, and College Knowledge Measures to Identify Students Not on Track For College: A Data-Driven Approach. Research & Practice in Assessment, Volume Twelve, Summer 2017. https://rpajournal.com
title: Data-reduction framework combining decision trees, random forests, lasso, and factor analysis to prioritize college-readiness predictors
description: This framework uses data reduction to select, from thousands of measures, the variables that maximize classification accuracy for college enrollment and persistence. Decision trees recursively split on the variable maximizing information about the outcome using the Gini index, with mean reduction in the Gini index (MDGI) as a variable-importance measure; random forests replicate trees to counteract sensitivity to the first split, and lasso provides a regression-based alternative. A subsequent factor analysis (bifactor model) identifies what the retained predictors measure. The article uses it to show that "enrolling in college and persisting for a semester can be predicted with almost 90 percent accuracy using a small set of predictors."
requirements: A dataset with both predictor measures and recorded postsecondary outcomes, split into training and test data to protect against overfitting
constraints: Decision tree models do not generally account for measurement error
The methods maximize classification accuracy, not how actionable a measure is for educators
Findings need replication with newer data, as NELS predates grit and growth-mindset instruments
target_learners: K-12 and postsecondary students being screened for college readiness supports
target_learning_goals: Identifying students not on track for college enrollment and persistence
examples: NELS data from 12,144 students tracked from 8th grade in 1988 through 2000, with roughly 8,800 persisting for a semester as the outcome

title: National Education Longitudinal Survey (NELS) dataset
description: NELS is a nationally representative longitudinal dataset tracking students from their 8th-grade year in 1988 through 2000, including recorded postsecondary outcomes and thousands of student survey items. Baseline data were collected on 12,144 students, of whom 9,601 (79 percent) attended college and roughly 8,800 persisted for a semester. The author chose NELS over the more recent ELS because it includes a broader range of student survey items, and used 8th- and 10th-grade measures to predict college readiness.

title: College-completion crisis framing of US post-secondary policy
description: The paper frames US post-secondary policy around a completion problem: the crisis arises not solely from too few students enrolling but from enrolled students not finishing. It argues states increasingly depend on a highly skilled and educated workforce, and it cites the estimate that "over 31 million students over the last 20 years have enrolled in but not completed post-secondary education." This framing motivates policies, such as articulation agreements, that aim to reduce students leaving school prior to earning a degree.

constraints: Framing applies to US public post-secondary education as described in the paper

reducing attrition before degree completion

article_title: A level playing field: College readiness standards
citation: Michael Dahlin and Beth Tarasawa. (2013). A Level Playing Field? How College Readiness Standards Change the Accountability Game. Northwest Evaluation Association. https://www.nwea.org
title: Hold schools accountable for student growth rates rather than status measures such as proficiency or college readiness rates
description: This principle holds that because status measures largely reflect socioeconomic composition, school accountability should rest on how much students grow. The report argues status metrics are "largely controlled by socioeconomic factors beyond school control" and that growth-based policies put every student's progress into play, making them a better measure of school effectiveness than NCLB's proficiency-driven approach. The study's equivalence of growth across poverty levels provides its evidentiary basis.
requirements: A longitudinal growth measure on an equal-interval scale so student progress can be tracked over time
constraints: The report states growth models are a necessary but insufficient measure of achievement in terms of equity, since existing achievement gaps persist when students enter school
target_learners: elementary and middle school students
high-achieving students
target_learning_goals: academic growth in mathematics and reading
college readiness
examples: The study used NWEA MAP assessments, a computerized adaptive test with an equal-interval cross-grade Rasch scale, to measure growth of top-10% students over three years in high- and low-poverty schools.
key_sources: Michael Dahlin and Beth Tarasawa. (2013). A Level Playing Field? How College Readiness Standards Change the Accountability Game. Northwest Evaluation Association. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-level-playing-field-college-readiness-standards-whitepaper/

article_title: A level playing field: College readiness standards
citation: Michael Dahlin and Beth Tarasawa. (2013). A Level Playing Field? How College Readiness Standards Change the Accountability Game. Northwest Evaluation Association. https://www.nwea.org
title: Recognize each school's top performers as an accountability subgroup when setting policy and evaluating school programs
description: The report recommends extending NCLB-style subgroup identification to high achievers, arguing each school has its own top tenth whose performance should affect the school's accountability score. It states we should "recognize the top performers in each school as a subgroup when setting accountability policy and evaluating school programs", so that schools attend to these students' needs just as they do for other subgroups. This leverages a mechanism the report credits with addressing achievement gaps.
requirements: State accountability systems must incorporate subgroup reporting so that each school's top performers are visible in evaluation
constraints: The report notes high achievers within a school may not be considered disadvantaged, so the case rests on compelling public interest rather than disadvantage mitigation
target_learners: high-achieving students in every school
minority and low-income high achievers
target_learning_goals: full academic potential of top performers
college readiness
examples: The foreword recommends policymakers reframe discussion to recognize that elite students should not be defined solely as the top 1%, 5%, or 10% of the standardized testing pool, since every school has its own group of elite students.

title: Competency-based micro-credentials as a credential type distinct from macro-credentials and learning programs
description: The eBook defines micro-credentials as a type of digital credential that verifies competency in a specific skill or set of skills, contrasted with macro-credentials such as degrees and certificates. Digital Promise specifies that micro-credentials are "competency-based, research-backed, personalized, on-demand, and shareable" and use badging technology to issue verifiable certifications. Crucially, the article states micro-credentials "are not learning or training programs like courses or MOOCs" and are not completion-based or time-based; they certify skills regardless of how they were acquired, through formal or informal learning, work, and life experiences.
requirements: Assessment requires the learner to implement the new skills in a workplace setting and show evidence of this implementation, judged against rubric criteria by the issuing organization
constraints: The definition varies depending on who uses the term and in what context; in this eBook micro-credentials represent the ability to apply learning rather than the learning program itself

Educators
Workforce and postsecondary learners
target_learning_goals: Verification of competency in a specific skill or set of skills
Reskilling and upskilling recognition
examples: An educator earns the Integrating Computational Thinking into Curriculum micro-credential by demonstrating how they support students using computational thinking

description: Digital Promise's Competency-Based Assessment Framework guides the design of its micro-credentials and "emphasizes principles like impact, equity, access, and language to ensure inclusiveness and relevance". description: The eBook enumerates the characteristics that distinguish the most rigorous and meaningful micro-credentials from lower-quality offerings. title: Relationship between digital badges and micro-credentials: badges as representation, metadata as verification
description: The eBook distinguishes digital badges from micro-credentials: per Education Design Lab, a micro-credential is the "learning/earning experience" while a digital badge is the "technology used to display it". Micro-credentials use Open Badges metadata — badge name, criteria, issuer, issue date, evidence URL, and more — to "connect evidence and criteria", conveying what the learner has demonstrated rather than only which program was completed.

article_title: Computational Thinking for a Computational World
citation: Digital Promise. (2017). Computational Thinking for a Computational World. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Three-competency framework distinguishing coding, computer science, and computational thinking
description: The paper organizes its argument around distinctions among three linked competencies: "Coding is the practice of developing a set of instructions that a computer can understand and execute"; computer science is the study of computers and algorithmic processes including their societal impact; and computational thinking is Wing's "a way of solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior that draws on concepts fundamental to computer science." It concludes coding is a technical skill, computer science an academic discipline, and computational thinking a problem-solving process applicable to any discipline. The framework underpins the paper's recommendation to integrate computational thinking across K-12 subjects without replacing computer science efforts.
requirements: Computational thinking should be recognized as valuable in its own right and simultaneously linked to coding and computer science
constraints: The paper notes current literature often fails to recognize the distinctions between computer science and computational thinking
target_learners: K-12 students
working adults
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
problem solving across disciplines
examples: The paper diagrams the three competencies as a mutually linked triangle and reviews Wing (2006) and Bundy (2007) as sources for computational thinking's broad applicability

title: Dispositional competency: ability, sensitivity, and inclination as three interrelated aspects of a developed competency
description: Drawing on Project Zero, the report argues that for a competency to be dispositional, a learner must develop it within three interrelated aspects. Ability ('I can...') concerns capability to apply a skill; sensitivity ('I should...') is recognizing when a skill should be applied; inclination ('I will...') is being comfortable and motivated to choose to apply that skill. The report contends these must be 'developed and used together, repeatedly over time, and across multiple contexts' to become ingrained dispositions.

constraints: Dispositional competency is harder to assess than academic or technical skill demonstration because it spans multiple dimensions, contexts, and abilities

article_title: Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career
citation: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244
title: Learning and Employment Record (LER) technologies as learner-curated lifelong skill portfolios
description: The report describes Learning and Employment Record technologies, sometimes called wallets, as records that 'enable learners to track and document their skills development across different contexts, from school to the workplace'. They are digital portfolios curated by learners, serving as repositories of competencies that transfer across disciplines, careers, and life experiences. The report recommends K-12 learners practice stewarding their own learning data and tailoring what they share with different audiences.
requirements: Interoperable systems connecting school, postsecondary, and workforce data
learner practice composing and tailoring a portfolio of achievements
constraints: Realizing the vision requires new models and systems of assessment co-designed inclusively across workforce, postsecondary, learners, educators, and researchers
target_learners: K-12 learners
postsecondary students
job seekers
target_learning_goals: documenting and showcasing transferable skills
learner agency over learning data
examples: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation's T3 Innovation Network, launched in 2018, works on data interoperability so credentials and LER technologies can make job-market information shareable
key_sources: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244

article_title: Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career
citation: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244
title: Design K-12 environments so learners make decisions, explore interests, and reflect, cultivating personal agency
description: The report argues learners need a sense of personal agency to actively participate in their learning journey, make informed decisions, and manage uncertainty, and that schools are uniquely positioned to foster this by creating environments where learners can explore, make decisions, and reflect on their learning. It recommends flexible learning pathways, learner-led conferences and portfolio reviews, and shifting teachers from keepers of knowledge to coaches. Practices should complement, not replace, tests and grades.
requirements: Investment in universal early childhood education programs designed with agency in mind
educator role shifts toward coaching learners in lifelong-learning mindsets
constraints: Many social structures, including socioeconomic status and educational attainment, impact an individual's ability to develop and exert their full sense of agency
target_learners: early childhood through K-12 learners
target_learning_goals: personal agency
decision-making
self-advocacy
lifelong learning mindsets
examples: Synergy High School in Mineola, New York was co-designed with students to facilitate interactive learning, digital badges, and self-directed spaces, and the district found the model worked particularly well for students who had struggled in less autonomous environments
key_sources: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244

article_title: Every Learner Everywhere and Lighthouse Institutions: First-Year Experiences
citation: Digital Promise. (2020). Every Learner Everywhere and Lighthouse Institutions: First-Year Experiences. https://www.everylearnereverywhere.org/
title: Multidimensional view of scaling educational innovations (Coburn)
description: The report adopts Cynthia Coburn's (2003) argument that scale in education cannot be measured by head counts or product purchases because innovations have multiple components present to varying degrees. Her conceptualization includes "depth (change in underlying pedagogical beliefs and practices), sustainability, and a shift in ownership" as well as spread measured as penetration within each educational unit. The report uses this framing to justify assessing institutional capacity rather than counting adoptions.
requirements: Assessment of scale must attend to depth, sustainability, ownership shift, and penetration within units, not just counts of participating units
target_learners: higher education institutions implementing innovations at scale
target_learning_goals: institutional capacity for improving teaching and learning
examples: The report applies this framing to judge that lighthouse changes involved only a minority of faculty and that sustainability after the grant was uncertain
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2020). Every Learner Everywhere and Lighthouse Institutions: First-Year Experiences. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/abf8db78-dc7a-4f4f-b06a-b00d1bda63e8

article_title: Every Learner Everywhere and Lighthouse Institutions: First-Year Experiences
citation: Digital Promise. (2020). Every Learner Everywhere and Lighthouse Institutions: First-Year Experiences. https://www.everylearnereverywhere.org/
title: Every Learner Everywhere lighthouse institution program and technical assistance model
description: A Gates Foundation-funded network of 12 organizations working with 12 lighthouse two- and four-year colleges to implement adaptive courseware in gateway courses serving first-generation, low-income students and students of color. Institutions committed to cross-functional project teams, summit participation, a community of practice, and research participation, receiving subgrants of $25,000 or $50,000. Technical assistance combined on-campus workshops, five to eight distance coaching calls, and two to four convenings, plus Digital Promise support for impact study design and data collection.
requirements: Cross-functional project team including a department chair or dean, academic affairs representative, faculty, and instructional technology staff
Commitment to redesign gateway courses and participate in data collection
constraints: Two of 12 institutions could not complete redesign in time for fall 2019 pilots due to a late project start
target_learners: first-generation students
low-income students
students of color in gateway courses
target_learning_goals: improved gateway course success rates and reduced equity gaps
examples: Ten institutions launched 41 redesigned courses across seven subject areas in fall 2019, involving products such as ALEKS, Lumen Waymaker, and Pearson MyMathLab, reaching an estimated 13,680 students

article_title: Identifying Indicators to Support Educational Attainment for Different Groups of English Learners in High School
citation: Allensworth, E.M., de la Torre, M., Franklin, K., & Xu, J. (2025). Identifying Indicators to Support Educational Attainment for Different Groups of English Learners in High School. (Working Paper). Providence, RI: Annenberg EdExchange. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1241
title: Use the same early warning and college readiness indicator systems for English Learners as for other students, but apply group-specific risk thresholds, especially for active English Learners in high school
description: The study concludes that schools can run one early warning and college readiness indicator system for everyone, because "the best indicators are the same for most students"; what differs is the threshold at which students become at risk. For example, active English Learners need attendance above 95% to be very likely to graduate, while former and never English Learners need 90% or higher. Applying group-specific thresholds lets schools use existing systems to identify at-risk English Learners accurately.
requirements: Schools must track GPA, attendance, and course failure data for all students, including English Learner subgroups.
constraints: Thresholds differ for active English Learners in high school, and outcomes were harder to predict for long-term English Learners with IEPs.
target_learners: High school English Learners, including former, long-term, and late-arriving English Learners
target_learning_goals: High school graduation, college enrollment, and college degree completion
examples: The study found active English Learners need attendance above 95% while former and never English Learners need 90% or higher to be very likely to graduate.
key_sources: Allensworth, E.M., de la Torre, M., Franklin, K., & Xu, J. (2025). Identifying Indicators to Support Educational Attainment for Different Groups of English Learners in High School. (Working Paper). Providence, RI: Annenberg EdExchange. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1241

citation: Illinois Workforce and Education Research Collaborative (IWERC), in partnership with the University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. (2024). title: Career-connected learning (CCL) as a districtwide framework unifying college prep and career readiness
description: The report describes CPS's vision and enactment of "career-connected learning" (CCL), a framework initiated in 2017, which aims to unify college preparatory and career readiness activities districtwide. The framework operates through two strategies: strengthening existing high school CTE programs and establishing a districtwide CCL framework for students from grades 6 through 12. Chicago is presented as one of many districts working to implement a modern CCL framework.

constraints: CPS is decentralized, so network and school leaders make program decisions, and funding for new initiatives is limited

target_learning_goals: College and career readiness
postsecondary planning
examples: District leaders focused on strengthening CTE programs of study and unifying initiatives through Learn.Plan.Succeed.
