article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students (2024)
citation: Mahaffie, S., Usher, A., Nagaoka, J., & McKoy, D. (2025). The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students: 2024. To&Through Project and UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/
title: Post-secondary Attainment Index
description: The report combines its three milestone rates into what authors call a "Post-secondary Attainment Index". It expresses attainment as a hypothetical cohort trajectory: "if 100 students started CPS in ninth grade today, 84 would graduate high school, 58 would enroll immediately in college, and 30 would complete a college credential within 10 years." The index turns graduation, enrollment, and completion rates into a single composite indicator for tracking progress over time.
requirements: Requires data on high school graduation, immediate college enrollment, and college credential completion for CPS cohorts
constraints: The completion component reflects rates for cohorts for which six years of post-secondary data exist, such as the class of 2018
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools students starting ninth grade
target_learning_goals: High school graduation, immediate college enrollment, and college credential completion
examples: The 2024 report expresses the index as 84 of 100 students graduating high school, 58 enrolling immediately in college, and 30 completing a credential within 10 years

article_title: Foundations for Young Adult Success: A Developmental Framework
citation: Nagaoka, J., Farrington, C. A., Ehrlich, S. B., with Johnson, D. W., Dickson, S., Heath, R., & Mayo, A. (2014). A Framework for Developing Young Adult Success in the 21st Century: White Paper — Defining Young Adult Success. University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research Working Paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/framework-developing-young-adult-success-21st-century
title: Integrated identity framework: young adult success as agency and motivation grounded in an integrated identity
description: The article's central framework conceptualizes a well-prepared young adult as one with an integrated identity and the agency to use internal and external resources toward self-set goals. It defines success as "being poised to work toward and achieve the goals a person sets for herself," with goals emerging from values and purpose. The framework names key factors — knowledge and skills, awareness, mindsets, strategies, and behaviors and habits — that come together in an integrated identity enabling directed action across life domains.
requirements: Adults across settings must help children internalize and make meaning of knowledge, strategies, mindsets, and awareness, not only teach content and skills
constraints: The article focuses on individual contributors to success, deferring the role of contextual constraints and facilitators to later project phases
The authors state the framework is their thinking at the end of Phase 1 and anticipate it will evolve
target_learners: children and youth from early childhood through young adulthood
target_learning_goals: developing agency, purpose, values, and identity to achieve self-set young adult goals
examples: The framework is grounded in a literature review and expert interviews conducted in Phase 1 of a four-phase project; later phases will examine developmental stages and settings
key_sources: Nagaoka, J., Farrington, C. A., Ehrlich, S. B., with Johnson, D. W., Dickson, S., Heath, R., & Mayo, A. (2014). article_title: Foundations for Young Adult Success: A Developmental Framework
citation: Nagaoka, J., Farrington, C. A., Ehrlich, S. B., with Johnson, D. W., Dickson, S., Heath, R., & Mayo, A. (2014). A Framework for Developing Young Adult Success in the 21st Century: White Paper — Defining Young Adult Success. University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research Working Paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/framework-developing-young-adult-success-21st-century
title: Four-part conception of agency: intentionality, forethought, self-reactiveness, self-reflectiveness
description: The framework adopts Bandura's (2006) four-part definition of agency to explain how young adults shape their life course. Agency means "taking an active role in shaping and managing one's chosen path rather than being at the mercy of external forces" (an internal versus external locus of control). The four parts are intentionality (action plan and strategies), forethought (setting goals and anticipating outcomes), self-reactiveness (self-regulation and competence to act), and self-reflectiveness (reflecting on efficacy and adjusting course).
requirements: The framework treats agency as resting on key factors — purpose, values, mindsets, competence, and relationships — that come together in an integrated identity
target_learners: adolescents transitioning into young adulthood
target_learning_goals: goal-setting, self-regulation, self-reflection, and directing one's own life course
examples: The article derives guiding questions such as "Who am I and what do I value?" and "Do I believe I can accomplish them?" from this agency conceptualization

description: Section 2 organizes the landscape of models the authors reviewed (over 20 existing models and frameworks) into named exemplars: the 21st century skills framework (the 4 Cs, media/information/technology skills, life and career skills); MHA Labs' six building blocks comprising 35 core skills; the NRC classification with "the cognitive domain... the intrapersonal domain... and the interpersonal domain"; CASEL's five interrelated SEL competencies; and Conley's four keys to college and career readiness. The framework positions itself as extending these toward a broader definition of success.

article_title: Using the Freshman On-Track Indicator to Improve High Schools in Chicago
citation: Using the Freshman On-Track Indicator to Improve High Schools in Chicago. (1990). Chapter 5 of Measuring to Improve: Practical Measurement to Support Continuous Improvement in Education, Harvard Education Press. https://www.harvardeducationpress.com
title: Freshman OnTrack end-of-year indicator used for goal-setting and accountability
description: The Freshman OnTrack indicator is an end-of-year data element signaling whether a ninth-grade student is likely to graduate. The article states it "signals a student is likely to graduate and is used for goal-setting and accountability", making it the anchor of Chicago's graduation-improvement data system.
requirements: Requires end-of-year data on ninth-grade students' course performance and attendance to compute on-track status
target_learners: ninth-grade high school students in Chicago Public Schools
target_learning_goals: successful completion of high school and graduation
examples: Chicago Public Schools used the indicator for goal-setting and accountability as part of a system developed over fifteen years

article_title: English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students
citation: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Franklin, K., Angeles, C., & Allensworth, E.M. (2024). English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Subgroup taxonomy of English Learners by classification history and disability status
description: The report organizes English Learners in high school into a taxonomy that disaggregates the broad active English Learner category into subgroups with distinct needs. Former English Learners "demonstrated English proficiency and exited EL status by the ninth grade"; long-term English Learners (with or without IEPs) had been in CPS six or more years without demonstrating proficiency on the ACCESS test; and late-arriving English Learners had been in CPS fewer than six years. The authors make this distinction because "the different experiences and needs of these subgroups are often not recognized" when districts report active English Learners as a whole. The taxonomy underpins every finding in the report.
requirements: Longitudinal administrative data on English Learner classification status, ACCESS test results, and IEP status at ninth-grade entry
constraints: Classification was based on student status at the beginning of ninth grade; a small group (2%) identified with a disability later remained in the without-IEP group
target_learners: High school English Learners in large urban districts
target_learning_goals: High school graduation and college access and persistence
examples: The report applied the taxonomy to 78,507 CPS students: 23% former, 4% long-term without IEP, 3% long-term with IEP, and 3% late-arriving English Learners
key_sources: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Franklin, K., Angeles, C., & Allensworth, E.M. (2024). English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/english-learners-in-chicago-public-schools-a-spotlight-on-high-school-students

article_title: English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students
citation: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Franklin, K., Angeles, C., & Allensworth, E.M. (2024). English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Report English Learner outcomes by subgroup, because aggregate reporting obscures both successes and groups needing support
description: The report argues that districts should disaggregate outcome reporting for English Learners rather than reporting only on active English Learners as a whole. Aggregate statistics "obscures the possible variability in the skills and needs that English Learners bring with them to high school," hiding former English Learners' successes and the distinct needs of long-term and late-arriving English Learners. Disaggregated reporting allows identification of which specific groups need more support and which supports differ by group.

constraints: The authors note there is a lack of information nationally because districts do not report outcome data for former English Learners separately
target_learners: English Learners in K-12 districts, especially high school students
target_learning_goals: Equitable identification of support needs for graduation and college access
examples: The report reported Freshman OnTrack, GPA, SAT, graduation, college enrollment, and persistence separately for four English Learner subgroups and an ever-English-Learner category

title: Post-secondary Attainment Index (PAI)
description: The Post-secondary Attainment Index is a district-level summary measure representing "the proportion of current CPS ninth-graders who would complete any degree or certificate from a two-year or four-year college within 10 years" if current rates held. It multiplies the four-year graduation rate by a weighted combination of enrollment and completion rates for four-year enrollees, two-year enrollees, and non-enrollees, combining data from multiple recent cohorts. The 2023 PAI synthesizes graduation data for the class of 2023, enrollment data for the class of 2023, and six-year college outcomes for the class of 2017.

target_learning_goals: District-level monitoring of high school graduation, college enrollment, and college completion attainment
examples: The 2023 PAI of 30.6% combines the class of 2023 graduation rate, class of 2023 immediate enrollment rates, and class of 2017 six-year completion rates

citation: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Amplify Science 1st grade curriculum: three phenomena-based units integrating science and literacy
description: The Amplify Science 1st grade curriculum consists of "three phenomena-based instructional units" covering life science, physical science, and Earth and space science, each 22 lessons of 45 minutes taught over 6–8 weeks. Lessons engage students in doing, reading, writing, talking, and visualizing science, with hands-on investigations, model building, and explanation writing. The package includes a digital teacher's guide, science kit materials with literacy supports, student notebooks, and books for read-aloud, shared, and partner reading.

constraints: Using the materials requires teachers to spend more instructional time on science than is typical based on national surveys of K–5 elementary teachers

reading development integrated with science
examples: In the study, intervention teachers implemented the three units within their district's NGSS-aligned science sequence while comparison teachers taught science as they typically would.

title: Integrate science and literacy in early-grade curriculum materials so more science instruction can be added without sacrificing reading development
description: The article finds that science curriculum materials using "the high-leverage strategy of integrated science and literacy" can improve science proficiency and vocabulary while simultaneously developing reading skills. Because day-to-day science lessons intentionally embed reading, writing, talking, and visualizing, teachers can devote considerably more instructional time to science with confidence that reading scores will not be negatively impacted. This integration may enable elementary teachers to create instructional space for regular science teaching.
requirements: Curriculum lessons must intentionally integrate science learning with literacy development, with an emphasis on reading in K–3, and teachers need professional learning on the integrated pedagogical approach
constraints: The reading result is from one randomized trial of 1st grade classrooms in three California districts; the authors note additional studies at larger scale will be needed as NGSS-designed materials become more widely used
target_learners: Early elementary (K–3) students, including multilingual learners and students in underresourced schools
target_learning_goals: Science proficiency with NGSS performance expectations
science vocabulary usage
reading comprehension
examples: Intervention teachers implemented Amplify Science units whose lessons engage students in doing, reading, writing, talking, and visualizing science; they spent considerably more time on science than comparison teachers in prior implementation research (Iveland et al., 2021).

citation: Harris, C. J., Murphy, R., Feng, M., & Rutstein, D. (2023). Supporting science learning and literacy development together: Initial results from a curriculum study in 1st grade classrooms. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Study-developed NGSS-focused assessments of 1st grade three-dimensional learning and science vocabulary in-use
description: Because no off-the-shelf 1st grade NGSS science assessments existed, the research team developed two NGSS-focused assessments designed to be fair to both study conditions. The science learning assessment presents six multistep phenomenon- or problem-based tasks requiring students to interpret data tables, draw, make predictions, and select tools for investigations. The science-vocabulary-in-use assessment presents 10 science terms with definition evaluation and appropriate-use questions. Interrater exact agreement exceeded 90 percent with Cohen's kappa greater than 0.8 across all items.
requirements: Scorers with science education expertise, rubric-based scoring with rigorous training, and blind scoring to research condition
constraints: Overall internal consistency was 0.674 (Cronbach's alpha) for the science learning assessment and 0.845 for the science-vocabulary-in-use assessment
target_learners: 1st grade students
target_learning_goals: NGSS performance expectations for 1st grade across Earth and space science, life science, and physical science
domain-specific science vocabulary use
examples: Both assessments were administered as whole-class activities in which teachers read scenarios and prompts aloud while students responded in their own booklets.

article_title: Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah
citation: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://web.stanford.edu/~mshanks/MichaelShanks/files/509554.pdf
title: Bring together a cross-department state team to design and deliver a resource allocation review.
description: The report's first lesson is that a state education agency should assemble staff from many departments to design and deliver the RAR, including the offices of the superintendent, student support services, teaching and learning, special education, state and federal programs, educator effectiveness, financial operations, assessment and accountability, and information technology. The authors argue that "Leveraging the perspectives of multiple departments in the design process enables the state education agency (SEA) to engage in a way that encourages creativity and shared responsibility," producing more effective resource allocation and support for schools.
requirements: The team should encompass key departments including superintendent, student support services, teaching and learning, special education, state and federal programs, educator effectiveness, financial operations, assessment and accountability, and information technology.
target_learners: state education agency staff
LEA and school leaders
target_learning_goals: designing and implementing an equitable resource allocation review process
examples: The report recommends tips such as using existing state-level academic, engagement, and financial data, connecting reporting requirements like the statewide comprehensive needs assessment and IDEA indicators, and leveraging Comprehensive Centers and other experts to guide design.

article_title: Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah

title: Establish a shared vision among educational leaders that equal does not mean equitable before designing resource allocation processes.
description: The report's second lesson holds that because individuals bring different lived experiences to resource equity work, states should build a shared vision establishing that "equal does not mean equitable." This mindset shift, spread across the SEA and the state, is described as necessary to develop a process that identifies equitable resource allocation methods addressing student needs and expanding student access to educational opportunities.

target_learning_goals: understanding equity versus equality in resource allocation
examples: Recommended tips include conducting a gap analysis of leaders' understanding of equitable resource allocation, providing ongoing equity-mindset training and technical assistance, and designing the process as an ongoing exercise in equity rather than compliance.

title: Dear Colleague Letter crosswalk of federal recommendations and R15CC considerations for resource equity provisions
description: Table 1 of the report is a crosswalk pairing the U.S. Department of Education's July 2023 Dear Colleague Letter recommendations (A.1 through A.9 on state resource allocation reviews and B.1 through B.4 on CSI and ATSI plans) with R15CC considerations drawn from the Utah technical assistance. The report explains that "The accompanying crosswalk (Table 1) includes the Department's recommendations, including considerations based on the technical assistance R15CC provided while designing the RAR from 2020 to 2023." Each row adds guiding questions for states on topics such as defining significant numbers of identified schools, defining financial and nonfinancial resources, aligning review timing, integrating with monitoring and budgeting, comparing allocation data, disaggregating by student group, stakeholder engagement, feedback, public posting, and plan templates and guidance.
requirements: States should use the crosswalk to align their RAR design with the Department's nonregulatory guidance on Title I, Part A resource equity provisions.
constraints: The crosswalk addresses the two referenced resource equity provisions: the state resource allocation review requirement and identifying and addressing resource inequities in CSI and ATSI plans.

LEA and school improvement staff
target_learning_goals: implementing ESSA resource equity provisions through resource allocation reviews

article_title: 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes
citation: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Move beyond numerical data alone because aggregate quantitative measures lack context, detail, and nuance
description: This principle holds that easily quantified data such as test scores, graduation rates, and attendance show big-picture patterns but miss the human side of teaching and learning. The brief explains such data "provide a high-level view but do not provide the context, detail, and nuance that are important for fully understanding and responding to student learning needs." It recommends adding qualitative data, including student, family, and teacher voices and documents such as syllabi, lesson plans, and student work.
requirements: Pair quantitative indicators with qualitative sources that capture voices and learning conditions
constraints: Quantitative aggregate data are described as useful for big-picture patterns and trends, not as worthless
target_learners: students whose learning needs require contextual understanding
target_learning_goals: fully understanding and responding to student learning needs within specific contexts
examples: The brief lists syllabi, lesson plans, and student work as document data offering insight into learning conditions and progress
key_sources: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655653

article_title: 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes
citation: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Satellite data: high-level aggregate measures that lack ground-level context
description: The brief adopts Safir and Dugan's (2021) concept of satellite data to name the kind of data education leaders most often rely on: easily quantified, aggregate measures such as test scores, graduation rates, and attendance. The brief states these data "provide a high-level view but do not provide the context, detail, and nuance" needed to fully understand and respond to student learning needs. The concept organizes the brief's argument for supplementing quantitative measures with qualitative data.
requirements: Should be paired with closer-to-the-ground qualitative sources to gain context, detail, and nuance
constraints: Applies to data that can be easily quantified and analyzed in aggregate
target_learners: all students in systems evaluated mainly through aggregate measures
target_learning_goals: understanding learning needs with sufficient context and nuance
examples: The brief applies the satellite-data label to test scores, graduation rates, and attendance data
key_sources: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655653

article_title: 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes
citation: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Attend to data quality before placing stock in an analysis, because high-quality data are a prerequisite for meaningful analysis
description: This principle instructs users not to take data at face value but to first examine how data were collected, managed, and retrieved. The brief asserts that "High-quality data are a prerequisite for any meaningful data analysis effort." It gives concrete checks: understanding the design, purpose, and administration of an assessment before analyzing results, and considering survey design and respondent representativeness before interpreting survey results.

target_learners: all students whose outcomes are measured by assessments and surveys
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of assessment and survey results
examples: The brief's example checks cover assessment data and survey data specifically

article_title: Using the EQUIP Observation Tool to Advance Equity in Math Classrooms
citation: Cunningham, J., Takahashi, S., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Using the EQUIP observation tool to advance equity in math classrooms. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: EQUIP observation tool for tracking and quantifying classroom participation patterns by demographic group
description: EQUIP (Equity Quantified In Participation) is an observation tool that helps educators "track patterns in student participation." Users upload a student roster with demographic information, optionally select discourse dimensions such as question types or talk time to cross-reference with demographics, and code each student contribution in real time or via video. The app then "automatically generate[s] analytics, including heatmaps, histograms, and various other data visualizations" that can surface participation inequities and prompt conversations about improving teaching practice.
requirements: Educators set up the app by uploading a student roster and associated demographic information they are interested in tracking
constraints: Discourse dimensions are optional; a user can simply record how many times a student participated
The report states the transformative power is not in the tool itself but in how it is used to enact change
target_learners: K-12 and community college mathematics students
target_learning_goals: equitable participation in classroom mathematics discourse
examples: A 1st-grade teacher's lessons were video-recorded and coded by researchers, who shared heatmap data reports in debrief conversations
A community college instructor used EQUIP six times in fall 2017 with a swivel camera and researcher coding
key_sources: Cunningham, J., Takahashi, S., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Using the EQUIP observation tool to advance equity in math classrooms. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655697

description: The interviewed researchers and teachers found it hard to envision a teacher using EQUIP alone, citing "real constraints on teachers' time." They recommend working in grade-level or department teams to collect and make sense of data together, which strengthens relationships, sustains focus on equitable participation, and mitigates difficult emotions the data can surface, since no single individual is to blame for inequitable participation.

Sophia used EQUIP with her co-teacher through the ARISE project

article_title: Cost and Cost Effectiveness of ASSISTments Online Math Support: Analysis from a Randomized Controlled Study in Middle School
citation: Feng, M., Weiser, G., & Collins, K. (2024). Cost and cost effectiveness of ASSISTments online math support: Analysis from a randomized controlled study in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: ASSISTments online math homework platform
description: ASSISTments is a free, web-based platform used in the study as an online tool for math homework, with many teachers also using it for classwork. It "provided students with instant feedback on their math work, while teachers received real-time data and progress reports on student learning." The platform contains textbook-based problems from schools' existing curricula plus prebuilt content, and developers built teacher-created practice problems into it on request. No specialized hardware or software was required beyond existing devices.
requirements: Teachers are expected to assign ASSISTments assignments for 20-30 minutes at least twice a week and regularly review data reports of student work

target_learning_goals: middle school mathematics achievement
examples: In the North Carolina RCT, intervention teachers implemented ASSISTments over two consecutive school years with 2-day summer professional development and coaching visits averaging three per teacher per year

article_title: Cost and Cost Effectiveness of ASSISTments Online Math Support: Analysis from a Randomized Controlled Study in Middle School
citation: Feng, M., Weiser, G., & Collins, K. (2024). Cost and cost effectiveness of ASSISTments online math support: Analysis from a randomized controlled study in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The ingredients method for educational cost analysis
description: The report applies the ingredients method (Belfield et al., 2018), a methodology that involves "systematically identifying all the resources necessary for implementing" a program, pricing each component, and calculating total and per-participant costs. It characterizes the "treatment contrast" as the difference in resource use, not just outcomes, between intervention and comparison groups, counting opportunity costs of resources regardless of who pays. Costs were organized into four categories: personnel, training, facilities, and materials, and managed with the CostOut tool.
requirements: Detailed information about the components of an intervention and its alternatives, including quantities and local prices of each ingredient
constraints: The analysis focused only on incremental costs above business-as-usual, excluding classroom space, technical infrastructure, and overhead rates
target_learners: district and school administrators making edtech adoption decisions
target_learning_goals: informed resource allocation and intervention adoption decisions
examples: The report identified ingredients collaboratively with the developers and local coach, refined the list through observations over two years, and clarified details by interviewing school leaders, coaches, and teachers

citation: Eisenberg, L., Krausen, K., & Caparas, R. (2024). Schools can't do it alone: Envisioning a statewide system of support to advance school-based behavioral health in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: California's Statewide System of Support (SSOS): a three-tiered structure for deploying technical assistance to local educational systems
description: The SSOS is California's unified structure, in place since 2017, for connecting school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools to TA, tools, and resources that build capacity for continuous improvement and reducing achievement gaps. It operates as a three-tiered model: "Tier 1 support (general assistance) is available for all LEAs and schools," Tier 2 (differentiated assistance) targets LEAs flagged by California School Dashboard performance, and Tier 3 (intensive intervention) serves persistent performance issues, though the SSOS has primarily focused on Tiers 1 and 2. COEs and Lead Agencies deliver support directly, while the CCEE, CDE, and SBE coordinate the system; the CCEE also hosts an online directory and a searchable Resource Hub.

constraints: The SSOS explicitly focuses on educational systems; behavioral health is generally addressed only when LEAs identify it as a Dashboard-linked strategy, and behavioral health indicators are not currently included on the Dashboard

target_learning_goals: Building local education leaders' capacity for continuous improvement and reducing achievement gaps

article_title: Schools Can't Do It Alone: Envisioning a Statewide System of Support to Advance School-Based Behavioral Health in California
citation: Eisenberg, L., Krausen, K., & Caparas, R. (2024). Schools can't do it alone: Envisioning a statewide system of support to advance school-based behavioral health in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Any statewide behavioral health TA model should combine cross-agency collaboration with a dual focus on student outcomes and sustainable service infrastructure
description: Research for this project suggests design features for capacity-building TA in school-based behavioral health. First, collaboration across county agencies (COEs, county behavioral health, SELPAs) is critical so services are coordinated and funding maximized; the existing AB 2083 cross-agency county-level MOU structure could be leveraged. Second, the brief recommends "the need for capacity-building TA on both of these areas of focus": improving student behavioral health outcomes (e.g., finding meaningful outcome measures) and building infrastructure for sustainable access (e.g., breaking down funding silos, increasing Medi-Cal reimbursements, developing data-sharing MOUs). Third, access should be expanded without making TA a requirement.
requirements: Collaboration between county agencies regardless of which agency leads TA at the county level
constraints: An analogous statewide measure for student behavioral health does not currently exist, so Tier 2 eligibility would have to rely on proxies such as LEA demographics, Dashboard data, or CHKS data

target_learning_goals: Improving student behavioral health outcomes and building sustainable infrastructure for integrated systems of care

citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: SCOE centralized school-based mental health services through an FQHC-eligible Medi-Cal billing model
description: SCOE hires clinicians and places them in schools under the Sacramento County Health Center, a Federally Qualified Healthcare Center eligible for Medi-Cal billing. The brief states these clinicians "provide clinical mental health services (Tier 3) to students and support Tier 1 and Tier 2 prevention and early intervention programs and services at school sites." SCOE also manages Medi-Cal billing centrally, which the brief says removes administrative burden from schools and allows centralized data tracking such as numbers of students served.

constraints: Described for Sacramento County schools under SCOE's purview
target_learners: K-12 students in Sacramento County schools
target_learning_goals: Access to school-based clinical mental health services and prevention supports
examples: SCOE manages Medi-Cal billing centrally and tracks data such as numbers of students served

article_title: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools into Centers of Wellness
citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: Coordination of Services Teams (COST) link students to mental health supports within a multi-tiered system of supports
description: COST is SCOE's coordination mechanism linking students in Sacramento County schools to mental health supports within a multi-tiered system of supports (MTSS). The brief states that "Rather than relying on direct referrals to clinicians, COST coordinates referrals using systematic and proactive approaches (e.g., universal screening data)." This is intended to ensure students' needs are met through appropriate channels, for example avoiding inappropriate referral to therapy when a classroom-based issue is present.
requirements: Universal screening data to drive proactive referral coordination
constraints: Operates within SCOE's multi-tiered system of supports in Sacramento County schools
target_learners: K-12 students in Sacramento County schools
target_learning_goals: Appropriate matching of students to mental health supports and services
examples: COST uses universal screening data rather than direct clinician referrals to coordinate support

article_title: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools into Centers of Wellness
citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: SCOE mental health career pathway employing peer specialists, graduate clinical interns, and associate clinicians
description: To address a shortage of available mental health clinicians, SCOE built a career pathway using peer specialists, graduate clinical interns, and associate clinicians in paid positions. The brief states these roles "provide career support while establishing a professional pathway for school-based mental health service providers." Internships for undergraduate and graduate students are available, and associate clinicians with graduate degrees can earn clinical hours while employed full-time. Recent partnerships also nurtured the School Based Mental Health and Wellness Path, one of SCOE's Career Pipeline Paths.
requirements: Paid positions for peer specialists, interns, and associate clinicians to sustain the pipeline
constraints: Designed to address the clinician shortage in SCOE's region
target_learners: Undergraduate and graduate students and aspiring school-based mental health professionals
target_learning_goals: Building a professional pathway into school-based mental health careers
examples: Associate clinicians with graduate degrees earn clinical hours while employed full-time

citation: Sacramento County Office of Education: Transforming Schools Into Centers of Wellness. (2024). WestEd. https://www.centersofwellness.scoe.net/our-work#collectiveimpact
title: Collective impact model aligning health and education systems for school-community mental health
description: SCOE leaders organize their county-wide mental health work through a collective impact model that aligns health and education systems. Partners include the County Department of Health Services, regional Medi-Cal plans, all districts and schools under SCOE's purview, and student, family, and community partnerships. Core values of relationships, collaboration, and equitable access to care shape the work, alongside a commitment to diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging.

article_title: Centering the Experiences and Perspectives of Educational Partners: Five Considerations for Schools and Districts
citation: Ojetunde, T., & Chavez, A. (2024). Centering the experiences and perspectives of educational partners: Five considerations for schools and districts. California Center for School Climate at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five considerations framework for engaging educational partners in school climate improvement
description: The resource organizes engagement with educational partners—defined as "essential collaborators such as students, parents, teachers, other school-based staff, and community members"—around five considerations: making authentic connections, seeking new perspectives, identifying areas to celebrate, highlighting promising practices, and fostering thoughtful solutions. Each consideration is paired with an example activity leaders can adapt. It is intended for "school site administrators, school district administrators, and other staff dedicated to improving the school climate."
requirements: Leaders must foster ongoing and authentic interactions anchored in genuine interest rather than engaging partners only to collect survey data or fulfill a mandate
constraints: Framed for K–12 school and district climate improvement and similar systems change efforts
target_learners: K-12 students, families, teachers, school staff, and community members as educational partners
target_learning_goals: School climate improvement
equity-centered systems change
inclusive decision-making
examples: The resource pairs each consideration with an example: listening sessions, empathy interviews, asset mapping, Start Stop Continue, and focus groups
key_sources: Ojetunde, T., & Chavez, A. (2024). Centering the experiences and perspectives of educational partners: Five considerations for schools and districts. California Center for School Climate at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655789

article_title: Centering the Experiences and Perspectives of Educational Partners: Five Considerations for Schools and Districts
citation: Ojetunde, T., & Chavez, A. (2024). Centering the experiences and perspectives of educational partners: Five considerations for schools and districts. California Center for School Climate at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Seek input from a diverse range of educational partners before deciding, to avoid solutionitis on complex school climate problems
description: The resource warns that rushed, isolated decision-making leads to "solutionitis," defined by the Carnegie Foundation as "the tendency to jump quickly on a solution before fully understanding the actual problem to be solved." Because school climate problems are multifaceted and intertwined with larger institutional challenges, and because an individual's perspective may be limited by personal experiences or biases, leaders should actively seek input from students, teachers, families, and community members to understand problems broadly before acting.
requirements: Leaders must pause and evaluate the situation in its entirety rather than defaulting to quick fixes made alone under time, resource, and staffing pressure
constraints: Especially important for multifaceted school climate issues such as safety and wellness, sense of belonging, and environment
target_learners: School site and district administrators and staff making budgetary, strategic, or instructional decisions
target_learning_goals: Accurate problem identification
inclusive and informed decision-making
equitable solution design
examples: The resource cites implicit-bias research (Gilliam et al., 2016) showing decisions made without checking biases can cause real harm, and co-design work (Daly-Smith et al., 2020) showing working with partners yields transformative solutions
key_sources: Ojetunde, T., & Chavez, A. (2024). Centering the experiences and perspectives of educational partners: Five considerations for schools and districts. California Center for School Climate at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655789

article_title: Pre-Referral Processes in California State Preschool Programs: How Practitioners Decide to Refer Multilingual Children for Special Education Evaluation
citation: Burr, E., Burho, J., & Perez, A. (2023). Pre-Referral Processes in California State Preschool Programs: How Practitioners Decide to Refer Multilingual Children for Special Education Evaluation. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Ensure high-quality early learning, including home language support, before referring an ML child for special education evaluation
description: The report holds that before referring an ML child for special education evaluation, programs must ensure high-quality early learning so that lack of opportunity to learn can be ruled out as a contributing factor. This includes supports for the home language and partnering with families to promote continued home language use. Interviewees described supplementary language programs, at-home activities, and social-emotional approaches used to rule out behavior before referral.
requirements: Supports for the home language, including partnering with families to promote continued use of the home language
constraints: Additional educator training may be needed so limited language fluency is not mistaken for a special need
target_learners: Multilingual children in California State Preschool Programs
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing language need from disability-related need before special education referral
examples: One site ran a supplementary weekly language program in which family members participated alongside children and received at-home activities; teams used trauma-informed care, Conscious Discipline, and Pyramid Teaching to rule out behavior.
key_sources: Burr, E., Burho, J., & Perez, A. (2023). Pre-Referral Processes in California State Preschool Programs: How Practitioners Decide to Refer Multilingual Children for Special Education Evaluation. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655866

article_title: How School Facilities Impact Student Health and Performance: Advancing Equity with Green Infrastructure
citation: Perez, Alyssa. (2024). How school facilities impact student health and performance: advancing equity with green infrastructure. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Causal chains as a research framework linking school building features to student health and performance
description: The brief describes "causal chains" as a method environmental health researchers developed to evidence how building features affect people where direct causal proof is impractical. Rather than showing a maintenance practice directly causes fewer asthma attacks, "researchers can test and evidence that the practice inhibits the growth of mold. Mold, causal studies can show, impacts asthma rates." The brief uses this framework to connect indoor air quality, heat, and lighting to attendance and achievement. It applies the framework to argue that sustainable school design can improve learning and well-being.
requirements: Requires identifying an intermediate mechanism (such as mold growth or absenteeism) that causal studies can individually establish
constraints: Evidencing direct causal relationships between building features and impacts on people is difficult due to how intricately people interact with their environments
target_learners: PK-12 students in California public schools
target_learning_goals: Student health, attendance, and academic performance as outcomes of the built environment
examples: The brief's asthma example: improved IAQ reduces asthma attacks, reducing chronic absenteeism and its educational harms
key_sources: Perez, Alyssa. (2024). How school facilities impact student health and performance: advancing equity with green infrastructure. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655919

article_title: How School Facilities Impact Student Health and Performance: Advancing Equity with Green Infrastructure
citation: Perez, Alyssa. (2024). How school facilities impact student health and performance: advancing equity with green infrastructure. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Catalogue of state and federal funding sources for sustainable school facility modernization
description: Figure 1 of the brief compiles federal and California-specific funding sources for sustainable facilities, including the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law's $500 million Renew America's Schools program and $5 billion Clean School Bus program, Inflation Reduction Act provisions, remaining ESSER funds ($7.68 billion unspent in California as of September 30, 2023), CalSHAPE ($20 million), ZESBI ($135 million), and the Green Schoolyard Grant Program ($100 million). Figure 2 adds guidance resources such as the Department of Energy's Efficient and Healthy Schools financing resources and Rewiring America's electrification handbook. The brief argues these can offset higher up-front costs of some green designs.
requirements: ESSER III facility spending must help reduce viral transmissibility or environmental health hazard exposure
constraints: Some approaches, like green schoolyards, carry higher up-front costs even when outweighed by mid-to-longer term benefits
target_learners: California PK-12 students in districts with outdated facilities
target_learning_goals: Financing learning environments that are more sustainable, healthy, and equitable
examples: U.S. DOE studies finding zero energy schools can be constructed at similar or lower costs than conventional schools while reducing operating costs
key_sources: Perez, Alyssa. (2024). How school facilities impact student health and performance: advancing equity with green infrastructure. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655919

article_title: Missing More than School: Reducing Chronic Absence for American Indian and Alaska Native Students
citation: Chang, H.N., & Leong, C. (2024). Missing more than school: Reducing chronic absence for American Indian and Alaska Native students. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Four-category taxonomy of root causes of chronic absenteeism: barriers, aversion, disengagement, and misconceptions
description: The brief organizes the reasons students miss school into four categories. As printed, "Figure 3 groups the reasons for absenteeism into four categories: barriers, aversion, disengagement, and misconceptions." Barriers include chronic illness, limited transportation, and housing and food insecurity; aversion includes unwelcoming school climate, anxiety, and biased disciplinary practices; disengagement includes boredom and lack of meaningful relationships with adults; misconceptions include beliefs that absences are only problematic if unexcused. The brief uses this taxonomy to argue that when large numbers of students are affected, systemic challenges beyond a student's or family's control are indicated.
requirements: Understanding the underlying causes of chronic absenteeism is treated as essential for devising effective solutions to improve attendance
constraints: The brief states these causes reflect systemic challenges in the community and in schools beyond a student's or family's control when large numbers of students are affected
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly American Indian/Alaska Native students
target_learning_goals: Regular school attendance and engagement in learning
examples: The brief maps issues commonly affecting AI/AN students' attendance, such as higher prevalence of chronic illness and limited health care access, onto these four categories
key_sources: Chang, H.N., & Leong, C. (2024). Missing more than school: Reducing chronic absence for American Indian and Alaska Native students. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655926

article_title: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems
citation: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Project Cal-Well three-component model for sustainable school-based mental health systems
description: The brief describes the Project Cal-Well model as "anchored by three components": Component 1 improves school climate for schoolwide prevention (policy changes, mental health literacy training, universal screening, MTSS and SEL programs, student-led clubs); Component 2 increases access to school-based behavioral health services (linkage protocols, staffing, referral tracking); Component 3 enhances community collaborations (partnerships, outreach, crisis response protocols). LEAs used this multifaceted approach emphasizing collaboration, community engagement, and infrastructure development.
requirements: LEAs implement all three components under state and county leadership with collaboration meetings and data sharing to build sustainable systems
constraints: Developed and evaluated within a SAMHSA Project AWARE State Education Agency grant program in California local educational agencies
target_learners: K-12 students in participating California local educational agencies
target_learning_goals: Student mental health awareness and access to school- and community-based mental health services
examples: Cohort 2 partnered with three county offices of education to support eight LEAs across five Northern California counties from 2019 to 2024
key_sources: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems. (2024). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655927

article_title: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems
citation: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: CHKS Mental Health Supports module and companion School Staff Survey Student Wellness Module
description: For the comprehensive Project Cal-Well evaluation, UCSF "created a custom Mental Health Supports module for the California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS)" to assess changes in students' mental health needs and access to support. In partnership with WestEd the module was expanded with trauma measures and is now part of the CHKS Behavioral Health Modules available to LEAs statewide. UCSF also developed a companion Student Wellness Module of the School Staff Survey to assess staff capacity to support student mental health over time.
requirements: Administered through the California Healthy Kids Survey system so LEAs statewide can use the behavioral health modules
constraints: Developed as part of the Project Cal-Well evaluation under the SAMHSA-funded grant
target_learners: K-12 students and school staff in California local educational agencies
target_learning_goals: Assessing student mental health needs, access to support, trauma exposure, and staff capacity to support student mental health
examples: The module was expanded to include additional measures on trauma and is now part of the CHKS Behavioral Health Modules available to LEAs statewide
key_sources: Project Cal-Well: Building Sustainable School-Based Mental Health Systems. (2024). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655927

article_title: Del Norte Unified School District: "A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services through Project Cal-Well"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Del Norte Unified School District: A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services Through Project Cal-Well. https://www.wested.org/
title: SAEBRS multi-informant universal mental health screening in DNUSD
description: The Social, Academic, and Emotional Behavior Risk Screener (SAEBRS) is a universal screening tool that DNUSD used with a "multi-informant approach," having "teachers and students complete" it, to monitor and respond to students' mental health needs. The brief reports that from fall 2020 through December 2023 the district conducted "nearly 11,000 student screenings," supported by Project Cal-Well's effort to build a culture of data-based decision-making about mental health supports and interventions.

District capacity to monitor and respond to screening results

Data-informed allocation of mental health supports
examples: Nearly 11,000 student screenings conducted from fall 2020 through December 2023

article_title: Del Norte Unified School District: "A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services through Project Cal-Well"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Del Norte Unified School District: A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services Through Project Cal-Well. https://www.wested.org/
title: Closed-loop referral system linking DNUSD wellness centers with community and county behavioral health providers
description: DNUSD established a closed-loop referral system with Project Cal-Well support after earlier referrals to community partners were often lost to waiting lists and lacked follow-up communication. The system "enables community-based service providers to refer students to the district's school-based wellness centers if they cannot meet their needs" and encourages regular communication with the county's Department of Behavioral Health, improving identification of unmet mental health needs in the district.

Regular communication between the district and county behavioral health
target_learners: Students needing behavioral health services beyond what community providers can supply

Identification of unmet mental health needs

article_title: Del Norte Unified School District: "A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services through Project Cal-Well"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Del Norte Unified School District: A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services Through Project Cal-Well. https://www.wested.org/
title: Project Cal-Well three-component school mental health model implemented in DNUSD
description: Project Cal-Well is a California Department of Education program, initiated in 2014 and funded by a SAMHSA NITT-AWARE grant, that "aims to expand mental health services in schools and communities." In Cohort 2 (2019–24) it supported DNUSD's multi-tiered system of support across three components: universal Tier 1 supports for positive school climate and social–emotional skills, Tier 2 school-based mental health services, and Tier 3 partnerships and cross-system collaborations. The district used the grant as a foundation to leverage additional pandemic-era funding.

Coordination with local and county behavioral health resources

Resilience
School safety
Access to mental health services

citation: Paradise Unified School District: Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery Through Project Cal-Well. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: RULER social–emotional learning approach adopted districtwide in PUSD
description: RULER is an SEL approach PUSD implemented as a primary objective to enhance student achievement. The name is "an acronym for Recognizing, Understanding, Labeling, Expressing, and Regulating," and it "focuses on developing these five key social–emotional intelligence skills." The district's initiative aims to establish a shared social–emotional vocabulary throughout all grades and schools within the district, positioning SEL as a Tier 1 universal support under Project Cal-Well.

In 2023/24 the district advanced this approach "by integrating data from monthly Kelvin real-time pulses," which allow "site administrators to customize monthly questions based on their specific goals." title: Universal mental health screening systems in Cal-Well districts
description: A district-level universal screening system in which every Project Cal-Well district in Stanislaus County now administers a mental health screener, such as the Covitality screening tool. article_title: Engaging English Learners with Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics
citation: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Three general approaches to reasoning about equivalence: convergent, relational, and transformational
description: Adapted from Cook and colleagues (2022), this framework describes three approaches students use to reason that two objects are equivalent. In the convergent approach, "Two objects are equivalent if they are related to a third object"; in the relational approach, objects are equivalent if they serve the same purpose or share characteristics; in the transformational approach, one object can be transformed into another via a sequence of allowable moves. The brief applies the framework across K-12 content and RAMPUP activities.
requirements: Educators are told they do not need to share the categories with students or require students to classify their reasoning; the framework serves teachers listening to student thinking
constraints: The brief notes the transformational approach was not applicable in the Perspective Plane context, so the framework does not apply uniformly across all mathematical contexts
target_learners: K-12 students, including students designated as English Learners
target_learning_goals: reasoning about mathematical equivalence across domains (arithmetic, algebra, geometry, statistics)
examples: In the Mean as Point of Balance activity, students employed a mix of transformational, relational, and convergent approaches to whether two dot plots share the same point of balance
key_sources: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED671702

description: RAMPUP (Reimagining and Amplifying Mathematics Participation, Understanding, and Practices) is a summer bridge program developed through the National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd to challenge and support rising 9th grade students transitioning from middle to high school. As the brief states, "RAMPUP is a 3-week program with three modules: patterns, networks, and equivalence." The brief draws examples of student reasoning from RAMPUP field trials.

article_title: Engaging English Learners with Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics
citation: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Equivalence reasoning progresses through three kinds of approaches — same value, related to each other, and transformable — across content strands
description: Across late elementary to middle grades, the brief organizes student approaches to equivalence in tables spanning fractions, rates, similarity of figures, algebraic expressions, and equations. Each strand is analyzed through the same three lenses: having the same value, being related to each other, and being transformable. As the brief puts it, "Table 1 presents some ways that students may reason about proportionality across the late elementary to middle grades," and Table 2 extends the same structure to expressions and equations.
requirements: Teachers should listen to students' reasoning across these approaches rather than requiring students to classify their own reasoning
constraints: The progression as printed spans late elementary through middle grades; high school work involves multiple representations across representational families
target_learners: late elementary, middle grades, and high school students, including English Learners
target_learning_goals: proportional reasoning, understanding the equals sign, equivalence of expressions and equations
examples: 4/8 and 2/4 are equivalent because they are both equal to 1/2 (same value); because 8 and 4 are twice 4 and 2 (related); or because multiplying 2/4 by 2/2 gives 4/8 (transformable)
key_sources: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED671702

article_title: Engaging English Learners with Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics
citation: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: RAMPUP uses six contextualized activity structures to elicit convergent, relational, and transformational equivalence reasoning
description: The brief illustrates equivalence reasoning through six RAMPUP contexts that overlap with but are not identical to typical school topics: mazes (connected components as equivalence classes), sliding puzzles, graphs of networks, the mean as point of balance, functions as alphabetic codes (integers modulo 26), and perspective drawing. As stated, "This section offers examples from observations of RAMPUP field trials and analysis of written student work." Table 3 maps student utterances in each context onto the three framework approaches.

target_learners: rising 9th grade students, including English Learners
target_learning_goals: connected components, graph equivalence, mean as balance point, modular arithmetic, coordinate geometry in perspective
examples: Students discover that multiplying by 2 modulo 26 makes encoded messages impossible to decode because A × 2 and N × 2 both yield B

article_title: Systems Alignment and Coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's Early Care and Education System
citation: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Alignment and coherence framework with six interrelated domains for system improvement
description: The report defines alignment as "all policies, practices, processes, and roles in a system working together in similar or consistent ways" and coherence as integration that mutually reinforces shared understanding and progress toward a clear vision. It organizes the features of alignment and coherence along six interrelated domains—goals, funding and policies, strategic communication, interest holder engagement, capacity building, and data use—situated within a five-step data-driven continuous improvement process and technical and adaptive approaches to change. Alignment can be internal, horizontal, or vertical.
requirements: A shared vision and theory of change established as the first step of the continuous improvement process
Inventory of whole-person initiatives and analysis of interrelationships before creating an action plan
constraints: The framework is presented for child-, youth-, and family-serving systems, applied here to early care and learning in Alameda County
target_learners: Young children from birth through age 12 and their families in Alameda County early care and learning systems
target_learning_goals: Kindergarten readiness and healthy learning and development through aligned, coherent early childhood systems
examples: The report applies the six domains to structure its analysis of First 5 Alameda's approach and opportunities for Measure C and the Oakland Children's Initiative
key_sources: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673491

article_title: Systems Alignment and Coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's Early Care and Education System
citation: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Measure C and the Oakland Children's Initiative early childhood funding initiatives
description: Measure C is a countywide transaction and use tax–funded initiative passed in March 2020 that will generate an estimated $150 million annually for a Child Care, Preschool, and Early Education Fund, with aims of expanded access to high-quality care, improved provider wages, and promotion of wellness and kindergarten readiness. The Oakland Children's Initiative, established through Measure AA in 2018, is expected to generate approximately $30 million annually, with about 62 percent of the remaining amount allocated to early childhood and 31 percent to college persistence and success implemented by Oakland Promise. First 5 Alameda administers Measure C and is the contracted implementation partner for the Oakland Children's Initiative Early Education Fund.
requirements: Public accountability and demonstration of impact, which the report calls of paramount importance because the initiatives are funded by sales and parcel taxes that increase the cost of living
constraints: Measure C was delayed by multiyear litigation and is currently being launched; the Oakland Children's Initiative prioritizes families in the public education system
target_learners: Children from birth to age 12 in Alameda County (Measure C) and children birth to age 5 plus students to and through college in Oakland (Oakland Children's Initiative)
target_learning_goals: Kindergarten readiness, school success, expanded access to high-quality early care and learning, and college persistence and success
examples: Measure C's initial investments include a 2-year Emergency Stabilization Fund as part of the initial investment of the 5-year plan
key_sources: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673491

citation: Walrond, N., Serwanga, R., & Farrell, G. (2025). Systems alignment and coherence: Opportunities for Alameda County's early care and education system. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Share early care information through trusted community channels and in families' routine settings and languages
description: The report presents strategic communication as both an engine and a by-product of alignment and coherence, and recommends bidirectional communication that builds awareness while gathering timely, honest feedback. Listening session participants "asked for materials to be shared in places that are part of their routines (such as faith communities or community resource centers)," translated into multiple languages, and delivered through trusted community leaders. The principle holds that outreach should meet families where they are.
requirements: Communication channels that are diverse and fully accessible to meet language, technology, and diverse ability needs
constraints: The report notes some communities, such as the Mam community, rely on word-of-mouth information sharing, requiring tailored channels
target_learners: Families with young children in Oakland and Alameda County, including communities that are often marginalized and harder to reach
target_learning_goals: Awareness of and access to high-quality early care and learning opportunities
examples: First 5 Alameda invests in trusted relationships through programs for providers (Quality Counts), families (Help Me Grow), the public (AlamedaKids.org), and policymakers (board of supervisors district data profiles)

article_title: Strengthening English Learner Reclassification in California
citation: Strengthening English Learner Reclassification in California. (2024). Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd, U.S. Department of Education grant #S283B190053. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/coe/indicator/cgf
title: OPTEL: an observation protocol standardizing teacher evaluation and parent consultation in English learner reclassification
description: The Observation Protocol for Teachers of English Learners (OPTEL) is a tool developed with the Region 15 Comprehensive Center for the California Department of Education. It "standardizes reclassification criteria 2 and 3" and is "intended to support teachers' evaluation of English learners' English proficiency while they are engaging in learning academic content, including during collaboration with peers." It can also be used formatively, for parent conversations, and in teacher preparation.
requirements: Relies on a robust understanding of the English learner development (ELD) standards released in 2014, whose proficiency levels align with OPTEL ratings
constraints: Early adopter LEAs had begun implementing; CDE encouraged statewide adoption starting in fall 2024
target_learners: English learners in California K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: Accurate, consistent, and equitable English proficiency evaluation for reclassification decisions
examples: California early adopter LEAs implementing OPTEL with statewide adoption encouraged starting fall 2024

article_title: Strengthening English Learner Reclassification in California
citation: Strengthening English Learner Reclassification in California. (2024). Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd, U.S. Department of Education grant #S283B190053. https://nces.ed.gov/programs/coe/indicator/cgf
title: California's four reclassification criteria under Education Code 313.3
description: The California Education Code (EC 313.3) outlines four criteria for reclassification of English learners: a proficient score on the state's English language proficiency assessment, teacher evaluation, parental opinion and consultation, and "a comparison of the pupil's performance in basic skills against a range of English proficient pupils of the same age." ESSA requires states to set a single standardized set of rules for all districts, making these criteria the operational definition of exiting English learner services in California.
requirements: Under ESSA, all schools and districts must use the same criteria for reclassification

target_learning_goals: Determining when students have met criteria to exit English learner services
examples: OPTEL standardizes criteria 2 and 3 of the four EC 313.3 criteria

article_title: Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations
citation: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://wested.org/
title: Five-domain framework for high-quality kindergarten entry assessments
description: The brief defines a high-quality KEA as an assessment whose content spans five child development domains designed to gather comprehensive student data: "physical well-being, social–emotional skills, learning approaches, language and literacy, and cognitive development." It uses this framework as the core content criterion for KEA quality, alongside clear administration guidelines and alignment with curriculum standards and other early childhood assessments. The framework is attributed to prior work by the K–3 Formative Assessment Consortium, Weisenfeld and colleagues, and Yun and colleagues.
requirements: Content must encompass the five developmental domains to gather comprehensive student data
constraints: The brief presents this as a characteristic of high-quality KEAs drawn from cited prior work, not as a tested result of its own
target_learners: children entering kindergarten
target_learning_goals: comprehensive assessment of developmental progress across physical, social-emotional, learning-approach, language and literacy, and cognitive domains
examples: State and national KEAs listed in the brief's appendix table are described against these domains, including language, literacy, math, science, executive function, and social-emotional skills for state KEAs
key_sources: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673515

article_title: Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations
citation: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://wested.org/
title: Do not use KEA data for accountability, kindergarten-entry delay, or disability diagnosis
description: The brief states that although KEAs serve many purposes, certain uses are inappropriate: "KEA data should not be used as part of an accountability system for students, teachers, or early learning providers." It further advises that KEAs should not be used to delay a student's kindergarten start or to diagnose a learning disability. The principle bounds appropriate KEA use to instructional guidance and planning rather than high-stakes or diagnostic decisions.
requirements: KEA use should be matched to a state's specific intended purpose, since a KEA cannot meet all possible uses simultaneously
constraints: Evaluating programs with a KEA depends on the presence of a dedicated study designed for that purpose
target_learners: children entering kindergarten
target_learning_goals: appropriate use of assessment data to support learning rather than for accountability or diagnosis
examples: The brief directs readers to Table 1 in the Appendix, which details potential KEA uses at classroom, building or site, district, and state levels, marking evaluation uses as requiring a dedicated study
key_sources: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673515

title: Commercially created KEAs most commonly offered by states
description: The brief identifies the most common commercially created KEAs used by states in its 2024 national scan: "Teaching Strategies Gold (offered by five states), the Desired Results Development Profile (offered by four states), and the Brigance Assessments (offered by four states)." These instruments appear in the appendix table as state-approved options that districts may choose from, alongside state-developed assessments such as state kindergarten readiness assessments.

constraints: The scan captured only publicly available information within the January-to-April 2024 research period

target_learning_goals: measuring kindergarten readiness across developmental domains
examples: Colorado offers ten state-approved options districts may choose from, including Teaching Strategies GOLD, Brigance Early Childhood Screens III, and FastBridge earlyMath

citation: Rolla, A., Mottesi, G., Wylen, M., & Akinola, Y. (2024). Kindergarten Entry Assessments: An Examination of Best Practices, National Trends, and Recommendations. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://wested.org/
title: Tiered uses of KEA data across classroom, building, district, and state levels
description: The brief organizes potential KEA uses by interest-holder level in an appendix table adapted from Garver and Yun and colleagues. At the classroom level, uses include tailoring individualized instruction and engaging families; at the building level, shaping schoolwide programming and tracking students in a data management system; at the district level, measuring curriculum effectiveness and informing resource allocation; and at the state level, evaluating progress toward state goals and allocating funding. Uses marked with an asterisk require a dedicated evaluation study.

constraints: KEAs cannot serve all of these purposes simultaneously
