article_title: Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: School and district leaders should fund ongoing, high-quality professional development with collaborative inquiry to build teachers' CRSE capacity
description: The brief argues that professional development is the key lever for building teacher capacity for CRSE in mathematics, since teachers vary in experience and comfort with the approach. It specifies that PD should be ongoing, deepen mathematics content knowledge alongside CRSE understanding, and involve collaborative inquiry that situates teachers in a community of practice where they design lessons and experiment with new practices. Promising methods named include lesson study, funds of knowledge study groups, and empathy methods.
requirements: PD must be ongoing and involve collaborative inquiry, situating teachers within a community of practice with opportunities to design mathematics lessons and experiment with new instructional practices
constraints: These professional learning opportunities require sufficient resources and time
target_learners: K-12 mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: Enacting culturally responsive and sustaining education in mathematics instruction
examples: The brief names lesson study, funds of knowledge study groups, and empathy methods as promising PD approaches, and suggests organizing PD into tiers so teachers move from novice to intermediary to advanced levels of practice
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673516

article_title: Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five criteria for mathematics curricular materials that support culturally responsive and sustaining education
description: The brief defines what CRSE-aligned mathematics curricular materials should do, listing five criteria: they should "affirm racial and cultural identities," "cultivate agency and belonging," "build critical consciousness," "center diverse perspectives," and "center student learning and academic success." The brief argues that such materials spare teachers the cognitively demanding and time-consuming task of making ad-hoc curriculum adjustments, enabling them to enact CRSE more effectively.
requirements: Materials must fulfill all five stated criteria: affirming racial and cultural identities, cultivating agency and belonging, building critical consciousness, centering diverse perspectives, and centering student learning and academic success
constraints: If adopting a new curriculum is not possible, the brief offers guiding questions for diversifying existing materials instead
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics learning grounded in racial and cultural identity, agency, belonging, and critical consciousness
examples: The brief points readers to the WestEd publication Essential Characteristics of Math Curriculum Materials That Advance Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education for more detail
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673516

article_title: Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Establish a learning culture that frames mistakes as improvement and uses data for inquiry rather than penalizing teachers
description: Because teachers will likely make mistakes while adjusting their practices as they learn CRSE, the brief urges leaders to examine how accountability structures affect teachers' willingness to adopt it. It notes that policies penalizing low standardized-test performance may encourage teaching to the test, leaving little room for experimentation. Leaders should frame learning from mistakes as a step toward improvement, clarify that data gathering supports inquiry rather than assessment or penalty, and create internal structures where experienced CRSE teachers coach colleagues.
requirements: Leaders must clarify that data such as test scores or climate survey results are gathered to support inquiry and learning rather than to assess or penalize teachers and students
constraints: Accountability policies that penalize low test performance may undermine teachers' willingness to experiment with CRSE practices
target_learners: K-12 mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: Sustained adoption of culturally responsive and sustaining instructional practices
examples: The brief suggests giving teachers more experienced with CRSE designated additional planning time to coach less experienced colleagues

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Air Tutors virtual high-dosage math tutoring program
description: Air Tutors is an online high-dosage math tutoring program for upper elementary and early middle school grades, delivered via "dynamic video conferencing and interactive whiteboards" at a ratio of four students per tutor. It offers 45-minute sessions four to five times per week over 10 weeks (30 intended hours), uses the i-Ready curriculum's scope and sequence, employs tutors with at least a bachelor's degree and 3 years of experience, and structures instruction within the gradual release of responsibility framework alongside an Ubuntu professional learning community.
requirements: Tutors with at least 3 years of math teaching experience and a bachelor's degree or higher
Sufficient scheduling, budget, and calendar time to deliver the intended 30-hour dosage over at least 10 weeks
constraints: In this evaluation, District B schools delivered far fewer hours than planned due to budget reductions, scheduling limits, late starts, and cancellations
target_learners: 4th through 6th grade students needing foundational math support
target_learning_goals: Foundational math skills including decimals, fractions, proportions, and basic geometry
examples: In the 2023–24 evaluation, 1,210 students across two districts attended at least one Air Tutors session, with tutors delivering instruction via the online platform
key_sources: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673538

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Gradual release of responsibility four-phase tutoring sequence
description: Air Tutors structures tutoring within the gradual release of responsibility (GRR) framework, a sequence of learning activities that shifts responsibility for learning from tutor to student across four phases: focused instruction ("I do it"), guided instruction ("We do it"), collaborative learning ("You do it together"), and independent learning ("You do it alone"). Tutors model cognitive processes so learners can understand metacognition and eventually replicate strategies independently. The framework need not be linear: educators may begin in any phase, and students move back and forth between components as they master skills.
requirements: Tutors introduced to the GRR framework during professional learning sessions before applying it in tutoring
constraints: The article notes the process can flow quickly or skip phases depending on the topic and student, and the framework does not have to be linear
target_learners: 4th through 6th grade students in small-group math tutoring
target_learning_goals: Building student independence and confidence as independent learners and thinkers in mathematics
examples: Air Tutors tutors apply the four GRR phases within 45-minute tutoring sessions, with the goal of equipping students to move forward as independent learners rather than remaining dependent on a tutor
key_sources: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673538

article_title: An Evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures Grant
citation: Fong, A., Chen-Gaddini, M., & Huang, M. (2025). An evaluation of the Air Tutors Program: Findings from an Arnold Ventures grant. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Align tutoring implementation with evidence-based dosage recommendations before launch
description: Because impacts appeared only when students approached the intended dosage, the report recommends that districts plan for sufficient time, stability, and support before adopting high-dosage tutoring. It states "it is important for districts to align their tutoring implementation with evidence-based dosage recommendations to ensure that sufficient time, stability, and support are available for the tutoring implementation," and that providers such as Air Tutors should ensure districts and schools are aware of dosage recommendations so students experience positive impacts.
requirements: District awareness of the program's recommended dosage (for Air Tutors, 30 hours via four to five 45-minute sessions weekly over 10 weeks)
constraints: In this evaluation, budget limitations, scheduling challenges, frequent cancellations, and delayed starts prevented District B from delivering the intended dosage
target_learners: 4th through 6th grade students in high-dosage math tutoring programs
target_learning_goals: Math achievement gains from tutoring delivered at the intended dosage
examples: District A scheduled tutoring so that 93 percent of participants reached the 24-hour threshold, while District B's budget cuts and cancellations left 62 percent of participants at 15 or fewer hours

title: Map of Portrait of a Graduate development approaches by state (Figure 1)
description: Figure 1 is a map classifying U.S. states by POG development approach, based on "a scan of publicly available documents and websites as of October 2024." Light blue states have documentation about district-led POGs with no formal statewide effort; dark blue states have a state-led POG effort in development or completed; white states lack publicly available documentation of either. The map operationalizes the brief's state-led versus district-led taxonomy.

article_title: Building Future-Ready Students: The State of Portraits of a Graduate Frameworks
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). Building future-ready students: The state of Portraits of a Graduate Frameworks. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Taxonomy of POG assessment strategies: state menu-based demonstration, experiential/performance assessment, embedded formative assessment, and competency-based progression
description: The brief organizes how states measure POG competencies into distinct approaches. Colorado uses Graduation Guidelines under which "Local school boards select from a state-provided menu of assessment options"; Nevada and Virginia use experiential learning demonstrated through "portfolios and capstones or hands-on learning opportunities"; Michigan emphasizes formative assessments embedded in learning alongside summative assessments of deeper learning; and New Hampshire integrates POG assessment into competency-based education where students advance on mastery rather than time in class.
requirements: Assessment systems must align with POG competencies and be supported by teacher training and resources, per the brief's policy discussion
constraints: The brief notes this aspect of POGs "remains fluid as states work to balance their accountability systems"
target_learners: high school students
target_learning_goals: demonstrating proficiency in POG competencies such as critical thinking, communication, and collaboration
examples: Colorado school boards select from a state-provided menu; New Hampshire students advance based on mastery of specific competencies rather than time spent in class

article_title: Building Future-Ready Students: The State of Portraits of a Graduate Frameworks
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). Building future-ready students: The state of Portraits of a Graduate Frameworks. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Policymakers should weigh locally developed versus state-mandated POGs, since local POGs reflect community values while state-mandated POGs offer uniform frameworks and consistent access
description: The brief recommends that policymakers explicitly consider the tradeoff between locally tailored and state-mandated POGs. Locally developed POGs "can reflect community needs and values," while state-mandated POGs "offer a uniform framework that can simplify the support structure for schools and ensure all students have access to a consistent set of competencies and resources." The recommendation follows the brief's finding that both approaches coexist nationally.
requirements: Coordination across multiple agencies and regions for state-led approaches; collaborative community processes for district-led approaches
constraints: The brief frames this as a policy consideration, not a tested comparison of outcomes
target_learners: all high school students
target_learning_goals: developing broad 21st-century competencies defined in POG frameworks
examples: The brief contrasts Indiana's statewide POG mandating academic mastery and career readiness with district-led POGs such as San Marcos Unified's emphasis on adaptability and relational competence

article_title: Implementing Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Three Tiers of Prevention and Intervention as Protective Factors
citation: Gage, N. A., Grasley-Boy, N. M., MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Ulrich, T. G. (2025). Implementing Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Three Tiers of Prevention and Intervention as Protective Factors. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: PBIS three-tiered prevention and intervention framework
description: PBIS is described as "a three-tiered, comprehensive, evidence-based framework aimed at improving and integrating all the data, systems, and practices that shape student outcomes." It organizes supports into universal Tier 1 schoolwide expectations taught and positively reinforced for all students, targeted Tier 2 small-group social skills supports such as Check In–Check Out for roughly 5–15 percent of students, and intensive individualized Tier 3 supports based on functional behavior assessment for 3–5 percent of students. It is a framework supporting ongoing professional development and capacity building, not a curriculum or scripted program.
requirements: Schools identify a leadership team, secure staff buy-in, evaluate data systems, identify training and coaching resources, develop an action plan, and monitor and adjust implementation, including completing the Tiered Fidelity Inventory
constraints: The article states universal Tier 1 PBIS is designed to prevent challenging behavior but not designed to address needs that are more intensive
target_learners: All students in a school, with Tier 2 supports for the approximately 5–15 percent nonresponsive to Tier 1 and Tier 3 supports for the 3–5 percent needing individualized intervention
target_learning_goals: Improving social, emotional, behavioral, and academic outcomes for all students and reducing disciplinary exclusions
examples: A midwestern state has trained over 800 schools in more than 280 districts since 2005 using a 2-year cohort model, representing 44 percent of all schools statewide
key_sources: Gage, N. A., Grasley-Boy, N. M., MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Ulrich, T. G. (2025). Implementing Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Three Tiers of Prevention and Intervention as Protective Factors. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673553

article_title: Navigating a Sea of Reforms: Sustaining School Health Centers through Statewide Initiatives
citation: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://WestEd.org
title: Certified Wellness Coach provider type
description: Certified Wellness Coach is "a newly defined provider type designed to increase the capacity of schools and community-based partners to support the behavioral health needs of youth." Coaches deliver nonclinical services—wellness promotion and education, screening, care coordination, individual and group support, and crisis referral—under supervision of Pupil Personnel Services credentialed holders or licensed clinicians. A state certification program launched in January 2024 with education and workforce pathways; SHC managers saw the role as aligned with existing unlicensed staff such as case managers and health educators.
requirements: Positions work as part of a larger care team under supervision of Pupil Personnel Services credentialed holders or licensed clinicians
Workforce-pathway applicants need an associate or bachelor's degree and at least 1,350 hours of related experience
constraints: Certified Wellness Coaches are not eligible providers in current FQHC prospective payment system rates, creating a disincentive for FQHC-sponsored SHCs to hire them
SHCs are reluctant to add positions without a clear picture of long-term sustainability through Fee Schedule billing
target_learners: Students and youth up to age 24 in Alameda County public schools
target_learning_goals: Behavioral health and well-being support for youth, including wellness promotion, screening, and care coordination
examples: SHCs identified schoolwide prevention activities, classroom presentations, care coordination, and case management as services fitting the wellness coach role
key_sources: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673564

article_title: Navigating a Sea of Reforms: Sustaining School Health Centers through Statewide Initiatives
citation: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://WestEd.org
title: Multi-Payer School-Linked Fee Schedule
description: The Fee Schedule is "a new, optional program that reimburses local educational agencies (LEAs) and school-linked designated providers for mental health and substance use disorder services provided to students 25 years of age or younger at or near a school site." It requires commercial and Medi-Cal managed care plans to reimburse school-based and school-linked providers, covering psychoeducation, screening and assessments, therapy, and case management. LEAs enroll in cohorts and may designate contracted or affiliate providers, with claims administered by Carelon.
requirements: Community-based providers such as SHC lead agencies must participate through an LEA enrolled as a Fee Schedule provider
LEAs must enroll as providers and designate other providers as contracted or affiliate members of their network
constraints: Outcomes of participation are still largely unknown; as of December 2024 only a small number of LEAs statewide had successfully submitted a claim
The program is not intended to replace existing service delivery covered by Medi-Cal specialty and nonspecialty mental health systems
target_learners: Students age 25 or younger receiving services at or near school sites
target_learning_goals: Access to mental health and substance use disorder services regardless of insurance type
examples: Six Alameda County districts with SHCs enrolled in Cohorts 1 and 2 (January and July 2024); five SHCs' potential revenue was estimated in Table 1
key_sources: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673564

article_title: Navigating a Sea of Reforms: Sustaining School Health Centers through Statewide Initiatives
citation: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://WestEd.org
title: Sustain school health centers with continued county operational funding alongside new billing initiatives
description: The report concludes that new billing revenues cannot by themselves sustain school health centers: "New funding through the CYBHI's Fee Schedule and CalAIM's ECM benefit do not offer an obvious pathway to replace the county's investment in SHCs with operational funds." County operational funds play a critical role in sustaining SHC staffing models, and most county-funded personnel have little or no billing pathway. The report recommends that Healthy Schools and Communities identify other sustainability strategies, new partners, or expanded county funds to maintain operations.
requirements: Continued county operational grants or alternative sustainability strategies and new partners to maintain current SHC capacity
constraints: Lead agencies face workforce shortages and are navigating multiple reforms simultaneously; SHCs cannot adopt state initiatives without support and buy-in from lead agency decision-makers
target_learners: Children and youth served by Alameda County school health centers
target_learning_goals: Sustained access to school-based health and behavioral health services supporting student well-being and attendance
examples: WestEd analyzed 2024–25 projected budgets for each lead agency and estimated Fee Schedule revenue for five SHCs to assess whether state initiatives could replace county funds

article_title: Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics
citation: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief.
title: A taxonomy of seven broad outcomes for culturally responsive and sustaining mathematics education
description: The brief organizes CRSE mathematics implementation around a set of outcomes beyond achievement: "students' development of mathematical identity, practice, and empowerment," plus co-construction of knowledge, broadened participation, competent doing, community and family alignment, critical consciousness and cultural competence, and mathematical talk. Table 1 pairs each outcome with a description and a potential classroom measure, positioning these outcomes as "critical drivers of mathematical competence and success" that systems should institutionalize alongside dominant outcomes.
requirements: Leaders and teachers systematize these outcomes so they are as important as dominant outcomes, including developing new measurement systems for identity, participation, and practice
constraints: The brief notes these outcomes are not typically prioritized at scale in large educational systems
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students, particularly students of color and marginalized learners
target_learning_goals: mathematical identity development
participation in mathematical discourse
competent doing of mathematics
critical consciousness and cultural competence
examples: Table 1 lists outcomes with measures such as regular student reflection writing on mathematical experiences and tracking the frequency and diversity of student contributions during discussions
key_sources: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673572

article_title: Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics
citation: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief.
title: Reframe achievement gap data using six critical criteria rather than gap-gazing
description: The brief argues that gap-gazing — "the all-out focus on achievement disparities, primarily between White students, students of color, and other marginalized groups" — narrows conceptions of learning and equity to achievement and produces stereotypes of marginalized students. It recommends keeping achievement gap data but reframing it through six criteria, each with guiding questions in Figure 1, so gap data is contextualized, systemic, and paired with data on nondominant outcomes and spaces of excellence.
requirements: Achievement gap data should be situated in historical, sociopolitical, and longitudinal context and presented as a systems problem
constraints: The brief warns gaps are often misunderstood as purely technical problems solvable by fixing an instructional strategy, when they are rooted in histories of injustice and systemic racism
target_learners: marginalized students, students of color, and their families in mathematics education systems
target_learning_goals: educational equity in mathematics
mathematical identity development
critical examination of achievement disparities
examples: Figure 1 pairs each criterion with questions such as how the gap has manifested over time, how the system produces the problem, and what students and families say about how they experience it
key_sources: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673572

article_title: Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics
citation: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief.
title: Practical measures as sensing mechanisms for CRSE implementation in mathematics
description: Practical measures are tools that "act as sensing mechanisms at the level at which work is carried out" and can be easily collected, analyzed, and used within practitioners' daily work lives. The brief describes them as reflecting practice and providing timely information to identify systemic breakdowns, focus educators' attention, propel improvement efforts, and build confidence in promising changes. In CRSE mathematics, they help teachers gauge whether instruction resonates with diverse cultural backgrounds and adapt their practice.
requirements: Teachers need support from school and district leaders to design and use practical measures connected to academic achievement and content standards
constraints: The brief presents practical measures as requiring regular collection, analysis, and reflection time within teachers' work lives
target_learners: mathematics teachers and school and district leaders implementing CRSE
target_learning_goals: assessing effectiveness of CRSE innovations
tailoring instruction to culturally and linguistically diverse learners
teacher reflection on equity-focused practice
examples: The brief lists gathering practices including formative assessment, self-reflection and peer observation, exit tickets, student feedback surveys, action research, supervisor feedback, and formative evaluations
key_sources: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673572

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Treat learning as multidirectional: school leaders and teachers should provide ample space to learn from and with families and communities
description: This principle holds that educators must not prioritize school-based knowledge in ways that devalue learning outside school. The brief urges that school leaders and teachers "provide ample space to learn from and with families, caregivers, and other respected leaders in the community," because "learning should be multidirectional." It is one of four recommendations for codesigning CRSE in mathematics.
requirements: A shift in educator mindsets and practices, and sustained, meaningful school–family partnerships, to welcome alternative ways of knowing and doing mathematics
constraints: The brief warns that prioritizing school-based knowledge can unintentionally undermine or devalue learning that takes place outside of the school context
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students and their families and communities
target_learning_goals: Mathematics learning that bridges students' home and school lives
examples: The brief instructs that educators' interactions with families and community members incorporate their feedback into meaningful decision-making processes
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Recognize and address power dynamics that make it hard for family and community members to show up authentically in schooling
description: The brief argues that in schooling, leaders and teachers hold relatively high power compared to family and community members external to the institution, visible in teacher-led parent conferences and unidirectional messaging. It recommends being intentional in showing families they are valued as people who use mathematics in everyday decision-making and that their knowledge has a place in schools.
requirements: Leaders must intentionally signal that families' everyday mathematical knowledge is useful and has a place in schools
constraints: Power dynamics show up in teacher-led parent conferences and unidirectional phone calls and email messaging; educators hold significant power in determining whose experiences hold valuable mathematical knowledge
target_learners: Families and community members of mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Valuing out-of-school mathematical knowledge and practices within school mathematics
examples: The brief notes research suggesting even early childhood teachers privilege some out-of-school mathematical practices over others, and that parents may feel pressure to conform to mainstream formal practices (Wager & Whyte, 2013; Takeuchi, 2018)
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Cultural brokers: school staff positions for soliciting family input through connection, education, and advocacy
description: Cultural brokers are a staffing investment the brief recommends for disrupting power dynamics in family engagement. It defines them as "school staff positions responsible for soliciting family input through connection, education, and advocacy" and says investing in them "can help solicit family input and bridge the gap between families and schools," citing Torres et al. (2015).
requirements: School investment in dedicated staff positions
constraints: The brief presents cultural brokers as one example among ways to disrupt power dynamics, not a tested intervention
target_learners: Families and community members of mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Bridging family and school communication around mathematics education
examples: The brief cites the University of Washington College of Education's cultural brokering brief (Torres et al., 2015)
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Engage families and communities through activities that are mutually beneficial and extend beyond the school setting
description: The brief frames family and community engagement as part of a mutually beneficial relationship, asking what role schools can play in improving outcomes for the broader community and how mathematics can make a difference locally. It states that "broadening engagement to encompass activities beyond the school setting shows an investment in families and communities," citing financial literacy campaigns and community garden planning as examples.
requirements: Activities should center the community's own needs and desires
target_learners: Mathematics students, their families, and the broader community
target_learning_goals: Mathematical learning applied to real-world community problems
examples: Financial literacy campaigns and community garden planning engage the broader community in mathematical learning; STEM fairs and community health assessments let students share mathematical learning with the community
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf

citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Table 1: seven community-based mathematics projects engaging students, families, and communities beyond the classroom
description: Table 1 lists learning projects supporting mathematics engagement beyond the school context: public art installation, environmental conservation project, urban planning simulation, community health assessment, financial literacy campaign, community garden planning, and STEM fair or expo. Each row describes how students participate, e.g., using "area, perimeter, and volume to calculate the space needed for planting" in garden planning.
requirements: Educators partner with local organizations and community stakeholders
constraints: The brief presents these as illustrative examples from cited sources, not as evaluated interventions of its own
target_learners: Mathematics students and their families and communities, including grades 6-8 in the cited garden task
target_learning_goals: Applying mathematical concepts such as geometry, measurement, statistical analysis, modeling, and budgeting to real-world community projects
examples: Public art installations use geometry, measurement, proportion, and budgeting; conservation projects use mathematical modeling and statistical analysis to study pollution, biodiversity, or climate change trends
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Support mathematics teachers in designing project-based learning opportunities centered on local community needs
description: The brief recommends that school leaders build relationships with local organizations and community leaders well respected by both students and their families, because partnering with such groups "can help level power dynamics and create pathways for teachers to design meaningful project-based learning opportunities" (citing Caires-Hurley et al., 2020). Leaders should provide access to curriculum and training so mathematical tasks can address local community needs.
requirements: Leaders should provide access to curriculum and training to support project-based learning
target_learners: Mathematics teachers and their students
target_learning_goals: Solidifying mathematical concepts through community-centered project-based learning
examples: Cited examples include public art installations, conservation projects, and urban planning simulations designed to solidify mathematical concepts

article_title: So, You Want to Create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and Considerations for the Field
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Governance taxonomy of POG development and implementation approaches varying by state involvement and local autonomy
description: The brief organizes POG development and implementation along a governance axis: "Approaches for developing and implementing POGs vary widely across states and districts, including the level of state involvement and local autonomy." It distinguishes a state-led standardized approach (e.g., Indiana, North Carolina, Virginia) that "ensures a level of consistency" from locally controlled approaches (e.g., California, Colorado, Illinois, Iowa) that allow customization, and notes most states do not mandate a POG at all, in which case districts may mandate and develop their own.
requirements: States or districts must decide how local goals align with or diverge from state policies, consulting the state department of education particularly on assessment and accountability requirements.
constraints: The brief states the locally controlled approach "can also lead to a diverse patchwork of graduate profiles," creating consistency challenges, while the state-led approach must balance "statewide consistency and the need for local relevance."
target_learners: high school students
target_learning_goals: demonstrating knowledge, skills, and abilities to graduate and contribute to families, workplaces, and communities
examples: States such as Indiana, North Carolina, and Virginia adopted a standardized state-developed POG; California, Colorado, Illinois, and Iowa provide districts flexibility to develop their own POGs.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673579

article_title: So, You Want to Create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and Considerations for the Field
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Establish a representative design committee and limit POG competencies to six or fewer
description: The brief recommends a design committee including representatives from state and local businesses and nonprofits, school and district leadership, students, and families, which creates, vets, and refines the competency list and outlines a high-level vision serving as the educational North Star. Researchers and practitioners recommend limiting competencies to six or fewer because "the power of a POG lies in its ability to align and focus educators." Common competencies include durable skills such as communication, critical thinking, and leadership.
requirements: A design committee with diverse interest-holder representation; third-party organizations are often engaged to facilitate feedback sessions and summarize information for the committee.
target_learners: high school students
educators and district leaders
target_learning_goals: defining and focusing instruction on durable skills and behavioral regulation competencies
examples: Core competencies most commonly reflected in POGs include communication, critical thinking, and leadership, with personal and interpersonal competencies such as creativity, adaptability, persistence, and relational awareness often included.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673579

article_title: So, You Want to Create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and Considerations for the Field
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Centralized online POG resource hub with advisory-group curation
description: Following assessment decisions, states and districts can support educators by creating a centralized resource hub offering guidelines and exemplars for effective assessment implementation. States like Colorado, New Hampshire, Utah, and Virginia have created online platforms where educators and administrators can access resources, share experiences, and learn from successful POG implementations. State and industry leaders can recruit a state POG advisory group to vet resources and tools and regularly convene to improve the site.
requirements: The hub should be regularly updated with new materials and case studies from districts and other states; an advisory group should regularly convene to discuss, improve, and bring fresh ideas and innovations to the site.
target_learners: educators and administrators
target_learning_goals: effective POG assessment implementation
examples: Colorado, New Hampshire, Utah, and Virginia created an online platform or hub for educators and administrators to access resources and share experiences.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673579

article_title: So, You Want to Create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and Considerations for the Field
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Translate POG competencies into measurable objectives aligned with state standards to guide teaching and assessment
description: The brief recommends that states and districts develop clear assessment criteria and align POG competencies with state standards. By translating competencies into measurable objectives, educators receive a clear roadmap for both teaching and evaluating the competencies, enabling assessments to serve as a guide for continuous instructional improvement. Alignment is fostered through collaboration among state education departments, district leaders, teachers, higher education institutions, and industry experts.
requirements: Collaborative efforts between state education departments, district leaders, teachers, institutions of higher education, and industry experts to ensure POG assessments reflect the rigor and quality of state standards.
constraints: Districts may struggle to balance POG competency assessments with state-mandated standardized tests, and may lack resources for time- and resource-intensive performance tasks, portfolios, and project-based learning evaluations.
target_learners: educators
high school students
target_learning_goals: teaching and evaluating POG competencies within the broader educational system
examples: Some states align standardized testing with POG competencies through crosswalks of state standards, revising test items for higher order thinking, or incorporating performance-based tasks in areas like communication and collaboration.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673579

article_title: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment
citation: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Ten Aspects of Community framework for organizing youth-supporting community assets
description: The Ten Aspects of Community, developed by the Forum for Youth Investment (Pittman et al., 2003, based on Pittman & Irby, 1996), is a taxonomy of community features that directly affect youth. The report states it "defines Ten Aspects of Community": Basic Services; Cultural and Artistic; Economic; Civic and Political; Education and Information; Health and Human Services; Individual Development; Physical; Social and Associational; and Spiritual and Religious. The needs assessment used this framework to organize and categorize the county's community assets and services data by aspect and by Supervisorial District.
requirements: Community assets and services data must be classifiable into the ten aspects for the framework to organize the inventory
constraints: Applied in this report to Yolo County community assets and services for children, youth, and families, organized also by Supervisorial District
target_learners: Children, youth, and families in Yolo County
target_learning_goals: Healthy youth development through access to community assets and services, including education and information resources
examples: The team refined and categorized Yolo County community assets and services according to the Ten Aspects of Community, sourcing data from Concordia's asset mapping and 211 Yolo's databases
key_sources: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673581

article_title: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment
citation: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Five-step community needs assessment process with engagement and interagency coordination throughout
description: The Roadmap Needs Assessment Five-Step Process structures the assessment as a pyramid of five sequential steps, with community engagement and interagency coordination as essential components throughout. The report states the team "used the Roadmap Needs Assessment Five-Step Process (see Figure 2) to conduct the needs assessment" and that the process "encompasses all aspects of the methodology." The steps move from identifying existing assets by the Ten Aspects of Community and district, to identifying needs, interviewing key informants, developing recommendations filtered through guiding principles, and aligning systems to achieve desired outcomes.
requirements: Community engagement and interagency coordination throughout the process
Data from multiple sources including asset databases, engagement sessions, interviews, and public quantitative data
constraints: Developed and applied for the Yolo County Roadmap to the Future initiative; recommendations are filtered through the initiative's three guiding principles
target_learners: Children, youth, and families in Yolo County
target_learning_goals: Coordinating and improving community assets and services that support children's and youth's healthy development
examples: Step 1 identified existing community assets and services organized by the Ten Aspects of Community and Supervisorial District; Step 4 developed recommendations and strategic actions filtered through the guiding principles
key_sources: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673581

article_title: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment
citation: Roadmap to the Future for Yolo County Children and Youth Needs Assessment. (2024). WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Ground community needs assessment and planning in guiding principles of youth and family voice, access and equity, and alignment and coherence
description: The Roadmap to the Future initiative developed three guiding principles—Youth and Family Voice, Access and Equity, and Alignment and Coherence—alongside four shared priorities, during Phase 0 convenings. The report states these "informed the Roadmap to the Future team's work to develop the needs assessment" and will continue to guide the long-term strategic plan. Recommendations and strategic actions were filtered through these principles, and the shared priorities span quality childcare and TK–12, mental health and wellness, welcoming beacons of community life, and thriving in young adulthood.
requirements: Principles developed collaboratively with elected officials and community leaders before the assessment, and applied as filters for recommendations
constraints: Principles are specific to the Roadmap to the Future initiative's vision and phases in Yolo County
target_learners: Children, youth, and families in Yolo County, including youth in foster care, experiencing homelessness, and those who are socioeconomically disadvantaged
target_learning_goals: Healthy development and educational advantage for every child and youth in the county
examples: Phase 0 convened three virtual Children, Youth, and Family Convenings attended by over 50 elected officials and community leaders to develop the principles and shared priorities

article_title: Bilingual Beginnings: Planning Kindergarten Entry Assessments for Spanish-English Speakers
citation: Rolla, A., & Mottesi, G. (2024). Bilingual Beginnings: Planning Kindergarten Entry Assessments for Spanish–English Speakers. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/kindergarten-entry-assessments-an-examination-of-best-practices-national-trends-and-recommendations/
title: Use bilingual profiles—assessments covering proficiency in both English and the home language—to identify supports and close opportunity gaps for Spanish–English bilingual kindergarteners
description: A bilingual profile is a detailed assessment including a student's proficiency in English and home language(s), literacy skills, and other developmental areas, providing a comprehensive picture of strengths and needs. The brief argues states should implement policies facilitating bilingual profiles because "These bilingual profiles can more accurately identify what supports students need, allowing states and districts to close opportunity gaps more effectively." Profiles should draw on skills and lived experiences in both languages, with continued screening allowing flexible categorization that avoids stigmatizing labels.
requirements: Assessment information must be usable at state, district, community, school, and classroom levels to inform equitable resource allocation and targeted, culturally and linguistically responsive interventions.
constraints: Including Spanish and English versions in all assessed domains may increase administration time and limit teacher capacity to collect evidence for specific areas; differences in home-language use policies across states and districts can affect reliability and validity.
target_learners: Spanish–English bilingual kindergarteners, including those classified as English Learners
target_learning_goals: School readiness in language, literacy, and mathematics; accurate identification of needed supports and interventions in both languages
examples: The brief recommends that states implement policies facilitating bilingual profiles and tailor assessments and instructional strategies to the unique needs of Spanish–English bilinguals across both languages.

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://www.wested.org/
title: Zone of proximal development (ZPD) as the frame for edge learning with English learners
description: The brief organizes its argument around Vygotsky's ZPD, which it defines as "the realm of what a student can do in interaction with others." Learning is less effective when too easy or too frustrating; the ZPD is the level of challenge "just beyond what students already know and can do." The brief extends this to English learners, arguing teachers should not wait for full English proficiency before offering rigorous edge learning, and links the ZPD to formative assessment as edge work for both teacher and learner.
requirements: Ongoing formative assessment to keep track of the ever-changing edge of students' abilities
constraints: The edge is always changing, so understanding of where it is requires ongoing intentional effort
target_learners: English learners (multilingual learners) in K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Engagement with rigorous, grade-level disciplinary content and language development simultaneously
examples: The brief's early elementary poetry lesson structures teacher and peer support so students analyze grade-level poetic devices at the edge of their competencies
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673601

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://www.wested.org/
title: Scaffolding is temporary, contingent support that is adjusted or removed as students grow in competence — not simplified content
description: The brief defines instructional scaffolding as "an intentionally designed and thoughtfully implemented system of temporary support that allows students to engage with content" they cannot yet accomplish independently. It explicitly warns against confusing scaffolding with doing the thinking for students or reducing access to grade-level content. Once students' independent capabilities expand, scaffolding is adjusted or removed, supporting emerging autonomy.
requirements: Support must be structured and contingent, provided by a teacher or peer for tasks students cannot yet do alone
Educators need ongoing professional learning to enact this work
constraints: Scaffolding should not be kept in place indefinitely
It must not mean simplifying content or reducing, postponing, or limiting access to grade-level content
target_learners: English learners at any level of English proficiency
target_learning_goals: Access to and participation in grade-level conceptual, analytic, and linguistic disciplinary practices
examples: The brief states students can engage in disciplinary practices such as using mathematical models or comparing character development in literature given appropriate support
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673601

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://www.wested.org/
title: Matching scaffolding practices to formative assessment evidence
description: The brief presents a table pairing scaffolding practices with the formative assessment evidence that would indicate their need — for example, visual aids when students struggle to connect word meanings to spelling, graphic organizers when students need help getting started, sentence stems when small-group discussion is challenging, modeling with think-alouds, structured partner work, whiteboard responses, story retells, and home-language translations. The pattern is that "these scaffolds and related contexts demonstrate the instructional adjustments teachers can make in response to evidence of learning."
requirements: Evidence of student learning that makes the need for a particular scaffold visible and audible
constraints: Practices are keyed to specific evidence conditions rather than applied uniformly to all students
target_learners: English learners across proficiency levels in elementary and secondary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of complex content, participation in disciplinary discussion, and language development
examples: The brief suggests visual aids such as pictures of different mammals along with the written word mammal
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673601

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Students Work Beyond the Edge of Their Current Abilities With Formative Assessment. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://www.wested.org/
title: 1st/2nd grade poetry-analysis lesson with differentiated poem sets and scaffolded edge learning
description: An early elementary lesson example, inspired by a lesson taught by Olivia Lozano at the UCLA Lab School, in which 1st and 2nd grade English learners and monolingual peers analyze poetic devices such as rhyme and repeated line. Students receive "sets of poems of varying complexity," first work through a sample poem with the teacher, then analyze independently with teacher conferences and peer feedback. The brief notes scaffolding "supports students to work at the edge of their competencies" and that learning would not have been supported had the teacher analyzed the poem for the whole class.
requirements: Differentiated materials, independent analysis opportunities, evidence-based planning, and peer and teacher support structures
target_learners: 1st and 2nd grade English learners and monolingual English-speaking students
target_learning_goals: Identifying and describing grade-level poetic devices while developing language in context
examples: Students conference with the teacher and get feedback from peers during independent work time
