article_title: School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices
citation: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy
title: Educators should be supported as full partners in developing and implementing AI tools in learning environments
description: The brief argues educators hold responsibility for classroom AI decisions and must be treated as partners, not mere adopters. It states educators must be "considered and supported as full partners in developing and implementing these tools in all learning environments." This grounds recommendations for developer-educator collaboration and teacher training.
requirements: Educators need awareness of AI technologies and positions of responsibility to advocate for appropriate classroom uses
constraints: Currently there are silos between research and practice that impede educator-developer partnership
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: informed educator decision-making about AI adoption and integration
examples: The brief recommends researchers partner with developers and disseminate findings to education practitioners to bridge research-practice silos
key_sources: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy

article_title: School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices
citation: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy
title: Evidence of effectiveness and implementation constraints should be provided for all educational technology, especially AI
description: The brief calls for transparency about how AI systems work, for whom, and their potential biases before classroom adoption. It states "Evidence of effectiveness as well as implementation constraints should be provided for all educational technology, especially when it involves AI," so educators can make informed choices about adoption and integration.
requirements: AI developers must document and share the underlying pedagogical approach and training constraints
constraints: AI-enabled tools are designed and evaluated under specific settings and operate most reliably under those tuned constraints
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: informed technology adoption decisions by educators
examples: The brief asks educators to evaluate questions like how the AI works, for whom, and what potential biases it might have related to their students
key_sources: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy

description: The brief urges developers to commit to designing with educators and clearly communicating design context, data collection, and use. target_learning_goals: equitable instructional practices and educator advocacy

teachers

article_title: Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity
citation: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185
title: An inclusive approach to learning transitions centered in the individual's life
description: Drawing on feminist scholarship and Colley (2007), the report reframes learning transitions away from a linear, androcentric pathway model toward one where "learning transitions defined by and centered in the life of the individual experiencing it, especially learners and workers from HSE communities." It treats change and time as a natural flow across multiple pathways, life as constant transition, and learning as a permanent state in "becoming" and "unbecoming." The change may occur at the level of knowledge, skills, attitude, or behavior, and how it is described depends on the individual's lived experience. The study applied this frame inductively, inviting HSE learners and workers to define what constituted an impactful transition to them.
requirements: Transitions must be studied in context, through events and practices in real-lived contexts rather than decontextualized methods
constraints: Most extant transition work assumes a traditional linear pathway conception the report explicitly departs from
target_learners: adult learners and workers from historically and systematically excluded communities
target_learning_goals: navigating education, career, and life transitions
examples: Participants defined impactful transitions themselves, producing stories such as losing a bar job during COVID, validating Cuban credentials in the U.S., and retiring from the Marine Corps after 26 years
key_sources: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185

article_title: Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity
citation: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185
title: Seven co-designed Learning Transition Design Principles for LER technologies
description: The report's central artifact is a set of seven design principles stating that LER technology should: connect people to supports; connect people to opportunities; include indicators of skills and learning; be inclusive of people's identity, movement, and language; empower people with skills-based practices; adopt a comprehensive approach to digital credentialing; and integrate with a variety of tools. "Together, 31 learners and workers from HSE communities co-designed seven learning transition design principles to guide the further development of LERs and associated LER technologies." The principles complement existing Inclusive Design and Interoperable Design Principles by focusing on the value and usefulness of LERs during transitions, and serve both as design guidance and as evaluation criteria for existing designs.
requirements: Design and development with (not for) HSE learners and workers, so context expertise informs the technology
constraints: The principles focus on value and usefulness during learning transitions and do not replace principles addressing ease of use, access, and data/tech design
target_learners: HSE adult learners and workers, including those experiencing poverty and multilingual learners
target_learning_goals: sharing and accessing skills data to pursue education, career, and life opportunities during transitions
examples: Principle 1 states LER technologies should, with user consent, match people to supporters, mentors and counselors, and career networking services

title: Four showcased LER technologies introduced via onboarding videos
description: The study introduced participant-advisors to four LER technologies: "Teacher Wallet (RANDA Solutions), MilGears (SOLID Inc), LearnCard (LEF), and Career Wallet (Velocity Network)." Each technology partner delivered a 30-45-minute product walk-through to the research team and created a five-minute introductory onboarding video shown during the first co-design workshop, so learners and workers unfamiliar with digital and verifiable credentials could react to the designs and practical functionality for people experiencing transitions. These reflections fed the perceived challenges, opportunities, and wishlist findings.
requirements: Introductory videos were needed because many participants had never heard of digital and verifiable credentials, LER, or digital wallet technologies
constraints: Participants reflected on showcased technologies via video rather than hands-on use
target_learners: HSE adult learners and workers with varying digital fluency and LER awareness
target_learning_goals: understanding and evaluating LER technologies for transition support
examples: Workshop groups responded to each video by discussing promotive or inhibitory factors of each LER design for individuals experiencing transitions

description: The article presents a framework defining digital fluency as moving beyond knowing how to use technology toward knowing why and when to apply it. For each problem, learners must decide which tools to use, why, and how to create something new with them.

article_title: Task Automation, Worker Augmentation: Opportunities for Career and Technical Education in the Heartland
citation: Jacobs, B. (2026, September). Task automation, worker augmentation: Opportunities for career and technical education in the heartland. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/317
title: Augmentation, automation, and displacement are distinct outcomes that CTE planning must not conflate
description: The brief defines three distinct concepts often used interchangeably: automation is the underlying technical capability of whether AI can perform a task, while augmentation and displacement describe human employment outcomes. Augmentation is "a scenario in which AI absorbs specific tasks within a job while the worker keeps the role," whereas displacement eliminates the position itself. The brief argues mistaking one for the other leads CTE programs to either abandon strong occupational tracks prematurely or credential students for disappearing roles.
requirements: CTE programs, employers, and policymakers must apply the distinction when making multi-year curriculum and investment decisions
constraints: The distinction concerns employment outcomes once AI capability is put to use, not the capability itself
target_learners: CTE students in Heartland-region secondary and postsecondary programs
target_learning_goals: Preparing learners for future-forward, automation-resilient employment in a labor market defined by change
examples: The brief treats occupations shaped by augmentation as future-ready, automation-resilient employment: work built to flex with the technology rather than compete against it
key_sources: Jacobs, B. (2026, September). Task automation, worker augmentation: Opportunities for career and technical education in the heartland. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/317

title: Shared dataset combining the Anthropic Economic Index with Census BTOS employer adoption data
description: The three-part brief series draws on "a shared dataset combining Anthropic's AI exposure index with the U.S. Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) employer adoption data." The AEI tracks how AI models are actually used on the job task by task, mapped to standard occupational classifications, while BTOS measures whether employers have actually adopted AI in their operations regardless of technical exposure. Together they let the brief distinguish task-level exposure from firm-level adoption.
requirements: Both sources are needed because task-level exposure to AI and firm-level adoption of AI are not the same thing
constraints: BTOS excludes farm businesses from its sample entirely and underrepresents small employers
target_learners: Policymakers, funders, and CTE practitioners using labor-market data for program planning
target_learning_goals: Translating labor-market data on AI into actionable next steps for CTE
examples: The brief uses the two datasets to triangulate that both exposure and adoption remain low for Heartland-heavy occupations

citation: Zachariah, I., Dallas, D., Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., & Karim. (2025). AI literacy for the Workforce. In Ruiz, P. et al. (Eds.), Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/271
title: Workforce AI literacy framework of six skill and competency domains
description: The brief defines AI literacy as "a set of foundational skills and competencies that enable individuals to understand how AI works, responsibly evaluate AI systems, and use AI effectively as a human-centered tool across various contexts." Table 1 organizes workforce-specific AI skills into six domains: Technical Knowledge, Practical Implementation, Analytical Skills, Interpersonal and Communication Skills, Ethical Evaluation, and Adaptive Skills. The framework is adapted from National Academies, OECD, Learning Guild, World Economic Forum, Microsoft, and AI Education Project sources.

constraints: The specific technical knowledge, skills, and competencies needed for AI implementation vary significantly across sectors

target_learning_goals: understanding how AI systems function and their limitations
evaluating AI outputs and mitigating risks
adapting to evolving AI technologies
examples: Table 2 illustrates sector examples in healthcare, finance, and creative fields, including an AI-powered wound assessment tool and AI-assisted restoration of The Night Watch

It extends to hiring, where companies must evaluate and verify AI tools for fairness and bias mitigation while maintaining human oversight and transparency.

article_title: El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233
title: Taxonomía del ecosistema de credenciales: macro-credenciales versus micro-credenciales basadas en competencias
description: El eBook organiza el ecosistema de credenciales en dos grandes ramas: macro-credenciales (títulos y certificados universitarios y de posgrado) y micro-credenciales, definidas como credenciales digitales que "verifica la competencia en una destreza o conjunto de destrezas específicas". Según la definición de UNESCO citada, una micro-credencial es un registro de logros de aprendizaje focalizados con evaluación basada en estándares claramente definidos, otorgada por un proveedor de confianza, con valor independiente y sujeta a garantía de calidad. El eBook enfatiza que las micro-credenciales no son programas de aprendizaje sino reconocimiento de la capacidad de aplicar lo aprendido, independientemente de cómo se adquirió.
requirements: Evaluación basada en estándares claramente definidos y otorgada por un proveedor de confianza
constraints: En este eBook, las micro-credenciales no son un programa de aprendizaje o adiestramiento, sino que representan la capacidad de aplicar el aprendizaje y el conocimiento
target_learners: Estudiantes de todas las edades, incluyendo educadores K-12, estudiantes postsecundarios y trabajadores
target_learning_goals: Reconocimiento y verificación de competencias y destrezas específicas adquiridas formal e informalmente
examples: El eBook distingue títulos de asociado, licenciatura, maestría y doctorado, y certificados universitarios y de posgrado como macro-credenciales, comparándolos en una tabla con créditos, duración y verificación
key_sources: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233

title: Características de diseño de micro-credenciales rigurosas y significativas
description: El eBook enumera las características que hacen que una micro-credencial sea rigurosa y significativa: "Las micro-credenciales se basan en competencias, son personalizables, se pueden compartir, están respaldadas por investigación, son evaluadas individualmente por un experto en la materia y se otorgan en función de la demostración satisfactoria de una destreza". Cada característica se define en el texto: las basadas en competencias articulan una destreza discreta con evidencias específicas; las respaldadas por investigación se apoyan en evidencia de impacto profesional; las personalizadas permiten elegir y completar a propio ritmo; las compartibles pueden añadirse a currículums y perfiles en línea. Se añade el reconocimiento del aprendizaje previo obtenido en cualquier contexto.

constraints: La calidad de las micro-credenciales varía

target_learning_goals: Verificación de destrezas profesionales y reconocimiento de aprendizaje previo

title: Marco de Evaluación Basado en Competencias de Digital Promise
description: El eBook describe el marco que fundamenta todas las micro-credenciales de Digital Promise. Sus primeros principios surgieron de profesionales de todo Estados Unidos: "construido sobre la base de destrezas demostrables, fundamentos basados en la investigación, múltiples formas de evidencia y evaluación y revisión transparentes y rigurosas". Tras una auditoría interna de contenidos en 2021, el marco se reiteró sobre principios de inclusión, equidad y accesibilidad, operacionalizados en cinco preguntas de revisión: impacto, equidad, acceso, lenguaje y el "Panorama General". El marco requiere que el estudiante presente evidencia de la aplicación de la destreza, evaluada por expertos objetivos contra rúbricas.
requirements: Los estudiantes presentan evidencia que demuestra su competencia y reciben una insignia digital si la evidencia cumple los criterios descritos en las rúbricas
constraints: El marco está destinado a reflejar la mejora continua y ha adquirido mayor especificidad según contextos de aprendizaje y tipos de destrezas
target_learners: Educadores K-12 y proveedores de desarrollo profesional que diseñan micro-credenciales
target_learning_goals: Evaluación rigurosa, equitativa e inclusiva de la aplicación de destrezas
examples: Julie Kasper describió la plantilla del marco como restrictiva en el buen sentido, obligando a su organización a reescribir lenguaje y citar investigaciones de libre acceso para su micro-credencial de educadores de refugiados

title: Estructura de tres componentes de una micro-credencial de Digital Promise
description: Cada micro-credencial de Digital Promise se desarrolla sobre el mismo marco con tres componentes principales. Según el eBook, "El primer componente está formado por tres partes: la Competencia, el Método Clave y los Componentes del Método", que ofrecen una visión general de las destrezas y cómo se demuestra la competencia. El segundo componente incluye la Investigación y los Recursos, con enlaces a estudios que respaldan la competencia y ayudas como publicaciones, vídeos y plantillas. El tercer componente comprende los Criterios de Presentación y las Rúbricas de Puntuación, que indican al estudiante qué responder y qué evidencia presentar, y sirven de guía anticipada y para los evaluadores.
requirements: La rúbrica de evaluación debe estar visible para el estudiante con anticipación

target_learning_goals: Demostración de competencia mediante portafolios de evidencia

article_title: Access to Powerful Technology as a Catalyst for Career Pathway Engagement
citation: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217
title: Engagement funnel framework: awareness, interest, and engagement as stages of influence on occupational identity
description: The paper adapts Callahan et al.'s (2019) funnel of influences on occupational identity into a narrowed "engagement funnel" of awareness, interest, and engagement, used as the organizing coding scheme for interviews and observations. The authors state they "focused our attention on the earlier stages of influence to create an 'engagement funnel' of awareness, interest, and engagement, where awareness and interest are a more nuanced view on exposure." Movement along the funnel is described as not necessarily linear, with the stages interrelated.
requirements: Data on student and educator experiences must be coded against the funnel stages to trace transitions
constraints: The paper states deep levels of participation were not expected within the implementation timeline, so participation stages were excluded
target_learners: historically and systemically excluded (HSE) high school students
target_learning_goals: career and technical education (CTE) pathway awareness, interest, and engagement; occupational identity development
examples: The authors analyzed Anaheim High School interviews and observations using the engagement funnel coding scheme, then examined examples for powerful learning principles

article_title: Access to Powerful Technology as a Catalyst for Career Pathway Engagement
citation: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217
title: HP Learning Studio at Anaheim High School
description: The HP Learning Studio is a school-community technology space launched in Winter 2024 at Anaheim High School, featuring "high-end HP workstations running Windows 11 and powered by the latest Intel processors, scholastic esports peripherals, and prosumer-grade audio-visual and broadcasting equipment." It is deliberately not tied to any one teacher's class or club, sits in the center of campus, and provides access to broadcasting, graphic design, podcasting, computer science, audiovisual, and esports equipment so students not enrolled in CTE pathways can explore interests. Equipment selection prioritized versatility, power, and long-term value, with modular PCs that can be upgraded.
requirements: A needs assessment and educator leadership team to inform space and equipment selection; school-community-industry partnerships to support CTE awareness, interest, and engagement
constraints: CTE facilities at the school were previously accessible only to enrolled pathway students; the studio addresses but does not eliminate broader access limitations
target_learners: high school students, including historically and systemically excluded youth not enrolled in CTE pathways
target_learning_goals: exploration of career interests, CTE pathway awareness and engagement, authentic project-based learning
examples: Launch stations included physics simulations, esports play, a HyperX ProCast podcasting station, and EV3 Mindstorms robot coding demonstrations
key_sources: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217

article_title: Access to Powerful Technology as a Catalyst for Career Pathway Engagement
citation: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217
title: Powerful learning principles: personal and accessible, authentic and challenging, collaborative and connected, inquisitive and reflective
description: The paper defines powerful learning as "a set of principles that guide educators to design learning experiences that meaningfully engage students": "personal and accessible, authentic and challenging, collaborative and connected, and inquisitive and reflective." The HP Learning Studio is presented as exemplifying these: it is centrally located and not tied to one class, supports authentic community-serving projects, enables collaborative creation of shareable learning artifacts, and fosters a safe space to fail and iterate. The authors cite research that authentic, project-based STEM environments feel more motivating and psychologically safe.
requirements: A centrally located, shared space not tied to any one teacher's class or club, so access is open to all students and educators
constraints: The paper notes multiple studies support the motivating character of authentic project-based environments, but the studio's own instantiation is documented only through qualitative examples
target_learners: high school students, particularly historically and systemically excluded youth
target_learning_goals: meaningful engagement, passion and interest discovery, preparation for future careers
examples: Students created products as learning artifacts shared locally or globally; Mr. Duarte's client-based website project exemplified collaborative and connected learning
key_sources: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217

article_title: Evaluation of the Expository Reading and Writing Course: Findings from the Investing in Innovation Development Grant
citation: Anthony B. Fong, Neal D. Finkelstein, Laura M. Jaeger, Rebeca Diaz, Marie E. Broek. (2015). Evaluation of the Expository Reading and Writing Course: Findings from the Investing in Innovation Development Grant. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: ERWC logic model: curriculum, professional learning, and materials as inputs leading to rhetorical classroom practices and improved college readiness
description: The ERWC theory holds that three inputs — curriculum, professional learning, and curriculum materials — produce classroom practices such as "extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation" to develop critical-thinking skills, interactive discussion to build oral language, and extended writing for varied tasks, purposes, and audiences. These practices are expected to yield improved outcomes measured by the EPT. The course rests on seven principles, including "A rhetorical approach that fosters critical thinking and engagement through a relentless focus on the text" and integration of interactive reading and writing processes.
requirements: Teachers must be certified through initial 20 hours of professional learning to teach the course
constraints: Designed for grade-12 students preparing for college-level English; targets expository, analytical, and argumentative reading and writing
target_learners: grade-12 high school students preparing for college-level English
target_learning_goals: critical reading and writing skills
rhetorical analysis of expository texts
college English readiness reducing remediation
examples: The course includes 12 modules organized by three domains — Reading Rhetorically, Connecting Reading to Writing, and Writing Rhetorically — with teachers expected to teach 8 to 10 modules
key_sources: Anthony B. Fong, Neal D. Finkelstein, Laura M. Jaeger, Rebeca Diaz, Marie E. Broek. (2015). Evaluation of the Expository Reading and Writing Course: Findings from the Investing in Innovation Development Grant. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559522

article_title: Evaluation of the Expository Reading and Writing Course: Findings from the Investing in Innovation Development Grant
citation: Anthony B. Fong, Neal D. Finkelstein, Laura M. Jaeger, Rebeca Diaz, Marie E. Broek. (2015). Evaluation of the Expository Reading and Writing Course: Findings from the Investing in Innovation Development Grant. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: ERWC Assignment Template: scaffolded module structure with six strands across three domains
description: The ERWC curriculum's 12 modules all follow the Assignment Template, "which presents a scaffolded process to help students read, comprehend, and respond to nonfiction and literary texts." Each module spans three domains — Reading Rhetorically (Prereading, Reading, Postreading strands), Connecting Reading to Writing (Discovering What You Think), and Writing Rhetorically (Entering the Conversation, Revising and Editing). Strands contain elements with activities, such as Surveying the Text and Making Predictions and Asking Questions. The template also embeds formative assessment recommendations and rhetorical grammar activities using curriculum readings and students' own writings.
requirements: Teachers are expected to teach 8 to 10 of the 12 modules over the school year, including one full-length book per semester
constraints: In some modules a given element may contain multiple activities, and in others an element may include no activities for the teacher to complete
target_learners: grade-12 high school English students
target_learning_goals: reading and comprehending nonfiction and literary texts
rhetorical reading and writing
academic writing conventions
examples: The Prereading strand includes elements such as Getting Ready to Read, Exploring Key Concepts, Surveying the Text, Making Predictions and Asking Questions, and Understanding Key Vocabulary

article_title: Rural Turnaround: Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Rural Turnaround: Challenges and Opportunities. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://centeronschoolturnaround.org/journeys
title: Cultivate an environment of success and collaboration to attract teacher and leader recruits to rural turnaround schools
description: The article's recommended approach to rural recruitment goes beyond incentives: rural schools and districts should "create an environment where enthusiastic, committed, and effective teachers and leaders want to be." As the handbook states, "An environment of success and collaboration is attractive to potential recruits." Amargosa's principal recruits by telling candidates the work will be challenging but that the school has a multiyear, comprehensive plan for helping students learn and thrive.
requirements: A credible, multiyear, comprehensive improvement plan that can be honestly presented to potential hires
constraints: Recruitment remains difficult in remote communities regardless; Amargosa still lost more than half its teachers before implementation
target_learners: Teachers and school leaders considering employment in rural turnaround schools
target_learning_goals: Recruiting and retaining effective educators in hard-to-staff rural schools
examples: Principal Robert Williams tells potential hires the work will be challenging but that Amargosa has a multiyear, comprehensive plan for helping students learn and thrive

citation: Rural Turnaround: Challenges and Opportunities. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://centeronschoolturnaround.org/journeys

It also produced a handbook on the state role in rural turnaround.

citation: Merging Cognitive Science and Curriculum to Strengthen Middle School Math. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://www.wested.org
title: Integrate visual images and verbal information in meaningful ways to promote understanding of key concepts
description: The Math Center's first design principle holds that integrating visual images and verbal information in meaningful ways promotes understanding of key concepts and development of critical skills. In the revised curriculum this meant removing decorative photographs and replacing them with sketches that more closely represent the details of the problem, as in the bumper car floor plan task.
requirements: Visuals must be directly related to the math of the problem rather than decorative
target_learners: middle school math students
target_learning_goals: understanding of key math concepts and development of critical skills
examples: In the revised sixth-grade area and perimeter unit, a photograph of an amusement park was replaced with a sketch of three possible floor plans, including one that does not meet the requirements

title: Structure practice to include both solving problems and studying already worked-out problems, some solved incorrectly
description: The second design principle states that practice structured to give students opportunities both to solve problems and to study already worked-out problems, some of which may be solved incorrectly, promotes deeper conceptual understanding. Davenport describes explaining incorrectly solved problems as increasingly seen as one of the most effective kinds of practice for students.

avoiding repeated errors

description: The third design principle holds that spacing out the presentation and review of key concepts and facts over time helps students better retain what they learn. article_title: Shared Data Reveal the Invisible Achievement Gap of Students in Foster Care
citation: Shared Data Reveal the Invisible Achievement Gap of Students in Foster Care. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://www.wested.org/bookstore
title: Linked California child welfare-education dataset of more than 43,000 students in foster care
description: The Invisible Achievement Gap report produced the first linked dataset joining California's two separate systems: CDE's California Longitudinal Pupil Achievement Data System and CDSS's Child Welfare Services Case Management System. WestEd staff "carried out a rigorous, multistep data-matching process, resulting in a linked dataset of more than 43,000 students ( ages 5-17) in foster care in California—the first set of that scope and magnitude." Matching large confidential datasets across unconnected systems required intense data security.
requirements: A formal data-sharing agreement between the child welfare and education agencies, brokered between CDSS and CDE
constraints: The two systems maintain separate data with no common identifiers to track children across systems, so linkage requires a meticulous data-matching process

target_learning_goals: Understanding and serving the academic needs of students in foster care

article_title: Academy Breaks the Isolation of Special Education Directors
citation: Academy Breaks the Isolation of Special Education Directors. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. https://www.wested.org
title: Special Education Leadership Academy (Massachusetts)
description: The Special Education Leadership Academy is a WestEd Learning Innovations program, funded by MA DESE and free to participants, offered since 2011 to experienced Massachusetts special education directors. It aims to build directors' capacities to do their jobs effectively and minimize burnout, and MA DESE funds it partly to retain veteran directors. Its structure combines an August session, follow-up sessions during the school year, and annual reunions for prior participants.

constraints: Funded by the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education and specific to Massachusetts directors

Legal and regulatory knowledge
Peer networking and support
Retention in the director role

Sessions are highly interactive and customized: prior to the Academy, participants are asked what their biggest issues are and what they want addressed, informing coverage of current topics such as transition planning.

citation: A Call to Action on Behalf of U.S. Babies. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://forourbabies.org/wp/
title: For Our Babies platform of supports organized around four pillars tracking development from pre-conception to age three

their families

PITC also worked with the U.S. Administration on Children, Youth, and Families to develop the Early Head Start program.

article_title: A Call to Action on Behalf of U.S. Babies
citation: A Call to Action on Behalf of U.S. Babies. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://forourbabies.org/wp/
title: The 'social womb': early brain development requires a safe, nurturing, and stimulating relational environment
description: Lally's 'social womb' framework holds that, for the first few years of life, the brain needs "a safe, nurturing, and stimulating environment in which babies can learn how to interact with others and use the tools of society to get their needs met." Responsive interaction—'When I cry, somebody comes. When I communicate, somebody listens'—shapes how babies function and relate to people for the rest of their lives. The For Our Babies initiative advocates a system of services to foster this sort of social womb.
requirements: A system of supports (prenatal care, paid leave, screening, quality care) that together provide safe, nurturing, stimulating environments
constraints: The framework is presented as an advocacy-oriented account grounded in brain science, not a tested model in this article

target_learning_goals: healthy brain development and capacity to interact with others and meet needs

article_title: Equity-Focused Schools Carry All Students to High Levels
citation: Equity-focused Schools Carry All Students to High Levels. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://www.wested.org
title: Professional learning communities (PLCs) with team structures and weekly scheduled meetings
description: Professional learning communities are structures that help educators inquire about and solve problems and reflect on their work together. In all four case study schools, staff studied the PLC concept, built common understanding, and carried it out with fidelity. Montgomery Center used PLCs to introduce team-level analysis of curriculum, instruction, and assessment, and created an Academic Student Support Team to track the impact of student interventions over time. All case schools have grade-level or multigrade teams, vertical teams to align curriculum across grades, team leaders, and scheduled meetings of at least an hour a week, and most also have data teams.
requirements: Scheduled team meeting times of at least an hour a week
A common studied understanding of the PLC concept implemented with fidelity
target_learners: teachers and other educators in K-12 public schools
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of instruction through collaborative inquiry and data use
examples: Montgomery Center School created grade-level PLCs, a middle school PLC, and an Academic Student Support Team tracking intervention impacts over time.

article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: QTEL approach: rigorous academic content and academic English taught simultaneously with expert support
description: The Quality Teaching for English Learners (QTEL) initiative holds that secondary ELL students can master rigorous academic content quickly and deeply rather than waiting years to learn English mechanics first. It works on the premise that students will rise to the challenge of rigorous subject matter if it sparks their interest, if they receive appropriate support, and if academic content and academic English language skills are taught simultaneously, as a single, integrated process. The article presents this as a counter to the traditional belief that ELL students need seven years of English before tackling complex academic content.
requirements: Teachers must make dramatic shifts in their beliefs and practices to master this instructional approach
target_learners: middle school and high school English language learners at intermediate English proficiency
target_learning_goals: academic content mastery
academic English listening, speaking, reading, and writing
examples: The Persuasion across Time and Space unit was piloted in five urban school districts through a partnership between the Understanding Language initiative at Stanford and WestEd's Teacher Professional Development Program.

article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: Persuasion across Time and Space: five-week CCSS-aligned ELA unit on persuasive text and media messages
description: A five-week, Common Core State Standards-aligned English language arts unit on persuasive text and media messages, targeting middle school English learners at an intermediate level of proficiency. It shows teachers how to help students build English language mastery in tandem with conceptual understanding of text, using texts from television commercials to the Gettysburg Address and Civil Rights Movement speeches, with tools such as Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos for evaluating arguments. The unit is available online with downloadable teacher and student materials.
requirements: Teachers learn how to differentiate instruction for ELL students and help them draw on background knowledge rather than simplifying text
target_learners: middle school English learners at intermediate English proficiency
non-ELL peers
target_learning_goals: reading, interpreting, critically analyzing, and creating persuasive texts
academic practices and the language required to express them
examples: Six school districts affiliated with the Council of the Great City Schools field tested the unit during the past year, and teachers in several other large districts reviewed and critiqued it.
key_sources: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela

article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: Apprenticeship model with tailored scaffolding builds ELL students' autonomy with complex texts
description: The unit emphasizes the apprenticeship model of learning, in which students participate in guided academic practices deliberately designed to provide opportunities for students to become autonomous experts over time. Teachers offer various levels of support, or scaffolding, tailored to each student's needs, and students progressively develop their ability to work independently. Students move from informal and collaborative group settings to formal group and individual presentations, practicing articulating ideas, interpreting information, and presenting and defending claims.
requirements: Scaffolding must be tailored to each student's needs
target_learners: secondary English language learners
target_learning_goals: independent academic reading and writing
articulating ideas and defending claims
examples: Assessments such as peer editing with clearly defined rubrics or finding textual evidence to support conclusions are designed to build students' autonomy as purposeful readers and writers over time.
key_sources: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela

article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: Progress from familiar texts and formats to unfamiliar content and text structures
description: Rather than simplifying text or assuming students cannot identify themes, teachers differentiate instruction and help students draw on background knowledge to build deeper understandings. By progressing from analysis of more familiar ideas and formats to analyzing unfamiliar content and text structures, teachers gradually enable students to explore complex texts in a purposeful way. Each lesson takes students through similar types of texts representing similar genres and conventions, thematically designed so new lessons build on prior concepts and skills.
requirements: Lessons must be thematically designed so each new lesson builds on prior concepts and skills
target_learners: secondary English language learners
target_learning_goals: comprehension and critical analysis of complex texts
examples: The unit's texts range from television commercials to Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address and pivotal speeches from the Civil Rights Movement.
key_sources: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela

article_title: Evaluation of the MIND Research Institute's Spatial-Temporal Math (ST Math) Program in California
citation: Staci Wendt, John Rice, Jonathan Nakamoto. (2014). Evaluation of the MIND Research Institute's Spatial-Temporal Math (ST Math) Program in California. WestEd. https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/elsi/
title: ST Math: game-based instructional software for K-12 mathematics using visual spatial puzzles
description: ST Math is "game-based, instructional software for K–12 students" created by the MIND Research Institute, aimed at boosting "math comprehension through visual learning." Students follow a penguin named JiJi and "help JiJi pass obstacles by solving spatial math puzzles." The software is integrated into classroom instruction but can also be used in a computer lab or at home. This evaluation examined its effects on California CST mathematics outcomes in grades 2-5.
requirements: Requires student logins and coverage of grade-level material; full implementation in this study was defined as at least 85 percent of enrolled students logging in and at least 50 percent of grade-level material covered.
constraints: The article evaluates ST Math only in California elementary grades 2-5 during 2010/11, with outcomes measured one year after first provision.
target_learners: K-12 students, evaluated here in elementary grades 2 through 5
target_learning_goals: Mathematics comprehension through visual learning
Elementary mathematics proficiency and advanced performance on state standards tests
examples: In this evaluation, 463 California grades in 212 schools were provided with ST Math beginning in 2010/11, of which 209 grades in 129 schools fully implemented it.
key_sources: Staci Wendt, John Rice, Jonathan Nakamoto. (2014). Evaluation of the MIND Research Institute's Spatial-Temporal Math (ST Math) Program in California. WestEd. https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/elsi/

article_title: Real Progress in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation
citation: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2014). Real progress in Maryland: Student learning objectives and teacher and principal evaluation. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. http://marylandpublicschools.org/MSDE/programs/tpe/index.html
title: Maryland SLO implementation process and state support tools
description: The Maryland SLO component is an instructional process embedded in the TPE evaluation system, in which SLOs are "the predominate measure of student growth for teachers and principals" and may account for 30%-50% of the total evaluation rating, with no single SLO counting for more than 35 percent. MSDE's Guidebook outlines a nine-step implementation sequence from professional development through data review, SLO development, review and approval, mid-interval and final reviews, to integration of results and setting the attribution roster. The state also developed SLO templates and guiding questions for teachers and principals, plus review criteria in four domains: priority of standard, rigor of target, quality of measure and evidence, and action plan.
requirements: Districts must provide SLO training to local school personnel in keeping with established state guidelines and document a verification process to validate consistency, comparability, quality and rigor of SLOs
constraints: Local districts, not the state, establish processes for setting, reviewing, assessing, and aligning SLOs, under Maryland's local control structure
target_learners: K-12 teachers and principals in Maryland public school districts
target_learning_goals: Improving educator effectiveness and student achievement through data-informed goal setting and instruction
examples: MSDE released over $1.5M in mini-grants to LEAs, with the largest share for school hardware/software investments (31.4% of grants) and teacher professional development on TPE, the Danielson framework, and SLOs (8.9%)
key_sources: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2014). Real progress in Maryland: Student learning objectives and teacher and principal evaluation. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. http://marylandpublicschools.org/MSDE/programs/tpe/index.html

article_title: Real Progress in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation
citation: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2014). Real progress in Maryland: Student learning objectives and teacher and principal evaluation. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. http://marylandpublicschools.org/MSDE/programs/tpe/index.html
title: In SLO implementation, the process of thinking through the inter-related components matters most
description: Drawing on fifteen years of SLO practice and research, the report holds that the value of Student Learning Objectives lies in the deliberative process rather than the compliance artifact: "The process of thinking through the inter-related components of the SLO and their implications for instruction is what matters most." The SLO process should foster planning and delivery of instruction through data use and systematic analysis, and motivate performance through growth targets set by both teachers and students. Districts must balance manageability with rigor and standardization with customization, and would benefit from state guidance on how much flexibility schools may use while preserving comparability and trust.
requirements: Districts must strike a thoughtful balance between manageability and a thorough, rigorous process, and between standardization and customization
constraints: The report presents this as a national lesson from fifteen years of SLO practice and research rather than a finding tested within this study's own data
target_learners: K-12 teachers and principals developing and implementing SLOs
target_learning_goals: Instructional planning and delivery informed by data, and student growth through teacher- and student-set targets
examples: The report cites a teacher who examined baseline data, found an initial goal less lofty than thought, and reset it to be an attainable but more challenging goal

article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Two overarching perspectives on what restorative justice in schools is: whole-school philosophy versus skill-based stand-alone practice
description: The article identifies two competing expert perspectives on RJ in schools. One treats RJ as "a philosophy, as a 'way of being,'" requiring a whole-school or whole-community approach to culture and climate. The other treats RJ as "fundamentally a skill-based exercise" that staff can learn through training and use as a stand-alone strategy for individual disciplinary actions, without opposing whole-system approaches. The article notes the definitional challenge stems partly from respondents' diverse backgrounds and that research is needed on critical program elements under either approach.
requirements: A working definition of RJ that school communities can embrace, which nearly all respondents identified as needed
constraints: The two perspectives are attributed to experts and practitioners with varied backgrounds and diverse experiences, not empirically tested in this brief
target_learners: K–12 students
school staff and administrators
target_learning_goals: restoring relationships after conflict as an alternative to punitive discipline
examples: The brief contrasts schools adopting RJ as whole-community culture change with schools using it as an add-on program focused on individual disciplinary actions
key_sources: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559727

article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Implement restorative justice with all adults in the school before implementing it with students
description: For whole-school RJ models, the article reports experts encourage a sequencing principle: build RJ practice among all adults in the school — "teachers, bus drivers, cafeteria staff, administrators, specialists" — before introducing it with students. Experts also note RJ is most successfully implemented when students, school employees, parents and guardians, and community members all embrace it, and that proper implementation requires understanding the school climate and the nature and source of the school's issues beforehand.
requirements: A clear understanding of the school climate and of the nature, extent, and source of the issues the school contends with before implementing RJ
constraints: Stated by experts for whole-school models; the article presents it as expert advice, not a tested finding
target_learners: all school adults including teachers, bus drivers, cafeteria staff, administrators, and specialists
K–12 students
target_learning_goals: school-wide adoption of non-punitive, relationship-restoring disciplinary practice
examples: Experts recommended implementing RJ with all adults in the school first when a whole-school model is desired
key_sources: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559727

article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: RP-Observe observation tool for measuring restorative justice in schools
description: RP-Observe is an observation tool that Rutgers University developed to measure RJ in schools, cited by experts among the very few instruments designed to measure RJ. The article reports that experts often created their own instruments, including fidelity instruments specific to the RJ model being implemented, and that some approach measurement through changes in school climate and relationships among students and staff. Interviewees agreed a resource should compile and disseminate existing evaluation tools and findings.
requirements: Sound measurement of RJ, which experts recognize is required to learn about its impact
constraints: Experts noted measuring RJ is challenging because RJ is about the overall school environment, communication, and a way of being
target_learners: K–12 students and school staff observed during RJ implementation
target_learning_goals: measuring implementation fidelity and outcomes of restorative justice practices
examples: Experts created their own fidelity instruments specific to the model of RJ being implemented

article_title: What Further Research Is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools?
citation: Hurley, N., Guckenburg, S., Persson, H., Fronius, T., & Petrosino, A. (2015). What Further Research is Needed on Restorative Justice in Schools? WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Strong principal leadership endorsing a change in discipline approach is essential for RJ implementation
description: Interviewed experts agreed on essential ingredients for implementing RJ in schools: strong leadership endorsing and advocating a change in the school's approach to discipline and culture, and training for school staff. The article reports that "a school principal who is committed to RJ and to creating a restorative environment in the school is essential for implementation to be successful," and that research is needed on leadership characteristics that best facilitate implementation and on sustainability.
requirements: Training for school staff alongside leadership commitment
constraints: Presented as expert consensus from interviews, not a tested relationship
target_learners: school principals and leaders
teachers and school staff

examples: Experts identified strong leadership and staff training as the first two essential ingredients for RJ implementation

article_title: Evaluation Brief: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: 2011-2014
citation: Reedy, K., & Lacireno-Paquet, N. (2015). Evaluation Brief: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: 2011–2014. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.kansasmtss.org/pdf/ex_eval/2015_KS_MTSS_Eval_Report.pdf
title: Kansas MTSS framework: a system-level change framework integrating core components for academic and behavioral outcomes
description: The Kansas MTSS is a statewide framework aiming to improve outcomes for all students through system-level change across classroom, school, district, and state. It integrates effective-schools components into "a single framework for improved social and academic outcomes for all students." Core components include evidence-based curriculum, high-quality instruction, a comprehensive assessment system, data-based decision making, effective intervention, fidelity of implementation, ongoing professional development, and empowering leadership culture. Implementation features "frequent data-based monitoring for instructional decision making" and a continuum of evidence-based systemwide practices enabling rapid response to each student's needs.
requirements: Evidence-based curriculum and high-quality core instruction and assessment
Data-based decision making supported by a comprehensive assessment system
Ongoing professional development and leadership within an empowering school and district culture
Fidelity of implementation
constraints: Sustaining implementation requires staff buy-in, institutionalization of MTSS practices, and sustained district and school leadership support; training, flexible scheduling, and resource purchases are necessary but not sufficient
target_learners: All K-12 students in participating Kansas public schools
target_learning_goals: Improved academic outcomes in reading and math
Improved behavioral outcomes and reduced special education referrals
examples: More than a third of all Kansas public schools were implementing MTSS, used as a key approach for turning around low-performing schools in the state
key_sources: Reedy, K., & Lacireno-Paquet, N. (2015). Evaluation Brief: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: 2011–2014. San Francisco: WestEd. http://www.kansasmtss.org/pdf/ex_eval/2015_KS_MTSS_Eval_Report.pdf

article_title: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report-2014
citation: Kristin Reedy, Ed.D., and Natalie Lacireno-Paquet, Ph.D. (2015). Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report—2014. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Kansas MTSS framework: a system-level change framework integrating core components for academic and behavioral outcomes
description: The Kansas MTSS framework aims to improve outcomes for all students through system-level change across classroom, school, district, and state, using "a coherent continuum of evidence based, system-wide practices to support a rapid response to each student's academic and behavioral needs" with frequent data-based monitoring. Its core components are evidence-based curriculum, high-quality instruction, a comprehensive assessment system, data-based decision making, effective intervention, fidelity of implementation, ongoing professional development, and leadership within an empowering culture. Curriculum, instruction, and assessment form the core supporting all students, supported in turn by leadership, professional development, and an empowering culture.
requirements: Implementation with fidelity requires systems change, including school- and district-level leadership, ongoing professional development, and alignment of school improvement initiatives under the MTSS framework
constraints: The report notes implementing MTSS with fidelity is challenged by staff and leadership turnover, secondary-level course and credit constraints, scheduling time, integrating multiple content areas, and staff skill in designing intensive interventions
target_learners: all K-12 students in participating Kansas public schools
target_learning_goals: improved academic outcomes in reading and math
improved student behavior
examples: Case study schools operated building leadership teams, three-times-per-year universal screening, weekly grade-level data review, and daily intervention blocks with groups regrouped based on screening and progress-monitoring data
key_sources: Kristin Reedy, Ed.D., and Natalie Lacireno-Paquet, Ph.D. (2015). Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report—2014. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559729

article_title: Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report-2014
citation: Kristin Reedy, Ed.D., and Natalie Lacireno-Paquet, Ph.D. (2015). Implementation and Outcomes of Kansas Multi-Tier System of Supports: Final Evaluation Report—2014. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: KSDE statewide MTSS support infrastructure (Core Team, Recognized Facilitators, Symposium, website, dissemination)
description: The Kansas State Department of Education maintains a statewide infrastructure to support and sustain MTSS implementation. Its components "include the MTSS Core Team, the cadre of Recognized MTSS Facilitators, the annual MTSS Symposium, an extensive and frequently updated website of materials, research, and resources on MTSS, and an ongoing dissemination plan" coordinated with the Technical Assistance System Network. In the 2014 survey, 77.4% of respondents reported KSDE established the necessary infrastructure to sustain and extend MTSS, 75.9% reported effective dissemination, and 76.0% reported sufficient resources.
requirements: Sustained leadership and support from KSDE, including the Office of the Commissioner, and investment in district-level capacity building and strengthening of the Core Team
constraints: Sixty-one percent of respondents agreed there are sufficient MTSS Facilitators to support MTSS statewide, indicating a perceived facilitator supply limit
target_learners: Kansas public schools and districts implementing MTSS
target_learning_goals: statewide implementation of MTSS with fidelity and sustainability over time
examples: Professional development materials are aligned with the Learning Forward standards (2012), and the annual Kansas MTSS Symposium was observed by evaluators each year

article_title: Underuse of Title VII Funding for Indian Education in Arizona, Nevada, and Utah
citation: RMC Research Corporation. (2015). Underuse of Title VII funding for Indian education in Arizona, Nevada, and Utah. Phoenix, AZ: West Comprehensive Center at WestEd. http://www.westcompcenter.org
title: Because knowledge of a funding program is the primary difference between funded and unfunded eligible agencies, improving program awareness should precede expectations of participation
description: The report's central interpretive finding is that the "primary difference" between eligible LEAs that received Title VII funding and those that did not "was in terms of knowledge about the program." Unfunded respondents were generally unfamiliar with the program and its eligibility requirements, and many learned about Title VII for the first time through the study itself. This implies that outreach and information provision are preconditions for eligible agencies to access available resources.
requirements: Information about the program's purpose, eligibility criteria, and application process must reach the LEA personnel knowledgeable about grants and AI/AN education.
constraints: Based on interviews in three states with a small sample; the report states findings should not be considered broadly generalizable.
target_learners: American Indian/Alaska Native students in eligible but unfunded LEAs
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to federally funded educational and culturally related academic programming
examples: Many unfunded respondents indicated participation in the study was the first time they had learned about Title VII as a mechanism to serve AI/AN students.
key_sources: RMC Research Corporation. (2015). Underuse of Title VII funding for Indian education in Arizona, Nevada, and Utah. Phoenix, AZ: West Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559751

article_title: The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, an Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3
citation: Jonathan Nakamoto, Sandy Sobolew-Shubin, Martin Orland. (2015). The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, An Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons: arts-integrated supplemental literacy curriculum with Units and teaching artist Residencies
description: The A4L Lessons Project is a supplemental literacy curriculum integrating reading, writing, and the arts, designed by Young Audiences, Inc. with University of Washington researchers. Its two main elements are Units of instruction delivered by trained classroom teachers, each focused on an art form (theater, visual arts, music, or dance) and built around central texts, and aligned Residencies in which "a trained teaching artist works in collaboration with the classroom teacher during five one-hour sessions." Each Unit comprises 10 to 19 Lessons with suggested instructional time of 13 to 20 hours, and students work in groups and practice public presentations while practicing 21st century skills.
requirements: Units are delivered by a classroom teacher trained by program staff
Residencies require a trained teaching artist collaborating with the classroom teacher
target_learners: students in grades 3, 4, and 5 in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: reading and writing achievement
literacy and life skills including critical thinking, creative problem solving, and teamwork
examples: Treatment students received two A4L Lessons Units and one teaching artist Residency each school year across 2011-12 through 2013-14
key_sources: Jonathan Nakamoto, Sandy Sobolew-Shubin, Martin Orland. (2015). The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, An Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED560945

title: How People Learn framework as the pedagogical foundation of the A4L Lessons curriculum
description: The report identifies the "How People Learn" framework (Bransford, Brown, & Cocking, 1999) as "the foundation for the program's pedagogy and strategies for student engagement." Under this framework, the curriculum emphasizes teacher-guided, student-initiated activities, encourages students to think and learn independently, and provides tools and strategies to help students approach challenging schoolwork. The arts-integrated curricula are described as giving students opportunities to excel through activities tapping a wide variety of skill sets and learning styles.
requirements: teacher-guided, student-initiated activity structures as designed into the Units
target_learners: elementary students in grades 3 through 5
target_learning_goals: independent thinking and learning
approaching challenging schoolwork
reading and writing achievement

article_title: The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, an Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3
citation: Jonathan Nakamoto, Sandy Sobolew-Shubin, Martin Orland. (2015). The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, An Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Comprehensive Cross Unit (CCU) Assessments measuring Cross-Unit DEEP literacy and life skills
description: The CCU Assessments (Joy, Ruth, and Jackie Tests) were developed specifically for the A4L curriculum by Dr. Diana Sharp with University of Washington experts, and assess Cross-Unit skills rather than Unit-Specific skills. Cross-Unit items assess "DEEP skills (Decision Enhanced by Empathy and Perspective)", including describing a character's or author's traits, emotions, thoughts, or internal motivations and analyzing how perspective impacts genre-specific elements. The tests use open-ended questions scored with rubrics of nine (Joy) or 12 (Ruth, Jackie) criteria, with printed Cronbach's alphas of .70-.75 (Joy), .77-.82 (Ruth), and .80/.79 (Jackie pre/post).
requirements: administered as fall pre-test and spring post-test after the Residency
scoring overseen by a trained literacy expert using shared rubrics
constraints: validity studies have not been conducted on the CCU Assessments and no parallel forms exist; convergent validity correlations with the OAKS ranged from r = .62 to r = .68
target_learners: students in grades 3, 4, and 5
target_learning_goals: literacy achievement
21st century learning and life skills such as empathy and perspective-taking
examples: The Joy Test was administered to grade 3 and the Ruth Test to grade 4 in all three study years

article_title: Incorporating Early Learning Strategies in the School Improvement Grants (SIG) Program: How Three Schools Integrated Early Childhood Strategies into School Turnaround Efforts to Improve Instruction for All Students
citation: Connors-Tadros, L., Dunn, L., Martella, J., & McCauley, C. (2015). title: Seven key components of effective school turnaround practices prevalent across the three case study schools
description: The brief identifies a set of turnaround components that were prevalent in each of the three studied schools, stating that "Key components of effective school turnaround practices were prevalent in each of the schools we studied." The components are strong leadership, effective teachers, redesigned schedules for additional time, rigorous and aligned instructional programs, use of data for continuous improvement, safe and healthy students, and family and community engagement. The pattern recurs across the three case studies, with early learning strategies woven into each component.

constraints: The brief notes these principles of good practice may look different from grade to grade and across state, district, and school contexts

target_learning_goals: Improved academic achievement and school climate in turnaround contexts

article_title: Incorporating Early Learning Strategies in the School Improvement Grants (SIG) Program: How Three Schools Integrated Early Childhood Strategies into School Turnaround Efforts to Improve Instruction for All Students
citation: Connors-Tadros, L., Dunn, L., Martella, J., & McCauley, C. (2015). Incorporating early learning strategies in the School Improvement Grants (SIG) program: How three schools integrated early childhood strategies into school turnaround efforts to improve instruction for all students. New Brunswick, NJ: National Institute for Early Education Research. https://www.nieer.org
title: Strong leadership at all levels—including leaders with early childhood expertise—is a basic strategy of school turnaround
description: The brief states that "A basic strategy of school turnaround is the application of strong leadership at all levels of the school." In the early years of a turnaround effort, knowledgeable principals and directors observe early learning teachers, provide actionable feedback, and support ongoing professional development in appropriate early learning environments. At Orchard Gardens, an assistant principal with a background as an early childhood specialist and instructional coach helped chart progress from age four through the tested grades.
requirements: Principals and directors with knowledge of early learning who observe teachers, give actionable feedback, and support ongoing professional development
constraints: Leadership turnover is a stated sustainability challenge; Orchard Gardens' principal was announced to depart in 2015
target_learners: Four-year-old preschoolers through eighth-grade students in turnaround schools
target_learning_goals: Continuous instructional improvement across the full pre-K–8 learning continuum
examples: Orchard Gardens' principal replaced 80% of the teaching staff and, with a new director of professional development and data inquiry, implemented instructional leadership teams with grade-level and content-area leaders

title: Boston Public Schools early learning strategy: uniform early math and literacy curricula, teacher training, coaches, and NAEYC accreditation support
description: Boston Public Schools enlists early childhood programming in its achievement acceleration agenda by "implementing uniform mathematics and literacy programs across early learning programs and including teacher training and coaches." Under early childhood director Jason Sachs, BPS expanded full-day kindergarten to every five year old, moved 35 schools toward NAEYC accreditation, and supported Orchard Gardens, which attained accreditation for its preschool and kindergarten classrooms in 2011 with the highest scores in the district. Internal and independent studies reveal positive effects on student performance in both the short and long terms.

constraints: The yearlong NAEYC accreditation process is described as rigorous and intensive

article_title: Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options
citation: Linquanti, R., & Cook, H. G. (2013). Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options. Council of Chief State School Officers. http://www.ccsso.org
title: Four-stage framework for a common English learner definition: identify, classify, establish an English-proficient standard, and reclassify
description: The paper organizes the entire EL definitional process around four stages adapted from a National Research Council panel report: "1) identify a student as a potential English learner; 2) classify (confirm/disconfirm) a student as an English learner; 3) establish an 'English-language proficient' performance standard on the state/consortium English language proficiency (ELP) test"; and 4) reclassify to former-EL status through multiple exit criteria. The framework is intended to help consortium member states "systematically review and document existing practices" and align instruments, policies, and practices within states, across states within a consortium, and across consortia.
requirements: Consortium member states must explicitly define their approaches to the four key steps and establish mechanisms to move toward sufficient convergence or alignment over time
constraints: The framework is adapted from an NRC (2011) panel report on comparability of state procedures for identifying, classifying, and reclassifying English learners
Fulfilling the common definition requirement is described as presenting substantial challenges requiring a carefully coordinated, multiyear effort proceeding in stages
target_learners: K-12 students potentially or actually classified as English learners
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency sufficient to access academic content instruction and participate fully in society
examples: Figure 2 presents the framework graphically, adapted from NRC 2011, p. 78

article_title: Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options
citation: Linquanti, R., & Cook, H. G. (2013). Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options. Council of Chief State School Officers. http://www.ccsso.org
title: Strengthen home language surveys by stating purposes, targeting construct-essential questions, setting decision rules, and validating forms
description: The paper proposes minimal guidance for states to strengthen the reliability, validity, and usefulness of home language surveys in moving toward a common EL definition. States should "Clearly state the purposes and intended uses of the HLS", evaluate questions as construct-essential, construct-associated, or construct-irrelevant, "Establish clear guidelines for administering the survey, and clear decision rules for interpreting and acting on the information", and conduct validation reviews examining over- and under-identification including hit rates based on false positives and false negatives.
requirements: Survey questions should reflect the stated purposes and uses of the HLS
Rigorous translation of survey questions into multiple languages and guidelines for oral administration where adult literacy is an issue
constraints: Resource constraints may limit the feasibility of multiple measures at this stage
target_learners: K-12 students entering school who are potentially English learners
target_learning_goals: Accurate initial identification of students needing specialized language and academic support services
examples: The paper lists example construct-essential questions such as which language the child most frequently speaks at home and which language(s) the child currently understands or speaks
