article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 1: The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.org
title: Early warning system methodology applied to school-level indicators of distress
description: The report proposes adapting early warning system methodology — commonly used to identify students at risk of not completing high school — to school-level indicators. An early warning system is defined as 'a process for identifying patterns and characteristics from previous events that turned out to be risky, testing those patterns in a local context to identify specific indicators and thresholds for risk, and then using the characteristics in a systemic way to identify scenarios of risk and to efficiently target interventions.' This report is presented as only a first step toward such a system for schools in distress.
requirements: Local validation: a historical reflection on characteristics of struggling schools must be done in each context to ensure identified data are those most likely to predict further struggling schools
constraints: The report does not itself build or validate thresholds; future publications are planned to support building context-tailored systems
target_learners: Charter school authorizers, charter support organizations, CMOs, and school boards
target_learning_goals: Identifying schools in distress before negative impacts on students are too severe to reverse
examples: The report suggests employing an early warning system may mean 'looking at existing data differently' in longitudinal fashion with an eye toward decline, rather than collecting vast reams of new data
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED609911

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 1: The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.org
title: Locally validate distress indicators before using them to flag struggling schools
description: The report cautions that charter contexts differ and early warning systems 'work best when locally validated.' The indicators it identifies 'should be the start to the conversation about what schools struggling in your jurisdiction look like, rather than the conclusion of the conversation,' ideally including stakeholders from varying levels of the charter sector working together to identify indicators.
requirements: A historical reflection on the characteristics of struggling schools must be conducted in each context before relying on the identified indicators
constraints: Not all authorizers have the capacity or policy directives to collect and examine all potential indicators; authorizers must tailor actions to their state's legislation
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and state education agencies
target_learning_goals: Accurate early identification of schools in distress in a given jurisdiction
examples: The report's methodology section and 'Context is Everything' sidebar both direct readers to validate indicators against local historical patterns of school struggle

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Seven-dimension blueprint for integrating equity, well-being, and academics in learning programs
description: The blueprint organizes program quality into seven overarching dimensions — equity, responsive relationships, climate and culture, instruction, instructional materials, professional learning, and leadership — each with specific indicators of success. It states that "The blueprint has seven overarching dimensions of quality that apply to all programs, and each dimension has specific indicators of success." The dimensions build upon each other, beginning with equity, and are interconnected with common themes and practices throughout. It applies to the full range of program formats, using in-person, remote, and hybrid as its distinguishing terms.
requirements: A multidisciplinary leadership team embeds itself in the blueprint as a whole and forms committees to lead specific improvement efforts, collaborating often rather than taking a divide and conquer approach
constraints: The blueprint explicitly does not provide guidance for reopening approaches focused primarily on remediating learning gaps to boost academic performance
target_learners: All K-12 students in in-person, remote, or hybrid learning programs
target_learning_goals: Academic excellence integrated with social and emotional well-being and equity
examples: School leadership teams use the blueprint's dimension-by-dimension goals and indicators to plan reopening and continuous improvement efforts
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Center equity in all aspects of a learning program, defined as comparably positive outcomes for all groups
description: The blueprint defines equity as "the attainment of comparably positive outcomes for all groups within, or served by, a program" and holds that equity exists when demographic characteristics are not predictors of outcomes. It directs that equity must be central to all aspects of a program — from leadership, professional learning, and instruction to digital inclusion, instructional materials, school culture, and relationships. Equitable programs build from the unique strengths and aspirations of students and provide the necessary support to overcome challenges.
requirements: An equity committee of diverse stakeholders that meets quarterly to establish a vision for program equity, lead the equity work, evaluate progress, and identify future priorities
An equity audit assessing the equity of services provided to student groups of interest and to teachers, staff, parents, and families
constraints: The blueprint warns that without addressing bias in the implementation of a multi-tiered system of support, schools may misinterpret student behavior and over-identify students for intensive support that they do not need
target_learners: Students of color, students learning English, students with disabilities, students from under-resourced communities, and all students served by the program
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to services and equitable opportunities for success across all program features
examples: The blueprint's equity audit covers policies and procedures affecting achievement, attendance, and discipline; program and classroom culture; instructional materials and assessments; professional learning; and stakeholder perceptions of equity, inclusion, anti-racism, and identity safety
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Prioritize responsive relationships as a prerequisite for learning, engagement, and well-being
description: The blueprint holds that "In order to effectively teach, learn, and thrive, humans must first feel physically and emotionally calm and settled and feel socially and emotionally connected through safe and responsive relationships." It therefore treats high-quality relationships as a prerequisite for student, teacher, leader, and family learning, engagement, and well-being, emphasizing interactions that are equitable, sensitive, and responsive to student and family identities. It notes these interactions are particularly critical in remote and hybrid environments where stakeholders are separated by distance and time.
requirements: Develop, implement, and monitor plans, policies, structures, and systems that support frequent, high-quality relational interactions among staff, between staff and students and families, and among students
A committee of diverse stakeholders that meets quarterly to establish a vision for prioritizing responsive relationships
target_learners: Students, teachers, leaders, and families in in-person, remote, and hybrid programs
target_learning_goals: Learning, engagement, and well-being supported by safe and responsive relationships
examples: Recommended structures include involving families in determining the timing, tone, and type of family-teacher connection, restorative practices and peer mediation, and protected time for professional learning communities
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Use a collaborative, data-driven cycle of inquiry with students and families as co-constructors
description: The blueprint "promotes a data-driven cycle of inquiry" intended as a collaborative process of ongoing self-reflection in which educators, leaders, students, and school communities question and adapt traditional methods based on input from, and co-construction with, students, families, and community stakeholders. Valuing student and family agency means co-creating services and supports with them rather than delivering services and supports to them. Issues identified during implementation should be seen not as deficits, but as fertile ground for growth.
requirements: Include representatives from all stakeholder groups, including students and families, to interpret and analyze data used to inform the decision-making process
Establish procedures to collect reliable and valid data multiple times per year to inform program planning, monitoring, and improvement
constraints: The blueprint acknowledges that embracing continuous improvement means taking risks and inevitably needing to deal with failures, since at least some well-planned interventions will not work out
target_learners: All students, with families and community stakeholders as co-constructors of the program
target_learning_goals: Continuous improvement of integrated equity, well-being, and academic outcomes
examples: The leadership dimension directs teams to allow stakeholders, including students and families, to co-design, co-lead, and co-refine the program with multiple ways to engage in evaluation and improvement
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: Growing Strong Learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District
citation: McCarthy, E., Morgan, C. & Sussman, J. (2020). Growing strong learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Academic Parent-Teacher Teams (APTT) dual-capacity building program
description: APTT is a family-engagement model in which teachers lead group parent meetings, share child assessment data against kindergarten-readiness benchmarks, and teach parents games to build targeted skills at home. The article describes that "teachers lead three group parent meetings throughout the year where parents learn about their child's curriculum, become better acquainted with each other and the teacher, and plan for supporting learning at home." Parents leave with their own game pieces and see progress data at the next meeting.
requirements: Teachers receive specialized training in implementing APTT meetings and activities, with trainer support across the school year
constraints: Implementation of the third APTT meeting was not possible due to COVID-19 shelter-in-place guidelines
target_learners: Pre-K children aged 3 to 5, including English learners, at Fairsite Preschool
target_learning_goals: Kindergarten readiness in language and literacy, mathematics, social-emotional, self-regulation, and physical development
examples: Teachers shared assessment data, parents played learning games, and families took home game pieces; parents who missed meetings reviewed content individually with a teacher or administrator
key_sources: McCarthy, E., Morgan, C. & Sussman, J. (2020). Growing strong learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613373

article_title: Growing Strong Learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District
citation: McCarthy, E., Morgan, C. & Sussman, J. (2020). Growing strong learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Bilingual Community Outreach Assistant (BCOA) position
description: The BCOA was a new staff position created to promote engagement of Spanish-language-dominant parents of English learners. The article states the BCOAs "answered questions for parents; reminded them of upcoming events, activities, and deadlines; forwarded helpful resources to parents; assisted parents in the enrollment process; and provided language interpreting for parents." BCOAs also hosted outreach events, supported EL parent leadership, coordinated recruitment, and, during COVID-19 closure, made weekly check-in calls, ran a daily tech hotline, and delivered distance-learning packets, Chromebooks, and hotspots to homes.

constraints: During school closure the role shifted to remote supports such as phone calls and home delivery of resources

article_title: The Toolkit before the Toolkit: Centering Adaptive and Relational Elements of Restorative Practices for Implementation Success
citation: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Four-element framework for restorative practices implementation: adaptive, relational, structural, and technical
description: The brief organizes restorative practices implementation around four interacting element sets. Adaptive elements are 'mindsets, paradigms, values, and belief systems, which lay the groundwork for any technical elements'; relational elements are intentional actions that build relationships and social capital; structural supports are infrastructure such as 'funding, people, time, discipline and other policies, and equity'; and technical elements are the concrete practices and toolkits. The guide treats the first three as precursors that make technical toolkits succeed.
requirements: Leaders and educators must attend to adaptive, relational, and structural elements alongside the technical elements for authentic, sustainable implementation
constraints: The brief states that aligning the elements is 'a journey, not a destination' and that results take years
target_learners: K-12 students and school communities
target_learning_goals: School climate and community transformation
equitable whole-person outcomes
examples: Part 1 covers adaptive elements, Part 2 relational elements, Part 3 structural supports, and Part 4 lists technical guides and toolkits
key_sources: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED615970

article_title: The Toolkit before the Toolkit: Centering Adaptive and Relational Elements of Restorative Practices for Implementation Success
citation: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Restorative practices as an adaptive paradigm rather than a program placed within existing school structures
description: The brief argues restorative practices should be understood not as a packaged program but as a paradigm — a worldview in which 'strong relationships are the conditions for learning and academic success' — within which educators shift the structures of schooling themselves. It contrasts this with the traditional paradigm in which academic learning is the priority and relationship-building detracts from it. The guide's oil-versus-food-coloring metaphor illustrates that a paradigm diffuses through and changes the system, while a program added to an opposing system is never fully absorbed.
requirements: Individuals must internalize restorative principles and shift their own mindsets and values for the paradigm to take hold
constraints: The brief notes restorative practices operate 'often antithetically with the traditional paradigm of our education system,' creating implementation tension
target_learners: K-12 students
educators and school leaders
target_learning_goals: Relationships and community as conditions for learning
equitable discipline and whole-person outcomes
examples: A comparison table contrasts traditional and restorative mindsets across paradigm, safety, time, power, teaching, discipline, and misbehavior
key_sources: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED615970

article_title: The Toolkit before the Toolkit: Centering Adaptive and Relational Elements of Restorative Practices for Implementation Success
citation: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Restorative justice tenets: harm to relationships rather than rule infractions, centered on people, trust, voice and agency, and equity
description: The brief defines restorative justice as 'a theory of justice [that] views crime, conflict, misbehavior, broken rules, and the like as harm to relationships, as opposed to infractions of societal laws,' aiming to center those harmed and create accountability that heals and prevents future harm. It traces the philosophy's origins to indigenous communities worldwide rather than its late-1970s Western criminal-justice emergence. Four guiding tenets are enumerated: centering people and relationships, trust, voice and agency, and equity.
requirements: Restorative justice is anchored by an inherent trust in people, communities, and their capacity to resolve their own conflicts
constraints: Within the restorative paradigm these relational elements are 'essential conditions for learning,' not add-ons
target_learners: Whole school communities including students, families, and staff
target_learning_goals: Accountability, healing, and prevention of future harm
voice, agency, and equity in school communities
examples: The brief lists tenets with named elements: Centering People and Relationships, Trust, Voice and Agency, and Equity
key_sources: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED615970

article_title: The Toolkit before the Toolkit: Centering Adaptive and Relational Elements of Restorative Practices for Implementation Success
citation: Trout, L. (2021). The toolkit before the toolkit: Centering adaptive and relational elements of restorative practices for implementation success. [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Ramp up for a year or more on adaptive, relational, and structural work before formal technical restorative practices training
description: The principle holds that schools should prepare the ground before formal technical training: 'Prior to implementing restorative practices, schools should "ramp up" by taking a year or more to focus on individual adaptive work, to build social capital, and to redesign structural supports in preparation for formal technical training.' After training, quick low-level successes may appear, but high-level success takes years and requires quality implementation and constant practice.
requirements: A year or more of adaptive, relational, and structural preparation prior to formal technical training
constraints: The brief cautions that high-level success such as improved behavior, academic growth, and cultural shifts 'will take three to five years or more' and depends on quality implementation
target_learners: School staff and leaders implementing restorative practices
target_learning_goals: Sustainable, high-fidelity restorative practices implementation
examples: The conclusion advises a ramp-up year before formal technical training, followed by constant practice

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ High School Students in California by Race/Ethnicity
citation: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/
title: California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS) as a disaggregatable school-climate and well-being assessment
description: The CHKS is an anonymous, modular student assessment developed by WestEd for the California Department of Education, administered voluntarily by districts, "usually at least every other year." It collects demographic items (race, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, Asian group identity, gender identity, sexual orientation) and 14 perception measures across five domains: school supports, school safety, mental health, school engagement, and academic performance. This report pools 2017–19 responses from 559,120 students in grades 9 and 11 and disaggregates them intersectionally.
requirements: Districts elect to administer the survey; participation by students is voluntary, and students may decline to respond to demographic items
constraints: Tables omit students who declined to respond to the gender-identity or sexual-orientation items; some subgroup cells rest on samples smaller than 10 and are flagged for caution
target_learners: California high school students in grades 9 and 11
target_learning_goals: Measuring school supports, safety, mental health, engagement, and academic performance to guide school improvement
examples: The report pools two academic years of CHKS data because most districts administer it biennially at times of their own selection
key_sources: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ High School Students in California by Race/Ethnicity
citation: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/
title: Intersectional disaggregation of school-climate survey data by gender identity, sexual orientation, race/ethnicity, and Asian group
description: This report's organizing method is to disaggregate one large survey dataset along intersecting identity axes rather than analyzing LGBTQ students as a single group. It disaggregates by "three gender identity categories" and "five sexual orientation categories" across seven race/ethnicity groups, then further disaggregates Asian students by 10 Asian-group identities, revealing that disparities "vary by race/ethnicity group" and that aggregate trends carry exceptions visible only at finer grain.
requirements: Survey items must collect the identity dimensions of interest; pooled multi-year data are used because districts administer biennially at different times
constraints: Subgroup samples can be extremely small (fewer than 10 for some Asian gender-identity cells), requiring caution when interpreting results
target_learners: High school students, including LGBTQ students of all race/ethnicity and Asian groups
target_learning_goals: Understanding how school supports, safety, and well-being differ across intersecting student identities to target supports equitably
examples: The report disaggregates 559,120 responses by race/ethnicity and gender identity (Table 5), sexual orientation (Tables 7–8), and 10 Asian groups (Tables 11–14)

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ High School Students in California by Race/Ethnicity
citation: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/
title: Provide targeted social and emotional supports for LGBTQ students, using disaggregated data to mitigate disparities
description: The report argues that because adolescence is a critical developmental period, schools should use disaggregated well-being data to target supports for LGBTQ students. It states that "providing them with targeted social and emotional supports that foster positive development can be crucial" and that the data "contribute to understanding how the provision of key supports may help schools and communities mitigate disparities in student outcomes."

constraints: The report presents descriptive survey data; it does not test which specific supports produce which outcomes

article_title: California Special Education Funding System Study, [Part 1]: A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California
citation: Jason Willis, Sara Menlove Doutre, Kelsey Krausen, Tyson Barrett, Tye Ripma, and Ruthie Caparas. (2020). Study of California's Special Education Funding System: Phase I Report — A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-component framework for education funding policymaking: allocation, distribution, expected expenditures, governance, and external accountability
description: The report introduces a framework for conceptualizing any education funding system, built around a funding formula with three components — "allocation (how amounts of funding are calculated), distribution (directing the funds to specific entities), and expected expenditures (requirements for or restrictions on how funds will be spent)" — plus decisions affecting local governance authority and external accountability. The report uses this framework as the lens for describing California's system in Sections 4 and 5 and states the next report will use it to detail implications and options for refining the system.
requirements: Policymakers consider all five components when revising a funding system, as the report states these are the components around which funding and practice decisions are made
constraints: The report notes every design choice in each component has tradeoffs, for example incentivizing overidentification versus underidentification of students with disabilities
target_learners: students with disabilities in California K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: correct, timely identification of students with disabilities; effective and efficient provision of special education services; provision of funding through effective mechanisms and agencies
examples: The report describes California's AB 602 system through this framework: state allocation by ADA with SELPA-specific rates, distribution exclusively through SELPAs, and expected expenditures including required and restricted spending rules
key_sources: Jason Willis, Sara Menlove Doutre, Kelsey Krausen, Tyson Barrett, Tye Ripma, and Ruthie Caparas. (2020). Study of California's Special Education Funding System: Phase I Report — A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616102

article_title: California Special Education Funding System Study, [Part 1]: A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California
citation: Jason Willis, Sara Menlove Doutre, Kelsey Krausen, Tyson Barrett, Tye Ripma, and Ruthie Caparas. (2020). Study of California's Special Education Funding System: Phase I Report — A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Statewide SELPA administrator survey and multi-LEA SELPA allocation plan review
description: The study's mixed-methods evidence base for Sections 4 and 5 comprises a statewide survey of SELPA directors administered February–March 2020, developed with input from the statewide SELPA Executive Board, plus a review of multi-LEA SELPA allocation plans. "Sixty SELPA administrators (from both single- and multi-LEA SELPAs) responded to the survey, representing nearly half of the state's SELPAs." Researchers triangulated survey data with review of allocation plans from 20 of the 54 multi-LEA SELPAs represented in responses; the intended systematic categorization of allocation methods could not be completed due to nonstandard formats and language.
requirements: Survey questions were developed with SELPA Executive Board input to solicit robust information about how multi-LEA SELPAs allocate and distribute state special education funding
constraints: The intended systematic review and categorization of allocation methods could not be completed due to the plans' nonstandard formats, nonstandard language, and the sheer variety of allocation and distribution mechanisms
target_learners: students with disabilities served by California SELPAs and LEAs
target_learning_goals: understanding how special education funds are allocated, distributed, and expended across California SELPAs and LEAs
examples: The survey and 20-plan review became the evidence base for the Section 5 description of multi-LEA SELPAs' role in allocating and distributing funds and establishing expenditure expectations
key_sources: Jason Willis, Sara Menlove Doutre, Kelsey Krausen, Tyson Barrett, Tye Ripma, and Ruthie Caparas. (2020). Study of California's Special Education Funding System: Phase I Report — A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616102

article_title: California State Special Education Funding System Study, Part 2: Findings, Implications, and Considerations for Improving Special Education Funding in California
citation: Doutre, S. M., Willis, J., Barrett, T., Ripma, T., Caparas, R., & Krausen, K. (2021). California State Special Education Funding System Study, Part 2: Findings, Implications, and Considerations for Improving Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Distribute state special education funds to LEAs rather than exclusively to SELPAs to promote coordination and inclusive practices
description: The report recommends transitioning over time from distributing state special education funds exclusively to SELPAs to distributing them to LEAs, which could then contract with regional entities for regionalized services. Because most students with disabilities spend most of the day in general education, the authors argue "Such coordination could be optimized by distribution of AB 602 funds directly to LEAs," aligning funding with LCFF accountability for all students.
requirements: LEA authority to make decisions about how best to use funds for coordination purposes
Maintenance of effort and excess cost fiscal requirements under IDEA must continue to be met
constraints: The need for some regionalized services persists, especially for students in high-cost categories and small LEAs
The funding system alone cannot bring forth necessary changes, though it can communicate state intent
target_learners: Students with disabilities in California K-12 schools, including those in general education classrooms 80 percent or more of the day
target_learning_goals: Access to and progress in the general education curriculum; coordinated services across general and special education
examples: The report's near-term option distributes funds for low- and mid-cost disability categories directly to LEAs while routing high-cost category funds to regional entities
key_sources: Doutre, S. M., Willis, J., Barrett, T., Ripma, T., Caparas, R., & Krausen, K. (2021). article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Indicators-of-distress framework: leading characteristics that occur early in charter school decline across six school domains
description: The report defines indicators of distress as "characteristics that occur early in a school's decline suggesting a school that is struggling to achieve or maintain high levels of quality." Unlike lagging indicators, they are leading indicators that "might predict future failure" and are "more difficult to measure but easier to influence." The framework organizes them into six interrelated domains—leadership, governing board, finance and operations, talent, culture, and instruction—adapted from the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement framework plus charter-specific functions, so stakeholders can identify distress early and intervene while improvement is feasible.
requirements: Requires an early warning system process that identifies patterns from previous school failures, tests them locally to set indicators and thresholds for risk, and applies them systematically to target interventions
constraints: Indicators emerged from interviews in 11 recently distressed charter schools in 7 states; distress is defined as difficulty achieving or sustaining the ESSA definition of a high-quality charter school, so transfer to other schooling contexts is an inference
target_learners: Charter school leaders and governing board members
Charter school authorizers and support organizations
target_learning_goals: Organizational capacity to identify early signs of school decline and intervene before failure
examples: The report categorizes indicators from Figure 1 into leadership, governing board, finance and operations, talent, culture, and instruction, with network-specific indicators flagged
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616211

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Build robust systems across school domains to prepare for and contain distress before it spreads
description: The report's first finding is that well-articulated and implemented systems running through key school processes prepare schools to overcome stressors. Systems act as "a backbone and intentionality to the school's operations, reducing confusion, unknowns, and opportunities for issues to go unaddressed and spiral into deeper decline." Robust systems buffer a stressor in one area so it does not spread to other domains; as the report puts it, "Stabilizing one domain allows you to stabilize others, isolating the spiral of distress to one area of the school."
requirements: Key systems in each core domain, including enrollment maintenance, leader and teacher development, consistent disciplinary processes, curricular alignment, and effective student support
constraints: Without systems, schools operate in crisis mode and institutional knowledge disappears when leaders leave; network-level systems inhibited school leaders when distant networks ignored local context
target_learners: Charter school leaders
Governing board members
Charter network leaders
target_learning_goals: Organizational preparedness, prevention, and response to school decline
examples: Schools that executed replication or expansion before readiness fell into distress; the report recommends readiness checks and leadership support structures before growing a school
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616211

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Charter ecosystem model: external stakeholders and environmental shifts as sources of and buffers against school distress
description: The report's second finding holds that school decline is systematic and partly external: "a charter schools' context—or ecosystem—can also be a source of challenges." The ecosystem model maps the school at the center of parents/community, district, network, authorizer, and state actors that shape its environment (Figure 3). "Being aware of these external stressors helped schools prevent a challenge from occurring," and ecosystems "can aid or impede a charter school's ability to overcome stressors," so schools should scan their context to anticipate shifts and prevent decline.
requirements: Ongoing awareness of the operating context so schools can prepare for and remediate potential challenges before they occur
constraints: Some circumstances, such as the COVID pandemic, arise suddenly and cannot be anticipated; the report's evidence comes from schools that had already experienced distress
target_learners: Charter school leaders and boards
Authorizers, districts, networks, and state policymakers in the ecosystem
target_learning_goals: Preventing organizational decline by anticipating environmental shifts affecting the school's learning conditions
examples: Figure 3 diagrams the charter ecosystem with school, parents/community, district, network, authorizer, and state as key actors
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616211

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Early warning system process for identifying school risk patterns and thresholds
description: The report defines an early warning system as "a process for identifying patterns and characteristics from previous events that turned out to be risky, testing those patterns in a local context to identify specific indicators and thresholds for risk, and then using the characteristics in a systemic way to identify scenarios of risk and to efficiently target interventions." The toolkit applies this process to charter school authorizing, helping authorizers spot declining schools before failure.
requirements: Local testing of patterns to identify context-specific indicators and thresholds for risk
constraints: Patterns from previous events must be validated in the local context before use
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and stakeholders supporting charter schools
target_learning_goals: Identifying schools in distress early enough to intervene before failure or closure
examples: The toolkit operationalizes the process through three tools for identifying, auditing, and assessing indicators of distress in authorizer portfolios
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Leading indicators of distress versus lagging indicators of failure
description: The report distinguishes two kinds of school-quality signals. Indicators of distress are "characteristics that occur early in a school's decline suggesting a school that is struggling to achieve or maintain high levels of quality," while indicators of failure are "output data points that occur later in a school's decline to measure how a school performed." Distress indicators are harder to measure but easier to influence; failure indicators are easier to measure but require more substantive interventions.
requirements: Authorizer data collection systems capable of capturing early, harder-to-measure signals
constraints: Indicators of distress tend to be more difficult to measure than lagging indicators
target_learners: Charter school authorizers
target_learning_goals: Monitoring school quality and identifying struggling schools prior to failure
examples: The toolkit recommends focusing on research-based indicators of distress rather than just indicators of failure such as standardized test scores
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Seven categories of charter school core functions for organizing distress indicators
description: The toolkit organizes indicators of distress around seven categories of charter school core functions. As the report states, "Research has identified seven categories of charter school core functions, and indicators of distress can arise within each one: leadership, governing board, operations, financial management, talent, culture, and instruction." Each category is elaborated with specific indicators and examples of how they appear in practice, data artifacts, and assessment scales.
requirements: Indicators should be interpreted in the authorizer's own context
constraints: Indicators do not necessarily show up all at once, in all categories, and may look different in different contexts
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and other stakeholders supporting charter schools
target_learning_goals: Structuring longitudinal review of school data with an eye toward decline
examples: Tools #1 through #3 each present tables organized by the seven categories
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Tool #1: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Your Portfolio worksheet
description: Tool #1 is a reflective worksheet for authorizers. Its stated purpose is to "determine how indicators may appear in data and in practice, reflect on these data, and identify indicators of distress in their own portfolio." Users review seven indicator tables, check which indicators struggling portfolio schools exhibited, add context-specific examples, and reflect on which indicators are most relevant and why schools in their context may be experiencing them. Estimated time is 1.5 hours.
requirements: Data collection reports, such as site visits, annual reports, and renewal reports from schools in the portfolio
constraints: Recommended for team use with members monitoring academic, financial, and operational performance
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and other stakeholders supporting charter schools
target_learning_goals: Recognizing distress indicators in their own portfolio of schools
examples: Users check boxes next to evidence such as high or increased leader turnover or decreased student enrollment
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Tool #2: Auditing Your Data Collection for Indicators of Distress
description: Tool #2 supports authorizers in "reviewing their data collection methods to determine where they are already collecting data on indicators and to close gaps to improve the identification of schools in distress." It maps each distress indicator to example artifacts and sources—board minutes, check-ins, audits, enrollment data, staff retention data—and asks authorizers to document informal versus formal collection mechanisms and identify gaps. Estimated time is 30 minutes.
requirements: Data collection instruments, such as site visit protocols, annual reports, performance management frameworks
constraints: The report advises that revamping data collection is not likely needed; minor modifications to existing methods suffice
target_learners: Charter school authorizers
target_learning_goals: Auditing and improving data collection to identify schools in distress
examples: The report suggests adding teacher attendance data to annual reporting and including a professional-culture question in site visit protocols
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Tool #3: Assessing Schools for Indicators of Distress rating scales
description: Tool #3 "provides an easy-to-use assessment to determine how schools fare on each of the indicators and the extent to which they are showing signs of distress." For each of the seven categories it presents 0–5 rating scales contrasting healthy and distressed poles, such as a leader who "Has the respect and trust of the staff" versus one who "Is not respected by the staff," plus additional user-defined measures and reflection prompts on strengths, weaknesses, and needed resources.
requirements: School-level data, such as performance frameworks, annual reports, site visit reports, information gathered during check-ins, and materials from board meetings
constraints: Estimated time is 30 minutes per school assessed
target_learners: Charter school authorizers, other stakeholders, and schools reflecting on their own performance
target_learning_goals: Assessing an individual school's performance across school functions to detect distress
examples: Culture scales include items on chronic absence, disciplinary actions, and disproportionate discipline across student subgroups
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Serving the Whole Person: An Alignment and Coherence Guide for Local Education Agencies
citation: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies
title: Conditions for equitable learning and development framework: personal, school, and system conditions
description: The guide organizes the conditions needed for equitable learning and development into three categories drawn from ecological models of development. As the guide states, "the conditions for equitable learning and development can be organized into three categories": personal conditions (health and well-being of students and adults), school conditions (climate, culture, safety, connectedness, belonging, and responsive relationships), and system conditions (policies, funding, and cross-agency collaboration beyond the school's direct control). The framework anchors Chapter 4's activity, in which teams rate each initiative's impact on the three condition types.
requirements: District teams must map each whole-person initiative against the personal, school, and system conditions to use the framework as intended in Chapter 4
constraints: System conditions are described as beyond the direct control of the school, so school-level teams depend on SEA and cross-agency collaboration for that category
target_learners: K-12 students
educators
families
target_learning_goals: equitable academic, social, and emotional learning and development
examples: In Chapter 4, a hypothetical district rates initiatives such as a family connection initiative and culturally responsive teaching professional learning on a 0-3 Likert scale for their impact on personal, school, and system conditions
key_sources: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies

article_title: Serving the Whole Person: An Alignment and Coherence Guide for Local Education Agencies
citation: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies
title: Whole-person development as integrated physiological, cognitive, social, and emotional domains
description: The guide defines serving the whole person as a comprehensive view of human development spanning multiple interrelated domains. It states that "Science shows that these domains develop together, and that health and well-being in one domain bolster the health and well-being of the others," citing Cantor et al. (2018), and that integrated approaches yield improved outcomes, citing Durlak et al. (2011) and Carneiro et al. (2007). Serving the whole person is presented as the foundation for outcomes such as success in school and the workplace, engaged citizenship, healthy relationships, personal purpose, and a sense of place in the community.
requirements: Whole-person efforts must be tailored to students' strengths, aspirations, and needs for students to develop to their full potential, as the guide states
constraints: The guide attributes the domain-integration evidence to cited external research rather than testing it itself
target_learners: K-12 students
the adults who care for them
target_learning_goals: cognitive, physiological, social, and emotional development leading to equitable outcomes
examples: The guide lists five general outcomes of serving the whole person: success in school and the workplace, engaged citizenship, healthy relationships, personal purpose, and a sense of place in the community
key_sources: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies

article_title: Serving the Whole Person: An Alignment and Coherence Guide for Local Education Agencies
citation: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies
title: Six-chapter alignment and coherence process from student understanding through strategic communication
description: The guide's core reusable design is a six-chapter team process: "Chapter 1. Identify the Strengths, Needs, and Aspirations of Your Students; Chapter 2. Describe How These Strengths, Needs, and Aspirations Inform Your Vision for Serving the Whole Person in Your District; Chapter 3. Identify a Focus Area for Coherence; Chapter 4. Tailor the Implementation of Your Whole-Person Initiatives for Alignment With Your Focus Area; Chapter 5. Create an Action Plan; Chapter 6. Plan for Strategic Communication That Reinforces the Work." Each chapter follows a consistent structure of purpose, collaborative activities, hypothetical district responses, and reflection questions.
requirements: A cross-departmental team with defined facilitation must carry out the chapters collaboratively; the guide also directs teams to assess readiness before starting
constraints: The guide recommends choosing no more than one or two focus areas to start, and notes teams may work more quickly or more slowly than the guide indicates
target_learners: K-12 students in the district
families
educators
target_learning_goals: aligned and coherent whole-person initiatives that advance equitable outcomes
examples: Chapter 3 directs teams to articulate a focus area using a 'so that' coordinating conjunction connecting the focus area to the district's broader whole-person vision

article_title: Balancing District Impacts and Community Interests: Considerations for District Charter Authorizers
citation: Chait, R. (2022). Balancing district impacts and community interests: Considerations for district charter authorizers. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: Charter authorizers should balance district impact assessments with six community- and district-oriented factors: demonstrated need, community demand, unique offerings, track record, fiscal impact, and long-term value to the district
description: The brief proposes that authorizers weigh six factors when deciding whether to authorize a new charter school: demonstrated need, community demand, unique offerings, track record, fiscal impact, and long-term value to the district. It argues this enables "informed and inclusive charter school authorizing decisions rooted in evidence of local communities’ wants and needs as well as analysis and projections about the impact on traditional public schools." Demonstrated need is assessed via achievement, performance, and attainment data; community demand via surveys and focus groups.
requirements: Conducting a community needs assessment reviewing existing student achievement, performance, and attainment data for all student populations
Assessing community demand through community surveys, focus groups, and other community engagement activities
Creating processes, collecting data, and conducting analyses for fiscal impact and long-term value considerations
constraints: The brief acknowledges that assessing negative long-term fiscal impact "is an admittedly complicated assessment"
Past performance as a track record indicator is described as not a perfect future predictor
target_learners: Students and families in communities served by district charter authorizers, including students with disabilities, English Learners, and students from low-income families
target_learning_goals: Ensuring new charter schools meet unmet student needs and community demand for schooling options and programs
examples: The brief illustrates the balancing problem with a hypothetical high-quality STEM charter application supported by families, located within 5 miles of an existing but poorly implemented and underenrolled STEM program, in an area with sufficient student population to support an additional school
The brief suggests authorizers may conduct needs and demand analyses on their own or in partnership with community-based organizations that have existing relationships with families
key_sources: Chait, R. (2022). Balancing district impacts and community interests: Considerations for district charter authorizers. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED620722

article_title: Teacher Residency Programs in California: Financial Sustainability Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Hirschboeck, K., Eiler White, M., Brannegan, A., & Reade, F. (2022). Teacher residency programs in California: Financial sustainability challenges and opportunities. WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org
title: Teacher residency model: LEA–IHE partnership integrating coursework with a yearlong clinical placement under an expert mentor teacher
description: The teacher residency model is a pathway into teaching developed and operated by a partnership between an LEA and a state-approved preparation program at an IHE. The brief describes it as focusing on rigorous "clinical preparation" whereby "a resident's credentialing coursework is integrated with a yearlong placement in the classroom of an expert mentor teacher," with the resident gradually assuming increased responsibility. Financial supports such as living stipends or tuition reductions are central, lowering barriers for candidates from underrepresented or low-income backgrounds. In California, grants of $20,000 per resident funded 38 LEA–IHE partnerships targeting STEM, special education, and bilingual credential areas.
requirements: A partnership between an LEA and an IHE with a state-approved teacher preparation program
Financial supports (stipends or tuition reductions) so residents can complete a year of intensive clinical placement and coursework
An expert mentor teacher providing mentorship and regular observations and feedback
constraints: The brief notes California's grant funding was one-time, and authorizing legislation initially capped administrative funding at 5 percent, so sustainability depends on LEA and IHE cost sharing over time
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates, particularly those in STEM, special education, and bilingual credential areas, and candidates of color or from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Rigorous clinical preparation for credentialing, including planning, teaching, and connecting with students and staff
Gradual assumption of increased classroom responsibility under expert mentorship
examples: California's Teacher Residency Grant Program released grants of $20,000 per resident to 33 LEA grantees in March 2019, funding 38 LEA–IHE partnerships, with residents expected to teach in their residency LEA for at least 4 years

Over 90 percent of residents reported strong mentor working relationships, regular observations with high-quality feedback, and coursework relevant to their clinical placement, even after the shift to virtual learning
key_sources: Hirschboeck, K., Eiler White, M., Brannegan, A., & Reade, F. (2022). Teacher residency programs in California: Financial sustainability challenges and opportunities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED620723

article_title: Instructional Equity and Respect for Diversity in Schools: Staff Perceptions Vary by Race/Ethnicity and by Role
citation: McCullough, S. N., Hashmi, S., Austin, G., & Cerna, R. (2022). Instructional equity and respect for diversity in schools: Staff perceptions vary by race/ethnicity and by role. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: California School Staff Survey instructional equity and respect for diversity scales
description: The CSSS includes a seven-item Instructional Equity scale (e.g., items on rigorous course enrollment, culturally reflective materials, and examining cultural biases) and a three-item Respect for Diversity scale, each rated on a four-point agreement scale. The brief reports that "Psychometric analysis shows that both scales have good internal consistency and reliability and no evidence of substantively meaningful bias across staff racial or ethnic groups." Higher agreement percentages reflect perceptions that schools foster equity or respect for diversity.
requirements: Administered online among all staff in grades 5 and above, with voluntary, anonymous, and confidential participation per CDE guidelines
target_learners: secondary school staff (teachers, administrators, paraprofessionals, counselors, resource officers, service providers)
target_learning_goals: assessing staff perceptions of school climate conditions supporting instructional equity and respect for diversity
examples: Used to analyze responses from 118,986 secondary staff across 433 districts and 3,132 schools in 2017/18 and 2018/19
key_sources: McCullough, S. N., Hashmi, S., Austin, G., & Cerna, R. (2022). Instructional equity and respect for diversity in schools: Staff perceptions vary by race/ethnicity and by role. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621215

article_title: Instructional Equity and Respect for Diversity in Schools: Staff Perceptions Vary by Race/Ethnicity and by Role
citation: McCullough, S. N., Hashmi, S., Austin, G., & Cerna, R. (2022). Instructional equity and respect for diversity in schools: Staff perceptions vary by race/ethnicity and by role. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: Disaggregate staff climate perceptions by race/ethnicity and role rather than relying on aggregate staff perceptions
description: Because aggregate staff perceptions may primarily reflect the views of the largest and most positive-perceiving groups, schools should examine perceptions disaggregated by race/ethnicity and role. The brief states these findings "highlight the need to look beyond the aggregate perceptions of staff, which may primarily reflect the views of White respondents (60% of the sample) and teachers (68% of the sample)." Staff in less positive-perceiving groups may have unique insights into unwelcoming aspects of school climate.
requirements: Survey data capable of being disaggregated by staff race/ethnicity and role, such as the CSSS
constraints: The brief notes staff of different races may work in different roles within schools, which can affect perceptions of the school environment
target_learners: school administrators and district leaders
target_learning_goals: identifying unwelcoming and inequitable aspects of school climate that aggregate perceptions mask
examples: The brief analyzed CSSS data disaggregated by six racial/ethnic groups and seven staff roles, finding consistent variation in both areas
key_sources: McCullough, S. N., Hashmi, S., Austin, G., & Cerna, R. (2022). Instructional equity and respect for diversity in schools: Staff perceptions vary by race/ethnicity and by role. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621215

article_title: Clark County School District Magnet Schools Assistance Program (MSAP): Spring 2022 Interim Evaluation Summary Report
citation: Nakamoto, J., Grant, A., Snipes, J., Allender, S., & Figueroa, T. (2022). Clark County School District Magnet Schools Assistance Program (MSAP): Spring 2022 interim evaluation summary report. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: STEM magnet school design combining themed pathways, project-based learning, blended learning with 1:1 devices, and STEM electives and extracurriculars
description: The three MSAP-funded magnet schools share a design built around a STEM theme with dedicated magnet coursework, project-based learning, and blended learning with 1:1 Chromebooks. Gehring used "Magnet coursework via STEM labs in computer science, engineering, and biomedical science" with PLTW Launch; Lied offered magnet pathways in architecture/construction, robotics/manufacturing, and computer science with inquiry-based learning; O'Callaghan offered tracks in video game design, video production, web design, and robotics/engineering. All schools added STEM electives taught by grant-funded teachers and STEM-related extracurricular activities.
requirements: MSAP grant funds to hire licensed teachers for STEM electives and extend instructional time
1:1 Chromebook access for blended learning
constraints: Design evaluated only during the first two years of magnet implementation and disrupted by COVID-19 school closures in 2019-20
target_learners: Elementary students in grades 1-5
Middle school students in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: STEM content knowledge in mathematics, science, and technology
Enrollment and completion of STEM courses
examples: Gehring extended the instructional day by 19 minutes for STEM enrichment and all students participated daily in PLTW lessons with frequent STEM lab access
Lied students enrolled in a STEM elective such as a robotics, automation, and manufacturing course taught by licensed teachers hired with MSAP grant funds

article_title: States' School Safety Centers: A Brief Look into History, Characteristics, and Activities
citation: McKenna, J., Russo, S., Sutherland, H., Boal, A., & Petrosino, A. (2022). States’ school safety centers: A brief look into history, characteristics, and activities. WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org
title: Proposed initial uniform definition of a state school safety center (SSSC)
description: The article proposes an initial definition of what constitutes an SSSC, based on its survey data: "A state-level resource that is funded through state appropriations, state/federal grants, or some combination of the two; that, at a minimum, serves the entire state as a central clearinghouse for school safety information and resources; and that may provide technical assistance and training and/or develop resources to support school safety efforts." The definition was developed because respondents varied in whether they counted agency-embedded offices as SSSCs.
requirements: Funded through state appropriations, state/federal grants, or a combination of the two, as the proposed definition states
constraints: The authors present it as at least an initial definition, subject to refinement through future data collection
target_learners: State policymakers and state education agency staff
target_learning_goals: Understanding and identifying what constitutes a state school safety center
examples: The definition was derived from a survey in which 28 respondents reported an operational SSSC and 3 respondents reported none, with terminology differences explaining some disagreement
key_sources: McKenna, J., Russo, S., Sutherland, H., Boal, A., & Petrosino, A. (2022). States’ school safety centers: A brief look into history, characteristics, and activities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621272

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Five key elements of a whole child approach
description: The guide enumerates five key elements that constitute a whole child approach: "positive developmental relationships; environments filled with safety and belonging; rich learning experiences and knowledge development; development of skills, habits, and mindsets; and integrated support systems." The fifth element, integrated support systems, is the guide's central focus, operationalized as integrated, school-based systems of care built through cross-sector collaboration. The list is grounded in the science of learning and development literature the guide cites.
requirements: Schools must coordinate policy, process, and practice across health, education, and social service sectors, since frameworks alone are described as insufficient without implementation
target_learners: All K-12 students in California local education agencies
target_learning_goals: Physical, social, emotional, and cognitive development; attendance, engagement, health, and academic performance
examples: The guide's Chapter 2 weaves six state initiatives (ACEs Aware, CYBHI, Children and Youth System of Care, community schools, early childhood, expanded learning) into the integrated support systems element
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child (WSCC) model
description: The WSCC model, from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, "aims to align the work of the public health and education sectors—which often serve the same students and share the same goals" so schools can adopt a whole child approach. It categorizes programs and services into 10 components: physical education and physical activity; nutrition environment and services; health education; social and emotional climate; physical environment; health services; counseling, psychological, and social services; employee wellness; community involvement; and family engagement. The guide uses it as an organizing framework, mapping local strategies (e.g., Solano County's school-based wellness centers) onto its components.
requirements: Families and communities must act as critical partners with education professionals, as the model emphasizes
constraints: The guide notes frameworks vary widely and there is no consensus in the field on how whole child frameworks relate to one another
target_learners: All K-12 students, with families and communities as partners
target_learning_goals: Student health, learning, and development through coordinated health and education services
examples: The Solano County Takin' CLAS to the Schools strategy is described as reflecting the family engagement, community involvement, health education, and counseling components of the WSCC model
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Build staff capacity for culturally responsive, asset-based family engagement
description: The guide holds that serving the whole child requires school staff equipped to build strong family partnerships through a culturally responsive approach sensitive to each family's lived experiences. "When schools put children and families first and leverage students' individual lived experiences, cultures, and languages, they strengthen the resilience of students and communities, create a culture of belonging, and maximize protective factors associated with well-being." It directs districts to the Dual Capacity-Building Framework, which offers guidance rather than prescribing specific actions.
requirements: Ongoing professional development for school staff, since without training and coaching the school–family divide persists
constraints: The Dual Capacity-Building Framework does not prescribe specific actions schools must take
target_learners: Historically underserved students and families, including Filipino-American, Latino, and LGBTQ communities named in the Solano County example
target_learning_goals: Student well-being, belonging, resilience, and achievement through strong family–school partnerships
examples: Solano County's ICCTM used pláticas y conocimiento—conversations and awareness about mental health among families with similar lived experiences—and the Cultural Game Changers workforce pipeline strategy
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: ACEs Aware Initiative
description: The ACEs Aware Initiative, driven by California's first surgeon general, focuses on screening children, youth, and adults for adverse childhood experiences, training medical providers, and improving public awareness. The guide reports "over 500,000 people have already been screened, and the ACEs Aware Initiative has the ambitious goal of reducing ACEs by half within one generation." ACEs are 10 categories of adversities in three domains experienced by age 18, linked to toxic stress and long-term health issues. Schools participate by building trauma-informed, healing-centered environments within local networks of care.
requirements: A whole school approach led by a principal and a cross-department leadership team, with staff attending to their own positive and adverse experiences before students'
constraints: One-time COVID-19 relief funds such as ESSER-1 and GEER must be used by September 2022
target_learners: Children, youth, and adults screened for ACEs; students from low-income backgrounds, English Learners, students experiencing homelessness or in foster care named for relief funds
target_learning_goals: Reducing toxic stress and creating trauma-informed school environments that support learning and well-being
examples: The guide recommends developing a leadership team, connecting one-time and ongoing funds (LEA BOP, SMAA, EPSDT Medi-Cal services), and educating personnel about PACEs science with time for buy-in
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
