article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Five-class taxonomy of knowledge sources for synthesizing STEM PLC knowledge
description: The synthesis organizes its evidence into five named classes of knowledge: Type 1, elaborated empirical studies since 1995 mostly in peer-reviewed journals; Type 2, empirical studies reported without method detail and non-empirical work such as theory building; Type 3, published expert knowledge and advice; Type 4, practice-based knowledge from an expert practitioner online panel; and Type 5, published model descriptions often with lessons learned. The authors explain that they "determined it would be useful to add an additional category that would explicitly attend to knowledge about models of conducting PLCs", finding "a considerable body of research in this category, some with “lessons learned” but without formal research". The framework lets the synthesis combine gold-standard and working knowledge while flagging where evidence is thin.
requirements: Restricting the synthesis only to empirical and descriptive studies in peer-reviewed journals would be too incomplete, so the additional non-empirical knowledge classes are needed to capture working knowledge.
constraints: The non-empirical sources may not meet the gold standard of empirical research, though the authors found them generally consistent with findings emerging from the empirical studies.
target_learners: K-12 STEM teachers
preservice STEM teachers
target_learning_goals: STEM teachers' content and pedagogical content knowledge
STEM instructional practice
student mathematics and science achievement
examples: The corpus profile: 78% qualitative only, 85% focused on inservice, 18% involving online components, twice as many studies in mathematics as in science, and two-thirds published in the last five years.
key_sources: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Three-component definition of a professional learning community with an inclusive STEM operating threshold
description: The synthesis defines a PLC through its three constituent components, each of which must be fulfilled for an activity to count: "professional – engaging educators in the development of their professional practice; learning – focused on both the learning of the educators and the learning of their students; and community – which requires common vision, goals, purpose, and a shared sense of trust". Operationally the study used an inclusive rather than restrictive threshold: groups of three or more teachers with a STEM focus, sustained rather than one-shot, excluding whole-school PLCs and two-person interactions such as mentoring pairs. This framework governed which studies were included and anchors the synthesis's design guidance.
requirements: Each component in the term Professional Learning Community — professional, learning, and community — should be fulfilled in order to regard some activity as a PLC.
constraints: The study's STEM focus precluded consideration of enterprises where whole schools are operating as PLCs, and collaborative work by two teachers, such as a single mentor-new-teacher induction pairing, was excluded.
target_learners: K-12 STEM teachers
preservice STEM teachers
target_learning_goals: educators' professional practice development
student learning
examples: Panelists questioned whether a thin lesson study enterprise should count as a PLC, worrying that including low-level endeavors with limited effects would make the PLC reputation that of a fad.

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Design elements for STEM PLCs: time and pacing, subject composition, protocols, and facilitation with administrator support and trust
description: The synthesis identifies recurring design considerations for STEM PLCs drawn across its knowledge sources. Designers must attend to "many aspects related to time and pacing", wisely factoring the relationship between desired PLC purposes and available conditions into decisions about how much and how often to meet. Group composition matters: "Comprising PLCs with teachers from multiple subjects (even limited to mathematics and science) can limit the depth or effectiveness of work on content knowledge or PCK." Protocols for group functioning and for examining student work are important but must be monitored, and facilitation, administrator support and trust-building are described as crucial.
requirements: Having facilitation, administrator support and trust-building are crucial; facilitators require professional development because facilitating adult learning is different than facilitating student learning.
Protocols for STEM PLC group functioning and for examining students' work should be built in, with design and use carefully considered and monitored.
constraints: Multi-subject composition, even limited to mathematics and science, can limit the depth or effectiveness of work on content knowledge or PCK.
The protocol can become the end instead of the means if not monitored.
Public discussion of content knowledge and PCK might be very foreign and threatening given the historical practice of teaching in isolation.
target_learners: K-12 STEM teachers in inservice PLCs
target_learning_goals: STEM content knowledge
pedagogical content knowledge (PCK)
collaborative examination of student work
examples: The reviewed lesson study articles ranged from one partial cycle in one semester to multiple cycles across two years, illustrating why level of effort must be factored into design decisions.
key_sources: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Taxonomy of studied STEM PLC models: lesson study, university course plus follow-up, collaborative action research, grade-level or department meetings, and discussion groups
description: The synthesis categorizes the PLC phenomena investigated in the reviewed research into face-to-face inservice modes — lesson study, university course plus follow-up, collaborative action research or collaborative inquiry groups, grade-level or department meetings, and discussion groups — plus separately tabled online PLC experiences and preservice PLC experiences. It reports that "The most common kind of PLC was variations of lesson study, but there was a wide range of phenomena among this group", with a full Japanese cycle involving joint planning, teaching, group revision and debrief, re-teaching and a final debrief, though most studied cycles omitted the revise and re-teach stages. The taxonomy exists because of great confusion in the literature about what a PLC is.
requirements: Readers need the level of effort — meeting frequency, duration, and time span — to accurately deliberate the findings' applicability, but many articles only state that groups met regularly or often.
constraints: Online and preservice phenomena are termed PLC experiences rather than PLCs because their informality, loose structure, or time constraints limit them from being fully conceived PLCs.
Only eight studies investigated online PLC experiences and only eight strongly focused on preservice teachers.
target_learners: K-12 inservice STEM teachers
preservice STEM teachers
target_learning_goals: collaborative improvement of STEM teaching practice
joint investigation of content and instructional practices
examples: The lesson study category spans one cycle in one semester, two cycles in one semester, one multi-lesson-unit cycle in one year, two stages over two years, and multiple cycles over one or two years.
key_sources: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching
citation: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf
title: Design and implementation principles of effective STEM learning teams
description: The synthesis identifies key design and implementation features shared by STEM learning teams that met high research standards: "shared goals and values, leadership support, issues of time and pacing, focus on student data and work products, collective responsibility for student achievement, good facilitation, and building trust." Teams should identify a STEM learning challenge, keep a steady focus on improving student learning, meet on common regular time, examine student data and work with common rubrics and protocols, and hold mutual accountability for student achievement. A single school subject focus is also identified as easing deep content engagement.
requirements: Teams need support of principals and administrators, including dedicated space and time to meet
Teachers need common time to meet on a regular and sustained basis
Teams should examine student data and work using common rubrics and protocols
constraints: It can take more than a few weeks or months for an unfamiliar team to open up about deeper aspects of STEM teaching
Cross-content teams need additional time and more complex strategies to engage meaningfully in subject content and pedagogy
U.S. school structure emphasizes individual teacher performance over teamwork, and pressure for rapid outcomes can trump the time and trust needed
target_learners: K-12 STEM teachers, including prospective teachers
target_learning_goals: Improving STEM teaching practice and student STEM learning
examples: The expert panel ranked shared values and goals as the most important factor
The report notes Shanghai middle school mathematics teachers each belong to two math learning teams
key_sources: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching
citation: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf
title: Three facilitation roles for STEM learning teams
description: Drawing on research the synthesis cites, facilitators of STEM learning teams fulfill three distinct roles: "facilitating knowledge, including helping to find relevant STEM or STEM education expertise if/as needed; processing facilitation to attend to the structure and interaction of the groups; and focusing facilitation to keep the group on target." Facilitation, whether face-to-face, online, or combined, requires engagement, tact, careful listening, and content and pedagogical knowledge. The framework treats helping adults learn as a distinct expertise from teaching children.
requirements: Facilitators need content and pedagogical knowledge plus engagement and tact
constraints: An expert teacher does not necessarily make an expert facilitator of a learning team
target_learners: Facilitators of K-12 STEM teacher learning teams
target_learning_goals: Supporting productive collaborative teacher inquiry in STEM PLCs
key_sources: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching
citation: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf
title: NCTAF STEM learning studios with cross-curricular teams and STEM professional volunteers
description: NCTAF's STEM learning teams work in "STEM learning studios": intentionally cross-curricular teams of science, math, and technology teachers joined by scientists and engineers from government, business, and industry who co-design and implement project-based learning activities addressing learning challenges the teachers identify. Implementation begins with a three-day summer workshop and quarterly design sessions, typically teaching one inquiry-based project module per quarter. Launched in 2009 with a NASA grant, the model reached eight high schools in three Maryland districts as of Spring 2011.
requirements: STEM industry and government volunteers recruited based on expertise matching the teachers' identified learning challenges
constraints: The report describes the model's first-year evaluation only; it does not present controlled achievement evidence for the studios
target_learners: High school and middle school teachers and students in participating Maryland districts
target_learning_goals: Enhancing STEM teaching through cross-disciplinary project-based learning
examples: An independent first-year evaluation showed an almost immediate positive impact on both teachers and students
Approximately three-quarters of students said what they learned in class helped them better understand the world around them
key_sources: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf

article_title: National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report: Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress
citation: Cook, G., Linquanti, R., Chinen, M., & Jung, H. (2012). National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report—Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress. American Institutes for Research, Washington, DC. http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/index.html
title: Set ELP performance standards through a deliberative process combining empirical analyses with informed, trained expert judges rather than empirical data alone
description: The report's foundational principle is that standard setting for EL accountability criteria is "not merely an empirical procedure" but requires empirical information plus informed judges in a rational, coherent, transparent deliberative process. Empirical methods ground policy deliberations and clarify implications of options, while qualified, trained panelists make the final judgment. The report applies this by pairing the analytic methods of Chapters II–IV with guidelines drawn from standard-setting best practices.
requirements: Panelists must be selected and trained, with appropriate qualifications and no vested interest in the standards set
A clear, sequential, documented process and a mechanism to validate decisions must be in place
constraints: No one empirical method gives a complete picture; methods seldom provide definitive answers and data are almost always imperfect, with missing cases common in AMAO analyses
target_learners: English Learners (ELs) in K–12 state assessment and accountability systems
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency and academic content proficiency in English language arts and mathematics
examples: The report applies decision consistency, logistic regression, and box plot methods to authentic state and district data sets in three states as worked examples supporting deliberative standard setting
key_sources: Cook, G., Linquanti, R., Chinen, M., & Jung, H. (2012). National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report—Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress. American Institutes for Research, Washington, DC. http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/index.html

article_title: National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report: Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress
citation: Cook, G., Linquanti, R., Chinen, M., & Jung, H. (2012). National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report—Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress. American Institutes for Research, Washington, DC. http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/index.html
title: Three accountability methods for taking ELs' ELP level into account when setting academic progress and proficiency expectations: progressive benchmarking, indexed progress, and status-and-growth accountability matrix
description: Chapter IV presents an organizing framework of methods for setting academic expectations for English Learners. "Progressive benchmarking methods are illustrated that adjust either EL students' content achievement scale scores or their weight (individual 'count'), based on each student's ELP level relative to their initial ELP level and time in the state school system." An indexed progress method uses ELs' ELP growth as a weighted, time-sensitive proxy for English language arts performance for newly arrived ELs entering at lower initial ELP levels. A status and growth accountability matrix method credits predetermined academic growth and proficiency attainment without considering ELP level.
requirements: Application requires student-level longitudinal data linking ELP assessments, content assessments, time in the state school system, and initial ELP level
constraints: The report notes the SGAM method explicitly ignores the EL's ELP level, contrasting with the two adjustment methods; each method is applied to one education agency's sample data set
target_learners: English Learners, particularly newly arrived ELs entering at lower initial ELP levels, in grade 3 and similar grades
target_learning_goals: Academic progress and proficiency expectations in English language arts and mathematics accountability systems
examples: All three methods were applied using the same education agency's sample data set (Education Agency 1, grade 3, N = 18,101 ELs in outcome comparisons)

article_title: Evaluation of "The Electric Company" Summer Learning Program
citation: McCarthy, B., Michel, L., Tiu, M., Atienza, S., Rice, J., Nakamoto, J., & Tafoya, A. (2011). Evaluation of The Electric Company Summer Learning Program. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: The Electric Company Summer Learning Program transmedia curriculum with Prankster Planet
description: The TEC Summer Learning Program is a 36-hour out-of-school-time transmedia curriculum for children ages 6 to 8 combining DVDs of 12 Electric Company episodes, scripted small- and large-group activities, and the Prankster Planet online game. The report describes it as "a transmedia curriculum that presents a narrative story to students that is presented across multiple forms of media, including television episodes and an online gaming experience." The curriculum is divided into 24 sessions with a repetitive structure of activity blocks (Watch and Learn, Stretch and Assess, Get Electric, Show Off Your Skills, Feel the Power), and Prankster Planet includes 12 missions centered on the vocabulary of each episode. The evaluation found it was well received and associated with pre-to-post skill gains.
requirements: Internet-ready computer access for students (sites were required to have at least one computer per two students)
teacher training via live or archived orientation webinars and a detailed curriculum guide with scripted facilitation
constraints: implemented in 5- to 6-week summer programs of 90 minutes a day; several shorter programs used a reduced 30-hour, 20-day model omitting two episodes
target_learners: students ages 6 to 8 between first and second grades, largely from low-income families and including English language learners
target_learning_goals: mathematics vocabulary
numeracy skills
literacy and phonics skills
motivation and confidence to engage in learning activities
examples: In the study, content was implemented in 5- to 6-week summer programs for 90 minutes a day for a total of 24 days by 16 teachers in 12 programs serving 152 students

article_title: A Climate for Academic Success: How School Climate Distinguishes Schools That Are Beating the Achievement Odds. Full Report
citation: Voight, A., Austin, G., and Hanson, T. (2013). A climate for academic success: How school climate distinguishes schools that are beating the achievement odds (Full Report). San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/
title: School Climate Index framework of five recurring climate dimensions
description: The report organizes school climate, a term with "no consensus definition," around five recurring themes identified in prior reviews: order, safety, and discipline; academic supports; personal and social relationships; school facilities; and school connectedness. Operationally it uses the California Healthy Kids Survey to build a School Climate Index combining two domains — supports and engagement, and low violence, victimization, and substance use — plus a truancy indicator, rescaled to a mean of 300 and SD of 50.
requirements: Requires student survey data such as the CHKS administered to the school's students
constraints: The report notes school climate "has no consensus definition" and the term has become something of a catchall for school-improvement targets
target_learners: middle and high school students
target_learning_goals: school connectedness and engagement
safe and supportive learning environment
examples: The study computed SCI scores for roughly two thirds of California public middle and high schools that administered the CHKS in 2008-09 or 2009-10

citation: Voight, A., Austin, G., and Hanson, T. (2013). A climate for academic success: How school climate distinguishes schools that are beating the achievement odds (Full Report). San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/
title: California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS) as a school-climate measurement instrument
description: The CHKS core module is described as "a 115-item student survey that is primarily designed to measure school climate." A factor analytic study identified eight latent constructs, which load onto two domains: supports and engagement, and low violence, victimization, and substance use. These domains combine with a reverse-coded truancy indicator to form the School Climate Index used as the study's climate outcome.
requirements: Administration was required of California districts receiving Title IV or TUPE funding during 2008-09 to 2009-10
constraints: Coverage is limited to schools that administered the survey — about two thirds of the state's traditional public middle and high schools
target_learners: middle and high school students
target_learning_goals: measuring school safety, supports, engagement, and connectedness
examples: The study used CHKS administrations from 2008-09 and 2009-10 to build school-level climate scores for 1,715 schools

description: The School Climate Index is a school-level indicator developed for the California Department of Education's Safe and Supportive Schools program. It is built from "aggregated student self-report data from the CHKS" and also includes truancy data from CBEDS. The report states "The SCI ranges from 100 to 500, with a mean of 300 and a standard deviation of 50." It served as the study's measure of school climate and is used in School Climate Report Cards.

CBEDS truancy data

target_learning_goals: School climate conditions supporting academic achievement

article_title: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science
citation: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three-component framework of academic language: content-domain vocabulary, general academic vocabulary, and discipline-specific sentence structures
description: The report defines academic language as school language valued by teachers, texts, and tests, structurally and lexically different from everyday spoken English. It divides academic language into three components: "(1) vocabulary related to the academic content domain; (2) general academic vocabulary related to the words used within the discipline to tie ideas together; and (3) sentence structures required by the content discipline." It illustrates the components with a butterfly life-cycle unit and echoes the bricks-and-mortar analogy distinguishing content-specific vocabulary from general academic terms like therefore and because.
requirements: Instruction must treat all three components so English learners can succeed in content-area instruction
constraints: The framework is illustrated with elementary science examples (butterfly life cycle, pendulum, rocks)
target_learners: English learners in U.S. K-8 schools
target_learning_goals: Academic language development in content areas
Content understanding in science
examples: In an elementary butterfly unit, egg, caterpillar, chrysalis are content vocabulary; grow, change, transform are general academic vocabulary; first, then, next, last structure sequencing sentences
key_sources: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580362

article_title: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science
citation: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Provide English language development and comprehensible content instruction simultaneously rather than delaying content until English proficiency
description: The report argues that equal educational opportunity for English learners requires ELD or ESL instruction combined with engaging content instruction made comprehensible through specific techniques, and that "Both of these instructional opportunities should be provided simultaneously." Delaying content instruction until sufficient English proficiency relegates students to a role where they lack the content knowledge expected at their grade level. Scaffolding—limiting contextual complexity and gradually removing limits—amplifies the language of content.
requirements: Teachers use scaffolds such as concept maps, graphic organizers, realia, pre-taught vocabulary, collaborative projects, and sentence frames
constraints: Without proper instruction, the language demands of content disciplines can compromise English learners' content understanding
target_learners: English learners, including newcomers and U.S.-educated students
target_learning_goals: Content knowledge and academic language acquired together
examples: The report's Montebello K-4 program blended science and language so student thinking came first and authentic language developed as students described their thinking
key_sources: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580362

article_title: Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex
citation: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED535250
title: Cognitive framework of data literacy as declarative, schematic, procedural, and strategic knowledge
description: The paper applies a cognitive framework from science education research to characterize the facets of data literacy. It states that "The cognitive framework identifies declarative, schematic, procedural, and strategic knowledge components that need to be addressed to ensure effective use of data by educators." Declarative knowledge is knowing that (language and terminology of data use), schematic is knowing why (purposes of data sources), procedural is knowing how (how data are organized and analyzed), and strategic is knowing when, where, and how to apply data literacy. The paper also identifies a volitional component of reflective, improvement-seeking educators that was neither expected nor found in the text analyses.
requirements: All four knowledge components need to be addressed to ensure effective use of data by educators
constraints: The volitional component was not identified in the text analyses and was not expected by the authors
target_learners: in-service educators
teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: using data effectively to inform educational practice
examples: Participants' pre-meeting definitions were cognitively analyzed using this framework to discern the knowledge and skills they saw as components of data literacy
key_sources: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582807

article_title: Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex
citation: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED535250
title: Eight-category content framework for professional development materials on data literacy
description: The materials analysis produced a coding framework for the knowledge and skills addressed by professional development texts on data use. The paper reports that "The content focus categories of the framework were assigned eight superordinate codes: precursor conditions, inquiry process, assessment, data, data analysis, instructional planning, programmatic planning, and understanding research evidence." Each code carries subcodes; for example, the precursor conditions code includes school vision, connection to other initiatives, authority, understanding of the change process, collaboration, focus on equity, cultural proficiency, school culture, and characteristics of professional development. Texts were rated for relative emphasis on each concept using page-coverage values consolidated into high, medium, and low levels.
requirements: The framework would need validation by an external advisory board and comparison to other researchers' frameworks for more rigorous use
constraints: The framework lacks sufficient robustness to support a quantitative comparison of raters
The analyses were initial and exploratory and were not a consumer's guide to professional development programs
target_learners: in-service educators receiving data literacy professional development
target_learning_goals: developing the knowledge and skills of data literacy
examples: Two research associates coded 31 remaining texts with the framework after moderation on the Love et al. (2008) text, and seven text authors confirmed in member checks that concepts and skills had been adequately identified
key_sources: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582807

article_title: Inequitable Opportunity to Learn: Student Access to Certified and Experienced Teachers
citation: Cardichon, J., Darling-Hammond, L., Yang, M., Scott, C., Shields, P. M., & Burns, D. (2020). Inequitable opportunity to learn: Student access to certified and experienced teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/crdc-teacher-access
title: Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) teacher access measures, 2014 and 2016
description: The Civil Rights Data Collection is a biennial survey of all U.S. public schools and districts collected by the Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights since 1968. The report uses the 2013–14 and 2015–16 waves, linked to the NCES Common Core of Data for locale, covering "a total of 92,602 schools serving more than 49 million students". It measures FTE teachers who are certified and in their first or second year, enabling school-level equity comparisons.
requirements: Data are collected at the school level, so the report notes these data cannot identify disparities at the student level within each school
constraints: Comparisons across years and subgroups examine percentage differences without weighting or other adjustments
target_learners: K-12 public school students
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to certified and experienced teachers as a condition of opportunity to learn
examples: The report divides schools into national and state-level quintiles by percentage of students of color enrolled and compares top and bottom quintiles

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers Leading Sustainable Professional Learning in Their Communities
citation: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading
title: Professional capital: human, social, and decisional capital that amplifies teacher effectiveness
description: The casebook invokes Hargreaves and Fullan's concept of professional capital as a strategy for changing education and strengthening the teaching profession. It is "the confluence of three other kinds of capital—human, social, and decisional—that amplify one another." The report states that "Professional capital combines teachers' professional knowledge and skills, their collective capacity to form networks and communities of learning and practice, and their use of experience to make decisions about teaching and learning that are in the best interests of their students." The ILC's teachers-teaching-teachers approach is presented as allowing teachers to develop professional capital and lead sustainable professional development.
requirements: Investing in the professional capital of individuals, the group, and the system, which the report says improves learning and achievement
constraints: The framework is cited from Hargreaves and Fullan as background theory, not tested in this report
target_learners: Practicing K-12 teachers and teacher leaders
target_learning_goals: Building collective professional capacity for standards-aligned instruction
examples: ILC teacher leaders aligned activities with school and district improvement goals, boosting capacity for instructional choices and enhancing their decisional capital
key_sources: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers Leading Sustainable Professional Learning in Their Communities
citation: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading
title: The Instructional Leadership Corps (ILC): a statewide teacher-led professional learning project
description: The ILC is a statewide collaborative teacher professional learning project launched in 2014 by the Stanford Center for Opportunity Policy in Education, the California Teachers Association, and the National Board Resource Center. Rather than outside consultants conducting one-shot workshops, "the ILC entrusts professional learning to local teaching professionals who have the training and support to lead ongoing learning within their own districts." Between November 2014 and September 2018, ILC leaders provided multisession workshops to more than 32,000 educators in more than 2,000 schools and at least 495 districts, with an initial cadre of 183 teacher and site leaders selected from an applicant pool of 500. Members are primarily teachers, augmented by administrators and coaches/ToSAs.
requirements: Intensive professional development for ILC members at statewide and regional conferences and retreats
Supportive institutional partners (SCOPE, CTA, NBRC) providing guidance, resources, and network upkeep
constraints: Growth depended on local fiscal commitment, embrace of the work, and valuing teacher expertise for the project to take root
target_learners: K-12 teachers and site administrators across California districts
target_learning_goals: Implementing CCSS and NGSS instructional shifts and building teacher leadership capacity
examples: Madera ILC leaders embedded workshops in new-teacher induction; North Orange County leaders ran Teachers Teaching Teachers conferences through CSU Fullerton
key_sources: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers Leading Sustainable Professional Learning in Their Communities
citation: Lotan, R. A., & Burns, D. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Teachers leading sustainable professional learning in their communities. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-teachers-leading
title: Iterative multisession professional development workshops with classroom application between sessions
description: Professional development workshops (PDWs) are a hallmark of the ILC. The pattern provides multiple learning sessions separated by opportunities for teachers to design and apply new strategies in their classrooms; the report states this is "a key element in helping teachers make lasting changes in instructional practice," in contrast to single-session workshops after which teachers may return to familiar practices. In the first workshop, participants experience instructional strategies and collaboratively plan lessons; in the second, they analyze student work samples, reflect, and exchange feedback for iterative improvement.
requirements: Multiple sessions separated by classroom application opportunities
Collaborative teams so teachers will attempt new approaches and refine them with feedback and practice
constraints: Follow-up involving modeling or observation-and-feedback of participant teachers is rare but important
target_learners: Practicing K-12 teachers implementing new standards
target_learning_goals: Sustained, standards-aligned changes in classroom instructional practice
examples: In the first of two consecutive workshops, participants experience strategies, study concrete examples often with videotapes of practice, and plan lessons; in the second they analyze student work artifacts

article_title: The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting Professional Learning in the Hands of the Profession
citation: Lotan, R. A., Burns, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). The Instructional Leadership Corps: Entrusting professional learning in the hands of the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-professional-learning
title: The ILC iterative professional development workshop model: multiple sessions separated by classroom application, reflection, and refinement
description: The ILC's hallmark is a sequence of professional development workshops (PDWs) in which teacher leaders demonstrate instructional shifts, support colleagues in trying new practices, and reconvene to analyze results. In the first of two consecutive workshops, "participants experience—rather than just observe—instructional strategies designed to deepen student learning" and collaboratively plan lessons; in the second, participants analyze student work samples, reflect, and exchange feedback for iterative improvement. This contrasts with single-session workshops after which teachers may return to familiar practices.
requirements: Teacher leaders trained in the instructional shifts; multiple learning sessions separated by opportunities for teachers to design and apply new strategies in their classrooms
constraints: The report notes meaningful follow-up was important but rare, and that achieving depth versus reach is a perennial dilemma in teacher professional learning initiatives

Site-based administrators
target_learning_goals: Implementing CCSS and NGSS instructional shifts
Sustained change in classroom instructional practice
examples: Two consecutive workshops in which teachers plan a lesson addressing an instructional shift, then return to analyze student work and refine practice

Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/instructional-leadership-corps-professional-learning
title: The ILC 'teachers teaching teachers' model of teacher-led, systemically connected professional learning
description: The ILC is a statewide collaborative in which expert teachers, trained through statewide and regional conferences, organize local professional development to spark iterative changes in practice. Its "purposeful approach" of "teachers teaching teachers" empowers teachers to lead sustainable professional development and advance instructional capacity within their districts. The model replaces one-shot outside-consultant workshops with ongoing, locally led learning, and its theory of action resonates with Jaquith's framework for enhancing instructional capacity, which calls for opportunities to develop professional knowledge, resources, recognition of instructional expertise, and organizational structures supporting collaboration and trust.
requirements: A corps of trained teacher leaders selected for instructional expertise and leadership, organized in local teams
Institutional partners providing guidance, resources, network upkeep, and recognition

Teacher leaders
Site and district administrators
target_learning_goals: Implementing new standards-aligned instruction
Building district instructional capacity and teacher leadership

article_title: Encouraging Social and Emotional Learning in the Context of New Accountability
citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability
title: CASEL's five-competency framework for social and emotional learning
description: The report adopts CASEL's widely used definition of SEL as "the process through which children and adults acquire and effectively apply the knowledge, attitudes, and skills necessary to understand and manage emotions, set and achieve positive goals, feel and show empathy for others, establish and maintain positive relationships, and make responsible decisions." Figure 1 presents five competencies—self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making—nested within classrooms, schools, homes, and communities. The report uses "competencies" as an umbrella covering skills, mindsets, and habits.
requirements: The framework spans skills, mindsets, and habits; the report notes mindsets include beliefs about belonging and effort, and habits include behaviors such as arriving prepared
constraints: The report notes the term SEL has expanded to include grit, resilience, perseverance, and growth mindset, and that some constructs such as growth mindset are still in development
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: social-emotional competencies including self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making

article_title: Encouraging Social and Emotional Learning in the Context of New Accountability
citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability
title: Multitiered accountability framework with four tiers of indicators under ESSA
description: The report conceptualizes accountability as a multilayered system rather than only federally mandated indicators. It distinguishes federal indicators used to identify schools for intervention, state-reported indicators for public information and improvement, state-supported indicators (tools districts may choose), and locally selected indicators. Different indicators belong in different tiers "depending on the nature of the data, who will be using it, and for what purpose." California's proposed ESSA system is presented as an example, and indicators may be shown on a dashboard as status or growth.
requirements: Federal indicators must be valid, reliable, comparable statewide, meaningfully differentiate schools, and be disaggregated by ESSA student subgroups
constraints: State-supported and locally selected indicators are not required and would largely inform ongoing improvement; some measures could fit in multiple tiers depending on state context
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: school quality and student success measurement, including SEL and school climate
examples: California's proposed multitiered ESSA system places chronic absenteeism and suspension rates among federal indicators and school climate surveys among locally selected indicators
key_sources: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability

article_title: Encouraging Social and Emotional Learning in the Context of New Accountability
citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability
title: Do not use measures of students' social-emotional competencies for high-stakes accountability
description: The report concludes that "States should not use measures of students' social and emotional competence for high-stakes accountability purposes, at least for now." Most such surveys are relatively new, were not designed for cross-school comparison, and are vulnerable to reference bias because students are not always the best judges of their own competence. States can instead support local use of these measures to inform teaching, learning, and program investments, with aggregate reporting for school decisions.
requirements: If used at all, measures should be used locally to identify students' strengths and needs, reported on an aggregate basis to inform school decisions
constraints: Measures may be particularly vulnerable to reference bias; attaching consequences may lead individuals to fake or game a measure, rendering it invalid
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of social-emotional competencies for improvement rather than sanction
examples: The report recommends student surveys of their own social-emotional competencies for state-supported and locally selected tiers, not the federal tier
key_sources: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability

article_title: Encouraging Social and Emotional Learning in the Context of New Accountability
citation: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability
title: Choose accountability indicators using four questions: actionability, intended use, reliability, and differentiation
description: The report offers four questions for policymakers choosing an indicator: what the indicator measures and whether data are actionable; for what use the measure was designed and how data might be distorted by high stakes; whether the measure generates consistent, reliable data; and whether it meaningfully differentiates between schools and subgroups. It invokes Campbell's law, noting the more a measure is used for decisions with negative consequences, the more likely it is to be misunderstood or distorted.
requirements: An indicator should have strong construct validity, and schools should be held accountable for outcomes they can reasonably affect
constraints: Surveys designed for one-on-one settings may not produce valid data when administered en masse; indicators lacking sufficient variability may be publicly reported but not used to rank schools
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: sound indicator selection for accountability and continuous improvement systems
examples: The report notes students used to greater supports may be more critical of a condition, rendering comparable ratings objectively unequal
key_sources: Melnick, H., Cook-Harvey, C. M., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Encouraging social and emotional learning in the context of new accountability. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/sel-new-accountability

article_title: The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers
citation: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency
title: Teacher residency model: district-university partnership grounding deep clinical training
description: A teacher residency is a certification pathway grounded in a full-year clinical apprenticeship alongside an expert mentor teacher, with tightly integrated coursework from a partner university leading to a credential and master's degree. The report defines it as "a mutually beneficial partnership between preparation providers and districts, one in which the integration of clinical experiences and coursework throughout the preparation program is co-designed". Residents receive financial support in exchange for a multi-year teaching commitment.
requirements: Strong district/university partnership with co-designed curriculum
Expert mentor teachers who co-teach with residents
Financial support exchanged for a three- to five-year teaching commitment
constraints: Attracting and developing a large pool of qualified mentors is a major challenge because monetary incentives are limited and time commitments considerable
target_learners: Prospective teachers in hard-to-staff urban and rural districts
target_learning_goals: Preparation for teaching in high-need schools and shortage subject areas
examples: The San Francisco Teacher Residency, founded in 2010 by SFUSD, University of San Francisco, Stanford, and the local teachers' union
key_sources: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency

article_title: The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers
citation: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency
title: Eight key characteristics of strong teacher residency programs
description: The report enumerates eight characteristics shared by high-quality residencies: strong district/university partnerships; coursework tightly integrated with clinical practice; a full-year residency teaching alongside an expert mentor; recruitment of high-ability, diverse candidates to meet district hiring needs; financial support in exchange for a three- to five-year commitment; cohorts placed in teaching schools; expert mentors who co-teach; and ongoing mentoring for graduates. The report states that "the success of residencies requires attention to each of the defining characteristics of the model, and the integrity of their implementation".
requirements: Attention to each defining characteristic and implementation integrity
target_learners: Teacher candidates and the districts that hire them
target_learning_goals: Rigorous preparation for teaching in high-need contexts
examples: SFTR places residents in a small number of teaching academies and provides two years of induction coaching after graduation
key_sources: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency

article_title: The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers
citation: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency
title: Integrate coursework tightly with a full-year clinical placement in expert classrooms
description: Residencies couple at least a full school year of clinical practice under an expert mentor with coursework designed to reinforce that practice, creating what the report calls "a more powerful learning experience" in which "the interconnectedness of theory to practice reinforces best, research-based practices for teacher residents". Most residents receive at least 900 hours of preservice clinical preparation versus 400-600 hours in traditional programs.
requirements: A partner university whose coursework is aligned to the clinical placement
Expert mentor teachers in whose classrooms residents apprentice

target_learning_goals: Connecting theory and research-based practice to classroom teaching
examples: SFTR residents take night courses tightly integrated with their clinical placement and participate in clinical instructional rounds modeled on medical rounds

article_title: Educating the Whole Child: Improving School Climate to Support Student Success
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., & Cook-Harvey, C. M. (2018). Educating the whole child: Improving school climate to support student success. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/educating-whole-child
title: Four-domain framework for whole child education
description: The report organizes its school implications around four major domains that research suggests schools should attend to: supportive environmental conditions, social and emotional learning, productive instructional strategies, and individualized supports. The framework states that "research suggests that schools should attend to four major domains," each elaborated with concrete practices: positive school climate and strong relationships; explicit SEL instruction, infusion, and restorative approaches; meaningful, inquiry-based, collaborative, mastery-oriented instruction with metacognitive opportunities; and integrated services, extended learning, and multi-tiered systems of support. It functions as the report's central explanatory structure linking the science of learning and development to school design.
requirements: Accomplishing the work requires an intensive focus on adult development and support so educators can design for and enact the practices
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Social and emotional skills
Healthy development
examples: The report elaborates each domain with practices such as looping, advisory systems, explicit SEL instruction, performance assessments, and multi-tiered systems of academic, health, and social supports.
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., & Cook-Harvey, C. M. (2018). Educating the whole child: Improving school climate to support student success. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/educating-whole-child

article_title: Educating the Whole Child: Improving School Climate to Support Student Success
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., & Cook-Harvey, C. M. (2018). Educating the whole child: Improving school climate to support student success. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/educating-whole-child
title: Personalize supports to each child's unique developmental path rather than designing learning around a mythical average
description: Because variability in human development is the norm, the report holds that effective teachers personalize supports and intervention for different children rather than assuming all children respond equally to the same teaching approaches. It warns that "when educators try to force all children to fit one sequence or pacing guide, they miss the opportunity to nurture the individual potential of each child," and can cause children and teachers to adopt counterproductive views about learning potential that undermine progress. Supportive schools avoid attaching labels to children or designing learning experiences around a mythical average.
requirements: Teachers need the capacity to personalize supports and intervention for different children
target_learners: K-12 students with diverse developmental pace and profile
target_learning_goals: Individual learning potential
Positive learning self-concept
examples: The report's principle that variability is the norm notes children of precisely the same age are at different developmental levels in different domains.

article_title: The Tapestry of American Public Education: How Can We Create a System of Schools Worth Choosing for All?
citation: Cookson, P. W., Jr., Darling-Hammond, L., Rothman, R., & Shields, P. M. (2018). The tapestry of American public education: How we can create a system of schools worth choosing for all? Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/tapestry-american-public-education
title: Choice systems improve quality only when paired with instructional improvement strategies that build capacity in all schools
description: The report argues that choice alone does not raise quality: "Simply creating new options does not lead automatically to greater access, quality, or equity." Districts that paired choice with intensive, content-based professional development, classroom walkthroughs with rubrics, and curricular support (NYC District 2, Milwaukee) saw achievement gains, while New Orleans, where central support was cut, produced an uneven set of schools. The principle directs policymakers to invest in teaching capacity across all schools rather than relying on choice dynamics alone.
requirements: A strong infrastructure of professional development and financial and curricular resources so all students have access to strong schools
constraints: Without a support system to help schools improve, the only recourse for school failure is closure, leaving students moving from one failing school to another
target_learners: All public school students in choice systems
target_learning_goals: Access to high-quality teaching and curricula in every school
examples: NYC District 2 built professional development and resources so all schools became higher quality; Milwaukee's gains began only after an instructional improvement initiative for district-run schools
key_sources: Cookson, P. W., Jr., Darling-Hammond, L., Rothman, R., & Shields, P. M. (2018). The tapestry of American public education: How we can create a system of schools worth choosing for all? Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/tapestry-american-public-education

article_title: The Tapestry of American Public Education: How Can We Create a System of Schools Worth Choosing for All?
citation: Cookson, P. W., Jr., Darling-Hammond, L., Rothman, R., & Shields, P. M. (2018). The tapestry of American public education: How we can create a system of schools worth choosing for all? Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/tapestry-american-public-education
title: The tapestry framework: choice as a means to an end within a system of schools worth choosing
description: The report organizes American school choice as a 'rich tapestry' of four public option types—open enrollment (intradistrict and interdistrict), magnet schools, charter schools, and schools based on distinct educational models—each described with its history, scale, and evidence. Its central framing is that "School choice is a means to an end and not an end itself": outcomes depend on how options are designed and managed, not on the existence of choice. The framework reframes the policy question from choice versus no choice to what kind of choice, to what ends, with the goal that every child chooses, and is chosen by, a school worth choosing.
requirements: Systems of choice must attend to quality and access for neighborhood schools as well as novel options, since parents' preferred choice is the neighborhood public school
constraints: The analysis addresses United States public school choice policy as of 2018 and draws on two prior Learning Policy Institute documents
target_learners: All students in American public education systems
target_learning_goals: Universal access to high-quality, publicly accountable, equitably available schools
examples: The report's four lessons: make all schools worthy of being chosen, ensure access for all, promote diversity and inclusion, and leave no school behind

article_title: A Coming Crisis in Teaching? Teacher Supply, Demand, and Shortages in the U.S.
citation: Sutcher, L., Darling-Hammond, L., & Carver-Thomas, D. (2016). A coming crisis in teaching? Teacher supply, demand, and shortages in the U.S. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/coming-crisis-teaching
title: Supply-and-demand framework defining teacher shortage as inability to staff vacancies at prevailing wages with qualified individuals
description: The report adopts "a theoretical framework of supply and demand that defines a teacher shortage as an inadequate quantity of qualified individuals willing to offer their services under prevailing wages and conditions." This departs from a narrow definition counting only new-teacher production against retirements, incorporating turnover, program changes, pupil-teacher ratios, and the attractiveness of teaching. The framework supports modeling projections of hires demanded and supply available, and yields clearer policy implications because shortages can be addressed on both the supply and demand sides.
requirements: Data on new entrants, re-entrants, projected hires, and attrition rates to model supply and demand
constraints: Shortage estimates depend on modeling assumptions about entrant rates and re-entry rates, producing upper- and lower-bound supply estimates
target_learners: U.S. K-12 public school students
target_learning_goals: Access to fully qualified teachers across all fields and school settings
examples: The report applies the framework using Schools and Staffing Survey, Teacher Follow-Up Survey, Baccalaureate and Beyond, and Title II data to project shortages by field, state, and school type

article_title: Building an Early Learning System That Works: Next Steps for California
citation: Melnick, H., Meloy, B., Gardner, M., Wechsler, M., & Maier, A. (2018). Building an early learning system that works: Next steps for California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/early-learning-ca
title: Promising county-level coordination practices: centralized eligibility lists, streamlined multi-agency collaboration, and pooled QRIS resources
description: Across its county case studies, the report identifies a recurring pattern of local practices that partially offset state-level fragmentation. San Mateo and San Luis Obispo counties "coordinate resources and have streamlined processes for families and providers"; San Francisco and Sacramento counties "maintain centralized waiting lists for ECE programs to efficiently link eligible families with available slots"; and seven Northern California counties "have pooled resources to develop a more comprehensive QRIS and offer stronger incentives and training than any county could offer on its own." These practices emerge where local agencies fund coordination themselves despite lacking state support.
requirements: Local funding sources to sustain coordination activities the state no longer funds, such as centralized eligibility lists
constraints: State and federal administrative structures still create the underlying tangle; local administrators "struggle to undo the administrative tangle created by the state and federal governments"
target_learners: Families and children birth to age 5 navigating county ECE systems in California
target_learning_goals: Access to subsidized early care and education and connection to programs matching family needs
examples: Sacramento's Child Action Inc. maintains a voluntary countywide centralized eligibility list using its own assessment process
San Francisco is piloting Child Care Connections, a centralized list designed to match slots with family preferences
Seven Northern California counties pool resources for a shared, more comprehensive QRIS

article_title: Understanding California's Early Care and Education System
citation: Melnick, H., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., & Wechsler, M. (2017). Understanding California's early care and education system. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/ca-ece-report
title: California's ECE system as a patchwork of uncoordinated programs administered by many federal, state, and local agencies
description: The report characterizes California's ECE system as "a patchwork of programs with distinct purposes and designs", built incrementally over more than half a century and enrolling over half a million children each year. Programs span school readiness (state preschool, Head Start, transitional kindergarten), working-parent support (Alternative Payment vouchers, General Child Care and Development), home visiting, and special education. Most programs are accountable to multiple agencies at county, state, and federal levels, which "can create confusion and increase the burden of administrative and reporting requirements" for providers and families.
requirements: An administrative structure allowing policymakers to see the whole system, such as a single agency or formal interagency team, to enable informed policy and funding decisions
constraints: Local ECE initiatives, which represent meaningful investments in some areas, remain largely outside the scope of the report
target_learners: Children birth to age 5 in California, particularly those living in or near poverty
target_learning_goals: School readiness and development of language, literacy, mathematics, executive functioning, and social-emotional competencies
examples: Figure 1 maps California's ECE programs by eligibility, ages, setting, and enrollment; Figure 2 depicts the many agencies controlling the programs

article_title: Effective Teacher Professional Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., Gardner, M. (2017). Effective Teacher Professional Development. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-prof-dev
title: Seven shared design elements characterize effective teacher professional development
description: The report's central framework: after coding 35 rigorous studies, the authors identify seven widely shared features of effective PD — content focus, active learning, collaboration, models and modeling, coaching and expert support, feedback and reflection, and sustained duration. They state that "effective professional learning incorporates most or all of these elements." The framework confirms and expands Desimone's earlier five-part consensus, adding specificity about active and collaborative practices.
requirements: PD models must incorporate most or all of the seven elements to be considered effective as defined by the report
constraints: Because studies typically examine comprehensive models incorporating many elements, the paper does not draw conclusions about the efficacy of individual program components
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: improving instructional practice
improving student learning outcomes
examples: The Reading Recovery program is described as an example possessing all seven elements and generating positive student gains

article_title: Community Schools as an Effective School Improvement Strategy: A Review of the Evidence
citation: Maier, A., Daniel, J., Oakes, J., & Lam, L. (2017). Community schools as an effective school improvement strategy: A review of the evidence. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/community-schools-effective-school-improvement-report
title: The four-pillar framework of community schools
description: The report organizes the community schools approach around four common features, or pillars: integrated student supports, expanded learning time and opportunities, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership and practice. The review states that although community schools vary by local context, four features—or pillars—appear in most community schools and support the conditions for teaching and learning found in high-quality schools. The framework structures the report's evidence review: each pillar is reviewed in its own chapter, and the pillars are mapped onto characteristics of high-quality schools (Table 3, Figure 1) and onto addressing out-of-school barriers to learning.
requirements: A comprehensive approach bringing all pillars together requires changes to existing structures, practices, and partnerships at school sites
constraints: Community schools vary in the programs they offer and the ways they operate, depending on their local context; successful community schools do not all look alike

children and adults served by community schools
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
attendance and engagement
social-emotional and physical well-being
closing opportunity and achievement gaps
examples: The report's Table 3 maps the four pillars onto characteristics of high-quality schools, and Figure 1 illustrates what the four pillars look like in action
