article_title: Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators
citation: Podolsky, A., Kini, T., Bishop, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/solving-teacher-shortage
title: Five-factor framework of teacher recruitment and retention
description: The report organizes the research on teacher shortages around five major factors that shape teachers' career decisions: "Salaries and other compensation", "Preparation and costs to entry", "Hiring and personnel management", "Induction and support for new teachers", and "Working conditions". Each factor is treated in its own section, with attention to how it operates in hard-to-staff schools. The authors stress the factors are interrelated and require a comprehensive policy response rather than isolated interventions.
requirements: Policymakers should implement mutually reinforcing policies across the five factors rather than any single policy in isolation
constraints: The authors note the factors are interrelated and the report treats them separately only for analysis
target_learners: policymakers and school and district leaders responsible for staffing classrooms with effective teachers
target_learning_goals: recruiting and retaining an effective, stable teaching workforce, especially in high-need schools
key_sources: Podolsky, A., Kini, T., Bishop, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/solving-teacher-shortage

article_title: Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators
citation: Podolsky, A., Kini, T., Bishop, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/solving-teacher-shortage
title: Improve working conditions—leadership, collaboration, and resources—because they define learning conditions and drive retention
description: The report argues that "Teaching conditions—which also define learning conditions for students—are a strong predictor of teachers' decisions about where to teach and whether to stay." It recommends investing in high-quality principals who include teachers in decision-making, surveying teachers about the teaching and learning environment (e.g., the TELL survey), and redesigning schedules and resources to enable sustained teacher collaboration, which improves efficacy and retention.
requirements: Sustained collaboration requires changes in scheduling and resource allocation so teachers have time for productive collaboration
constraints: The report cautions that one policy in isolation will do little; working-condition improvements should be part of a mutually reinforcing policy set
target_learners: teachers in high-need schools and the principals and district leaders who shape their working environments
target_learning_goals: improving teacher retention and the quality of teaching and learning conditions in schools
examples: The TELL survey asks about school culture, principal leadership, and collegial relationships that predict job satisfaction and career plans
Effective principal preparation programs include problem-based learning, field-based internships, cohort groups, and district collaboration
key_sources: Podolsky, A., Kini, T., Bishop, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). Solving the Teacher Shortage: How to Attract and Retain Excellent Educators. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/solving-teacher-shortage

article_title: Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity through the Every Student Succeeds Act
citation: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa
title: Four Pillars of Opportunity framework for leveraging ESSA toward equity
description: The report organizes its analysis of ESSA around four pillars of opportunity: "(1) access to learning opportunities focused on higher-order thinking skills; (2) multiple measures of equity; (3) resource equity; and (4) evidence-based interventions." The framework is presented as a bridge from an inequitable "factory model" of schooling relying on rote thinking and memorization toward a 21st-century model offering deeper learning. Each pillar is treated in a dedicated section with policy provisions and state and district examples.
requirements: Thoughtful regulation and implementation of ESSA provisions by federal, state, district, and school actors
constraints: The report notes concerns that ESSA's emphasis on state control of accountability systems may lead states to overlook the needs of low-performing schools
target_learners: students of color
low-income students
English learners
students with disabilities
students who are homeless or in foster care
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking skills
deeper learning
equitable access to college- and career-ready curriculum
examples: Figure 1 depicts the four pillars bridging the factory model to a 21st-century model of education
key_sources: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa

article_title: Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity through the Every Student Succeeds Act
citation: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa
title: San Francisco International High School as a case of the four pillars serving new immigrant English learners
description: San Francisco International High School (SFIHS), part of the Internationals Network for Public Schools, serves new immigrant English learners; in 2015, "82% of students were classified as newcomers, and 35% were classified as non-readers in their native languages." The school requires an "activity-based curriculum" with projects, internships, and college-preparatory coursework for all students from day one, and evaluates students through portfolios showcased and defended twice per year. The report presents it as the four pillars operating at school, district, and state levels.
requirements: Portfolio assessment requiring students to write about, revise, and present their learning before teachers, staff, peers, and community members
constraints: The report presents this as a single school case rather than an experimental evaluation
target_learners: new immigrant English learners
newcomers with interrupted formal education
low-income students
target_learning_goals: college readiness
applied knowledge and skills
synthesis and evaluation of learning
examples: More than three-quarters of students in each of the school's first two graduating classes met the rigorous requirements for admissions to California's state university system, and 83% of 2013-14 graduates were enrolled in college in fall 2014
key_sources: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa

article_title: Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity through the Every Student Succeeds Act
citation: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa
title: CORE districts' multiple-measures accountability system spanning academic and social-emotional domains
description: The California Office to Reform Education (CORE) districts, a network of 10 districts that secured an ESEA flexibility waiver in 2013, use a multiple measures accountability system with two domains: Academic Achievement, including growth and achievement on state English Language Arts and math tests, graduation rates, and an 8th grade on-track-to-graduate rate; and Social/Emotional and School Culture and Climate, including "measures of social-emotional skills; suspension/expulsion rates; chronic absenteeism; culture/climate surveys from students, staff, and parents; and English learner redesignation rates." The indicators are organized into a dashboard on a school report card used to evaluate progress and plan improvements.
requirements: Indicators must be valid, reliable, comparable, and disaggregated by subgroups
constraints: The report states districts have found that attending to these indicators has improved outcomes, but presents no experimental evaluation of the system
target_learners: all students in the CORE districts
English learners
students at risk of disengaging from school
target_learning_goals: academic achievement and growth
social-emotional skills
positive school climate
examples: Figure 2 depicts the CORE district accountability system with academic and social-emotional/culture-climate domains aimed at elimination of disparity and disproportionality

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Four models for integrating performance assessment into state systems
description: The paper organizes state performance assessment options into four models: "Performance items or tasks as part of traditional 'sit-down' tests", curriculum-embedded tasks implemented during the school year, "Portfolios or collections of evidence that aggregate multiple tasks", and comprehensive assessment systems combining all of these, "each serving distinctive complementary purposes". The models "can also be combined in various ways" and all "have been used successfully at scale in states and nations around the world". The paper describes design, implementation, and scoring for each.
requirements: States must manage task selection and scoring to assure validity, reliability, and comparability
constraints: Under ESSA, states must assess students annually in ELA and math in grades 3-8 and once in high school, and at least once in each grade span in science
target_learners: K-12 students in state assessment systems
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking skills and understanding
application of knowledge to complex problems
examples: New York Regents tests, GCSE through-course assessments, New Hampshire's comprehensive system, and the Performance Assessment Resource Bank
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Assessment continuum from standardized tests to student-designed investigations
description: The paper presents assessment strategies as a continuum (Figure 2) running from "Standardized, multiple-choice tests of routine skills" through standardized tests with performance tasks, systems of performance items, multi-week performance tasks, to "Longer, deeper investigations (2-3 months) & exhibitions, including graduation portfolios". Along the continuum, "tasks become more complex, measuring progressively larger and more integrated sets of knowledge and skill". The student's role shifts "from passively receiving and responding to external questions" to "taking increasing initiative for finding and making sense of information".
requirements: Tasks are scored based upon a set of pre-determined criteria, usually codified in a rubric; when comparability is needed, scorers are trained and often moderated
constraints: The paper notes multiple-choice and close-ended items "cannot measure higher level thinking skills or the ability to apply them"
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: deeper learning skills including communication, meta-cognitive and learning-to-learn skills, and resilience
examples: MARS and BAM tasks, SCALE/CCSSO Performance Assessment Resource Bank tasks, NY Performance Standards Consortium portfolios, IB and AP assessments
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Curriculum-embedded performance tasks contributing a substantial share of summative scores
description: Curriculum-embedded performance tasks are conducted during the school year, extend over days or weeks, and are scored with common rubrics; several can be combined into a summative score or paired with an end-of-year test. Internationally, such tasks "typically comprise 30-60 percent of the total score". In the GCSE English exam, through-course assessments "count for 60 percent of the total score; the remainder is from a written exam". The paper notes students and teachers do not experience these tasks as formal tests because they are embedded in instruction.
requirements: States or districts need to put aside professional development time for scoring the tasks; moderation or auditing systems assure comparability of teacher scoring
constraints: The paper notes these tasks should not be thought of as part of testing time but as part of teaching and learning time
target_learners: secondary students in state and national examination systems
target_learning_goals: research, inquiry, writing, and presentation of findings in content areas
examples: GCSE English classroom assessments in reading, imaginative writing, and speaking and listening; the GCSE ICT controlled assessment; Connecticut's acid rain science task; Victoria, Australia practical tasks
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Performance Assessment Resource Bank of reviewed curriculum-embedded tasks
description: The Performance Assessment Resource Bank is a nationwide bank of curriculum-embedded performance tasks "developed by the Council for Chief State School Officers (CCSSO) in collaboration with the Stanford Center for Assessment, Learning, and Equity (SCALE) and the Stanford Center for Opportunity Policy in Education (SCOPE)". Tasks are "reviewed for quality by a team of assessment experts and, frequently, piloted and revised", and are presented with their embedded units, rubrics, and scored samples of student work. The bank includes "tools and protocols for training educators to develop, review, revise, and score tasks with consistency".
requirements: Tasks are reviewed and validated before sharing; educators use the bank's tools and protocols for training in task development and scoring
target_learners: K-12 students whose teachers draw on the bank's tasks
target_learning_goals: application of concepts to real-world contexts, data collection and analysis, and communication of findings
examples: The Rising Cost of a College Education mathematics task, in which students collect and analyze data, develop equations and graphs, and write an article; New Hampshire, Colorado, and Kentucky are drawing on the bank while developing their own task banks
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Involve practicing teachers as scorers of performance tasks to strengthen instruction
description: The paper recommends that practicing teachers serve as primary scorers of performance tasks in statewide assessments, as California, New Hampshire, and New York have required. It states that "Evidence shows that this involvement strengthens teachers' understanding of the standards and the assessments and informs classroom instruction", and that "Teachers learn significantly and can improve their practice from the scoring process". Allocating professional development days for scoring or including teacher scoring in test administration contracts can enhance teacher learning and reduce costs.
requirements: Reliable scoring requires training, moderation processes, and auditing; strong task design and careful rater training
constraints: Human scoring adds modest costs; the paper notes SBAC and PARCC developed systems for reliably scoring tasks for a few dollars per item per student
target_learners: K-12 students in states using performance tasks, and their teachers
target_learning_goals: teacher understanding of standards, curriculum, and assessment; classroom instruction aligned to higher-order skills
examples: New York teachers score extended writing tasks on professional development days set aside at the end of the school year, with a proportion of tests audited annually by the state education agency
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Taking Deeper Learning to Scale
citation: Noguera, P. (2017). Taking deeper learning to scale. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/deeper-learning-to-scale
title: Deeper learning as a reform framework of higher-order competencies
description: The report frames deeper learning as a set of learning experiences and capacities that schools should make available to all students, particularly the disadvantaged. It defines deeper learning as "the utilization of higher order thinking capacities and learning experiences that include critical thinking, problem solving, independent research, evaluation, comparative analysis, and the opportunity to acquire the skills needed for college and career readiness." It links this to Common Core goals of flexible content understanding, collaboration, effective communication, and learning how to learn, and uses the framework to analyze three school-improvement cases.
requirements: Schools must create fewer, higher and deeper curriculum goals and build teacher and school capacity rather than relying on accountability pressure alone
constraints: The report states these learning goals are currently not available in many schools, particularly to the most disadvantaged students
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly economically disadvantaged and historically underperforming students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
problem solving
collaboration
communication
college and career readiness
examples: Brockton High School adopted deeper learning as its high-leverage improvement strategy through a schoolwide literacy program
key_sources: Noguera, P. (2017). Taking deeper learning to scale. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/deeper-learning-to-scale

article_title: Taking Deeper Learning to Scale
citation: Noguera, P. (2017). Taking deeper learning to scale. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/deeper-learning-to-scale
title: Make school improvement teacher-led rather than administration-driven
description: The report argues that school-improvement initiatives should be led by teachers rather than imposed top-down by administrations. In Brockton, a Restructuring Committee of veteran teachers framed the work, designed the literacy goals, and won over colleagues; the report states "the literacy initiative was teacher led, and this was undoubtedly a key factor responsible for the success that was achieved." It contrasts this with districts that expect compliance with central-office orders rather than building genuine buy-in.
requirements: Willingness of site and district leadership to accept a gradual approach rather than demand immediate widespread adoption
constraints: Initially the teachers' union objected and supported teachers who refused to participate; the strategy relied on working with the willing
target_learners: high school students in large urban schools
target_learning_goals: literacy across content areas
higher order thinking
examples: Teachers calling themselves the Restructuring Committee began by posting MCAS scores with the question: Is this the best we can be?
key_sources: Noguera, P. (2017). Taking deeper learning to scale. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/deeper-learning-to-scale

article_title: Supporting Principals' Learning: Key Features of Effective Programs
citation: Sutcher, L., Podolsky, A., & Espinoza, D. (2017). Supporting principals' learning: Key features of effective programs. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/supporting-principals-learning
title: Four building blocks of high-quality principal preparation and professional development programs
description: The report proposes a framework of four building blocks for effective principal preparation and professional development: organizational partnerships between programs and districts, program structures such as cohorts and networks, meaningful and authentic learning opportunities, and learning content focused on instruction, collegial organizations, and data use. The authors state that "Research points to several key building blocks of such programs," derived from a review of studies connecting program components to improved school outcomes such as student learning, principal and teacher retention, and school climate.
requirements: Programs must be built on strong working relationships between the district and the preparation or training program, which the report says provide "a foundation for the other features of effective programs"
constraints: The framework summarizes features associated with positive outcomes in studies published within the past two decades, not experimentally isolated causal components
target_learners: aspiring principals
practicing school principals
target_learning_goals: instructional leadership
school improvement leadership
creating collegial school organizations
examples: Figure 1 depicts the building blocks as partnerships, cohorts and networks for collegial learning, applied learning, and a focus on instruction, organizations, and using data for change
key_sources: Sutcher, L., Podolsky, A., & Espinoza, D. (2017). Supporting principals' learning: Key features of effective programs. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/supporting-principals-learning

article_title: Evaluation of the Comprehensive School Reform Program Implementation and Outcomes. Fifth-Year Report
citation: Orland, M., Hoffman, A., & Vaughn, III, E. S. (2010). Evaluation of the Comprehensive School Reform Program Implementation and Outcomes: Fifth-Year Report. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/reports.html#title
title: NCLB eleven-component comprehensive school reform framework
description: The NCLB legislation defines comprehensive school reform as a coordinated approach requiring that "school reform should be comprehensive in nature, strengthening all aspects of school operations—curriculum, instruction, professional development, parental involvement and school organization." The framework specifies 11 components assumed to work together, including proven methods based on scientific research, comprehensive design, professional development, measurable goals, staff support, parent and community involvement, external assistance, evaluation, coordination of resources, and use of scientifically based research models with evidence of effectiveness in multiple settings.
requirements: Schools must implement all 11 components together for reform to be comprehensive as legislatively defined
constraints: The framework was legislatively specified under NCLB Title I, Part F, Section 1606
target_learners: K-12 public school students in low-performing Title I schools
target_learning_goals: Meeting state performance standards in mathematics and reading
examples: The ECSRIO study surveyed 436 CSR and 382 non-CSR schools to measure implementation of these 11 components
key_sources: Orland, M., Hoffman, A., & Vaughn, III, E. S. (2010). Evaluation of the Comprehensive School Reform Program Implementation and Outcomes: Fifth-Year Report. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/reports.html#title

article_title: Elementary School Principals' Professional Learning: Current Status and Future Needs
citation: Levin, S., Leung, M., Edgerton, A. K., & Scott, C. (2020). Elementary school principals’ professional learning: Current status and future needs. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/professional-learning-principals
title: Components of High-Quality Principal Professional Learning framework
description: The report proposes a conceptual framework (Figure 1) in which high-quality principal professional learning has two components: content and delivery. The content component “addresses” managing change, creating collegial environments, and improving instruction, the latter including whole child education and equitable opportunities. The delivery component “includes” applied learning, mentors or coaches, and network building. The framework derives from a 2017 LPI literature review identifying attributes of professional learning related to improved school outcomes, and it structures both the survey design and the report's policy recommendations.
requirements: Professional learning must pair relevant content topics with authentic, job-embedded delivery formats such as applied learning, mentoring or coaching, and PLCs
constraints: The report notes the literature on the impact of professional learning for principals is minimal, especially compared with the literature on teachers
target_learners: Elementary school principals
Early-career and experienced school leaders
target_learning_goals: School leadership capacity
Leading schoolwide instructional improvement
Leading equitable schools and whole child education
examples: The NAESP-LPI survey measured principals' access to content topics and participation in applied learning, mentoring/coaching, and PLCs, mirroring the framework's two components
key_sources: Levin, S., Leung, M., Edgerton, A. K., & Scott, C. (2020). Elementary school principals’ professional learning: Current status and future needs. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/professional-learning-principals

article_title: Restarting and Reinventing School: Learning in the Time of COVID and Beyond
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Schachner, A., & Edgerton, A. K. (with Badrinarayan, A., Cardichon, J., Cookson, P. W., Jr., Griffith, M., Klevan, S., Maier, A., Martinez, M., Melnick, H., Truong, N., Wojcikiewicz, S.). (2020). Restarting and reinventing school: Learning in the time of COVID and beyond. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/restarting-reinventing-school-covid
title: A ten-priority framework for restarting and reinventing school around equity, authentic learning, and stronger relationships
description: The report presents an overarching framework organizing research, state and local examples, and policy recommendations into ten priorities: closing the digital divide, strengthening distance and blended learning, assessing student needs, supporting SEL, redesigning for relationships, authentic culturally responsive learning, expanded learning time, community schools, educator preparation, and equitable funding. It states that the framework 'focuses on how policymakers as well as educators can support equitable, effective teaching and learning regardless of the medium through which that takes place.' The priorities are intended both for the 2020-21 restart and as a long-term vision for addressing educational quality and inequity.
requirements: Universal broadband and device access is described as 'the absolute minimum for ensuring that every child can continue learning'
constraints: The report does not replicate health and safety reopening guidance, focusing instead on equitable teaching and learning regardless of medium
target_learners: All k-12 students in the United States
target_learning_goals: Equitable, effective teaching and learning across in-person, online, and hybrid media
examples: Figure 1 diagrams the ten priorities as a framework for restarting and reinventing school

article_title: Restarting and Reinventing School: Learning in the Time of COVID and Beyond
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Schachner, A., & Edgerton, A. K. (with Badrinarayan, A., Cardichon, J., Cookson, P. title: Community schools built on four evidence-based pillars coordinate supports for children and families
description: The report describes community schools as a vehicle for coordinating services for children and families, grounded in 'four evidence-based pillars: integrated student supports, expanded and enriched learning time, active family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership practices.' Local policies, regional technical assistance agencies, blended funding streams, and Children's Cabinets are recommended to launch and sustain such initiatives at scale. The report states community schools 'have demonstrated their capacity to meet students’ needs during the pandemic.'
requirements: Reliable blended and braided federal, state, and local funding streams to provide integrated health, mental health, and social services alongside instruction
constraints: Regional technical assistance is described as needed to coordinate state and county services from multiple agencies and support strategic planning

target_learning_goals: Coordinated academic, health, mental health, and social supports enabling learning
examples: Children's Cabinets at federal, state, and county levels are recommended to coordinate services across agencies

article_title: Community Schools the New Mexico Way
citation: Oakes, J., & Espinoza, D. (2020). Community schools the New Mexico way. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/improving-education-new-mexico-way
title: Community schools framework: four pillars for a whole-child, whole-school, whole-community approach
description: The report describes community schools as an approach in which schools partner with local communities to provide high-quality teaching plus additional resources and supports that mitigate barriers poverty erects. It is explicitly "an approach to schooling based on evidence-based principles, rather than a 'program'" and is built on "four pillars—integrated health and social supports, expanded learning time and opportunities, strong family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership and practice" that meet community needs and use community assets. Together the pillars provide more than wraparound services, using a whole child, whole school, whole community redesign of schools.
requirements: A foundation of powerful teaching of challenging academic content and support for students' mastery of 21st-century competencies
constraints: The report notes New Mexico's community schools vary considerably in the extent and quality of their implementation and, as a consequence, in their achievements
target_learners: students in high-poverty schools
students from low-income families
English learners
Native American students
students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: improved attendance, behavior, and academic achievement
more positive school climate
closing opportunity and achievement gaps
key_sources: Oakes, J., & Espinoza, D. (2020). Community schools the New Mexico way. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/improving-education-new-mexico-way

article_title: Improving Education the New Mexico Way: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Oakes, J., Espinoza, D., Darling-Hammond, L., Gonzales, C., DePaoli, J., Kini, T., Hoachlander, G., Burns, D., Griffith, M., & Leung, M. (2020). Improving education the New Mexico way: An evidence-based approach. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/improving-education-new-mexico-way
title: Five fundamental elements of a high-quality education system
description: The report organizes its recommendations around a framework of five system elements that states and nations that have improved education have strengthened: "Meaningful learning goals, supported by Knowledgeable and skillful educators, Integrated student supports, and High-quality early learning opportunities, all made possible with Adequate and equitably distributed school funding." The report argues policy changes in all five are possible in New Mexico and could bring significant improvement, and that inadequacies in each area were cited by the Martinez/Yazzie court.
requirements: Policy changes across all five elements, plus a thoughtful accountability system, since the report states the five elements alone are not enough to establish and sustain a high-quality education system
constraints: Framed for state-level system change in New Mexico's context of diversity, local control, and high poverty
target_learners: All New Mexico public school students, particularly at-risk students defined by the Martinez/Yazzie case
target_learning_goals: Meaningful 21st century learning across academic, cultural-linguistic, social-emotional, and college-and-career domains

title: Four domains central to meaningful learning goals
description: The report defines meaningful 21st century learning goals through four domains: "Both research and local knowledge suggest four specific domains that are central to meaningful learning" — high-level cognitive skills in core academic disciplines; culturally and linguistically responsive curriculum and instruction; social and emotional learning developing self-regulation, collaboration, problem-solving, conflict resolution, perseverance, and resilience; and pathways integrating college and career preparation. title: Community schools strategy with four key pillars
description: The report describes the community schools approach as "an evidence-based approach for increasing the school success of students living in communities of poverty that should become the norm in New Mexico's high-poverty schools." Although community schools vary to reflect local conditions, "they are built with four key pillars: integrated supports, expanded learning time and opportunities, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership." The report recommends making the strategy the norm in schools where at least 80% of students come from low-income families, and notes Albuquerque, Las Cruces, and Santa Fe have created more than three dozen community schools.

title: Use supportive accountability that builds state and local capacity rather than sanctions
description: The report recommends an accountability system that, beyond monitoring and oversight, "includes comprehensive data and processes that New Mexico's districts and schools can use regularly to inform and support educator learning, high-quality implementation, and continuous improvement." Such accountability provides "the constructive balance between state leadership and local control that New Mexico needs," including fiscal auditing followed by constructive assistance, training and technical assistance in data use, and authentic collaboration with tribal governments in Native-serving districts.

description: The report presents Gateway's assessment approach as a design principle: "Assessment at Gateway is designed to support learning rather than competition or labeling." title: Three-component framework for high-quality, equitable kindergarten entry assessments: content, administration, and validity
description: The report organizes research and policy recommendations on early childhood assessment into three components. A high-quality KEA should 'have content that effectively measures essential developmental domains in ways that are developmentally appropriate and culturally relevant and can be connected to a system of ongoing formative assessment across p–3,' have administration procedures that are practical and fair for all young children, and yield results that are accurate for all children assessed. The framework is summarized in Table 1 as guiding considerations for choosing high-quality KEAs and draws on recommendations from the National Research Council, CEELO, NIEER, NAEYC, CCSSO, and other bodies.

constraints: An assessment that measures only discrete reading or numeracy skills is not appropriate as a KEA
target_learners: children entering kindergarten
target_learning_goals: whole child development across social-emotional, cognitive, language and literacy, mathematical and scientific reasoning, and physical domains

description: Georgia's Readiness Check, used since 2016, is the first part of the GKIDS assessment system, 'a yearlong suite of kindergarten assessments connected to state content standards that provides teachers with ongoing information needed to guide instruction.' It covers social and emotional learning, English language arts, and mathematics while remaining relatively brief: 10 of 20 items are direct assessment performance tasks such as naming letters and counting aloud, and 10 are observation-based. It aligns with the Work Sampling System used in Georgia's preschool program, and all new kindergarten teachers must complete initial professional development on the GKIDS system.

title: Illinois KIDS: a statewide observational KEA based on the DRDP-K with mandatory professional development
description: Illinois has used the Kindergarten Individual Development Survey statewide since 2017; the report calls it 'the most populous state in the United States to require a comprehensive KEA.' KIDS is based on the DRDP-K, and of three assessment versions only the shortest, the State Readiness Measures, is required, including 14 items measuring approaches to learning, social and emotional learning, language and literacy, and mathematics. Scores are based on teacher observation over multiple authentic activities in children's natural classroom settings. The state provides mandatory implementation workshops with substitutes, tailored coaching, and an annual summit, and publishes aggregated state-level KEA data annually.

constraints: Only the shortest version, the State Readiness Measures with 14 items, is required for Illinois districts

Georgia prominently labels its KEA a formative tool, Illinois proactively briefs reporters, Colorado offers districts a menu of assessments, and Illinois permits a longer optional version. States and districts also maintain at least one staff position responsible for KEA oversight, professional development, data reporting, and resources, and implementation is supported by a gradual phase-in, adequate funding, and ongoing improvement processes.

article_title: Design Principles for Schools: Putting the Science of Learning and Development into Action
citation: Learning Policy Institute & Turnaround for Children. (2021). Design principles for schools: Putting the science of learning and development into action. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Guiding Principles for Equitable Whole Child Design framework
description: The report presents an organizing framework, the Guiding Principles for Equitable Whole Child Design, comprising five elements: positive developmental relationships, environments filled with safety and belonging, rich learning experiences and knowledge development, development of skills habits and mindsets, and integrated support systems. It states that "The organizing framework to guide transformation of learning settings for children and adolescents is reflected in the five elements shown in Figure 1.1". Each element is linked to research from developmental and learning science and to structures and practices for changing conditions, adult practice, and student learning. The framework aims at healthy development, learning, and thriving that is transformative, culturally affirming, empowering, and personalized.
requirements: Implementation across classroom, school, district, and larger macrosystem levels, joined together to produce an intentionally integrated developmental enterprise
constraints: The report notes the elements "have not yet been widely used to develop and create learning settings, nor have they been engineered in fully integrated ways"
target_learners: k-12 students

deep understanding and application of content
self-awareness and positive identity
healthy life choices
empathetic and ethical contribution to community

title: Organize schools through structures and practices that build positive developmental relationships
description: The report recommends that schools be deliberately organized so educators can form continuous, secure relationships with students, collaborate with colleagues and families, and build community. It states that "Schools can be organized to foster positive developmental relationships through structures and practices that allow for effective caring and the building of community". Named structures include small learning communities, advisory systems, looping, home visits, staff collaboration time, and shared decision-making; practices include trust-building behaviors and pedagogies that develop deep knowledge of students and their cultural contexts.

motivation and self-efficacy
sense of being known and valued at school

citation: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity. (2021). Spencer Foundation & Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/summer-learning-creating-equity
title: Engage students' and families' knowledge and experiences in disciplinary learning rather than treating home lives as deficits
description: This principle holds that human learning is ecological and cultural, and that academic learning expands when it connects to learners' prior knowledge, experiences, and identities. The report warns that deficit views of students of color, low-income families, and multilingual learners drive remediation-oriented pedagogy, and urges that "children actively construct knowledge based on their experiences, relationships, and social contexts." Teachers build on this by inviting family and community expertise into disciplinary study, as in the Algebra Project's use of urban transit experiences for mathematics.
requirements: Educators must seek to understand learners' experiences and provide multiple opportunities to connect knowledge-building to personally relevant topics and lived experiences
constraints: The report notes learning environments all too often view students and families through a deficit lens, which must be actively countered
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly students of color, low-income families, and multilingual learners
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary learning in literacy, mathematics, and science connected to students' lived experiences
examples: In science classrooms studying plant growth, students measure plant height and soil moisture and interview family members who garden about how they keep plants healthy

citation: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity. (2021). Spencer Foundation & Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/summer-learning-creating-equity
title: Six Design Principles for Summer Learning and Beyond framework
description: The report's organizing framework is a set of six interrelated design principles, or stances toward learners and learning: center relationships; create a culture of affirmation and belonging; build from students' interests and take a whole child approach; engage students' and families' knowledge in disciplinary learning; provide creative, inquiry-based forms of learning; and address educator needs and learning. The report states these are "essential for creating intellectually rigorous and equitable learning settings" and provide "a holistic framework for designing goals, practices, and activities for summer learning and beyond." The principles are grounded in a view of learning as cognitive, physical, emotional, social, and cultural at once, and are meant to be used together.

constraints: The framework was developed for post-pandemic summer learning design and beyond, in response to pandemic and racialized trauma contexts

target_learning_goals: Intellectually rigorous and equitable learning; social-emotional development; academic engagement
examples: The Cajon Valley Union School District applies the principles through advisory spaces, the Launchpad career and interest center, TEDxKids@ElCajon, co-design sessions with families, and Camp Cajon summer programming

These principles ground the report's account of what educators must know.

constraints: The report presents these as syntheses of scientific advances linked to educational research, not as new empirical findings of this report

title: Guiding principles of equitable whole child design: five environmental features schools must provide
description: The report identifies five features of environments, structures, and practices attuned to students' learning and developmental needs: "positive developmental relationships," "environments filled with safety and belonging," "rich learning experiences that support deep knowledge development," development of social, emotional, and cognitive skills, habits, and mindsets, and "integrated support systems." Figure 1 presents these as the Guiding Principles of Equitable Whole Child Design, framed as transformative, culturally affirming, empowering, and personalized, sourced to the Learning Policy Institute and Turnaround for Children design principles.
requirements: School staff and leaders need a common knowledge base about child development across all domains to enact these features
constraints: The report notes these features are not easily achieved in factory-model school designs originating more than a century ago
target_learners: all K-12 students
target_learning_goals: healthy development, learning, and thriving through supportive school environments
examples: The School Development Program teaches all members of the school community to use principles of child and adolescent development to create a positive developmental environment

article_title: Educator Learning to Enact the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776
title: NAE framework for teacher education: three knowledge areas joined with skills and dispositions to form adaptive expertise
description: Drawing on the National Academy of Education report Preparing Teachers for a Changing World, the report describes three general areas of knowledge beginning teachers must acquire: knowledge of learners and how they learn and develop within social contexts, understanding of subject matter and curriculum in light of the social purposes of education, and understanding of teaching in light of content and learners as informed by assessment. These areas "must be joined with skills of curriculum design and instruction, inquiry, reflection, and diagnosis to produce the adaptive expertise that enables teachers to make the connections between children and content that are necessary for learning," further joined to dispositions supporting empathy, cultural competence, and equity.
requirements: Development of a vision for teaching relies on the fusion between coursework and clinical work—theory and practice
constraints: How People Learn II does not change this central conception but emphasizes sociocultural and motivational influences on learning more clearly
target_learners: teacher candidates in preservice preparation
target_learning_goals: adaptive expertise in connecting children and content for deep learning

article_title: Educator Learning to Enact the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776
title: Five key practices for educator preparation: grounding in human development, theory-practice integration, authentic practice with feedback, inquiry, and professional learning communities
description: The report enumerates key practices for educator preparation that "research has shown make a strong difference in the capacities of educators": anchoring candidate learning in the study of human development and learning; integrating theory and practice through clinical experiences and coursework; "providing opportunities for authentic practice, assessment, feedback, and reflection to accelerate learning"; engaging in inquiry and analysis strategies that guide reflection and application; and collaborating in professional learning communities offering mutual support and modeling.
requirements: These practices operate within program designs built on pedagogical alignment and clinical experiences tightly linked to coursework
constraints: The report characterizes the supporting research collectively without reporting specific effect sizes in the text provided

target_learning_goals: mastery of developmentally grounded teaching practices and adaptive expertise

article_title: Teacher Shortages during the Pandemic: How California Districts Are Responding
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., Burns, D., Leung, M., & Ondrasek, N. (2022). Teacher shortages during the pandemic: How California districts are responding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/899.809
title: District strategy pattern: compensation increases, high-retention pathways, recruitment capacity, and added student-support staff
description: The report identifies a four-part pattern of district responses to shortages: "increasing teacher compensation, improving recruitment and hiring capacity, developing high-retention pathways into teaching within the district, and adding new staff to improve teaching and learning conditions." Districts used state and federal recovery funds for wage increases, stipends, and bonuses (especially for hard-to-fill positions and substitutes), Grow Your Own initiatives and teacher residencies, streamlined hiring such as open contracts and 24-hour offer turnaround, and new counselor, psychologist, social worker, and instructional coach positions intended to ease teacher workloads and support retention.
requirements: State or federal recovery funding to finance compensation increases, pathway development, and additional staffing
constraints: The report notes a rural district offered a $15,000 signing bonus and $3,000 moving stipend for high school mathematics and music positions but had not received any applicants, showing limits of compensation alone for hard-to-staff rural locales
target_learners: K-12 students in California districts facing teacher shortages
target_learning_goals: Stable staffing with fully prepared teachers; smaller class sizes; learning recovery and social-emotional support
examples: Chula Vista USD raised substitute daily pay from $122 to $200 and long-term substitute pay from $132 to $283; one district offered contracts within 24 hours of interview
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., Burns, D., Leung, M., & Ondrasek, N. (2022). Teacher shortages during the pandemic: How California districts are responding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/899.809

article_title: Protecting Education as a Civil Right: Remedying Racial Discrimination and Ensuring a High-Quality Education
citation: Robinson, K. J. (2021). Protecting education as a civil right: Remedying racial discrimination and ensuring a high-quality education. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/407.455
title: A progressive, capacious framework of education as a civil right combining antidiscrimination protection and an affirmative right to high-quality education
description: The report defines a civil right to education in two complementary ways: protection from discrimination and an affirmative entitlement. It states that "Civil rights also include affirmative rights to a body of law that protects the capacity of individuals to participate in society and flourish," and that the report "embraces both definitions of civil rights to provide a comprehensive approach." The framework holds that remedying identity-based discrimination is necessary but insufficient: the nation must also make an affirmative commitment ensuring all children access to a high-quality education so they can participate in society and flourish.
requirements: Adoption by both federal and state governments of complementary legal and policy guardrails embracing the strengths of each level of government
constraints: The report focuses on racial discrimination and leaves examination of other bases for discrimination, such as religion, national origin, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, and disability, to others
target_learners: All U.S. public schoolchildren
target_learning_goals: Equal educational opportunity
Access to a high-quality education enabling participation in society and flourishing

article_title: Developing Effective Principals: What Kind of Learning Matters?
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Wechsler, M. E., Levin, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Tozer, S. (2022). Developing effective principals: What kind of learning matters? [Report]. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/641.201
title: Theory of Action for Principal Professional Learning
description: The report's guiding framework holds that professional learning opportunities, defined by content (what principals learn about, e.g., instructional support, school improvement, meeting diverse students' needs) and strategies (applied learning, internships, coaching and mentoring, cohorts and networks), shape principals' leadership knowledge, skills, and dispositions. These influence school climate, teacher practices and retention, and ultimately student opportunities and learning, all embedded in state, district, school, and community contexts and policies. The report states that "These aspects of professional learning influence leadership knowledge, skills, and dispositions—how principals lead, the school climates they establish, and their goals and actions." It also acknowledges principals bring prior knowledge, skills, and dispositions from lived and job experiences that interact with formal learning.
requirements: Learning opportunities must address both the content of learning and how principals learn, including structures (practicums, internships, coursework) and pedagogies supporting learning by doing
constraints: The framework acknowledges principals bring different knowledge, skills, and dispositions beyond formal training, and that formal learning interacts with prior experiences in widely varying ways

novice principals
experienced principals

school climate construction
management of change
focus on equity
development of people

article_title: Developing Effective Principals: What Kind of Learning Matters?
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Wechsler, M. E., Levin, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Tozer, S. (2022). Developing effective principals: What kind of learning matters? [Report]. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/641.201
title: Comprehensive principal preparation programs combine recruitment, coherent curriculum, applied learning, mentoring, and cohorts
description: The report defines "comprehensive principal preparation programs" as those incorporating features identified in Preparing Leaders for a Changing World: "close partnerships between districts and programs; proactive recruitment into the program; well-supported cohorts and/or networks for collegial learning; a coherent curriculum enacted through applied learning (e.g., internships longer than 20 weeks with a mentor, action research or inquiry projects, field-based projects); and a focus on leading instruction, developing the organization, developing people, and managing change." Studies of such programs examine principals' self-reports of preparation, teachers' views of leadership, and student outcomes.
requirements: District–program partnerships
proactive recruitment
cohort or network structures
applied learning including extended internships with mentors
curriculum focused on instruction, organization, people, and change
constraints: All studies meeting the review's criteria focused on programs incorporating all or many of these critical features, so findings may not generalize to programs lacking them

teacher leaders

organizational development
change management

article_title: Preschool Quality and Child Development: How Are Learning Gains Related to Program Ratings?
citation: Sussman, J., Melnick, H., Newton, E., Kriener-Althen, K., Draney, K., Mangione, P., & Gochyyev, P. (2022). Preschool quality and child development: How are learning gains related to program ratings? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/422.974
title: Quality Counts California (QCC) quality rating and improvement system
description: Quality Counts California is a quality rating and improvement system, a collaboration between First 5 California, the California Department of Education, and the California Department of Social Services. Early learning and care sites are rated on seven elements and assigned a final quality rating in a tiering system ranging from Tier 1 (lowest) to Tier 5 (highest). The seven elements are child observation; developmental and health screenings; lead teacher qualifications; teacher–child interactions; teacher–child ratios and group size; program environment rating scales; and director qualifications, with ratings assigned by trained assessors based on program documentation and classroom observations. Participation is voluntary; 28% of licensed early learning centers participated during the 2020–21 funding year.
requirements: Ratings are assigned by trained assessors based on program documentation and classroom observations
constraints: Participation in QCC is voluntary
target_learners: preschool children ages 4.5 to 5.5 in publicly funded early learning programs
target_learning_goals: early learning and development across social-emotional, language and literacy, and mathematics domains
examples: The study analyzed QCC ratings alongside DRDP scores for approximately 70,000 children in 1,700 rated programs

title: Desired Results Developmental Profile (DRDP) teacher-administered developmental assessment
description: The DRDP is a developmental assessment administered by children's classroom teachers, completed based on teacher and family observations in five essential readiness domains: social and emotional development, language and literacy development, mathematics, approaches to learning–self-regulation, and physical development. It is completed in fall and spring, providing a measure of children's learning and development over the preschool year. The article reports the assessment is valid for formative and summative assessment with diverse groups of children, including multilingual learners, children with disabilities, and children from different racial/ethnic groups.

mathematics

article_title: Building School Communities for Students Living in Deep Poverty
citation: Cookson, P. W., Jr., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2022). Building school communities for students living in deep poverty. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/121.698
title: Deep poverty–responsive schooling framework: funding adequacy, community schools, and whole child culture
description: The report extends Richard Milner and colleagues' "poverty-responsive" framework to deep poverty, organizing school reform around three strategies: "1. Begin with funding adequacy and equity. 2. Develop community schools and partnerships. 3. Develop a whole child teaching and learning culture." It argues the framework requires shifting "deficit-based conceptions of students in poverty to those that are asset-based", developing community partnerships, and creating schools students living in poverty can depend on because many are "school dependent". The framework targets structural reform of funding, school organization, and pedagogy rather than fixing students.
requirements: Adequate and equitable school funding as the foundation for all other strategies
Partnerships with community agencies to respond to out-of-school issues
Asset-based educator mindsets that build on students' strengths
constraints: Education alone cannot eliminate childhood deep poverty; the report states a suite of policies including housing, health care, and employment is required
target_learners: Students living in deep poverty in the United States
Students in communities of concentrated poverty
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement and graduation
Social-emotional well-being and healing from trauma
Equality of educational opportunity
examples: The report addresses Milner's three steps in reverse order, beginning with funding because money matters, then community schools, then whole child culture

citation: Cookson, P. W., Jr., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2022). Building school communities for students living in deep poverty. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/121.698
title: Community schools as a place-based integrated-support strategy
description: Community schools are "a place-based strategy in which schools partner with community agencies and allocate resources to provide an integrated focus on academics, health and social services, youth and community development, and family and community engagement". Many operate on all-day and year-round schedules serving both children and adults, functioning as academic and social centers for innovative learning, recreation, health care, and social services. The report describes them as associated with reduced absenteeism, improved academic outcomes, and more positive school climates, and notes statewide initiatives in California, Maryland, New Mexico, New York, and Vermont.
requirements: Partnerships with community agencies
Resources allocated to integrated academic, health, social, and engagement supports
constraints: The report notes deep poverty can be found throughout regions, prompting some communities to move beyond a single school to a broader geographic area
target_learners: Students from deep-poverty households
Children and adults in high-poverty communities
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Attendance and engagement
Health and social-service support for learning
examples: Districtwide community school plans in Oakland, Hartford, New York City, and Tulsa; the New York City Community Schools Initiative studied by Rand

article_title: Magnet Schools and Metropolitan Civil Rights Planning: A Strategy to Revitalize and Stabilize Distressed Communities
citation: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312
title: Stable Metropolitan Racial Integration framework for affirmatively furthering fair housing
description: A proposed classification system that divides metropolitan areas into three community types — areas of minority concentration, racially mixed areas, and predominantly white areas — and sets different fair housing requirements for each. The report states: "The proposed Stable Metropolitan Racial Integration system divides metropolitan areas into three types of communities." Under the framework, magnet schools are encouraged in areas of minority concentration to reintegrate and revitalize them, encouraged in racially mixed areas to preserve integration, and discouraged or disallowed in predominantly white areas.
requirements: Jurisdictions conducting AFFH planning would be encouraged or required to consider magnet school creation consistent with their neighborhood classification
constraints: The report notes a centralized HUD taxonomy could elide regional distinctions, and classifying communities entirely on economic characteristics while omitting racial demographics is inadvisable
target_learners: K-12 students in metropolitan school districts
target_learning_goals: Racial and socioeconomic integration of schools
Access to high-quality integrated education
examples: HUD or entitlement jurisdictions could determine classification criteria during AFFH rulemaking or Consolidated Plan processes
key_sources: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312

article_title: Magnet Schools and Metropolitan Civil Rights Planning: A Strategy to Revitalize and Stabilize Distressed Communities
citation: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312
title: Combined geographic-zone and open-enrollment attendance policy for revitalization magnets
description: A magnet attendance design combining a residential attendance boundary with voluntary regional open enrollment, so the school both serves its immediate neighborhood and draws integrating families from the wider region. The report describes "implementing an attendance policy in which 50% of a school's enrollment is drawn from a particular geographic zone and 50% is drawn as open enrollment from the larger region." In a low-income segregated area, zone students are likely nonwhite and lower-income while open-enrollment students are more likely white and affluent, and strong demand can make the attendance zone housing attractive, supporting residential integration.
requirements: Strong demand for magnet seats so families seek housing in the geographic attendance zone
constraints: The report warns poorly designed magnets can lose their ability to attract enrollment, and high-demand schools risk becoming heavily white and affluent without enrollment-weighting policies
target_learners: K-12 students in racially and economically segregated urban neighborhoods
target_learning_goals: School integration
Neighborhood revitalization through school quality
examples: The report cites successful magnets in the Hartford, CT, and San Antonio, TX, regions that weight enrollment by socioeconomic strata

article_title: Magnet Schools and Metropolitan Civil Rights Planning: A Strategy to Revitalize and Stabilize Distressed Communities
citation: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312
title: Pair Low-Income Housing Tax Credit projects in qualified census tracts with magnet school development as concerted community revitalization plans
description: The report proposes giving substance to the federal requirement that tax credit projects in qualified census tracts contribute to a concerted community revitalization plan by incorporating magnet schools. It states: "a proposed Low-Income Housing Tax Credit project in a qualified census tract could be paired with a proposal to develop a new magnet school in the vicinity of the project." The magnet serves project-zone children while drawing affluent families, integrating the neighborhood and potentially revitalizing it through housing demand and an improved tax base.
requirements: The project proposal must show existing or planned magnets can absorb new students without intensifying school segregation
constraints: The report notes the current statutory requirement is threadbare, with no federal guidance defining a concerted community revitalization plan
target_learners: Children in low-income housing projects and surrounding districts
target_learning_goals: Access to integrated, higher-quality schooling
examples: The Department of Education's Magnet School Assistance Program could provide priority grants to magnets created as part of such plans

article_title: Magnet Schools and Metropolitan Civil Rights Planning: A Strategy to Revitalize and Stabilize Distressed Communities
citation: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312
title: Metropolitan civil rights planning organized around three goals: diversification, stabilization, and revitalization
description: The report frames metropolitan civil rights planning as pursuing economically and racially diverse neighborhoods across a whole metropolitan area through three goals. It states: "Metropolitan civil rights planning can be roughly divided into three broad goals: 1. Diversification of affluent and white-segregated communities in outer-ring suburbs and exurban areas 2. Stabilization of diverse and integrated communities, particularly in inner and second-ring suburbs 3. Revitalization of economically distressed and nonwhite-segregated communities, particularly in urban centers and inner suburbs." Because government cannot force families to relocate, policymakers must indirectly increase the appeal of distressed areas, and the report calls well-designed magnet schools one of the few proven methods for doing so.
requirements: Policymakers must find indirect ways to increase the appeal of distressed or unstably integrated neighborhoods to wider socioeconomic groups
constraints: Stabilization and revitalization are harder than diversification because discrimination, disinvestment, and white flight push demographics toward segregation and poverty concentration
target_learners: Students and families across an entire metropolitan region
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to integrated schools and neighborhood opportunity
examples: The report builds on the 1968 Kerner Commission's recommendation of exemplary metropolitan schools designed to attract students of varying racial and socioeconomic backgrounds

citation: Campoli, A. K., & Darling-Hammond, L. (with Podolsky, A., & Levin, S.). (2022). Principal learning opportunities and school outcomes: Evidence from California. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/438.376
title: Professional Learning Theory of Action: principal learning shapes leadership behaviors that influence teacher and student outcomes
description: The report's organizing framework "assumes connections between principal professional learning—both the content of learning and strategies for learning—and principal enactment of specific leadership behaviors." Leadership behaviors in turn relate to teacher practices and retention, school climate, and student opportunities and learning, all unfolding within state, district, school, and community contexts and policies. The framework distinguishes content areas (instructional leadership, school improvement, school conditions, developing people, meeting diverse students' needs) from learning strategies (applied learning, internships, coaching and mentoring, cohorts and networks), and applies to novice principals, experienced principals, assistant principals, and teacher leaders.

Experienced principals
Assistant principals and teacher leaders

Developing people

Meeting diverse students' needs

article_title: Creating Identity-Safe Schools and Classrooms
citation: Hernández, L. E., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2022). Creating identity-safe schools and classrooms. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/165.102
title: Identity safety framework: four practice areas that counteract social identity threat in schools
description: The report organizes identity-safe schooling around four research-backed practice areas: trusting relationships and interpersonal connection; caring, consistent, purposeful communities; restorative practices; and teaching that promotes "understanding, student voice, student responsibility" plus cultivating "diversity as a resource for teaching." It rests on the science-of-learning premise that social, emotional, and cognitive experiences are intertwined, so threat reduction and belonging are preconditions for achievement. The framework is offered as the antidote to stereotype threat.

Consistent routines and structures (advisories, looping, community meetings) that let positive connections flourish
constraints: The report frames these as supports for students facing social identity threat from stigma based on race, ethnicity, gender identity, language, immigration status, disability, or other features
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those from minoritized or stigmatized groups
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging and membership in school
Student achievement and engagement
Reduced effects of stereotype threat
