article_title: Positive Conditions for Mathematics Learning: An Overview of the Research
citation: Fitz, J. (with Price, H.). (2025). Positive conditions for mathematics learning: An overview of the research. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/967.472
title: Science of learning and development (SoLD) framework: students learn best in environments offering safety, positive relationships, belonging, purpose, and affirmation
description: The report organizes its synthesis around the science of learning and development (SoLD), a body of research from neuroscience, psychology, and developmental and learning sciences. It "provides evidence that students learn best in environments where they feel a sense of physical, emotional, and identity safety; hold positive relationships with adults and peers; and experience belonging, purpose, and affirmation." These conditions support cognitive, physical, psychological, social, and emotional development and can counter stress and trauma that biologically impair learning. The report applies this framework to K–12 math classrooms, where math anxiety makes supportive conditions especially important.
requirements: Teachers must attend to students' social-emotional developmental needs through interpersonal relationships, classroom management, and instructional strategies
constraints: The report states the four condition divisions are heuristic in nature, with considerable overlap between conditions
target_learners: K–12 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement and engagement
Reducing math anxiety
STEM identity and persistence
examples: The report reviews more than 70 articles identified through comprehensive database searches and citation mining, focused on malleable conditions teachers can influence
key_sources: Fitz, J. (with Price, H.). (2025). Positive conditions for mathematics learning: An overview of the research. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/967.472

article_title: Positive Conditions for Mathematics Learning: An Overview of the Research
citation: Fitz, J. (with Price, H.). (2025). Positive conditions for mathematics learning: An overview of the research. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/967.472
title: Math anxiety mechanism: emotional threat responses divert attention and reduce working memory during mathematical engagement
description: The report describes math anxiety as prevalent psychological fear of math among students and adults, including many elementary math teachers. Neuroimaging research finds children with high math anxiety "perceive math as threatening," showing elevated neural activity in emotion-processing brain areas and lower activity in mathematical reasoning areas. Researchers hypothesize the emotional reaction diverts attention from the task, co-opting deep mathematical cognition and reducing working memory. Math anxiety is linked to reduced achievement and avoidance of math courses and careers, and may also arise from early struggles, kicking off a vicious cycle.
requirements: Classroom conditions must address students' social and emotional experiences alongside instructional quality, since anxiety can result from early math struggles
constraints: The mechanism is presented as researchers' hypothesis about neural findings, and the review notes anxiety can be a consequence as well as a cause of low achievement
target_learners: K–12 mathematics students, especially those with high math anxiety
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Deep cognitive engagement with math
Reduced avoidance of math courses and careers
examples: The report argues teachers can ameliorate anxiety by cultivating conditions that develop the sense of safety necessary for deep cognitive engagement with math
key_sources: Fitz, J. (with Price, H.). (2025). Positive conditions for mathematics learning: An overview of the research. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/967.472

article_title: Design Principles for Teacher Preparation: Enacting the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Rushing, J.). (2025). Design principles for teacher preparation: Enacting the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/115.854
title: Guiding Principles for Enacting SoLD-Aligned Teacher Preparation framework
description: The report's organizing framework, the Guiding Principles for Enacting SoLD-Aligned Teacher Preparation, specifies the content, pedagogy, organization, processes, and norms of teacher preparation aligned with the science of learning and development. It comprises five elements: "curriculum rooted in a deep understanding of learners, learning, and development", "development of skills, habits, and mindsets of an equitable educator", "rich, experiential learning opportunities", "pedagogical alignment and modeling", and "supportive developmental relationships in communities of practice". These elements are designed to enable teachers to enact the design principles for equitable whole child school design, producing teaching that is efficacious, reflective, culturally responsive, student-centered, and deeply knowledgeable.
requirements: Programs must be clinically intensive and coherent; the report notes such models are typically time- and resource-intensive
constraints: The report states close attention to supports and resources is beyond the scope of this report
The principles are not explicitly aligned with any particular type of educator preparation pathway
target_learners: Teacher candidates in educator preparation programs
target_learning_goals: Understanding learners, learning, and development
Equitable whole-child teaching practice
examples: The framework is illustrated with a vignette of an Alverno College teacher candidate teaching a collaborative math lesson at Walker Elementary School

title: Root teacher preparation curriculum in a deep understanding of learners, learning, and development
description: The report holds that a curriculum rooted in a deep understanding of learners, learning, and development is the most important foundation teacher preparation programs can offer, ensuring candidates have the knowledge and skills to teach and support children well. Programs should model learning rooted in culture, experience, and relationships and equip educators to understand interrelated conditions for optimal brain development. This includes a curriculum that connects subject matter with strategies for an asset-based approach to learning about students' backgrounds, families, and communities.
requirements: Knowledge of all aspects of child and adolescent development, including brain development; pedagogical content knowledge and pedagogical learner knowledge; and language development including academic language
target_learners: Teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: Understanding child and adolescent development
Adapting curriculum and assessment for individual students
examples: Programs should prepare educators who evaluate, modify, and adapt curricular materials for individual students and create assessment experiences that allow students to learn deeply through relevant inquiry

title: Develop the skills, habits, and mindsets of an equitable educator
description: Because students learn best when school connects to their cultural contexts and their identities are affirmed, the report argues that EPPs must be designed to develop educators with mindsets that support all students well and equitably. Program faculty should model empathy, demonstrate social and emotional learning and cultural competence, and prepare educators to use restorative practices. This includes strengthening candidates' understanding of how to create environments of trust and belonging and build partnerships with families, community members, and other educators.

Support for candidates to understand how contextual realities impact students' experiences and social identities

target_learning_goals: Creating environments of trust and belonging
Negotiating school policies toward equitable ends
examples: Programs should prepare educators who understand how contextual realities impact the experiences of their students and their perceptions of social identities

title: Immerse teacher candidates in rich, experiential learning opportunities with performance-based assessment
description: The report states that all learners, including prospective teachers, actively construct knowledge based on their experiences, relationships, and social contexts, so EPPs should immerse teacher candidates in active and compelling learning opportunities paired with authentic and performance-based assessments. Programs should coordinate coursework and fieldwork to provide a full range of adult learning experiences, including practice, feedback, skill development, and growth in adaptive expertise. title: Align pedagogy across coursework and clinical work so candidates experience the teaching they are expected to use
description: The report identifies pedagogical alignment in both coursework and clinical work around a coherent vision of whole child development, learning, and teaching as a critical program strategy. New teachers should experience the very kinds of teaching strategies they are expected to develop for their pupils. Instructors, supervisors, and cooperating teachers should enact and unpack the approaches they expect candidates to use, integrating theory and practice around SoLD-aligned principles through close partnerships between programs, schools, and districts.

title: Structure supportive developmental relationships in communities of practice for teacher candidates
description: The report argues that teacher candidates benefit from professional learning communities within university classrooms, clinical placement schools, and disciplinary and professional groups. These communities provide supportive environments for engaging with real problems of practice and promote active, interactive, constructive, and iterative learning. article_title: Successful Teacher Residencies: What Matters and What Works
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Successful teacher residencies: What matters and what works. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/480.783
title: Teacher residency model: LEA–EPP partnerships providing a full-year clinical placement with integrated coursework in exchange for a teaching commitment
description: The teacher residency model, "modeled after medical residencies," consists of "partnerships between local education agencies (LEAs) and educator preparation programs (EPPs)" in which "residents" spend "a full year in a clinical placement alongside an expert teacher while completing highly integrated coursework focused on skills for successful teaching." In paid programs, residents typically make a multiyear teaching commitment to the host LEA in exchange for financial support during preparation. The report uses this model as the organizing framework for its cross-case analysis of five California programs.
requirements: A partnership between an LEA and an educator preparation program
A full-year clinical placement alongside an expert mentor teacher
Integrated coursework aligned with clinical practice
constraints: Considerable variability exists between programs that are nominally referred to as teacher residencies, and non-grant-funded programs may lack important features required by the TRGP

Readiness to teach in high-need subject areas and LEA contexts

article_title: Successful Teacher Residencies: What Matters and What Works
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Successful teacher residencies: What matters and what works. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/480.783
title: Eleven characteristics of high-quality teacher residencies: eight research-based characteristics plus three emerging from the case studies
description: Across the five case study programs, eleven practices emerged as promoters of success. Eight align with characteristics previously identified by the Learning Policy Institute and Pathways Alliance: strong LEA–EPP partnerships; selectively recruited diverse candidates; a full-year teaching experience alongside an expert mentor teacher; expert mentor teachers who coteach; tightly integrated coursework and clinical practice; cohorts of residents; financial supports for residents; and ongoing mentoring and support for graduates. Three additional characteristics emerged from the current study: "Proactive whole person supports that residents can easily access through a 'go-to person,'" ongoing program capacity development, and an explicit focus on promoting equity for residents and their students.
requirements: Programs must implement the characteristics in context-specific ways that fit partner LEA needs and available funding
constraints: The report notes that because programs drew on different funding sources, not all practices discussed aligned with TRGP requirements
target_learners: Teacher residents in postbaccalaureate residency pathways
target_learning_goals: High-quality preparation for teaching in high-need shortage areas
Equity-focused teaching practices
examples: Case study programs served between 15 and 325 residents, offered hybrid, online, and in-person formats, and ranged from 10 to 18 months in length

title: California Golden State Teacher Grant (GSTG) Program
description: A California service scholarship administered by the California Student Aid Commission that provides teacher candidates and Pupil Personnel Services candidates "an upfront grant as part of their overall student aid package to offset a substantial portion of their cost of preparation." In exchange, recipients commit to teach in a priority school or California State Preschool Program for 2 years, repaying the grant (prorated for partial completion) if they do not. The program has provided over $570 million since 2020–21 and its parameters—award amount, eligibility, service length—have changed repeatedly as funding varied.
requirements: Recipients must be enrolled in an approved, California-based preliminary teaching or PPS credential program through a student teaching or residency pathway and commit to serve in a priority school, where at least 55% of enrolled students are eligible for free or reduced-price meals, are English learners, or are living in foster care
constraints: The maximum award was reduced from $20,000 to $10,000 in July 2024, interns were excluded from eligibility, and lower-income applicants are prioritized when funds run short

Pupil Personnel Services credential candidates (school counselors, social workers, psychologists)
target_learning_goals: Recruiting and retaining a well-prepared, diverse educator workforce for high-need schools and shortage subjects
examples: In 2023–24, 45% of California's new teacher candidates received a GSTG; over the first 5 years the program supported 22,851 teacher candidates and 5,812 PPS candidates

citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., Espinoza, D., & Oakes, J. (2025). Community schools certification: An approach for implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/220.412
title: Essentials for Community Schools Transformation framework: six key site-level practices supported by enabling conditions
description: The Community Schools Forward partnership, convening a national task force of leaders from 45 organizations, produced a definition, framework, theory of action, and indicators resource for community schools. The framework identifies six key site-level practices: "(1) expanded, enriched learning opportunities; (2) rigorous, community-connected classroom instruction; (3) a culture of belonging, safety, and care; (4) integrated systems of support; (5) powerful student and family engagement; and (6) collaborative leadership and shared power and voice." These practices are best implemented when there is a shared vision, trusting relationships, and data-informed, inclusive decision-making, supported by sustainable resources, shared governance structures, and continuous improvement infrastructure.
requirements: Implementation depends on shared vision and purpose, trusting relationships among school community members, and data-informed, inclusive decision-making.
constraints: While programs and services vary according to local context, the six key site-level practices are shared.
target_learners: K-12 students in community schools
target_learning_goals: student well-being and engagement
academic outcomes
school climate and belonging

title: University of Central Florida Center for Community Schools certification system for the Community Partnership Schools model
description: The UCF Center houses a state-funded certification process for the Community Partnership Schools (CPS) model throughout Florida, based on 12 standards with substandards divided into nonnegotiable "fundamental practices" and an overall assessment scored on a four-point rubric. Schools apply once key partnerships and positions are filled, then spend up to 5 years self-assessing, gathering artifacts, and receiving "technical assistance, coaching, and peer-to-peer mentoring" before a readiness assessment and a 3-day external review. In fiscal year 2024, $20.1 million in state funding was appropriated to UCF Center, which currently serves 43 schools.
requirements: Schools must have a memorandum of understanding with each of the four required core partners (nonprofit agency, university/college, school district, and health care provider), the director position in place, and programming aligned with community needs.
constraints: The model requires certain staffing and features to be in place, which can limit who and how many schools can participate in certification; some participants felt the standards were too rigid or difficult to achieve in their context and the data collection process was cumbersome.
target_learners: K-12 students in Florida Community Partnership Schools
target_learning_goals: implementation fidelity of the community schools strategy
continuous improvement
examples: Planning grants are awarded for up to $80,000 with a 25% match; implementation grants typically range from $150,000 to $200,000 per year for the first 5 years.

title: Georgia Department of Education LEAD staged certification and recognition pilot for whole child education model schools
description: From 2021 to 2023, the Georgia Department of Education piloted a certification and recognition process for community schools implementing a whole child education model. The process recognized schools as they progressed through stages characterized by the acronym LEAD (Learning, Emerging, Achieving, Distinguished), each with benchmarks for structures and processes; later stages expected evidence of integration with the schoolwide improvement plan, impact, and outcomes. The finalized standards and coaching were praised by educators, but the pilot faced capacity challenges and was shut down for consolidation and reorganization.

constraints: The pilot faced challenges throughout due to capacity issues within the Department of Education and a rush to begin before certification materials were completed.

whole child education

title: Design certification processes to focus on continuous improvement rather than compliance and accountability
description: The report finds certification processes offer the most value when organized around continuous improvement rather than compliance. Promising strategies include "offering general and targeted technical assistance; creating peer and mentor networks for community schools coordinators; having an assigned coach; building in check-ins and feedback sessions, including peer reviewers in the certification process; and maintaining a resource library for participants." Establishing phases or tiers with clearly defined thresholds lets schools achieve baseline implementation, celebrate growth, and strive for excellence, keeping certification formative rather than punitive.
requirements: The certifying entity must invest sufficient resources to support onboarding and ongoing coaching of district and school personnel, staff the evaluation process, and expand as more schools apply.
constraints: The tension between formative support and compliance orientation remains; the amount of time allotted for schools to attain certification should be long enough to engage meaningfully and deepen implementation year over year.

continuous improvement
examples: All three certification systems examined were designed to center on continuous improvement.

article_title: Community Schools Impact on Student Outcomes: Evidence from California
citation: Swain, W., Leung-Gagné, M., Maier, A., & Rubinstein, C. (2025). Community schools impact on student outcomes: Evidence from California. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/541.498
title: Community schools four-pillar whole-child framework
description: The report describes community schools as an evidence-based strategy in which students, families, educators, and community partners organize in- and out-of-school resources, aiming to "improve learning conditions and support the well-being of students, families, and communities through four core pillars of integrated student supports, expanded learning opportunities, collaborative leadership, and family engagement." California's state-approved CCSPP framework extends this into four areas (pillars, key conditions for learning, cornerstone commitments, proven practices) broken into 16 features that grantees align to. The framework functions as a design anchor for transformative systems change rather than isolated service expansion.
requirements: Grantees are expected to align their work and reporting with the framework's four areas and 16 features to ensure a comprehensive whole-child approach
constraints: Specific programs and services vary by local context; the approach depends on local adaptation rather than a fixed model

target_learning_goals: Improved attendance and engagement
Academic growth in math and English language arts
Reduced exclusionary discipline
Student social and emotional development

description: The report distills research on quality early childhood teacher preparation into program design principles: programs should establish a shared vision informing courses, clinical work, and partner school selection; ground candidates deeply in child development as a lens for other coursework; and integrate coursework with field-based experiences. The report states that "Integrating coursework and field-based experiences makes for a more powerful learning experience" and that a unified vision "enables success." It applies these principles in profiling eight preparation programs across four states.

description: A program-level design pattern in which candidates complete sustained and intensive supervised clinical experiences, ideally full-year placements, with strong mentorship and individual and group reflection opportunities. The report's research summary states that "Providing sustained and intensive supervised clinical experiences, such as full-year supervised clinical placements with strong mentorship and opportunities for reflection individually and in groups, strengthens practice." Required clinical length varies across the four study states from one semester to a full year, with Louisiana requiring a full-year placement.

Partnerships with schools that instantiate best practices and provide a well-supported setting to learn to teach

article_title: Keeping Schools Safe? The Research on Behavioral Threat Assessments
citation: DePaoli, J. L., & Loewe, S. B. (2025). Keeping schools safe? The research on behavioral threat assessments. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/808.437
title: Four major school-based behavioral threat assessment models (FBI, NTAC, CSTAG, Salem-Keizer)
description: The report organizes school-based behavioral threat assessment into four major models that states adopt or reference in legislation and policy: "federal models from the Federal Bureau of Investigation and from the National Threat Assessment Center (NTAC), the Comprehensive School Threat Assessment Guidelines (CSTAG) model, and the Salem-Keizer model." All models define serious threats, establish multidisciplinary teams, guide threat handling, and require team training. The FBI model uses threat categorization and a four-pronged assessment; NTAC provides site-level guidance with an eight-step process; CSTAG uses a five-step decision tree distinguishing transient from substantive threats; Salem-Keizer begins with screening questions and can extend to a communitywide team.
requirements: Each model identifies appropriate threat assessment training as a key component of high-quality implementation, including training for all adults, students, and parents on the reporting and assessment process
constraints: Many districts and schools adopt BTA practices that do not follow any of these specific models; the Salem-Keizer model has only one published research study on its implementation or outcomes
target_learners: K-12 students
school threat assessment team members
target_learning_goals: preventing school violence
responding appropriately to student threats of violence
examples: Virginia created its own model policies based on NTAC guidance; Florida adopted CSTAG as its statewide BTA system

It is part of a broader city infrastructure that includes the Long Beach Early Childhood Education Committee, a partnership created in 2003 that unites district, city, nonprofit, and health partners around a shared strategic plan, and annual outreach events and a citywide conference for early educators across the mixed delivery system.

description: The San Francisco Department of Early Childhood (DEC) is a dedicated local governing agency for early childhood, reporting to the mayor, formed in 2013 and renamed in 2022 when it merged with First 5 San Francisco. title: Blended-funding classroom alignment: uniform curricula, assessments, quality measures, and ratios across funding streams
description: This pattern, observed in Lindsay Unified School District, aligns preschool classrooms funded through different streams by braiding funding and applying identical standards everywhere. The district blends CSPP, TK, and other funding sources, integrates TK and CSPP staff in professional development, and prioritizes fully inclusive environments where children with disabilities learn alongside peers. A districtwide strategic plan and a district leader with ECE expertise supported this consistency.

Ability to braid multiple funding streams

Children with disabilities in inclusive classrooms

description: A framework developed by Community Schools Forward that organizes community school transformation around the traditional four pillars—integrated student supports, expanded learning time, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership—extended with two added core features. The report states it "extends the traditional four pillars of community schools—integrated student supports, expanded learning time, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership—by adding two core features: (1) a culture of belonging, safety, and care, and (2) rigorous, community-connected classroom instruction." LAUSD's CSI is explicitly aligned with this framework, and the added classroom-instruction feature motivates the report's focus on teaching and learning rather than services alone.

title: LAUSD community school common roles and processes (coordinator, community rep, assets and needs assessment, benchmarks)
description: Each LAUSD community school implements common roles, processes, and structures codified in the collective bargaining agreement. The report states: "These common positions—codified and outlined in the CBA between the district and the union—include the community school coordinator (CSC) and the community representative (community rep)." The CSC builds community partnerships, family engagement, and leads the assets and needs assessment (ANA), a comprehensive stakeholder-data process revisited annually; community reps support day-to-day implementation and home–school relationship building. article_title: Building a Positive School Climate.
citation: Knight, James A. (1985). Building a Positive School Climate. Paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the Midwestern Educational Research Association, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED265663
title: Ten strategies for building a positive school climate
description: The paper enumerates ten strategies said to rise out of a broad research base on achievement, discipline, teaching effectiveness, and business productivity: "make students feel important, (2) make students feel invited, (3) deal with needed changes in others from a positive point of view, (4) learn to make appropriate nonverbal cues, (5) get to know each student personally, (6) learn to empathize, (7) establish parameters, (8) use student-centered instruction, (9) learn to know and understand the difference between discipline and punishment, and (10) be enthusiastic about teaching." citation: Haycock, Kati. (1998). Good Teaching Matters: How Well-Qualified Teachers Can Close the Gap. Thinking K-16, v3 n2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED457260
title: El Paso Collaborative for Academic Excellence
description: A comprehensive effort created in 1992 by the University of Texas-El Paso and the three El Paso-area school districts (El Paso, Ysleta, and Socorro) to raise student achievement kindergarten through college. Its goal was to prepare every young person in the city to enter college without remediation, reflected in the El Paso Standards. Teachers received intensive assistance including summer institutes and regular on-site coaching, funded through NSF dollars and redirected federal and state funds, while the University changed teacher preparation. The article reports improved achievement and a narrower gap between ethnic groups on TAAS math passing rates from 1992-93 to 1997-98.

Prospective teachers at UTEP

citation: Haycock, K., Lynch, M., & Engle, J. (2010). Opportunity Adrift: Our Flagship Universities Are Straying From Their Public Mission. The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: Redirect institutional grant aid from high-income students who do not need it to low-income students whose enrollment and graduation depend on it
description: The report argues that public research universities, as the wealthiest public institutions and the largest source of undergraduate grant aid, should shift their own aid dollars toward low-income students. It notes Pell Grants "only cover about 36 percent of the cost of attending a four-year public college" and that increased aid improves low-income students' graduation chances while having little or no effect on high-income students. Redirecting aid is presented as a direct lever on both access and success.
requirements: Institutions must have discretionary institutional grant aid resources and data on recipient family income to retarget awards.
constraints: The report notes institution-specific data on reordered aid priorities are unavailable, so it cannot confirm how many institutions have actually changed.

target_learning_goals: Access to and completion of bachelor's degrees at public research universities
examples: The report highlights financial aid pledges at at least nine flagships, including no-loan guarantees at Indiana University, the University of Virginia, and the University of Florida that ensure the lowest-income students pay nothing beyond their EFC.

title: California Assembly Bill 490 (2004): education rights and district responsibilities for students in foster care
description: AB490 (Steinberg), Chapter 862, became law in January 2004 and establishes specific education rights for children and youth in foster care in California and responsibilities for school personnel, judges, attorneys, social workers, probation officers, and caregivers. Its provisions are designed to give these students access to the same educational opportunities and resources as other students. Provisions include the ability to finish the school year in the school of origin, immediate enrollment even without records, school records transferred within 2 days, and full or partial credits for previous coursework accepted by schools.

Depends on rigorous performance evaluations perceived as tools to improve practice rather than punish

article_title: A Step Forward or a Step Back? State Accountability in the Waiver Era
citation: Daria Hall. (2013). A Step Forward or a Step Back? State Accountability in the Waiver Era. The Education Trust. http://www.edtrust.org
title: Good accountability systems pair ambitious, achievable expectations with mechanisms that prompt meaningful action
description: The report argues that well-designed accountability systems rest on two priorities: expectations and action. Good systems set "improvement and gap-closing expectations that are both ambitious" and achievable, and they go beyond evaluation to "celebrating and rewarding schools that exceed expectations and acting when schools repeatedly fall short." The report uses these two priorities as the criteria against which it judges every state waiver plan, organizing ten diagnostic questions for educators, advocates, and policymakers.

Performance against goals must be incorporated into school rating or grading systems so that meeting goals actually matters.

target_learning_goals: Raising achievement and closing achievement and graduation-rate gaps for all student groups
examples: Minnesota makes the percentage of students overall and in student groups meeting cut-the-gap-in-half goals a meaningful component of its Multiple Measure Rating.
Massachusetts bases a district's performance rating on the designation of its lowest performing school, making the district only as strong as its weakest link.

article_title: Core to College Evaluation: Statewide Networks. Connecting Education Systems and Stakeholders to Support College Readiness
citation: Bracco, K. R., Klarin, B., Broek, M., Austin, K., Finkelstein, N., Bugler, D., & Mundry, S. (2014). Statewide networks: Connecting education systems and stakeholders to support college readiness. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Social network analysis framework of nodes, ties, and social capital for understanding educational reform sustainability
description: The report applies social network theory to statewide reform: a social network is "a group of actors connected to one another through a set of relations or ties." Nodes are the actors (people, groups, organizations); ties are the connections or flows between them, which link up to form paths allowing nodes to directly or indirectly influence one another. Strong ties support transfer of tacit, non-routine and complex knowledge, while weaker, less dense networks suit simple routine information. Social capital is "an investment in a system's social relations through which the resources of other individuals can be accessed, borrowed, or leveraged." The report uses this framework to analyze how AD networks spread the initiative and may sustain it.
requirements: Mapping of both formal and informal structures, since informal ties can impact the success of formal structures
constraints: The report notes it did not find examples fitting the transforming level of interaction, so that level was not used in its analysis

target_learning_goals: Understanding and sustaining cross-sector collaboration for college readiness reform
examples: The report maps networks in Hawaii, Louisiana, Tennessee, and Washington, categorizing interactions as information sharing, feedback, or collaboration

article_title: How Arizona's Dropout Crisis Affects Communities, Creates Economic Losses for the State of Arizona
citation: How Arizona's Dropout Crisis Affects Communities, Creates Economic Losses for the State of Arizona. (2014). A Project of WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Lifetime-profile economic loss model for calculating social and fiscal costs of dropouts and disconnected youth
description: The report applies an established economic framework that "operates by comparing lifetime profiles" of dropouts versus graduates and disconnected versus other youth, calculating differences in earnings, taxes, health, crime, and welfare as present values. "All money amounts are expressed in present values at age 18 or age 20 using a discount rate of 3.5%", in 2013 dollars weighted to Arizona's price level. The model had been applied nationally and in other states but, as the report notes, had not previously been applied to Arizona.
requirements: National research evidence disaggregated by sex and race, Arizona-specific earnings and expenditure data, and local data from Census PUMAs, school districts, and local government departments where available.
constraints: The dropout analysis rests on a thought-experiment where at age 18 a dropout switches to being a high school graduate following the typical low-income graduate path; the disconnected-youth analysis assumes five years of disconnected status.
target_learners: High school dropouts
Disconnected youth aged 16-24
target_learning_goals: Quantifying economic losses from incomplete education
Informing state and local investment policy
examples: The report applies the model to Arizona and ten localities (Miami, Avondale, Mesa, Tucson, Phoenix, Goodyear, Sahuarita, Gilbert, Tempe, and Oro Valley), adapting national estimates with local educational attainment, economic conditions, and wage rate indices.
key_sources: How Arizona's Dropout Crisis Affects Communities, Creates Economic Losses for the State of Arizona. (2014). A Project of WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED559628

article_title: One-Shot Deal? Students' Perceptions of Assessment and Course Placement in California's Community Colleges
citation: Venezia, A., Bracco, K. R., & Nodine, T. (2010). One-shot deal? Students' perceptions of assessment and course placement in California's community colleges. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org
title: High schools and community colleges should align efforts toward informing and preparing students well before placement
description: The report's central recommendation is to replace the one-day, arrival-time placement experience with "a more seamless, longer-lasting set of processes wherein high schools and community colleges align their efforts toward informing and preparing students." Students should learn requirements early in high school so they can master needed knowledge, skills, and cognitive strategies, and should have ways to gauge their preparation and get support in both high school and college. The principle responds directly to findings that students arrive knowing next to nothing about what to expect.
requirements: Coordination between K-12 and postsecondary systems despite the structural divide between them
Communication to students about readiness requirements early in their high school years
constraints: The report states improvements will be extremely challenging to implement in the environment of budgetary crisis and program instability, and what students most want is more one-on-one counselor time, an expensive intervention
target_learners: Incoming community college students, particularly recent high school graduates
target_learning_goals: College readiness in English and mathematics and informed navigation of assessment and placement
examples: The report also recommends efficiencies such as a common assessment system and centralized Assessment Warehouse, and notes 97 percent of surveyed colleges offer student success courses teaching study skills and college habits of mind.
key_sources: Venezia, A., Bracco, K. R., & Nodine, T. (2010). One-shot deal? Students' perceptions of assessment and course placement in California's community colleges. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566386

article_title: Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase?
citation: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: Mentor Tech mentoring and support program at Texas Tech University
description: Mentor Tech is a Texas Tech program for underrepresented students pairing them with faculty mentors matched on "ethnicity, gender, hobbies, and career and academic interests," with required weekly contact and twice-monthly in-person meetings. It runs about 60 workshops a year on academics, career, and personal development, connects students to community groups, and awards $500–$1,000 scholarships. Started with 46 students in 2002, it now serves more than 1,000 students (45 percent black) with a waiting list.
requirements: Students must attend four workshop or social events each semester and maintain required mentor contact frequency
target_learners: underrepresented students at Texas Tech University, 45 percent of participants black
target_learning_goals: degree completion and first-year retention
examples: Among black students at Texas Tech, graduation rates are now 56 percent, 19 points higher than a decade ago; Mentor Tech participants' first-year retention is 88 percent, 6 points above the university rate for underrepresented students
key_sources: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566672

article_title: Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase?
citation: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: Do not accept overall graduation-rate gains as evidence that all student groups are benefiting; examine disaggregated outcomes and be intentional about closing gaps
description: The report argues that institutions must be intentional about success for black students because aggregate improvement can mask stagnation or decline for subgroups. It states "we shouldn't accept wholesale that increases in overall graduation rates lead to gains for all student populations," noting that 31.5 percent of improving institutions showed no gains for black students. Institutions that disaggregated and acted — Buffalo, Ohio State, NC State, Rutgers — narrowed gaps, showing "demographics aren't destiny."
requirements: Institutional data systems that can track graduation rates by race/ethnicity over time
constraints: The report's analysis covers four-year public institutions with at least 30 first-time, full-time black and white students; HBCUs were excluded
target_learners: black students at four-year public colleges and universities
target_learning_goals: closing racial graduation-rate gaps and equitable degree completion
examples: The report urges paying closer attention to the 73 institutions that did not improve graduation rates for black students at all and to the 39 with both declining black rates and widening gaps
key_sources: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566672

article_title: Community Schools: An Evidence-Based Strategy for Equitable School Improvement
citation: Oakes, J., Maier, A., & Daniel, J. (2017). Community Schools: An Evidence-Based Strategy for Equitable School Improvement. Boulder, CO: National Education Policy Center. http://nepc.colorado.edu/publication/equitable-community-schools
title: Community schools framework: four pillars creating conditions where all children learn
description: The brief describes community schools as a place-based strategy in which "schools partner with community agencies and local government to provide an integrated focus on academics, health and social services, youth and community development, and community engagement." Four pillars appear in most community schools: integrated student supports, expanded learning time and opportunities, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership and practices. The pillars emerged from a comprehensive review of community schools research, are often organized by a full-time community schools coordinator, and align with evidence-based features of good schools.
requirements: A full-time community schools coordinator typically organizes the pillars and conducts needs assessments, partners with agencies, and tracks program data
constraints: Community schools vary in the programs they offer and the way they operate, depending on local context, needs, assets, and school system capacities
target_learners: Students in high-poverty neighborhoods
Students of all backgrounds
Children and adults served year-round
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Attendance and behavior
Social, emotional, and physical development
examples: The Tulsa Area Community Schools Initiative used a holistic community schools model including all four pillars, offering comprehensive services and community voice in governance
key_sources: Oakes, J., Maier, A., & Daniel, J. (2017). Community Schools: An Evidence-Based Strategy for Equitable School Improvement. Boulder, CO: National Education Policy Center. http://nepc.colorado.edu/publication/equitable-community-schools

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Loss and Momentum Framework for community college student progression
description: The loss and momentum framework organizes the community college experience into four stages of student progression — connection (interest to application), entry (enrollment to completion of gatekeeper courses), progress (entry into a course of study to 75 percent of requirements completed), and completion (complete course of study to credential with labor market value). For each stage it pairs common loss points, such as poor college counseling or part-time enrollment, with momentum strategies such as mandatory advising and accelerated programs. The guide states that "understanding when and why a college's students are slowed down or sidetracked in efforts to earn a credential is essential" for developing completion pathways, and the framework anchors the initiative's data-intensive Pathways Analysis.
requirements: A student data system spanning from day one to completion, plus student engagement and leadership focused on completion, frame the framework's use
constraints: Loss points and momentum strategies are presented as common impediments and responses, not as a validated causal model
target_learners: community college students, especially low-income students
target_learning_goals: timely attainment of credentials of value for further education and the labor market
examples: The framework diagram pairs loss points like delayed entry and limited advising with momentum strategies like dual enrollment, intrusive advising, and emergency aid
key_sources: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Completion pathways as integrated institutional designs for student progress
description: Completion pathways are the central design concept of the guide: "integrated sets of institutional policies, practices, and programs that are intentionally designed to maximize students' progress at each point of their community college experience, from the time students first consider attending the community college to their attainment of a credential." The guide positions developing strong completion pathways as a key attribute of a high-performing college and the chief means of raising completion while containing costs, maintaining open access, and ensuring quality. It stresses that pathways require systemic and structural change across all instructional programming and student support services, not isolated best practices at a single stage.
requirements: Colleges must revisit and be prepared to redesign all aspects of their education endeavor, with faculty, staff, and administrators working across organizational silos
constraints: The guide states there is no single model for developing effective completion pathways across colleges
target_learners: community college students, especially low-income students
target_learning_goals: increased credential completion rates
examples: The guide's eight design principles and the loss and momentum framework operationalize what a completion pathway must address
key_sources: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Eight design principles for effective completion pathways
description: The guide enumerates eight design principles drawn from research and practice: seamlessly connecting academics, career and technical education, professional development, and student supports with K-12 schools, transfer partners, and employers; providing coherent, clearly communicated course sequences and enrolling students quickly in a program; defining student competencies and learning outcomes within and across programs; improving engagement through education and career planning and interactive alerts and messaging; customizing, contextualizing, and differentiating instruction; making academic catch-up a responsibility of all programs using acceleration, modularization, and integrated developmental education; integrating student services with instructional supports and gatekeeper courses; and leveraging technology to broaden, improve, and reduce costs of curricular options and services.
requirements: Curricular redesign such as contextualization requires consideration of assessment, curriculum development, staffing, scheduling, and faculty professional development
constraints: The guide notes contextualization can increase time to completion unless mathematics competencies are reduced to those critical for the technical subject matter, and that technology is not a panacea
target_learners: community college students, including developmental education students and first-generation students
target_learning_goals: program completion, deeper learning, timely progress through gatekeeper and developmental courses
examples: The guide describes three emerging acceleration models: linking developmental and college-level courses, compressing two levels of developmental courses, and mainstreaming developmental students
key_sources: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Five attributes of high-performing community colleges
description: The guide identifies attributes common to high-performing colleges that support completion pathways: learning- and outcomes-focused leadership in which faculty, staff, administrators, and trustees make student learning and completion their top priorities; student-centered change that gathers information about student experiences and engages students in developing reforms; a culture of improvement and use of data examining loss and momentum points and costs; faculty engagement and professional development built into organizational and reward structures, including incentives for adjunct faculty; and technology capacity to increase effectiveness and efficiency of service and instructional delivery. All attributes, the guide notes, require teamwork across roles and functions since they are directed toward system integration.
requirements: Teamwork across roles and functions, since the attributes are directed toward system integration
constraints: The guide presents these attributes as hypothetical examples of the attribute in action rather than evaluated cases
target_learners: community college students, including nontraditional students
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes and completion rates
examples: Example attributes in action include collegewide Pathways Analysis teams, structured peer mentoring among full-time and adjunct faculty, and hybrid or blended formats in large entry-level courses
key_sources: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center

article_title: California College Promise: Program Characteristics and Perceptions from the Field
citation: Rauner, M., Perna, L. W., & Kanter, M. J. (2018). California College Promise: Program Characteristics and Perceptions from the Field. WestEd. https://californiacollegepromise.WestEd.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/College-Promise-Landscape-Scan-2018.pdf
title: California College Promise programs (42 programs, fall 2017)
description: A set of 42 place-based college affordability and support programs active in California in fall 2017, documented in the CCPP database. All programs "offer direct financial support for students" and "serve all students who meet the program's eligibility criteria," and all but one is led by or partnered with a community college. Programs combine last-dollar or first-dollar financial awards with academic counseling, career counseling, summer bridge programs, and K–12 and four-year partnerships.
requirements: Programs must offer direct financial support, target students by residence or school attendance, serve all eligible students without caps, and have begun serving students by fall 2017 to fit the scan's definition
constraints: Programs offering only out-of-school-year support or serving only particular demographic groups were excluded from the scan
target_learners: Recent high school graduates entering California community colleges
Low-income and underrepresented community college students
target_learning_goals: Increase college access and enrollment
Improve persistence, completion, and transfer
examples: The Richmond Promise, funded through a community benefits agreement with the local government and Chevron Corporation
San Marcos Promise (PACE), which requires participants to attend CSU San Marcos
key_sources: Rauner, M., Perna, L. W., & Kanter, M. J. (2018). California College Promise: Program Characteristics and Perceptions from the Field. WestEd. https://californiacollegepromise.WestEd.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/College-Promise-Landscape-Scan-2018.pdf

article_title: Examination of Data Usability Options for Assessing Eligibility for Higher Education in California
citation: Fong, A., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2018). Examination of data usability options for assessing eligibility for higher education in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Before using CALPADS course records for eligibility studies, align CALPADS A-G categorization with UC/CSU categorization for each year and school
description: The report recommends reviewing how courses are categorized into A-G categories in CALPADS so that categorization matches what the UC/CSU systems use. It states that "A review of the categorization of courses into A-G categories in CALPADS so that it matches, for each year and school, the categorization used by the UC/CSU system would solve that challenge," addressing the very low elective (G) matching rate. This recommendation follows directly from the alignment analyses showing G-course non-alignment.
requirements: Access to CALPADS course records with A-G indicators and course labels
Knowledge of the UC/CSU categorization used for each year and school
constraints: Applies to the elective (G) categorization problem the report identified; the report notes 2011-2015 CALPADS data may preclude estimating 2015 graduate eligibility rates
target_learners: California public high school students being assessed for UC/CSU eligibility
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of A-G course completion for higher education eligibility
examples: The report's alignment tables (Tables 3-12) showed G-course exact alignment of only about 20-30% while other A-G areas reached 70-87%
key_sources: Fong, A., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2018). Examination of data usability options for assessing eligibility for higher education in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED592524

article_title: Examination of Data Usability Options for Assessing Eligibility for Higher Education in California
citation: Fong, A., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2018). Examination of data usability options for assessing eligibility for higher education in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: CALPADS student-level longitudinal course record dataset
description: CALPADS is the California Longitudinal Pupil Achievement Data System, "a federally funded student-level longitudinal dataset designed primarily for K–12 federal reporting purposes." Course records include a unique student identifier, school code, local and state course codes and descriptions, A-G indicator and admissions requirement code, instructional-level code, academic term, marking period, final grade, and credits attempted and earned. The report evaluated whether these records could surrogate transcript data for UC/CSU eligibility studies.
requirements: LEA submission of course data; mandatory from 2014-15 onward (98-99% submission) versus voluntary earlier (62-93%)
constraints: Data are certified for federal reporting deadlines and "are not as current or specific as data submitted in the UC/CSU enrollment applications"; 2011-2014 course data are known to be incomplete
target_learners: California K-12 public school students
target_learning_goals: Tracking course completion and grades for federal reporting and higher education eligibility assessment
examples: WestEd examined over 18 million course records for 428,410 2015 graduates across four school years
key_sources: Fong, A., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2018). Examination of data usability options for assessing eligibility for higher education in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED592524

article_title: College-Ready in the California State University System: Campus Experiences Implementing EO 1110
citation: Bracco, K. R., Schrager, C., Calisi, G., Gutierrez, P., Salciccioli, M., & Finkelstein, N. (2019). College-ready in the California State University system: Campus experiences implementing EO 1110. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.calstate.edu/eo/EO-1110.html
title: Support data-driven, iterative curriculum redesign when implementing large-scale course reform
description: The report recommends that campus leadership and the Chancellor's Office "support data-driven, iterative curriculum redesign to assess the efficacy of curricular reforms and consider improvements to further support student success." Campuses were already engaged in iterative redesign and expected continued changes; the recommendation is grounded in the observation that one year was too early to know which models work best.
requirements: Capacity for ongoing data collection on student progress through different course models
Time and support for campuses to make successive refinements across semesters
constraints: The report states it is too early to understand the full policy impact or determine which curricular changes are most effective and why
target_learners: First-year CSU undergraduates in entry-level written communication and math/quantitative reasoning courses
target_learning_goals: Meeting General Education written communication and quantitative reasoning requirements in the first academic year
examples: Bakersfield faculty administer a diagnostic reading exam twice during the term and will use results to inform further refinements to the course
San Francisco State's Statistics for Social Justice courses, piloted fall 2018, continue to be refined
key_sources: Bracco, K. R., Schrager, C., Calisi, G., Gutierrez, P., Salciccioli, M., & Finkelstein, N. (2019). College-ready in the California State University system: Campus experiences implementing EO 1110. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.calstate.edu/eo/EO-1110.html

article_title: College-Ready in the California State University System: Campus Experiences Implementing EO 1110
citation: Bracco, K. R., Schrager, C., Calisi, G., Gutierrez, P., Salciccioli, M., & Finkelstein, N. (2019). College-ready in the California State University system: Campus experiences implementing EO 1110. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.calstate.edu/eo/EO-1110.html
title: Program-wide portfolio assessment in composition as a professional-development and consistency practice
description: An assessment practice in which writing-program faculty review sampled student portfolios across sections to gauge consistency and improve instruction. Interviewees "identified program‑wide portfolio assessment as a best practice, but the practice has not yet been widely implemented." Faculty engaging in it report value both for gauging cross-section consistency and for improving their own classroom activities through shared discussion of assignments.
requirements: Resources and capacity to support faculty time for cross-section norming and review
constraints: One campus dean noted the campus no longer has resources for paid lecturer time to read assignments across sections for norming purposes
target_learners: First-year writing students across course sections
target_learning_goals: Consistent instructional quality and assignment expectations across writing course sections
examples: At program meetings, faculty bring in a sampling of assignments, read them, and give each other feedback on what is working
key_sources: Bracco, K. R., Schrager, C., Calisi, G., Gutierrez, P., Salciccioli, M., & Finkelstein, N. (2019). College-ready in the California State University system: Campus experiences implementing EO 1110. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.calstate.edu/eo/EO-1110.html

article_title: Corequisite Remediation in Mathematics: A Review of First-Year Implementation and Outcomes of Quantway and Statway
citation: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/
title: Quantway College with Corequisite and Statway College with Corequisite one-term course sets
description: Two one-term course sets developed by the Carnegie Math Pathways for corequisite remediation, each pairing a college-level course with a developmental-level corequisite. As the report describes them, "Each is designed as a one-term stand-alone course set: a college-level course with some embedded learning supports and a corresponding corequisite course that provides learners with additional support." Both courses in each pair use the pedagogy and learning supports of the original two-term pathway courses, and developmental-level lessons were designed to be independent so faculty can skip lessons. Institutions could use separate or single enrollment, and contact hours for the pair ranged from four to six across the six implementing institutions.
requirements: Faculty time before each course pair starts to review lessons, select content, and structure course timelines to fit the local implementation configuration
constraints: Learning must take place in a shorter time frame than the two-term pathways, and faculty reported too little time for student learning as the chief challenge
target_learners: College students placed into developmental mathematics at two-year and four-year institutions
target_learning_goals: College-level quantitative reasoning or statistics credit earned in a single term
examples: Six institutions delivered the offerings via 15 faculty across 21 sections reaching 410 students in spring 2018 and fall 2018
key_sources: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/

article_title: Corequisite Remediation in Mathematics: A Review of First-Year Implementation and Outcomes of Quantway and Statway
citation: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/
title: Same-faculty cohort pairing of college-level and corequisite courses
description: All six implementing institutions delivered the paired courses as a cohort, with one instructor teaching both the college-level and the developmental-level course to the same group of students. Faculty reported that this continuity supported student comfort, consistent social support, and continuity of pedagogical approaches, and let them make ongoing adjustments to content and timeline. As the report prints it, "All institutions used a cohort model for course delivery, with the same faculty member teaching each of the paired courses (college-level and developmental-level) to the same group of students." Faculty at the two multi-section institutions also met weekly and visited one another's classrooms to improve strategies during the term.
requirements: The same faculty member teaches both paired courses to the same group of students
constraints: The report states that since no other strategies were attempted, the effect of using the cohort strategy versus other strategies needs further investigation
target_learners: Developmental math students in corequisite course pairs at community colleges and four-year institutions
target_learning_goals: Persistence and success in college-level quantitative reasoning or statistics
examples: Faculty at the two multi-section institutions held weekly meetings and classroom visits to adjust lessons, homework, and exams throughout the term
key_sources: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/

article_title: Corequisite Remediation in Mathematics: A Review of First-Year Implementation and Outcomes of Quantway and Statway
citation: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/
title: CMP active, collaborative pedagogy with productive struggle and productive persistence in the corequisite pairs
description: The instructional design carried from the original Quantway and Statway pathways into the new corequisite courses: student-centered, collaborative problem solving in authentic contexts, small-group productive struggle, and productive persistence supports for mindset and belonging. The report states that "the pedagogy centers on active, collaborative learning within rich, authentic contexts," using themes such as citizenship, personal finance, medical literacy, and social justice. Both the college-level course and the developmental-level corequisite use this pedagogy. Faculty reported initial student resistance to struggling in groups with minimal instructor support, followed by deeper engagement once students adapted, and noted that time pressure sometimes pushed them back toward direct instruction.
requirements: Faculty preparation time or prior experience with CMP curricula to build familiarity with the pedagogy and materials
constraints: Under time constraints, faculty reduced time for collaboration, exploration, and discovery and used more direct instruction, selecting which rich tasks students could fully explore
target_learners: College students placed into developmental mathematics
target_learning_goals: Engagement, persistence, and deep learning of quantitative reasoning or statistics concepts
examples: Faculty observed that social-emotional supports helped develop students' persistence and nurtured a sense of community and belonging in the classroom
key_sources: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Create culturally affirming school environments whose goals and values align with those of teachers of color
description: Case-study principals retain teachers of color by aligning school vision with teachers' personal values: a whole-child focus, community service expectations, positive racial identity development, and equity commitments. The report found "teachers of color stay in schools that have a commitment to equity, social justice, and the dismantling of racism." Leaders set this culture through their own mindset, language, and staff-wide conversations about racism and bias.
requirements: School leaders must model and message a genuine belief in the promise of students of color, since the principal's mindset trickles down to teachers and students.
constraints: The report cautions these recommendations "may seem straightforward" but the educator voices make clear "how difficult they are to put into practice."
target_learners: K-12 teachers of color
target_learning_goals: Teacher retention and workforce diversity
examples: One school implemented mandatory weekly 45-minute "cultural proficiency seminars" where teachers have candid conversations about race and bias; another principal revised the whole PD plan around teacher-expressed needs.
key_sources: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603193

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Affirm teachers' humanity and racial identity so teachers of color can be their authentic selves at school
description: Case-study principals deliberately create space for teachers to be themselves as individuals and as people of color, including freedom in dress, hair, and cultural expression. Teachers described being able to wear culturally affirming clothing and wear natural hair, and one school ran a building-wide "Woke Wednesdays" initiative demonstrating "their commitment to consciousness and social justice." Administrators of color were noted as making teachers feel safer and heard.
requirements: Administrative support, including administrators of color, so teachers do not feel they must leave their identity at the school door.
target_learners: K-12 teachers of color
target_learning_goals: Teacher retention, authentic professional identity
examples: Teachers wore shirts such as "I'm Rooting for Everybody Black" without reprisal; a leader transitioning to dreadlocks felt comfortable not hiding her hair under a wig.
key_sources: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603193

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Empower and invest in teachers through responsive professional development, leadership pathways, and classroom autonomy
description: School leaders retain teachers of color by securing growth resources, funding conference attendance, embracing distributive leadership, and allowing discretion over materials and course content. One principal scrapped planned PD to "make sure that we're feeding our staff and we're giving them what they want," showing teachers their feedback is valued and implemented. The report states the space to advocate on students' behalf "makes it more likely a teacher will stay."
requirements: Principals must budget for professional development and be willing to cede control over aspects of schooling, including purchasing culturally relevant materials teachers request.
target_learners: K-12 teachers of color
target_learning_goals: Teacher retention, professional growth, instructional autonomy
examples: Principals sent groups of teachers to the Black Male Educators' Convening in Philadelphia and bought class sets of The Hate U Give and Pushout at teachers' request.

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Build a schoolwide family with formal and informal mentorship, pairing novice teachers of color thoughtfully with veterans
description: Case-study schools foster strong relationships among teachers, students, and administrators so teachers of color feel they belong; principals schedule team-building, off-site PD, and informal rapport-building time. Formal mentorship assigns new staff a veteran teacher, and pairings must be strategic: when teachers "experience bias, stereotyping, and racism, it requires a partner teacher who can help with those problems because they have experienced them first hand."
requirements: Mentor pairings must be chosen thoughtfully, including shared content areas and shared lived experience, with required check-ins.
constraints: One principal cautioned a familial culture can become "a dysfunctional family that often has led to complacency and comfortability," so professionalism boundaries must be maintained.
target_learners: Novice and veteran K-12 teachers of color
target_learning_goals: Teacher retention, induction, professional belonging
examples: New hires received two and a half days of onboarding on school culture and were assigned veteran teachers as resources, with a required number of check-ins.

article_title: Promising Models for Preparing a Diverse, High-Quality Early Childhood Workforce
citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: Family Child Care Apprenticeship: job-embedded pathway to Child Development Permits for home-based providers
description: The FCC Apprenticeship is a pilot program implemented by the SEIU Educator Training Center with partners at four California sites, designed for licensed family child care providers. It pairs accessible college coursework with on-the-job training: "Apprentices enroll in college courses that are conveniently offered during evening hours at community sites, in partnership with local community colleges." Apprentices receive home-visit coaching, site-coordinator advising, cohorts of 25 peers, wage enhancements from $100 to $500 per month, and stipends covering tuition, books, a laptop, and fees, making coursework free.
requirements: Partnership among a union educator training center, employers, child care resource and referral agencies, community colleges, and funders to deliver coursework, coaching, and financial supports
constraints: Designed for licensed family child care providers who work independently, a segment whose earnings are very low
target_learners: Current licensed family child care providers, predominantly low-income women of color
target_learning_goals: Child development knowledge and skills for early childhood teaching; attainment of California Child Development Permits
examples: In the FCC program's 2-year existence, 95 apprentices have earned new permits.

citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: Skyline College Education/Child Development Program: community college lab school with mentored clinical practice
description: Skyline College's Education/Child Development Program is a traditional community college department preparing early educators for classroom teaching toward an associate degree or Child Development Permit. Its on-campus Child Development Laboratory Center provides "high-quality mentoring and teaching practice early in their academic careers." A Teacher Track Learning Community lets some students gain early student teaching experience and earn a Child Development Associate Teacher Permit in their first year, and faculty use engaging teaching strategies tied to practice with a prescribed guided pathway.
requirements: An on-campus lab school, faculty collaboration to align coursework and field experiences, and ECE-specific academic and career advising

examples: Alumni speak extremely highly of their preparation and readiness for teaching.
