article_title: 5 Things for Advocates to Know about Chronic Absenteeism
citation: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://EdTrust.org
title: Address chronic absence through tiered prevention and early intervention rather than punishment
description: This principle holds that solving chronic absence requires understanding and addressing the underlying challenges causing students to miss school. The brief states "What works is a tiered response, beginning with universal supports that promote positive conditions of learning and then bolstering with additional interventions that provide more personalized and increasingly intensive interventions, as needed." Such prevention-oriented approaches are described as more effective and less costly than punitive, legal-system-dependent approaches.
requirements: Tiered approach specifics tailored to local realities, challenges, assets, and strengths
Partnering closely with students and families to understand their challenges and strengths
constraints: A cookie cutter approach is much less effective, especially post-pandemic given greater differences in families' economic, social, and health conditions
target_learners: K-12 students at risk of chronic absence
Preschool and kindergarten students
target_learning_goals: Consistent school attendance
Access to classroom instruction and learning conditions
examples: The brief urges school and district leaders to implement locally tailored multi-tiered systems of support to identify and connect students with needed resources, and states to provide guidance and professional development helping districts take a tiered approach.
key_sources: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627994

article_title: 5 Things for Advocates to Know about Chronic Absenteeism
citation: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://EdTrust.org
title: Reducing chronic absence requires authentic partnerships with students, families, and communities
description: This principle holds that schools cannot solve attendance problems alone. The brief states "Unless school leaders draw upon the knowledge of their students and families, they are unlikely to create effective solutions, especially given the diverse and rapidly changing realities that affect student attendance." Schools should partner with community organizations and public agencies to resolve barriers to attendance and build relationships, engaging marginalized communities in co-developing solutions.
requirements: Strong relationships with students and families, especially from marginalized communities
Educators and staff examining their own biases and learning about students' and families' identities and experiences
constraints: Effective only when engagement is authentic co-development rather than top-down; the brief stresses drawing on family knowledge
target_learners: Students from marginalized communities
K-12 students facing attendance barriers
target_learning_goals: Reduced chronic absence
Belonging and engagement in school
examples: The brief recommends organizing youth and families to work with schools and districts to identify attendance barriers and develop solutions, and asking for state funding and technical assistance to forge authentic partnerships.
key_sources: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627994

article_title: 5 Things for Advocates to Know about Chronic Absenteeism
citation: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://EdTrust.org
title: Chronic absence is a reflection of the school and community environment, so improve conditions for learning
description: This principle frames chronic absence as an indicator of systemic conditions rather than individual failing. The brief states "Chronic absence reflects the challenges students face in school, such as bullying, lack of an engaging curriculum or meaningful relationships, and feeling physically or emotionally unsafe." It also results from insufficient community resources like unstable housing, inadequate healthcare, and poor transportation. High absence levels reflect systemic challenges and historical discrimination requiring programmatic or policy solutions.
requirements: Policymakers and practitioners creating environments where students and families feel welcome and valued
Professional development helping adults build relationships and support students from diverse backgrounds
constraints: Barriers are cyclical: lack of meaningful relationships leads to disengagement and absence, which then prevents building belonging
target_learners: K-12 students affected by adverse school or community conditions
target_learning_goals: Engagement in school
Positive, equitable learning conditions
examples: The brief urges leaders to use school climate data for improvement, ensure curriculum is rigorous and reflective of students' diverse experiences, and use chronic absence data to allocate resources where disparities are greatest.
key_sources: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627994

article_title: Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators
citation: Nicholas Munyan-Penney and Sarah Mehrotra. (2023). Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Four equity pillars framework for federal assessment policy
description: The report develops four "equity pillars" — ensuring consistent, high expectations for student success; encouraging relevant, inclusive assessments; providing timely, actionable, and easily accessible results; and making assessment results meaningful — as criteria for improving federal assessment policy. The pillars are grounded in the focus group findings and Ed Trust's equity-centered values, and are intended as a framework for forthcoming federal policy action including ESSA reauthorization. The report states the pillars "set clear priorities for what we believe should be the future of statewide assessments" and hopes they will be used by other advocates to assess future policy proposals.
requirements: Federal assessment policy proposals must maintain comparable, disaggregated statewide summative assessment data for the pillars to apply as intended
constraints: The framework addresses statewide summative assessments and federal policy, not classroom or local assessment design
The report notes faster results are in direct tension with developing more complex, authentic test items that take longer to score
target_learners: students of color
students from low-income backgrounds
students with disabilities
English learners
target_learning_goals: college and career readiness
equitable access to grade-level standards
examples: Pillar 3 cites Maryland releasing spring 2022 results in late January 2023, and suggests initial results be usable by educators while data-quality reviews are completed
key_sources: Nicholas Munyan-Penney and Sarah Mehrotra. (2023). Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators. Ed Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628034

article_title: Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators
citation: Nicholas Munyan-Penney and Sarah Mehrotra. (2023). Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Typology of four assessment types: statewide summative, diagnostic, formative, and interim
description: The report's sidebar defines the four assessment types schools use. Statewide summative assessments are year-end tests administered to all students across a state, and "provide insights on the extent to which students have mastered grade-level content that is aligned to state college and career readiness academic standards." Diagnostic assessments are administered near the beginning of the year to identify skills, strengths, and weaknesses; formative assessments are classroom-based checks such as exit tickets, quizzes, and unit tests; interim assessments are administered a few times per year to track progress toward grade-level mastery and monitor interventions. The report argues the four types should ideally form a coherent, aligned picture of student achievement.
requirements: Each assessment should be aligned with a high-quality curriculum and state standards, and stakeholders empowered to use each for its intended purpose
constraints: The report notes different assessments are not always aligned with one another, state standards, and/or the curriculum
target_learners: K-12 students in grades 3-8 and high school
target_learning_goals: mastery of grade-level content aligned to state college and career readiness standards
examples: Federal law requires math and ELA summative assessments in grades 3-8 and once in high school, and science assessments once in grades 3-5, 6-9, and 10-12
key_sources: Nicholas Munyan-Penney and Sarah Mehrotra. (2023). Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators. Ed Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628034

article_title: How School Discipline Impacts Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Blair Wriston, Nancy Duchesneau. (2023). How School Discipline Impacts Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Adopt evidence-based, restorative, relationship-focused discipline instead of punitive and exclusionary measures
description: The brief argues schools should replace harmful exclusionary and punitive practices (suspensions, expulsions, corporal punishment, seclusion, restraint, hardening measures) with evidence-based approaches such as restorative justice and PBIS. Restorative approaches "can be used to build and repair relationships while also holding students accountable for their actions," keeping students in the classroom where they can learn from conflict and supporting holistic development.
requirements: Implementation with a race-equity lens so practices are fairly applied and do not reproduce disparities
constraints: The brief warns hardening practices such as school police and metal detectors have not been shown to increase school safety and disproportionately harm underserved students
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Social, emotional, and academic development; safe and inclusive school climates
examples: The brief points to restorative justice and Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) as positive, evidence-based discipline approaches, and to DC's guidance and funding for restorative implementation.
key_sources: Blair Wriston, Nancy Duchesneau. (2023). How School Discipline Impacts Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628035

article_title: How School Discipline Impacts Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Blair Wriston, Nancy Duchesneau. (2023). How School Discipline Impacts Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Is Your State Prioritizing Social, Emotional, and Academic Development? 50-state scan
description: Released in 2022 by Ed Trust in partnership with CASEL, building on the 2020 report Social, Emotional, and Academic Development Through an Equity Lens, this 50-state scan "shows how states support the social, emotional, and academic needs of students in their discipline policies, as well as four other key policy areas": professional development, rigorous and culturally sustaining curriculum, student/family/community engagement, and wraparound services. Educators, advocates, and policymakers can use it to compare their state's discipline policies.
requirements: States' discipline and SEAD policy documents must be publicly available for scanning and comparison
target_learners: P-12 students across all 50 states
target_learning_goals: State policy support for social, emotional, and academic development
examples: The brief suggests educators, advocates, and policymakers use the scan to evaluate how their state's discipline policies compare to other states.

article_title: How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: States should set equity-centered discipline goals, publish disaggregated discipline data, and promote positive approaches such as restorative justice
description: The brief argues harmful discipline and dress codes damage students' SEAD and disproportionately exclude students of color and students with disabilities. It recommends states "adopt more positive approaches to discipline, such as restorative justice, which empowers students to build, maintain, and repair relationships and resolve conflicts," set goals to reduce disparities, and make discipline data publicly transparent.
requirements: Clear state goals to reduce disparities and overuses in discipline
Publicly transparent discipline data
constraints: Many of these policy areas are led at the local level; states influence districts through goals, guidance, and funding rather than direct control
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to learning opportunities free from exclusionary discipline
examples: Texas limits out-of-school suspensions for students below third grade to offenses involving weapons or drugs and publicly reports district-level discipline data disaggregated by race
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628037

article_title: How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: Professional development should build educators' culturally affirming environments, relationship-building skills, and asset-based mindsets
description: The brief states educators "must have the skills to create culturally affirming environments, build relationships with their students, and support students' academic success," plus mindsets geared toward removing systemic barriers. It recommends high-quality professional learning in asset-based pedagogies, belonging and inclusiveness, adult self-awareness, and environments supporting holistic student development.
requirements: High-quality and relevant professional learning opportunities for all adults in schools
target_learners: P-12 educators and the students they serve
target_learning_goals: Educator capacity to support students' social, emotional, and academic development with an equity lens
examples: Texas identifies a network of intermediary organizations providing high-quality professional development for equitable practices and requires teacher preparation programs to train educators to integrate students' SEAD
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628037

article_title: How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: Students need equitable access to rigorous, culturally sustaining curricula and advanced coursework to thrive
description: The brief argues students "should have access to rigorous, deeper learning and culturally sustaining curricula," because when students see themselves in the work and feel challenged, their belief in reaching their goals strengthens. It recommends guidance and funding for standards-aligned, culturally sustaining curricula and equitable, even automatic, enrollment in advanced coursework.
requirements: Guidance and a review process for selecting curricula aligned to learning standards and culturally sustaining criteria
State education agency staff to support districts with implementation
target_learners: P-12 students, including those inequitably enrolled in advanced coursework
target_learning_goals: Rigorous learning, cultural relevance, and equitable access to advanced coursework
examples: Texas provides guidance for selecting standards-aligned curricula, funding to expand advanced coursework enrollment, and publicly reports advanced coursework data disaggregated by student demographics
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628037

article_title: How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: Multi-tiered or integrated systems of support (MTSS) as wraparound services framework
description: The brief describes MTSS, "also known as wraparound services," as frameworks districts and schools can use to connect services to students, providing access to resources to overcome academic and non-academic barriers to success. When schools identify and provide targeted supports, meet students' health and well-being, and ensure students feel they belong, students can better engage in schools. The brief recommends districts conduct student-level and system-level strengths and needs assessments and measure fidelity of implementation.
requirements: Districts monitor effectiveness of MTSS and conduct strengths and needs assessments
Funding and guidance for evidence-based multi-tiered systems of support
target_learners: K-12 students needing targeted social-emotional, physical and mental health, or family supports, including students experiencing homelessness
target_learning_goals: Removing academic and non-academic barriers so students can engage in school
examples: Texas includes a Children's Commission coordinating interagency services and provides health, housing, and oral health supports and homelessness guidance
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628037

Its toolkit includes a diagnostic tool organized around "key questions" for identifying problem areas, plus practical guidebooks offering actions to address them. The brief highlights relevant key questions under each SEAD policy section for district leaders and advocates.

target_learning_goals: Diagnosing and addressing equity problems in the student experience

article_title: How Does Tennessee Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Tennessee Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: SEAD framework: six policy areas for equitable social, emotional, and academic development
description: The brief defines SEAD as "A HOLISTIC APPROACH TO SUPPORTING STUDENTS' DEVELOPMENT AND LEARNING THAT IS INTEGRAL TO ENSURING POSITIVE OUTCOMES IN SCHOOL AND BEYOND." It organizes state policy action into six areas: inclusive discipline and dress code policies, meaningful professional development for all adults, equitable access to rigorous and culturally sustaining curricula, engaging students and families as full partners, integrated wraparound services, and diversifying the educator workforce. The framework treats academic, social, and emotional development as inseparable and equity-centered.
requirements: State and district leaders coordinate policies across all six areas rather than treating SEAD as a single program
constraints: Many of these policy areas are led at the local level, with state leaders playing a supporting role
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color, students from low-income backgrounds, and other underserved students
target_learning_goals: Holistic social, emotional, and academic development and positive school outcomes
examples: The brief audits Tennessee's policies against each of the six areas, listing bright spots and improvement priorities for each
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Tennessee Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630070

article_title: How Does Massachusetts Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Massachusetts Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. EdTrust.org. https://edtrust.org
title: Multi-tiered or integrated systems of support (MTSS) as wraparound services framework
description: The brief describes MTSS, also known as wraparound services, as 'frameworks that districts and schools can use to connect services to students,' providing access to resources to overcome academic and non-academic barriers to success. When schools identify and provide targeted supports, meet students' health and well-being, and ensure students feel they belong, students can better engage in school. Massachusetts supports MTSS through guidance, funding, and Medicaid billing authorization without IEP or IFSP documentation.

article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: SEAD as a holistic approach to supporting students' development and learning across six policy areas
description: The brief frames social, emotional, and academic development (SEAD) as "A HOLISTIC APPROACH TO SUPPORTING STUDENTS' DEVELOPMENT AND LEARNING THAT IS INTEGRAL TO ENSURING POSITIVE OUTCOMES IN SCHOOL AND BEYOND." It organizes state policy support for SEAD into six areas: inclusive discipline and dress code policies, professional development for adults in schools, equitable access to rigorous and culturally sustaining curricula, engagement of students and families as partners, integrated wraparound services, and diversifying the educator workforce. The framework is used to audit Washington's policies and to generate questions district leaders and advocates can ask about local implementation.
requirements: State leaders must set expectations and provide guidance and funding so local leaders can implement SEAD with an equity lens
constraints: Many of these policy areas are led at the local level, so state policy alone does not determine implementation
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color, students from low-income backgrounds, and other underserved students
target_learning_goals: Healthy development and rigorous learning that produce positive outcomes in school and beyond
examples: The brief audits Washington's policies in each of the six areas, listing bright spots, improvement priorities, and key questions for district leaders
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: States should set equity-centered discipline goals, transparent data, and positive approaches such as restorative justice
description: The brief argues that harmful discipline practices and dress codes damage students' social, emotional, and academic development, and that students of color and students with disabilities are disproportionately excluded from school. It recommends that "States can influence district and school disciplinary actions by setting clear goals to reduce disparities and overuses in discipline, ensuring a strong set of data is publicly transparent, and adopting more positive approaches to discipline, such as restorative justice." Washington's bright spots include banning corporal punishment, zero-tolerance policies, exclusionary discipline for young learners and minor offenses, and discriminatory hair and grooming codes.
requirements: Guidance and funding for restorative discipline policies, professional development in positive discipline practices, and state agency staff to support districts with technical assistance
constraints: Washington still needs equity-centered goals to decrease exclusionary discipline and reduce disparities, and discipline data disaggregated beyond race and gender
target_learners: P-12 students, especially students of color and students with disabilities who are disproportionately excluded
target_learning_goals: Opportunities to learn and develop holistically without exclusionary discipline
examples: Washington bans corporal punishment and harmful practices including zero-tolerance policies and discriminatory hair and grooming codes
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: Professional development should build educators' culturally affirming skills, relationships, and anti-racist mindsets
description: The brief holds that to equitably support students' SEAD, educators must have the skills to create culturally affirming environments, build relationships with students, and support academic success, with mindsets geared toward anti-racism. It states that "Professional development (PD) ensures that educators learn these mindsets and skills," and urges states to support professional learning in asset-based pedagogies such as culturally responsive practices, diversity, equity, and inclusion, adult social-emotional learning or adult mindsets, and evidence-based, equity-focused systemic SEL for students. Washington already requires preparation programs to train teachers in culturally responsive pedagogy and provides online SEL modules for staff.
requirements: Preparation-program training requirements, licensure renewal tied to mastery of SEAD-supporting skills, and state agency staff to help districts identify and fund high-quality PD
constraints: Washington lacks clear equity-centered goals articulating a vision for PD addressing adult mindsets and SEL, and does not publicly report educators' perceptions of district PD offerings
target_learners: Educators in schools serving P-12 students
target_learning_goals: Culturally affirming environments, educator-student relationships, and support for students' academic success and well-being
examples: Washington requires preparation programs to provide training in effective, culturally responsive pedagogy and offers online SEL modules for staff
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: Students need access to rigorous, culturally sustaining curricula with equitable advanced-coursework enrollment
description: The brief argues that students must be challenged and encouraged to meet high expectations through rigorous, deeper learning and culturally sustaining curricula. It reasons that "When students can both see themselves in the work and feel their teachers challenging them to excel, what follows is a stauncher belief in themselves to reach their goals." Washington's bright spots include state goals calling on districts to equitably enroll students in advanced coursework, guidance for adopting culturally sustaining curricula and standards-aligned curricula, automatic enrollment in advanced coursework in high school, and public reporting of dual credit completion disaggregated by demographics.
requirements: State education agency staff to support curricular needs, guidance on selecting culturally sustaining curricula aligned to learning standards, and a review process for determining whether curricula meet these criteria
constraints: Washington's goals do not explicitly state curricula should be rigorous and culturally sustaining, and lack specific actions for equitable advanced-coursework enrollment or disaggregated enrollment and success data by course type
target_learners: P-12 students, with attention to equitable access for underserved students
target_learning_goals: Rigorous, deeper learning; self-belief in reaching goals; access to advanced coursework and college and career preparation
examples: Washington requires automatic enrollment in advanced coursework in high school and publicly reports dual credit completion disaggregated by student demographics
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: Multi-tiered or integrated systems of support (MTSS) as wraparound services
description: The brief describes multi-tiered or integrated systems of support (MTSS), "ALSO KNOWN AS WRAPAROUND SERVICES," as frameworks districts and schools can use to connect services to students, providing "STUDENTS WITH ACCESS TO RESOURCES TO OVERCOME ACADEMIC AND NON-ACADEMIC BARRIERS TO SUCCESS." When schools identify and provide targeted supports, meet students' health and well-being, and foster belonging, students can better engage in school. Washington supports MTSS adoption with guidance and funding, health and housing supports, an anti-bullying policy naming targeted groups, transgender-inclusive athletics and facilities policies, and requirements that districts monitor MTSS progress using student data.
requirements: Districts must conduct student-level and school-level needs and strengths assessments, and monitor the progress and impacts of support systems for continuous improvement
constraints: Washington does not explicitly prioritize multi-tiered systems for students with the highest needs, does not require fidelity-of-implementation reporting, and lacks mandated school counseling at the 250:1 ratio recommended by the American School Counselor Association
target_learners: P-12 students needing targeted social-emotional, physical and mental health, or family supports, including students experiencing homelessness
target_learning_goals: Overcoming academic and non-academic barriers to success; student engagement and sense of belonging in school
examples: Washington prohibits lunch-shaming for unpaid meal debt and provides oral health supports and information for supporting students experiencing homelessness
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: The four-pillar framework of community schools: integrated student supports, expanded learning time, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership
description: The report organizes community schools implementation around four evidence-based pillars, or features: "(1) integrated student supports, (2) expanded learning time, (3) family and community engagement, and (4) collaborative leadership." State grant programs use these pillars to structure allowable uses of funds—New Mexico implementation grants, Vermont grants, and Georgia's certification process all fund activities mapped to the pillars. The framework functions as the report's organizing account of what a community school is and does, alongside practices grounded in the science of learning and development such as trauma-informed supports.
requirements: Implementation requires organizing in- and out-of-school resources, supports, and opportunities across educators, families, community members, and students as partners.
constraints: The report notes the strategy "takes time and resources to put into place" and, when implemented well, is associated with improved student outcomes.
target_learners: K-12 students in high-need schools and districts
target_learning_goals: Student attendance, academic achievement, high school graduation, and healthy development
examples: New Mexico implementation grant funds support a full-time community school coordinator with flexibility for expenditures supporting the four pillars; Georgia's Whole Child Model pairs the pillars with five whole child tenets (healthy, safe, engaged, supported, challenged).
key_sources: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: Provide ongoing funding through school funding formulas because it is more predictable and sustainable than time-limited grants, especially for coordinative staffing
description: The report recommends ongoing investments through school funding formulas (set-asides or entitlement grants) because "ongoing funding is a more predictable and sustainable source of support for districts and schools than grant programs that might be discontinued—an especially important consideration for the additional coordinative staffing required to implement community schools." Multiyear and ongoing commitments matter because the community schools strategy is complex and takes time to fully implement. Grant funding can still be increased over time and can precede an ongoing stream.
requirements: A stable state funding mechanism (formula set-aside or entitlement grant) and funded coordinator positions at school and LEA levels.
constraints: Grant programs are time-limited and may be discontinued; the report presents grants as a precursor or complement, not a replacement, for ongoing funding.
target_learners: Students in high-need schools and districts receiving community schools funding
target_learning_goals: Sustained implementation of community schools programming and coordinative staffing
examples: Maryland's Concentration of Poverty entitlement grant provides annual personnel grants of $248,833 per eligible school; New York's Foundation Aid set-aside reached $250 million annually.
key_sources: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: California Community Schools Partnership Program (CCSPP): a $4.1 billion state grant and technical assistance investment
description: The CCSPP is the nation's largest state investment in community schools: "In 2021, California passed a historic $3 billion investment in the CCSPP, followed by an additional $1.1 billion investment in 2022." It provides three grant types—planning grants up to $200,000 per LEA for up to 2 years, implementation grants of $150,000–$500,000 annually per school for up to 5 years, and extension grants up to $100,000 annually for 2 years—plus approximately $140 million for a network of regional technical assistance centers with a lead center. The first funding round awarded planning grants to 192 LEAs and implementation grants to 76 LEAs representing 458 school sites.
requirements: Applicants must serve a student population in which 50% or more of pupils are from low-income households, English learners, or youth in foster care, or exceed state-average rates of dropout, suspension and expulsion, homelessness, foster care, or justice involvement.
constraints: The state prioritizes applicants serving 80% or more high-need pupils; the statute requires an annual formative evaluation from 2023 through a final report by December 31, 2031.
target_learners: Low-income students, English learners, and youth in foster care in California high-poverty schools
target_learning_goals: Pupil well-being and engagement through integrated supports, expanded learning, family engagement, and collaborative leadership
examples: Grants can cover staffing, needs and assets assessments, partnership development, service coordination, family engagement, data collection and evaluation, and professional development on trauma-informed practices.
key_sources: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: Maryland Concentration of Poverty (CoP) entitlement grant program
description: Established by the Blueprint for Maryland's Future in 2020, the CoP program provides all eligible Maryland schools two complementary state funding sources: personnel grants of $248,833 annually for essential community schools staff (a community school coordinator and a licensed health care practitioner), and per-pupil grants on a sliding scale. "In 2022, the CoP grant program distributed a total of $116.7 million in state aid to 300 eligible schools (approximately 21% of all public schools in the state)." Eligibility phases in over time, starting at an 80% free or reduced-price meal threshold and decreasing by 5% each year.
requirements: Personnel grant eligibility is determined by the greater of the proportion of students receiving free or reduced-price meals, identified in a Community Eligibility Provision school, or identified through direct certification.
constraints: Per-pupil grant eligibility thresholds differ from personnel grant thresholds (80% in fiscal year 2022, declining to at least 55% starting in 2027).
target_learners: Students in high-poverty Maryland public schools
target_learning_goals: Expanded and enriched learning time, integrated student services, family and community supports, and staff professional development
examples: Per-pupil grants fund integrated student services (medical, dental, vision care, transportation, healthy food, attendance support), family supports, trauma-informed professional development, and additional support staff such as social workers and restorative practice coaches.
key_sources: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: State certification processes for community schools: Florida's UCF Community Partnership Schools and Georgia's Whole Child Model School certification
description: Two states support community schools through university- or state-led certification. Florida funds a certification process administered by the University of Central Florida's Center for Community Schools, with $7.1 million in state funding in fiscal year 2022 serving 36 schools; certification rests on 12 standards in the UCF-Certified Community Partnership Schools Fundamental Practices 3.0 and a partnership of a nonprofit, a university or college, a school district, and a health care provider. Georgia's Department of Education created a Whole Child Model School certification process whose "overarching goal ... is to help community schools develop and independently sustain a whole child education model," combining the four community schools pillars with five whole child tenets.
requirements: Florida schools submit quarterly progress reports and complete a self-study reviewed by four to six external reviewers including site visits; Georgia participating schools must employ a whole child coordinator and establish a collaborative leadership team with a needs-assessment-based improvement plan.
constraints: Georgia participation is voluntary with no direct state funding for pilot schools; certification lasts 3 years with recertification contingent on growth in at least one whole child area. Florida grants step down after certification as schools blend and braid funding.
target_learners: Students in participating Florida and Georgia community schools
target_learning_goals: Whole child education, sustainability of community school models, and nonacademic barrier reduction
examples: Florida planning grants are awarded up to $80,000 with a 25% community contribution match; implementation grants typically range from $150,000 to $200,000 per year for the first 5 years.
key_sources: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402

article_title: Educating Teachers in California: What Matters for Teacher Preparedness?
citation: Patrick, S. K., Darling-Hammond, L., & Kini, T. (2023). Educating teachers in California: What matters for teacher preparedness? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/956.678
title: CTC teacher preparation program completer survey system
description: A statewide survey system administered by the California Commission on Teacher Credentialing since 2016–17, embedded in the online preliminary credential application so that "the survey responses across all years are high." Between 2016–17 and 2020–21, "59,140 completers from 107 different California TPPs responded to the survey." The survey captures completers' perceptions of preparedness across the six California Standards for the Teaching Profession domains, clinical pathway, clinical support, student teaching hours, cooperating teacher behaviors, and opportunity to learn reading, writing, and math teaching. Since 2019 the CTC has also fielded cooperating teacher and employer surveys.
requirements: Completion is tied to the credential recommendation and application process, which the report credits for high response rates
constraints: It excludes California TPP completers who never applied for a preliminary credential in California and teachers prepared out of state; response rates for CSU completers must be estimated because CSU's data system does not track respondents
target_learners: teacher candidates completing approved California TPPs
target_learning_goals: assessing completer preparedness across the teaching performance expectations
supporting program accreditation and continuous improvement
examples: Survey results are integrated into a public data dashboard showing statewide trends, while institution-level results are available to programs to support programmatic improvement
key_sources: Patrick, S. K., Darling-Hammond, L., & Kini, T. (2023). Educating teachers in California: What matters for teacher preparedness? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/956.678

article_title: Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System
citation: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://edtrustmidwest.org
title: Weight school funding toward districts with the highest concentrations of poverty using an Opportunity Index with weights of 40%-100%
description: The brief recommends Michigan replace its flat 11.5% At-Risk weight with a Massachusetts-style Opportunity Index in which "districts with the most students living in poverty receive the highest additional funding." Massachusetts's 2019 Student Opportunity Act used funding weights of 40% to 100% for students experiencing poverty. The brief argues targeted funding maximizes learning gains relative to across-the-board increases.
requirements: A funding formula mechanism that identifies district poverty concentration and applies graduated weights
constraints: The brief estimates full implementation would cost approximately $5.3 billion annually, against $747.5 million currently spent on At-Risk funding
target_learners: students from low-income backgrounds
students in districts with high concentrations of poverty
target_learning_goals: equitable access to educational resources needed for academic success
examples: Massachusetts's 2019 Student Opportunity Act prioritized equity with funding weights of 40% to 100% for students experiencing poverty while keeping a lower base foundation amount than Michigan's
key_sources: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630507

article_title: Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System
citation: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://edtrustmidwest.org
title: Fund English Learners through a weighted student funding formula of 80%-100% based on English language proficiency
description: The brief recommends that Michigan lawmakers "implement funding weights ranging from 80% to 100% based on students' language proficiency," in line with leading states and research. It argues English Learners need additional resources and instructional supports for language acquisition, including adjusted student-teacher ratios and one-on-one tutoring.
requirements: Weights graduated by students' English language proficiency
District capacity to provide varied support services and curricula and engage with parents and the English Learner community
constraints: Fully implementing the MPEO weights would cost approximately $500 million annually versus $26.5 million currently spent, a gap the brief puts at $474.4 million
target_learners: English Learners in K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: English language acquisition
access to instructional supports necessary for language acquisition
examples: Maryland is phasing in a weight of 85% more and Georgia now allocates 160% more funding to English Learners, per the brief's comparison
key_sources: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630507

article_title: Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System
citation: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://edtrustmidwest.org
title: Fully fund the foundation allowance for students with disabilities and close the special education shortfall gap
description: The brief recommends Michigan provide districts the full foundation allowance for students with disabilities plus reimbursements for special education delivery, prioritizing closure of the "shortfall gap" between district spending and state reimbursement. Michigan currently provides only 75% of the foundation allowance for these students and reimburses just over 28% of special education service costs.
requirements: Replacing the partial reimbursement system under which districts shoulder much of the funding responsibility
Lawmakers should investigate options for creating a weighted funding formula for students with disabilities
constraints: One early-2023 estimate put the shortfall gap at $343 million; cited research suggests adequately funding students with disabilities may require weights of at least 185% of base funding
target_learners: students with disabilities
peers without disabilities in underfunded districts
target_learning_goals: access to needed special education services and supports
examples: Michigan's fiscal year 2023 budget invested deeply in closing the shortfall gap, which the brief calls a first step toward funding equity
key_sources: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630507

article_title: Equitable & Inclusive Hiring Practices: A Reference Guide of Strategies to Grow & Diversify the Educator Workforce
citation: Equitable & Inclusive Hiring Practices: A Reference Guide of Strategies to Grow & Diversify the Educator Workforce. (2023). Rhode Island Department of Education, Office of Educator Excellence. https://www.ride.ri.gov/
title: PAUSE framework for interrupting bias in recruitment and hiring decisions
description: The PAUSE framework, developed by Vanderbilt University, is presented as a tool that "can encourage critical self-reflection and interrupt the effects of unchecked biases." The guide recommends applying it to recruitment and hiring decisions to "reveal the ways in which bias might be manifesting in the process." It sits alongside measures such as the Harvard Implicit Association Test, which the guide calls "a starting point" for individuals and teams working to interrupt bias.
requirements: Hiring teams work to understand their biases and identify strategies to manage them before applying the framework
constraints: Project Implicit is quoted as stating that durably changing implicit preferences may require more than a quick five-minute intervention
target_learners: school and district leaders
HR professionals
school-based hiring teams
target_learning_goals: interrupting implicit and explicit bias in recruitment, hiring, and workplace interactions
examples: The guide positions PAUSE within Part IV on anti-bias strategies, alongside establishing objective criteria and diverse finalist pools
key_sources: Equitable & Inclusive Hiring Practices: A Reference Guide of Strategies to Grow & Diversify the Educator Workforce. (2023). Rhode Island Department of Education, Office of Educator Excellence. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED633258

article_title: Braiding Funds to Support an Effective and Diverse Educator Workforce
citation: Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. (2022). Braiding Funds to Support an Effective and Diverse Educator Workforce. https://www.wested.org/
title: California Educator Effectiveness Block Grant as a braiding hub for professional learning, school climate, and student well-being strategies
description: An element of the braiding toolkit: the Educator Effectiveness Block Grant 'can be used to address areas of need related to professional learning, school climate, social-emotional learning, mental health, restorative justice, implicit bias, and discrimination and harassment prevention.' Table 1 lists fundable strategies, including 'professional learning, coaching, and mentoring opportunities for administrators and teachers, as well as paraprofessionals and classified staff,' covering coaching, instruction across subjects, reengagement and accelerated learning, trauma-informed practices, English Learner instruction, inclusive practices, and early childhood education. Six other funding sources can be braided with it.
requirements: Uses must supplement proportional costs aligned with the grant's allowable activity areas
constraints: Applies to California LEAs under the state's Educator Effectiveness Block Grant rules
target_learners: Administrators, teachers, paraprofessionals, and classified staff who work with pupils
target_learning_goals: Educator effectiveness: improved instruction, positive school climate, and student well-being
examples: Diversity-prioritizing uses include contracting with 'PD providers that specialize in anti-racist practices and culturally sustaining pedagogies' and supporting veteran teachers of color as coaches and mentors
key_sources: Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. (2022). Braiding Funds to Support an Effective and Diverse Educator Workforce. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED633297

article_title: Accountability for Postsecondary Readiness. A 50-State Analysis
citation: Mitchell P. Herz, Lamar L. Johnson, and Eric W. Crane. (2023). Accountability for Postsecondary Readiness: A 50-State Analysis. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three-type taxonomy of postsecondary readiness measures: academic, career, and military
description: The brief organizes the measures states use in postsecondary readiness indicators into three types. As the authors state, "Three main types of measures were identified: academic, career, and military." Academic measures include advanced course completion, SAT/ACT thresholds, on-track-to-graduate status, advanced diplomas, multilingual certificates, and college enrollment or remediation. Career measures include industry credentials, CTE course completion, work-based learning, and WorkKeys thresholds. Military measures include ASVAB thresholds or enlistment. The taxonomy emerged from coding the measures across all ESSA plans.
requirements: States must define which specific measures count within each type in their ESSA plans; where plans lacked detail, state agency websites were consulted.
constraints: The taxonomy reflects only measures documented in federally approved ESSA plans as of May 1, 2023.
target_learners: high school students
target_learning_goals: postsecondary readiness for college, career, and military pathways
examples: Pennsylvania's plan used the Career Standards Benchmark as its sole postsecondary readiness measure; North Dakota's plan included 23 separate measures.
key_sources: Mitchell P. Herz, Lamar L. Johnson, and Eric W. Crane. (2023). Accountability for Postsecondary Readiness: A 50-State Analysis. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED633301

article_title: Survey Development for Assessing Student Computing Career Intentions. Technical Report
citation: Kao, Y., Murphy, D., Hubbard Cheuoua, A., Kannan, P., Tsan, J., Jennings, K. E., Smith, H., Emanuel, S., & Miller, E. R. (2023). Survey development for assessing student computing career intentions: Technical report. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Seven-construct framework of computing career intentions spanning individual, situational, and social factors
description: The article organizes its survey around seven constructs derived from a literature review of career intentions research: coding self-efficacy, barrier-coping self-efficacy, interest in coding, intention to pursue a coding career, practical support, social support, and sense of belonging in computing. Constructs are grouped as "Individual Factors", "Situational Factors", and "Social Factors". Each construct is defined by the degree to which an individual holds a specific belief or perception, such as "The degree to which an individual feels they can be successful in coding-related tasks".
requirements: Items for each construct are administered as 5-point Likert matrix questions with agreement response options
constraints: The framework was operationalized for computing career intentions among participants of computer science education programs, not general career measurement
target_learners: participants of informal and formal computer science education programs, from high school students to adults
target_learning_goals: measuring individual, situational, and social factors shaping students' intentions to pursue computing careers
examples: The draft survey contained 32 computing-related items across the seven constructs, plus demographic questions
key_sources: Kao, Y., Murphy, D., Hubbard Cheuoua, A., Kannan, P., Tsan, J., Jennings, K. E., Smith, H., Emanuel, S., & Miller, E. R. (2023). Survey development for assessing student computing career intentions: Technical report. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED638631

article_title: Survey Development for Assessing Student Computing Career Intentions. Technical Report
citation: Kao, Y., Murphy, D., Hubbard Cheuoua, A., Kannan, P., Tsan, J., Jennings, K. E., Smith, H., Emanuel, S., & Miller, E. R. (2023). Survey development for assessing student computing career intentions: Technical report. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Computing career intentions survey instrument (32-item full version and 12-item short form)
description: A brief, culturally sensitive survey measuring computing career intentions, developed by WestEd with Google and validated through cognitive interviews, a small-scale field test, and a large-scale field test. The full version has 32 computing-related items across seven constructs, administered as 5-point Likert items in matrix questions. A reduced 12-item version was selected for embedding in longer program evaluation surveys, with items chosen for content, readability, factor loadings, DIF categories, and classical statistics.
requirements: Designed to be short enough to embed in a longer program evaluation survey without being burdensome for participants
constraints: Some items showed ceiling effects, making them less than ideal for measuring changes over time; several demographic comparison groups fell below the recommended minimum group size of 200 for DIF analysis
target_learners: computer science education program participants across age groups, including minors and adults
target_learning_goals: assessing coding self-efficacy, interest, career intention, practical and social support, and sense of belonging in computing
examples: Participants responded between August 22, 2022, and October 24, 2022, spending an average of 5.5 minutes to complete it
key_sources: Kao, Y., Murphy, D., Hubbard Cheuoua, A., Kannan, P., Tsan, J., Jennings, K. E., Smith, H., Emanuel, S., & Miller, E. R. (2023). Survey development for assessing student computing career intentions: Technical report. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED638631

article_title: The Search for More Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books
citation: Tanji Reed Marshall, Ph.D., and William H. Rodick, Ph.D. (2023). The Search for More: Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/booktool
title: Tool for Representational Balance in Books
description: A 10-criterion rubric, developed by The Education Trust after convening experts, consulting publishers, and synthesizing existing cultural-responsiveness and bias tools, designed to "guide a reader through any text to determine how people, cultures, and topics are represented." Its four sections cover creator and character identity, people, cultures, and topics, with each criterion framed as a question (e.g., "Are people of color multidimensional?"). The team applied it to 300 K-8 trade books from EdReports-favorably rated curricula, coding representations as complex, partial, or limited, and offers it publicly at edtrust.org/booktool for publishers, district leaders, educators, caregivers, and students.
requirements: Applied to texts by readers analyzing how people, cultures, and topics are represented; in this study it was applied to core trade books identified by publishers as expected reading for all students
constraints: The report acknowledges its ethnoracial grouping methods are imperfect and obscure distinctions across and within groups; identities present in the sampled books were not complex, limiting intersectional analysis
target_learners: K-8 students reading ELA curricula texts
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking about how people, cultures, and historical and social topics are represented in texts
examples: Applied to 300 K-8 books selected from trade book lists of publisher partners whose curricula partially or fully met EdReports quality measures, reaching at least 25% saturation per publisher and per grade band (K-2, 3-5, 6-8)
key_sources: Tanji Reed Marshall, Ph.D., and William H. Rodick, Ph.D. (2023). The Search for More: Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/booktool

article_title: The Search for More Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books
citation: Tanji Reed Marshall, Ph.D., and William H. Rodick, Ph.D. (2023). The Search for More: Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/booktool
title: Representational balance framework (complex, partial, limited representation)
description: The report's conceptual framework holds that curricula quality includes how people, cultures, and topics are represented, not only standards alignment, knowledge building, and usability. It defines "representational balance" as representation "that allows all students to see themselves and others in rich and varied ways that more accurately reflect the realities of people's lives," countering what Adichie calls "a single story." Representation is coded on three levels — complex ("mirrors the complexity of people, cultures, and topics"), partial ("not quite complex"), and limited ("perpetuates the marginalization of people, cultures, and topics") — using criteria of multidimensionality, agency, positive influence, stereotype avoidance, cultural immersion, equal value, and non-sanitized, multi-perspective, student-connected topics.
requirements: Assessing authorship alongside portrayal, since the framework treats who writes the stories as integral to how people, cultures, and topics are represented
constraints: The framework's initial analysis found so little diversity in sexual orientation, disability status, justice-system status, and other identity aspects that the report's analysis focuses on people of color
target_learners: K-8 students in English language arts classrooms
target_learning_goals: Seeing self and others represented complexly; developing critical thinking about texts
examples: The framework's people criteria (multidimensional, agency, positively influential) echo media tests like the Bechdel, DuVernay, and Vito Russo tests and align with ELA standards on character development analysis
key_sources: Tanji Reed Marshall, Ph.D., and William H. Rodick, Ph.D. (2023). The Search for More: Complex Racial and Ethnic Representation in Grade School Books. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/booktool

article_title: Increasing Access to Advanced Coursework in Texas
citation: Kristen Hengtgen, Hector Biaggi. (2024). Increasing Access to Advanced Coursework in Texas. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: OnRamps dual credit program (University of Texas)
description: OnRamps, established in 2011 by the University of Texas, offers virtual dual credit courses "taught by high school teachers but designed and supported by OnRamps staff and UT faculty." Courses require no placement assessment, so students whose test scores or grades may not convey readiness can still access advanced coursework, and students can choose to accept or decline college credit depending on their goals and performance. The program also offers free online professional development for virtual and hybrid educators on the TEA website and has served as a model for other institutions of higher education across Texas.
requirements: High school teachers deliver courses designed and supported by OnRamps staff and UT faculty
target_learners: Texas high school students, including those whose test scores or grades may not convey college readiness
target_learning_goals: Earning college credit and accessing college-level coursework while in high school
examples: OnRamps courses do not require a placement assessment, and students may decline college credit depending on their goals and course performance
key_sources: Kristen Hengtgen, Hector Biaggi. (2024). Increasing Access to Advanced Coursework in Texas. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED641978

article_title: School Funding Effectiveness: Evidence from California's Local Control Funding Formula
citation: Johnson, R. C. (2023). School funding effectiveness: Evidence from California's Local Control Funding Formula. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/529.194
title: California Local Control Funding Formula (LCFF)
description: The LCFF is California's school funding formula, enacted in 2013, which allocates state funding "by the proportion of unduplicated 'high-need' students in the district" rather than by district property wealth. It has three components: a base grant varying by grade span, a supplemental grant equal to 20% of the adjusted base grant per high-need student, and a concentration grant equal to 50% of the adjusted base grant per high-need student in districts with more than 55% high-need students. It rolled out from 2013 through 2019 with guaranteed multiyear distributions and minimal restrictions on district use of funds.
requirements: Districts must devise a Local Control Accountability Plan identifying how resources are principally directed to high-need students
constraints: Basic Aid districts with local revenue per pupil in excess of LCFF targets do not receive state funding and are not subject to LCFF requirements
Roughly 10% of state funding, including special education and transportation, is outside the LCFF
target_learners: K–12 public school students in California, particularly students from low-income families, English learners, and students in foster care
target_learning_goals: Reducing socioeconomic achievement gaps through equitable school funding
examples: In 2018–19, allocations totaled approximately $8,000 per pupil in base grants, $1,600 per high-need student in supplemental grants, and $5,300 per high-need student in concentration grants in districts with more than 55% high-need students
key_sources: Johnson, R. C. (2023). School funding effectiveness: Evidence from California's Local Control Funding Formula. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/529.194

article_title: Coaching at Scale: A Strategy for Strengthening the Early Learning Workforce
citation: Schachner, A., Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Barajas, J. (2024). Coaching at scale: A strategy for strengthening the early learning workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/984.909
title: Effective coaching combines a strong coach-educator partnership, reflection and individualized feedback, focused observations, intentional coaching plans, and job-embedded active learning
description: The report identifies a set of research-based characteristics of effective early childhood coaching models. As the executive summary states, "effective coaching relies on a strong partnership between coaches and educators; reflection and individualized feedback; focused observations; intentional coaching plans to guide sessions; and job-embedded learning opportunities for active learning." Each feature is grounded in reviews of coaching research, with the coach-coachee relationship described as the foundation of coaching effectiveness. The principle also encompasses coach knowledge: successful coaches need knowledge of the coaching model, general coaching and consultation skills, and knowledge of child development and teaching.
requirements: Coaches with knowledge of the specific coaching model and practices, general coaching and consultation skills such as understanding adult learning principles and building rapport, and knowledge of early childhood development and teaching
constraints: The report notes coach knowledge and skills "has received much less research attention than the other areas"
target_learners: Early childhood educators (lead and assistant teachers, home-based educators, site leaders)
target_learning_goals: Implementation of evidence-based instructional practices and improved adult-child interactions
examples: The five studied coaching systems aligned coaching content to quality standards, used classroom assessment tools to inform practice, and paired coaching with other professional development efforts.
key_sources: Schachner, A., Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Barajas, J. (2024). Coaching at scale: A strategy for strengthening the early learning workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/984.909

article_title: Coaching at Scale: A Strategy for Strengthening the Early Learning Workforce
citation: Schachner, A., Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Barajas, J. (2024). Coaching at scale: A strategy for strengthening the early learning workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/984.909
title: Coaching as a collaborative expert-practitioner relationship distinct from technical assistance, mentoring, and supervision
description: The report defines coaching as a distinct professional learning mechanism: "there is general agreement in the field that coaching involves a collaborative relationship between an expert and a practitioner with the aim of developing specific knowledge and skills through the use of planning, observation, action (e.g., modeling), feedback, and reflection." The report distinguishes coaching from technical assistance (which may not involve a collaborative relationship and can address noninstructional topics), from mentoring (typically between colleagues in similar roles), and from supervision (which evaluates job performance). In its purest form, coaching is distinct from supervisory and compliance functions.
requirements: A collaborative relationship between an expert coach and a practitioner aimed at developing specific knowledge and skills
constraints: Coaching is distinct from supervisory and compliance functions in its purest form, though some supervisors may act as coaches
target_learners: Early childhood educators and program leaders
target_learning_goals: Development of specific instructional knowledge and skills
examples: Coaching recipients are typically lead classroom educators, but coaches may also work with teaching teams including assistants and aides, and with program leaders on leadership knowledge and skills.
key_sources: Schachner, A., Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Barajas, J. (2024). Coaching at scale: A strategy for strengthening the early learning workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/984.909

article_title: Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and Implications from the Grant's First 4 Years
citation: Brannegan, A., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and implications from the grant's first 4 years. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/support/formative-evaluation-of-the-california-teacher-residency-grant-program
title: Teacher residency pathway: LEA-IHE partnership integrating credentialing coursework with a yearlong placement in an expert mentor teacher's classroom
description: A teacher residency is an intensive preparation pathway in which "a resident's credentialing coursework is integrated with a yearlong placement in the classroom of an expert mentor teacher." It is developed and operated by a partnership between a local educational agency and an institution of higher education with a state-approved preparation program, and residents typically receive financial support in exchange for a multi-year teaching commitment in the host LEA. The brief treats residencies as a route to well-prepared, retained 1st-year teachers responsive to local hiring needs.
requirements: A partnership between an LEA and an IHE with a state-approved teacher preparation program
Financial support for residents, typically tied to a several-year teaching commitment in the host LEA
constraints: The brief notes residency evidence is cited from prior studies (e.g., Guha et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2015) rather than tested in this brief
target_learners: teacher residency candidates in shortage fields such as special education, bilingual education, and STEM
target_learning_goals: rigorous clinical preparation for teaching
responsiveness to local LEA workforce needs
examples: TRGP residencies prepared 516 residents in special education, 366 in bilingual education, and 350 in STEM between 2019-20 and 2022-23
key_sources: Brannegan, A., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and implications from the grant's first 4 years. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/support/formative-evaluation-of-the-california-teacher-residency-grant-program

article_title: Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and Implications from the Grant's First 4 Years
citation: Brannegan, A., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Scaling California's Teacher Residency Grant Program: Findings and implications from the grant's first 4 years. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/support/formative-evaluation-of-the-california-teacher-residency-grant-program
title: Spread-and-depth framework for assessing the scale of a funded preparation pathway
description: The brief organizes its analysis of the TRGP around two dimensions of scale: "Spread considers the total number of residency partnerships and residents funded by the TRGP and their geographic distribution across the state," while "Depth considers the extent to which TRGP-funded residencies are beginning to make a meaningful impact on the teacher workforce in their host LEAs," including whether programs approach a size supporting sustainability and cost effectiveness. The framework lets policymakers see that a grant can spread widely yet remain shallow locally, and it frames the brief's tension between broadening access and deepening impact.
requirements: Administrative data on program and resident counts, geographic distribution, and local hiring needs to compute both dimensions
constraints: The brief notes its analysis presents a limited view: 2023-24 and 2024-25 data were unavailable, and extant data do not address resident effectiveness, resident experience, or LEA perceptions
target_learners: state policymakers and grant administrators scaling educator preparation programs
target_learning_goals: evaluating whether a funded pathway achieves meaningful local workforce impact and sustainability
examples: The brief applies the framework to the TRGP's first 4 years, finding growing spread but limited depth in most host LEAs and IHEs

article_title: New Mexico Community Schools: Improving Student Opportunities and Outcomes
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief
title: New Mexico's six key practices framework for community schools
description: The New Mexico Public Education Department's community schools framework identifies six site-level practices for implementation: collaborative leadership, shared power, and voice; powerful student and family engagement; rigorous, community-connected classroom instruction; expanded, culturally enriched learning opportunities; a culture of belonging, safety, and care; and integrated systems of support. The brief states these practices are "grounded in research and the expertise of community school practitioners participating in the national Community Schools Forward task force" and were integrated into the strategic vision and daily operation of the profiled schools.
requirements: State implementation grants and a full-time community school coordinator at each school to pursue the practices
constraints: Practices must be tailored to the local school community, per the brief's statement that integrated implementation is "tailored to the local school community"
target_learners: K-12 students in New Mexico public schools
target_learning_goals: Student well-being, engagement, attendance, and academic achievement
examples: The three profiled districts (Albuquerque, Peñasco, Roswell) integrated the six practices into school transformation efforts supported by PED implementation grants.
key_sources: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief

article_title: New Mexico Community Schools: Improving Student Opportunities and Outcomes
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief
title: Community schools as a whole-child strategy partnering with local organizations and families
description: The brief defines community schools, quoting the New Mexico PED, as "a whole child, comprehensive strategy to transform schools into places where educators, local community members, families, and students work together to strengthen conditions for student learning and healthy development." Schools achieve this by partnering with local organizations and families to organize in- and out-of-school resources such as health services, meals, and after-school programming. The strategy is positioned as an equity-centered, evidence-based approach to school transformation.

target_learners: K-12 students, particularly in under-resourced communities
target_learning_goals: Conditions for student learning and healthy development
examples: Los Padillas, Peñasco, and Roswell sites organized health clinics, food distributions, after-school programming, and family engagement structures under the strategy.
