title: Reflection systems rest on three mechanisms: interactive feedback, verbal reinforcement, and external verification with self-correction
description: The review describes reflection systems as underpinned by three complementary mechanisms that let AI agents evaluate performance and iteratively refine outputs: "These mechanisms include interactive feedback loops, verbal reinforcement, and external verification and self-correction." CRITIC operationalizes interactive feedback through a verify-then-correct cycle with external tools such as search engines and code interpreters; Reflexion converts feedback into episodic memory for iterative self-improvement; SELF-REFINE iterates generate-critique-refine within a single model using few-shot prompts. The review presents these as a hybrid structure combining internal evaluation with external tools.
requirements: Mechanisms combining internal evaluation processes and external tools to address error detection, adaptability, and knowledge gaps
constraints: Self-generated assessments can be limited by the model's inherent knowledge gaps or biases, which external verification addresses
target_learners: learners using AI-supported tutoring, feedback, and assessment tools
target_learning_goals: iterative improvement of outputs and feedback quality
metacognitive self-assessment
examples: Section 4.1.1 details CRITIC, Reflexion, and SELF-REFINE as exemplars of the three mechanisms

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding for Cognitive Engagement in an Intelligent Tutoring System
citation: Tithi, S.D., Alam, N., Yasir, T., Shi, Y., Tian, X., Chi, M., Barnes, T. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding for Cognitive Engagement in an Intelligent Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07308
title: ICAP-based operationalization of cognitive engagement levels through worked example types in an ITS
description: This framework maps the ICAP engagement modes onto concrete problem representations in an intelligent logic tutor. Problem Solving is treated as "Interactive in the ICAP framework, since students receive explicit accuracy feedback on each step"; Guided worked examples, adapted from the Parsons format with subgoal structure, represent the "activeengagement level in ICAP"; and Buggy worked examples, containing expert-designed errors students must find and fix, represent the "constructiveengagement level in ICAP". The article uses this mapping as the theoretically grounded basis for adaptive scaffolding policies that select among engagement levels.
requirements: The tutor must provide problem-solving interleaved with the two worked-example types, and the ICAP level of each activity must be assigned; the article notes that "defining the ICAP level of a learning activity is non-trivial" because feedback-driven reflection could make either type more interactive.
constraints: The operationalization was implemented and evaluated in one logic tutor in an undergraduate discrete math course; the authors state the design "should be replicated in other problem-solving domains" to establish generalizability.
target_learners: undergraduate students in a discrete math / computer science course
target_learning_goals: propositional logic proof construction and rule application
examples: In the study tutor, Guided examples presented partial solutions with missing node connections students complete by applying rules, while Buggy examples presented solutions with expert-designed bugs students identify and correct.

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: Persona progression model: a four-stage AI-instructor persona (Guide→Collaborator→Peer→Launcher) operationalizing the Gradual Release of Responsibility framework for AI-mediated instruction
description: The persona progression model ties the AI instructor's tone and scaffolding depth to the learner's position in the module sequence across four stages: Guide (patient teacher, explains every concept), Collaborator (working partner, asks before telling), Peer (senior colleague, terse and direct), and Launcher (states the goal and steps back). The article states that "The curriculum defines four personas, each specified as a prompt engineering directive in every module file", mapping 1:1 to GRR's four phases, with "I do it" reinterpreted so the learner is always hands-on. Persona boundaries are set at onboarding from three experience-level schedules (4/3/2/1, 3/3/3/1, 1/3/5/1) and can shift at module boundaries via the adaptive system. Implementation uses descriptive prompt directives alone, without fine-tuning, RLHF, or RAG.
requirements: Each module file must contain an explicit persona directive metadata line consumed by Claude Code when reading the module
constraints: The article notes a static tone either underwhelms beginners or patronizes experts, motivating stage-dependent personas; the adaptation is validated only for structural consistency, not instructional effectiveness
target_learners: professional software engineers learning an agentic AI coding tool, at beginner, intermediate, or advanced experience levels
target_learning_goals: compositional mastery of an agentic AI coding tool's features, from setup through multi-agent orchestration
examples: Module 1–3 use the Guide persona; the intermediate schedule assigns Guide to modules 1–3, Collaborator to 4–6, Peer to 7–9, and Launcher to module 10
key_sources: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: cc-self-train adaptive learning system: a three-layer hook-based engagement observation and scaffolding adjustment mechanism
description: The adaptive learning system observes learner engagement quality through keyword-heuristic classification of each learner message into six engagement categories with quality scores from 1 to 5, accumulated in a local learner profile. Layer 1 is a silent Stop hook that fires after every Claude response and computes streak booleans; Layer 2 injects a teaching note into Claude's context at session start based on the productive/unproductive ratio; Layer 3 adjusts the learner's Effective Level at module boundaries. The article describes "a two-timescale system" in which a slow clock adjusts the persona schedule at module boundaries using aggregate statistics while a fast clock triggers scaffolding changes mid-module using sequential patterns, governed by an asymmetric response principle that is quicker to increase scaffolding than to withdraw it.
requirements: Operates entirely through Claude Code's hook system with no external dependencies, no API calls for observation, and no web backend
constraints: Observation uses keyword heuristics rather than LLM-based classification, so individual classifications are noisy; Effective Level changes occur only at module boundaries; level changes are silent to the student
target_learners: developers learning an agentic AI coding tool through the cc-self-train curriculum
target_learning_goals: sustained productive engagement and appropriately paced scaffolding during tool-mastery learning
examples: A struggle streak (three or more consecutive answer_seeking or passive_acceptance classifications) produces the priority alert "Offer more scaffolding NOW"
key_sources: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: Cross-domain unified curriculum: five project paths teach identical feature sequencing to enable transfer of tool mastery
description: This pattern fixes the instructional sequence across multiple parallel project domains so that tool knowledge transfers between them. The article states: "all five paths teach the same 10 Claude Code feature sets in the same order, designed to facilitate cross-domain transfer of tool mastery." Each path (Canvas portfolio site, Forge CLI toolkit, Nexus API gateway, Sentinel code analyzer, and BYOP) produces a different software artifact while adapting the same exercises to its domain; a feature coverage matrix documents that all covered features are taught in all 5 paths, enforced by an automated test class. The BYOP path serves as the ultimate transfer test, requiring learners to identify where each feature applies in their own codebase with no pre-specified exercises.
requirements: A feature coverage matrix enforced by the TestModuleConsistencyAcrossProjects test class, which fails the suite if a feature is added to one path but not the other four
constraints: The feature sequence is fixed; only project-specific application changes across domains
target_learners: developers choosing a project path by interest, including first-time users (Canvas) and learners applying the curriculum to an existing codebase (BYOP)
target_learning_goals: domain-independent transfer of agentic AI tool mastery
examples: Module 7's guard-rail exercises teach the same three hook mechanisms (deny, inject context, and modify input) in all five paths, contextualized per domain
key_sources: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: cc-self-train auto-updating sync pipeline: an onboarding agent that detects upstream tool changes and updates teaching materials before instruction begins
description: The sync pipeline (/sync skill) addresses the content decay problem of curricula for rapidly evolving tools. The article states: "when a learner begins the curriculum, the onboarding agent checks whether its teaching materials cover the learner's installed version of Claude Code. If not, it updates the modules before instruction begins, so the learner always receives a current snapshot." The six-step pipeline detects the version gap, fetches and triages the upstream changelog, maps features to affected modules, researches new features, updates module and context files, and verifies structural integrity, reverting any file that fails. A safe-append rule never modifies or renumbers existing steps, inserting new content before the Checkpoint section.
requirements: A predefined feature-to-module mapping and a parametrized test suite that verifies structural integrity of updated files
constraints: During onboarding only the learner's chosen project variant is updated; standalone maintainer invocation updates all five variants in bulk
target_learners: developers learning agentic AI coding tools whose features change on a cadence measured in days
target_learning_goals: learning current tool features rather than outdated curriculum content
examples: Adding BYOP as a 5th path required generating 10 module files, which the pipeline then maintains alongside the original 40
key_sources: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460

article_title: A Formative Study of Brief Affective Text as a Complement to Wearable Sensing for Longitudinal Student Health Monitoring
citation: Tamunotonye Harry, Johanna Hidalgo, Matthew Price, Yuanyuan Feng, Kathryn Stanton, Connie Tompkins, Peter Sheridan Dodds, Mikaela Irene Fudolig, Laura Bloomfield, and Christopher Danforth. 2026. A Formative Study of Brief Affective Text as a Complement to Wearable Sensing for Longitudinal Student Health Monitoring. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. 10, 4, Article 219 (December 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14360
title: Use ultra-brief affective prompts to enrich the psychological interpretability of passive physiological data at minimal participant burden
description: The article's design guidance is that a single open-ended affective question, answered in the participant's own words, can complement passive wearable sensing by supplying psychological context the sensors cannot recover. Responses were extremely short — the median was three words — yet still associated with within-person variation in sleep and activity outcomes. The article concludes that "ultra-brief affective prompts enrich the psychological interpretability of passive physiological data at minimal burden", positioning this as a lightweight alternative to infrastructure-intensive sensor-language models.
requirements: A single open-ended concern prompt integrated into an existing study protocol (here, a bimonthly ecological momentary assessment delivered via a study mobile application), paired with concurrent wearable outcome data aggregated over the same two-week window.
constraints: The concern prompt is negatively valenced by construction, selectively surfacing worry and distress; the authors state findings should be read within that scope.
The bimonthly interval is a design constraint representing a middle point in the burden-versus-sensitivity tradeoff, not an optimum established by the study.
Associations are formative and exploratory; none survived correction for multiple comparisons.
target_learners: university students
first-year university students in longitudinal health monitoring studies
target_learning_goals: psychological context for physiological monitoring
early detection of distress
timely clinical outreach

article_title: Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named
citation: Nama, R. (2026). Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named. Author's accepted manuscript, AI and Ethics (Springer Nature). https://arxiv.org/
title: Agentic literacy debt: a compounding societal deficit from deploying agentic AI without literacy infrastructure
description: The paper defines agentic literacy debt as the accumulating deficit that grows "when agentic AI systems are deployed at scale without the literacy infrastructure users need to govern them." Borrowed from technical debt, it compounds through three reinforcing channels: normalization of opaque delegation (a ratchet effect of inherited, rarely revoked permission grants), multi-agent ecosystem complexity, and institutional path dependence. It extends Ladson-Billings' education debt and Petrozzino's ethical debt to systems that act autonomously on citizens' behalf.
requirements: Deployment of autonomous agents without frameworks enabling users to understand, supervise, and contest their actions is what adds to the debt.
constraints: Unlike ethical debt, incurred at design, it is incurred at the point of deployment and compounds with every user interaction without adequate literacy infrastructure.
target_learners: users, patients, consumers, and citizens on whose behalf agents act
target_learning_goals: governing autonomous AI agents: understanding, supervising, and contesting agent actions
examples: The author cites OpenClaw walletdrain attacks and the EchoLeak vulnerability as visible consequences of the gap.

title: Treat user literacy as a first-class design objective, because design defaults are literacy interventions
description: The paper argues that engineers must recognize that "design defaults are literacy interventions whether or not they are intended as such": the single undifferentiated permission grant, the invisible action log, and execute-first reporting for irreversible actions each decide whether users develop capacity to govern agents. It recommends transparency-by-design embedding literacy into agent interactions, AI tutoring simulating agentic scenarios, and contextual micro-learning at the point of risk.

target_learning_goals: capacity to see, constrain, and contest agent actions

title: Three validation targets for educational simulation: behavioral believability, educational mechanism fidelity, and institutional counterfactual usefulness
description: The paper argues that educational simulators are too often evaluated only on surface realism, and distinguishes three targets that are often conflated. As printed: "Behavioral believabilityasks whether generated dialogue resembles what teachers and students might say.Educational mechanism fidelityasks whether the internal process producing that dialogue corresponds to learning theory, such as knowledge restructuring, scaffolding, or misconception repair.Institutional counterfactual usefulnessasks whether the simulator can support 'what-if' reasoning about policies, spaces, or AI-mediated teaching arrangements that do not yet exist." AgentSchool is designed around the latter two targets, making internal learning states explicit and allowing scenarios to depart from present-day templates.

title: A4L Analytics Pipeline
description: The A4L Analytics Pipeline is a component of the Architecture for AI-Augmented Learning that performs statistical analyses on learner interaction data from educational AI assistants. It is "defined as a state machine that runs in a cloud environment" taking "a JSON-formatted analysis configuration payload as input". A data fetch module retrieves specified datasets into a staging area, and an analysis module performs pre-processing, transforms, and analysis, uploading results to durable object storage for the Visualization Pipeline's role-specific dashboards. Daily scheduled runs monitor the published data store for new data and run affected payloads.

target_learning_goals: understanding AI assistant adoption, performance, need for cognition, and sense of belonging through learning analytics
examples: The pipeline ran Welch's t-tests, contingency tables, and power calculations across the JW, VERA, and SAMI research domains using one codebase.

title: Highly Configurable System design for cross-domain learning analytics
description: The pipeline applies Highly Configurable System (HCS) principles, "enabling a single underlying codebase to be applied to different scenarios through flexible configuration". Each statistical option's parameters — alternative hypothesis, dataset, independent and dependent variables, and result storage location — are programmed as variables whose values are read from keys in the JSON analysis configuration payload, so the same analysis-module code serves different domains. Santana et al 2025 found this yields a pipeline that is extensible and flexible while maintaining structural coherence, defined as the absence of invalid system configurations.
requirements: Analysis configuration payloads must supply valid values for each configurable key (statistic name, dataset, variables, result file name).
constraints: Structural coherence depends on configurations being valid; the balance between flexibility and structural coherence was established in prior work by Santana et al 2025.

target_learning_goals: reproducible cross-domain analysis of learner interaction data

description: The article defines agentic systems as digital actors with three core behavioural traits: "autonomy to function without continuous human intervention, proactiveness to initiate goal-directed actions, and reactiveness to adapt to changing contexts". Unlike conventional dialogue systems, proactive AI agents can anticipate outcomes, take initiative, and strategically plan. A key functional advantage is the ability to use external tools (databases, APIs, microservices) while leveraging persistent memory across sessions and communicating across multi-agent networks. The article uses this framework to analyse how such systems interact with established pedagogical principles.

The matrix is intended to bridge theory, system architecture, and practice, demonstrating how intentional instructional friction and dynamic scaffolding fading can be embedded across diverse learning contexts.

By engineering strategic "instructional friction," agents can force the critical thinking and active inquiry necessary to cement knowledge, ensuring the learner remains the primary driver of the intellectual journey. Examples include an AI that asks the student to explain how their hobby relates to a new topic rather than explaining for them, and an AI that pauses the interface when it detects rapid clicking or superficial answers.

description: The article proposes that AI scaffolding be inherently transitional, explicitly designed to retreat as student competence increases. To prevent learned helplessness, agentic systems require robust, real-time analytics capable of distinguishing between temporary task completion and long-term mastery, allowing the AI to dynamically withdraw intermediate supports and systematically yield full cognitive autonomy back to the learner. title: Adaptive Virtual Patient framework: separating behavioral state transitions from language generation
description: The AVP framework inserts an explicit behavioral-state module between the trainee's turn and the virtual patient's reply: LLM evaluators score empathy and exploration each turn, a dynamics module accumulates the scores into an ordinal disclosure level (G/M/H) using weights derived from a psychotherapy-data SEM, and an LLM generates the next utterance conditioned on that level. title: Four measurable properties for evaluating adaptive virtual patients: responsiveness, gradual build-up, faithful realization, and skill sensitivity
description: The article proposes four measurable properties an adaptive virtual patient should satisfy, each with its own metric: P1 Responsiveness (state changes in the direction the data predicts), P2 Gradual Build-up (the state "climbs steadily across the session and only as the user earns it"), P3 Faithful Realization (generated text matches the intended state), and P4 Skill Sensitivity (different users get visibly different sessions). Each property comes with its own metric, so evaluators can locate exactly where a system fails rather than collapse the question into one number.

description: Phoenix is a "voice-based, non-embodied conversational agent that joins real-time group discussions through spoken dialogue with multiple participants", positioned as an equal peer supporting knowledge co-construction rather than an authoritative tutor. Its architecture integrates Google speech-to-text, Microsoft Azure text-to-speech, and OpenAI's GPT-4.1-mini on a Django backend, with a GPT-4.1-mini-based gatekeeping classifier analyzing the eight most recent dialogue turns to decide when Phoenix should respond. Phoenix was implemented with Indian, British, and African American accents while keeping the LLM prompt and tasks constant.
requirements: Runs on a shared laptop at the group table with a web interface displaying spoken output alongside a live transcript
A gatekeeping classifier that analyzes the eight most recent dialogue turns to determine when the agent should respond
The LLM generating responses is not informed of the synthesized accent type, to prevent accent-related cultural biases in outputs
constraints: Designed for one-off, lab-based workshop interactions in this study rather than longitudinal classroom use
Technical constraints, including latency and limited model transparency, affected interaction flow and trust
target_learners: K-12 teachers in small-group problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: Collaborative problem-solving and consensus building
Equitable, human-led participation in group discussion
examples: In the study, 33 teachers in 11 groups of three interacted with Phoenix across an icebreaker, a survival-task consensus activity, and an open-ended brainstorming task, with accents varied between groups via Azure voices Arjun, Bella, and Lola with pitch adjustments for gender neutrality

article_title: AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction
citation: Yanjie Zhang, Jiajun Zhu, Minyu Wu, Huamin Qu, and Sicheng Song. (2026). AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633
title: AdaPT: an LLM-powered system supporting lesson plan structuring, learning profile analysis, and one-click transformation
description: AdaPT is an interactive LLM-powered web application that reframes lesson preparation from creation to transformation. It supports (S1) parsing uploaded plans into structured components, (S2) summarizing natural-language student descriptions into structured profiles, and (S3) one-click transformation with traces and reasons for each change. The abstract states it "features an interactive interface that allows teachers to input student profiles, offers structured lesson representation" and supports iterative, teacher-in-the-loop refinement. It was implemented with Vue.js frontend and a TypeScript NestJS backend hosting LLM agents.
requirements: Teachers must upload an existing lesson plan and provide a natural-language description of the target students' learning situation
constraints: Evaluated only with K-12 IT lesson plans and Chinese school contexts
target_learners: K-12 teachers adapting plans for rural, lower-performing, or weaker parallel classes
target_learning_goals: Contextually appropriate, differentiated lesson plans aligned to curriculum standards
examples: In the walkthrough, urban transportation examples were replaced with local agricultural scenarios for rural students

article_title: AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction
citation: Yanjie Zhang, Jiajun Zhu, Minyu Wu, Huamin Qu, and Sicheng Song. (2026). AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633
title: Four-component lesson plan representation schema grounded in curriculum studies and differentiated instruction
description: AdaPT decomposes lesson plans into four components: curriculum standards, learning objectives, learning profile analysis, and learning tasks. The design draws on the Encyclopedia of Curriculum Studies' four common features of instructional design models and on Tomlinson's differentiated instruction framework, operationalizing readiness via Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. The authors state they "designed a structured representation that decomposes a lesson plan into four key components." Learning tasks are refined into atomic units with task, expected answer, detailed plan, implementation method, and design intent, enabling reuse and reflection on standards alignment.
requirements: Plans must be parsed into schema-conformant components before transformation
constraints: Knowledge readiness remains initially unknown until enriched from teacher input or LMS data
target_learners: K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Structured, pedagogically coherent lesson plans aligned with national curriculum standards
examples: The Learning Profile Analysis dimension covers collaboration, discussion, independent learning, and preferred thinking styles (analytical, practical, creative)

article_title: AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction
citation: Yanjie Zhang, Jiajun Zhu, Minyu Wu, Huamin Qu, and Sicheng Song. (2026). AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633
title: Multi-agent backend with LessonPlan Agent and LearningProfile Analysis Agent providing traceable transformations
description: AdaPT's backend is a multi-agent system in which each agent encapsulates distinct reasoning responsibilities. The LessonPlan Agent parses uploaded plans into schema-conformant components (using RAG over a tree-structured knowledge graph of national curriculum standards) and transforms them by recalibrating objectives and iteratively adjusting tasks. The LearningProfile Analysis Agent generates structured profiles from teacher natural-language descriptions, optionally retrieving knowledge readiness from the school's LMS via tool-calling. The authors state "The backend of AdaPT is designed as a multi-agent system (Figure 5), where each agent encapsulates distinct reasoning responsibilities aligned with the design requirements." Outputs are schema-validated JSON with references and localized reasons for traceability.
requirements: A curriculum standards knowledge graph for semantic alignment; teacher-provided context descriptions
constraints: Traceability depends on agents generating references and reasons linked to source spans in the original plan
target_learners: K-12 teachers, including those with limited ICT skills
target_learning_goals: Interpretable, editable, pedagogically grounded lesson plan adaptation
examples: Each transformed component is linked back to its source span with References and Reasons, e.g., lowered difficulty justified by weak debugging skills

citation: Yanjie Zhang, Jiajun Zhu, Minyu Wu, Huamin Qu, and Sicheng Song. (2026). AdaPT: Adaptive Lesson Plan Transformer for Cross-Regional and Differentiated Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17633
title: Design AI lesson tools to support transformation of existing plans rather than generation from scratch
description: The article argues educational AI tools should align with teachers' actual practice of modifying existing high-quality plans rather than creating new ones. The formative study found the from-scratch generation prototype "was rejected because teachers' actual practice is often one of modification." AdaPT therefore reframes preparation as transformation: parsing existing plans, analyzing target student profiles, and adapting content with traceable changes. The authors derive design implications for future AI-based educational technologies that support adaptation practices and help mitigate educational inequality.
requirements: Systems must parse unstructured existing plans into editable structured formats and retain teacher agency over each change
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in Chinese K-12 contexts and cross-regional teaching support settings
target_learners: In-service K-12 teachers, especially those in cross-regional or differentiated teaching contexts
target_learning_goals: Efficient, contextually adapted lesson plans promoting educational equity
examples: AdaPT's one-click transformation generates adapted drafts with traces and reasons for each change, which teachers accept, modify, or regenerate

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: GenAI adaptive AI agent with response-contingent prompting and withheld solutions
description: The study's adaptive AI agent is a generative large language model configured via a structured system prompt defining its instructional role, response scope, and escalation logic. During pretesting it applied "response-contingent prompting": targeted probes for misconceptions, elaboration requests for superficial responses, and advancement for adequate engagement. "Direct solutions and posttest-relevant answers were explicitly excluded from the agent’s allowed outputs during pretesting." In the adaptive retrieval condition it additionally reviewed prior session performance signals to adjust conceptual depth.
requirements: A structured system prompt defining the agent's instructional role, response scope, and escalation logic, with direct solutions excluded from allowed outputs during pretesting
constraints: The study was conducted within a single instructional context; the article states replication across domains and task types is needed to assess generalizability
target_learners: undergraduate students in an upper-division applied statistics course
target_learning_goals: multiple linear regression concepts including predictor selection, multicollinearity detection, model comparison, and interpretation of regression coefficients
examples: In condition G1 the agent reviewed prior session performance signals, increasing conceptual depth for weaker content areas while maintaining challenge in stronger areas
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: Observed practice effort rubric scored from AI conversation logs
description: Observed practice effort is a behavioral engagement measure derived from students' submitted AI-agent conversation logs collected after each of three scheduled practice sessions. Two raters independently applied a consensus-developed rubric distinguishing substantive engagement (E), surface engagement (SE), compliance-driven submissions (CE), and non-engaged submissions (NE). Each student earned up to three engagement credits converted to a proportional 0.00–1.00 score, with qualitative adjustments within a band, yielding "an ordinal measure of behavioral engagement distinct from self-report or time-on-task."
requirements: Submitted AI-agent conversation logs after each scheduled practice session and two raters reaching agreement through structured discussion prior to scoring
constraints: The article states the measure "reflects behavioral indicators rather than internal motivational states"
target_learners: undergraduate students completing AI-supported practice sessions
target_learning_goals: behavioral engagement during AI-supported retrieval or study practice
examples: Scores took proportional values such as 0.00, 0.33, 0.66, 1.00, with within-band adjustments such as 0.77 or 0.88 where strict proportional scoring did not fully capture engagement patterns
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: Follow GenAI-enabled adaptive pretesting with structured spaced retrieval practice rather than learner-directed AI study to preserve gains
description: The article concludes that adaptive pretesting elevates initial understanding but that "sustained learning depends on how subsequent AI-supported practice is structured." When pretesting is followed by retrieval-based practice — especially adaptive retrieval — gains in retention and engagement persist; when followed only by learner-directed AI interaction, benefits may attenuate. AI access should be structured to elicit retrieval rather than enable passive review.
requirements: AI-supported practice sessions held constant in number and timing across learners, with interaction structure designed to elicit retrieval attempts
constraints: Evidence comes from a single instructional context (one applied statistics course and topic); the article calls for replication across domains and task types
target_learners: undergraduate students learning applied analytical content with GenAI support
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and near-transfer of concepts after AI-assisted pretesting
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to adaptive spaced retrieval, fixed spaced retrieval, or learner-directed AI study after a common adaptive pretesting and instruction phase, with the same posttest at semester's end
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: Knowledge Debt: a developer-level analogue of Technical Debt incurred when agents change code the developer does not fully understand
description: Knowledge Debt is the article's central explanatory construct: "a developer-level analogue to Technical Debt, incurred when an agent makes changes to the codebase that the developer does not fully understand". Like Technical Debt, it "compounds silently and surfaces only when independent capability is required, at which point repayment through relearning becomes costly". The authors propose operationalizing it as a measurable construct as future work.
requirements: Applies in settings where developers delegate code changes to AI agents whose reasoning the developer does not fully verify.
constraints: The article presents Knowledge Debt as a posited construct; empirical operationalization is explicitly future work.
target_learners: Professional software developers using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Maintaining independent debugging, adaptation, and extension capability while working with AI-generated code
examples: The paper frames the accumulating gap between AI-generated code and developer understanding, building on prior work in cognitive offloading and skill atrophy.
key_sources: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: Six design principles for embedding incidental learning into developer-agent interactions
description: The article proposes six early design principles that "any approach embedding incidental learning into human-agent interactions should satisfy": Contextual (tied to the specific code or decision just engaged with), Grounded (based on the agent's reasoning, not artifacts alone), Ambient (out-of-band, flow-respecting), Selective (intervening only on genuine learning moments), Adaptive (calibrated to developer expertise), and Closed-Loop (verifying internalization via comprehension checks). They "do not specify a system" but "define what any such system must do".
requirements: Learning opportunities must be grounded in the agent's reasoning trace, which carries information such as alternatives considered and uncertainty that cannot be reconstructed from code artifacts alone.
constraints: The authors present the principles as early proposals and "invite the community to refine and extend them".
target_learners: Software developers at varying expertise levels using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Incidental acquisition of concepts such as API choices, design decisions, alternatives, and trade-offs during agent-assisted coding
examples: SHIELD is presented as an early instantiation that operationalizes these principles.
key_sources: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: SHIELD: a multi-agent system for embedding incidental learning in developer-agent interactions
description: SHIELD (Safeguarding Human Expertise and Incidental Learning in Software Development) is a multi-agent prototype operating within the developer's IDE alongside their AI coding agent. It instruments the agent to emit telemetry on every code change, then a Telemetry Observer Agent, Learning Orchestrator, Teachability Triage Agent, Probe Generator Agent, Knowledge Assessor Agent, and Microlearning Generator Agent identify genuine knowledge gaps and surface probes and microlearning asynchronously. It is implemented as a VSCode extension using CrewAI, Neo4j for the Concept Map, and GPT-5.1, currently instrumented for Claude Code.
requirements: Requires instrumenting the developer's AI coding agent to emit structured telemetry capturing changes, rationale, alternatives considered, and confidence.
constraints: The current prototype works only with Claude Code as the AI coding agent; no empirical user evaluation has been conducted yet.
target_learners: Professional software developers delegating coding tasks to AI agents
target_learning_goals: Repaying Knowledge Debt by addressing emerging knowledge gaps as they arise without interrupting development flow
examples: A walkthrough shows a developer delegating a webhook retry issue; the agent replaces fixed retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter, and SHIELD surfaces a probe, assesses partial understanding, and delivers microlearning followed by a comprehension check.

article_title: Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation
citation: Saqib Shouqi, Abdullah Nazly, Januki Wanniarachchi, Ravisha De Alwis. (2026). Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation. ADScAI Conference, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03166
title: Multi-agent adversarial evaluation framework coordinating Interrogator, Target, and Judging agents
description: The article proposes a modular multi-agent framework in which "a strategy-driven Interrogator Agent that applies six progressive adversarial strategies" probes a Target Agent representing the RPLA under evaluation, while "an automated Judging Agent that scores behavior across role fidelity, drift, ethical deviation, and consistency dimensions" evaluates the full transcript afterward. The Judging Agent does not participate in dialogue generation, ensuring evaluation does not alter the behavior measured. The framework treats the Target Agent as a black box and supports multiple LLM providers through a unified abstraction layer.
requirements: A persistent database storing experiment metadata, conversation transcripts, and evaluation results to enable replay, comparison, and auditing
A unified LLM provider abstraction layer so the same experimental setup runs across models without changing evaluation logic
constraints: The Target Agent is treated as a black box, reflecting deployment conditions where internal model parameters are not accessible
The framework focuses on prompt-based adversarial attacks and does not consider vulnerabilities arising from training, fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning processes
target_learners: Developers and researchers evaluating role-playing language agents for education, healthcare assistance, and customer support
target_learning_goals: Assessing robustness, reliability, and alignment of role-playing language agents under sustained adversarial conditions
examples: Experiments ran 10-turn interactions per experiment across three personas (Healthcare Assistant, Customer Support Agent, Financial Advisor) with three random seeds per condition
key_sources: Saqib Shouqi, Abdullah Nazly, Januki Wanniarachchi, Ravisha De Alwis. (2026). Adversarial Stress Testing of Role-Playing Language Agents using Multi-Agent Evaluation. ADScAI Conference, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03166

title: Open-source adversarial stress-testing platform for RPLAs with FastAPI backend and React dashboard
description: The article releases "an open-source platform to support AI safety and reproducible RPLA benchmarking." The system follows a client-server design in which "A FastAPI-based backend manages experiment configuration, agent execution, scoring, and data persistence, while a React-based frontend provides an interactive interface for experiment creation, monitoring, and analysis." Metric computation code is available in the repository under agents/judging_agent/metrics.py, enabling reproducibility and community auditing of scoring algorithms.

constraints: The authors caution the framework could be misused to exploit deployed systems and emphasize responsible access and usage; automated evaluation should not be solely relied upon for critical decision-making
target_learners: AI safety researchers and developers of role-playing language agents
target_learning_goals: Systematic discovery of RPLA failure modes and reproducible benchmarking of agent robustness
examples: All experiments were executed using the proposed orchestration pipeline with 10-turn interactions per experiment across Groq, OpenAI, and Anthropic providers

description: The paper proposes an organizational framework in which a stable student-elected administrative board governs a dynamic portfolio of student-led projects, with faculty acting as mentors. title: Forca Libras: computer-vision hangman game for Brazilian Sign Language learning
description: Forca Libras, developed within the GAIA project, is an AI-powered game that "employs computer vision techniques to recognize hand gestures corresponding to the Brazilian Sign Language (LIBRAS)." It adopts a dual pedagogical approach: hearing students practice LIBRAS through gesture recognition, while deaf students use it to support Portuguese literacy through visual representations, contextual images, textual hints, and Portuguese words. The system was published at the Brazilian Symposium on Collaborative Systems (SBSC) 2026.
requirements: Integration of computer vision, software engineering, educational game design, and accessibility concepts
target_learners: hearing students learning LIBRAS
deaf students developing Portuguese literacy
target_learning_goals: Brazilian Sign Language manual alphabet
Portuguese literacy for deaf learners
examples: GAIA applications are demonstrated during university extension events, school visits, and technology exhibitions to promote digital inclusion

article_title: The 5P Reflection Model for Education in the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Era
citation: Rajan Kadel, Samar Shailendra, Islam Mohammad Tahidul, Urvashi Rahul Saxena, Aakanksha Sharma, and Sabitra Kaphle. (2026). The 5P Reflection Model for Education in the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Era. Pre-print submitted to IEEE Transactions on Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03413
title: 5P reflection model: an iterative five-stage GenAI-aware reflection model
description: The 5P Reflection Model is an iterative reflective model with five stages: Purpose, Process, Product, Pitfalls and Plan, with emotional factors considered across all stages. It synthesises features from experiential, transformative, reflective-practitioner, affective and self-regulated learning theories and incorporates the technological dimensions of GenAI. The article states it is proposed "to manage greater demand for reflection, ii) to address the limitations of the existing reflection models, iii) to consider technological aspects of GenAI."
requirements: Learners document prompts, iterations and output evaluations during the Process stage, and validate GenAI output against reliable sources in the Product stage
constraints: The article presents the model as a design-based research proposal without empirical validation of learning outcomes in the text provided
target_learners: higher education students using GenAI tools
target_learning_goals: authentic and ethically sound reflection
responsible GenAI use
metacognitive engagement
examples: Each stage is operationalised: Purpose sets goals and intended GenAI use; Process documents prompting and iteration; Product validates output and distinguishes human from GenAI contribution; Pitfalls reflects on factual, ethical and privacy risks; Plan sets refined future goals
key_sources: Rajan Kadel, Samar Shailendra, Islam Mohammad Tahidul, Urvashi Rahul Saxena, Aakanksha Sharma, and Sabitra Kaphle. (2026). The 5P Reflection Model for Education in the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Era. Pre-print submitted to IEEE Transactions on Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03413

title: Five-category taxonomy of reflection models
description: The article organises the reflection literature into five families, each analysed for strengths, limitations in the GenAI era and application areas in Tables I-V: experiential (Kolb, Gibbs, DIEP), transformative (Mezirow and successors), reflective practitioner (Schön, Brookfield, CARL and others), emotional/affective (Boud and others), and self-regulated learning (Zimmerman, Pintrich, Winne and Hadwin, Boekaerts). The article states: "In this study, we classify reflection into five commonly recognised categories" spanning these traditions.
requirements: Understanding of each family's theoretical basis to select models suited to a given educational context
constraints: The article concludes that none of these families adequately addresses GenAI's technological aspects
target_learners: higher education students
professional practitioners in health sciences, STEM and teacher education
target_learning_goals: structured reflective practice
understanding of reflection model selection
examples: Tables I through V summarise each model's strengths, GenAI-era limitations and application areas, e.g. Gibbs' cycle for nursing and health sciences, Zimmerman's model for STEM education

title: Integrated reflection framework fusing features from five theory families with a technology-enhanced layer
description: The article's model design adopts enumerated key features from each reflection theory family: staged reflection and iterative cycles from experiential learning; assumption re-examination from transformative learning; reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action from the reflective practitioner; emotion handling from affective models; and goal setting, self-monitoring and adaptive adjustment from self-regulated learning. As the article states, "the following key features are adopted from existing reflection and learning practices in the literature", integrated with GenAI technological aspects in a framework illustrated in Fig. 1.

constraints: Emotional factors are considered across all stages rather than confined to one stage

target_learning_goals: authentic reflection
responsible GenAI use
metacognitive self-regulation
examples: Reflection-in-Action is operationalised as iterative prompting and refinement; Reflection-on-Action as reviewing and analysing the final output

title: Re-centre reflection on process over product in GenAI-rich learning
description: Because GenAI challenges the authorship and authenticity of learner-produced artefacts, reflection models should focus on the reflective process rather than the product. The article argues existing models assume the product is created by learners themselves, and advocates a "process over product" philosophy so that learners' reasoning, prompts and iterations become observable and assessable even when GenAI assists.
requirements: Learners document their interactions with AI tools, the prompts used, and the iterative thinking that unfolds through human-AI collaboration
constraints: The article frames this as necessary for authenticity assessment in GenAI-rich environments rather than as a universally tested recommendation

academic integrity
deep learning with GenAI support

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: Preserved metacognitive demand: hold what the learner must decide constant and let carried load vary with demonstrated need
description: The principle states that "An AI learning system should hold the learner's metacognitive demand approximately constant, and let the cognitive load it carries vary with demonstrated need." It rests on the paper's separation of two quantities that giving-more-or-less designs run together: the load the system carries and the demand placed on the learner before help arrives. CoMeT implements it by escalating support at decision points on failure and fading on take-up, so the learner keeps deciding while the tutor's labour varies.
requirements: The tutor must be able to identify decision points and detect take-up from the learner's turns, via authored coverage patterns plus a take-up judgement
constraints: Demand is held approximately constant, not exactly; the principle was tested on adult learners on short Python tasks with authored decision points
target_learners: adult novice programmers learning Python
target_learning_goals: planning and monitoring decisions in programming problem solving
self-regulated learning during AI-assisted coding
examples: Tutor C asks first, gives more help each time the learner does not use it, and pulls back as soon as the learner does, conceding one decision point at a time after three asks
key_sources: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: The contingency dimension: separating the load a system carries from the demand it places on the learner
description: The paper defines a design axis on which tutor designs sit: "We call the line those positions lie on thecontingency dimension, and contingent tutoring is movement along it during a task." Structuring changes how much load the system carries; problematizing changes how much demand the learner faces. Existing LLM tutors fix one position at design time; contingent tutoring moves along the dimension during a task, escalating after failure and fading after success. The theory has three parts: direction (the contingent shift rule), unit (decision points), and warrant (what justifies fading).
requirements: A signal the tutor can read from the learner's writing to decide when support rises and falls
constraints: Positions of prior systems on the dimension are illustrative; the warrant part was tested only on a text-channel tutor with authored decision points
target_learners: adult novice programmers using AI tutors
target_learning_goals: regulatory work such as deciding, articulating and judging before help arrives
examples: Table 1 places prior LLM systems and the three study tutors on the dimension as five properties: withholds, structures, gates, escalates, fades

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: CoMeT: a browser-based contingent AI programming tutor with a support ladder over authored decision points
description: CoMeT is "a browser-based environment in which a learner works through a short programming task beside a chat tutor", with a sketchpad and code editor. Tasks run three gated phases (Planning with the editor locked, Monitoring, Evaluating), and correctness is decided by authored test cases, never by the model. Tutor C escalates one rung at a time through three asks (Socratic question, specific hint, contrasting case), concedes a point after R = 3 rounds, and returns to the first rung on take-up; coverage is decided by authored patterns rather than holistic model judgement.
requirements: Decision points must be authored per task and phase, with coverage patterns and scaffold wording, so the difference between tutors is auditable
constraints: All three tutors ran on the same model backbone (Claude Haiku 4.5); take-up where patterns do not settle it falls to a one-word model judgement and a length threshold that errs on the learner's side
target_learners: adult learners with no prior programming threshold through over five years of Python experience
target_learning_goals: settling the decisions a program turns on before code is written
monitoring and evaluating one's own solution
examples: In the study, 131 adult learners met all three tutors across three Python tasks (bus-fare calculator, pizza order, staffing roster), one tutor per task in a Williams square design

article_title: AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories
citation: Buyankhishig Enkhjargal, Himanshi Lalwani, Hanan Salam. (2026). AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24245
title: AdaptED Stories: practitioner-guided AI web application for authoring, personalizing, and delivering Social Stories
description: AdaptED Stories is a practitioner-facing web application for Social Story interventions with autistic children. Per the abstract, "The system uses student profiles to draft story text and visuals, supports review and refinement by practitioners, and includes reading-session support with comprehension activities and session records." Student profiles capture comprehension level, preferred story and sentence length, goals, interests, and a photograph converted into a reusable cartoon avatar. The library is pre-loaded with 200 validated Social Stories from the SS-GEN dataset across six thematic categories. Reading sessions use child-like text-to-speech narration, and analytics aggregate comprehension and behavioral scores with AI-generated recommendations.
requirements: Practitioner review and approval of AI-drafted text and visuals before use with children
Student profile information defined by the practitioner to ground personalization
constraints: Background inconsistencies may still occur in personalized visuals
Evaluated only for usability and acceptance, not yet for child outcomes
target_learners: Autistic children in special-education contexts, including non-speaking or minimally verbal children
target_learning_goals: Understanding and preparing for everyday social situations
Target behavior change and comprehension of social narratives
examples: Phase 3 participants completed five structured tasks: creating a student profile, generating a story, personalizing a library story, conducting a reading session, and reviewing analytics and recommendations.
key_sources: Buyankhishig Enkhjargal, Himanshi Lalwani, Hanan Salam. (2026). AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24245

article_title: AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories
citation: Buyankhishig Enkhjargal, Himanshi Lalwani, Hanan Salam. (2026). AI-Assisted Social Story Intervention for Special Education: The Design of AdaptED Stories. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24245
title: Keep practitioners in control of AI-assisted authoring: treat AI outputs as reviewable drafts, not finished products
description: The article's first design goal holds that AI should reduce authoring effort while practitioners remain the main authors and decision-makers. As stated, "Our first goal was to keep practitioners as the main authors and decision-makers, with AI used to draft story text and visuals that are always subject to review and editing." In AdaptED Stories this is realized through staged workflows in which generated text and each scene visual are reviewed, edited, or regenerated and explicitly approved before saving. This preserves professional oversight and alignment with evidence-based practice.
requirements: Staged approval workflow separating text approval from visual approval
Practitioners with formal training in behavioral assessment and intervention design
constraints: Positioned for practitioner-facing rather than parent-facing authoring, since parent-centered authoring may create tensions between parental priorities and therapeutic goals
target_learners: Autistic children in special-education contexts
target_learning_goals: Therapeutically grounded, personalized Social Story interventions
examples: Across generation and personalization workflows, AI outputs are treated as reviewable drafts rather than finished products, with per-scene regeneration available.

article_title: Ticket to Nowhere: The Gap between Leaving High School and Entering College and High-Performance Jobs.
citation: Haycock, Kati, Ed.; Barth, Patte, Ed.; Mitchell, Ruth, Ed.; Wilkins, Amy, Ed. (1999). Ticket to Nowhere: The Gap between Leaving High School and Entering College and High-Performance Jobs. Thinking K-16; v3 n2 Fall 1999. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED457262
title: The K-16 Square: four interlocking commitments linking K-12 and higher education to bring all students to high standards
description: The K-16 Square is a framework drafted by state education CEOs from seven states (with the National Association of System Heads and the Education Trust) representing four interlocking and equally important commitments as the corners of a figure: ensure all high school graduates meet high standards; accept only teachers who can bring all students' performance to high standards; accept into college only students who meet high standards; and ensure all teacher candidates produced are prepared to bring student performance to high standards. The framework holds that "Change in one sector cannot be accomplished without change in the others," with standards for K-12 graduation congruent with college admission standards. The CEOs propose that about a third of states achieve the universal goal by 2010 and the rest by 2020.
requirements: Strong interaction among sectors: standards for graduation must be congruent with standards for college admission, and teacher preparation standards congruent with school employment standards
Publicly available, accurate data on the performance of schools, colleges, universities and their students
constraints: Each state must establish its own timetable because socioeconomic and political circumstances vary and may change suddenly
target_learners: all K-12 and college students, especially low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: meeting high achievement standards from elementary through postsecondary education, preparation for work and citizenship
examples: The CEOs' statement cites El Paso, Texas, where a five-year collaboration between higher education, K-12, and community leaders raised academic performance for all students and reduced the minority achievement gap by about two-thirds

article_title: Priced out: How the Wrong Financial-Aid Policies Hurt Low-Income Students
citation: Mamie Lynch, Jennifer Engle, and José L. Cruz. (2011). Priced Out: How the Wrong Financial-Aid Policies Hurt Low-Income Students. The Education Trust. https://www.collegeresults.org
title: Evaluate financial-aid policies by whether they primarily benefit low-income students, remove access barriers, and provide awards large enough to influence choices and success
description: The report proposes that policymakers apply a set of screening questions to any financial-aid policy at the federal, state, or institutional level. The questions ask whether the policy "primarily benefit[s] low-income students," whether low-income students can "fully tap financial assistance" without technical barriers, and whether awards are "large enough to influence the choices—and success rates—of low-income students." The report grounds this in its finding that current aid choices increasingly steer funds toward affluent students.
requirements: Policymakers at federal, state, and institutional levels must apply the criteria when setting financial-aid policy
constraints: The report notes net-price data cannot show how institutions allocate aid across income brackets, only what low-income students pay after all grant aid
target_learners: low-income undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: college access and affordability
postsecondary attainment
examples: The report's executive summary and conclusion both print the three-question test for decision makers setting financial-aid policy

title: VCU University College model: cohort-based first-year core curriculum with centralized support and proactive advising
description: Virginia Commonwealth University's University College, launched in 2006, is built around "a cohesive core curriculum with a limited set of course options and small class sizes," taught by dedicated cross-disciplinary faculty, with a full-year cohort class. It pairs this with proactive advising — required advisor meetings twice a semester, faculty attendance reporting, and outreach at the first sign of trouble — plus learning, writing, and supplemental instruction centers. After implementation, DFW rates in core courses decreased significantly and retention rose.
requirements: Significant investment and commitment at the highest levels of the institution
Dedicated faculty hired to work across disciplines
Professionally trained advisors tracking student data
constraints: The article attributes the model's success to VCU's context; it reports institutional self-attributions rather than a controlled evaluation
target_learners: First-year undergraduates, including undeclared majors at risk of dropping out
target_learning_goals: First-year course success, retention, and on-time graduation
examples: VCU narrowed its black-white gap from 7.4 points in 2004 to near parity by 2010, with black students graduating at 49.8 percent
The investment in University College was repaid in retention terms in less than three years, per the vice provost

description: EOP is a state-sponsored access-and-support program at Stony Brook serving nearly 600 low-income students and students of color whose high school preparation was incomplete. It provides "a five-week summer 'boot camp' program, personal counseling and academic advising at least three times a semester, and a mandatory study skill workshop" including an academic success contract.
