citation: Mary Nguyen, Erin Ward Bibo, and Jennifer Engle. (2012). Advancing to Completion: Increasing degree attainment by improving graduation rates and closing gaps for Hispanic students. The Education Trust. https://www.collegeresults.org
title: STEM Smart outreach programs and LSAMP at Stony Brook University
description: STEM Smart is Stony Brook's umbrella outreach program including over 10 federally funded programs providing "mentors, internship and research opportunities, career preparation workshops, and tutoring services for students all along the STEM pipeline from middle school to Ph.D." LSAMP, one component, provides a four-year curriculum for underrepresented minority STEM majors plus a Bridge to the Doctorate with a full NSF fellowship. Participants show retention and completion rates substantially higher than the institution as a whole.
requirements: External funding (NSF, NIH, NASA among others)
Mentors, research opportunities, and tutoring infrastructure across the pipeline
constraints: Program leader Ferguson states the programs "have not yet achieved transformative potential" and lack an institutional infrastructure supporting diversity
target_learners: underrepresented minority students
low-income and first-generation students
middle school through doctoral students in STEM
target_learning_goals: STEM degree completion
diversity in STEM education and careers
examples: 80 percent of a recent LSAMP cohort received bachelor's degrees within four years
key_sources: Mary Nguyen, Erin Ward Bibo, and Jennifer Engle. (2012). Advancing to Completion: Increasing degree attainment by improving graduation rates and closing gaps for Hispanic students. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED535510

article_title: Doing away with Debt: Using Existing Resources to Ensure College Affordability for Low and Middle-Income Families
citation: Michael Dannenberg and Mamie Voight. (2013). Doing Away With Debt: Using Existing Resources to Ensure College Affordability for Low and Middle-Income Families. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: College Results Online web tool comparing four-year colleges' graduation rates within peer groups
description: College Results Online (CRO, www.collegeresults.org) is an Education Trust web tool that "compares each four-year college's graduation rate, disaggregated among demographic groups, relative to its peer institutions." Each peer group is determined by an algorithm of 14 variables, including measures of selectivity, student demographics, and institution size and sector, shown in research to correlate with graduation rates. The report proposes CRO peer groups as a benchmarking mechanism for states setting institutional eligibility standards for state grant funds, with both a performance floor and an upper limit above which colleges automatically qualify.
requirements: Peer-group benchmarking should be paired with an absolute performance floor and an upper automatic-qualification limit
constraints: The report notes a peer-grouping indicator cannot justify investment where the proportion of students graduating is extremely low
target_learners: postsecondary policymakers
low-income college-bound students and families
target_learning_goals: institutional selection and consumer empowerment
college completion improvement
examples: The report uses CRO data to show Western New Mexico University's 17.5 percent six-year graduation rate and to note Carnegie Mellon graduates 86 percent of first-time, full-time students within six years yet ranks only 10th in its peer group
key_sources: Michael Dannenberg and Mamie Voight. (2013). Doing Away With Debt: Using Existing Resources to Ensure College Affordability for Low and Middle-Income Families. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED543214

article_title: The Pell Partnership: Ensuring a Shared Responsibility for Low-Income Student Success
citation: Andrew Howard Nichols. (2015). The Pell Partnership: Ensuring a Shared Responsibility for Low-Income Student Success. The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org/resource/pellgradrates
title: Pell Grant Graduation Rate Database and Institution Profile tool
description: A publicly accessible database built by The Education Trust from a yearlong collection effort using four sources: state higher education systems, colleges and universities, U.S. News and World Report, and IPEDS. It covers "graduation rates for Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients at nearly 1,150 institutions, the percentage of Pell Grant recipients attending each school, the cost for each, and much, much, more." The report states this is the first time such information is widely available to the general public.
requirements: Institutions must report six-year graduation rates for first-time, full-time Pell recipients in their IPEDS graduation-rate cohorts, as defined in the report's Appendix A
constraints: For-profit and non-specialized colleges were excluded
Private institutions are underrepresented, and participating institutions tended to be slightly larger and more selective than the surveyed population
For some colleges the gap was calculated by combining U.S. News Pell data with IPEDS overall rates, which the authors note could produce small discrepancies
target_learners: prospective low-income and working-class college students
policymakers
campus presidents and administrators
target_learning_goals: informed college choice by low-income students
institutional accountability for low-income student completion
examples: The report's Table 1 lists 36 standout institutions meeting criteria including Pell graduation rates at or above the national Pell rate of 50 percent and gaps at or below 3 percentage points
key_sources: Andrew Howard Nichols. (2015). The Pell Partnership: Ensuring a Shared Responsibility for Low-Income Student Success. The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org/resource/pellgradrates

article_title: Creating Accountability for College Access and Success: Recommendations for the Higher Education Act and Beyond
citation: Kayla C. Elliott, Tiffany Jones. (2016). Creating Accountability for College Access and Success: Recommendations for the Higher Education Act and Beyond. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Apply consequences gradually and tiered by infraction, reserving loss of Title IV eligibility for last after support and time have been exhausted
description: The report argues that accountability measures threatening Title IV aid "could cripple or close institutions that enroll high numbers of underserved students," so consequences should be gradual and intermediary first — such as removing tax benefits, program-level targeting, improvement plans, and mandatory alerts — with Title IV elimination only after other steps fail and two years of failing to meet standards.
requirements: Apply consequences and penalties only after the first four principles are pursued and exhausted, and only after two years of failing to meet standards
constraints: The report states campus closures can have the most impact on college opportunity for low-income students and students of color, who already have limited access
target_learners: students from low-income families
students of color
target_learning_goals: protecting college access while enforcing institutional accountability
examples: The report proposes allowing reduced consequences and waivers for institutions showing continual growth rather than punishing progress
key_sources: Kayla C. Elliott, Tiffany Jones. (2016). Creating Accountability for College Access and Success: Recommendations for the Higher Education Act and Beyond. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org

article_title: Hard Truths: Why Only Race-Conscious Policies Can Fix Racism in Higher Education
citation: Tiffany Jones and Andrew Howard Nichols. (2020). Hard Truths: Why Only Race-Conscious Policies Can Fix Racism in Higher Education. The Education Trust. https://www.EdTrust.org
title: Race-conscious policies are necessary because income-based proxies do not close racial gaps
description: The report's central principle is that policies substituting income or other proxies for race fail to achieve racial justice because "Black and White students and families with the same income often have vastly different experiences and circumstances that can affect educational and financial outcomes." It argues race must be addressed explicitly and in the design of policies providing access, opportunity, or support to students of color.
requirements: Policies that explicitly address race in their design rather than relying on income, geography, or other proxies
constraints: The report focuses its data and discussion on Black students, noting the case generalizes to all students of color
target_learners: Black students
students of color in higher education
target_learning_goals: Racial equity in higher education access, opportunity, and outcomes
examples: The report cites simulations showing income-based affirmative action yields less racial diversity than race-based policies, and performance-funding studies where low-income enrollment rose while Black enrollment stayed flat or fell
key_sources: Tiffany Jones and Andrew Howard Nichols. (2020). Hard Truths: Why Only Race-Conscious Policies Can Fix Racism in Higher Education. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603265

article_title: Teaching the Way Students Learn Best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School
citation: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale
title: A framework of four principles for whole child education derived from the science of learning and development
description: The report organizes its case around four principles for educational practice drawn from syntheses of neuroscience, cognitive science, and the developmental sciences: (1) environmental conditions supporting positive, trusting relationships, safety, and belonging; (2) intentional development of social, emotional, and cognitive skills, mindsets, and habits, with "supports for behavior should be educative and restorative"; (3) curricular designs and instructional strategies featuring "well-scaffolded instruction and ongoing formative assessment"; and (4) multi-tiered systems of support based on a shared developmental framework. Figure 1 presents these as a Framework for Whole Child Education, and Appendix B maps Bronxdale practices onto the principles.
requirements: School structures and classroom practices must support positive, trusting relationships, physical and emotional safety including identity safety, and a sense of belonging and purpose.
constraints: The report presents the framework as derived from recently published research syntheses rather than testing it empirically in this case study.
target_learners: K–12 students, especially diverse learners and students experiencing adversity
target_learning_goals: Academic capacity, competence, motivation, metacognitive skills, social-emotional skills, and resilience
examples: The report uses the framework to structure its account of Bronxdale's culture, SEL teaching, instruction, and systems of support, with a mapping table in Appendix B.
key_sources: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale

article_title: Teaching the Way Students Learn Best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School
citation: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale
title: Whole-school design pattern combining community vision, inquiry instruction with social-emotional supports, restorative discipline, and a professional community of practice
description: The report identifies a constellation of four mutually reinforcing school-design factors that it argues produced Bronxdale's outcomes: "a compelling vision of students and school as a caring, safe, collaborative community," "the integration of inquiry instruction with social-emotional supports," "educative discipline that puts restorative practices into action," and a faculty committed to "teaching the way that students learn best" while "continuously learning together in a community of practice." The pattern treats culture, pedagogy, discipline, and adult learning as one integrated design rather than isolated programs.
requirements: Structures such as small class size and advisory to build close relationships; distributed leadership; intensive ongoing professional development; and multi-tiered academic, health, and social supports.
constraints: The report notes the school's evolution took about 7 years and that its first year, before these practices were in place, was "in disarray" with fights and an unsafe climate.
target_learners: Diverse high school learners, including students from low-income households and students with disabilities in inclusion settings
target_learning_goals: Self-reliant, independent learning; curiosity; creative problem-solving; agency; academic and emotional self-regulation
examples: Bronxdale implemented advisory, Peer Group Connections, restorative circles, peer mediation, youth court, small classes of about 22 students, and a senior capstone project presented to a jury of peers and faculty.
key_sources: Ancess, J., Rogers, B., Duncan Grand, D., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2019). Teaching the way students learn best: Lessons from Bronxdale High School. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-bronxdale

article_title: Taking the Long View: State Efforts to Solve Teacher Shortages by Strengthening the Profession
citation: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view
title: Teacher residency model with eight key characteristics of strong programs
description: A teacher residency is an accelerated certification pathway in which candidates "work as paid apprentices to skilled expert teachers while completing highly integrated coursework" during a full-year clinical placement in a high-need classroom, with tuition and living support repaid through a multi-year service commitment. The report lists eight characteristics of strong residencies drawn from a research review, including strong district-university partnerships, tightly integrated coursework, expert mentor co-teaching, cohorts in partnership teaching schools, and ongoing mentoring for graduates. States including California, Texas, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Louisiana fund or mandate residency models.
requirements: Strong district and university partnerships
A full year of residency teaching alongside an expert mentor teacher
Financial support for residents in exchange for a 3- to 5-year post-residency teaching commitment
Expert mentor teachers who co-teach with residents
constraints: Programs are typically targeted to postbaccalaureate candidates and hard-to-staff positions in sponsoring districts
target_learners: Postbaccalaureate teacher candidates
Career changers and paraprofessionals entering teaching
target_learning_goals: Effective teaching in high-need fields and school districts
Retention of new teachers in hard-to-staff positions
examples: California invested $75 million in a Teacher Residency Grant Program for special education, STEM, and bilingual shortage areas, funding more than 3,500 new teachers with up to $20,000 per teacher matched by districts
Louisiana adopted regulations requiring a yearlong residency as a pathway to licensure, with $7.3 million in transitional funding for stipends and mentor training
key_sources: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view

article_title: Taking the Long View: State Efforts to Solve Teacher Shortages by Strengthening the Profession
citation: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view
title: Address teacher shortages with a set of mutually reinforcing policies rather than any single policy in isolation
description: The report argues no single policy solves teacher shortages if enacted alone: research on hard-to-staff schools indicates it is important "both to raise salaries and to provide for more collegial, supportive, well-resourced environments," and induction works best alongside school-level collaboration and mentorship policies. It recommends that policymakers consider how to ensure a set of mutually reinforcing strategies spanning recruitment, preparation, induction, leadership, compensation, and retention. Washington State's comprehensive approach, profiled in the report, illustrates this combined strategy.
requirements: Coordination across multiple policy areas (scholarships, pathways, induction, leadership, compensation, recruitment)
constraints: Effectiveness hinges on the size, scope, and comprehensiveness of the policy, quality of implementation, and responsiveness to state, local, and labor market context
target_learners: State policymakers designing teacher workforce systems
Prospective and practicing teachers in shortage fields
target_learning_goals: Recruiting, developing, and retaining a strong, stable, diverse teacher workforce
examples: Washington State combined service scholarships, high school pathways and Grow Your Own programs, mentoring and induction, school leadership investment, competitive compensation, and recruitment policies in a single comprehensive approach
The report concludes states should continually evaluate implementation and outcomes to strengthen the effectiveness of their actions
key_sources: Espinoza, D., Saunders, R., Kini, T., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2018). Taking the long view: State efforts to solve teacher shortages by strengthening the profession. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/long-view

article_title: Next Generation Accountability: A Vision for School Improvement under ESSA
citation: Adams, C. M., Ford, T. G., Forsyth, P. B., Ware, J. K., Olsen, J. J., Lepine, J. A., Sr., Barnes, L. B., Khojasteh, J., & Mwavita, M. (2017). Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability
title: Next generation accountability framework: shared accountability, adaptive improvement, and informational significance in a two-stage design
description: The report advances a framework for school accountability under ESSA governed by three principles: shared accountability, in which "performance responsibility is distributed across the system's components"; adaptive improvement, acknowledging that school capacities differ greatly; and informational significance, replacing a single composite with a broad palette of functionally significant indicators. It features a two-stage design: Stage One is formative, providing schools useful information for their own improvement decisions; Stage Two is aggressive, identifying and transforming schools in catastrophic failure. Schools are viewed as systems whose outcomes result from the quality of their resources and processes.
requirements: A support infrastructure capable of serving the developmental and resource needs of schools with differing needs
constraints: Stage Two applies to schools in catastrophic failure; Stage One is more formative than summative
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: deeper learning
college and career readiness
examples: The framework is operationalized in the Educational Quality and Improvement Profile (EQuIP) with resource, process, and outcome indicators
key_sources: Adams, C. M., Ford, T. G., Forsyth, P. B., Ware, J. K., Olsen, J. J., Lepine, J. A., Sr., Barnes, L. B., Khojasteh, J., & Mwavita, M. (2017). Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability

article_title: Next Generation Accountability: A Vision for School Improvement under ESSA
citation: Adams, C. M., Ford, T. G., Forsyth, P. B., Ware, J. K., Olsen, J. J., Lepine, J. A., Sr., Barnes, L. B., Khojasteh, J., & Mwavita, M. (2017). Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability
title: Educational Quality and Improvement Profile (EQuIP): a multi-indicator school reporting profile
description: EQuIP is the report's proposed accountability instrument, reporting data on school resources (organizational and home/community capacity), processes (instructional and learning capacity), and outcomes (cognitive and noncognitive). By reporting data on school resources, processes, and outcomes, "an EQuIP provides vital information for making judgments of school quality and helps focus school improvement efforts." It is envisioned as a comprehensive profile with multiple uses, with example pages for each capacity and outcome area and an online version (EQuIP Online).
requirements: Indicators should be collected with appropriate frequency and minimal disruption to the learning process
Indicators and measurement methods should have substantial evidence to support their validity and reliability
constraints: The report acknowledges no measure is perfect in its ability to accurately capture the phenomenon under study
target_learners: K-12 students
school stakeholders including parents, educators, and policymakers
target_learning_goals: deeper learning outcomes
college and career readiness
school quality improvement
examples: Example EQuIP pages are shown for organizational capacity, home and community capacity, instructional capacity, learning capacity, and cognitive and noncognitive outcome indicators

Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability

article_title: Building a System of College and Career Pathways in New Mexico
citation: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education
title: College and career pathways framework integrating CTE, core academics, work-based learning, and personalized supports
description: The report proposes a comprehensive high school redesign framework in which pathways "integrate CTE and core academic curriculum, combine classroom and work-based learning, and align secondary and postsecondary programs." Its state framework should include four essential components: college preparatory core academics "emphasizing real-world application, project-based learning, and performance assessment"; a sequence of four or more challenging CTE courses aligned to industry standards with dual enrollment and certifications; a continuum of work-based learning from career awareness in grade 9 to internships or school-based enterprise by grade 12; and personalized student supports including counseling, accelerated instruction, and social-emotional learning. The framework is grounded in the MDRC and SRI evidence the report reviews.
requirements: A task force to develop a state pathways framework and quality standards guiding pilots and eventual system design
constraints: The report notes H.B. 91 continued to situate CTE largely in isolation from the rest of students' high school experience
target_learners: All high school students in grades 9-12
target_learning_goals: College and career readiness
High school completion and postsecondary transition
Industry-related knowledge and skills integrated with core academics
examples: The report recommends New Mexico create demonstrations of pathways systems in 6 to 10 districts as part of the H.B. 91 CTE pilot.
key_sources: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education

article_title: Building a System of College and Career Pathways in New Mexico
citation: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education
title: Seven-dimension pathway quality standards spanning outcomes-driven practice, equity culture, industry themes, project-based learning, work-based learning, supports, and distributed leadership
description: The report proposes state quality standards for college and career pathways mirroring the seven dimensions on which certified Linked Learning pathways produced positive impacts. Standards include that "The progress of every student is the driving focus for evaluating pathway quality," a culture of high expectations with nondiscriminatory and inclusive practices, an industry-themed program of study offering dual credit, inquiry- and project-based learning that is "relevant, rigorous, outcome-focused, and collaborative in nature," a personalized continuum of work-based learning for every student, personalized academic and social-emotional supports, and shared responsibility among staff, leaders, and community partners.
requirements: A pathway quality assessment rubric tied to state quality standards, plus metrics and incentives for increasingly higher levels of quality implementation
constraints: The report warns tracking should ensure pathways do not regress into old systems that led to tracking and inequitable outcomes by race, ethnicity, gender, and special needs
target_learners: All high school students in pathway programs, including students with low prior achievement
target_learning_goals: College and career readiness
Mastery of college- and career-ready learning outcomes
Academic and professional skills demonstrated through work-based learning
examples: The report recommends metrics such as percentage of students participating in industry-centered, multidisciplinary project-based learning and percentage of students earning dual college credit aligned with their pathway.
key_sources: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education

article_title: California Teachers and COVID-19: How the Pandemic is Impacting the Teacher Workforce
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., Leung, M., & Burns, D. (2021). California teachers and COVID-19: How the pandemic is impacting the teacher workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/california-covid-19-teacher-workforce
title: Teacher residency programs as district-preparation partnerships for high-need positions
description: Teacher residency programs are "partnerships between school districts and teacher preparation programs designed to recruit and prepare a diverse pool of candidates to teach in high-need positions." They are yearlong apprenticeships modeled on medical residencies, providing residents extensive clinical practice under an expert mentor teacher while completing tightly integrated coursework. Districts with residencies reported certainty about the number and quality of teachers they could expect to hire.
requirements: District-preparation partnership capacity; state or local investment to fund resident supports
constraints: The report notes many residents struggle financially and such programs can be out of reach for smaller districts with lean administrative teams
target_learners: Teacher candidates in high-need subjects and locations
target_learning_goals: Fully prepared, retained teachers for shortage fields
examples: Districts expanded residencies leveraging state investments; leaders valued predictable hiring from yearlong preservice cohorts

article_title: Students Experiencing Homelessness: The Conditions and Outcomes of Homelessness among California Students
citation: Burns, D., Espinoza, D., Ondrasek, N., & Yang, M. (2021). Students experiencing homelessness: The conditions and outcomes of homelessness among California students. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/students-experiencing-homelessness
title: Multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) as a school-level structure for supporting students experiencing homelessness
description: MTSS is described as a school-level coordinative structure that integrates academic, behavioral, and social-emotional supports in tiers. The report states that "School-level structures like multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS) can support students experiencing homelessness by providing an intervention framework that integrates academic, behavioral, and social and emotional competencies." It recommends districts implement MTSS so services reach students who need them without cumbersome procedures, and notes MTSS can be tailored to individual students' specific needs, which matters given this group's complex needs.
requirements: Well implementation to provide services effectively, which the report notes can be made challenging by the highly mobile nature of homelessness
constraints: Implementation is challenged by the highly mobile nature of homelessness, as the article states
target_learners: K–12 students experiencing homelessness
target_learning_goals: Integrated academic, behavioral, and social and emotional competencies
examples: The report recommends districts implement school-level coordinative structures such as MTSS to efficiently identify and meet student needs, alongside community school wraparound supports
key_sources: Burns, D., Espinoza, D., Ondrasek, N., & Yang, M. (2021). Students experiencing homelessness: The conditions and outcomes of homelessness among California students. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/students-experiencing-homelessness

article_title: Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans
citation: Mustaffa, J. B., & Davis, J. C. W. (2021). Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/black-student-debt-study/
title: National Black Student Loan Debt Study (survey of 1,272 Black borrowers plus 100 in-depth interviews)
description: A sequential, equal status mixed-method study of Black borrowers' experiences with student loans, conducted by The Education Trust with Jalil B. Mustaffa. "In total, 1,272 Black borrowers completed our survey," recruited via social media ads, email alerts, and word of mouth, followed by in-depth interviews with 100 volunteers selected on demographic characteristics and analyzed with the constant comparative method. The sample is largely four-year and graduate-degree holders, women, borrowers aged 25 and older, earning $50,000 or more annually.
requirements: Participants must identify as Black borrowers; survey instrument elicits perspectives on mental health, information quality, pandemic impact, return on investment, and solutions
constraints: Non-random sampling scheme; sample skews toward degree holders, women, and borrowers earning $50,000 or more annually, so findings may not generalize to all Black borrowers
target_learners: Black student loan borrowers in higher education, including graduate-degree holders and parent borrowers
target_learning_goals: Understanding Black borrowers' lived experiences of student debt to inform student loan and college affordability policy
examples: Survey data were cleaned, recoded, and analyzed using frequencies and descriptive statistics; the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Pennsylvania
key_sources: Mustaffa, J. B., & Davis, J. C. W. (2021). Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/black-student-debt-study/

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: California
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: California. EDTRUST.ORG. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: California Classified School Employee Teacher Credentialing Program (Grow Your Own)
description: A California Grow Your Own program that provides grants to adults who work in schools (classified staff) so they can complete their undergraduate education and prepare to become teachers. In July 2021 the state appropriated $125 million to expand the program for another five years. The California Center on Teaching Careers is described as an extension of the Credentialing Grant Program that supports classified staff pursuing teaching degrees. The brief rates California green on providing funding, guidance, and public support for GYO programs that attract candidates of color.
requirements: State-level funding and guidance for developing GYO programming
constraints: Described as serving adults already working in schools; the brief reports no outcome evaluation of the program
target_learners: classified school staff and paraprofessionals seeking teacher credentials
adults already working in schools
target_learning_goals: completing undergraduate education and teacher preparation
entering the teaching profession
examples: The brief cites Texas' Grow Your Own grant program as another state earning a green in this category
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: California. EDTRUST.ORG. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing educator workforce diversity
description: The brief organizes state-level action into six strategies: making educator diversity data "visible and actionable to stakeholders"; setting clear state and district goals; investing in educator preparation programs; targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting and hiring a diverse workforce; investing in retention through working conditions and growth opportunities; and using federal COVID relief funds for diversity strategies. Each strategy is operationalized as criteria rated on a three-level scale (meets all or most, some, one or no requirements), and Illinois is rated against each. The framework treats workforce diversity as a policy-design problem spanning data, goals, preparation, recruitment, and retention.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share useful and timely educator workforce data so stakeholders can set goals and chart a path forward
constraints: The framework addresses state-level policy conditions; it rates what states do, not district or classroom practice
target_learners: K-12 public school students in Illinois, particularly students of color
target_learning_goals: Equitable student access to a racially diverse, high-quality educator workforce
examples: Illinois earned greens for scholarship programs, GYO funding, residency pathways, and numeric diversity goals, but reds or no-evidence ratings for investing in minority-serving institutions and for leader cultural-competence training
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622786

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Make educator diversity data publicly visible and actionable at the school level
description: The brief argues that increasing workforce diversity requires that "all stakeholders must have access to useful and timely educator workforce data to set goals and chart a path forward." State education agencies, as keepers of state data systems, should publish school-level racial demographics of the educator workforce in dashboards, report cards, or reports so stakeholders can make targeted decisions. Illinois posts only district-level data, and the brief recommends adding school-level data and easier interpretation, citing Massachusetts' dashboard as a model.
requirements: Data should be publicly available and easily accessible, at school level, in a dashboard, report card, or state report
constraints: Illinois currently meets only some requirements: it posts district-level rather than school-level data
target_learners: K-12 public school students

citation: Byon, A. H., & Elliott, K. C. (2022). Equity First: Priorities for Higher Education Partnerships and Investments. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/how-to-end-the-hunger-and-homelessness-crisis-among-college-students/

students from low-income backgrounds

article_title: Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847
title: A three-indicator framework for describing state teacher compensation conditions
description: The report organizes teacher compensation analysis around three indicators: "(1) average annual starting salary for public school teachers, (2) average annual starting salary for public school teachers adjusted for cost-of-living differences across states, and (3) average weekly wage competitiveness". Together, the authors state, "these indicators signal the overall wage conditions underlying efforts to attract and retain well-prepared teachers across a state." Each indicator is presented as a national and state-level map and table.
requirements: Starting-salary data collected from district teacher salary schedules or district compensation plans
Cost-of-living adjustment requires Regional Price Parity data
Wage competitiveness requires comparison wages for other college-educated workers in each state
constraints: Teacher starting salaries and cost of living vary by district, so within states there are districts higher or lower than the state average on these indicators
target_learners: Public school teachers (K-12 workforce)
target_learning_goals: Understanding state teacher compensation conditions that underlie teacher recruitment and retention
examples: The report applies the framework to all states and the District of Columbia, with a final table showing all three indicators and ranks for each state.
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847

article_title: Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847
title: Teacher wage competitiveness index
description: An indicator defined as "the average public school teacher weekly wage as a percentage of the estimated weekly wage for other college-educated workers within each state". Weekly wages are used because they "adjust for any differences in the work year across occupations". The report transforms Economic Policy Institute weekly wage penalty data to a 0-100% scale and bands states from less competitive (below 75%) to more competitive (90% or above).
requirements: Population Survey data controlling for factors that typically influence wages
Weekly wage estimates for other college-educated workers in each state
constraints: State estimates are based on data from 2014 through 2019, and the national estimate is based on 2019 data
target_learners: Public school teachers (K-12 workforce)
target_learning_goals: Assessing how competitively teacher pay compares with other college-educated occupations in a state
examples: The report reports state index values ranging from Wyoming at 98.0% down to Virginia at 67.3%, with a U.S. average of 80.8%.
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847

credential holders
career changers
high school students in dual enrollment

ECE coursework completion
bachelor's degree attainment for early educators

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions into six strategies: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, investing in educator preparation programs, targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting a diverse workforce, investing in retention of teachers of color, and using federal COVID-related relief funds. district and school leaders
educator preparation programs

recruiting, preparing, and retaining teachers of color

article_title: Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators through Teacher Residencies
citation: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797
title: Common features of a high-quality teacher residency
description: The brief enumerates characteristics that research has identified in high-quality teacher residency programs: residencies "consist of strong partnerships between school districts, universities, and sometimes other organizations," tightly integrate coursework with classroom practice, require a full year of residency teaching alongside an accomplished mentor teacher, recruit diverse candidates for specific district needs, provide financial support in exchange for a teaching commitment, place cohorts in teaching schools modeling evidence-based practices, and offer ongoing mentoring for graduates. The brief presents these features as making early childhood-focused residencies part of a multipronged solution for preparing qualified, diverse teachers.
requirements: Strong district–university partnerships
Yearlong clinical experience with an accomplished mentor teacher
Financial supports for residents
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates preparing for TK–3 or elementary credentials
target_learning_goals: Preparation of credentialed teachers with early childhood expertise
examples: Fresno Unified's TK–3 residency and UCLA's IMPACT ECE program both exhibited these features, including paid apprenticeships, integrated coursework, and cohort placement in partner schools.

article_title: Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators through Teacher Residencies
citation: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797
title: Fresno TK–3 Teacher Residency Program
description: An 18-month residency (2017–2019) within Fresno Unified's workforce pipeline, run with California State University, Fresno, leading to a Multiple Subject credential and a master's degree in curriculum and instruction. The program focused on "early literacy, developmentally appropriate practices, and social and emotional learning" plus family engagement, with all credential coursework co-taught by district leaders paired with university faculty and quarterly curriculum meetings used to redesign syllabi around a developmental focus. Residents received an $11,000 stipend, clustered school-site placements, and courses held at a school site near their clinical placements.
requirements: District–university co-instruction of all credential coursework
Federal TQP grant funding for the resident stipend
constraints: The stipend was not enough to fully cover residents' cost of living; some residents substituted one day a week to supplement income
target_learners: Recent college graduates, career changers, and uncertified educators seeking TK–3 credentials
target_learning_goals: Developmentally appropriate pedagogy, early literacy, STEM integration, and social-emotional learning for TK–3
examples: Residents applied the project approach, investigated puzzles of practice, and taught literacy skills within content areas using informational text as starting points for science, social studies, or fine arts explorations.
key_sources: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797

article_title: Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators through Teacher Residencies
citation: Cathy Yun. (2022). Preparing Transitional Kindergarten to 3rd Grade Educators Through Teacher Residencies. Learning Policy Institute & EDPREPLAB. https://doi.org/10.54300/139.797
title: UCLA IMPACT ECE/Multiple Subject Program
description: A social justice–focused urban teacher residency run by LAUSD and UCLA Center X (2010–2014), through which candidates earned a Child Development Master Teacher Permit, Multiple Subject certification, and a Master of Education degree in 18 months. It began with a weeklong institute on child development and inclusion, required the eight early childhood core courses (the CAP 8) for the child development permit, and included extensive clinical placements in early childhood settings (6 hours a day, 4 days a week) and elementary classrooms (approximately 30 hours per week). Residents received a $10,000 fellowship; mentors received a $3,000 stipend and monthly "Methods With Mentors" professional development organized around UCLA's five dimensions of mentoring quality.
requirements: Completion of the CAP 8 early childhood core courses for the child development permit
Mentor selection and matching based on effective teaching and program values
constraints: The program required a large number of courses because residents pursued two certifications and a master's degree; the director noted integrating ECE and multiple subject courses would be a value add
target_learners: Candidates interested in early childhood education in traditionally underserved urban communities
target_learning_goals: Child development expertise, developmentally appropriate practice, social justice–oriented instruction, and inquiry-based reflective practice
examples: Residents' inquiries addressed puzzles of practice such as creating environments in which families feel welcome, differentiating instruction, and implementing classroom management strategies.

citation: Jinann Bitar, Gabriel Montague, Lauren Ilano. (2022). Faculty Diversity and Student Success Go Hand in Hand, So Why Are University Faculties So White? The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org

Metrics 1-3 produce 0-100 scores converted to letter grades: faculty diversity relative to student diversity, equity in tenure-track versus contingent hiring, and equity in tenure distribution. The framework is designed so advocates can "use these metrics and findings to see what's happening at institutions and push for change."

policy advocates
state and federal policymakers
target_learning_goals: increasing Black and Latino faculty representation
improving college completion for students of color
examples: Bluefield State College scored 99 (A) on Black faculty diversity because 9.5% of faculty were Black versus 9.6% of students; Ball State scored 105 (A) on Latino hiring equity

description: The report profiles three initiatives it identifies as promising practices for diversifying the professoriate. The Southern Regional Education Board's State Doctoral Scholars Program provides "tailored faculty mentoring, networking, and financial support throughout their doctoral journey" and has helped more than 1,100 underrepresented students earn a Ph.D., with an 83% participant graduation rate. The California Pre-Doctoral Program funds disadvantaged juniors, seniors, and graduate students for doctoral preparation, including GRE preparation and faculty mentoring.

undergraduate and graduate students facing economic or educational disadvantages
faculty hiring committees

reducing bias in faculty hiring
building the professoriate pipeline for students of color

article_title: Authentic Student Work in College Admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business
citation: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774
title: Ross Admissions Portfolio (Business Case Discussion + Artifact)
description: A required student-created portfolio added to the Ross School of Business BBA first-year application in fall 2016. Per the report, "The Ross Admissions Portfolio consists of two components: a Business Case Discussion and an Artifact." The Business Case Discussion is a 500-word essay asking applicants to identify and solve a personally meaningful business-related issue; the Artifact is a 250-word description accompanying multimedia work showing learning applied in or beyond school. Every first-year BBA applicant completes it alongside University of Michigan application materials.
requirements: Aligned to central admission processes without altering University of Michigan deadlines or timelines

article_title: Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study
citation: Duchesneau, N., & Zapata, M. (2023). Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Five-type spectrum of school safety approaches, from school-to-prison pipeline schools to school-to-possibility pipeline schools
description: The report's authors categorize schools on a five-point spectrum of safety approaches. At one end, "School-to-prison pipeline schools" are "hardened schools with a high emphasis on physical security, no guardrails to prevent the harm that physical security can cause, and little to no attention on student well-being." Intermediate types add guardrails and scale up well-being practices while scaling down physical security. The ultimate goal, school-to-possibility pipeline schools, have fully adopted practices addressing root causes of violence and removed physical security. Leaders are advised to locate their schools on the spectrum and plan next steps toward the goal.
requirements: Leaders must first assess where their school or district currently stands on the spectrum in terms of current policies before planning next steps
constraints: The spectrum is a framework proposed by the report's authors based on this two-district case study and other research, not a validated measurement instrument
target_learners: students in urban districts serving majority Black, Latino, and/or low-income populations
target_learning_goals: creating safe, inclusive learning environments that support students' social, emotional, and academic development
examples: The report situates both case-study districts as retaining physical security while adopting well-being practices, placing them in intermediate spectrum categories rather than at the school-to-possibility end
key_sources: Duchesneau, N., & Zapata, M. (2023). Creating Safer Schools: A Case Study. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED641760

article_title: Universal Prekindergarten Expansion in California: Progress and Opportunities
citation: Wang, V., Leung-Gagné, M., Melnick, H., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Universal prekindergarten expansion in California: Progress and opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/597.103
title: California universal prekindergarten mixed-delivery system and the 2022–23 UPK Planning and Implementation Grant Survey
description: California's UPK system is a mixed-delivery early learning arrangement comprising transitional kindergarten (TK), the California State Preschool Program (CSPP), Head Start, and locally funded early learning programs. The report states "California UPk includes several early learning programs, including transitional kindergarten (Tk), the California State Preschool Program (CSPP), Head Start, and locally funded early learning programs," with TK the only program that is free and universally available as part of the public school system and CSPP serving income-eligible 3- and 4-year-olds. Implementation is supported by the Universal Prekindergarten Planning and Implementation Grant (about $200 million in 2021 plus $300 million added in 2022), and monitored through the California Department of Education's August 2023 survey of all grant recipients, analyzed here for 1,384 LEAs (95% of public school districts and 65% of charter schools serving elementary grades).
requirements: All public LEAs are required to offer TK; offering CSPP and Head Start and partnering with community-based providers is encouraged but not required

TK curriculum must align with the California Preschool Learning Foundations, and state-funded TK classes must meet staffing requirements including the 2025–26 credential and early childhood coursework requirements
constraints: TK eligibility expands gradually, with all 4-year-olds eligible only by the 2025–26 school year
The report's findings describe the 2022–23 school year as captured in one survey administration
target_learners: All California 4-year-olds
Income-eligible 3- and 4-year-olds
Multilingual learners and students with disabilities in early learning programs
target_learning_goals: Universal access to prekindergarten education
School readiness across developmental domains
Developmentally appropriate early learning instruction
examples: In 2022–23, 25% of LEAs (343) operated a CSPP contract; 19% applied to expand their existing contract and 12% planned to apply in future years
The 2021 grant allocated $200 million to all LEAs serving kindergarteners, and the 2022 budget added another $300 million with funds released in 2023
The survey analyzed responses from 1,384 LEAs, representing 817 of 862 public school districts and 567 of 875 charter schools offering elementary grades

citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Ideal pathways system: intentional, supported trajectories with consistent guidance from middle school through adulthood
description: The brief defines pathways as "the full universe of intentional and supported trajectories that every learner understands and participates in as they move from adolescence through adulthood." The framework spans CTE, work-based learning including internships and apprenticeships, early postsecondary opportunities (advanced coursework, AP, IB, dual enrollment, early college), and postsecondary programs leading to industry-recognized credentials or degrees. Learners receive "consistent, knowledgeable guidance, beginning in middle school, from well-qualified counselors and navigators" and are supported over time to find, experience, and move among pathways aligned with their desired social, economic, and personal outcomes.
requirements: Well-qualified counselors and navigators with knowledge of the full range of options and capacity to connect students to opportunities
Guidance beginning in middle school and continuing through transitions
constraints: The current patchwork of programs and funding streams is described as inadequate to address the scale and urgency of the challenge
target_learners: Students ages 16-24, particularly low-income, first-generation students and students of color
target_learning_goals: College and career navigation and informed pathway choice
examples: The brief's convening of national partners in fall 2023 produced this collective definition to guide federal policy recommendations

citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Five elements of an ideal pathways system: clear choices, smart start, access for all, guided beginnings, final prep
description: The brief enumerates five essential elements an ideal pathways system ensures for students and families: "1. Clear choices: a clear understanding of all their options 2. A smart start: early outreach before entering high school 3. Access for all: information that is accessible and in multiple formats 4. Guided beginnings: regular touchpoints with a navigator 5. Final prep: dedicated and targeted support in high school." Each element is paired with promising state practices, such as Indiana's College Core planning tool, Connecticut's Student Success Plans, DCPS language access, Illinois' PaCE Framework, and Pinellas County college and career centers.
requirements: Dedicated pathways counselors in every school to connect students to these systems
Federal investment at scale, since implementation varies across states and underfunded districts struggle to offer additional resources
constraints: The brief notes other important elements exist (greater ROI, long-term economic mobility, employers seeing qualified employees) but focuses on the five navigation and counseling elements
target_learners: High school students and their families, particularly students of color and students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Understanding and accessing college and career pathway options
examples: Connecticut requires individualized Student Success Plans starting in sixth grade; Illinois' PaCE Framework organizes career exploration, postsecondary preparation, and financial aid literacy

citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Pathways counselors: highly trained specialists providing personalized navigation support alongside grade-level counselors
description: The brief calls for "the creation and support of highly trained pathways counselors who can work in conjunction with grade-level school counselors and educators, but whose sole job is to provide students with a clear understanding of their options and outcomes; provide personalized, regular touchpoints to help students stay on track; and offer dedicated, targeted support on students' college and career journeys." The rationale is that it is nearly impossible for one school counselor to serve as general practitioner, provide grade-level supports, fulfill administrative tasks, offer mental health support, and be trained on all pathways. The brief also proposes national training and certification for this role.
requirements: Sufficient funds and clear expectations for districts to hire and support enough navigators
Professional learning, supports, and tools so school personnel can prepare all students for a high-quality pathways journey
constraints: The brief states solving the school counselor shortage is not possible anytime soon, motivating the specialist role
target_learners: High school students, especially traditionally underserved students
target_learning_goals: Clear understanding of college and career options and outcomes; staying on track toward postsecondary goals
examples: Pinellas County Schools staff every high school with a college and career center with a dedicated coordinator and trained volunteers, freeing counselors for more substantive conversations

title: Residency clinical faculty site coordinator role
description: The site coordinator is a clinical faculty role at residency partner educator preparation programs, described by US PREP as a "critical linchpin" to transformed residencies and much expanded compared to typical clinical field supervisor assignments. Beyond observing and coaching candidates, site coordinators provide mentor training and professional development, facilitate EPP–district partnership governance meetings, and compile and present resident clinical performance data to inform partnership improvement. As one US PREP staff member noted, "They're engaged with all stakeholders. They're the one responsible for gathering the data and supporting residents, mentors, and principals during the actual yearlong residency."
requirements: Site coordinators are EPP faculty embedded in school districts to work directly with mentor teachers, school leaders, and district administrators

mentor teachers

partnership governance and continuous improvement
examples: In TCLAS-supported partnerships, site coordinators participated in regular professional development sessions featuring data-driven discussions of resident progress

title: Provide resident stipends covering living expenses so candidates can fully participate in yearlong clinical placements
description: Paid residency stipends intended to cover living expenses are an essential feature of Texas residencies. "Set by the TCLAS grant program at $20,000 per resident, stipends were aimed at eliminating the need for residents to take outside jobs during the yearlong clinical placement." Stipends made residencies a realistic option for a broader pool of candidates, and current residents consistently shared they could only participate because of the stipends. Implementing residencies without stipends may create barriers to full resident participation.
requirements: Stipend levels sufficient to eliminate the need for residents to take outside jobs during the clinical year
constraints: Implementation of residencies without stipends may create barriers to full resident participation in local contexts
target_learners: teacher residency candidates

examples: TCLAS set stipends at $20,000 per resident to support living expenses during the yearlong placement

description: Texas interwove responsibility for teacher preparation across educator preparation programs (EPPs) and districts, with grants built on the assumption that the two work in tandem. As the TEA described, "In high-quality teacher residency models, the EPP and [district] have shared ownership over the preparation, support, and success of the teacher resident." Partnership requirements were instantiated through shared governance meetings that specified attendance by both parties, identified topics for collaborative planning, and called for joint data-informed decision-making, creating feedback loops for continuous improvement.

examples: Shared governance enabled EPPs to iterate on coursework, revisit assignments, and improve alignment to district contexts after practice-based redesigns

article_title: Humanizing Teacher Preparation: Claremont Graduate University's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Humanizing teacher preparation: Claremont Graduate University's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/338.812
title: Claremont Critical Social Justice Teaching Competencies and classroom ecology framework with nine domains
description: Claremont's Teacher Education Program uses its Critical Social Justice Teaching Competencies as the foundation for coursework and clinical programming, so that every assignment and class develops skills to interrupt deficit schooling. The framework centers relationships and interactions between and among students and teachers, emphasizing humanizing classroom experiences. The competencies explicitly address nine domains: "(1) philosophy of education, (2) pedagogy, (3) science of learning (data-driven instruction), (4) socio-emotional learning and experience, (5) funds of knowledge, (6) school climate and culture, (7) community and cultural wealth, (8) socio-political identity, and (9) worldview and global perspectives." Faculty operationalize the stance through concrete, observable teaching practices.
requirements: Competencies must be integrated into all courses, clinical observations, resident self-reflection, and evaluations rather than confined to one course
constraints: Applies to Claremont's own teacher preparation program; the report does not test the framework's effects experimentally
target_learners: teacher preparation candidates (residents) earning preliminary California credentials
target_learning_goals: critical social justice teaching practices
culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy
humanizing classroom relationships
examples: The program aligned clinical observations, resident self-reflection, and evaluations with the competencies and centered the work of diverse scholars as course texts

Consider: Who or what is included or excluded in those assumptions and values? 4. How can you reimagine or reenvision it." Residents reported that reflecting on positionality and implicit biases also builds community, with one resident noting team-building discussion "makes us feel bound together in community."

The model is organized around seven prioritized teaching practices aligned to California's Teacher Performance Expectations and the Danielson Framework for Teaching.

article_title: Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students
citation: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn
title: Human capital theory as the framework linking education investment to productivity and societal returns
description: The report adopts human capital theory as its organizing framework, which "has established that education, or human capital more broadly, enhances a person's skills and increases productivity in the workplace, and that investments in education anticipate a wide range of benefits." The framework treats aggregate human capital as the nation's combined skills and attainment, weighted by demographic composition, and predicts both individual and collective economic gains, externalities, and nonmonetary benefits. The report cites empirical rates of return of about 10% for an additional year of education.
requirements: Requires treating education as an investment whose returns can be estimated and compared against costs
constraints: Returns estimates typically focus on increased earnings and the individual, though the report argues for broader accounting including externalities
target_learners: All students, with particular attention to those from historically disadvantaged racial/ethnic and income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Educational attainment, skills, productivity, and long-term economic and social outcomes
examples: The report applies the framework to justify benefit-cost analysis of interventions from preschool through higher education.
key_sources: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn

article_title: Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students
citation: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn
title: Design education investments with sufficient quality, intensity, duration, and dosage to yield strong benefit-cost ratios
description: The report's economic evaluations indicate that intervention design features drive returns: "the quality, intensity, and duration of the interventions are important, as higher benefit-to-cost ratios are usually associated with more resource-intense programs and those with stronger dosage effects and/or with longer exposure." This principle directs policymakers and program designers to resource interventions adequately rather than scaling back inputs, since under-resourced versions may fail to reproduce the returns documented in evaluations.
requirements: Programs must be funded and implemented at the quality, intensity, and duration levels associated with higher benefit-to-cost ratios in the evaluation literature
constraints: Higher benefit-to-cost ratios are associated with more resource-intense programs, implying greater upfront cost
target_learners: All students, with particular benefit for the most disadvantaged children
target_learning_goals: Maximizing net economic and educational returns on educational investment
examples: The report's synthesis of economic evaluations found stronger dosage effects and longer exposure linked to higher returns.

article_title: Building Futures: Strengthening the Educator Workforce through Teacher Apprenticeships
citation: Nathan Kriha, Diarese George, Jonathan Feinstein, and Anna Skubel. (2025). Building Futures: Strengthening the Educator Workforce Through Teacher Apprenticeships. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Registered Teacher Apprenticeship Programs (RTAPs) and the National Guidelines for Apprenticeship Standards
description: RTAPs are a form of registered apprenticeship recognized by the U.S. Department of Labor in which apprentices hold paid positions with progressively increasing wages, complete at least 2,000 hours of structured on-the-job training under an experienced mentor, receive supplemental classroom instruction, and earn a portable, nationally recognized credential. The Pathways Alliance's National Guidelines add teacher-specific elements: competency-based completion, at least one academic year of on-the-job learning with a mentor-teacher at a ratio not exceeding two apprentices per mentor, at least 144 hours of related technical instruction, and no service as teacher of record. The report describes RTAPs as an "earn and learn" model intended to make teaching more accessible and affordable and to attract a more diverse candidate pool.
requirements: Programs must be registered with the U.S. Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency and operate as partnerships between districts and educator preparation programs
constraints: The report notes little research exists on the efficacy of these programs to produce high-quality, well-prepared, and diverse educators, and many programs have yet to graduate any apprentices
target_learners: adult learners and currently employed non-teacher school staff such as paraprofessionals and long-term substitutes seeking teacher licensure
target_learning_goals: full state teacher certification or licensure through competency-based, job-embedded educator preparation
examples: Programs studied in Tennessee and Texas placed apprentices in schools four to five days per week while completing coursework at night and on weekends, lasting one to three years depending on entry credentials

description: The brief describes American higher education quality assurance as a "program integrity triad" established under the Higher Education Act of 1965, designed to ensure Title IV funding flows only to institutions meeting standards for quality and integrity. article_title: AI-Assisted Autonomous Learning and Reduced Academic Accomplishment in Vocational Higher Education: The Mediating Role of Hardiness
citation: Wang W and Zhang Q (2026). AI-assisted autonomous learning and reduced academic accomplishment in vocational higher education: the mediating role of hardiness. Front. Psychol. 17:1848291. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1848291
title: Psychological resource account of AI-mediated learning grounded in Self-Determination Theory
description: The article frames AI-assisted autonomous learning as a learning context that reshapes students' experiences of autonomy, competence, and challenge rather than merely a tool for efficiency. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, it argues that when AI "functions as a scaffold" students retain ownership, but when it replaces effortful engagement, "the learning process may appear autonomous but become externally guided in substance." Hardiness (commitment, control, challenge) is positioned as the psychological resource transmitting these effects to academic self-evaluation, with Cognitive Load Theory as a complementary explanation for reduced deep processing.
requirements: Students must retain opportunities for independent decisions, effortful problem solving, and challenge appraisal for hardiness to be activated
constraints: The account is tested only cross-sectionally among vocational college students at one Chinese institution and the mediation is partial, so other mechanisms remain
target_learners: vocational higher education students
target_learning_goals: academic adaptation and self-evaluated competence in AI-supported self-directed learning
examples: The study modeled AI-assisted autonomous learning as a second-order latent variable predicting hardiness and reduced academic accomplishment in an SEM

description: The article recommends that AI tools be integrated "as supportive scaffolds rather than replacement systems": teachers should "intentionally retain moderately challenging tasks in AI-supported courses" and design activities requiring students to explain, reflect, revise, and decide independently. AI should provide prompting questions, step-by-step hints, alternative perspectives, or reflective feedback rather than complete solutions, so students keep a sense of control, persistence, and ownership while benefiting from AI support.

constraints: The recommendation rests on cross-sectional correlational evidence, not on a test of the designed activities themselves

article_title: AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning
citation: Minji Kim, Cheolil Lim. (2025). AI chatbot design principles to enhance the collective efficacy in collaborative learning. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-025-10080-z
title: Four-element design framework for AI chatbots enhancing collective efficacy in collaborative learning
description: The article proposes a design framework for educational AI chatbots organized into four design elements: group cohesion support, affective cohesion support, support for collaborative learning activities, and inducing conversation (facilitation of dialogue). These elements are operationalized through ten design principles and 46 sub-guidelines. The framework is grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, Social and Emotional Learning, Social Presence Theory, and Transactional Distance Theory, and positions chatbots as "dynamic members of collaborative teams" that scaffold both social and cognitive processes.
requirements: The chatbot must automatically deliver team-specific feedback by analyzing accumulated conversation logs, without requiring learner prompts
constraints: The principles were developed as general guidelines across age groups; the authors state context-specific principles for project-based, maker, and discussion-based learning require further research
target_learners: learners working in collaborative learning teams across age groups
target_learning_goals: collective efficacy
collaboration
communication
problem-solving

article_title: Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human-AI co-regulation in learning
citation: S P, Joseph J, Jose M, S M A, N R and Joseph J (2026) Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human–AI co-regulation in learning. Front. Dev. Psychol. 4:1835258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdpys.2026.1835258
title: Human–AI co-regulation framework: cognitive regulation is distributed between the learner and an external intelligent system
description: The article proposes that interactions with AI be conceptualized as a co-regulation process in which planning, monitoring, and control of cognition are shared between a human learner and an adaptive intelligent system. It integrates sociocultural theory, executive function and metacognition research, and distributed cognition, extending classical developmental accounts to non-human regulating partners. The authors state they "hypothesize that the interaction with AI can be viewed as a co-regulation process, where cognitive regulation is distributed between the learner and the external intelligent system."
requirements: An adaptive AI system capable of real-time response generation, feedback, and decision support, not merely passive information presentation
constraints: The framework is conceptual and not yet empirically validated; the authors note there are "still only limited empirical findings, which are frequently inconsistent"

problem solving

title: Four roles of AI in cognitive regulation: scaffolding, metacognitive support, memory augmentation, and decision assistance
description: The proposed co-regulation model distinguishes four primary roles through which AI participates in cognition. As a scaffold, AI enables performance beyond independent capability; as metacognitive support, it prompts reflection and strategy evaluation; as external memory, it stores and generates content that offloads internal processing; as decision partner, it offers recommendations that shape action. The article states: "The model highlights four primary roles of AI in cognitive regulation: scaffolding, metacognitive support, memory augmentation, and decision assistance."
requirements: AI systems that actively engage in organizing cognitive activity rather than only storing or presenting information
constraints: The nature and intensity of AI involvement vary across developmental stages, becoming more prominent in later stages where metacognitive capacities are more developed

citation: Stenbom, S., & Garrison, D. R. (2026). Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences. The International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 27(2), 114–131. https://doi.org/10.19173/irrodl.v27i2.9314
title: The Community of Inquiry framework as a coherent theoretical framework for guiding educational adoption of AI
description: The article positions the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework as the theoretical lens needed to navigate the tensions of generative AI in education, stating that "this article argues for the necessity of a coherent theoretical framework to guide the educational adoption of AI." It uses CoI and collaborative inquiry to show how AI can be integrated "in ways that preserve human agency and sustain deep and meaningful learning." The authors conclude the framework "has considerable potential to provide understanding and guidance in the adoption of AI tools."

constraints: The framework guides adoption; the article argues its necessity rather than empirically testing it
