article_title: The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector is Lack of Training
citation: Vinicius Santana Gomes. (2026). The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector Is Lack of Training: How a Structured Method Accompanied Productivity Gains in Two Brazilian Government Cases. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01517
title: The AI House: a four-layer pedagogical method for public-sector AI adoption (Foundation, Walls, Finishing, Roof)
description: The AI House is the article's named four-layer pedagogical method for adopting generative AI in the public sector, described as "a four-layer pedagogical method for the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the public sector". The Foundation teaches what generative AI is and how the model produces text; the Walls teach prompt construction (the PACTO method, Chain of Thought, zero-/one-/few-shot modes); the Finishing ties AI functionalities to the public servant's concrete document tasks and marks where human review is mandatory; the Roof integrates data-protection law, procedural confidentiality, public-administration principles, and international AI governance frameworks. The layer order is deliberate: skipping a layer generates a specific, predictable mode of failure, and "the house collapses entirely if the foundation is unstable".
requirements: All four layers must be taught in order; the article states each layer fulfills a function and skipping any generates a specific, predictable mode of failure.
constraints: The method was designed to operate on free-tier versions of commercial AI platforms, without corporate licensing or proprietary infrastructure.
target_learners: Public servants in government control and administrative units, with or without legal training
target_learning_goals: Safe, methodical, legally compliant use of generative AI for official document production, including prompt construction and data-protection compliance
examples: The method was materialized as a 20-hour, five-class official EGOV-DF course, 'Artificial Intelligence in the public sector: techniques, risks, and applications', with classes mapped to the four layers.
key_sources: Vinicius Santana Gomes. (2026). The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector Is Lack of Training: How a Structured Method Accompanied Productivity Gains in Two Brazilian Government Cases. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01517

article_title: The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector is Lack of Training
citation: Vinicius Santana Gomes. (2026). The Main Barrier to AI Adoption in the Public Sector Is Lack of Training: How a Structured Method Accompanied Productivity Gains in Two Brazilian Government Cases. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01517
title: Custom AI assistants with curated legal knowledge bases, queried in de-identified form
description: The method's operational key tool in both units was a custom AI built on free-tier platform functionality (Projects in ChatGPT and Claude, Gems in Gemini) loaded with the unit's applicable normative base. As the article describes it, "By loading into the custom AI the normative base and the correct documents pertinent to the unit’s subject matter, the public servant obtains answers anchored in that base, with persona and tone configured for the institutional context." At SES/CONT the base comprised ten legal instruments (decrees, normative instructions, laws, manuals); at UCI/SEDET, modular custom AIs were built per recurring subject (e.g., Public Procurement under Law No. 14.133/2021). Queries were made de-identified, under a Data Anonymization Protocol, so submitted content ceases to be personal data under Article 12 of the Brazilian Data Protection Law.
requirements: A curated documentary/normative knowledge base pertinent to the unit's subject matter, loaded into the custom AI before use.
constraints: Queries must be de-identified: no names, case numbers, or identifiable data of the concrete case enter the tool; conversation-training features are deactivated and temporary conversation modes used.
target_learners: Public servants producing legal and technical administrative documents in internal control units
target_learning_goals: Drafting legally grounded documents, answering normative questions, and standardizing technical writing without exposing protected data
examples: SES/CONT's custom AI loaded ten legal instruments including Decree 39.701/2019 and Complementary Law 840/2011; UCI/SEDET built modular custom AIs per subject, migrated from Gemini Gems to Claude Projects.

article_title: AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education
citation: Mahinpei, R., Dean, V., Fong, R., Liu, L. T., & Ribeiro, M. H. (2026). AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03095
title: AI drafts as editable scaffolds that lower initiation barriers for discretionary work
description: The article proposes that AI-assisted drafts function as "editable scaffolds" for discretionary work: they provide personalized starting points that help workers begin a task they intend to do but often skip, rather than reducing the total effort of producing the output. Interviews show TAs use drafts to articulate implicit judgments, verify interpretations, and refine tone, treating them as "intermediate artifacts" rather than final outputs. The framework distinguishes increasing participation (whether work happens) from improving efficiency (how well required work is done).
requirements: The human must retain full control to use, edit, or ignore the draft at their discretion
constraints: Preserving human oversight may constrain how much total effort AI can remove, as the article notes drafts did not reduce measured time per unit of feedback
target_learners: teaching assistants in higher education
instructors managing discretionary feedback provision
target_learning_goals: increasing provision of personalized feedback to students
supporting TA articulation and verification of feedback
examples: In the field experiment, TAs described drafts as helping them "get started with a template and then fine-tune it as we go on" and as an "attention check" catching errors they missed
key_sources: Mahinpei, R., Dean, V., Fong, R., Liu, L. T., & Ribeiro, M. H. (2026). AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03095

article_title: AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education
citation: Mahinpei, R., Dean, V., Fong, R., Liu, L. T., & Ribeiro, M. H. (2026). AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03095
title: Separate AI-assisted feedback from grading to preserve independent evaluation and reduce over-reliance
description: The article recommends introducing AI assistance only after the primary evaluative task is complete. Instructors "raised concerns about potential over-reliance on AI-mediated feedback," and the design responded by having TAs "first completed grading independently, and only then proceeded to the feedback stage." This sequencing preserves the grader's independent judgment of student work while still lowering barriers to the discretionary feedback step, and it was reinforced by formative-study concerns about graders deferring to drafts without verification.
requirements: A workflow where the primary evaluative task (grading) can be completed before AI assistance is introduced
A platform integration that surfaces drafts only after the primary task is submitted
constraints: Validated in a single 300-level ML course with structured rubric-based grading; generalization to other workflows is not tested
target_learners: teaching assistants in higher education
target_learning_goals: preserving independent evaluation of student work
reducing over-reliance on AI-generated feedback
examples: The Chrome extension displayed feedback drafts only after TAs clicked a Done Grading button, ensuring AI assistance was introduced after grading was complete

title: LLM-backed Chrome extension surfacing AI feedback drafts within Gradescope
description: A lightweight, LLM-backed Chrome extension integrated into the Gradescope grading platform, powered by o4-mini (selected via Bradley-Terry analysis of TA rankings). After grading, TAs click a "Done Grading" button inserted by the extension; in treatment submissions a personalized AI feedback draft is shown, which TAs "can use the feedback draft as-is, edit it, or ignore it." The extension also logs behavioral data (provision, length, time) and embeds in-situ surveys on draft usage and helpfulness.

A prompt incorporating problem description, instructor solution, grading rubric, and student submission
constraints: Drafts shown only after grading to reduce over-reliance, per instructor and formative-study input
target_learners: teaching assistants grading written assessments in higher education
target_learning_goals: increasing personalized feedback provision on student submissions
examples: A pilot during a practice assignment (HW0) validated the extension and integration plan with no issues requiring changes

title: Generated Animated Traces (GATs): AI-generated, analogy-based, narrated animations synchronizing code, execution state, and conceptual analogy
description: GATs are AI-generated instructional videos for CS1 that synchronize a Source Code View with the currently executed line highlighted and a Conceptual Analogy View, e.g., "searching for abunnyin physical boxes to illustrate awhileloop". They were produced through a human-in-the-loop pipeline in which an AI-driven system generates scripts, traces, manim-based animations, subtitles, and voiceover, with light human editing for pedagogical clarity. The study compared GATs to textual explanations matched in learning objectives, conceptual scope, and line-by-line execution order.

citation: Tomohiro Nagashima, Mirella Hladký, and Vera Rief. (2026). Warning About AI Fallibility Increases Help-Seeking in an Intelligent Tutoring System. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03822
title: Math intelligent tutoring system with fox-shaped pedagogical agent Maddox and rule-based hard-coded hints
description: A math intelligent tutoring system built with the Cognitive Tutor Authoring Tools to support secondary students practicing systems of linear equations. Students begin with "drag-and-drop manipulations, selecting the next strategic step from a set of predefined options" and later move to free-text input. A fox-shaped pedagogical agent, Maddox, provides hints and targeted feedback that are "rule-based and hard-coded, without reliance on LLM-generated responses." The study compared two versions differing only in the popup message shown.

hints and feedback must be hard-coded to guarantee identical system behavior across conditions

so the warning concerns fallibility that is not actually present

target_learning_goals: solving systems of linear equations using substitution, equalization, and elimination methods

citation: Tomohiro Nagashima, Mirella Hladký, and Vera Rief. (2026). Warning About AI Fallibility Increases Help-Seeking in an Intelligent Tutoring System. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03822
title: Give both conditions a matched popup message to isolate the effect of disclosing AI fallibility
description: When testing transparency cues about AI fallibility, the control condition should receive a comparable popup that omits only the fallibility disclosure. The authors explain that "the distinction focused on whether the warning message mentioned the possibility of hallucination or not, instead of, for example, giving no warning to students in the control condition," so the design isolates the disclosure effect rather than the general effect of any warning popup.
requirements: A control message matched in format and tone that differs only in mentioning potential mistakes
constraints: This design tests disclosure of fallibility, not the general effect of providing popup warnings

target_learning_goals: critical engagement with potentially fallible system output
examples: The NoMistake condition received "Please read Maddox's messages carefully!" while the Mistake condition received the fallibility warning

article_title: Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose
citation: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed.
title: Oracle and tutor metaphors: how students' figurative framings of LLMs shape expectations that exceed the systems' pedagogical and epistemic capabilities
description: The chapter analyzes the two most prevalent student metaphors for LLMs: an oracle, conveying swift authoritative access to information, and a tutor, conveying personalized pedagogical support. Metaphors act as "cognitive scaffolding that helps people navigate and interpret unfamiliar tools" while also shaping uptake. The author argues the tutor metaphor "risks overstating the reliability of LLMs and wrongly imbues them with pedagogical intentionality," since LLMs do not track understanding or scaffold misconceptions, encouraging trust precisely where students' ability to evaluate accuracy is weakest.
requirements: Metaphor analysis draws on questionnaire responses in which students themselves articulated the metaphors and their associated hopes and worries
constraints: Analysis is based on a single 100-respondent questionnaire plus literature, not generalizable on its own per the author
target_learners: higher-education students, predominantly engineering
target_learning_goals: critical understanding of what LLMs are and are not
epistemic vigilance in AI-supported learning
examples: Students described LLMs as an expert truth-teller for search and synthesis, and as a low-barrier individual explainer, while simultaneously reporting hallucinations and verification burdens

citation: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed.
title: Adopt AI in education only in a purpose-driven, context-sensitive way, weighing pedagogical benefits against known risks including environmental costs
description: The chapter proposes that "Any potential adoption of AI in education should be purpose-driven": educators clarify why GenAI is needed in a course or assignment, what added value it represents, and how it contributes to learning objectives, then assess controlled experimentation against that initial motivation. If evidence does not support the intentions, educators should object to AI use for that purpose, positioning pedagogical benefits against known risks, including environmental and water costs of GenAI.
requirements: Educators clarify purpose via questions such as what added value the technology represents for the learning objectives
Controlled experimentation assessed for evidence against the initial motivation
constraints: In cases of doubt or no clearly supported purpose, the author urges erring on the side of caution and not using GenAI
target_learners: higher-education students, predominantly engineering
target_learning_goals: alignment of AI use with learning objectives
sustainability awareness in technology choices
examples: The author cites the UNESCO report figure that ChatGPT's roughly 1 billion daily queries add up to roughly 310 GWh per year, urging educators to keep such environmental costs in view

article_title: AI-Driven Assessment of Human Tutors: Linking Training Performance to Real-Life Practice
citation: Thomas, D. R., Kamikazi, M. C. A., Brandt, C., Borchers, C., & Koedinger, K. R. (2026). AI-Driven Assessment of Human Tutors: Linking Training Performance to Real-Life Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18617
title: AI-driven tutor training and real-life assessment system linking scenario-based lessons to transcript-based evaluation
description: The article introduces a pipeline that trains tutors on research-supported "tutor moves" via immersive scenario-based lessons, then uses generative AI (Gemini-2.5-pro) to evaluate real-life application in tutoring transcriptions. A two-stage prompting strategy first uses "an 'opportunity prompt' identified relevant moments where a tutor move was applicable (0/1)" and then "an 'evaluation prompt' scored the quality of the tutor action" (0-ineffective, 1-effective). The system maps three validity types to stages: content validity via expert judgment, predictive validity via training-to-transcript correlation, and construct validity via AI scoring accuracy. If proficiency is not met, a remediation loop of self-reflection or lesson retake is triggered.
requirements: LLM prompts derived from expert-validated human scoring rubrics, with documented inter-rater reliability procedures
Transcripts of authentic tutoring sessions (audio processed via Whisper and merged with chat logs)
constraints: The article states LLM prompts require continuous auditing given the wide range of IRR scores
Manual session uploads may introduce selection bias where more confident tutors submitted more data
target_learners: undergraduate volunteer and paraprofessional math tutors tutoring middle school students remotely
target_learning_goals: pedagogical tutor moves such as praising, reacting to errors, determining what students know, affirming correct attempts, guiding thinking, and prompting explanation
examples: 86 undergraduate tutors completed six scenario-based lessons within a three-phase interrupted time series design, with audio transcriptions and Zoom chat logs collected in the resumed tutoring phase

article_title: What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue
citation: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225
title: Complementary-affordances account: AI dialogue as supported monologue versus human dialogue as interactional-competence practice
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that AI and human dialogue "create distinct but complementary conditions for L2 practice." AI dialogue "structurally approximates supported monologue": sustained output with fewer, longer turns, slower responses, less floor competition, and more fluent within-turn production, shifting learners "from reactive turn management to more deliberate, content-focused production." Human dialogue instead exercises interactional competence through rapid turn exchange, floor competition, and negotiation sequences. The framework predicts AI's pedagogical contribution is specifically structural (syntactic priming), while human partners scaffold turn competition, clarification requests, repair, and collaborative floor management.
requirements: An AI interlocutor configuration whose verbose, syntactically regular input creates favorable conditions for short-term structural alignment
constraints: The AI condition reflects one system configuration (model, voice, prompt, VAD setting, and task interface) with university German learners performing one task type
Uptake measures cannot fully separate priming from parallel activation driven by shared task context
target_learners: second- and third-year university L2 German learners
target_learning_goals: L2 spoken interactional fluency
lexical and morphosyntactic uptake
interactional competence
examples: The spot-the-difference study showed human dialogue rapid and interactive versus AI dialogue with fewer, longer turns and more within-turn fluency
key_sources: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225

article_title: What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue
citation: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225
title: Transcript-based pipeline for measuring interactional fluency and direction-sensitive uptake from diarized ASR output
description: A reusable analysis pipeline that operationalizes interactional fluency and direction-sensitive linguistic uptake for spoken AI practice "using metrics extractable from diarized ASR output without manual linguistic annotation." The fluency component extracts seven features from word-level timestamps (conversation length, turn count, mean turn duration, words per turn, response latency, floor ratio, within-turn pause ratio). The uptake component tracks lexical adoption via a global timeline with a first-use, first-source-wins rule, and syntactic uptake via four German morphosyntactic template types parsed with the Stanza UD pipeline, with correctness checked against a 91,270-noun gender lexicon. The authors provide it as "a reusable analysis pipeline for rapid, scalable evaluation of conversational AI in educational settings."
requirements: Diarized, timestamped ASR transcripts with verified speaker labels; a baseline monologue preceding each dialogue to establish learner-specific vocabulary baselines
constraints: Transcript-based analysis excludes prosody, pronunciation, stress, intonation, and segmental accuracy
NLP pipelines trained on Standard German may degrade on disfluent L2 speech; word-level ASR errors were not systematically corrected
target_learners: second- and third-year university L2 German learners
target_learning_goals: measuring interactional fluency and linguistic uptake in L2 spoken dialogue practice
examples: Applied to 78 AI dialogues and 39 human-human conversations from four sites, with three AI transcripts' speaker label swaps corrected via a disfluency-rate classifier

article_title: AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning
citation: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337
title: Human–AI Coaching Game: coaching as a non-cooperative two-player POSG targeting independent competence
description: The Human–AI Coaching Game is a formal model casting AI coaching as a two-player partially observable stochastic game with distinct objectives for the two agents. The article argues that "coaching is fundamentally anon-cooperativegame" because "the learner seeks to maximize the task performance, while the coach optimizes a pedagogical objective, namely the learner'sindependentcompetence." The coach's reward is the Value of Independence (VoI): the learner's expected return acting without AI assistance. The learner's latent skill is private information the coach infers via a belief state. This contrasts with cooperative Assistance Games, which the article notes have been used almost exclusively for humans teaching robots.
requirements: A latent, totally ordered skill level for the learner that governs a skill-conditioned policy class
A coach reward measuring the learner's capacity for independent performance rather than assisted task performance
constraints: General POSGs are intractable, so the framework requires the reduction techniques of the L2C pipeline to be solvable
The VoI reward is counterfactual and expensive to estimate directly
target_learners: human learners of motor skills, primarily novices in the evaluated domain
target_learning_goals: long-term independent motor-skill competence rather than short-term assisted task performance
examples: The formalism is instantiated for FPV drone racing, where the coach maintains a per-gate belief over learner skill and blends expert and learner commands
key_sources: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337

article_title: AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning
citation: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337
title: Learning to Coach (L2C): an RL pipeline combining adaptive blending, a skill-change PFA, and a surrogate reward
description: L2C is the article's trainable coaching framework built on the Coaching Game formalism. Its contributions are "threefold: (i) a closed-loop blending rule that adapts the assistance levelλto the coach's observations of both the physical environment and the learner behavior; (ii) a reformu-lation of theCoaching Gameto a single-agent POMDP, solvable via RL, through a probabilistic model of the coach's causal influence on learner skill; and (iii) a tractable surrogate reward that is provably consistent with the counterfactual V oI objective." A hybrid probabilistic finite-state automaton models skill change on success and failure events with sigmoid rates over skill; the coach policy is trained with PPO against skill improvement and deployed with Bayesian runtime skill inference and multimodal feedback.
requirements: A pretrained expert policy to anchor the blending rule
A learner model expressible as a skill-parameterized policy class
Privileged access to learner skill during simulation training
constraints: The Boltzmann learner model is one tractable choice; the article states accurately modeling skill-conditioned learner behaviors remains an open problem
Verbal and visual cues are predefined and triggered by fixed rules; only assistance modulation of physical control is learned
target_learners: human learners practicing motor skills such as FPV drone racing, mostly novices
target_learning_goals: accelerated development of independent motor-skill competence, measured by unassisted lap time and failure count
examples: Deployed in a 40-minute FPV drone racing coaching session with shared control, verbal instructions, visual cues, and guided re-attempts of failed segments

citation: Kashika Khurana and Ally Liew. (2026). An exploratory behavioral and electroencephalographic study of artificial intelligence-assisted learning modes in high school students. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/allyliew/participant-data
title: Three-mode taxonomy of educational AI interaction: Tutor, Collaborator, and Solver
description: The article creates and uses three measurable "modes" for human-AI interaction because, as it states, "no common taxonomy exists that strictly defines different AI interaction types." Tutor mode is high learner contribution with Socratic prompting and hints but no final solutions; Collaborator mode shares contribution between learner and AI with fluctuating executive control; Solver mode is low learner contribution where the AI provides the solution with no student input. The modes operationally define distinct student use cases to provide experimentally controllable conditions, implemented via standardized ChatGPT prompt templates.
requirements: Standardized prompt templates per mode (executed in temporary ChatGPT sessions) to minimize variations in responses
Random rotation of modes across task blocks to prevent order effects
constraints: The taxonomy is the authors' own operationalization for this pilot study, not an established classification
target_learners: high school students (ages 14-18)
target_learning_goals: problem-solving across convergent, divergent, and analytical thinking tasks
examples: Participants completed two counterbalanced quizzes in which each task block paired one with-AI and one without-AI question under a rotating mode

article_title: 'A bit of chaos and madness: The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform'
citation: Perkins, M., Postma, D., Roe, J., Sisay, S., & Holdcroft, C. (2026). 'A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform. Preprint.
title: The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) as a structured framework for embedding GenAI into assessment design
description: The AIAS is a scale-based framework providing structured guidance for embedding generative AI into assessment design across the dimensions of integrity, equity, and pedagogy. It assigns levels that specify permitted GenAI use, functioning in practice as "a shared language" through which faculty, students, and institutions negotiate expectations. This study examines its enactment at two universities, showing its value depends on implementation conditions rather than framework choice alone.
requirements: Requires interpretation by staff and students, who must negotiate limits, declarations, and appropriate levels of use
constraints: Can degrade into a compliance layer when disconnected from learning outcomes, disciplinary context, and staff capacity
Levels can be read as permissions attached to unchanged tasks rather than specifications of task type and evidence
target_learners: higher education academic staff implementing GenAI assessment guidance
university students using GenAI in assessed work
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
assessment design aligned with learning outcomes
critical and responsible GenAI use
examples: A private international university in Vietnam adopted the first AIAS version institution-wide; a UK public university adopted the revised version in one school
key_sources: Perkins, M., Postma, D., Roe, J., Sisay, S., & Holdcroft, C. (2026). 'A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26729

citation: Perkins, M., Postma, D., Roe, J., Sisay, S., & Holdcroft, C. (2026). 'A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform. Preprint.
title: Invest in implementation conditions — sustained faculty development, consultative governance, equitable access, and programme-level consistency — when adopting GenAI assessment frameworks
description: This principle holds that the value of a GenAI assessment framework is realised through its implementation conditions, not its selection. The study concludes that "structured frameworks are most useful when they are embedded within sustained faculty development, consultative governance, equitable access, and programme-level consistency". It directs institutional investment toward faculty development, equitable tool access, programme-level guidance, and assessment redesign capacity as core infrastructure for GenAI-era assessment reform.
requirements: Institutions must invest in faculty development, equitable tool access, programme-level guidance, and assessment redesign capacity
constraints: Without these supports the framework risks becoming a compliance layer or another discursive response leaving the validity problem untouched
The study reports faculty perceptions rather than measured generalisable outcomes

target_learning_goals: valid assessment of learning in a GenAI context
academic integrity
equitable student access to AI tools

article_title: AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI
citation: Taelin Karidi, Ofra Amir, and Ido Roll. (2026). AI in the Wild: A Large Scale Analysis of Authentic Interactions of College Students with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29442
title: Two-dimensional annotation framework: cognitive intent (Bloom level) and interaction context
description: The article introduces a two-dimensional annotation framework for characterizing student–AI interaction units. Dimension 1 captures the "cognitive intentunderlying each student turn", operationalized with Bloom's revised taxonomy (remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create). Dimension 2 captures the "interaction context, specifying what the student is directing the AI to engage with": own_work, task_domain, ai_output, or administrative. The framework was informed by established educational taxonomies and developed through iterative inspection of authentic interactions.
requirements: Annotations are assigned at the interaction unit level based on the inferred intent expressed in the student's message, with the AI response used only as contextual information when the request is underspecified.
constraints: Bloom's taxonomy "remains agnostic to the object of that request", which motivates the second dimension; the framework was applied via an LLM-based procedure without human-agreement evaluation in this study.
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI in coursework
target_learning_goals: characterizing how students engage generative AI during authentic academic work
examples: Applied with gpt-5-mini to annotate 15,887 interaction turns from 821 students across six courses, revealing distinct course-level interaction profiles.

article_title: 'Why Put in This Much Effort?": How AI Availability Shapes Students’ Motivation in Introductory Programming'
citation: Keith Tran, Colton Harper, and Thomas Price. 2026. "Why Put in This Much Effort?": How AI Availability Shapes Students' Motivation in Introductory Programming. In Proceedings of the ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research Vol. 1 (ICER 2026 Vol. 1). https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811653
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT) as a framework for analyzing how AI availability reshapes motivational judgments
description: The study uses Situated Expectancy-Value Theory as its analytical framework, decomposing motivation into expectancy plus four subjective task values. As the article states, "Intrinsic value refers to the enjoyment or satisfaction derived from doing the task itself," alongside attainment value, utility value, and cost, which "works against motivation." SEVT is situated: beliefs are shaped by task context including available alternatives, making it suited to analyzing how AI availability enters students' motivational reasoning. The article also draws on Flake et al.'s cost sub-components: effort cost, opportunity cost, and loss of valued alternatives.
requirements: The framework requires analyzing which specific motivational dimensions students describe as most affected, since AI does not uniformly raise or lower motivation
constraints: The article notes cost has received the least theoretical and empirical attention despite its practical significance for understanding student disengagement
target_learners: engineering majors in introductory programming
end-user programmers who are not CS majors
target_learning_goals: sustained effort and engagement with programming practice
examples: The interview protocol structured questions around all five SEVT dimensions, asking general questions then AI-specific questions for each dimension

title: Course design should shift from valuing what students produce to supporting how they learn, since students found motivation in the learning process itself
description: The article's implication is that external constraints are not the only lever: most students already valued independent effort but struggled to act on those values. The authors write that "Students who managed the tension found motivation in the learning process itself, suggesting that course design may need to shift from valuing what students produce to supporting how they learn." Students who succeeded used reframing toward the learning process and explicit boundaries on AI use, such as P12's litmus test of being able to recreate the work without AI.
requirements: Requires course contexts where students have agency over AI use and explicit policies, as in the study's six-level AI Assessment Scale-inspired policy
constraints: The authors note their qualitative sample does not support claims about prevalence, and self-selection may have biased the sample toward students with stronger opinions about AI

engineering majors using AI tools in coursework
target_learning_goals: sustaining engagement with programming practice
protecting learning through independent effort
examples: Students set boundaries such as restricting AI to syntax checking or checking work after giving it their best, and reframed focus onto the learning process rather than the product

article_title: Using AI-based Learning Assistants in Higher Education: A Large-Scale Descriptive Analysis
citation: Kristina Schaaff, Quintus Stierstorfer and Valerie Hekkel. (2026). Using AI-based Learning Assistants in Higher Education: A Large-Scale Descriptive Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08748
title: Syntea AI-based learning assistant at IU International University of Applied Sciences
description: Syntea is an AI-based learning assistant developed by IU and integrated into its learning platform, also accessible via web and mobile applications. It supports "factual question answering, open-ended chat, interactive tutoring, and personalized exam training" and employs deep-dialog learning methods inspired by the Socratic approach. It can provide personalized feedback, track learning progress, and personalize content to career goals. article_title: AI Advice Suppresses People's Willingness to Say \"I Don't Know\", Even When the Advice Is Wrong and Accuracy Is Incentivized
citation: Chiara Marcoccia, Walter Quattrociocchi, Valerio Capraro. (2026). AI advice suppresses people's willingness to say "I don't know", even when the advice is wrong and accuracy is incentivized. https://osf.io/nwx6r/overview?view_only=a03ae0ca587c4c84a442c44d55ab97b6
title: Epistemia: acceptance of AI output for surface fluency lowers the metacognitive threshold for answering
description: The article reads its findings through epistemia, "the tendency to accept AI outputs for their surface plausibility and syntactic coherence rather than through verification". Because an LLM must always produce an output and does not itself suspend judgment, users who delegate judgment to it may inherit that lack of suspension. The authors propose that a fluent available answer lowers the threshold at which people decide they know enough to respond, reducing suspension, inflating confidence, and lowering accuracy when the advice is wrong.
requirements: An AI system that always produces a fluent output, so that an answer is available even when the user lacks knowledge
constraints: The article states it is untested whether suspension collapses to the same degree when AI advice is usually correct
The design did not record whether participants who overrode the AI consulted other sources, limiting inferences about verification
target_learners: Adult online participants answering knowledge questions
Users of AI assistants, search summaries, and writing tools
target_learning_goals: Calibrated judgment about whether one knows enough to answer
Willingness to withhold an answer under uncertainty
examples: The authors propose that the availability of a fluent answer lowers the threshold for responding, with stakes one condition under which this mechanism partly re-engages.

citation: Veronica Pimenova, Chris Lee, Baramee Bhakdibhumi, Simon Chu, and Andrew Begel. (2026). Leveling the Playing Field: Temporal Video Segmentation for Individuals with ADHD in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24612
title: Logic-aware segmented video intervention with fixed 4-second system-defined pauses
description: A post-hoc video processing intervention for instructional programming videos: after recording, content is cut at logical action boundaries and a fixed pause is injected after each step. The article explains that "a pause was manually inserted immediately after the completion of a logical action (e.g., snapping a block into place), but before the explanation of the subsequent step." Pausing is system-defined rather than student-initiated, chosen because student-initiated pausing often has negligible learning effects. Pause duration was set to 4 seconds after piloting 2-, 4-, and 6-second intervals with 13 participants.

constraints: The 4-second pause duration is fixed; the article acknowledges a one-size-fits-all pause duration may not be optimal for every learner
Evaluated with adult novices with no programming experience in the Scratch environment, which the authors note may limit generalizability

individuals with ADHD in computing education
target_learning_goals: following instructional video steps to build a Scratch game
reducing errors and hesitations during programming tasks

title: Cognitive load framing of instructional video barriers for learners with ADHD
description: The article organizes its intervention around Cognitive Load Theory's three load types and working memory constraints. It states that "CLT emphasizes that reducing extraneous cognitive load while optimizing intrinsic and germane loads should enhance comprehension," and draws on the phonological loop account to explain why ADHD learners may lose verbal instructions before acting on them. Segmentation with pauses is presented as reducing extraneous load and supporting dual-channel integration in line with Mayer's segmenting principle.

title: Personal agency as an empirically merged self-efficacy/self-regulated learning factor in AI-use motivation modeling
description: In this study's measurement model, exploratory factor analysis of adapted self-regulated learning and self-efficacy items produced a single combined factor rather than two separate constructs. The authors "labeled personal agency to reflect a combined sense of being able and ready to act on academic demands", capturing confidence in handling challenges, planning, and integrating new knowledge. This factor then served as a baseline latent predictor in the SEM of perceived AI outcomes, where it negatively predicted perceived relief from competence frustration. The interpretation aligns with prior work treating self-efficacy and SRL as conceptually distinct but closely related.

constraints: The merge is an empirical result of this sample's EFA, not assumed a priori; one help-seeking item (SR4) was removed for weak and conceptually inconsistent loading

target_learning_goals: motivation and psychological need fulfillment in AI-supported learning
examples: EFA on baseline items (KMO = .862) suggested a four-factor structure in which SRL and self-efficacy items loaded on a common factor

article_title: Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth
citation: Liu, A., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., He, K., & Sun, M. (2026). Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth. Preprint, no identifier printed in text.
title: Code-level division-of-labor framework for allocating qualitative coding between human coders and LLMs
description: A two-dimensional classification that triangulates how often human and LLM coders converge (human-LLM Jaccard) with which source an independent blind expert prefers when they diverge (endorsement on contested applications). The article states the division of labor "cannot be determined from agreement alone; it requires a two-dimensional classification considering both how often sources converge and which source an expert prefers when they diverge". Applied to the 72-code instrument it yields four categories with full code lists in the article’s Appendix B: Automatable (6 codes), LLM-assisted (16 codes), LLM-preferred (12 codes), and Human required (15 codes).
requirements: Model evaluation on the target instrument should precede deployment, since the gap between the best and worst model is far larger than the gap between the best model and the best human coder.
The division of labor should be set at the code level using the two-dimensional assessment; the article states blanket decisions in either direction are suboptimal.
Confidence-based triage should be used only after testing that high-confidence annotations are in fact endorsed more often than low-confidence ones for the chosen model.
constraints: Findings rest on a single codebook and a single dataset, so the specific codes identified as automatable or human-required may not generalize to other domains, data structures, or coding approaches.
The aggregate finding of no human-LLM preference is conditional on the mix of five verified models selected under a fixed verification budget.
target_learners: Researchers designing large-scale qualitative coding pipelines
Education researchers evaluating LLM-assisted annotation of educator or learner data
target_learning_goals: Valid, reliably evaluated qualitative coding of educational data at scale
Appropriate delegation of coding work between human coders and LLM systems
examples: Automatable codes combine Jaccard above 0.40 with comparable or higher LLM endorsement; four codes meet both criteria fully (Grading, Special Education (IEP), Entire Lesson Planning, Unit Planning) and two are automatable with light human review.
LLM-assisted codes show moderate agreement (Jaccard 0.20 to 0.40) with adequate LLM endorsement, where the confidence lift averages 40 percentage points.

LLM-preferred codes such as Inquiry and Deep Questions and Research and Source Analysis show low agreement but consistent verifier endorsement of LLM application, so replacing human coding there would improve rather than degrade quality.

article_title: Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth
citation: Liu, A., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., He, K., & Sun, M. (2026). Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth. Preprint, no identifier printed in text.
title: Blind, source-symmetric expert verification protocol for evaluating qualitative coding without a gold standard
description: A transferable evaluation protocol in which an independent domain expert judges anonymized pairwise comparisons of code sets without knowing which source produced which, treating human and machine sources symmetrically. The verifier "selects one of four responses: Set 1 preferred, Set 2 preferred, Both adequate, or Neither adequate", with position randomized. In this study the protocol comprised 855 stratified pairs: 555 Human vs. LLM, 210 LLM vs. LLM, 85 Human vs. Human, and 5 code supplement pairs for rare codes, supporting a binomial preference test, a Bradley-Terry model, per-code endorsement rates, and tie rates.
requirements: A verifier with domain expertise who was not involved in the original coding and has no knowledge of which sources produced which annotations.
A stratified sample large enough that each comparison stratum retains enough pairs for meaningful analysis, sized to the practical capacity of the single expert verifier.
constraints: Verification was limited to five focal models so each stratum retained enough pairs; models outside the focal set did not enter verification.
The study relies on a single independent verifier; a panel would provide stronger normative evidence and allow assessment of inter-verifier reliability.
target_learners: Social science and education researchers delegating qualitative coding to LLMs
Research teams making automation decisions about annotation pipelines
target_learning_goals: Evaluating coding quality without presupposing either human or machine superiority
Detecting shared bias that agreement-with-human-codings metrics cannot detect
examples: The verifier was a researcher with a doctoral degree in education, extensive educational research experience, and K-12 teaching experience, blind to source identity.
Human coders were placed under the same anonymized scrutiny as the models, which the authors call the study’s central methodological design move.

citation: Howard Ziyu Han, Nikolas Martelaro. (2026). Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04166
title: Antagonistic AI design agent with steerable stakeholder pushback in Miro
description: An LLM-powered agent built in Miro (Next.js, Miro SDK, GPT-4.1, Whisper, GPT-4o) that enacts constructive conflict for interaction design students. In the Agent Intervention Space, "the agent generates a first round of four pushback points anchored in the designer's current proposal; the designer interacts with those points to steer the design direction; the agent then generates a second round informed by that steering." Each pushback point pairs a stakeholder perspective with a specific challenge. Designers steer via point-level tagging (useful, not useful, custom) and stance-level Consensus and Command frames. A sub-agent retrieves a database of prior constructive-conflict examples to ground critiques.
requirements: Multimodal context gathering (text, visuals, think-aloud) so pushback is anchored in the designer's contextual exploration
Steering mechanisms (tagging and Consensus/Command frames) so designers retain agency while engaging with critique
constraints: The agent could not infer relationships between linked ideas from think-aloud input
It cannot show how common, important, or grounded synthetic concerns are in lived experience and does not substitute for engagement with the real public
A few Miro actions not exposed by the open API were handled by the researcher via a predefined, bias-avoiding protocol
target_learners: Novice interaction designers (design students trained in interaction design but novices at navigating stakeholder conflict)
target_learning_goals: Engaging constructively with multi-stakeholder tension during early design ideation
Reconsidering and revising design decisions in light of stakeholder pushback

title: Constructive conflict grounded in agonistic pluralism as a design-learning framework
description: The article grounds its agent in agonistic pluralism, which "reframes collective decision-making as “grounded in productive conflict,” where competing values are continuously contested rather than reconciled." Building on this, adversarial design creates "spaces of confrontation" to challenge assumptions, positioning constructive conflict as a means to reveal hidden assumptions and negotiate design implications. The framework treats stakeholder disagreement as productive rather than something to be resolved, and the authors operationalize it as sustained, steerable pushback rather than one-shot critique.
requirements: Approaches that help designers actively engage with stakeholder tensions, since simply inviting tensions into the room does not automatically translate into better design outcomes and can fall into tokenism
constraints: In participatory design practice there is often a push toward harmony and consensus, which can inadvertently silence important disagreements
target_learners: Novice designers working on multi-stakeholder design problems
target_learning_goals: Surfacing hidden assumptions and stakeholder tensions rather than resolving differences prematurely
examples: The Stepwise Guidance condition translated the framework into written prompts mirroring the agent's system prompts

description: The study's dataset comprises 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials from U.S.-based, credit-bearing, upper-division university courses offered between Fall 2023 and Fall 2026. Courses were identified through structured Google searches and screened for three content criteria: explicit GenAI framing, software engineering lifecycle coverage across at least two SDLC domains, and required GenAI use in graded software engineering tasks. The dataset yielded 32 institutionally eligible candidates, of which 23 met all content criteria.
requirements: Public availability of course materials; courses must satisfy the three content criteria including required GenAI use for graded software engineering tasks.

article_title: AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques
citation: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990
title: AI-Guided Learning: integrated support for the Consume-Understand-Imitate cycle
description: The dissertation proposes AI-Guided Learning, an integrated approach in which deep learning systems provide adaptive support at each of three interrelated stages of learning from audio and video: Consume (efficient content consumption), Understand (deep comprehension), and Imitate (skill acquisition). The author states the framework "provides necessary support at each stage as learners progress through three interconnected phases" and stresses that AI functions as a guide that reduces cognitive load while maintaining learner autonomy, rather than automating tasks wholesale. Three subsystems (AIxSpeed, FastPerson, Profy) instantiate the stages.
requirements: Deep learning models capable of extracting features from audio, video, and text streams for each stage
Coordination among subsystems so learners can move cyclically between stages
constraints: The author notes the CUI model is an organizing framework proposed in the dissertation rather than an empirically established sequence
Current limitations include the need for long-term effect validation and extension beyond audio-visual domains
target_learners: Self-directed online learners of long-form audio and video content
Second-language learners practicing pronunciation
target_learning_goals: Efficient consumption of long-form audio-visual content
Deep comprehension of lecture content
Skill acquisition through imitation of expert models

citation: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990
title: FastPerson multimodal video summarization system with chapter-level summary/full switching
description: FastPerson is a video-to-video summarization system that analyzes both visual and audio streams of lecture videos to generate condensed videos, using voice cloning to maintain the original speaker's voice and preserve continuity with the original lecture. Its interface "allows learners to seamlessly switch between summary and full versions on a chapter-by-chapter basis", letting learners select viewing granularity according to their comprehension level. In evaluation it cut viewing time by 53% on average without a significant quiz-score difference.
requirements: Multimodal analysis of visual (slides, board writing, gestures) and audio streams
Voice cloning technology to preserve the original speaker's voice
constraints: Existing text-only summarization loses the multimodal nature of video and breaks continuity with the original content, which this system is designed to avoid
target_learners: Learners of long-form lecture videos
target_learning_goals: Efficient grasping of core lecture content while retaining access to detail
examples: In the 40-participant evaluation, participants watched educational videos under summarized and normal playback conditions and completed comprehension quizzes

citation: Kazuki Kawamura. (2025). AI-Guided Learning: Research on Knowledge and Skill Acquisition Support Methods Using Deep Learning Audio-Video Processing Techniques. Doctoral dissertation, The University of Tokyo. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08990
title: Profy data-driven pronunciation feedback system learned from unannotated audio
description: Profy is an automated feedback system for imitation-based skill learning, instantiated for second-language pronunciation. It constructs a deep learning model that "directly learns what constitutes good and poor performance from unannotated audio data", avoiding the annotated error-pattern databases of conventional CAPT systems. The system highlights waveform regions emphasized by the classifier and shows model-derived acoustic distances from native-speaker distributions in latent space, giving learners localized feedback on where their performance deviates.
requirements: Large amounts of native (expert) speech data and only small amounts of learner data
Self-supervised learning techniques for representation learning
constraints: Conventional systems provide only binary correct/incorrect judgments or overall scores and cannot localize individual learners' specific difficulties; Profy is designed to address this granularity gap
target_learners: Japanese learners of English (and, by extension, learners of imitable skills)
target_learning_goals: Objective evaluation and improvement of pronunciation and other imitated skills
examples: The English learning application highlights classifier-emphasized waveform regions and visualizes latent-space distances from native-speaker distributions during practice

title: Design AI learning support around adaptivity, integration, and transparency
description: The dissertation states that AI-Guided Learning rests on three design principles: "Adaptivity: Dynamic adjustment according to learners' individual needs, comprehension speed, and skill levels"; "Integration: Seamless coordination and mutual support between Consume-Understand-Imitate stages"; and "Transparency: Presentation of AI's judgments and recommendations in a form learners can understand". The principles position AI as a guide that reduces cognitive load at each stage while maintaining learner autonomy, in line with augmentation-rather-than-replacement perspectives.
requirements: AI subsystems capable of per-stage adaptation and of explaining their judgments to learners
constraints: Many current educational technologies are point solutions focused on a single stage and lack integrated support across the whole learning process
target_learners: Self-directed learners using AI-supported audio-visual learning systems
target_learning_goals: Efficient knowledge acquisition and skill development from audio-visual content
examples: The three subsystems instantiate the principles: AIxSpeed adapts speed to estimated listening difficulty, FastPerson integrates multimodal summarization, and Profy visualizes model-derived feedback

title: SINE: a domain-agnostic pipeline generating choice-based interactive-fiction scenarios from structured educational content
description: SINE is the stimulus-generation system used in this study: "a previously described domain-agnostic pipeline that generates choice-based IF scenarios from structured educational content using an open -weight LLM, with deterministic validation and a repair stage". In this study the pipeline was kept unchanged, with the inference backend moved to Qwen3 14B via the OpenRouter cloud API. It produced a controlled pool of 48 scenarios from 20 media-technology seeds after automated playability and validation filtering.

article_title: Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: From Provision to Student Enactment
citation: Omar Alsaiari, Nilufar Baghaei, Jason M. Lodge, Naomi Winstone, Dragan Gašević, Hassan Khosravi. (2026). Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11625
title: Feedback literacy as a developmental capacity exercised through structured feedback encounters
description: The article adopts an ecological view of feedback literacy in which productive feedback engagement is not a natural response to good feedback but a learned capability developed through participation in purposefully structured feedback encounters. It draws on the account that "Carless and Boud [3] identify four interrelated dimensions: appreciating feedback, making judgements, managing affect, and taking action." These capacities intersect with self-regulated learning, and evaluative judgement supports assessing the relevance of AI-generated suggestions. The theory motivates treating workflow structure, not comment quality alone, as the primary lever for intervention.
requirements: Feedback environments must create structured opportunities for students to develop and exercise feedback-literacy capabilities
constraints: The article treats feedback literacy as developmental and shaped by the learning environment rather than as a fixed individual attribute
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: interpreting, evaluating, and acting on feedback
evaluative judgement
self-regulated learning
examples: The Enacted Feedback workflow operationalised this theory by prompting selection, evaluation, and selection-anchored dialogue before submission

title: Enacted Feedback workflow: staged selection, evaluative prioritisation, and selection-anchored AI dialogue
description: A reusable workflow pattern in which AI-generated feedback comments are the entry point to a staged process rather than a completed output. As the article states, "The workflow scaffolded three behaviours associated with productive feedback use that theDirected FeedbackandSelf-Directed Feedbackconditions left to students' discretion: student agency through selection, evaluative judgement through prioritisation, and dialogic engagement through targeted AI assistance." Students receive initial comments (A1), select improvement suggestions (A2), and enter AI dialogue anchored to those selections (A3), while retaining paths to bypass the structured pathway.
requirements: AI-generated feedback comments organised as strengths and suggestions for improvement
an interface that renders suggestions as selectable items and passes selections into the dialogue context
constraints: Students who bypass selection receive unanchored dialogue resembling the optional, student-initiated interaction of the Self-Directed condition
target_learners: higher education students authoring learning resources
target_learning_goals: feedback enactment
evaluative judgement
revision of drafted work
examples: In RiPPLE, 63.0% of Enacted Feedback resources moved from AI Feedback to selected suggestions, and the condition showed the highest uptake and revision counts

description: RiPPLE (Recommendation in Personalised Peer-Learning Environments) is the platform in which the study was conducted. citation: Praveen Pathak, Siddharth Tiwary, Charudatt Kadolkar, Vijay Singh, David Rakestraw, Shirish Pathare, and Anwesh Mazumdar. (2026). Large-scale AI grading of handwritten physics assessments: Score agreement and Olympiad team selection outcomes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20521
title: Use AI grading of handwritten physics assessments as a second reader or audit tool under examiner control, not as the grader of record
description: The article's central design recommendation is that multimodal AI can support high-stakes physics grading but should not replace examiners. Because "The main difficulty remained exact partial-credit grading, especially in experimental work," the authors conclude AI "should be used as a second reader or audit tool under examiner control." In this role AI can flag submissions with large differences from official scores, provide additional comments, and help examiners check grading consistency, while expert examiners remain central to final marks.

Some high-confidence AI parts still differed from official scores by more than one point

target_learning_goals: Accurate, reliable scoring of handwritten physics examinations including partial credit
examples: In both rounds the AI top five for OE2 contained the same five students as the human top five, and RII matched 34 of 40 QM course grades exactly

title: Before AI grading is attempted, rubrics should state as explicitly as possible the conditions for awarding marks, common deductions, acceptable alternatives, and carried-forward-error rules
description: The article finds that rubric detail was central to strong AI–human agreement and that disagreements arose where rubrics stated a broad goal while leaving the required physics implicit. It recommends that "the rubric should state as explicitly as possible the conditions for awarding marks, common deductions, acceptable alternative solutions, and carried-forward-error rules." Focused refinements making such conditions explicit reduced AI–official differences on the tested questions.

constraints: Refined-instruction gains were demonstrated on the specific refined questions and should be confirmed on a holdout set, per the article

target_learning_goals: Reliable AI-assisted partial-credit grading aligned with official examiner standards
examples: The refined OE2 T–S graph rubric stated required branch shapes and temperature ordering, after which AI stopped awarding shape credit in incorrect-curvature cases

title: Sentinel AI-powered security game platform with LLM-driven adversarial persona and badge system
description: Sentinel is an AI-powered mobile game platform offering subgames on phishing detection, password cracking, text scams, and phone call scams. Its core interaction engine uses a Large Language Model (Google Gemini API) fine-tuned with system prompts defining the attacker's persona, with LLM output piped through a low-latency ElevenLabs text-to-speech engine for realistic voice modulation. The platform "provides player analytics and a badge-reward system to enhance motivation and sustained engagement," and adjusts scam sophistication based on the user's initial streak.

A bounded adversarial framework that filters user inputs to prevent jailbreaking the scammer bot

Voice profiles are randomized in gender, tone, and accent to avoid reinforcing stereotypes about attacker demographics

password security

social engineering awareness
examples: The Phone Scam game simulates a call in which a trained AI bot acts as a scammer attempting to extract sensitive information, and switches to subtler soft-sell tactics if the user easily detects the first clue

title: Distinction between gamification as a motivation layer and game-based learning as a fully integrated environment
description: The article's background section organizes game-infused education around two approaches: gamification, the application of game design elements such as points, levels, badges, and leaderboards within non-game contexts, and game-based learning (GBL), which employs complete games or interactive simulations as the primary medium of instruction. title: Four-domain account of university AI adaptation: perceived usefulness, self-reported competence, academic integrity concerns, and institutional policy clarity
description: The study is guided by the premise that "patterns of AI use and trust are associated not with any single variable but with a combination of four domains: perceived usefulness, self-reported competence, academic integrity concerns, and institutional policy clarity". Usefulness is understood as a subjective assessment that AI makes educational or administrative activity more efficient, effective, or convenient; policy clarity is treated as a potential resource for institutional governance; and responsible use entails checking accuracy, understanding model limitations, following local rules, and maintaining reflective control. The framework treats AI as embedded in university assignments, communication, planning, assessment, and administrative processes rather than as a single tool.

article_title: AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice
citation: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417
title: Evidence-present versus evidence-effectively-available distinction for AI assessment of documents
description: The article proposes a methodological distinction for AI-based assessment: evidence contained in a student report is not the same as evidence the model can actually retrieve during processing. As the article states, "the fact that evidence is present in a report does not necessarily mean that such evidence is effectively available to the model during processing." An equation may be in the document yet inadequately retrieved, and a graph may be uninterpretable if axes, units, or legends are not legible. This distinction explains why model-instructor differences may reflect document processing rather than physics reasoning, and it conditions the information on which the model operates.
requirements: Assessment with AI requires attention to how reports are processed and what information can actually be retrieved, not only to model capabilities.
constraints: The article notes OCR systems and multimodal models still show limitations with visually complex documents, and high character-recognition accuracy does not guarantee preservation of document structure and meaning.
target_learners: higher education students in experimental physics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment and feedback on laboratory reports
examples: The article notes a graph may contain relevant information that cannot be interpreted if its axes, units, or legends are not legible during processing.
key_sources: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417

title: Treat AI-generated scores as input for guiding review, not as grades interchangeable with teacher grades
description: The article recommends incorporating AI as a support tool that organizes and focuses review while professional teacher judgment guides interpretation and final assessment decisions. It reports that "AI-generated scores are not interchangeable with teacher grades" even when the model uses the same rubric criteria, so system output "should be considered an input for guiding the review rather than a definitive grade." The instructor confirms, modifies, or rejects the model's observations, retaining responsibility for assessment decisions.
requirements: Teachers must verify evidence, contextualize observations, and determine whether AI observations are appropriate for assessment and feedback.
constraints: AI feedback reliability varies by evidence type: descriptive criteria are more useful for initial review, while criteria requiring interpretation of equations, graphs, units, or uncertainties need careful teacher verification.
target_learners: higher education instructors assessing laboratory reports
target_learning_goals: reliable assessment and feedback on student laboratory work
examples: AI produces a first structured reading identifying possible strengths and difficulties organized by rubric criteria, which the instructor then confirms, modifies, or rejects.

article_title: AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice
citation: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417
title: Rubric-item guidance table for delegating AI feedback by criterion
description: Table 1 of the article provides per-criterion recommendations for instructors using AI feedback on laboratory reports, elaborated by the authors from the analyzed experience. Objectives may be accepted after general review as the safest item to delegate; theoretical framework feedback, especially formulas and mathematical notation, should be manually reviewed; comments on experimental setup referring to images or apparatus diagrams should be verified before acceptance; data analysis requires prioritized teacher review of calculations, units, graphs, and uncertainties; conclusions should be compared with the graphical evidence cited before validating the score; and the overall assessment should be used only as an orienting input.
requirements: Instructors review AI feedback differentially by rubric item, with heavier verification for items depending on mathematical and visual evidence.
constraints: The table is based on the authors' own elaboration from one analyzed experience in experimental physics laboratory report assessment.
target_learners: higher education instructors assessing physics laboratory reports
target_learning_goals: calibrated use of AI feedback across rubric criteria
examples: The table marks Objectives as "the safest item to delegate to AI" and the Overall assessment as usable "only as an orienting input."

article_title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
citation: Amin Jalali. (2026). AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06207
title: AI-decision checkpoints framework: one explicit AI-adoption decision point per BPM lifecycle phase
description: The framework uses the BPM lifecycle to structure explicit, phase-related decisions about AI adoption across identification, discovery, analysis, redesign, implementation, and monitoring. At each checkpoint students "identify AI-candidate subprocesses, establishing the baseline, evaluating expected benefits and risks using the analytical instruments of the corresponding lifecycle phase, and documenting a reasoned decision to adopt, adapt, postpone, or reject specific AI components". It decomposes AI adoption from a monolithic yes/no judgment into locally grounded assessments producing a traceable decision trail.
requirements: Each checkpoint aligns with one of the six BPM lifecycle phases and uses that phase's analytical instruments
constraints: The framework does not prescribe a correct answer at any checkpoint; it foregrounds reasoning quality
individual checkpoints can be weighted or combined without disrupting the logic
target_learners: Master-level Business Information Systems or Computer Science students
future process developers
target_learning_goals: reasoning about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes
justifying AI adoption decisions with phase-appropriate evidence
examples: In the Master-level course, CP1 yielded an AI opportunity register, CP3 a baseline performance report, CP4 a comparative redesign-and-simulation dossier, CP5 an implementation feasibility and governance dossier, and CP6 a mining-based evaluation summary

Document B proposes AI agents, prioritizing email-based registration extraction and RAG-based fraud screening; the fraud-screening agent is "deliberately constrained by a known class-imbalance problem (the data science team reports high recall but imperfect precision)". article_title: Are Students Dependent on AI in Writing Courses? Analyzing Factors Influencing Dependence on Generative AI Through the I-PACE Model
citation: Liu L, Zhuang M and Wang J (2026). Are students dependent on AI in writing courses? Analyzing factors influencing dependence on generative AI through the I-PACE model. Front. Psychol. 17:1905037. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1905037
title: I-PACE model extended to generative AI dependence in academic writing
description: The study applies the I-PACE (Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution) model, originally proposed to explain internet-use disorders, to college students' dependence on generative AI in academic writing. The Person component covers pre-existing individual traits such as academic self-efficacy and AI literacy; the Affect and Cognition components are represented by academic stress, perceived trust, and performance expectations; and the outcome is dependence. As the article states, "The 'Execution' component serves as the outcome variable, referring to the excessive reliance on generative AI, encompassing an individual'scognitivereliance,emotionalreliance,andtoolreliance on AI tools." The SEM results extend the model by showing a trust transmission mechanism from social influence to dependence.
requirements: Requires measurement of personal-trait, emotional-cognitive, and execution constructs in a specific technology-use context, as the study operationalized via adapted Likert scales
constraints: The article notes research on problematic AI-dependence behavior in educational generative-AI contexts is still in early stages
Tested in a cross-sectional, single-source Chinese undergraduate writing-course sample
target_learners: Chinese undergraduate students in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: Responsible use of generative AI in academic writing and prevention of excessive AI dependence
examples: The study mapped academic self-efficacy and AI literacy to the Person component, academic stress, perceived trust and perceived usefulness to Affect/Cognition, and AI dependence to Execution, testing the paths with SEM on 229 responses

article_title: The impact of artificial intelligence literacy on learning engagement among university students: the mediating role of psychological capital and the moderating role of professional identity
citation: Wang, N. (2026). The impact of artificial intelligence literacy on learning engagement among university students: the mediating role of psychological capital and the moderating role of professional identity. Frontiers in Psychology, 17:1892204. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1892204
title: Resource-gain spiral moderated mediation model linking AI literacy, psychological capital, and learning engagement
description: The article's core framework, anchored in Conservation of Resources Theory with complementary perspectives (Social Cognitive, Broaden-and-Build, Self-Determination, Social Identity, and Self-Verification theories), is a moderated mediation model in which AI literacy acts as a technological cognitive resource that builds psychological capital, which drives learning engagement. The authors posit "a 'resource gain spiral' pathway wherein AI literacy, as a technological cognitive resource, accumulates into psychological capital and subsequently enhances learning engagement", with professional commitment as a contextual amplifier.
requirements: The model requires measures of AI literacy, psychological capital, professional commitment, and learning engagement, and was tested with PLS-SEM path analysis including an interaction term (psychological capital × professional commitment).
constraints: Tested in a cross-sectional survey of Chinese undergraduates; the article notes the AI literacy–engagement relationship "may not simply be linear and positive" across cultural and educational contexts.
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: learning engagement
AI literacy
psychological capital
examples: The model was tested on 1,198 undergraduates using the College Students' AI Literacy Scale (22 items), the Positive Psychological Capital Questionnaire (27 items), the Professional Commitment Scale (27 items), and the UWES-S (17 items).
