article_title: Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model
citation: Olaoye DD, Owolabi HO and Olaoye OT (2026). Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model. Front. Educ. 11:1669504. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1669504
title: Automated Extended Essay Grading Software (AEEGS)
description: AEEGS is an AI-based web application developed by the researchers to score extended mathematical essay responses in senior secondary Economics without manual training on many model answers. It uses "contextual similarity, which is a pre-trained scoring algorithm used in this study in awarding scores to students extended essay responses which return index of 0–1", multiplied by the marks allotted in the marking scheme. It was built with HTML, CSS, MYSQL, PHP, Laravel, Python and FastAPIs on the waterfall model, and includes a candidate login interface, test-item interface and an online database of responses and scores.
requirements: The examiner must supply both the question items and the expected model answer (marking scheme) against which student responses are matched
constraints: Validated only on two Economics mathematical items; the article states the scores of other pieces of software were not correlated with it
target_learners: Senior secondary school III students studying Economics in South-west Nigeria
target_learning_goals: Scoring mathematical, graphical and computational Economics extended essay items at senior secondary certificate examination level
examples: Used to score 1,008 students' responses to Economics Paper II Section A mathematical items, with scores displayed in an online database backend

citation: Olaoye DD, Owolabi HO and Olaoye OT (2026). Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model. Front. Educ. 11:1669504. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1669504
title: Contextual similarity scoring model for automated essay grading
description: The article's scoring framework matches a student's response to an examiner-supplied model answer using semantic contextual search similarity, returning a similarity index of 0–1 that is multiplied by the item's allotted marks. Its matching phase "combines the similarity algorithm (answer matching), which are Generic Words (GW), Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), and Semantic Distance (SD)", weighted by each algorithm's strength. The model begins with tokenization or normalization of the two strings and considers all possible ways examinees could phrase responses, so it awards scores without manual training on many model answers.
requirements: An examiner-supplied marking scheme with model answers and stipulated marks for each item
Student responses collected in a web-based environment
constraints: Applied and validated in this study only for mathematical extended essay items in senior secondary Economics
target_learners: Senior secondary school students taking certificate examinations in Economics
target_learning_goals: Accurate automated scoring of extended mathematical computation responses against a marking scheme
examples: The AEEGS implementation returns a 0–1 similarity index and multiplies it by the marks stipulated in the marking scheme to produce the item score

article_title: From automated scoring to learning diagnosis: a mechanism study of AI-supported formative assessment in English writing
citation: Yao X-C and Fan L (2026) From automated scoring to learning diagnosis: a mechanism study of AI-supported formative assessment in English writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1905455. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1905455
title: The diagnostic-review mechanism: AI issue-level diagnosis passing through student interpretation, revision, teacher review, and reflection
description: The article proposes a classroom sequence in which AI diagnostic feedback becomes formative only through downstream activity. "The classroom sequence was task submission, AI diagnosis, student interpretation, independent revision, structured teacher review, reassessment, and reﬂection." The framework integrates formative assessment, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and teacher-feedback research, ordered by how diagnostic information moves through interpretation, revision, reassessment, and reflection. Teacher review comprises "conﬁrmation, correction, supplementation, and re-explanation of AI feedback", connecting automated evidence with situated writing judgment and making review workload observable.
requirements: Issue-level AI diagnosis that separates problem diagnosis from revision suggestions and does not rewrite the composition
Structured student interpretation before revision (restating problems, explaining effects, identifying uncertainties, specifying a revision plan)
Structured teacher review after revision, followed by reassessment and reflection
constraints: Evidence comes from two intact classes taught by one instructor, leaving class selection and instructor effects in the observed group contrast
Student time-on-task was not recorded, and the contrast may include additional interpretation, reflection, and revision time
Cycle order coincided with task type, and no delayed post-test was administered
target_learners: University EFL students in English writing courses
target_learning_goals: L2 writing quality and revision skill
Feedback literacy and self-assessment accuracy
Self-regulated revision behavior
examples: In the study, Diagnostic Review students completed an interpretation sheet requiring them to restate problems, explain their effects, identify uncertainties, and specify a revision plan before independent revision, while Control students received AI score/standard feedback with routine checking

article_title: A systematic mapping review at the intersection of artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning
citation: Banihashem, S. K., Bond, M., Bergdahl, N., Khosravi, H., & Noroozi, O. (2025). A systematic mapping review at the intersection of artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 22(50). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00548-8
title: Chatti et al.'s Who-What-How-Why framework adapted to map the AI-SRL research intersection
description: The review adopts Chatti et al.'s (2012) learning analytics framework and applies it to AI-supported SRL, structuring the field along four aspects: "Who (stakeholders), What (theory), How (methods), and Why (objectives)". Who covers stakeholder groups targeted; What covers the theoretical frameworks underpinning studies; How covers AI implementation categories such as profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive systems and personalization, and assessment and evaluation; Why covers direct impacts on SRL and end outcomes. The review argues the framework captures aspects the prior SMA Grid review omitted, including AI's purposes, methodologies, and underlying theory.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable along the four aspects of stakeholders, theory, implementation, and objectives
constraints: The framework was originally designed for learning analytics and was adapted, with the review distinguishing AI from LA by AI's ability to autonomously adjust to the learner
target_learners: higher education students
K-12 students
educators
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
examples: The review used the framework to structure four research questions on stakeholders, theoretical frameworks, implementation, and purposes

article_title: Anticipatory governance and leadership for AI implementation in higher education: A scoping review
citation: Sandra Baroudi. (2026). Anticipatory governance and leadership for AI implementation in higher education: A scoping review. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00616-7
title: Anticipatory governance as a proactive, participatory, adaptive decision-making framework for higher education facing AI-driven futures
description: The review adopts anticipatory governance as its main theoretical framework, defining it as "a proactive, participatory, and adaptive deci-sion-making model that calls upon educational leaders to engage with uncertain futures". It rests on foresight tools, stakeholder co-creation, and flexible, inclusive policy frameworks to shape possible futures rather than react to crises. The framework distinguishes anticipatory leadership (the micro-level mindset and actions operationalising it) from AI governance (the ethical, policy, and regulatory mechanisms guiding responsible AI use), with participatory governance as a key dimension. Required competencies named include imagination, systems thinking, ethical reasoning, and technological and AI literacy.
requirements: Stakeholder co-creation and engagement of leaders, educators, students, and communities who collaboratively imagine, experiment, and learn iteratively
Data analytics to inform strategic decisions and policies
Foresight tools and flexible, inclusive policy frameworks
constraints: The review states it must be adapted to institutional, cultural, and infrastructure conditions of different regions rather than applied as a universal framework
It must go beyond managerial rationales and ground itself in participatory and inclusive leadership
target_learners: Higher education leaders and policymakers
Educators and faculty
Students and institutional stakeholders
target_learning_goals: Preparing institutions for AI-driven transformation
Building foresight, ethical reasoning, and AI literacy
Fostering inclusive, equitable governance of educational technology
examples: The review cites Finland's strategic foresight and scenario-based policy-making in sport education programs, and Egypt's Egyptian Knowledge Bank and free digital access initiatives as early examples of anticipatory governance in action
key_sources: Sandra Baroudi. (2026). Anticipatory governance and leadership for AI implementation in higher education: A scoping review. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00616-7

article_title: Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions
citation: Feng Z and Huang K (2026) Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions. Front. Psychol. 17:1879982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1879982
title: Integrated framework combining Bayesian cognitive diagnosis, knowledge space theory, and cognitive load theory for personalized path optimization
description: The article proposes and validates "a personalized learning path optimization framework that integrates Bayesian cognitive diagnosis, knowledge space theory, and cognitive load theory." Bayesian DINA estimation supplies attribute mastery probabilities on sparse data; knowledge space theory supplies prerequisite ordering so that "prerequisite attributes must be learned before target attributes"; and cognitive load theory supplies the psychological mechanism, since prerequisite-respecting sequences are held to reduce extraneous load. The framework links diagnosis, sequencing, and mediation testing in one pipeline.
requirements: A Q-matrix mapping items to cognitive attributes and a specified attribute prerequisite hierarchy
Sufficient response data for MCMC estimation of the Bayesian DINA model
constraints: The attribute hierarchy is a theory-driven specification based on Bloom's taxonomy rather than an official structure provided by EdNet
The framework was validated on foundational probability content with undergraduates and on EdNet KT1 listening/reading skill tags interpreted as general cognitive attributes
target_learners: undergraduate students learning foundational probability theory
online platform learners in large-scale educational datasets
target_learning_goals: mastery of prerequisite-ordered cognitive attributes such as foundation concepts, rule application, logical reasoning, procedural knowledge, and analytical thinking
examples: The experimental group followed personalized paths generated by the shortest remediation path algorithm while the control group followed a fixed A1→A2→A3→A4→A5 sequence over the same content.
key_sources: Feng Z and Huang K (2026) Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions. Front. Psychol. 17:1879982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1879982

article_title: Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions
citation: Feng Z and Huang K (2026) Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions. Front. Psychol. 17:1879982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1879982
title: Shortest remediation path algorithm converting diagnosed knowledge states into prerequisite-respecting learning sequences
description: The shortest remediation path algorithm is "the core technical component of this study for transforming cognitive diagnostic results into personalized learning sequences." It takes a student's current knowledge state vector, a prerequisite graph, and a target state; computes each missing attribute's dependency depth; sorts missing attributes by ascending depth; inserts any missing prerequisites before their dependents; and recommends three unanswered questions per attribute sorted by ascending difficulty. Its design goal is minimum path cost while respecting prerequisite relationships.
requirements: A diagnosed binary knowledge state vector and a directed acyclic prerequisite graph over attributes
A Q-matrix for selecting unanswered practice questions per attribute
constraints: Path cost counts each missing attribute and each inserted prerequisite as one step; efficiency is measured as path length, not learning outcomes
target_learners: online learners with partial attribute mastery diagnosed from response data
undergraduate students in the validation experiment
target_learning_goals: remediating missing cognitive attributes in prerequisite-consistent order toward full mastery
examples: For a student who mastered only A1, the algorithm produced the sequence (A2, A3, A4, A5); for a student who mastered A1 and A2, it moved A4 before A5 to yield [A3, A4, A5].

description: The principle directs students to engage actively with course material through AI interactions instead of using AI to bypass the work. The article states: "By interacting with AI to rephrase, question, edit, or elaborate on key concepts, students become more conscious of the content, reinforcing understanding and promoting deeper learning." It is grounded in the article's aim of improving retention of course content by using AI "as a means to actively reflect, process, and engage with the material explained in class."

title: Critical digital pedagogy approach to fostering students' ethical and effective engagement with AI tools
description: The article adopts a critical digital pedagogy approach as its framing for AI integration in higher education. Rather than restricting AI use, the approach aims "to foster students' awareness of ethical and effective engagement with AI tools." It works by embedding reflective practices, critical analysis of AI-generated content, and clear responsible-use guidelines into course activities, positioning students as critically aware users of AI rather than prohibited users. The approach sits within the broader context of digital transformation in higher education and evolving demands of academic integrity.
requirements: Course activities must be designed to encourage reflective practices and critical analysis of AI-generated content

academic integrity
digital literacy

citation: Ali Bicer, Tugce Aldemir, Unggi Lee, Jewoong Moon, Karen Rambo Hernandez, Miriam Sanders. (2026). How generative AI guided-professional development supports teachers' engagement with mathematical creativity, content knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge. ZDM–Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01816-1
title: Generative AI as a cognitive and instructional partner in teacher professional learning
description: The study conceptualizes generative AI not as a content-delivery tool but as "a cognitive and instructional partner" that supports teacher learning through contingent prompting, feedback, rehearsal, and guided reflection. Guided by Rhodes' 4P framework (person, process, press, product) and constructivist and socio-constructivist perspectives, the AI responds to teachers' ideas, prompts explanation and revision, simulates student reasoning, and scaffolds reasoning within teachers' zone of proximal development. Teachers experienced the system as a "knowledgeable partner" rather than a static content provider.

Teachers retain interpretive authority and the system's role remains transparent and bounded
constraints: Open-ended AI coaching may produce generic feedback or overextend beyond teachers' professional judgment

target_learning_goals: mathematical creativity
content knowledge for proportional reasoning
pedagogical content knowledge
examples: The chatbot used GPT-4 via the OpenAI API, configured through module-specific system prompts, few-shot examples, and conditional prompt templates with guardrails against direct solution-giving

title: Ten-module AI-guided asynchronous PD program on proportional reasoning with eight designed AI-mediated mechanisms
description: The AI-guided PD comprised ten asynchronous modules completed across one academic semester, typically requiring 30-45 hours, each centered on rate and proportional reasoning. Eight intentionally designed AI-mediated mechanisms structured engagement: adaptive prompting, real-time feedback, progressive scaffold fading, simulated student reasoning, supportive nonjudgmental tone, flexible pacing, representational nudges, and cycles of creative challenge and reflection. Teachers solved tasks, generated multiple strategies, posed problems, interpreted simulated student thinking, and reflected on instruction.

citation: Buket Bilgiç and Demet Sever (2026). Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights from faculty members and students. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00601-0
title: Researcher-developed Likert-type surveys on ethical AI use for students and faculty members
description: The study's quantitative phase used Likert-type surveys prepared separately for students and faculty members to measure views on ethical AI use in education. Both surveys showed high internal consistency ("students: α = 0.906, ω = 0.906; faculty members: α = 0.948, ω = 0.952"). Exploratory factor analysis yielded a four-factor structure for the student survey explaining 38.00% of total variance and a five-factor structure for the faculty survey explaining 56.33%. The instruments were developed by the researchers and revised through expert review and pilot applications before use.
requirements: All data collection tools were developed by the researchers and revised through expert review and pilot applications.
constraints: The article states that additional analyses are required for the instrument to be considered a validated scale.

faculty members

examples: The surveys were administered under stratified sampling by academic unit, with responses analyzed descriptively in JAMOVI.

title: Six-theme multidimensional ethical structure of AI use in higher education
description: Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with faculty members and students organized perspectives on ethical AI use into six themes: "Ethical Risks, User Approaches to Ethical Risks, Ethical Risk Management, Resources and Support, and Long-Term Effects", alongside participants' AI tool use and perceived benefits. Together these themes reveal what the article calls "a multidimensional ethical structure in the use of AI in education", spanning risks, user orientations, management practices, support structures, and anticipated long-term consequences. Faculty and student perspectives are presented separately within each theme.
requirements: Semi-structured interviews with both stakeholder groups, analyzed through Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis combining inductive and deductive coding.
constraints: The study is situated within a specific context, and the results reflect participants' reported views and experiences regarding the ethical use of AI in education.

title: Adaptive AI-based STEM instructional program: rule-based mastery sequencing in Moodle with machine-learning analytics for monitoring only

title: Mastery-based branching across micro-learning units with misconception-triggered redirection
description: Each lesson was decomposed into micro-learning units aligned with deep learning dimensions, with decision rules governing progression based on learner performance. "Mastery-based branching mechanisms were embedded at both the diagnostic entry point and within lesson-level assessments to differentiate beginner and advanced tracks." Redirection logic targeted specific misconceptions (e.g., orbital positioning, axial tilt, tide–gravity causal links) with scaffolded models, hint sequences, and worked examples, while rapid mastery unlocked enrichment challenges.

description: The study developed its intervention through the ADDIE model, treating it not merely as a procedural sequence but as an organizing design logic ensuring coherence among objectives, adaptive mechanisms, activities, and assessment. They argue rapid prototyping lacks explicit mechanisms for aligning adaptive decision rules with assessment, and backward design does not address data-driven adaptation.

article_title: Bounded Reliance: A Source Credibility Perspective on EFL Students' Engagement with AI-Generated Writing Feedback
citation: Serpil, H., & Mor, M. K. (2026). Bounded reliance: A source credibility perspective on EFL students' engagement with AI-generated writing feedback. Journal of Language Pedagogy and Linguistics, 1(1), 1-27. https://doi.org/10.0.20.161/zenodo.22828386
title: Source Credibility Theory as a lens for evaluating algorithmic feedback providers
description: Source Credibility Theory holds that message effectiveness depends on perceived source credibility across three dimensions: expertise (knowledge and competence), trustworthiness (honesty, dependability, lack of bias), and goodwill (caring and responsiveness to the recipient). The article applies this lens to AI-generated writing feedback, arguing that "learners apply to an algorithmic provider the same multidimensional source judgments the theory was developed to explain for human communicators." It uses the three dimensions to organize its thematic analysis of student interviews.
requirements: Learners must have sustained direct experience with the feedback source before evaluating its credibility
constraints: The study examined perceptions in one undergraduate translation-studies writing course, not causal effects of credibility on learning outcomes
target_learners: undergraduate EFL students in higher education
target_learning_goals: evaluating and selectively using AI-generated feedback in academic writing revision
examples: The study coded interview themes abductively against the three SCT dimensions (expertise, trustworthiness, goodwill) in a 15-week GROK-supported writing course

article_title: The Devil is in the Details: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World
citation: Aras Bozkurt, Helen Crompton, & Caroline Fell Kurban. (2026). The Devil is in the Det[ai]ls: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World. Open Praxis, 18(1), 1–12. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.1.1145
title: The ghost student: agentic AI as mind plus AI browser as body producing a verification gap in digital education
description: The article's organizing framework describes the ghost student as a digital surrogate created by coupling Large Language Models (the mind) with agentic AI browsers (the body). Agentic AI is defined as systems designed to operate autonomously, adapt dynamically, and execute multi-step processes to achieve predefined goals with minimal human intervention, and the browser supplies embodied actions such as clicking, scrolling, and submitting work. The result is a verification gap: a digital entity that satisfies every metric of success while the human learner remains entirely disengaged, making the learner's presence optional and eroding credential trust.
requirements: Institutional systems that infer learning from logged-in activity and output-based submissions, which the surrogate can satisfy without a human present
constraints: The framework addresses agentic AI browsers acting with valid authenticated credentials; it is an argument-based editorial account, not an empirically tested model
target_learners: higher education students
K-12 students
open, online and distance education learners
target_learning_goals: verified human presence in learning
academic integrity
credential trust
examples: The editorial describes AI browsers logging into an LMS with valid credentials, navigating modules, watching videos, responding to quizzes, and submitting assignments without further human input
key_sources: Aras Bozkurt, Helen Crompton, & Caroline Fell Kurban. (2026). The Devil is in the Det[ai]ls: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World. Open Praxis, 18(1), 1–12. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.1.1145

title: Design assessment for verified human presence rather than relying on output-based submissions
description: Because agentic surrogates master the product but cannot demonstrate a process, the article recommends moving away from output-based assessments toward presence-required models such as oral examinations and defenses, live presentations with spontaneous questioning, in-person demonstrations, and dialogic assessment and reflective portfolios. These methods remain resistant to automation because they value the process of becoming, not just the product of doing. The article frames this as a structural redesign rather than better detection.
requirements: Faculty understanding of how AI browsers and autonomous agents function, what they can access, and what tasks they can complete
Time, funding, and professional support, since oral defenses and portfolios do not scale with the same frictionless ease as a quiz
constraints: Assessment models relying heavily on oral articulation or sustained reflection can inadvertently disadvantage students with disabilities, language barriers, or neurodivergence, so inclusive presence must be designed
target_learners: higher education students
online and hybrid course learners
target_learning_goals: authentic demonstration of learning
resistance to automated completion
articulation of reasoning in real time
examples: The editorial's audit questions ask educators where student presence is actually required, where learning is inferred rather than verified, and which assessments assume a human behind the keyboard

title: Agentic AI browsers (e.g., Perplexity Comet, OpenAI Atlas) as autonomous interfaces that act inside institutional systems
description: AI browsers embed LLMs directly into the browsing environment, enabling autonomous perception of on-screen content and execution of embodied actions such as clicking, scrolling, opening new tabs, completing forms, uploading files, and submitting responses across live web systems. Named examples include Perplexity's Comet browser and OpenAI's Atlas, which integrate reasoning, retrieval, and browser-level action into a continuous loop of perception and execution. The article characterizes the browser as the body through which agentic AI enacts agency, occupying the same interactive space as the authenticated user.
requirements: A user's valid, authenticated credentials to institutional systems, which the browser uses to navigate institutional perimeters
constraints: These are general-purpose agentic interfaces, not purpose-built for education; the article describes them as functioning as a digital parasite when deployed in learning environments

online learners

digital citizenship and institutional responsibility

article_title: A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching
citation: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632
title: CDM-AIR: a capability–decision model ordering AI-TPACK upstream of TPB beliefs with context as antecedent and moderator
description: CDM-AIR is a theoretically grounded framework explaining teacher readiness to integrate AI in teaching. It separates capability from belief: AI-TPACK constitutes a capability system, while TPB constructs form a belief-mediated decision pathway. As the article states, "AI-TPACK constitutes a teacher’s capability system for designing and enacting AI-integrated pedagogy, whereas TPB constructs operate as a belief-mediated decision pathway through which teachers form intentions and translate them into observable classroom behaviour." Contextual facilitating conditions shape subjective norms and perceived behavioural control and moderate the PBC–behaviour link. The model is specified as thirteen hypotheses in five families and admits full structural, staged, and diagnostic modes of use.
requirements: Capability must be conceptualised as competence and measured with performance-based evidence where feasible, ordered upstream of decision beliefs
The teacher remains the accountable decision-maker; the model assumes AI functions through teacher-mediated adoption choices
constraints: The model does not model moment-to-moment distribution of agency between teacher and AI system during instruction
It has not yet been empirically validated; causal ordering remains theoretical until tested with longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs
Should classroom AI evolve to the point where systems adopt teachers rather than the reverse, the TPB decision core would require replacement rather than extension
target_learners: in-service and pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: readiness to integrate artificial intelligence in teaching
key_sources: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632

article_title: A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching
citation: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632
title: Worked lesson-design capability task with a 0–9 scoring rubric for performance-based AI-TPACK measurement
description: A performance-based assessment instrument operationalising the capability construct: teachers design a short AI-integrated lesson segment and justify the role of AI. The exemplar prompt asks the teacher to "Design a 40-minute Grade 10 biology lesson segment on enzyme activity in which a generative AI tool is used to produce differentiated formative feedback on learners’ predictions about reaction rates." Responses are scored 0–3 per criterion on pedagogical alignment, justification quality, and verification and ethical safeguards (total 0–9, Table 2). The article recommends double-scoring a random 20% of responses with inter-rater agreement of at least κ = .70 before single-scoring.
requirements: Double-scoring of a random 20% of responses with inter-rater agreement of at least κ = .70 (or intraclass correlation of .75 for continuous rubric totals) as the acceptability threshold
Parallel exemplars for prompt-evaluation and content-validity tasks seeded with discipline-typical errors
constraints: Completion requires approximately 30–40 min in piloting
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers in teacher-education programmes
target_learning_goals: AI-integrated lesson design, output verification, and ethical safeguarding competence
examples: The article provides the Grade 10 biology enzyme-activity prompt and the three-criterion rubric in Table 2 as a worked exemplar of the first of four indicator types

citation: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632
title: Treat AI readiness as pedagogical capability rather than tool familiarity, and evaluate whether targeted mediators moved
description: From the capability-to-belief bridge (H6, H7) and mediated pathways (H10, H11), the article recommends that teacher-education programmes "treat AI readiness as pedagogical capability rather than tool familiarity, prioritising integrated AI-TPACK development through lesson-design tasks, prompt-evaluation activities, content-validity judgements, and artefact-based reflection." Programme evaluation should measure whether the targeted mediators (PBC and attitude) moved before intention, not only whether participants report greater willingness, because technological knowledge may align with perceived benefits while integrated competence lags.

constraints: Technological knowledge may align strongly with perceived AI benefits while pedagogical and content knowledge show weaker associations, producing confidence without integrated competence

target_learning_goals: integrated AI-TPACK capability development
examples: The article links this principle to the performance-based tasks operationalised in its Section 4.3.3

article_title: Artificial intelligence assisted design of a novel cooperative learning technique for higher education
citation: Özgür Tutal. (2026). Artificial intelligence assisted design of a novel cooperative learning technique for higher education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-50770-1
title: Curriculum Concept Constellation Technique (CCCT)
description: CCCT is a cooperative learning technique in which small heterogeneous groups of 4–5 students map key curriculum concepts as "stars" into visual "constellations" using metaphors. It uses a "Metaphorical and visual approach" in which "The CCCT uses the metaphor of stars forming constellations in the night sky to represent key concepts in curriculum development." Students take roles (Star Finder, Constellation Designer, Metaphor Maker, Visual Artist, Navigator) ensuring individual accountability and positive interdependence, work over two weeks, and close with a gallery walk and reflection/group processing.
requirements: Small heterogeneous groups of 4–5 members with assigned roles; simple materials (canvas, markers, sticky notes); a two-session format within a theoretical course
constraints: Designed for abstract theoretical course content without a practical component; implemented over two weeks in a curriculum development course
target_learners: sophomore prospective teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding the theoretical foundations of curriculum development
cooperative regulation of learning
positive attitudes toward cooperativeness
examples: Groups identified 5–7 key concepts such as John Dewey's philosophy, behaviorism, societal needs and developmental psychology, connected them into constellations, and described relationships with metaphors such as behaviorism as a gravitational force pulling ideas toward measurable outcomes.

article_title: Artificial intelligence assisted design of a novel cooperative learning technique for higher education
citation: Özgür Tutal. (2026). Artificial intelligence assisted design of a novel cooperative learning technique for higher education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-50770-1
title: Structure cooperative learning so that group work embeds the five essential elements rather than merely placing students in groups
description: The article argues that effective cooperative learning depends on intentional structuring, not group formation alone. It states that "merely placing students in groups does not guarantee effective cooperation or learning" and that without structuring, group work "may devolve into unproductive or even counterproductive interactions." The five elements—positive interdependence, individual accountability, face-to-face promotive interaction, interpersonal and small group social skills, and group processing—guided both the design of CCCT and its evaluation rubric.
requirements: Careful planning, clear expectations, and ongoing support so that students engage in meaningful and productive collaboration
constraints: Stated for cooperative learning generally; the article notes that without built-in inclusion mechanisms some students, such as shy students, non-native speakers, or students with learning disabilities, may be marginalized or disengaged
target_learners: students in small-group instruction across educational levels
target_learning_goals: meaningful collaboration, individual accountability, and productive peer interaction
examples: CCCT operationalized the elements through assigned roles ensuring individual accountability and positive interdependence, face-to-face collaboration during constellation creation, and a closing reflection and group processing activity.

article_title: Leveraging generative AI to facilitate peer feedback in collaborative argumentation learning
citation: Chang, Y., Liu, Q., Lu, Y. & Miao, E. (2026). Leveraging generative AI to facilitate peer feedback in collaborative argumentation learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00586-w
title: Scaffold students' GenAI dialogue with prompt scaffolding built on context, objective, and role elements to improve peer feedback quality
description: The study designed prompt scaffolding that structures students' dialogue with GenAI during peer feedback, combining "the elements of context, objective, and role in the prompt model". Context supplies argument content and background knowledge; objective specifies the evaluation tasks GenAI should perform; roles such as approvers or detractors let the model conduct thought experiments. The scaffolded condition (PS-GenAI-PF) produced the strongest argumentation gains, supporting scaffolded over unscaffolded GenAI use.

The prompt scaffolding must be tailored to the peer feedback task, specifying evaluation targets such as supporting arguments, rebuttals, and counterarguments
constraints: Students were reminded not to rely exclusively on GenAI-generated content, given the cognitive offloading risk the article notes
Evidence comes from one course with 45 third-year Educational Technology student teachers in 12 groups
target_learners: higher education students
pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: collaborative argumentation quality
peer feedback quality
examples: Groups used prompts such as "evaluate the argument from X perspective" and role prompts like "You work as an education policy maker" while reviewing peers' argumentation artifacts with ERNIE Bot

article_title: Let's Chat: Leveraging Chatbot Outreach for Improved Course Performance
citation: Meyer, Katharine, Lindsay C. Page, Catherine Mata, Eric N. Smith, B. Tyler Walsh, C. Lindsey Fifield, Michelle Tyson, Amy Eremionkhale, Michael Evans, Shelby Frost, and Eye Eoun Jung. (2026). Let's Chat: Leveraging Chatbot Outreach for Improved Course Performance. (EdWorkingPaper: 22-564). https://edworkingpapers.com/ai22-564
title: Non-generative AI academic chatbot with TA-supported knowledge base and #quizme practice function
description: A text-based chatbot with non-generative AI capability that sent 2-3 scheduled, customized messages per week (about 40 per semester) to students in large online courses. Messages provided "timely reminders about course requirements", customized feedback on individual progress, connections to academic supports, and an additional communication channel. When students texted in, the bot responded from a pre-programmed knowledge base; low-probability matches were flagged to the course TA, whose manual responses updated the knowledge base. A #quizme function in Government let students request multiple-choice practice quizzes before exams.
requirements: Faculty buy-in and a course TA embedded in both the course and chatbot administration to maintain the knowledge base and review bot responses daily for quality control
Students opted in to receiving text-based communication from the university
constraints: The #quizme function was deployed only in Government, since Microeconomics did not have exams
Messages required timely gradebook information from the TA to customize outreach to students' performance each week
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large-enrollment, asynchronous online courses at a minority-serving public university
target_learning_goals: Course engagement and assignment completion
Course performance and completion
Connection to academic supports such as tutoring
examples: In a spring 2021 pilot in Government, 90% of end-of-course survey respondents recommended that GSU continue the bot, and weekly digests were redesigned to be customized to students' course performance to date

article_title: Students' experiences of using ChatGPT for English language learning: a qualitative study in a Malaysian higher education institution
citation: Annamalai N, Nasor M, Din Eak A and Ayoub Alkubaisy AA (2026) Students’ experiences of using ChatGPT for English language learning: a qualitative study in a Malaysian higher education institution. Front. Psychol. 17:1875727. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1875727
title: AI-mediated motivational ecology: an extension of Self-Determination Theory in which basic psychological needs are partly met through AI interaction
description: The article extends SDT, which conceptualizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as human-centered constructs grounded in interpersonal and instructional contexts, by proposing that learner needs can be "partly met through AI interaction rather than solely through instructor and peersupport". In this account, ChatGPT's personalized feedback and conversational responsiveness reshape how autonomy, competence, and relatedness are negotiated in human–AI interactions, e.g. relatedness experienced as perceived communicative support rather than human connection. The study uses this lens to interpret Malaysian EFL undergraduates' experiences of ChatGPT-mediated English learning.
requirements: Learners actively engage with AI feedback and make informed decisions about their learning strategies for agency and self-regulation to be encouraged
constraints: Whether AI interaction fully satisfies the psychological need for relatedness remains debatable because authentic relatedness traditionally involves human interactions
target_learners: undergraduate EFL students with limited English proficiency (MUET Bands 2–3)
target_learning_goals: English language competence in grammar, writing, speaking, and vocabulary; learner motivation and self-directed learning
examples: The study interviewed 25 Malaysian undergraduates who used ChatGPT 3.5 or 4.0 voluntarily for course-related English activities over a 5-month semester, coding themes deductively against autonomy, competence, and relatedness

title: The Pedagogy Benchmark: 1143 curated MCQs of pedagogical knowledge from Chilean teacher exams (920 CDPK + 223 SEND)
description: The Pedagogy Benchmark is a publicly released dataset of multiple-choice questions testing LLMs' pedagogical knowledge, built from the Chilean Ministry of Education's ECEP teacher exams administered 2017–2023. Questions were extracted, de-duplicated, translated, and manually curated by a pedagogy expert, yielding "1143 high-quality, annotated MCQs". The 920 general questions form the CDPK benchmark and 223 form a separate SEND benchmark, each tagged with education level, subject, and pedagogical subdomain.

article_title: Assessing the Quality of AI-Generated Exams: A Large-Scale Field Study
citation: Calvin Isley, Joshua Gilbert, Evangelos Kassos, Michaela Kocher, Allen Nie, Emma Brunskill, Ben Domingue, Jake Hofman, Joscha Legewie, Teddy Svoronos, Charlotte Tuminelli, Sharad Goel. (2025). Assessing the Quality of AI-Generated Exams: A Large-Scale Field Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08314
title: Iterative LLM refinement strategy for generating course-tailored exam questions
description: A two-stage generation procedure, similar to Self-Refine, in which an LLM generator produces multiple-choice questions from instructor-provided course materials and an AI judge labels each question "good" or "bad"; labeled questions are fed back into the generator's prompt as few-shot examples, and the loop repeats until 20 judge-approved questions exist. A final judging round assesses difficulty, appropriateness, and answer correctness, and the 10 hardest approved questions become the class-specific exam. All generation and judging used OpenAI's o3-mini model, with five 2012 AP Statistics practice questions as "good" examples in every prompt.
requirements: Instructor-provided course materials (course description, syllabus, prior homework or exams) converted to plain text as context for both generator and judge
An AI judge applying appropriateness criteria such as no syllabus-logistics questions, mentally solvable calculations, and no duplicated concepts
constraints: Question generation was limited to multiple-choice questions solvable in about 1-2 minutes each
If final judging removed more than 10 questions, an additional 20 questions had to be generated and the full group of 40 re-evaluated
target_learners: college students in STEM and quantitative courses
target_learning_goals: assessment of course-specific conceptual understanding
examples: For each class the loop ran until 20 judge-labeled good questions were generated; a rejected 'bad' biochemistry question tested knowledge of class logistics rather than substantive content

article_title: Assessing the Quality of AI-Generated Exams: A Large-Scale Field Study
citation: Calvin Isley, Joshua Gilbert, Evangelos Kassos, Michaela Kocher, Allen Nie, Emma Brunskill, Ben Domingue, Jake Hofman, Joscha Legewie, Teddy Svoronos, Charlotte Tuminelli, Sharad Goel. (2025). Assessing the Quality of AI-Generated Exams: A Large-Scale Field Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08314
title: Large-scale field study dataset and code release for AI-generated exam evaluation
description: The article releases the code and datasets behind its exam-generation and evaluation pipeline via GitHub, alongside a field-study corpus of student responses: 91 classes comprising 1686 students who completed both a common quantitative-reasoning pre-test and a semester-end tailored exam, of whom 1208 students in 71 classes received AI-generated exams and 478 students in 20 statistics classes received AP Statistics practice questions. Responses were analyzed with a hierarchical Bayesian 2PL IRT model fit with cmdstanr.
requirements: Student pre-test responses used as anchor items to establish a common θ scale across exam types
constraints: Exam type was not randomly assigned, so comparisons across groups are descriptive
The constant-θ assumption across the semester is required for the common scale
target_learners: college students across dozens of US colleges
target_learning_goals: measuring student ability with course-tailored assessments
examples: In rare cases (less than 2%) of multiple submissions, responses were superscored by retaining the highest score per question

article_title: BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation
citation: Hanchen David Wang, Clayton Cohn, Zifan Xu, Siyuan Guo, Gautam Biswas, Meiyi Ma. (2026). BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13280
title: Competency bias and the multi-dimensional fidelity problem for LLM student simulation
description: The article names competency bias as "the inherent tendency of preference-tuned models to produce correct solutions even when prompted to simulate novice students", and frames simulating learners as a multi-dimensional fidelity problem with behavioral, epistemic, and perceptual components. Behavioral infidelity is the linear construction trap avoiding iterative trial-and-error; epistemic infidelity is the curse of incompetence, where LLMs act as masked experts who diagnose errors before execution; perceptual infidelity is RLHF-flattened output diversity. BEAGLE is designed explicitly against these three objectives.
requirements: Authentic student behavior is treated as emerging from SRL processes (cognition, metacognition, motivation/affect) rather than outcome quality, so fidelity objectives must be defined over process distributions, not correctness
constraints: The framework targets open-ended problem-solving trajectories in coding-embedded domains; porting requires a knowledge component taxonomy and action schema
target_learners: novice learners in open-ended programming and physics problem-solving environments
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning behaviors including planning, enacting, monitoring, and reflecting during problem solving
examples: Fig. 1 contrast: real students debug persistently (D→D: 28%) while LLM-generated students dominate continuous construction transitions and bypass debugging
key_sources: Hanchen David Wang, Clayton Cohn, Zifan Xu, Siyuan Guo, Gautam Biswas, Meiyi Ma. (2026). BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13280

article_title: BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation
citation: Hanchen David Wang, Clayton Cohn, Zifan Xu, Siyuan Guo, Gautam Biswas, Meiyi Ma. (2026). BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13280
title: Enforce novice-like simulation architecturally rather than through prompting or context engineering
description: The article's central design recommendation is that realistic synthetic student behavior cannot be elicited from preference-tuned LLMs by persona prompting or context injection alone; it requires architectural enforcement. Symbolic control (semi-Markov dynamics, BKT with flaw injection) and a decoupled Strategist/Executor constrain what the model can do, so that "sequence-level student simulation cannot be recovered through context engineering alone; architectural enforcement closes the gap." The +M baseline variants, which inject BEAGLE's metacognitive vocabulary without the architecture, empirically isolate prompt effects from architectural ones.
requirements: A calibrated symbolic-control layer (semi-Markov transitions and Gamma durations fit on historical student logs) plus a knowledge model with explicit flaw injection
constraints: +M variants never beat DKL = 0.63 or Realism = 1.64, and removing the semi-Markov controller while preserving prompts pushes DKL to 6.81
target_learners: researchers and builders of adaptive tutoring systems and pedagogical agents needing synthetic novice data
target_learning_goals: generation of high-fidelity synthetic learner trajectories for training tutors and stress-testing pedagogical interventions
examples: BEAGLE implements the principle via three mechanisms: semi-Markov behavior control, BKT+EFI knowledge constraints, and the Strategist/Executor split with observation filtering

article_title: Bots and Blocks: Presenting a Project-Based Approach for Robotics Education
citation: Tobias Geger, Dominique Briechle and Andreas Rausch. (2026). Bots and Blocks: Presenting a project-based approach for robotics education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14529
title: Digital Technologies project framework: semester-spanning agile Scrum projects as an integral third of a robotics-relevant CS curriculum
description: The article proposes a project-based learning framework in which students work in small teams on industry-relevant problems across multiple semesters. The bachelor's program comprises 180 ECTS points, of which 60 are project-based courses worth ten ECTS each, organized with the Scrum framework. The authors state that "the project team is not driven by consecutive tasks to develop a product but by the development of a minimum viable product (MVP)" defined by user stories. Projects are consecutive: early semesters teach project skills, later ones mix cohorts for interdisciplinary work.
requirements: A multi-semester study program structure so that application modules and skill refinement can span several projects rather than a single course
Scientific staff acting as Product Owner and a senior student acting as Scrum Master for each team
constraints: The framework is described for the undergraduate program of one applied computer science degree (Digital Technologies); the authors note transferability to other domains is future research
target_learners: undergraduate bachelor's students in applied computer science (Digital Technologies)
target_learning_goals: practical robotics and software engineering skills alongside theoretical knowledge
agile self-managed teamwork on industry-relevant problems
examples: In the winter semester 2025/2026 project, a student team developed a ROS2-based disassembly software ecosystem over seven two-week sprints

title: Schools: interactive lecture-demonstration-exercise sessions embedded in the project timeline
description: Schools are the article's format for teaching base qualifications within the project. "Each school covers a different topic and always begins with a short lecture of around sixty minutes." After a live demonstration by a supervisor, students work on a matching exercise with instructor support, then present, reflect on and discuss results in the plenum, with critical parts addressed explicitly. Some schools are followed by tasks that feed the next session or an intermediate exam. In the robotics project, schools covered ROS/ROS2 and object detection with YOLO.

Exercises matched to the demonstrated concepts and plenum discussion of student results

title: ROS-based disassembly station with two robots and conveyor belts as the project hardware platform
description: The student project used a hardware disassembly station consisting of two robots and two conveyor belts, with a ROS backbone controlling the robots and adjunct installations. The system exposes topics for moving, rotating, grasping, digital outputs and inputs, joint states, conveyor and clamp control. Because some components were implemented in ROS 1, "a ROS bridge is required in order to integrate all functionalities into the new ROS2 system that the students are implementing." Students aligned the AI camera frame with the world frame via the /tf2 node for precise grasping.

title: Consecutive semester project sequence: methodological foundation first, then full-stack preparation, then domain projects with mixed-level cohorts

Later projects mix students from higher bachelor levels or master's students, allowing collaboration on more complex interdisciplinary projects and letting newer students benefit from more advanced peers.

citation: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: AICoFe: an AI-based collaborative feedback system for peer, self-, and teacher assessment in higher education
description: AICoFe is a human-centered AI system that supports peer and self-evaluation in educational settings using customized rubrics integrating quantitative scores and qualitative observations. It is "organised into four main modules": a Visualization Module with role-specific dashboards, a Management Module for data storage, a Feedback Generation Module orchestrating multi-LLM feedback production, and a Recording Module capturing student performances in video and audio. Video recordings of presentations support reflective learning and more thorough evaluation.

constraints: Participation in video recording is strictly opt-in via informed consent, and all audiovisual data are stored in compliance with GDPR

critical reflection
evaluative judgment
oral presentation skills
examples: Deployed at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid with approximately 80 students and 5 teachers across one undergraduate course and one master's course

citation: Alvaro Becerra, Alejandra Palma and Ruth Cobos. (2026). AICoFe: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Collaborative Feedback System for Higher Education. LASI Spain 26: Learning Analytics Summer Institute Spain 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0003-7793-2682
title: Multi-LLM feedback generation pipeline combining three independently fine-tuned models
description: AICoFe's Feedback Generation Module extends prior single-model work to a multi-model setting in which "three independent feedback instances are generated, one per LLM" (GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.1). Each model receives the same structured prompt built from average rubric scores, validated qualitative observations, rubric level descriptions, and instructional materials. Using three distinct models is argued to enrich feedback with diverse perspectives while reducing the risk of single-model biases or systematic errors reaching students. Each instance follows a three-paragraph structure: strengths, areas for improvement, and an action plan.
requirements: All models are fine-tuned on teacher-validated feedback instances from the SOPHIAS dataset, and a post-processing validation stage enforces teacher-defined constraints such as length, coherence, and exclusion of restricted terms
constraints: All data sent to the generative models are anonymised prior to transmission to commercial LLM providers

target_learning_goals: actionable personalized feedback on assessed skills
examples: GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned via the OpenAI API for 3 epochs; Gemini 2.5 Flash via Vertex AI for 40 cycles; Llama 3.1 locally via LoRA with 4-bit NF4 quantisation

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: The evolutionary spiral: co-evolution of intent and build across agent-mediated turns
description: The evolutionary spiral is the article's central conceptual contribution: a project runs as a sequence of turns in which work inside a turn is fast and loose while between turns intent is pinned down, the specification is updated and the context file absorbs what was learned. It synthesises Boehm's risk-driven spiral model, the design-research account of co-evolution of problem and solution spaces, and Brooks's contracting-point refinement of iterative process. The article states that "Across many turns the project converges on a definite version of what was actually wanted, even though no single turn could have known the final destination." It is taught in Module 18 and operationalised through two judgment skills, the commit point and drift detection.
requirements: Practitioners must learn commit-point and drift-detection judgment skills, which the article says are learned through practice rather than instruction
constraints: The article notes the two judgment skills cannot be taught the way verification gate design can; a companion pre-print will develop the contrast with spec-driven approaches at full length
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students with foundational computer science knowledge
target_learning_goals: managing iterative human-agent software projects
discovering requirements through build-evaluate-revise cycles
examples: A semester project that takes a small software product across at least three full turns of the evolutionary spiral, graded on mid-project commit-point decisions and recoveries from drift
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: Agentic software engineering as a discipline: humans frame, specify and judge; agents execute
description: The article's opening conceptual move is that agentic software engineering is a discipline rather than a tool skill: it has principles, named artefacts, recognised failure modes and standards. Its central division of labour is that "humans frame, specify and judge, and agents execute, which means that the human's job is to equip the agent and to verify what it produces." The article names three collapse modes (hand-editing output and losing the audit trail, delegating judgment along with execution, delegating framing itself) and four structural risks: skill atrophy, code opacity, diffuse accountability, and models reproducing training-corpus assumptions.
requirements: Practitioners must be trained to expect the four structural risks and to maintain the division of labour, since none of the risks disappear with experience
constraints: The article states the division of labour is straightforward to state but difficult to maintain in practice, and collapses in predictable ways when violated
target_learners: undergraduate software engineering students
practising developers transitioning to agent-mediated work
target_learning_goals: understanding the human role in agent-directed development
recognising discipline failure modes and structural risks
examples: The curriculum teaches the ACE side of Hassan and colleagues' SASE workbench split while developing enough AEE understanding to direct and verify agent output
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: Auditability principle and the seven-part anatomy of an agentic workflow turn
description: The article defines auditability as the discipline's defining principle: "a workflow that cannot be inspected, replayed or evaluated after the fact is craft, while engineering is accountable and reproducible." Its operational artefact is the audit trail, a frozen record linking intent to specification, context, agent trajectory and verification, which agentic work produces as a byproduct of normal operation. Each workflow turn has seven constituents running as a single act rather than sequential phases: intent, specification, context, plan, execution, verification and the audit trail, each with a corresponding curriculum module.
requirements: The practitioner must preserve, name and make navigable the material the workflow generates, so someone other than the original engineer can reconstruct what was decided, why, and what happened
constraints: The article notes classical software engineering struggled to produce audit trails routinely because engineers wrote them by hand after the fact; the principle's low cost depends on agent-generated records
target_learners: undergraduate software engineering students
target_learning_goals: designing auditable human-agent workflows
verification before trust
examples: Module 4 names the seven-part anatomy and the auditability principle; Module 13 develops verification gates with verification theatre as a named failure mode
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: ASE-26: a twenty-one-module undergraduate curriculum for agentic software engineering
description: ASE-26 is a comprehensive undergraduate curriculum deposited on Zenodo under CC BY-ND 4.0, organising agentic software engineering into twenty-one modules across four parts plus a closing module. Part 1 covers the discipline, Part 2 the environment, Part 3 the engineering (Modules 10 through 18, the largest part), and Part 4 the market, with Module 21 teaching practitioners to keep their mental model of the field fresh. The article states the structure "follows the order in which a practitioner builds capability rather than the order in which the literature was published," and the full text with reference lists is deposited as the canonical reference.
requirements: Students are expected to already have foundational knowledge of computer science and some experience with software engineering
constraints: The curriculum is designed to be revised; Module 21 distinguishes durable principles from contingent capabilities tied to current model and ADE features
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students with foundational computer science knowledge
target_learning_goals: framing and specifying agentic projects
context engineering
verification gate design
multi-agent workflow design
code review against the MRP standard
security and governance of agentic systems
examples: Module 11 covers context engineering; Module 12 covers safety with Git as the primary safety layer; Module 14 introduces five multi-agent workflow patterns from Anthropic's engineering writing
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: Grade the discipline, not the artefact: assess what the agent cannot satisfy
description: Because the delivered artefact in an agentic course is co-produced with an agent, the article's assessment principle is that "the grading scheme grades the discipline rather than the lines of code." Criteria are chosen so the agent cannot satisfy them in itself: framing, specification, context engineering, verification design, code review against a structured standard, multi-agent coordination, and security and governance analysis. Three commitments follow: the audit trail is gradable, the spiral is gradable as a rhythm across turns, and verification is gradable as a deliverable, with Hassan and colleagues' MRP framework as the final-deliverable standard.
requirements: Students must submit chat transcripts, commit history, context files, lessons-learned notes and verification records alongside the artefact; without these the artefact is opaque and cannot be assessed
constraints: Audit trails that are absent, opaque or evidently retrofitted score zero on process traceability regardless of artefact quality; an artefact satisfying four of five MRP criteria is treated as not merge-ready
target_learners: undergraduate students in agentic software engineering courses
target_learning_goals: demonstrating framing, specification, verification design and review judgment co-producing work with an agent
examples: A student taking three turns to converge with a clear audit trail scores higher than one reaching a similar end state in one turn with no record of the reasoning; weighting is 50 per cent continuous coursework, 40 per cent project, 10 per cent closing artefact
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction
citation: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph.
title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: a three-level metacognitive construct explaining cognitive transfer from mathematics to AI understanding
description: The article proposes Awareness of Technological Isomorphism, "defined as a student's metacognitive realization that their own mathematical cognitive operations (e.g., observing trends, inducing patterns, and making predictions) share an underlying logical structure with AI technical operations". It comprises three progressive levels — existence, recognition, and internalization of isomorphism — and is anchored in Ausubel's transfer theory and Flavell's metacognitive theory. The article distinguishes it from computational thinking: students need not "think like a computer scientist" but discover their reasoning is already mirrored by machine processes, which the authors argue is more developmentally accessible in elementary school.
requirements: Instructional guidance must reveal that AI performs a task with the same underlying logic students have just used, so recognition can occur
constraints: The article notes the construct was conceptualized and operationalized for the elementary 'Data and Prediction' continuum, with Stage 3 (internalization) left open for further operational development
target_learners: elementary school students (Grades 1-6)
target_learning_goals: understanding AI predictive principles
trend estimation and data reasoning in mathematics

description: The framework translates principles derived from learning theories into observable pedagogical variables — properties of a resource that can be explicitly identified in terms of content, representation, and conceptual organization — represented as metadata. citation: Mario Brcic, Stjepan Frljic. (2026). The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26181
title: The six moves: Prime, Probe, Point, Attach, Strengthen, Test as a model of learning one new idea
description: The article models what a student knows as a knowledge map of dots and links, and learning one new idea as growing a new dot and tying it into the map through six ordered moves. As printed, "We call them the six moves: Prime, Probe, Point, Attach, Strengthen, Test, shown on Figure 1." Probe and Test are the protected moments where the student's own work must remain visible; Point, Attach, and Strengthen are guarded-support moments. Each move is mapped to a teacher role, a permitted AI role, and supporting evidence in Table 1.
requirements: A motivated, engaged student; the article states the sequence assumes what it cannot itself supply
constraints: Scope is one idea, on first encounter, in a single pass; long-term retention via review and spacing is a separate layer above the model
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students learning a new idea
target_learning_goals: Building durable, transferable understanding of a new concept
examples: The article runs survivorship bias through all six moves as a worked lesson plan (Table 4, Figure 2), with AI in at Prime, Attach, and Strengthen and out at Probe and Test

article_title: The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning
citation: Mario Brcic, Stjepan Frljic. (2026). The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26181
title: Place AI by cognitive role: secure the first hard attempt and final unaided check, allow guarded AI in between
description: The article's central design rule is per skill, not per course: "AI belongs wherever it increases feedback, practice density, or professional realism without obscuring the evidence that the student can think and perform unaided." Concretely, teachers protect Probe and Test as AI-out moments, permit guarded AI (hints, examples, feedback, drill) in the middle moves, and open AI for authentic work once unaided competence is shown. The diagnostic is that if letting AI in makes the task feel effortless, it is in the wrong place.
requirements: A secured, AI-free check that shows the student can perform unaided; guarded rather than answer-giving AI during scaffolded moves
constraints: The rule is per skill, not per course; the same student may need AI kept out of one skill and welcomed into another in the same hour
target_learners: All students in AI-supported courses, from high school through higher education
target_learning_goals: Protecting productive struggle and unaided skill demonstration while scaling feedback and practice
examples: Mapped onto the six moves, the access pattern is protected attempt, guarded support, protected proof; the survivorship-bias lesson keeps AI out only at Probe and Test

citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02432

description: A publicly available web platform supporting prompt-based programming through dialogue with a GenAI assistant (GPT-4o-mini), hidden-test execution, and direct code editing. The bug injection pipeline acts as middleware that intercepts correct generated code and replaces it with validated, runnable near-miss variants containing subtle faults. Students receive a problem specification, craft a natural-language prompt, and can iterate by reprompting or editing code directly. The platform was deployed in a CS1 course at the University of Auckland with five programming tasks covering arrays, matrices, and binary operations.

citation: Victor-Alexandru Pădurean, Kaitlin Riegel, Alkis Gotovos, Jyotika Mahapatra, Ahana Ghosh, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, James Prather, and Adish Singla. 2026. title: Deliberate bug injection into correct GenAI code to create code review opportunities
description: A pedagogical design pattern where realistic, runnable bugs are deliberately injected into otherwise correct GenAI-generated code, requiring students to read and repair generated outputs rather than passively accepting them. The design creates structured opportunities for students to inspect generated code, verify its behavior, and make localized repairs. Injected bugs are small, realistic, and accompanied by feedback mirroring authentic development workflows. The pattern addresses the problem that modern models often produce correct solutions for CS1-level tasks, reducing students' incentive to closely inspect outputs.
requirements: A GenAI code-generation workflow with hidden tests
A validation mechanism ensuring injected bugs compile and fail tests
Explicit warnings to students that the model is likely to make mistakes
constraints: Not intended to undermine students' trust in GenAI or their own abilities
Injected bugs are introduced only after the assistant first produces a correct solution, so comparisons with natural bugs reflect response context rather than causal difficulty
target_learners: introductory programming (CS1) students
target_learning_goals: code review and verification
debugging near-miss solutions
critical evaluation of AI-generated code
examples: In a CS1 course deployment, 917 students worked on five prompt-based programming tasks in which the pipeline replaced passing code with validated near-miss buggy variants
